Q47 Is that in the UK or internationally?

Professor Joshi : It is international for development studies , together with the University of Sussex , for the 10th year running , so we have a long-standing reputation in development work . We are a bunch of about 200 staff , of which more than half are researchers , and we work in interdisciplinary teams . W e are not disciplinary based . W e work very much on applied problems in the real world , so we are not doing research for pure research ’ s sake . W e are very much engaged in real-world problems across the g lobal s outh — and increasingly now in the g lobal n orth.

Yes, absolutely. Can I take this moment to say that we are here every Tuesday and would welcome it if students or academics want ed to come and join the C ommittee session ? We will send them an invitation. People do not tend to take the opportunity and we find that curious. Harry, who are you?

Thank you very much ; i t is good to be with colleagues. I am Harry Anderso n. I am d eputy d irector at an organisation called Universities UK International. We are a membership body, a representative body , and have 142 UK universities with us , including Sussex and all the universities that you have just been hearing from. They are large research-intensive and small specialist universities , and everything in between.

The team that I am very fortunate to lead covers our policy and global engagement work . That is international-focused. The reason that team exists is because UK higher education is highly international, both in its composition and its outlook . Our universities are recognised right around the world for their quality. They produce graduates whose skills and qualifications are recognised by employers both in the UK and internationally by G overnments and by professional bodies.

As we have just been hearing, our universities lead on research to solve global challenges , so we are highly international. T hat leads me to probably one of the key things I would want to land during this session, which is —
Briefly, or maybe it will come out in the questions.

Secondly , I think that investing in development support s countries around the world , but there is also enlighten ed self-interest in the soft power that benefits the UK. Also, given what we have just been hearing about scarcity and cuts, we need a bit more of a clearer strategy that focuses on longer-term development and how we can focus the work that universities do with the funding that is available. I will leave it there.

Q48 Thank you. Anu, you touched on this in your opening — and Harry has expanded on it — but I wonder if you could give some thoughts and reflections on how the Government can balance the objective of growing UK education exports with supporting and developing higher education in low and middle-income countries.

Professor Joshi : You are talking about transnational education, I assume. Increasingly it is evident that there is a huge demand for this kind of education, and universities in the UK obviously are attractive places to get this education, but in many places — such as my own country, India — there are not enough opportunities to do that . H aving this export out there in their own locations , with the expertise that we bring , would be very important. There is a huge opportunity there in many places, many places are already doing this kind of thing and more could be done in that field. We ourselves are not doing it at the moment . IDS do not do transnational education. Maybe you have more of an understanding of that, but it seems to me that there is a huge opportunity there that could be taken up.

That also feeds very well into the international development agenda, because this would be strengthening capacities and strengthening partnerships of people who are based there . Y ou do not have the kind of problem we were talking about with people not staying in their own countries because they are already there. They are not going to move abroad.

Q49 I am not sure if you heard what my colleague David Mundell said in the first session about people getting the skills and opportunities , using them to further their own career s and leaving their countr ies . We see that particularly when it comes to nursing and healthcare around the world. I s that a risk?

Professor Joshi : It is always a risk . Y ou cannot curtail people or corral them in particular countries , but the more opportunities you create in the countries through our development partnerships, the better you can feed these people with the education into those spaces , so that the opportunities are attractive. At the moment, as you know —and again, speaking from the Indian experience —there is huge unemployment. You have been watching the news. There is a h uge unemployment crisis , and youth are out on the streets demanding all kinds of things. Unless those opportunities are created there, and education through exporting some of our skills , robustness and credibility of the quality systems that we have, we will not be able to solve that kind of problem. I think there is an opportunity there. It has to be done very carefully , because UK universities are a good and attractive option, but they are not for everybody.
Q50 Harry, do you have any examples from the organisations that you work with of where investment has led to sustained growth in the country?

Yes. T he G overnment funded a scheme a number of years ago — I think it closed in 2022 —k nown as the strategic partnerships for higher education , innovation and reform programme . That programme was reviewed , and I think was seen to have met a number of objectives in supporting development around the world. There are probably a couple of examples that could helpfully be drawn from that.

First, UK universities in Somaliland , working with local partners , helped to reform the healthcare curriculum. I think about five universities ended up reviewing their curriculum, making changes and looking to support skills development locally . A number of the universities that were not even involved in that partnership ended up following that model because they recognised that it worked and was successful. You could then remove the UK support , and that is a kind of long-term sustainable support in-country.

There were a couple of examples from a project in Sierra Leone . One was where an institution was able to get university status by looking at reviewing modules and accreditation and making sure that it was at a sufficient level and standard required for university status in that country, working with the regulator. That creates local infrastructure that can provide support. The final example , again within Sierra Leone , was around working with local regulators and professional accreditation bodies to essentially redesign some of the quality assurance mechanisms so again the rest of the sector within country can meet certain standards.

W hen we are talking about TNE , often one of the big drivers from other G overnments as to why they want to see UK support and to partner with the UK —when it could be support from Australia , for example, or other countries that do TNE— is the reputation and quality of our academics and our institutions , which can help increase capacity locally. There has been huge focus on India recently. My understanding is that when our previous P rime M inister led the trade mission to India, it was the Indian G overnment that was pushing for UK universities to be involved in that mission . I think we sent about 14 vice-chancellors. That was driven from the Indian side rather than the UK side or by UK universities. T here is a huge opportunity there.
You could look at many other countries. The Premier of Indonesia recently came to the UK looking to see UK universities to help set up local support. There is huge potential there through using TNE .

Q51 Harry and then Anu , c an I ask you about successor programmes to SPHE IR and the Global Research Fund and what you think the form of successor programmes should be in order to increase their strategic effectiveness?

First, we would welcome a successor programme . My understanding was that there was a move towards a possible successor programme , focusing more specifically on female participation in education We had a number of conversations with FCDO about that scheme . T here is huge appetite and demand from our universities to be involved in a successor scheme , but at present I do not think we know that that scheme is going to be taken forward.
Q52 Do you know what the budget of the first iteration was?

Not off the top of my head , but we could definitely get that information for you. I think colleagues heard it from the first panel , but what would make it successful is that it needs a long-term funding envelope. It needs clear prioritisation and focus for what it is doing . That allows our members, the UK universities, to work with local partners to rebuild the trust that I think has been undermined by the recent cuts we have seen in some of those programmes.
I have discovered that i t ran from 2016 to 2022 and cost £45 million.

Professor Joshi : We did not have experience with the SPHE IR programme , but we thought that the Global Challenges Fund was very important . S everal of our researchers have been involved in some of those. As Harry said, any successor would be most welcome.

What I wanted also to submit is that there are other ways of doing these things in relation to supporting research partnerships and particularly combining them with higher education. We have experience of an FCDO then DFID-funded programme called the multi-methods research course that was delivered jointly by IDS and the Partnership for African Social and Governance Research . It was set up as a way of improving capacity for research in Africa because it was considered not as strong as we would like it to be. It was designed primarily for mid-career researchers .

S ince then, the first few iterations ran for about five years and IDS staff were very heavily involved — along with other staff, faculty from the UK — but in a few years the first cohort that had gained capacity just took over . I t has trained over 3,000 researchers , who are now doing their own education in the countries with the quality assurance that was given in the programme. T hat is another example of how this can be made to go forward.

Q53 Can I just ask you, Harry, whether among UK universities there has been any contraction of international partnerships ? For example, when we were in Nigeria , we heard about a partnership with the University of Dundee. Now , very unfortunately, the University of Dundee has run into very serious financial issues , and I think we are all aware of other universities running into financial issues. Has that led to withdrawal from some of these international activities that it would previously have pursued?

The short answer is yes. As you alluded to , we are a sector facing quite an acute financial crisis , particularly when G overnment funding is withdrawn . These are partnerships that cannot be sustained through higher education funding alone. Increasingly, you are seeing that on the domestic side too , with a much closer focus on R&I-related activity , which needs to be aligned much more with frontier technologies and G overnment priorities because the funding is so tight within the sector at the moment.
Q54 We heard earlier about scholarships . T urning to the visa brake , how will students in higher education institutions be affected by the G overnment ’ s visa brake on certain countries?

Professor Joshi : We are already experiencing some of the effects of this visa brake because , as an international development institute, we get a lot of students from developing countries , many of whom are funded through Ch eve ning and other scholarships . I n the past , many of them have com e from the countries that have been experiencing visa brake s — Myanmar and Afghanistan, for example. This affects the kind of development goals that we have. For example, if you stop women from Afghanistan — that came up in the earlier conversation —they just do not have access to education . It is something that the ir country ’ s G overnment are not providing and it is very central to one of our development goals to provide some of those things.

We currently have a PhD student who started off as a scholar from Afghanistan and now is doing a PhD. It is unlikely that she will go home because of the constraints that she currently faces. In that sense, yes, the drop has been quite significant. In 2025-26 , we had 24 funded scholars at IDS. This year we have seven. The drop has been considerable. From what I understand, there are lots of Chevening scholars who came up and were almost ready to be given scholarships and t hen the visa brake came in and they have been denied . I understand — I can check the figures — that about 30 were from Afghanistan, which is quite substantial. In a sense, it is undermining our other development goals.

I completely endorse what has just been said. In the light of what we have been discussing, I think the impact was on the perception of the UK as a trusted partner when it comes to global development efforts, because we are essentially just shutting the door. We are acutely aware that the G overnment ha ve legitimate concerns when it comes to immigration overall. I think successive G overnments have been elected on promises to reduce net migration , and there are concerns around asylum -seeking and related issues. Our challenge is where immigration policy often cuts across wider G overnment objectives . The visa ban is quite acute for global development objectives .

T he Home Office will probably always think that it only has a blunt mechanism and so it had to be a visa brake . I do not see why the Home Office could not have exempted certain students , such as Chevening scholarship students or others. That is where that policy has been the most harmful and most impactful. If there had been a n earlier conversation about recognising and flagging that , this could be an easy exemption . I think that would have been most welcome and done a lot to help preserve some of the UK ’ s reputation. My only other comment is that the visa brake impacts students looking to come to the UK. One thing that I have been pleased to see is that UK universities are looking to try to step up and support those students who have been impacted by the ban.

A charity called Mosaic is looking to set up part - funded scholarships with UK universities to enable those students who are not able to physically travel to study via online or distance learning or in another campus — a branch campus of the UK ’ s around the world — so that they are not denied the opportunity still to benefit from a UK education, even if they cannot come to the UK.
Q55 Is Mosaic a charity ?
I believe they are a charity, ye s.
Q56 Could you find some more information ?

Yes, absolutely, we can share some further information there. This is new . I cannot remember , but I think they call what they have set up the global development platform . T his is a very recent thing, I think , since the ban.
Q57 If you could connect us, we would be grateful.
Yes, absolutely.

Q58 I read an article from the New Humanitarian about Sudan students who cannot come to the UK, the US or Australia anymore. T he quote used is , “T he only place left is the moon .” M y question is more serious than that. Are there other countries those students will therefore go to rather than those w estern countries?

Professor Joshi : As everyone knows, the US is not an attractive destination either for students from some of the countries affected by the UK visa ban. I think Australia is getting stricter, as far as I can tell. A lthough Europe is still offering scholarships and they could go, there are often language issues there that prevent people from going. T he UK is an attractive destination , and we should be attracting these students , particularly the Chevening scholars . They have been vetted ; they have proven themselves through multiple interview processes. If they were given an exemption, that would have been fantastic.

I t is not just the m who benefit . P eople who are already here, other students , benefit from their experiences. It creates what we were talking about earlier : the soft power — a network of individuals across the globe, particularly from these very conflict-driven countries where soft power becomes even more important later on , when these people become powerful and take up positions of power , and you want to negotiate or network around other issues that are critical or solve global challenges that require collective action. This is the power that is going to be useful and we are just sort of —

Q59 David and I have just come back from Bangladesh , where the P rime M inister studied in England and is, as a result , very keen on our country. To both of you, what could be the tangible benefits of an increase in ODA-funded scholarships for your organisations?

We are a membership body, so there would not be a tangible benefit for us as an organisation, but our members would benefit massively if additional ODA scholarships were available. Also , I think a number of universities will often match - fund or provide support through other means if funding was made available . I think it would increase the number of students who would be able to come to the UK as a result , so we would be very supportive of an increase.

Professor Joshi : I would echo what Harry said. A s an institution that does mainly global development, most of our students are from the g lobal s outh. If student scholarships were increased, that would mean that our numbers would go up and we would be able to offer more support. What we are unique in is that we bring our research directly into the classroom because we are such a research - intensive institution . I ncorporating our students right from the classroom into research projects and then having them take this education back to their countries would be a huge benefit.
Q60 Why?

Professor Joshi : Because we think that we inculca te UK values and approaches to development that are important in the current climate , l ooking at global challenges, looking at public good being important, not taking on just a very privatised agenda , things like that — a lthough growth is important of course and we are not denying that — and finding innovative ways to do that. I think it would be very important.

Another thing is benefit to the UK. F or example, we know from our research and working with our students that examples of community healthcare from Brazil have been brought into the UK as a potential approach to help ing solve some of NHS problems. There are other example s as well . I t is not just us providing all the expertise and knowledge , it is also them bringing innovations and examples from their situations to the UK.

Q61 This is a similar question to what I asked the first panel. H igher education institutions are increasingly looking to the private sector for investment to fill the gaps created by the reduction in ODA. What do you think are the risks in relying on private capital for developing research, particularly where the commercial returns are uncertain, but the need is high?

Professor Joshi : If I might start, I think the earlier panel did respond in very strong terms that there are possibilities and good opportunities in certain areas. In particular, I think private capital is essential because G overnment capital will not be able to fund everything that is needed. However, in other places there are areas where private capital is not going to step up. R egulation is one important element, as was pointed out earlier. Funding dependencies on private capital should be also looked at a bit carefully —there is a risk there , as well as in unequal investment in certain areas versus others. We have seen this in the health sector, for example. We need to be careful that we secure public funding for public goods that are not likely to be invested in by the private sector.

I would probably agree with what we have just heard , as well as with what the previous panel said. There is clearly a role there. The worry would be if private finance and capital was seen as an easy replacement for what public and G overnment funding could do. Where we have seen it be successful is in the catalytic impact it can have in crowding in and unlocking other funding. T he British Council run s a very successful global partnerships scheme called Going Global , which looks to put up some funding that allows institutions in the UK to partner with others around the world to test models on a small scale and then work out if they are scalable and could be developed. That is where private finance could be incredibly helpful, but I think it needs to be done within a quite close regulatory framework to ensure that it is focusing on the longer - term goals that we all have.

Q62 Harry, on the international education strategy , w e have heard criticism that there was a very limited focus on development objectives within it. Would you agree with that criticism and what would you — or rather , your members — like to have seen included?

We are very supportive of the international education strategy. It has been refreshed a number of times, but most recently at the start of this year, which is the first time since the change of G overnment. We would say that the international education strategy has responded to a lot of the concerns that our members would have , in that it is broader in focus. There was a previous concern , if you were to look at the previous iteration of the strategy , that it was overly focused on export earnings and that that was quite problematic when you were going to meet other G overnments, other universities in other countries, because it quite frankly could look exploitative.

What we have seen therefore is a welcome move away from just focusing on an export target to the broader contribution that international education can make . I think that reflects the breadth of contributions that universities can make. It is not just about international student recruitment anymore , it is about international research partnerships and it is about TNE , as we have just been hearing .

The opportunity that we have is that the FCDO has joined as a co-owner of that strategy. Previously it would just have been the Department for Education and DBT , as was. FCDO ’ s role in being a co-owner of that strategy gives a huge opportunity to make sure that there is a greater focus on global development. That is where we would always encourage the G overnment to think of universities as pieces of critical infrastructure of global development. Wherever the UK is looking to talk to other G overnments around the world, our members will more than likely have a partnership or expertise or support that they could utilise in that sense , so I think there is a real opportunity there.

The challenge we face is that we have seen reductions in the headcount for what was previously the Department for Business and Trade in its colleagues based in-country. We still have a fantastic embassy network. The British Council provides fantastic in-country support to help with UK universities looking to partner with others overseas. However, I think that reduction is problematic and could undermine some of those wider development objectives.

Q63 Harry, coming to the reach of UK universities , about 650,000 students are located overseas , and UK universities are working and supporting them. How do you think that that infrastructure could be used more strategically as part of our development offer?

This year I believe we crossed over a quite important tipping point and threshold. I do not think this will be reflected in our submission because the data only came out very recently , but we have now reached a point where there are almost 700,000 TNE students — UK students — studying for a UK degree overseas. Given policy in the UK, we are seeing a decline in the number of international students coming to the UK , so those two figures have now crossed over. The short answer is that we are seeing a huge renewed interest from UK universities in establishing TNE partnerships. Probably a number of vice - chancellors and senior leaders within universities are looking at TNE in a far more strategic way , and I think the international education strategy helps with that.

What we are looking to see, and what is often happening is that the breadth of TNE provision is huge. It is not just campuses. Overseas campuses are often what attract the attention, but I think they are , off the top of my head, less than 1% of all TNE provision . There is validated provision, franchise provision and other types of provision , so there is a huge opportunity there for universities to be working with partners overseas to meet the local skills needs and local development needs of those institutions in - country to make sure that the offer is responding to what is needed locally. That is the opportunity we have . That is what I was talking about before, why overseas G overnments often come to the UK and want our UK universities to help with setting up campuses and joint provision with their local universities.
Q64 I will come to you as well, Anu. What explicit role could TNE have in our aspirations around soft power and international development ?

Professor Joshi : There are lots of opportunities , as I said , and things are moving. One of the things that we could be more strategic about is to link th e TNE export role with the development aspirations of the countries in place. For example, if we are doing TNE and we have simultaneous research partnerships with those places and locations, we can co-create research — as was being talked about in the earlier panel — in - country, in situ, in a much stronger , creative and innovative manner that responds to local realities in a way that perhaps sitting here with international partnerships might not do as well. T here are ways of thinking strategically about linking these two things much more closely that we could be doing.

An other point to add , which I should have mentioned , is that TNE partnerships are incredibly helpful in essentially helping to export UK soft power , because often we will end up as the UK G overnment, as UK universities , working with overseas G overnment s and overseas regulators to essentially set the parameters and the framework for what that TNE provision looks like in - country. We will often be one of the first countries working with say country X to set this provision up. A recent example is Nigeria . I think the UK helped to develop the TNE guidelines in Nigeria , and that essentially helps to sprea d our reputation , but is also what underpins and makes the UK ’ s HE system successful : rigorous quality assurance mechanisms, research - informed teaching, academic freedom, freedom of speech — helping to promote those kind s of fundamental principles to underpin other HE systems around the world.
Q65 What are the risks for the FCDO and for universities as they are thinking about increasing their TNE offer?

The key thing we need to stay focused on is that the UK is in a very privileged position when it comes to our reputation when we are talking about other countries and other G overnments looking to work with the UK. We need to keep a laser focus on quality . There is a huge amount of interest , as we alluded to, in India at the moment. Lots of UK universities are setting up provision in India. We need to make sure that the first few cohorts of those students are happy and successfu l and go on to very fulfilling careers and that we keep laser focused on the quality of our provision because that is the advantage we have over other countries when they are looking to set up TNE provision.
Anything to add, Anu?
Professor Joshi : No, I think I would say the same.

Q66 While we have you here, Harry, I will push you on something that is not related to international development but is very much university - related, which is what came up on 30 September , around the MI5 warnin g universities about China using a public company to front some of its intelligence operations. What is your perspective on that , and what is the link and the risk for universities of working overseas or working closely with foreign powers? What is the risk back here in the UK?

First, universities take incredibly seriously their responsibilities when it comes to national security. This topic has increased in salience and has established itself very much as a board - level issue within UK universities. Looking at what has happened over recent years, institutions have strengthened their due diligence, risk assessment processes and research security processes. My organisation, UUK, has been instrumental in helping to set up the research collaboration advice team — RCAP — now within G overnment, and which is there to support universities when they are looking to set up new partnerships.

We are always going to be a target for this , first because of the quality of our institutions , the sort of research that we are producing and the collaborations that we have, but also because of what I said at the start, which is that we are an inherently open and internationally facing sector and we are therefore always going to face these challenges. The question therefore is about how we mitigate those challenges . I think we have had a very constructive and good relationship when it comes to working with the G overnment on this. RCAP is one example. We had the d irector g eneral of MI5 come to our annual conference to address our vice - chancellors and highlight that this is a major concern that institutions need to be aware of.

We also work very closely with NPSA and other parts of the security services to make sure that that guidance is being shared among academics and universities , so it is not just at the board level but is cascaded down through and across institutions. We have made huge progress on this , but I think there is always more to be done. A t the start of this year , we had another meeting with MI5 , the d irector g eneral and Security Minister Dan Jarvis , and we have now set up the academic interference reporting route , so there is a confidential mechanism through which senior university leaders can report concerns. There is always more to be done , but this is an issue that universities take very seriously.

Q67 I have a couple thousand Hong k ongers in my Rushcliffe constituency in Nottinghamshire, and since I was elected , they have been raising concerns around the Confucius i nstitutes. As Universities UK, do you have confidence in universities needing and benefiting from Confucius i nstitutes , or do you think there are some aspects of policy that universities need to review?

I think universities will always keep international partnerships under review , whether they be Confucius i nstitutes or other partnerships . My understanding is that we do not believe that there is any kind of immediate need to revisit that at this point. There is not much more I could say on that . We recognise the risk , given how international we are , but I do not think we are looking to take any immediate action on Confucius i nstitutes.

Q68 We would be very grateful if you wrote to the Committee about that, either in private or public . I think you have painted a very good contemporary position. Thirty years ago , there was a mad rush of UK universities chasing the Chinese renminbi , and I think it is well documented that that has exposed us. At the time China was a middle-income country, so we were absolutely delighted to help it with its development needs.

If I can just give you some context, my closest university is Sheffield Hallam , and the way academics there were psychologically terrorised was quite acute. The reason probably that you had the meeting at the beginning of the year with MI5 and the S ecurity Minister was because we realised that we did have a big gap in security because we had such an open profile to Chinese universities.

That is kind of done , and I think it is good that there is now an embryonic reporting mechanism for academics who feel uncomfortable. However, are you looking for the next risk ? B ecause 30 years ago, it was absolutely right that we were helping and supporting all our institutions in helping and supporting China with its development. Are you , as an organisation — or are our universities — looking at where that next potential risk could be and making sure that our partnerships are equitable , but also secure for both parties?
Yes, absolutely. The framework around the governance , research security and what you could call responsible international partnerships has come a long way in 30 years , but even in five years.
I would agree.

Just look at the expansion of ATAS — the Academic Technology Approval Scheme . T hat was previously just for academics but has now been expanded to students. I think there is a much greater recognition of the risks here , and of going into these things with eyes wide open. We will always look to support our members with this.

One observation I would make about China is that we have built a higher education model that is reliant on the income of overseas students , so as a G overnment and as a country we need to ask ourselves whether it is wise to fund what we think is a critical piece of national infrastructure in the UK , but also of global development , such as we have been talking about , through the income streams from international students.

I think the top point that our c hief e xecutive , Vivi enne Stern , would always be making is about the need to develop a long - term , sustainable funding model for our universities. I think she has been on record at a p arliamentary C ommittee saying that , in the past , international students were the cherry on the top of a cake , but now they are the flo ur that underpins the whole operating model. I think we need to recognise our over - reliance and the dependencies that that creates , particularly where institutions do have single - market dependencies or two or three - market dependencies and support those institutions where possible.

Q69 Anu, a final question from me. You raised the case of the Afghan woman student who you have now taken on as a PhD student , and said how it is unlikely that she will be able to return home. Do you put — “ protections ” is probably too heavy a word — support systems in place when you have overseas students who you know , for example, may be doing research into LGBT rights , for example , which you know would be controversial at home ? Are you minded of that and would you put protections in place , or would you just not encourage research in that area?

Professor Joshi : We do put protections in place —we do research on LGBTQ rights ; we do research on all kinds of gender - related issues —s o that would be very much part of it , in the classroom as well as outside. We are also very mindful that some of our students are first - generation learners . I n fact , we are just talking with a couple of countries , including Timor-Leste , about sending us cohorts of students who are first-generation learners on G overnment scholarships , and that they come as a cohort so that they can be supported . A lthough we rely on international students , as Harry was saying , and they contribute enormously to the classroom , it is a very difficult experience for them , or it can be a very difficult experience for them , so it is important that we do this in a careful - minded way.

Another thing to say is that although you might count international students in the immigration figures , these are people who are contributing. They are not dependent. It is very important to keep that in mind as well — these are people who have come here to get the best education. They may not, as in the case of this Afghan woman , be able to go home because of the situation there , bu t they are contributing here and we should respect that.

I have written down your phrase, Harry — “critical infrastructure”. I think that our universities and research facilities absolutely are that . A s a state , I think we have not done enough to protect and nurture them . You are in a situation where we, for the wrong reasons, recognise how critical you are to us. Thank you both so much for sharing your skills and expertise. We do appreciate it.

sessions.iT: Inquiry into the recommendations of the Infected Blood Inquiry (Stage 1)
sessions.w: Cindy Butts

segs.tx: Public Administration and Constitutional Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: Inquiry into the r ecommendations of the Infected Blood Inquiry (Stage 1), HC 113
Tuesday 13 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 13 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Simon Hoare (Chair); Richard Baker; Charlotte Cane; Sam Carling; Lauren Edwards; Peter Lamb; John Lamont; Luke Taylor.
Justice Committee member present: Sarah Russell.
Questions 103 - 14 0
Witness
I : Cindy Butts, Independent Public Advocate for England and Wales .
Examination of witness
Witness: Cindy Butts .

Q103 Good morning , colleagues, and welcome back after what I hope was a successful and enjoyable conference season. I am delighted to welcome Cindy Butts, the independent public advocate. Thank you for finding the time to see us . I am also really pleased to welcome Sarah Russell, our parliamentary colleague from the Congleton constituency, who sits on the Justice Committee. Sarah was involved with the pre-appointment hearing for the role . Sarah, it is delightful that you could be with us this morning. We are grateful to you.

We are looking at the role of the IPA , principally in relation to public inquiries. I will kick off with the first question s. You are the first independent public advocate and have been in post for almost a year. How would you describe, hitherto, the main functions that you have been carrying out?

F irst , I was deployed to the Heaton Park synagogue attack four days after starting the role. My role is to be an independent, visible presence, there solely to advocate for the needs of victims, survivors and the bereaved. A big part of that in the immediate aftermath is making sure that people have the support they need, finding out where they do not and being a strong and independent voice . N ot to provide it , but to ensure that those organisations that are responsible do , to try to avoid, dare I say, what happened nine years ago in Grenfell, where people were falling through the cracks. That is the immediate role .

As you all know, the complicated processes begin to kick in from there : the inquests, the reviews and the public inquiries. It is my responsibility to make sure people understand those processes, can navigate them and are able to play an important, meaningful role in them . The mere fact that they have to navigate them , in and of itself , tells us quite a lot about the recovery and the system, and about the architecture of support that exists in the aftermath , because it is very complicated. I n essence , my role is to make sure they can play a meaningful part in those processes .

Q104 You have a tripartite role : a signposter to the services available to those who need them, an advocate to G overnment service providers on their behalf, and someone who holds service providers’ toes to the fire to make sure they meet demand in a reasonable way.

Yes, but not just service providers. The reason my role is officially called the standing advocate is that it is my responsibility to understand the system as a whole, where there are gaps, what systemic and thematic issues are present that are not meeting the needs of people, and to bring those to the attention of Ministers and Government. There is also more systemic learning and challenge that comes with the role.

Q105 It is coming up to a year since you started the job . Has it proved hard to differentiate between not being part of Government , because you are not part of Government, and the office being part of the architecture, if you will, of society, and being a n advocate without fear or favour for those who need it ?

That is a really good question. I do not think it has been hard in the sense of being really clear that my role is independent and I am not there for the comfort of Government; I am in part there to challenge Government , where appropriate and necessary, and to work constructively alongside them. I do not think there has been a difficulty in being able to articulate that, and in people understanding it. Quite frankly, people have been approaching me in droves because they understand the independent nature of my role. T he difficulty comes in being such a small outfit. There are three of us , including me . The architecture is that we do not have an independent, physical office ; some processes in the way we do things depend on the Ministry of Justice. For example, we do not have our own finance and budget official , so we very much rely on the MOJ to help us with that function. That is where the bureaucracy becomes difficult . It is the very thing that I am sure you will hear from so many other people.
Yes. Welcome to our world.

Quite frankly , there are times when I ask myself how on earth the Government get anything done , because of the tranche of business cases and approvals , going round the house s speaking to this one and that one an d then being told , “N o , you should have never spoken to me in the first place .”
Then that one moves mid-conversation . W e should form a self-help group or something.

We really should. That is a strain on an office that, first, is not properly resourced and , secondly, at times needs to act quickly. I do not have the time because people’s needs are immediate. That is where the administrative challenge comes in , as opposed to the sort of independence piece you mentioned.

Q106 I am sure we will come on to it in later questions, but the first months of experience in a new role are usually the most informative. Do these views — your experiences — get fed into the Secretary of State, the Permanent Secretary or the Treasury?

They get fed into various places : t he Secretary of State, the Victims Minister, officials or individual Departments , depending on what the issue is . U ltimately , they get fed through to the Minister .
Q107 In your experience, h ow does the job description bear up to the daily reality ?

From my experience , having been deployed after only four days in the role , major incidents do not wait for you to be ready. That is the first thing. Being able to respond quickly and have the systems and processes ready to spring into action has reinforced the need for the role to be properly resourced and ready to respond when needed. The Heaton Park synagogue attack was not a Grenfell or a Hillsborough. In the event that we have a major incident that is larger in scale, how we are able to respond to that raises a number of questions , challenges and issues that really need to be resolved.

Q108 Good morning, Cindy. You are only able to support people following a major incident, and the major incident is defined by the Secretary of State for Justice. Does that restriction — the definition of major incident — limit your ability to help people?

Yes and no. Obviously I support where I have been deployed but there are cases that are, if you like, legacy cases . There are a n umber of legacy cases where families and campaigners have approached me for help and support . W hile I cannot support in the way that I do if I am deployed, I have been supporting in ways that I can.

The first thing, and one of the things that has become quite stark, is the value of listening to those who might have lost people in the Chinook crash , as a result of the Primodos scandal or , indeed , the Summerland fire in 197 3 . The value of listening is so important, which is why I have not just been supporting those following the Manchester A rena attack but also listening to those affected by the cases that have gone before that I am not, in a statutory sense, supporting. Also , we know that people’s experience and the learning s do not follow a neat statutory definition, so getting the learning s from people who are still fighting for justice and still waiting for answers is really important because it tells us about the system. The other area that is really important , and it is why I engage with people from those cases , is that it helps to inform how I operate and how the office wo rks .

Y ou may or may not be aware of the review that Dame Anne Owers carried out into the death of Harry Dunn. She recommended that the MOJ consult on whether I should have exceptional circumstances provisions to be able to support those families where there might have been just a single death but the impact on that family or the complexity of issues that they might be dealing with are very tricky. For example, in Harry Dunn’s family’s case : international statecraft and Donald Trump . Where the families have to deal with that on their own, and where there is a public interest, I should be able , in exceptional circumstances, to support them through that really difficult process. I support that. The MOJ agreed to consult on it, but it has not done so just yet.

Q109 That is helpful. For those legacy cases, is there a threshold for you to determine that it is sufficiently serious to get involved, or are you listening to everybody who comes to you who falls into that legacy category?

I try to listen to everybody, to be honest. I sometimes listen to people where , if my role had existed at the point the disaster or the death happened, I may not have been deployed, but it is still really important for me to listen to those experiences because they still tell me something about the system. I r ecently met Will Powell, who lost his son , Robbie , many years ago. He is still fighting for justice. I listen, I learn and I try to take those messages forward in the work we are doing.

Q110 I know others are going to come on to your workload and staffing, but in terms of your workload and the balance between th os e legacy cases and supporting those affected by major incidents as defined by the Minister , what is the current split?

That is a really good question. It is really difficult to define the split . For example, at Heaton Park , the Jewish community was deeply affected. One of my challenges in a new role was to try not just to demonstrate that I am useful and can make a difference as the new kid on the block. I actually had to exercise restraint , because I knew and understood that the community has its own infrastructure and support network. Some of that is because it has been under sustained attack and has had to look after itself , and s ome is because of religious and cultural needs . P art of our work is about being trauma-informed, and a big part of that is understanding the community first and foremost, recognising where we could add value and exercising restraint so that we are not duplicating what other organisations are meant to be doing or trying to usurp their infrastructure.

I say that because , when the attack happened, one of the immediate things I did was check in on them to find out whether they had sufficient trauma-informed support. They said, “T hank you very much, but we have flown in four or five trauma-informed specialists from Israel. ” It is about understanding their specific needs . It is about being quiet-ish in the beginning , but then needs emerge over time as the process unfolds. People have been coming forward with issues and concerns that we have been picking up on and trying to pursue. It ebbs and flows , and it depends on need and our ability to respond . When it ebbs , that is when we can spend a bit more time on other cases. It has been a mixture. Sorry, I will try to be a bit more succinct.

Q111 Sarah Russell: Your description of your work is immensely impressive, if I might say so , but I am left wondering how you manage all this in two days a week. Is two days a week sufficient for this role?

Officially, I am two days a week , and then I go up to full - time when I am deployed. At some point—I am not quite sure when—it is up to the Secretary of State to decide when to stand me down; that is the phrase used in the legislation. I go back up if something happens, then back down, then back up, and so on . I am actually full-time right now because I was deployed four days after , but o fficially it is part-time. That is not the right thing for a role like this, not least because there is work to be done between deployments. I have already articulated just how important preparedness and resilience are . This role does not just kick in when I am deployed, as important as deployment is , which is a mistake.

The structure and the way it is designed can limit the kinds of people who can go for this role. I took this role knowing it was two days , and then it went up and I thought it is madness. I took it anyway , because my view is that you take it and make it different when you are in there. The part-time role would have put so many people off . I am still in the prime of my career. I do not have a rich husband , a rich wife , a lovely pension or whatever to prop me up. I need to earn . The idea that you can just do the role part-time and perhaps get another employe r to say, “ I will take you on, ” knowing full well that you could be off if something happens is for the birds. It designs out people who could be really good at this role, and it is a diversity issue. As I say , I took it anyway , and my view was to take it and make it different for myself and for future IP A s.
Sarah Russell: It seems quite problematic that the role is non-pensionable , but I will leave it there.

I should also say that it is so important for a role like this because , although I have two staff — I love them dearly , and they are absolutely brilliant — they are civil servants. He who holds the pen holds the power. A s much as I love them, I am not happy for them to be holding the organisation when I am not there . I t is about the independence, and that is so crucially important. There is also that issue to consider in terms of full-time or not . Who is holding the pen? Who has the power? This role is about the independence.

Q112 Sarah Russell: I quite agree . In respect of that independence, you have said that you have concerns about your staffing levels . For comparison, although the roles are not directly comparable, I note that the Children’s Commissioner is a full-time role with a staff of 28 and , as I understand it , you have a staff of three. Can you talk about how that limits your ability to do your role? I presume that it must.

We could do more if we had more resources. I would quite like to get into the depth of some of the systemic policy issues. We could do more work in terms of that. The key thing for me is around being able to scale up when we need to, which is why I have put in a business case for more resources . It would mean that we are able to get to a steady state . At the moment we are not in a steady state because , quite frankly , there was not enough proper scoping and sizing at the beginning to understand what this organisation need s in steady state and what it needs when it needs to scale up . T hose are the key issues.

I would quite like what the Children’s Commissioner has. Even something that is not quite that but substantially more than what I have . That is what is needed to be able to respond in a way that Parliament expect s , and the way that victims, survivors and bereaved families deserve. I am hopeful that the business case will be approved soon.

Q113 Those are two key points for us as a C ommittee , and for Sarah to take back to the Justice Committee . The two germane points are : first , how can you do the job in two days and then drop everything for potentially four months ? That narrows down , by definition, who might apply . Secondly, as far as the public are concerned, the key word is “independent”. Is the role an independent advocate ? I echo your respect and admiration for the c ivil s ervice , but when it hold s the pen while you are stood down by the Secretary of State, the c ivil s ervice is a servant of the Government. How can it be independent of the Government it serves ? It is asking too much.

The other thing that is important to say is that this is difficult, hard work. You are dealing with people in grief and in trauma . O ne of the key things that additional funding will allow me to do is to put in place proper trauma-informed support for myself and my staff. That is also linked to the whole issue of part-time and full-time. When I go down to part-time, I am still always switched on because I never know when something will happen and I will need to kick in. I have to remain spiritually— if I can use that word —r esilient and ready at all times .
Q114 When can you have comfort and confidence to book a holiday , for example? It can be something like that.
I actually have one coming up, mainly because my staff are forcing me to make sure I take a break.
Do not publicise the dates , because that will put a curse on it.

Q115 You have talked about your deployment to the terrorist attack at Heaton Park . I n your annual report, you raised how best you could provide useful services without adding further burden when people are already overwhelmed by multiple approaches and requests for engagement. You have touched to some degree on how you managed that. Are there any other lessons that you learned from that deployment?

There are a couple of things. I have talked about the issue of understanding the community, exercising restraint and understanding that needs emerge at different times. On your point about burden, one of the strongest messages from people in the community wa s , “W e feel overwhelmed. ” DCLG is not the right acronym now, is it?
It is MHCLG now. I was a Minister in the Department , and it changes its title more than I change my socks . It is something to do with housing and local Government and communities and stuff .

MHCLG, the Home Office, the Mayor, organisations such as Victim Support and other people descending on them wanting updates and information. We understand they were working in their best interests. It is not as if they were deliberately trying to overwhelm them. They wanted to know and understand what was going on. The burden they were being placed under was absolutely immense. That reinforced for me why it is so important to be very clear about our added value, not trying to duplicate, and not imposing ourselves on them.

Some of the other more specific learning that has come out of Heaton Park is that the synagogue itself was an interested party in the inquest process — as am I — but the synagogue was not able to access legal aid because it is an organisation. That is one of the areas that we have identified. There is clearly a gap there. The synagogue community was at the heart of the attack . It happened there. It has affected that community deeply . It is an interested part y within the process, but it does not have access to legal aid. The only way it could access it was through exceptional circumstances applications, which are very complicated, particularly for the volunteers who oversee the synagogue, and they then have to try to get pro bono support. There are systemic issues and gaps that we are identifying.

Another gap is around support for carers : p eople who suddenly become carers by dint of supporting people who have been attacked ; there is no proper mechanism for supporting them through that in terms of benefits. Again, we are trying to pursue this by working with the relevant Departments to understand the gap and see how we can plug it . Does that help?
Q116 Yes , it does . It goes back to your point that once you are stood down, there is still a lot of follow-up work to make sure those gaps are filled.

Absolutely, which is not to mention the fact that I talked about the immediate support and then all the complicated processes kick in , but do they? Sometimes they do , but sometimes it takes ages before those complicated processes kick in. An inquiry could happen years later. The MOJ and I need to do some deeper thinking . I do not sit here before you with all the answers. It has been one year. As I said, in large part it has sometimes felt like I am running just to stand still . I do not have all the answers ; there are some things that still need to be worked out, including : how do you stand down? When is the most appropriate support? Is there a hybrid where you stand down but stay ready to support when those other processes kick in? One of the really crucial questions for me is when you get stood down, where is there still a need? Who will pick that up? If not me, then who? T here are still some important things that need to be figured out.
Q117 You talked earlier about the timescale for people who have suffered from the incident. They may still need you for their own reasons, even if a formal process has not kicked in.

In particular , they do not respect the stood - down piece, and neither should they because their needs will emerge whenever their needs emerge , or when they come forward with them . The key is that we can identify other ways, even if it is not me, to help and support them throughout that really long and painstaking journey.

Q118 That brings us on to the announcement the Government made yesterday that there is going to be a public inquiry. Could you talk us through how you were involved in the process of making that decision , if you were involved ?

That is not a decision for me ; that is a decision for the Chief Coroner who presided over the inquest. I have counsel that represents the IPA within those processes . W e have been involved in those deliberations, and in what the issues are in terms of the security services. We have had disclosures in respect of the thinking around that and the evidence amassed that indicate d it needed to go to a statutory inquiry. I have been apprised via that disclosure process and have had the opportunity to make submissions , which I took . I pointed out the drawbacks of going to a statutory inquiry , in that there would be no jury and some evidence would be heard in closed session, and I reinforced the fact that even within those parameters , people affected should be able to understand those processes and play a meaningful part , and that decisions need to be timely . M y submissions and my views have really tried to reinforce all that .

I am really pleased that the decision was announced yesterday in relatively swift time, which is good, but of course a chair needs to be identified and terms of reference need to be set up , all of which can take time. The longer it takes, the more anxious the community rightly is, and they do not have the answers they so desperately want and deserve. Being able to keep pushing and pressing for that to be done speedily , while making sure that they are at the heart of those decisions even with the constraints that it brings , is important.
Q119 Will you be able to input into the terms of reference of the public inquiry , and so on ?

I hope so. To be clear, the legislation says that wherever I am deployed , I automatically become an IP in an inquest. It is silent in respect of inquiries ; it does not say that I ought to immediately become a core participant. Once the chair is appointed, we still need to work out what status I will have. I am still undecided about what status is right, whether core participant status is right. Part of being a core participant is that you serv ic e the inquiry chair , if you like. Is that the right thing for the independent public advocate to be doing? It means that you have access to swathes of disclosure : thousands upon thousands of documents. Sometimes servicing the inquiry chair means you need to get beneath all the disclosure documentation if they ask you to look at this or to respond to that on their behalf. You need more than three people to do that. I have not quite worked out my role, but I will .

In early November, I am convening a roundtable to look at the issue of public inquiries in all their forms. What is the right thing? Where can I add value to that process? What are the things that victims and survivors would want from me in an inquiry process, whether statutory or non-statutory? I am co-hosting that with Professor Andrew William s , who I know you have taken evidence from, and other academics, practitioners and people with lived experience to try to get under the skin of it and think more deeply about what our roles should and ought to be. I am happy to report back to you on that if you like.
T hat is really helpful. Thank you.

Q120 Can I ask a very quick supplement ary on standing down? The Secretary of State decides when you should be stood down from an active engagement. I know we are talking hypothetically here because the situation has not arisen, but suppose you take a different view . Suppose you believe that the Secretary of State has it wrong , that there is still work that your office could or should be doing , and that it would be premature to stand you down. Does the Secretary of State have the final say , “N o, sorry, you are stood down ,” and that is the end of it ? Or is there a higher being to whom you can appeal?

T he statutory guidance says that the Secretary of State’s decision to stand me down is made in consultation with the IPA. There is no higher being , other than I have a relationship with the Justice Committee and I have the ability to produce discretionary reports to Parliament, which is perhaps another lever if I feel strongly that I should not be stood down.

There is a need to have a better and more transparent process for standing up , in particular . That is really important. At the minute, it is a bit opaque. People do not really understand it. It could reduce the credibility of my role, if it is very clear that I ought to be stood up but I am not. There is a lack of transparency . It would bring greater public understanding and victim awareness if there were a clear route in which I can give my views, knowing those views have been fed up to the Secretary of State, and that the Secretary of State has to give public reasons for not standing me up. That is really important for transparency. It also protects Ministers . T he last thing I want is for them to be accused of using my role as a political football.

Q121 That is very helpful. What is your assessment of the mindset of the Government ? It is a new , evolving role . Is it the Government’s position that this is organic and evolutionary and that they will respond proactively to how your role is evolved, defined and expanded as lived experience dictates ? Or is it that you have signed on the dotted line , “T here is the job descriptio n and the job spec ,” i t is encased in aspic and that is the end of it?

They are much more aligned to your first description. It is going to evolve. We have an 18-month review , there will be learning from that , and we will be able to flex and adjust accordingly. That is the camp they are predominantly in . It is certainly the camp that I am in.

T hat is helpful. You referenced the good professional working relationship you have with our sister C ommittee, the Justice Committee. This Committee has general oversight of arm’s length public bodies, and so on . I f you make a written submission that is pertinent and germane to our work , and if you think we could be of help, please feel free to make sure this Committee is on the circulation list.

Q122 Sarah Russell: Y our role is not to give legal advice but to support engagement in relevant processes for victims and their families , to advocate for them and even to act as a spokesperson for them. There are quite a lot of those different processes potentially : coronial inquests, Government reviews, and statutory and non-statutory public inquiries. How do you advise them on which of these routes is most appropriate in their case? Or do you not? How does it work?

T hus far I have not had the need to do that. In terms of how it might work in practice, my starting point is that victims, survivors and bereaved families are not a monolith. They have a diversity and range of views of what ought to ensue. An important part of my role is to be able to explain the differences in terms of those processes and, crucially, to try to help them to surface what the issues are that they want answered. That is where it has to start: the context. What are the issues that they want to be addressed? Is this an issue that is really technical that might require a particular kind of set-up where there might be a sole chair supported by technical experts? Or does it require a review process with a wider panel? Might it be better to have a statutory inquiry?

For me, the issue starts with what they want answered , w hat the actual issues are , and h elping them to understand the different avenues, the pros and cons of those, where they might be overly lengthy or where they may not best fit the answers that they seek. The place to start is helping them understand those differences and articulate them based on need. Another key value I bring is not trying to package those differences neatly. Sometimes Ministers and politicians want a neatly packaged answer, with a bow , “T his is what victim-survivors need. ” They want a neat answer , and s ometimes there is no neat answer. It is my job to represent those views in all their complexit y . It does not mean I would not have conversations with the bereaved and survivors to ask whether we can try to align view s that are not far away from where they might be. There might be a proper role for that too , because I also believe that you should try not to give institutions any quarter ; i f they are together and they are not easily divided, they will be stronger. There is a role for me to try to get coherence, but where that is not possible, it is to represent those views in all their complexity.

Q123 One of the recommendations of the Infected Blood Inquiry was that there should be a role for Parliament in calling for inquiries and that this Committee should have such a role, reflecting support more broadly across Parliament for an inquiry. In those circumstances, how would you anticipate your role interacting with Parliament when it comes to the support that might be there to call for an inquiry?

The statutory guidance currently gives me the ability to advise the Secretary of State on what form of review or inquiry ought to take place, having taken soundings from those affected. I have that ability. For me, it goes back to the response I gave earlier. It is about having those discussions, listening to families and survivors, being alert to the fact that there might be really vociferous views, but there might be those who are being ignored because of that , as well as quiet voices in terms of their needs and what they want . To listen and be able to articulate those back to Ministers is an important role that I can play.

Q124 Do you feel you have the flexibility in your remit to have those discussions directly with this Committee or other C ommittees on the potential for an inquiry if they were considering those matters as well, and on whether there should be a call for an inquiry?
Yes . The Chair has invited me to stay in touch and build on the relationship, and that would be one way in which I would expect to do so.

Q125 Your annual report highlights the issue of trust . O ne previous complaint has been that Government Departments and Ministers decide whether to hold a public inquiry, sometimes into their own potential public failures or the failures of their Department. Do you think that the creation of the independent public advocate is enough to combat that criticism, or do you think there is more that can be done to address any perceived conflict of interest concerns?
Sorry, can you break that down for me a little ?

Do you think the creation of your post and your office is enough to give the kind of independence that is needed around Ministers potentially still having a role in saying whether a public inquiry should go forward, even if they or their Department are involved in the circumstances that led to it ?

No, I do not think it is enough , which is why Parliament has a really important role to play in scrutinising the decisions that Ministers make on whether to launch a public inquiry. There is a need for greater transparency, particularly where there are calls for an inquiry or a review and t hose calls are not heeded. Often , the rationale for why an inquiry has not been set up is not given , which erodes trust. People tell me that they want answers. This is an important lesson I have learned . I often meet families face-to-face ; I often meet them virtually. O ne thing that strikes me over and over is how much families become investigators and campaigners, trying to fight for the truth. Not only does the trauma they experience of losing a loved one pass down generationally, but the fight for truth passes down generationally too.

I met a woman who lost her father as a result of a major incident. She is fighting for a public inquiry. She inherited that fight from her mum. Her mum no longer fights for it because she is too old. She has passed it on to her daughter. She spoke to me from her living room , and I could see stacks and stacks of papers, documents, correspondence and files. It had b ecome her life . She said to me, “ I want to know what happened to Dad because I feel like I owe it to him. Even more than that, I cannot leave that inheritance to my three-year-old daughter , who will then have to fight for the answers. ” There is something about understanding the impact of when people do not get answers , and then do not get answers to why an inquiry has not been set up ; there is no transparency. I can put my views across , and I will do that vigorously and independently , but there is something about the system that needs to change as well.

Q126 You have been very helpful in highlighting your ability to advocate on their behalf, particularly if you feel that an inquiry is needed, and Parliament’s role. Do you think there should be a formal role for those who are affected in the way you have just described , and who may take on that campaigning role?
Yes.
Q127 Lauren Edwards: What would that look like? How do you envisage that working?

There is a question that I should ask you : what do you mean by role? If you mean a formal role in being able to influence what happens in terms of the kind of review , then they have that in part through me . As we develop, I would like to think that could also extend to trying to influence the plumbing and mechanics of any such review and what it might look like, making sure I could see myself being an important advocate, ensuring that the terms of reference, for example, address the issues that they want addressing. There are other ways that I could play a part.

Q128 That makes a lot of sense. It is probably something that you will see coming through the process , and something that would maybe be picked up in the 18-month review where you consider the mechanisms and how you can engage with the people who have been affected. You have already talked a lot about the sense of overwhelm that happens when people go through a major incident , so the timing of getting them involved in calls for a public inquiry would be quite important. You also talked a lot about trying to reach those quieter voices. Looking forward to the 18-month review, do you have any thoughts about what you would like to see , or what conversations you would like to have with Government about how you can structure your office in a way that mean s you could be an even stronger advocate for those people ? You have now had experience of it , but I imagine that will continue to build .

T hose conversations are happening internally . A s I sa id , I am convening the roundtable , which will be a really good opportunity to get under the skin of different inquiries and how we can best represent and be a strong advocate within those processes. A lot will bubble out of that session , and then we will push forward with those views to Government and officials . As I said, I will feed back to you too.

This is more of an aside than a question. Given the very real lived example of Northern Ireland and the intergenerational longevity of the impact of unanswered events in the troubles , it is extraordinary that any institution in these islands would need to have a masterclass on what happened. You referenced the lady with all the document s and her heartfelt feeling that she did not want to pass on this great burden she had inherited from her mother , and that i f the questions about what had happened to her father were not resolved , it was going to be passed down to her child. That is not new.

As a country, we have been listening and hearing about the impact of the troubles in Northern Ireland. I find it surprising that officialdom—not your office , but officialdom in broad terms—would need to have a masterclass in defining the varying ways that trauma manifests itself in the human spirit. As I say , this is more of an aside than a question , and it is a worrying one. Let us turn to somebody who is not worrying, Sam Carling.

Q129 Thank you very much for coming in this morning, Cindy. Apologies that I missed the first part of the session. Just thinking about the other end of inquiries—when they have reported and made their recommendations , and when we are monitoring the Government ’s implementation of them —I saw in your annual report that you fully support the establishment of a national oversight mechanism or independent body responsible for collating, analysing and following up on these recommendations. Could you expand a bit on your reasons?

My reason s are that , all too often , we set up public inquiries at huge expense, not just in monetary terms but all the things we have been talking about: the burden, pressure, unanswered questions and impact on families still waiting for those answers. The inquiries take too long and cost huge amounts of money. We sometimes learn the lessons. Sadly , we all too often do not implement the learning s from those lessons or make sure there is meaningful change. All too often , those reports languish on shelves and nothing is done.

There is something else and , again , it goes back to previous conversations. When there is no body charged with making sure that recommendations are implemented and are making the desired change, who takes responsibility? It is the families. They carry that burden to make sure those recommendations are fully implemented. They become super - monitors and monitor the institutions, review websites and try to have meetings and get updates. That burden falls on them, which is not right.

That is why I support an independent body that has the expertise, is established in statute as having that responsibility, can be held to account and has a single individual who is held accountable for ensuring that those recommendations are implemented and lead to meaningful change. That is why I support a national oversight mechanism , which I believe is the only way it can be done.
Q130 Do you think it is necessary to have a body apart from Parliament , or do you think it is a function of Parliament and that perhaps this Committee should focus on it in more detail?

It is really important to have a separate body. There should be a close working relationship with perhaps a C ommittee such as yours, working and scrutinising not just that independent body but also the Government and Ministers on enacting and carrying through on recommendations. That should be an oversight role that sits and hovers above a national oversight mechanism , because that independence is so important. The independence and expertise are really important.

Frankly, there are swathes and swathes of reviews and recommendations. It is not just out of major incidents; it is out of incidents more broadly. It is inquests and prevention of future d eaths reports . It is a lot of work. I just cannot fathom a C ommittee being able to do it justice. It could do it but it probably would not do it well because it would not have the expertise or independence.

The other question is : what gives? You all have a really important role in respect of holding the National Audit Office to account. You named the others . S orry , I should be able to reel them off. Come on, C lerk. What are the other things that you do?
There is too much to mention; we could go on until teatime. We are omnipotent in this Committee.

What gives if you are doing that and not doing it properly? I am a pragmatist. On the one hand , I think to myself, “Good grief, I can’t imagine Government wanting to set up yet another arm’s length body.” If there were ever a time, function and need for another arm’s length body, in my view it is this.

Q131 You mentioned prevention of future deaths reports , in which I have an interest. Would you say there should be a difference in how recommendations from those, non-statutory inquiries or other investigation bodies should be followed up? Should it be different from inquiries , or should it all be looked at by the national oversight mechanism in one place?
I would probably say in one place.
Q132 Would you see a role for you and your office in that body , or would you think it is best kept separate?

What I would not support is that we could do the NOM role. I know Professor Andrew Williams made the suggestion , and I thank him for it because I know he has confidence in our work. That would dilute the very purpose and role that we are there to perform. We could work closely with them in partnership without assuming that responsibility ourselves . A gain , feeding in the views and experiences of those who are affected is where we could play a meaningful role.

Q133 This has been touched on in various ways, largely in terms of what it should not be rather than what it should be. What do you feel the role of Parliament should be in monitoring the implementation of recommendations in the event that we have this national oversight body? Presumably there is still a role for Parliament there.

Yes, there is a role for Parliament. The body ought to report to Parliament as a whole; there is value in that. Parliament can play a really important role in scrutinising and challenging Government on their response to recommendations, whether that is Departments or Ministers themselves.

Q134 Thinking about central Government, given that to some extent all this comes about because there are failures in central Government and the way in which they try to respond to recommendations, how do you think that role could be improved in future? Is it purely through having greater watchmen ensuring that this thing is being carried out , or is there something else that we could try to implement to improve the way Government approach it?
What is something else?
I do not know . T hat is what I am asking you.
