In 2024, I was then able to have that reset. In the last two years, I have reopened 10 new police stations—particularly in rural communities—that my predecessor had closed. Giving people a front counter not only gives them the ability to come in and speak to the police when they need to, but provides reassurance. The people sitting on the front counters are not just sitting there waiting for someone to come in, but are processing all the online crime reports as well.
Q173 So you have administrative staff doing this?

Absolutely. They are doing that to help police officers. The key thing for me has been having a visible presence and giving people back their local bobbies. In January 2024, I brought back a named local police officer for every single community, so every village and every hamlet has one. Those local bobbies are never abstracted to deal with 999 calls; they are proactive only. They should know the local headteacher, barber and hairdresser. They should really be a part of their communities, and that is what I have been striving to do.

Investing in the rural crime taskforce was a significant investment on my part. That was about my priorities, but also about my representing a large swathe of rural communities across Hampshire and the Isle of Wight. If you do not have buy-in from your mayor or PCC, it is incredibly difficult, because a chief constable will always have a greater threat and harm assessment in other areas. If it is not led by people like us, it is probably not happening, to be honest.
Q174 I was particularly interested in your point about the front desk. Have you seen an uptick in reporting of crime since that was reopened?

Yes, we have, but the great impact has been something else. I will use the market town of Petersfield, which is in Damian Hinds’s constituency, as an example. In June last year, I opened a police station there for the first time in 10 years—it had been closed 10 years ago by my predecessor. We have seen a 19% reduction in crime in that market town, not so much because people are going in and reporting crime but because there is a more visible policing presence. I have both 999 responders and neighbourhood policing teams working from there, and that has been a visual deterrent—so prevention is better than cure. That has been really key, and we need it for rural communities too.

That is really interesting. In my rural community in North Cornwall, Launceston has been trying to get a front desk for a long time, and our PCC Alison Hernandez has refused to do that. I agree that it would increase confidence in policing, not necessarily from increasing the number of police officers, but from having the access to the police to report crime, and from having confidence and trust.

Q175 The view of the professor from the first panel was that, if you had a pot of money, it would best be spent on investigations and zapping up your investigative capacity. I am sure you are right that it is reassuring to have something that looks like a police station in Petersfield, but the question is whether the money you spent on that would have been better spent on increasing the investigative capacity of the officers dealing with the complicated, serious crimes.

I guess it is about whether you want to be reactionary or preventive, and there is a balance to be struck there. We do not want too few detectives, or for the detectives we do have to carry too high a caseload, because victims drop off, cases fall away and you end up with people being repeat victims and criminals getting away with it.

To go back to Andy’s point, if there was a never-ending porridge pot, we would of course have more money and more detectives, please. I do think that prevention is better than cure, and that is very much the approach I have taken. I have weaved a trauma-informed practice into everything I am doing through my office: the £11 million of services that I commission, victim support and perpetrator support programmes, jointly with the Probation Service. Tackling the root cause of why someone has been a heroin or crack cocaine addict for the last 10 years is better than locking them up, because if you can prevent them from wanting to burgle houses and steal tractors, or whatever it is, that is surely a better thing.
Q176 Mr Allen, do you want to add anything?

You asked me about priorities and how we prioritise. A lot of that is the function that we carry out—all being well, mayors and deputy mayors will follow us in it—which is to hold to account. I started off my life as a village bobby. I was a rural sergeant, when we had rural police stations in Cumbria. They were closed down in austerity—16 police stations. Unlike Donna, I have not had the funding to be able to reopen them.

What I have done is invest 44% more into our neighbourhood policing teams. That is 44% extra staff—PCSOs and constables. That is how you start to restore trust and confidence. It is about the contact with the public. Policing is a contact sport; I have frequently described it as such.

When I knocked on doors prior to my election in 2024, everybody was telling me, “I want to see a police officer; I want to know who my police officer is.” Yes, they cover huge areas—huge swathes of Cumbrian countryside—but if they are active, engaged and in all the community groups, they will get the trust and confidence, the reporting and the local buy-back.

In relation to your question about whether you invest in investigation or prevention, I would always go prevention to start with because it is cheaper. For example, I invest heavily in youth and community groups from the community fund money we take from criminals. For every £1 that I invest, I can show you that we are actually saving £3 in terms of criminality, social care and so on. In the areas that we have invested in, antisocial behaviour has gone down by 40%, and crime has come down by 8%. Prevention works. You have to have an investigation capability as well, but if you invest in prevention first, you can reduce the burden on the back end.

Part of our role is to promulgate best practice across the country from all 43 forces. I regularly get asked, “What would be the one thing you would recommend to any rural area police force around rural crime?”. The one thing I repeatedly say is investment in their rural watch scheme. As you have heard, this is not about putting more police officers. You can move the deckchairs around the Titanic as much as you want, but the bottom line is that, if you have got the community and where we see the strength in the community, it works really well.

For forces that use rural watch and use WhatsApp, which is a very contentious issue, it is very effective, to the point that—we know this from the research and the criminals we deal with—they think there is a secret society that occurs because there is this group. It is because the community has come together to help deal with criminality. It makes it a more hostile place for criminals to operate in. I would certainly encourage investment in that. It will bring you far greater rewards, but it needs the neighbourhood policing teams to help deliver it.
I am very conscious that we spent quite a long time on that section, so let us move on to drugs and county lines.
Q177 What is your strategy for tackling drugs in rural areas, and how does it differ from your wider approaches on crime.

Again, drugs is one of the four priorities for Cumbria police. I spent most of my career in the NCA and its precursors tackling that nationally, internationally and locally. I have invested in tackling drugs locally. There are lots of days of action, but I fund additional days of action using money taken from criminals. Thus far, I have spent about £800,000 on that—on one occasion, we recovered half a million pounds from a single job, so it pays for itself.

It is about publicising very heavily and ensuring that the criminals understand that they will be targeted and tackled. It gets more people to report instances of drug use, drug trafficking and so on, especially in our rural areas. We did one in Penrith last week. That is a very rural area—a little market town—so you would not think it would have a drugs problem. We got quite a bit of drugs back-end money from that one job. That will lead to other jobs. Again, it is all about prioritisation and holding to account.

It is also about the force itself working together—our force intelligence bureau working with the neighbourhood policing team, with roads policing and with response. What we find is that you have to do this locally. The ROCUs in particular are very good, and we fund part of that. But Cumbria never ever hits the MoRiLE score—the index that lets the ROCUs come and do work in your area. The bigger urban areas—be that Manchester or Liverpool—get all the resources in terms of ROCU function. We need some resource ourselves. We make good use of what we have and work really closely with our neighbouring forces. That causes a bit of an issue as well, because we are part of North West ROCU but a lot of our organised crime comes from the north-east, so we have to co-ordinate it. We do it very well, because we have to.
Q178 Would you say that the major difference between your wider approach and the approach to drugs is the amount of resource applied to rural areas as opposed to non-rural ones?

It is, but it is a difference of scale as well . We do not have the scale of drug use and drug trafficking that , say , Manchester or Liverpool do , b ut we are able to tackle it. A good example is Barrow - in - Furness , which had a problem with county lines. It is on the route from Liverpool, be that rail or road , and we had a real issue there. We focused on that and tackled it . W e got assistance from a group called 1-CLIC, working with the Well, and it was able to go in with the addicts and the dealers and work with them.

N ow we do the enforcement and take out the level of drug dealers —that is manageable in a rural area, whereas in bigger areas it may be less so —and then 1-CLIC is going behind to put in the help and assistance around the addicts and the people affected by the drug dealing . T hat works really well : a s of last account, Barrow had no county lines in it. There are s till drugs — of course there are—b ut we have taken out the out - of - county involvement and the mass transshipment of drugs into our county , so we can keep a handle on things better in a rural small area.
Q179 I will ask the same about your strategy, Donna.

I will be absolutely honest with you : drugs consumption is everywhere . B ut the drug consumption in rural communities does not concern me. What concerns me about rural communities when it comes to drugs is the storage, concealment, processing and distribution of drugs. It is more about drug supply networks in rural communities , where you have areas with secluded premises , reduced footfall and lower visibility . D rug supply networks and organised crime gangs working in drug supply will suddenly pop up in the middle of a high street in a disused shop . T hey wi ll then move their model to being out in a rural area.

What have I been doing to try to tackle this? I have invested in a lot more ANPR cameras to cover some of our rural roads . W e have the intelligence — we are good at developing intelligence in policing across England and Wales — but our ANPR cameras are largely on our key route networks, on busy roads and in urban centres. We need to ensure that we are adapting as the OCG model adapts with drug supply , so that that those rural communities are not left vulnerable.

As I said earlier, OCGs working in rural communities are all about mone y—t hat is their motivation . It i s about making income and as much money as they can under the radar as quickly as they can without being caught. Linked to that, as I said at the beginning , you also have violence. W here you have violence and drug supply, you have firearms, and then you have to look at how the OCGs working in rural communities are linked to the illegal black - market firearms supply and distribution across the UK. That is a real and present threat, and that play s out into our urban areas as well.

As I say , I am not so concerned about drug consumption in rural communitie s; it is very much about how rural communities are being exploited for the distribution, concealment and processing of drugs coming into this country. You then have to factor modern slavery into that as well, because people who are in this country illegally get exploited by OCGs in the drug world and will be concealed in outbuildings and places like that in very remote rural communities.

Q180 F orgive me , my geography is terrible and I c annot remember exactly where these places are , but have you had any issues with areas that have a licence to grow cannabis, for example ? H ow has that been impacted ?

No. My biggest issue from an OCG perspective in rural communities in Hampshire is the p ort of Southampton. We have one of the busiest ports in Europe , a nd as a consequence, we get OCGs that operate very sophisticated ly, which Andy and the team nationally are focused on l ooking at.

We had a big OCG operation about 18 months or two years ago . They were coming from the outer areas of Birmingham down into Hampshire, stealing plant and machinery to order . They would steal a trailer or quad bike a t 1 or 2 in the morning , and it would be in the p ort of Southampton by 4 or 5 o’clock in a container and gone by 6 a m. By the time the farmer ha s woken up, it is gone —it is in a container , leaving the UK and going to the e astern b loc , where they were literally buying things to order . T he OCGs were just thriving on that . T hat has been a big piece of work . Th e NCA got involved in some of that; Andy will give you more information on it.

W e have been very vulnerable to that from rural OCG s across the country that come into a very large rural area in Hampshire because the port is right there at the end of the M3 motorway . T hey can steal in Winchester, Basingstoke and the beautiful shire areas we ha ve and go straight into Southampton , to the port at the bottom of the motorway , and it is gone and away.

My counsel on this would be that OCGs—organised crime groups—are diversifying. They have seen that the risk for reward for the theft of high-value machinery is far more likely to bring you less attention from a police force or ROCU . There is lots of evidence to show that it is a commodity for drugs in return.

Since 2014, we have seen a 75% increase in vehicle thefts, including farm vehicles. At the same time, we have seen a reduction in the number of qualified stolen vehicle examiners. When we are doing operations at ports and chop shops around the country, it is harder to find those machines and identify them as stolen.

In terms of sophistication, as you have heard from the PCC, we had a machine stolen in North Yorkshire, and 24 hours later it appeared in Poland with a completely new identity. It had been cloned on the move in the back of a lorry. That is the level of sophistication that we are seeing from OCGs; the average member of the public would not know how to do that.

To be honest, this is where I would like more involvement from the ROCUs. They do a great job in tackling drugs and firearms in the urban areas, but when it comes to rural crime, we are seen as a soft touch; big areas with low police cover because of the nature of where we live.

A good example is a job that involved Cheshire, Cumbria and a number of other rural forces. More than £1 million worth of plant equipment was stolen. Cheshire eventually took it on because the ROCU could not or would not—it did not hit their MoRiLE score at the time—and individuals have been charged as a result. But the forces had to work to get there individually to bring them to account; it did not meet the ROCU criteria. That is one area where it is needed.

Forces work perfectly well. We have got small but really well-performing rural crime teams and very good detectives and FIBs, but the ROCUs need to be more plugged into what is an emerging and developing area. Criminals will always go for the soft touch; if it is easier and has less risk, that is where they will go.

Operation Siren is a fantastic example of that working very well, but it is thwarted by the fact that we have a court date of May 2028. Early releases mean we are now dealing with the same people. We had an incident where somebody was released sooner than I could give the commendation to the officers for the job that they did. It is a big challenge.

Q181 Before we move on, how do you ensure that all officers are able to spot the signs of things like human trafficking, modern slavery and drug trafficking? Thinking about my own area, the PCSO or police officer attending the parish council meeting may come into contact with somebody or get some indication that something is not right. Donna, you mentioned the isolated places where the drugs can be grown or stored. How do you ensure that all those officers have the training needed to spot those signs and flag them?

That is a really good point. We are asking a lot of our officers. Some of them are very young in service and they are coming up against issues such as modern-day slavery. They may not have known what that meant before becoming a police officer at the age of 18, 19 or 20. We are asking a lot of them.

It is about regular training. With the rural crime taskforce that I funded about 18 months ago, we have given them very specific training on the risks of sheep worrying, hare coursing and the salmon season, which we came into a couple of months ago. I have invested in off-road vehicles, so that they have the right tyres on the right vehicles to be able to pursue people in Subaru Imprezas who are chasing across farms for hare coursing.

We have also taught them about different sorts of guns and how to disarm them. A lot of them have never held a gun before even though they are a police constable—why would they if they have never been a firearms officer? We have given them all that training.

In terms of modern-day slavery and some of the additional risks to look out for, that is part of their core training. They undergo annual refreshers and reviews, but it is difficult because it is asking a lot of them to look out for some of those wicked problems in rural communities, where you do not often see that.

This is one where the rural crime comes in and definitely proves its worth. We have invested and put additional resources into ours. As Donna said, we have given them additional vehicles using money taken from criminals, so that they have got the latest, decent and best kit that we can get.

We are also getting new recruits into the training school. In Cumbria, 60% of our frontline constables have got less than three years’ service, so it is a continual churn of training. The rural crime team does that well. There are only a few of them—there are five of them in the team—and they cannot be everywhere. A lot of the training is about, “This is what to look for, this is how to spot it and here is what to do when you do”, as well about as working with farmers so they lock up diesel and do not leave keys in vehicles. It is a strategic function, but it is one that delivers big results if you do the training and education properly.

We benefit from a really good relationship with industry. We get funding from the NFU and the Construction Equipment Association, and we do training annually across the UK. About 1,600 officers have been trained in the last two years in how to identify stolen equipment and how to work with the knowledge around livestock, because it is unreasonable to expect every police officer to know what a movement order for some cattle is or what a sheep book is. That is where, again, through the funding from NFU Mutual, we have been able to have a dedicated police staff member who can help advise police officers on how to investigate those offences. That is where it becomes really helpful to provide that specialist knowledge. It is not about everybody knowing everything; it is about knowing where to go to get the answer.

Q182 I am going to ask you another question on waste crime, but I wanted to pick up on something you just said. Did you say that you take the money from the criminals and use it to buy equipment for policing?

Yes, absolutely. It is the ARIS fund—our asset recovery incentivisation fund. We get half of whatever we seize. Of the half a million pounds from the one drugs raid I mentioned, half goes to the Treasury and half comes back to me as the arbiter for the force—the holder of the money. Then the force put forward certain suggestions of what they would like to use the money on. I also use some of the money for my community fund, for local youth groups and so on. It is a very good use of resource in Cumbria, because of our arterial links. I think that certainly last year we seized the fourth highest amount of money in the entire country—not per capita, but in total.

Q183 Thank you. I didn’t know that; that is interesting. I am going to ask you something about waste crime now, specifically about fly-tipping, which is a big problem where I am from. I was at the Suffolk Show over the summer, and I was horrified to learn about this problem—there were people from the National Farmers’ Union there explaining what was going on. It seems that there is a massive problem in my bit of the world of fly-tipping on farms, and then it is the responsibility of the farmer to clear away, at their expense, the stuff that has been tipped on to their tracks and fields. I know that when the Prime Minister was campaigning to be the Prime Minister, there was a massive, great fly-tip somewhere close to his constituency, which has been cleared. My question is about this waste crime and how effective the current policing and associated strategies are at dealing with this in rural areas.

I will go first. This is an issue largely led by local authorities that could be better at leading the prosecutions under the Environmental Protection Act powers that they have. We then have the Environment Agency on the larger, more complex scale, which has definitely started coming to the table a bit more. What we know from the Prime Minister’s recent announcements is that there is going to be a move towards empowering police forces—I hope that comes with some resourcing and some money—to help support the investigative skills that are required for the Environment Agency and for environmental health officers and councils. Some councils are really good at this, but for others, it is very hit and miss—it is a postcode lottery when it comes to this. But the impact is absolutely horrendous.

Very often, with some good investigative skills, you can find out where a dump has come from by photographing it, putting it on social media and someone saying, “Oh yeah, that’s the stuff that came from my garden. I can tell you who came and picked it up.” Of the public, 85% of us or maybe more are generally law-abiding, and we do not want to see stuff from our gardens tipped in the local country lane.

We also know that illegal fly-tips are costing the UK economy over £1 billion a year. In my area alone, we have had over 1,001 incidents of fly-tipping reported in the last 12 months in the south-east region. My colleagues, the police and crime commissioners for Surrey, Sussex, Kent, Thames Valley and I have set up a policing south-east rural waste crime board so that we can work with the Environment Agency and others. We have had a particularly horrendous case on the border between Sussex and Kent called Hoads Wood. That site will be out of action for five years because of the toxic waste that was there before it can be used again for its natural environmental habitat reasons. It is horrendous.

What I would say is that you can stretch policing resources only so far, and I would really love to see councils utilising their quite effective legal powers a lot more. They are not doing that to their full capacity at the moment, and if they were, we could see some much lengthier custodial sentences given for what is actually a very impactful crime.

I agree with Donna. For my part, Cumbria has not had the large-scale things like Hoads Wood or Kidlington in Oxfordshire, where 23,000 tonnes of waste was dumped—of course, we all saw that on the TV. But it is an issue; we have had over 5,000 incidents of low-level fly-tipping just in the north of Cumbria, which is one of my local authority areas.

I would like to see clarity on how the councils deal with it. My asks are a clearer intelligence picture, so better intelligence-sharing, and prompt investigation. The police have a part to play and can do more, but this remains—and should remain—a local authority lead. Local authorities should have responsibility for it going to court and being prosecuted, but there is no reason why the police cannot assist. It is no different to what we do with dodgy shops and trading standards.

Through prompt investigation, we should be able to identify who is doing the large-scale dumping—it is not that difficult—and then take the prosecution forward. Lastly, it is obviously limited to public land, but there has to be some recourse to assist private landowners; otherwise, they will not report and the dump gets bigger and bigger.

Q184 There is a big difference between stuff that is tipped on to the road and stuff that is tipped into a farmer’s field. What do you think about the idea of councils actually collecting the rubbish themselves from people’s properties at no cost? The reason this is happening—I think—is because criminals are going around with their trucks, offering to take people’s stuff away for a small fee, and they are then dumping it. If the councils did that, there would be less of an incentive, which seems to be a preventive approach that is happening in some places.

For me, the incentive to carry on fly-tipping would go up if it just got collected by councils. What I think would be fair for taxpayers would be councils collecting the waste for them, and then properly investigating and prosecuting the person who did it. Through the courts, the prosecuting officer or environmental health officer who went to court could then put in a compensation claim to say, “It cost us £3,500 to collect this waste, take it to a local tip and incinerate it”—or whatever it is they do with it. They should be keeping a log of those costs and then recharging that through the courts, as part of the conviction and compensation order to the perpetrator of the crime.

We work with the Environment Agency very closely, and we assist it with training. It will come as no surprise that a lot of the machinery used on these sites is stolen. The powers are there, but we have found that it is about the capacity within those organisations to prosecute. There is definitely a link to the organised crime that we are dealing with, as it is the same people who are doing waste crime. My only ask, if I can be so bold, is that we move away from calling this “fly-tipping”. Fly-tipping seems to suggest that it is a nuisance. I would much prefer that we refer to it as “waste crime”; these are criminals who are doing this, because they are there to make money from it.
I agree.

Q185 I want to touch on the importance of partnership working. I mentioned in the previous session that Devon and Cornwall worked with other regional forces in the south-west on Operation Scorpion, which was quite effective in tackling county lines gangs. Can you tell us a bit more about partnerships with industry? Andrew, I suspect that we might come on to the Act that you referenced earlier, but it would just be interesting to hear about best practice.

I would be very happy to. In fact, I would not be sat here if not for what I would say is a groundbreaking partnership between the police, NFU Mutual, the Construction Equipment Association and, even now, finance companies, which are seeing a benefit in having a national co-ordination role that is performed by ourselves, working with those forces.

All the 43 forces now benefit from that funding in training and assistance with on-the-ground operational deployments. Without a doubt, the partnership is key to both the national unit and, on the ground level, what you see from the local neighbourhood Rural Watch schemes, the parish council, the local NFU Mutual office that works there and the farming groups. They are fundamental to tackling the problems we face.

In terms of support going forward and legislation, the Equipment Theft (Prevention) Act came on the back of a big push from the NFU to help address these issues, and we have really seen the power of that in helping to improve things. Ultimately, while people may disagree over the necessity for it and the cost of implementing it, it is done and comes from a point of view of trying to make things better.

Q186 Can I pick up on that point? I think that Act was passed in early 2024, and we are obviously in late 2026 now. We have the opportunity to raise that with Home Office Ministers when they come before us. Why is that so difficult to implement? We have heard from all the panels today about billions of pounds-worth of machinery and theft from farms. Why can we not pass that Act and actually have the protection on that expensive machinery, which would massively undermine these gangs that we have heard about?
There are some very good people who you could call upon, including the likes of Greg Smith MP, who helped push for this. This was not just about machinery; this was also about tool theft.

If you look into it, tool theft is actually one of the greatest acquisitive crimes across the country, but it is hidden behind theft from vehicle, burglary and things like that. This was about helping to get stolen property back to people and helping make it harder to steal in the first place. It is where those discussions have come to with manufacturers as to the cost to them of doing this and where the benefit sits. My request would be to say, “Look, what is the greater pressure here?” That is where Ministers have to make that difficult decision as to what the benefit of reducing crime is, what the cost to manufacturing is and the cost that might be put on to members of the public by it.

Obviously, I sit on the fence of wanting to see crimes go down, and I think we should have better security on machinery and have forensic marking. At the moment, the Act is still waiting to come through, which would have forensic marking on quad bikes. Quad bikes remain a consistent problem every year for thefts, and it is organised crime that is behind those thefts. Hopefully, it will help, but as yet, it is not in place.

Partnership working is absolutely key. I come back to the point I made earlier: with so many thousands of square miles of rural countryside area across this country, we cannot possibly ever imagine an Exchequer where we can afford to police every single village green; therefore, partnership working is absolutely key. I have a rural crime taskforce that I chair once a quarter. The senior police officer leads that with me; in my force, that is my assistant chief constable head of local policing. Our rural policing team sits under his watch. I have the NFU, the Countryside Land Association—the CLA—and BASC. They all sit on my rural crime taskforce, and we are sharing best practice. We also have barn meetings with farmers, landowners and gamekeepers. When we have a specific issue, we will surge in and help them from that perspective as well.

I had a half-a-million-pound rural crime prevention fund that I launched last year. It was open for three months. Parish councils, Members of Parliament, councillors, district parish councils, community groups and neighbourhood watch groups could bid into that for anything from £500 up to, I think, £20,000. That could have been for some deployable CCTV, for some more lighting in a rural community, to cut back some hedgerows or something that enables criminals to work in a certain way. That has been really helpful, but the key thing for me is that, without rural communities, we could not possibly hope to have the levels of community safety that we have in the country.

The final thing from me around partnership working is that, in Hampshire, we were the first police force in the country to have something called HADs, which is the humane animal dispatch scheme. We have 46 volunteers. When a deer or another animal is hit on a road, the police control room can deploy them, 24 hours a day, and they are all firearms trained and trained in how to dispose of animals in a safe way. It saves police officers or the firearms unit going out and spending half an hour driving across a rural community to deal with, let’s say, a very injured deer. Our volunteers do that. Wiltshire and Thames Valley police have now taken on the scheme that we are running, and it is now also part of the College of Policing’s best practice on how to humanely deal with animals injured predominantly on our roads.

I will add one key thing. What PCCs, mayors and deputy mayors have is the power to convene—to pull the various partners together, get them round a table and get them to work together. I know Donna does this. I do this to great effect in Cumbria across a whole range of things from rural crime to drug dealing and dodgy shops. But also, Cumbria has twice the national incidence of male suicide in some of our areas, and one of the things we have started doing recently is bringing the key parties together and saying, “How can we fix this? How do we fix this major issue?” That works. You are sitting them down; you have the key players, they go out and task their teams, and you are bringing back intelligence and a practical ability to make a difference on the ground. To my mind, that is what the mayors and the PCCs bring to the table. It is the power to convene, the power to persuade and the power to get things done.

Q187 Can I ask about the c lear, h old, b uild model ? We have obviously been hearing about that in urban areas, and I am going to look at it in Staffordshire in a couple of days’ time. How effective is it in rural areas?
We have used two clear, hold, build sites in Hampshire: one in Gosport and one in Southampton. We have not done one in a rural community.

Could I see it working? Yes, I could, but in terms of competing demands, with 2.2 million people in my patch and the number of urban centres, I am going to estimate that I would have probably 100 other areas that I would put ahead of any rural community in terms of risk. It is just not on the same scale in terms of the impact on people, children, sexual exploitation, risk from drug supply and violence. It is in a different league. O ur clear, hold, build sites are very much targeted towards serious violence and drug supply. That is where we are focused. We have not used that tactic in a rural community, and I am not sure there has ever been one, but Andy may be able to give you clarity on that.
No, there has not, as far as I am aware.
I can add a bit. We have one in Cumbria, but not in a rural area. It is in a place called Hindpool in Barrow-in-Furness, which is on the edge of the town. We call it “Happy Hopeful Hindpool”.

It works in an urban / semi-urban setting. As Donna said, your difficulty is that you do not have the scale or continuation of the issues and the offences. Some of the practices from clear, hold, build can be transferred—clearing out the issue, putting in the good stuff, dealing with the addiction and the problems that caused it, and then putting in actually decent living conditions for people and so on. You can put those principles in anywhere, and we should. However, I have only ever seen it in an urban setting, and I think it is probably more suited to urban than rural areas.

Q188 That is helpful; thank you. I will finish on policing reform. I will not make any preamble, because you have heard me previously, but I would like to hear your views on policing reform and how it might impact your ability to tackle organised crime in rural areas.

If it happens—that would be my opening gambit . It has already been pushed back three times; I think we are now looking at February next year. You will probably be better informed than me on that one.
I am not sure we are.

Fair enough. I am not actually against police reform. I think change can be a very good thing. We have 43 police forces across England and Wales, and some of them are very small, to the point where they have had to get rid of all their police community support officers. That is a real pity. Some of them are really struggling financially. Do y ou know what? There is a really practical issue here as well. We are struggling to recruit chief constables in this country—we really are. The number of police officers who want and aspire to get to that level is something that perhaps this Committee might want to look into.

There is the creation of the NPS, the National Police Service—the central part that will run BlueLight Commercial and the Police Digital Service. David is the chair of the PDS; I was on its board for a couple of years. We can l ook at some of the centralised bodies, such as NPAS, the National Police Air Service, which has just been blighted with issue after issue, particularly recently, with a lot of its planes and helicopters grounded for servicing issues. That has been far from ideal. However, when you look at some of the national policing bodies, it is right that there should be some central co-ordination, and I am optimistic that that stuff will happen fairly quickly without any significant reform, because it is just business as usual—common sense.

In terms of the police forces, I know it is rumoured that Lord Hogan-Howe’s review could take us from 43 police forces down to as few as nine , 12 or 20—w ho knows? I think it is right that the Prime Minister, if my information is correct, has intervened to say, “Let’s look at what we are doing with the mayoralties to see if we can tie that up with the boundaries of the new police forces.” That would make sense, rather than having a police force that perhaps had two mayors, with one covering only a section of it, which is messy.

I am not against reform; I think it could be a good thing. However, I am very concerned about the scale that has been mooted, going down to as few as nine police forces. The country currently has nine regions, including Wales. Those police forces would be so enormous. There is no way that there would not be a slip in service for the public on that basis. Bigger is not always better.

Policing as a public service is very constrained financially now. Times are really tough. Some of the smaller police forces are struggling to deliver the operational need that is required of them in their communities. We know that criminals will exploit gaps and voids that have been created. I am not against it, but let’s wait and see where the detail and the scale of it land. Then I will be able to form a proper opinion on it.

They were talking about police reform 40 years ago, when I was a young constable, in much the same vein. I agree with Donna on having the national police service in the centre. I am the chair of PDS and I sit on BlueLight Commercial . Have your IT and procurement set up in one place. That should be mandated. As long as the vehicle you drive is a general purpose car, and it meets the criteria that policing need, the type of vehicle you drive does not matter . That makes sense.

It also makes sense to look at the National Crime Agency and Counter Terrorism Policing. There are a lot of really hard to fill roles in there, from surveillance to interception—take your pick. A whole plethora of specialist services are competing against each other for the rare individuals who have gone through all that training. That makes a lot of sense: you get more bang for your buck. You have to have clear governance, oversight and holding to account, because it will be a very powerful body. It is probably not enough just to have the Home Secretary having the oversight and control. You need some local oversight from mayors or whatever.

We should do the middle bit well, do the NPS well and create a centre of excellence that works. You have some good organisations that are keen to do this now. In terms of mergers of forces, I would go for evolution rather than revolution any time of the week. Cumbria is a good example: we are a small force with a tiny population—half a million people—but we have a very constrained geography. We meet all our KPIs, and that includes attending grade 1 and grade 2 incidents, both police and fire. We do it, and if we can do it in Cumbria, you can do it anywhere. Likewise, we are pretty financially viable . We have had issues through austerity, but we are coming through those, and our numbers are increasing and we are doing more.

To my mind, we should look at the mayoralties and the deputy mayor model, which is a clear follow-on from the PCC model, which we know works. If you have engaged PCCs who care, get stuck into dealing with it and working, and hold their chief constable to account, that works. If my area merges with Manchester, Cheshire, Liverpool and Lancashire, what benefit does Cumbria get? We are the best performing force in our region. What on earth would I get from merging with forces that are not as good? It is as simple as that. We would lose resource, and people would be pulled away to go to Blackpool, Preston or—if we go the other way—Northumbria. For example, Windermere still has a police station, and Ambleside has a police station. They are about a mile apart. The reason is that, in summer, it will take you two hours to get between those, and 18 million people visit that part of this country.
That is the unique thing that you have, as I have in my area—tourists.

Absolutely. One size does not fit all. As Donna said, bigger is not always more efficient or more effective. If it was, the Metropolitan police would be the most effective police force in the world. It is not, by a long way.
Q189 As the MP for Alton Towers, I definitely have tourists coming to my constituency. Andy, do you want to finish off?

Just briefly, Chair. I think there is a benefit to our national unit sitting nationally, rather than with an independent police force. You talked about your Three Shires Head problem; central co-ordination is still needed to perform that . Whether it is over eight forces, as it has been recently for the GPS thefts, or whether it is over three forces that are larger, there is still a necessity for co-ordination to bring people together. We have it now with the ROCUs: they cannot always agree who is going to pick up a job. That needs central co-ordination. Lastly, big is not always beautiful. We have seen this with some of the big forces that have big rural areas. They are not always the best. Some of the smaller forces are exceptional at what they do.
Thank you so much for that. Are there any further comments—no? Thank you for your time. It has been really informative and helpful for this inquiry.

sessions.iT: The taxation of the hospitality and tourism sectors in Northern Ireland
sessions.w: Northern Ireland Tourism Alliance; Grant Thornton Ireland

segs.tx: Northern Ireland Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: The t axation of the hospitality and tourism sectors in Northern Ireland , HC 544
Wednesday 14 October 2026 , Derry/Londonderry
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 14 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Tonia Antoniazzi (Chair); Simon Hoare; Adam Jogee; Mike Kane; Mr Paul Kohler; Katrina Murray; Gavin Robinson.
Questions 65 - 1 16
Witnesses
I : Dr Joanne Stuart, Chief Executive Officer, Northern Ireland Tourism Alliance;
II: Aidan Lyons, Director, Indirect Tax, Grant Thornton Northern Ireland .
Written evidence from witnesses:
– Northern Ireland Tourism Alliance, [ THT0015 ]
– Grant Thornton Ireland, [ THT0023 ]
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Dr Joanne Stuart and Aidan Lyons.

Q65 Welcome to the final evidence session of our inquiry into taxation of the hospitality and tourism sectors in Northern Ireland. We are really pleased to be taking our evidence today from St Columb’s Hall in Derry/Londonderry. This is the first time that the Committee has taken public evidence in Northern Ireland since March 2024, and the first time outside Stormont since June 2018, so this is quite the achievement.

We are joined by Dr Joanne Stuart, chief exec of Northern Ireland Tourism Alliance, and Aidan Lyons, director of indirect tax at Grant Thornton Ireland. Thank you ever so much for joining us. How would you assess the financial health of the hospitality sector in Northern Ireland?

Thank you very much for the invitation to speak to you today. As you said, I represent the Northern Ireland Tourism Alliance, which represents the whole of the tourism ecosystem in Northern Ireland. We are the voice of tourism in Northern Ireland, and that covers everything from transport to tour guiding, accommodation, attractions and so on.

In July, we had the 2025 figures for tourism, which showed that tourism—the number of visits and trips—is growing. However, the associated spend and the associated days or nights that people are staying have not increased at the same level. We are doing well, but we have more work to do with regard to increasing the spend and giving visitors more reason to stay in Northern Ireland.

The latest Tourism NI industry survey ran to assess the first six months of this year. The majority of companies are doing the same as, if not better than, last year, but from a challenge perspective, we are looking at the value. An increase in visitors does not necessarily mean an increase in revenues, which goes through to the bottom line.

We have a number of challenges, particularly in the hospitality industry. I know that representatives from Hospitality Ulster have spoken to you. The challenges are things like business rates, the inflation costs in food and the increase in salaries and wages, which was a particular challenge for all businesses in the tourism industry. Primarily, we are made up of small and medium-sized enterprises, and the increase in the NIC threshold and the rate of NIC were huge costs to be assumed by the industry.

As a result, that did not leave companies with enough reserves to get into the investment that is needed, or to put forward competitive pricing, because of the costs that have to be assumed. I have prepared a more detailed brief for the Committee on the back of this, and I have given a full breakdown of the differentials between Northern Ireland and the Republic of Ireland across all the different operating costs. That is stark, with regard not just to VAT but to payroll, pensions and so on.

Q66 You have gone through basically what the problems are—the VAT, employer NI contributions, increases to the national minimum wage, businesses’ energy costs—but to what extent do you think difficulties are caused by the VAT rate, as opposed to the other factors?

VAT is one factor, but there are also a number of costs when you look at this from my perspective—I look at the whole trip. Our case is based on looking at it from the consumer perspective—the visitor, business viability and future investment. When we look at the visitor or the tour operator choosing where to go, VAT is one of the costs that potentially makes us less competitive. Then we are looking at the increase in travel costs—APD and ETA—and a number of aspects add costs on to our trip.
Which we will come to.

Therefore, because we have a higher rate of VAT, all that is coming together. We believe that we need a sustained reduction in VAT. However, that does not mean that we do not need to look at the costs that are within our control.
I will go to Aidan with the same question.

I echo Joanne’s thanks for the invitation to appear before you today. I specialise in indirect tax, in VAT principally. The standard rate of VAT in the UK is 20%. There is a differentiation from the Republic of Ireland, where it is 13.5% and 9%—there is a difference.

It is a consumer tax, so it is the consumer who pays the tax, and it is added on to the cost or the price that they pay, whether that is staying at a hotel, going to a restaurant or whatever it may be. It can have an impact on the overall price paid. I am not an economist, although our submission included quite a lot of economic analysis and reference, so I would certainly defer to Joanne in that and in her understanding and knowledge of the sector. Potentially, a reduction in VAT might help—it can help—but there is a wider policy here. Clearly, costs are going up—utilities, wages and other costs that the sectors have to face—and they all factor into the overall position.
Q67 I suppose this is one for you, Joanne: would you say that tourism and hospitality businesses in Northern Ireland are struggling compared with similarly sized businesses in other sectors?

I could not say yes or no; I think it is different across the piece. We have some very successful tourism businesses, but smaller businesses can be struggling. That is common across the economy in Northern Ireland. The increase in NIC definitely had a major impact in tourism and hospitality. It really did halt investment and recruitment in those businesses. It was also difficult for businesses, because once you started to change at the lower end, there were increases all the way up. With the cost of pensions and so on, that made a big difference. Businesses have to think very carefully about recruiting people.

The Republic of Ireland has announced a budget, which we are working through at the moment, but certainly based on figures from before the budget came out, there was a difference of nearly 7% in the per-person cost. Those in Northern Ireland were paying 7% more than those in the Republic, and that makes a lot of difference when you are trying to recruit.

A lot of the costs that we are dealing with are similar across the economy. There are specific ones, like business rates for example, where there is support in the rest of the UK, but we do not have the same support here. Again, when we are looking at costs and where decisions can be made, they are divided between Westminster and the Northern Ireland Executive, which can cause a challenge.
Q68 On that note, Joanne, do you think that the tourism and hospitality sector requires more support from the UK Government than businesses in other sectors?

I do, because of the type of businesses we have. We are also very much people-focused and people-facing. Although we are utilising technology to make business efficiencies, we are never going to replace people; we would never want to do that. That is what creates the welcome for visitors, so we are an important sector for providing those jobs on a regional basis. As we start to see AI develop further, there will be people who need to look at different jobs and opportunities. That is where tourism and hospitality can step into the breach, but we have to make sure that our businesses are there and will have the capacity for investment.

Q69 Thank you both for coming this afternoon. It is good to be back here in Northern Ireland. Can you touch on the cost pressures facing the tourism and hospitality sectors in the United Kingdom and the Republic of Ireland? What do they look like? Give us a flavour of that comparison.

As Aidan set out, obviously there are the differences in VAT. It is more about food. Alcohol is charged at a higher VAT rate in the Republic of Ireland, so it does not include alcohol. We talked about wages and the differences. There is a slight difference in the minimum wage. I think the Republic of Ireland is more or less where we are now, but obviously national insurance and the minimum employer pension are both higher for businesses up here. It works out at roughly £1,800 more per employee in Northern Ireland.

Business energy prices in Northern Ireland are definitely different, whether that is for small or large users. I have included all my sources in the briefing paper. It is between 9% and 14% higher across those bands. Then we have inflation: overall consumer inflation in the UK is 3.1% and in the Republic of Ireland it is 3.7%. There are a number of different things.
One thing that I would say about VAT—I am sure Aidan agrees—is that it is very complicated and complex.
Yes.
There are multiple different things, but we have tried to provide some information to simplify that. Does that answer your question?

Q70 It does. Out of interest, can you give us a flavour of how effective sharing best practice and mitigating the impact between businesses is? What is that relationship like? Is there one? Could it be better?
Between—?
Between business in the Republic of Ireland and in Northern Ireland, and some of their representative bodies.
Them supporting us?

No, sorry. You have just talked through some of the challenges felt by businesses on both sides of the border. I am interested in knowing what co-operation and engagement takes place between businesses and their representative organisations to mitigate some of that, to share best practice or to say, “This is how we should do things differently.”

I think there is a lot of collaboration and networking across the industry. Tourism NI has a workplace excellence programme—it is just about to announce 15 businesses going on to that—which is all about sharing best practice. NITA itself has our skills forum, which again is about bringing employers together to learn from each other and share. We have just launched the apprenticeship ambassador scheme, which is about trying to encourage businesses to look at different ways to bring in new staff and increase staff.

There are a number of costs that we cannot do anything about, such as ETA, APD and all that, but we come together so that we can understand what those costs are and how we can work on that. I work very closely with the Northern Ireland Hotels Federation, Visit Belfast, the councils and the Association of Leading Visitor Attractions so that we can find what the common themes are and what we need to do to make the case.

As I say, we have to work with three jurisdictions, obviously including Westminster and the Executive. We look at Tourism Ireland funding and what the Irish Government are doing to support tourism, and we are trying to leverage some of that. In the current budget, Fáilte Ireland has received an additional €6.5 million to promote the Republic of Ireland across the island of Ireland. Tourism Ireland has received more money, and rural pubs have received €15 million because they are seen as an important part of the ecosystem, and they really are struggling. It is sometimes hard for businesses up here to see the funding and support that is being given to their industry.
And there is the inevitable competition that goes with that. If you are not that far away, you can go and spend your money there.

Yes, that is the thing. We will probably come on to talk about the pilot. The thing we have to remember with Northern Ireland is that we are promoted as the island of Ireland. People come to the island of Ireland and then decide whether to spend time in Northern Ireland or in southern Ireland. We have that competition right on our doorstep, and people can make decisions at the last minute. That is why it is really important that we are able to articulate the value and the reasons that people come to Northern Ireland. That is why the promotion budget for Tourism Northern Ireland is really important. It is obviously very difficult at the moment, because we do not have a budget in Northern Ireland. We are talking about VAT, which is important, but it is also part of a larger problem.
Thank you; that is a really helpful answer. Aidan?

There is not too much that I can add to that, because Joanne has set it out eloquently. It speaks to her experience, in terms of her role. We see from our clients that, across Northern Ireland, there are cost pressures, whether it is from utility bills or NIC. I think that is true of all businesses. There are some tremendously successful businesses in Northern Ireland. Clearly, the hospitality and tourism sector does have some specific pressures. There is a difference in the taxation rates as far as VAT is concerned between the Republic and Northern Ireland.
Q71 Do you think that it is helpful to make a comparison between the two?
In terms of—?
The experiences of businesses in the sector on either side of the border. It is not a trick question; I am just interested.

It is an interesting question, and I am sure that Joanne can bring something to it. If you are a tourist, I think you choose where you are going because there are things you want to see; that drives why you go to a certain place. On the island of Ireland, if you fly to Dublin, you can be in Belfast in an hour and three quarters. If you want to go to the Titanic museum, that is where you are going to go. If you are coming from the US to the island of Ireland, you might want to spend some time in Northern Ireland—why wouldn’t you, if you wanted to go to the Giant’s Causeway and are specifically driven by that? We should make that as attractive as possible.

Q72 Dr Stuart, I want to ask about the Great British summer savings scheme—although it should really have been called the “Great United Kingdom summer savings scheme”. You will remember that it introduced a temporary reduction of 5% of VAT on children’s meals, tickets and family attractions. The Committee is keen to hear, in broad terms, your members’ experience of the scheme, and in particular how many businesses participated, whether you are able to tell us what that is as a percentage of eligible businesses, and to what extent those VAT savings were passed on directly to customers through lower prices. Did the scheme lead to increased footfall, sales or visitor numbers?

I have done a lot of work to find information from our members on this. NITA had weekly calls with our members as soon as it was announced. Detail was quite sparse and difficult to get, to begin with, but it caused a lot of implementation problems. There was not a very big lead-in time, and businesses were therefore having to change prices. Also, for that summer period, there are a lot of incentives that go out, particularly from attractions, so you get a lot of pre-bookings. A lot of time was spent understanding the refunds and that type of thing. So there was a cost.

I also worked with ALVA. It looked at the UK and did a survey of UK members, which includes members from Northern Ireland. The implementation and additional business costs were highlighted by everybody who responded—I think it had 20 responses to its survey. Everybody passed through the full discount to the customers. However, the evidence showed that there was very little additional business to what would be expected over the summer period. It also seemed to catch the tourism agencies on the hop, so there was not very much promotion of it. A lot of customers were not aware of it. Obviously, the attractions had passed that on so were able to inform them when they arrived, but it was very hard to quantify real additional footfall to what would be expected at that time of year. The visitor was receiving the saving, but there was no significant increase seen coming through to the business as additional revenue or profit.

Q73 In terms of striking the balance between a beneficial financial outcome to the business as a result of an uptick in footfall, versus the costs of administering and understanding the scheme, making refunds, doing the paperwork and so on, was it financially neutral or was there a negative cost?
It is sort of anecdotal based on a survey, but for the majority of people I have spoken to, it was a cost.

Q74 I do not mean this question to be as anti-Treasury and churlish as possibly it sounds. There was very good intention from the Treasury, but the detail was very sketchy at the time of the announcement and there was not enough lead-in time. Is it too churlish to describe it as a bit of a damp squib and a gimmick on behalf of HMG?

The public were not really aware of it, so that was the challenge. We are certainly not saying that that is not something, but we think that if you are doing something like that, it has to be designed with business. This is part of the problem, and it was one of the problems that we faced with covid as well.

Businesses understand their business, and by working closer with business we can make the implementation easier and support it by having clear eligibility rules and sufficient lead-in time. We can then have co-ordinated promotion by the tourism agencies and the businesses, which we think would have a much bigger impact.
Q75 Although I do not want to be accused of leading the witness in any way, shape or form, I am going to suggest that your answer to this question will be yes.

I am not sure what answer I am going to get, but it links back to the Chair’s opening set of questions. Would my hunch be correct that in order to do what the Treasury wishes—to provide beneficial support to UK hospitality, but in the Northern Irish context here—an endemic, permanent, long-term approach to a differential on VAT for the hospitality sector, due to its permanence and ease of understanding and so on, would be a far greater benefit to NI hospitality than the scheme that we had this summer and indeed than any nascent successor schemes that Treasury Ministers may have in mind?

Any VAT reduction has to be sustained. There has been talk about a pilot, but you are talking about three to five years of that to really understand how things are feeding through—not just for the consumer, because that impact should be immediate, but to the businesses: are we seeing more investment and an increase in jobs and so on?

It is about engaging with business to ensure that we have ironed out any potential issues before starting, and about making sure the tourism agencies are also engaged so that everybody is lined up at the same time and we can get the best benefit from it.

From a VAT perspective, for any VAT rate change there will be system changes that need to be implemented, and a determination has to be made whether to pass some or all of the savings on to the consumer. When you have a rate change for a short period, you are making a change to your systems at the start and then you have to change your systems back at the end of that pilot period. Clearly, there is a cost to doing that. It is probably easier for the larger corporates to deal with that; they may have more sophisticated systems and a bigger IT department and can therefore implement the sort of changes required. If you are a smaller business, it may be more challenging.

On the Great British summer savings scheme, there was a degree of complexity in what it did and did not apply to. It was very much aimed at families—children’s food and what have you—but from a VAT point of view, you need to understand which parts are in and which parts are out. I am a VAT adviser, so if the tax is complex that is great for me, because clients need more support. But you want it to be something that they can easily understand so they can implement those changes: what supplies are subject to the reduced rate and what supplies are outside?

You also need a lead-in period for this, as much as anything. For any IT change, you typically do not just ring up or email the IT department and say, “Can you make this change?”, because they have other things to do as well, so it needs to feed into their overall list of priorities.

It is about trying to understand that where there is a change, there is a time and cost commitment for the business to implement that change, and then it will have another, similar cost and time commitment at the end when it has to change it. It is very clear that if a reduced rate of VAT were to be introduced, you would want a good lead-in period. There would need to be a decent amount of time while that rate applies to understand the implications and whether it makes the changes that you want it to make. Then, at the end of the three years, five years or whatever it may be, you cannot leave businesses on a cliff edge, going, “Is it going to change? Is it going to go back? Is it not?” They need to know, and it feeds into their margin and has an impact as they plan for the future.
Q76 So it has to be long-term? Changing it just for the summer has no impact or little impact.

I cannot talk to the economics, but I can certainly talk from a VAT perspective. If you were to make a change, you would want it to be over a longer period of time, because then you get a better idea of whether it is actually working.
It is very hard to measure the impact over such a short period of time.
I think so. I think that is true of many things. It may be hard to determine the overall impact of a two-month or two-and-a-half-month sample period.

Q77 Thank you for joining us today. I am Paul Kohler, the MP for Wimbledon. I also own a bar in Covent Garden in central London, so I know all about the pressures that hospitality is facing across the UK. I also recognise that there are particular pressures in Northern Ireland because of the land border and competition from the south. While you were talking, I looked up Wetherspoons in Belfast and Wetherspoons in Dublin to see the difference in prices. It looks to me as if a pint is about 30% cheaper in Dublin. Is that right? If you buy a pint of Guinness in the north or the south, is there that sort of price differential?

I cannot talk to that from personal experience, but we know that the hospitality industry has been really struggling with the increase in costs. We came out of the back of covid with very low reserves, and, when you look at industry surveys, people have less and less of those reserves to call on, so costs cannot be brought in by the business. That may be seen in higher prices, but that is not my area of expertise.

Q78 I am going to ask you about costs and VAT in particular in a moment. I am just wondering: if a consumer walks into a comparable pub in the north or south, are they paying a lot less for their pint in the south than in the north? I am just wondering about that point, rather than looking at costs. Do you know?
I do know that alcohol VAT is higher in the south—
Not the cost; I mean what the consumer is spending on a pint. I want to get a feel for that.
I really cannot answer that.

I can only talk as a consumer here, rather than on a professional basis. It depends on where you go. Dublin probably has a reputation for being quite expensive. Certainly, if you go to Temple Bar it is expensive.
Q79 What about for a comparable place, though? That is why I looked up Wetherspoons in Belfast and Dublin.
But I also think that Belfast can be quite expensive as well.
Well, exactly.

But that is because of the cost base and the pressures that are attached to it. I have friends who love coming over to Belfast, but in certain places it can be quite expensive. That is my anecdotal experience as a consumer, rather than as a tax adviser.

Q80 It would be interesting to know what the actual consumer is paying in both places, because on that competition argument, we need to compete with the south. Costs are one thing, but it would be really interesting to know what the consumer is paying in both those places. I would like to see that at some point. Is the call for a VAT rate the same as the south: 9% on hospitality?

In our written submission, we called for 9% across the board with regard to tourism and hospitality, but we caveated that by saying that more work is required around the evaluation and what would work. I know that there are calls for 10%. Just thinking about the mechanics of that, 10% is probably more straightforward than 9%. We have said that a better understanding of the base is needed, as well as an understanding of any costs associated with a VAT that is capped. We would not want to see any impact on the block grant, for example. There is a bit more work to be done, but we are happy with 10% or 9%. That would sort of be where we are looking.
Q81 It looks like a back-of-the-envelope calculation, but the Treasury is saying that it would cost £300 million to £400 million a year. Does that sound right to you, as a gross cost for the VAT?
Is that across the UK?

No, it is £5 billion across the UK. It has said, in a very rough approximation, that it would be £300 million to £400 million pounds just in Northern Ireland. Does that sound right to you, or are you not able to say?

I would want to come back to you on that, to be honest. I do not know; I need to look at those figures. I have not actually seen that, so I apologise, but I will come back to the Committee on that. There are aspects here—again, I do not know how it has calculated them. Obviously, if we can make businesses more successful, there are more corporation tax receipts.

Q82 I want to ask you about that, because that was just, “How do we cost this, full stop.” Having gone back to 9% in the south in July, you have quoted that it will cost € 633 million over the year. Again, that is just the headline cost of the VAT reduction. Has anyone done any studies on the overall cost-benefit analysis in the south? That would help us in our calculations about the north. Does that exist?
I don’t know, from an economic perspective. I know that some work was done, but I don’t know whether it was that detailed.

I am not sure. There have certainly been a couple of reports on the impact of the changes in VAT rate and looking at pass-through, but also on whether it drives more investment and whether it increases tax receipts overall. I do not know whether there has been anything specific to look at the overall thing, but that is certainly something that we can check further.
That is absolutely crucial, isn’t it?

The other thing we are saying is that we need to see an increase in employment as well. There are taxes in regard to that. That is what I am saying: more evaluation is required. That is what we talk about. It is not just about the consumer; it is about business viability, but it is also about future investment. We need our businesses to be investing to develop that and make it more attractive to come to Northern Ireland so that you get longer stays and more money. When visitors come and stay, according to Tourism Ireland figures across the island, 37% of spend is in food and drink; over 25% is in accommodation, and you have retail and transport. If you can extend the stay and extend that value, that will create the add-on.
Q83 I hear all the arguments. You have a wonderful test bed in the south: that has happened, and it would be interesting to see all that analysed to see what it shows.

I have one last question and then I will shut up, because the Chair will tell me off. I see that, as I understand it, off sales in the south have a 23% VAT rate. Did that come in in tandem with the reduction in hospitality, or has it always been 23%?
It has always been 23%, but I would need to check that.
Ireland obviously has the 23%, which is the standard rate of VAT.
Oh, it’s a standard rate?

Yes, it is a standard rate of VAT at 23%. It is higher than the UK’s rate of 20%, but it has reduced rates of 13.5% and 9%, which apply to different parts of the two sectors that we are talking about. I suppose that is the other thing: there are two rates, which can bring complexity, both in terms of which sits where and in terms of the cost.
Q84 I was just wondering whether a solution for the whole of the UK would be upping the VAT on off-sale alcohol to pay for lowering it for hospitality. Has that ever been considered by anybody?
I don’t know. It is not something I have been privy to.

Q85 Good afternoon. It is a pleasure to see you both today. I want to continue the discussion about VAT. I completely understand why the sector has identified VAT as the campaign. In a world of greater devolution, with different parts of the United Kingdom having different regimes and powers, this is a nice simple tax because it is all controlled by the Treasury. What I cannot understand is why it would be a better use of money than other interventions and options that might be more complex but are still on the table.

There are three aspects to the VAT that a consumer sees. There is the reduction in VAT, and maybe that encourages them to go out more. There is also the ability to have a blend, where you give a discount to the customer because of the VAT cut but you bring some of that discount into the business to enable us to develop and grow. It is about the perception of being really good value for money, which then helps us to attract visitors.

There are other things we need to look at. VAT is not the sole answer, but it goes a long way. We need to look at how we can mitigate the impact of the ETA; I have spoken to the Committee about it before and have done a lot of work on that. We are now starting to see more businesses and tour operators identifying ETA as one of the barriers to coming to Northern Ireland. The APD is another area. We need to look at all these aspects and who controls them.

Obviously business rates are a devolved matter, and the Northern Ireland Executive are in a very difficult position at the moment with regard to budget. I suppose the VAT is a headline; it is very easy to understand the concept of it, and it is something that everybody has got behind.

Q86 We are seeing reform on business rates in other parts of the UK, and the recognition that the value of some properties and establishments has increased considerably, which is having knock-on impacts on business rates. Could that be a priority for the Executive to support tourism and hospitality?

Yes, it is a very important aspect when you look at the operating costs of a business. We had the rates revaluation last year, which we then sort of overturned. Primarily, a lot of that was from the hospitality industry. That is now being reviewed to see whether we can have a rates system that is fairer across all sectors and reflects the challenges faced by tourism and hospitality businesses when it comes to business rates. That campaign has been going for a number of years. We did get support through covid, which was very welcome, and the campaign will continue. But that is another element, and it would not take away from saying that we think a VAT cut would bring more benefit to the whole of the tourism ecosystem and the consumers.
Aidan, what is your view?

You are probably looking at a holistic approach again if you want to support the sector. VAT is clearly one element, and quite an obvious element, because as a consumer you are the one who pays the tax. It is a concept that is quite easy to get your head around when you say, “Well, if you reduce VAT, there should be a reduction in prices.” But it does give businesses a bit of flexibility. They can choose to pass the saving on, or they can choose to retain that for investment and what have you, so it does give them a bit of flexibility.

In terms of wider support to the sector, business rates is absolutely one thing, and in terms of supporting skills or supporting people entering the sector. There are a number of things that can be done to support it, but clearly VAT is something that has a lot of traction; I can understand that.

Q87 What has come out of the last couple of questions is that it is very hard to draw any parallels to see whether there would be a benefit in reducing VAT in Northern Ireland compared with the Republic, because the data is not there. Is the data there to show that it would be beneficial to cut it in Northern Ireland? That is basically a question for you, Aidan.

The difference in the VAT rates is noticeable: 20% to 13.5% and 9% is a chunky number, whichever way you look at it. If there were a reduction in that VAT rate, it certainly would give a business in the sectors affected the ability to pass that on to the consumers.
Q88 In Ireland, when they reduced it to 9%, they specifically said that it was not to be necessarily passed on.

Yes, in terms of restaurants and so on. Because they have had a lower rate of VAT for longer and more consistently, not just because of covid—the rates are longer-standing—I think they have identified that as a way of supporting the sector and making it more attractive to tourists. They have obviously made a strategic decision that if we can reduce VAT rates, that does have an advantageous impact on the sector.

From a Government perspective, they had that cut before, then it went back up again to 13.5%, and then they brought it back down again to 9%, so they have obviously seen that there was a positive impact in those businesses having the 9% VAT rate, because they have now put that back in place. I think there is more there to see on how that is helping.
Q89 Before I start my questions, I wanted to take this opportunity to echo the words of the Prime Minister at the start of PMQs today.

I am deeply saddened at the death of my friend Pat Karney. Pat was one of those larger-than-life characters who made Manchester the city it is today, a proud Irishman and a proud Mancunian who dedicated almost half a century to serving the people of the great city of Manchester. I knew Pat for many years, and his warmth and wit always struck me, as did his absolute passion for the city. From helping to rebuild Manchester after the 1996 IRA bombing to championing our Christmas markets and introducing our annual Manchester Day, Pat’s fingerprints were all over our modern city. Manchester has lost a giant, and many of us have lost a good friend. My thoughts and prayers are with his family today. Thank you, Chair; it is very appropriate that I could say that at the Northern Ireland Affairs Committee.

Joanne and Aidan, thank you very much for being here. We know that Paul Kohler has a massive cash pile there in Covent Garden, which clearly pulls in more than £90,000 a year and more than meets the VAT threshold. Could I get a hint from you, even if it is a back-of-an-envelope analysis, as to what proportion of hospitality and tourism businesses would benefit from a VAT cut in Northern Ireland?

According to NISRA, there are just under 6,000 VAT-registered businesses in tourism and hospitality in Northern Ireland, so obviously they would benefit from a VAT cut. I think there are probably between 7,500 and 8,000 businesses in this sector in Northern Ireland, but 6,000 would be VAT-registered.
Q90 Can you give the Committee a sense of how the Irish VAT registration threshold compares?

The UK VAT registration threshold is £90,000 per annum. I cannot remember what the Irish one is, but it is lower. The UK traditionally had the highest threshold in the EU 27, before Brexit. Some EU member states have a threshold of zero, so if you make a sale you are in their VAT net. But with VAT, there are two things. If you are VAT-registered, you charge VAT on your sales, but it also gives you the ability to recover VAT on your costs, so clearly that gets factored into your cost of sales in terms of your profit margin.
Q91 It might be useful, for the Committee to be able to compare pears and oranges, to know what the threshold in the Republic is.
