The UK Government have said that restricting any VAT cut to Northern Ireland would introduce divergence. I cannot imagine why Treasury orthodoxy would say that—well, I can—“potentially weakening Northern Ireland’s place in the UK internal market.” What do you make of that argument? Do you want to put on the record your response to the UK Treasury?

There is diversification in other aspects. For example, you can look at APD. If we want to go to the UK mainland, flying is really our only option, and we have to pay APD on both—leaving Belfast or Derry, and landing in GB. So there are other areas where the UK has in some ways disadvantaged Northern Ireland. What we are saying is that with this sort of cut it makes sense to have a pilot, and we are suggesting that Northern Ireland would be a good location for that, because we are a shared-island destination. We are sitting with the land border; somebody can decide whether they want to come to Northern Ireland. And they can change their mind: they might decide, “No, I’m not going to go up.” I don’t think you get the same within any of the regions in GB, especially when you are looking at external visitors. You can see an immediate impact.

Tour operators that put itineraries together for the whole of the island make decisions. I know you have the results of the survey by the Inbound Tourism Operators Association of Ireland. VAT and the cost of a trip are one of the things that make their decision on whether they are going to come to Northern Ireland. Add ETA on top of that, and we have examples of tour operators deciding to drop Northern Ireland out of the itinerary.

A pilot ensures that you can see, in a shorter time, whether the VAT cut is having an impact, and then in the longer term it is about how our businesses are investing and employing people and what the impact is on the price to the customer. One of the things that we have to remember is that you do not want to get to a point where you are racing to the bottom. This is about how we ensure that businesses have the capability and the reserves to increase the value of any experience that people are having. What more can we add to that experience, so that people are prepared to pay for the experience? You need to invest, and businesses need to invest, as well as tourism agencies and so on, and Government. It is also sort of closed, in that you have a really good example of two different jurisdictions that you can measure.

Q92 As somebody who represents an airport seat in Manchester, I am acutely aware of airport passenger duty. It was probably introduced in the ’90s to stem the overheating of Heathrow and other London airports. I would argue for APD holidays for new routes, which I think would hugely benefit a city like Derry/Londonderry, that could prove commercially that those routes could happen. I am sure the Treasury would also argue that we do not pay VAT on the tickets or the fuel, but a lack of a level playing field is a massive disincentive on the island of Ireland, when the Republic does not charge as much—or any APD at all. I do appreciate that.
The Dublin to Derry/Londonderry flight is going to have APD on it as well. Again, that will be both ways.
But it is good news that you are getting that flight.
Absolutely: it is good news, but we are adding potentially another £18 or £30 to the cost of a return trip.
Q93 I have strayed from VAT. Do you think that there would be any administrative burdens on your businesses from having a differential VAT tax burden in Northern Ireland?

VAT is a UK tax, so there are no regional variations on it. When the British summer savings scheme came in, it was laid by statutory instrument and applied to the whole of the UK. I do not think that there has been an instance in which there has been a different VAT rate based on a region: that has not been done by the UK before. I do not see that they would devolve VAT decisions to Stormont, because it is a UK tax.

If you are a business operating in Northern Ireland, England, Scotland and Wales, you would then have two different rates, so there would be a complexity there. Certainly, the larger businesses and more sophisticated systems would be able to make certain changes to do that, but if you were operating on a UK-wide basis, you would have a different rate of VAT applying in Northern Ireland as opposed to England, Scotland and Wales.

Q94 Good afternoon to you both. You had the benefit of getting evidence from a former Aviation Minister there on the air passenger duty. Joanne, you know that this is an inquiry into hospitality and tourism, and you represent the Tourism Alliance, so tourism is your mainstay. What proportion of the money that would be saved in a VAT reduction would apply to tourists, and what proportion would be for general hospitality?

It is very hard to answer that, Gavin, because when you look at the different attractions, for example, and different organisations, they have a hospitality element to them—they would have restaurants, cafés and different things in them. Then you look at hotels, where it is accommodation, restaurants and so on, so hospitality is part of those businesses. I think that the reason from a tourism perspective is that tourism is about ensuring that we get the best value from our tourists—how do we attract more overseas tourists to Northern Ireland? When you look at hospitality from restaurants and pubs, they are primarily a domestic market, and it is tourism that brings the external visitors and more money in and increases the size of the pie.
Aidan, do you know the answer to that question?
No.

Q95 I think it is an important question, because this would apply to every café, restaurant and bar, no matter where they are or who is going in. What the VAT rate is makes no material difference to where I as a Belfast-based person go for my tea—I am not driving across the border to save pennies in the pound on VAT—but in a cross-border area such as this city of Londonderry, it could make a material difference if you are organising a wedding and spending £20,000, £30,000 or even £40,000, so there are degrees to it all.
There are also business events, Gavin, where you are talking about 500 or 1,000 delegates, and catering is part of that, so that can make a significant difference.
Q96 Of course, but there are degrees to all of this. It would be good to get a sense of the balance and to know where it sits between general hospitality, domestic spend and tourism.

Joanne, we have been asking this question of many, and you have given a taste of it in your written evidence. If there were a reduction in hospitality and tourism VAT, how should it be used by the businesses that save money?
That will differ per business.
Let ’ s think first about how it should be used, and then about how it will be used.

Having talked to members, I think we would see a blended approach. Some of the VAT cut would go to the customer, so they would be able to see exactly the price that they are paying and the VAT, and some would remain in the business to handle the costs. The problem is that each business will be different depending on what situation they are in. We would look to have a blended approach where, depending on the business, you would see a reduction in costs to the customer, not an increase. However, we also need to make sure that our businesses are viable and have the reserves to spend to increase employment and investment. In the detailed brief, which we will send through, I have given some examples of how that may look with full pass-through, a lower level of pass-through and no pass-through.

Q97 In your evidence, you said that 75% of respondents to a survey you did in 2026 stated that they would pass the VAT reduction through in reductions in price, but one third—that takes us over 100% already—would increase staffing, 25% would improve wages for staff and 83% would increase investment in the business. When you add all that together, we are well over 200%. When you say a blended approach, it really is people saying both. You might get a bit of a price reduction, a bit of investment, a bit of staffing and so on.
I think people had the choice to say which ones they would do, rather than split it out by percentage.

Q98 There will be those who say that it is hard to stimulate increased business if the customer is not incentivised by reduced cost, yet we have had evidence from others during this inquiry that the bottom line is that it is not about reduced cost, but about increased margins, or at least making margins more sustainable—that is probably a fairer way to put it. People feel that they are not making a profit and that a reduction would at least allow them to make a profit. When you did your survey, did that come through as a damaging aspect to the argument to pursue a VAT reduction? The south had a reduction in 2011, and 88% of it was passed through. They had a reduction in 2019, and 50% of it was passed through. They had a reduction in 2020 and in 2023, and they stopped passing it through to consumers. If a credible argument is to be mounted, how should it be mounted to show that it would benefit not just the industry, but the economy?

That is what our case is around. We want to see businesses being able to invest. I understand the argument about a sustained margin, but it is what they do with that margin. It is not about creating profits that are not going anywhere. We want to see that margin being invested in the businesses, in creating jobs and in creating much better value. We want to create experiences that people want because they are prepared to pay for them, but we are not at that point yet. Northern Ireland tourism has a way to go before it is as mature at the Republic of Ireland. How do we prove our value so that people go, “Actually, I am prepared to pay for that because that is such a good experience”?

I cannot say that everybody will pass it on. It will very much depend on the businesses. Most of the businesses that we are talking to are those in which hospitality is an element but not necessarily the only thing they provide. Restaurants and pubs could be in a slightly different situation and could require the cut to be retained in the business. You will have heard about that from others.

That could support business resilience. I suppose it is about trying to understand the clear objectives of a VAT reduction—if that is what happens—because it will depend on the business and its specific circumstances.

We referenced what was passed through in Ireland in 2011 and 2019. Circumstances were maybe different—they were coming out of a very challenging economic environment in 2011—but it gives a business a bit of flexibility to say, “I can retain some of that margin for myself so I can invest in the business, or get the business through this sticky stage.” If they get through that, the business can start to make other decisions beyond that, and it helps support the business going forward. Clearly, we want to have a thriving sector in the long term, and this is one element that can potentially help that.

Q99 Aidan, tax is your bailiwick, so let me ask you this. The Tax Policy Associates said that a reduction in VAT for tourism and hospitality would cost more than all the reliefs that are currently applied put together, although that would probably apply to a greater degree in GB than in Northern Ireland. Do you agree with that?
I have seen that. Clearly they have done their research, but I cannot say one way or the other because I do not have the detail that they have used to arrive at that.

Q100 Have you given any consideration to whether blanket application to all businesses is the best approach? Should it be more targeted, whether towards tourism, hospitality or certain parts of the hospitality industry? Whenever I think about tourism, I think about how every global, multimillion-pound corporation would benefit from this—every Caffè Nero, Starbucks, KFC and McDonald ’ s . So would Michael Deane ’ s , but of all those, there is probably only one that you would travel to Belfast for .

We have not done anything specific at this point, but you are absolutely right : it applies to everybody. When we are look ing at a pilot scheme for a potential VAT reduction , it is about looking at which areas we are going to apply it to and what that looks like.

It is really important to have clarity : “T hese are the services , or the goods , that we are going to apply it to , and this is why. ” If you have a reduction for restaurants, among others, then yes, Michael Deane will benefit from that, but so will the chains of restaurants, because they are present in Northern Ireland and provide services within the scope of VAT. I do not think that you could carve out chains, for one thing because of fiscal neutrality, never mind the level of complexity and the noise that would be associated with that.
Thank you both very much indeed.

Q101 I am going to press you on a point I was exploring with you earlier. When you say, “Look, we need to cut VAT to compete with the south, where they have a lower VAT rate,” the crucial issue is what people are paying in the north and the south. I have just looked it up. Now, this is Copilot—it is AI, so I give that health warning—but it tells me that in Belfast it is £6 for a pint of Guinness and in Dublin it is €7 , so it is comparable. Outside Belfast and Dublin, it is between £5.50 and £6.50 in the north, and €1 more in the south, so again it is comparable. It also says that comparable hotels tend to be more expensive in the south than the north. While there are many reasons to cut VAT across the UK, does that not undermine the argument that a VAT reduction is needed to put you on a level playing field with the south?

We have taken the perspective that it is about the cost of the whole trip. When tour operators are looking at it, they are looking at the cost of the whole trip, not just one element of it. We would have a higher VAT rate. Pricing also depends on where you are going. Obviously, Belfast is really important for our tourism, but it is also a gateway to the rest of Northern Ireland. We want to see a sharing out of that tourism, and regional growth as well as growth in the capital.

VAT applies to a number of aspects, so a VAT cut can really help to reduce the price of the whole visitor trip. That is what we are looking at. I do not think visitors are checking the price of a pint in Belfast compared with Dublin before they come and then deciding that they are going to stay in Dublin. They are looking at the whole piece. It is when you add them up that you start to see that difference.

Q102 I see all that, but surely to mount your case you have to show that the costs of hospitality are more expensive in the north than in the south. Otherwise, the argument that we need to get our VAT rates down to the same level does not work. If, for whatever reason, the cost of hotels is higher in the south than in the north, and the cost of alcohol is comparable, the argument is not there, is it?
We have looked at the different costs in the south compared with Northern Ireland, and when you take into account the fact that we have higher operating costs in Northern Ireland—

I do not doubt that, but I am asking about the person paying over the counter. If they are paying more in the south than the north, the argument that you need to reduce VAT to compete with the south doesn’t work, does it?

It does, because we are not in a position to reduce or maintain prices because of the operating costs of the business. That is where this has been looked at. We are saying that hospitality is one element of that, but you need to look at the whole trip and what we are able to change. When you look at the whole trip, that is where you start to see differences in cost. Yes, if you compare one hotel in Dublin with one hotel in Belfast, you may see that the Belfast one is less expensive, but when you put the whole trip together, the cost is higher.
I don’t think I can add to that, because that is a fair comment. You are looking at the whole. Yes, there is a price that the consumer pays, but there is also a cost base.

Q103 Mr Robinson asked a number of my questions on passing through the impact to consumers, which hopefully demonstrates the consistency of interest among members of the Committee. I shall let him off because he lent me a tie today—just for clarity, if anyone wondered where I had bought a tie like this, I must attribute it to its owner.
In all seriousness, Aidan, will you give us a flavour of how VAT cuts have been used in other sectors of the economy and what impact they have had?

Studies have been done on where VAT reductions have been made, and it does vary. Gavin referred to the cuts in Ireland, where more of it was passed on initially. I think there was a VAT rate reduction in Finland, and there was a pass-through, but it was quite low. It does vary, and it will typically depend on the amount of the reduction in VAT. If it is a low amount, it might be easier to make the decision to pass all of it on or none of it on, because the reduction does not make much difference. You will see that there is pass-through, but there is not a consistent approach across sectors, countries and the like.

Q104 So in some other sectors—my question was about how they have been used in other sectors—it has supported businesses as opposed to consumers, who have their role to play in spending their money, growth and the rest of it. So it is a mixture.
Yes.
Q105 Would there be any other factors in that?

If you look at the reduction of the VAT rate on domestic utility bills to zero, that is clearly designed to support consumers: rather than paying VAT at the reduced rate of 5%, we are paying it at 0%. If you are to have a VAT rate reduction, the policy objectives need to be clear. In that case, the 0% in GB is clearly designed to try to alleviate some of the pressures on households. Again, I do not think there is a one-size-fits-all solution; you will never get that. It depends on the rate reduction, and it depends on how it applies—is it industry specific? Does it impact everybody? Those things all play a role in how the rate is dealt with. But it is fair to say that generally, if there is a rate reduction, there can be pass-through, but there can also be retention to support further investment in the business or to provide business resilience.
Q106 Interesting—thank you. Can you give us a flavour of the lessons to learn and the trends to observe from the VAT cut in the UK from 2020 to 2022? What can we pick up from that?

Clearly, that was designed during the covid pandemic, and there was some complexity to that. It was 5% for a period, then it went up to 12.5% for six months, I think, and then it ended in March 2022. There were some exceptions to the reduction in the VAT rate, for example alcoholic drinks—presumably there were public health reasons behind that. The other thing that you need to factor in is whether, if a combination of goods and services is bought, different VAT rates apply, and how you deal with that. That brings complexity from a VAT perspective as well.

A lesson you can draw, both from that specifically and more generally, is that, because it is a complex tax, you need to be clear about what is within the scope of the reduction, you need support from HMRC through clear guidance, and you need good timelines. I appreciate that in the pandemic people had to react quickly to an unprecedented position, but here you should clearly communicate any pilot scheme so that everybody knows, as much as possible, what is in and what is out, because it is a complex tax. It is about trying to bring simplicity to what could be complex.

Q107 That is very interesting. I have heard you very clearly on certainty, clarity and simplicity. With those three factors in mind, as well as your answers to my previous questions about how cuts have been used in other industries, and the balance between consumers and businesses in terms of whether they go further—this is not meant to be a silly question; I am interested in getting a snapshot response from you—would a VAT cut now be helpful, would it work, and if one were issued for this sector, would it do some of the things we have discussed around alleviating pressures and supporting growth?
I think my Northern Irish client base would say yes.
Notwithstanding the various elements that go with—
Yes—that is a simple answer to a complex question. It is complex, but are there benefits to business? Absolutely.

Going back to the previous VAT cut, we have to remember that people were not travelling then, so from a tourism perspective, even when we had the VAT cut, business was on its knees and we did not have the demand. The evaluation on that would probably show that it did not really have a big impact, because people were not travelling, so even though businesses may have been able to keep VAT within the business, they did not have the level of business needed for it to show a big impact.

Yes, that is a fair point. People were not going out because they could not go out. There was a very particular reason behind that. It was designed to try to alleviate pressures on a sector that was facing an unprecedented situation.
Q108 And therefore any assessment of that VAT reduction during covid is not really comparable to today.
That’s right.

Q109 Joanne, what impact, if any, has the VAT differential had on competitiveness between Northern Ireland and the Republic? What impact has it had on tour operators from Northern Ireland and from the Republic? We have the ITOA report here.

Yes, and that really helped to show that VAT is one element that is looked at, but it is the whole cost that tour operators are looking at. Again, the VAT cut would help to alleviate some of the other costs of a trip. We know that there is a £20 cost per person for ETA, and there is potentially APD. Having a VAT cut would help, when looking at the total cost, to mitigate those additional costs that people only have if they come to Northern Ireland.
Q110 Do you have evidence of coach companies from Northern Ireland missing out and losing business?

Yes. With the work that we did previously on ETA, we had specific examples where business had been lost due to ETA. Since we did that work, you have seen costs increasing anyway, so it is one of the factors. Tourism NI does its industry survey every six months; the last one covered the first six months of this year. When we did that last year, just 12% of people said ETA was having an impact on overseas visitors; that has jumped to 24% now. 2025 was the first full year—well, nearly a full year—since the ETA was implemented. It was implemented fully in April. We are starting to see businesses being able to say that there is a specific impact on them as that is rolled out.
Q111 Is there evidence that group tour operators are changing their itineraries to avoid requiring their customers to obtain an ETA?

Yes, and ITOA has said that. We have examples, especially where a tour operator had maybe only one or two days in Northern Ireland. The thing with tour operators is that they are offering services that include that administration. There were a number of problems. You usually have older people on the tours, and they need more support, but also, with the price increasing to £20 per person, that suddenly added a lot on to the cost of the trip, and we still had our normal costs. That is what I am saying: it is the whole trip that we are looking at. What are the costs that you do not have if you stay in the Republic? ETA is one of those, as is APD.
Q112 Should the Home Office introduce an exemption to the ETA scheme for group tour operators visiting Northern Ireland?

As you know, that is one of the things that we have discussed. Where we are at the moment is that I think the Home Office wants to see the economic impact. Obviously, it is very difficult to say, “This is the lost business,” because the people have not come. It is lost opportunity. Rather than someone saying to me, “I’m not coming because of the cost of the ETA,” they just decide not to come to Northern Ireland because of the administration, the cost and so on. All the information becomes quite anecdotal, which is very difficult. All I can say to you is that, much more than they were before, businesses are now saying that it is an issue. We are able to show where tour operators have changed itineraries and decided not to come to Northern Ireland.

We still do not know—again, it would be good to have information from the Home Office on how ETA is working—whether people are deciding not to bother with ETA. It is a very difficult one. As you know, we would like to see exemptions, because we do not think that it is stopping the type of people the Home Office wants to stop. These are tourism visitors, and they are probably the one set of people who will do what they have to do, but then they may make the decision not to bother.

Q113 Are people actually getting out of Dublin and the south-west? Are the tour groups that historically would have come to Belfast and here even avoiding Donegal, Galway and Sligo—the parts of the Republic that are literally within spitting distance of here?

That is part of the challenge. The sort of people we are talking about—visitors—want to make sure they are doing the right thing. You are obviously in Derry/Londonderry. You don’t know that you have really passed the border. This location would benefit from visitors from Donegal, across the border. The ETA does stop that, because if a family wants to come and spend a day or a night here, and they are staying in Donegal, suddenly you are talking about an extra £40 or £50 for an ETA, plus the administration in getting it, and that adds on to all your other costs. Once you have got it, you can use it multiple times, but when you are looking at overseas visitors, probably the highest return rate is from those from GB, where it doesn’t count.

Q114 O n ETA—we have talked about this for many a year , assisted in early engagement with the Home Office, talked about an exemption and so on—I think the exchange between you and the Chair has been quite illuminating, Joanne. The Home Office will ask for the economic impact, but is the truth not that, at least in the first year of operation, you cannot demonstrate anything because of sectoral growth? The one big tourist attraction that you and I both know in my constituency, which was most perplexed about the introduction of an ETA, had 100,000 additional visitors last year, in the first full operative year of ETA. While there might be anecdotal evidence, it will be hard to demonstrate economic loss when there has been sectoral growth.

If you look at our 2025 figures, the biggest overseas growth area is GB. We have seen a really significant increase, as has that attraction, but when we look at North America and Europe, we have not seen the growth, and we are not getting the spend from those markets. I agree with you that the sector has grown, but it is not necessarily in the market that we want to grow, which is the international market. GB is great; about 70% of the overseas business is from GB, which is brilliant. We have a challenge in sustaining that, but we also need to increase the other international markets, and that is not happening. That is where ETA could form part of the reason.

Q115 I do not disagree with the point that there are challenges, but it is hard to demonstrate that it was as cataclysmic as was feared, when there are 100,000 additional visitors to one attraction alone in the first full year of operation.

Again, we want to see the additional visitors, but we need more diversity. GB visitors do not spend as much as a North American does when they come to stay. That is what I am saying. We have seen an increase in overnight trips, but not in the duration, in the spend or in the markets, such as North America and Europe, that spend more. I get your point; it is just about having to go down into more detail of where that growth is coming from.
Q116 It would have to be more granular, wouldn’t it? I have one final question. Sorry to use the pun, but for tourism and hospitality in Northern Ireland, is VAT the problem—yes or no?
It’s not “the” problem, but it is one of the problems.
It is a contributory factor.
Thank you very much.

sessions.iT: Resilience of the UK's food supply to disruptions
sessions.w: Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs; Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs; Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs

segs.tx: Public Accounts Committee
Oral evidence: Resilience of the UK’s f ood s upply to disruptions , HC 671
Thursday 15 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 15 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown (Chair); Mr Clive Betts; Anna Dixon; Rachel Gilmour; Sarah Hall; Rupert Lowe ; Blake Stephenson .

Gareth Davies, Comptroller and Auditor General, National Audit Office, Rich Sullivan-Jones, Director, National Audit Office, and George Osborne, Alternate Treasury Officer of Accounts, HM Treasury, were in attendance.
Questions 61-1 18
Witnesses

I : Paul Kissack, Permanent Secretary, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs; Emily Miles, Director General for Food, Farming and Biosecurity, DEFRA; and Helen Dallas, Interim Deputy Director, Food Preparedness and Response, DEFRA .
Report by the Comptroller and Auditor General
Resilience of the food supply chain to disruptions ( HC 587 )
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Paul Kissack, Emily Miles and Helen Dallas .

Q61 Welcome to the Public Accounts Committee on Thursday 15 October 2026. Today is the second instalment of our farming week, in which we are examining the resilience of UK food supply to disruptions.

On Monday, we heard from expert witnesses on topics such as the preparedness of the farming sector for major disruptions, as well as the Government’s engagement with food retailers, manufacturers and farmers about food supply and resilience. Today, we will explore how DEFRA and the Government are organised to improve food supply chain resilience, assess DEFRA’s preparedness for a severe supply chain disruption, and look to understand how the Department engages with industry and learns from other sectors and countries. We will also take a local angle on this issue by questioning DEFRA on the level of local and societal preparedness for food supply disruptions.
May I thank all our witnesses very much for coming? As is our usual practice, it would be helpful if you introduced yourself and said how long you have been in post.
Thank you, Chair. My name is Paul Kissack . I am the permanent secretary at DEFRA and I have been in post for almost exactly one year.
I am Emily Miles, director general for food, farming and biosecurity. I have been in post for two years, and before that I ran the Food Standards Agency.
I am Helen Dallas, the deputy director for food preparedness and response. I have been in that role since April but have been working in this area for coming on for five years now.
Q62 Thank you all very much. Before I ask the first question, I should declare my interests as a practising farmer and chartered surveyor.

Paul, f arming and food resilience are two sides of the same coin. In 202 3 , we had a major disruption to the food chain, so you had plenty of warning about what actions DEFRA needed to take to ensure the resilience of our food supply chain. This summer—this year, really—saw major problems for farmers, with a spike in input prices. We have now seen the whole debacle of the SFI, as Harry Metcalfe told us about on Monday, with five hours to get applications in. As if it was not enough for the price of fertiliser to increase by 30% to 40%, there is now a new fertiliser tax , imposed by the Government on 1 January. It does seem to me as though , in both instances , DEFRA is behind the curve. What can you do to make sure that DEFRA is more prepared for these quite seismic world events, which affect the resilience of our food and farming?

I would not recognise your characterisation of DEFRA as being behind the curve, but I absolutely recognise your characterisation of the challenges facing farming at the moment, and particularly over the last couple of years. For your assurance, nobody in DEFRA at official or ministerial level is under any illusions about how difficult it has been over the last year or two in particular for many farmers. As your witness on Monday pointed out, it varies by sector and by area of the country , but overall it is definitely the case that farmers have had a particularly difficult time over the last couple of years.

On how that plays into questions about the overall food system, perhaps I could start by offering a reflection on the R eport itself, which is not about farming but about the broader food system. W e absolutely recognise what the Report sets out, and I think we share its analysis almost entirely. It is very helpful and very well timed from our perspective, as we ramp up a programme of work. It sets out a food system that is extremely resilient, and probably one of the most resilient food systems in the world, in its ability to respond to some of the acute challenges it has faced over recent years, be that as a result of geopolitical events, the pandemic or the changes that came with the exit from the European Union. W e have discovered that we have a very resilient food system led by the private sector. There is a role for Government, but the resilience comes from a sophisticated private sector food chain.

When it comes to farming —we absolutely recognise that domestic production underpins that food system—the Government have set out, I think unusually for Government, a clear commitment to at least maintain , and ideally grow , domestic production over the coming years . That was set out in the land use framework earlier this year and also in the farming road map, which I think is the first time a Government have set out a long-term vision for farming in quite some time. That is underpinned by sector growth plans—we are currently developing two sector growth plans around poultry and horticulture, and we published the organic farm plan yesterday. There is a lot of work going on to try to build the growth potential of the food system as a whole, both from domestic farming and from other parts of the food system, including manufacturing.

On Government funding in this area, it is worth recognising that we are now coming to the end of what has been at the very least a seven-year transition away from basic payments. Some might argue that that transition has actually been going on for decades as we have moved away from unlinked payments. Government funding to farmers is now focused broadly in two areas. One is the sustainable farming incentive and ELMs more broadly, to support farmers to move to more resilient farming. That works alongside food production, so that is good for food production and good for long-term resilience in terms of addressing some of the climate issues that you just referenced. The second type of funding is more in the innovation and technology space, to try to move to higher-productivity farming. That is how the Government now spend their money—or taxpayers’ money—on farming, rather than on the unlinked payments we had previously. That is a huge change for the sector.

As I say, we are coming to the end of that enormous change that has taken place over the last seven years. We are now seeing record levels of demand from farmers for SFI schemes—maybe we will come on to the SFI particulars you mentioned. This year, for example, we have committed close to £800 million of new funding for farmers to support them to move to more resilient systems over the coming years. That is in addition to pre-existing commitments that will be out there through ELMs and so on.
Q63 I am going to ask two quick questions before I pass over to Rachel Gilmour, who has questions on both the farming and food-resilience elements.

To stick with the farming element for a minute, I am glad that you cited the land use strategy. Savills estimates an average loss of farmland of 26,000 hectares every year since 2000. That would be more than 500,000 hectares over two decades—nearly 10%, as the land use strategy envisages. If we carry on taking that amount of land out, if we get global shocks in terms of world events, and if we get climate change, how are the Government going to maintain farming outputs as they are at the moment?

I heard you use those figures earlier in the week, and we did what good people do when they hear something and think, “Is that true?” We went back and looked at some of the data, and I think that is a UK figure rather than an England figure. As the DEFRA perm sec, I am better placed to talk about the England figure.

The amount of farmland in England is just shy of 9 million hectares. That is about 68% of the total land in England. That is by far a larger proportion of our landmass than in any comparable country. If you look at most European countries or at the States, it is much closer to about 50%. We are very unusual in having quite so much of our land under agriculture. I do not say that as a good or bad thing, just as a statement of fact. In terms of where we might have been 10 or 15 years ago, we now have 1% more land in England under agriculture than we did 15 years ago.
Q64 I would like to examine that in greater detail; we will do some work on that.

On food resilience, there has been quite a lot of criticism, as you will have see n from the NAO Report, that DEFRA has worked up some plans but has not worked them up well enough in concert with the private sector by testing them out and discussing them with the private sector. It is all very well working up plans, but if you do not have the buy-in of the people who have to operate them, they cannot be as effective as they should. What do you plan to do to change that?

That is a very fair analysis, so I completely agree with it. To clarify, the reference in the NAO Report is to our playbooks and the fact that we have not shared them. I would not share those playbooks because I do not think they will add any value for the people we would share them with. It is basically a playbook of how we stand up particular operations within the Department: how we set up teams, how we communicate with Ministers and with the press office, and so on. They are very much internal manuals for DEFRA to make sure that we are equipped to set things up fast. We similarly have a playbook on a national power outage—which we all hold in hard copy, as you can imagine—for what happens in a national power outage. They are internal manuals for how we respond quickly in the event of certain crises.

That said, the NAO is absolutely correct to identify a gap in not having a shared plan with different stakeholders for different events. We are working towards exactly that. We had a first meeting of a new food readiness group—I think it was last week or the week before—through which we are bringing together people from right across the food chain, including logistics, the cold chain, retailers, and a lot of the local responders, be they LRFs or the voluntary sector, to try to form a clearer national framework that will run through various different scenarios that we all need to collectively respond to, and to have clearer agreements on the triggers and intervention points, and the roles and responsibilities. That will be a shared plan, both in its development and in who can access it.

Q65 A final point from me—I also raised this on Monday—is about what the NFU calls, in its submission, multiple and compound threats to our food resilience. You have a major climate change problem, as we had this year, and you then get a massive disease outbreak somewhere else. In your discussions with the private sector parts of the food chain, did you discuss the whole issue of compound and several different disruptions occurring at the same time?
I have a couple of points on that. The short answer is yes—that is exactly the sort of thing we want to talk about with that group, which will meet on a regular basis.

To distinguish a bit between the different sorts of risks we face—I think the NAO Report helps a bit with this—when we say that we think the food system is pretty resilient and has demonstrated itself to be resilient, we are primarily talking about acute risks. We know it is resilient because we face a number of acute risks and we have therefore stress-tested it to real effect.

I am more worried about two different sorts of risks. One is chronic risks, the most obvious being what we are seeing in the changing climate and the more extreme weather we are facing. As I talk to farmers, that is increasingly the thing they are talking about. To be honest, they were talking about that before summer, heat waves, the droughts and the wildfires. That is a systemic challenge that we face, both in this country and globally, in respect of the changing nature of the climate and the loss of biodiversity. That is absolutely something we are focused on. To my earlier points, that is why we are investing in the environmental land management schemes to help farms to become more resilient.

The second sort of risks I worry about are what we call the catastrophic risks. They are untested. It is a good thing that they are untested—we do not want to have to face catastrophic risks—but the changing geopolitical circumstances mean they are becoming more apparent. A national power outage is a particular risk that would be very challenging not just for the food sector but for many critical national infrastructures. It is about understanding not just the compounding effect of those different risks but how you respond to different varieties of risk over time.

It is worth noting that DEFRA has moved over probably the last five years—so mainly not under my watch; it started prior to me but I have continued the process. Six years ago, when we went into the process of some of the EU exit planning and particularly the pandemic, we were not set up in the way that you might expect a national security Department to be set up, in terms of having a central professional cadre with clear lines into Cobra and the national security apparatus. We very much are now—over the last five years we have built up that capacity—and there is a particular role for that central resilience unit to deal with concurrent risks and ensure that we are moving resource and capability around the Department to do that.

I am sure other Members will wish to probe other questions. This is not totally a matter for your Department; there is an inter-dependency with other Departments and it is all to do with critical national infrastructure planning as well. I am sure Members will wish to probe that.
Q66 When will you actually have tangible plans and targets to support your objective to improve the resilience of the food supply chain?

We already monitor a very wide range of data on exactly that question. Every three years, as required by statute, we publish a food security report. I cannot remember which chapter it is, but I think it might be chapter 3 that is specifically about food chain resilience. That sets out a range of information. It is not targets and metrics in that sense, but it is a range of information, including data, that we track to see how we are doing on the overall state of food resilience and security in the country.

Alongside that, last year we produced the 10 “Good Food Cycle” outcomes, which are referenced in the NAO Report. One of the criticisms we have faced is that we have not produced metrics underpinning those. We are in the process of producing those metrics, and I expect us to be putting them out relatively early next year, all being well. Of course, there is a range of other public data and statistics that come out—further statistics came out today—which we can put together and use to judge the overall resilience of the system.

I do not think there is a single metric you can use. The NAO Report includes the production-to-supply ratio. That is quite a useful metric, but if I am honest, I do not think it is that useful a metric when we are talking about food security and resilience; it has quite a lot of flaws. It needs to be used alongside quite a lot of other things, so that we have a basket that we can assess.

Q67 I do not know whether you picked up on the news on Monday of a severe problem in France, where refrigerators were hacked and the temperatures were increased, which of course had disastrous outcomes. With that sort of thing in mind, where have you got to with the planned update to your departmental outcomes framework? Do you have anything that reflects complex hacking and incidents like that?

If I may, I will hand over to Helen to say a bit more about the work we are doing on cyber specifically. The case on Monday was interesting. I do worry about cyber. When I think about the things I worry about most, I worry about the chronic changes around climate, I worry about things like a national power outage as a catastrophic but hopefully very low risk, and I worry a lot about cyber.

The reason I particularly worry about cyber is that the risks are getting greater and the focus on critical national infrastructure is getting greater, as the chief exec of the National Cyber Security Centre has set out publicly. Aspects of the food system, from farm to fork, are connected to the internet to a degree that people are not necessarily au fait with. Who would have thought that French fridges would be the subject of a cyber-attack? There are lots of areas that could be susceptible to that kind of attack.

One of the characteristics that makes the food system as a whole quite different from some other critical national infrastructure systems is that it is very dispersed. Unlike the energy sector, which has a relatively small number of big critical assets, or the transport sector, where you can talk about airports and so on, it is very dispersed; there are tens of thousands of firms out there. To some degree that is a vulnerability, because you would have to guarantee the cyber-security of all those tens of thousands of firms. On the other hand, it is a strength, because if one of those firms goes down, there are substitute firms that will step in. Even recently, when we saw a couple of supermarkets subjected to cyber-attacks, the overall food supply for the country was fine.

Nevertheless, the growing level of risk is something that I am concerned about. A couple of years ago, we would not have had a particularly strong understanding within the Department about the cyber-security risks facing the sector, but since then we have made quite a lot of progress. Let me hand over to Helen to say a bit more.

We obviously learned a lot from the attacks on the retailers last year. One of the key things is the relationships across Government—with the National Cyber Security Centre, across the Cabinet Office and with us, too—that need to step into place when those sorts of attacks happen. We have been doing a lot of more intensive work at the retail end of the supply chain, including some benchmarking exercises on what their cyber-security levels are looking like and using the cyber assessment framework, which is a National Cyber Security Centre tool.

Because, as Paul says, there are tens of thousands of businesses, getting that intensive reach is incredibly difficult—well, it is not possible—so we also have things like the PAS 96 guidance, which has the title “ Food Defence – Protection and Prevention from Deliberate Acts ”. That provides a wealth of guidance to businesses, mostly aimed at SMEs, about how to protect themselves against these things. The French supermarket attack is a really good example: when we heard that news, we quickly stepped up the National Cyber Security Centre and were in touch with our retailers and checking with our stakeholders to see whether there were any impacts here.
So there was a lot going on behind the scenes when this happened.
Absolutely—always.

Q68 One of the Committee’s continuing themes is that the Government have an awful lot of legacy equipment. DEFRA has a lot of it, including in its ALBs. They are much more susceptible to cyber-attacks. Is it a real priority for DEFRA to do something about that?
For its own systems?
Yes.

Yes, it is. Cyber is always at the top of the Department’s risk register. There are one or two other things there as well, like the current position of the Weybridge site—the National Biosecurity Centre site—but cyber-security is basically at the top of the list, and we devote quite a lot of time to it as an executive committee, to understand where we have got to in terms of our overall position.

You are right that we have a very large legacy stack. The NAO identified a few years ago that we had what I think was the second largest legacy stack in Whitehall—I have always wondered who has the largest. We thought that about 300 applications in that legacy stack were potentially vulnerable. We have remediated over 200 of them, and we continue to work through that, so we are in a much stronger place now.

There is also quite a strong cross-Government drive, now led out of DCMS, to ensure that all Departments are applying a clear framework that regularly tests our cyber-security. Within the Department, we have also identified a small set of business-critical systems on which we want to do even more work just to double-check their cyber-security.

The biggest cyber-security challenges, both for a Department like ours and for the sector, are sometimes not the most sophisticated cyber-attacks but the relatively unsophisticated ones, as well as human behaviour in large organisations that makes them open. Some of this is also about training our staff to guard against that.
Q69 I should declare, like you, Sir Geoffrey, that I have been an active farmer in the Cotswolds for 40 years, with arable and sheep operations.

Paul, you mentioned the SFI. I am one of the farmers who missed out from the bugger’s muddle, as I would describe it, of your opening and closing of the window within less than a day. Large numbers of farmers missed out, and they do not know what is happening now. You underspent your critical agricultural budget by over £350 million across consecutive cycles, while cutting direct support to farmers. I think most farmers would like to know fairly quickly what you will do to put right the fact that a lot of people did not get into that short-term window. The first question I want to ask is whether you think farming and food production and resilience is a long-term or a short-term project.
It is a long-term project, and a more long-term project than in most industries that we would talk about.
Q70 Right, so do you think that opening and shutting a window for farmers to do long-term planning in less than a day, turning it into a complete charade, is a good indication of long-term planning?

The long-term aspect comes from the length of the agreements that people secure, which are a minimum of three years in the case of SFI and up to five years, or indeed 20 years, when it comes to the higher tiers.
Q71 That is a different answer. Do you think that opening and closing a window for long-term grant applications based on long-term planning is good management?
Let me take a step back—
Do you think that is good management?
I recognise that the window has caused huge levels of irritation, frustration, anger and stress, even for some of the people who managed to get an agreement. I completely recognise that.
So how do they plan?

The scenario facing the Department is that we have gone from a world where, three years ago, we would open an SFI window and very few farmers would come forward seeking SFI agreements, to a world where the opposite happens: we open a window and the demand from farmers far exceeds the finite sum of money that we have to pay them. We need to work out what we do in that scenario.

We did various things in SFI26 to try to mitigate that risk. The first thing we did was to open a window, which was available to small farmers only, to give them privileged access, and to those who had no standing ELM agreement. That window, which went live sometime in the summer, worked very well and was very orderly. We made £70 million available and I think we spent £67 million before, basically, the demand ran out.

We knew, going into window 2, that demand was going to outstrip the available resources. At the beginning, in about August, the amount of money available in that pot for SFI window 2 was about £180 million. The Prime Minister, having visited farms over the summer and seen some drought, added £50 million into the pot. We subsequently added a further £20 million and, finally, the £3 million that had not been spent, so we had increased the pot by 40% in the weeks leading up to the window. Even that was not enough. When it opened, the level of demand from farmers far exceeded the amount of money available.
You must have known that. You underspent the budget—
Of course we were expecting that level of demand—
Q72 Look, I don’t want to go down a rabbit hole. I asked you the question, and I think in most people’s view, that is not good management. We will just park that for now.

What I want to go on to, because the Committee is very concerned about this, is the long-term resilience of food. In covid, the private sector largely dealt with the issue, not the Government. I was quite concerned when I when I read: “Defra is less confident about the ability of businesses to withstand shocks without government intervention in the next five to 10 years because of increasing risks and the potential for more severe disruptions.” That, to me, says it all, because I disagree with you when you say that you are not behind the curve—I think DEFRA is massively behind the curve. If you will indulge me, I will go through why I think you have systemically weakened our food production and our entire food distribution—our machinery, distribution chains—basically everything that we rely on for a long-term plan for food resilience, which on an overpopulated island is crucial.

The British countryside is in a state of manufactured crisis—decades of top-down eco-bureaucracy, ideological tax rates, structural underfunding and urban-biased planning laws, which have pushed our foundational rural economies to the brink of collapse. That is my view. Farmers have been let down repeatedly, financially and culturally, by DEFRA’s poor administration, with decades of chaotic mismanagement under successive Secretaries of State. Global events such as those in Ukraine and Iran have caused massive spikes in energy, fuel and fertiliser prices. As a result, the UK’s food industry and our food security and supply chain are fractured. That is where I think it is.

I look at what you have done over my 40 years in farming. Most recently, the APR issue for agricultural land will dissuade people from investing in farms, as will BPR for small businesses. Yesterday, we had fertiliser tax on top of massive increases in fertiliser prices. Staff continuity and ability at DEFRA are appalling, and I have had first-hand experience of that. We have had the banning of sprays such as pyrethroids and fungicides, as well as tinkering with seed dressings, but no addressing of the supermarket oligopolies. Planning complexities have been stopping diversification. Energy costs, as a result of net zero, are now the highest in the world. We have a weakening supply chain, basically as a result of a lack of profitability. We have an ageing workforce in farming, as you know, at about 63 years of age on average—not an ideal situation if you are looking for long-term security. The health and safety mafia have caused endless problems, and farmers are going bust.

In your road map, which I have had a look at, you mention “resilience” 15 times more often than you mention income, profit, prices and so on. I am afraid that it is just verbal baby food. I look at things like this and I think, “What on earth does that mean? Not much to me.” I think, Paul, that this is a systemic problem. When you go into a company that has a cultural problem, you have to change the culture, so do you think you need to change the culture at DEFRA? That is my question, as an elected MP and someone who is concerned about Britain’s food resilience.
I am always open to feedback on how the Department is doing—
What do you think?

I think the Department is getting an enormous number of things right, and there are various things that I would like to improve. That is always to be the case in a large, complex organisation that trying to deliver difficult things.

To talk about the SFI for a minute from an administrative perspective, we could have been sat here in a world in which the system fell over because the RPA could not administer it, but we are not. We are in a world in which the RPA administered a new application every two seconds during that window. That is an extraordinary achievement by the people in that organisation. So do I think they are broken? No, I do not. I think they are administering things in extraordinarily difficult circumstances.

When it comes to the overall state of farming in this country, it is worth remembering that the domestic production of food in this country across most sectors is going up, and has been over 10 years. The supply ratio, which I referenced earlier and is in the NAO Report, has been stable for about 20 years. We are producing in this country about 60% of the food that we eat. That is twice as much as we were producing before the second world war.

British farming continues to be a success story, and we should be proud of it. There is a role for DEFRA in supporting it through the incredibly difficult circumstances at the moment, which are playing out on the ground through extreme weather and drought. That is what we are focused on doing, through investing in environmental land management, which farmers want—it turns out that they want more than we can afford to pay for—and through paying them through innovation grants and other productivity grants to move to robotics and more precision farming. That is what we are doing to try to help modernise the farming sector. We are putting more money into the sector than ever before as a result of the spending review settlement.

Q73 I couldn’t disagree more, and I think that if you had a poll of farmers, they would agree with me, not with what you just said. I think you are deluding yourself if you say that you have got it right now. You have not been getting it right during my time in farming. I have watched the state undermine farming. The question is: are you turning farmers into gardeners? Is that what you are trying to do? In Monday’s hearing, you heard Harry say that he has to take a risk planting crops now. He is being encouraged not to plant food, grow crops or do the vocational things that a farmer is designed to do.
The sustainable farming incentive is specifically designed—
But do you—
Hang on, Rupert. Let the permanent secretary answer, please.

The sustainable farming incentive is specifically designed to work alongside food production. If anything, I would say that under this Government there has been a shift in emphasis around SFI and ELMs towards more support for food production to make sure the schemes that we run work alongside food production.

Actually, the future of food production on these farms depends on the quality of the soils and the quality of the water—the things that we are investing in now. That demonstrates a seriousness about the long-term future of resilience and profitable farming.
I’m done, Geoffrey. I am done.

Q74 You heard Harry in our session on Monday. I have quarterly meetings with my farmers. I have been doing that for the 34 years for which I have been a Member of Parliament, and I have never before heard those farmers say that they are thinking about whether they should plant crops or not because, when they plant, they do not know whether they will make a profit. That shows to me a pretty downcast industry.

Added to that, whatever you think—you put a gloss on it—the management of the SFI was appalling. It is self-defeating, because some of my farmers who had SFI or its predecessor schemes, and who now have not got it, will plough up all the environmental benefits that have been gained by this country over 20 or 30 years of subsidy. That seems ultimately self-defeating.

Add to that the fertiliser tax, which I referred to earlier. If you, as a Ministry, having seen the huge spike in fertiliser prices—most farmers, whatever they farm, require fertiliser to a greater or lesser degree—actually impose a fertiliser tax on 1 February, you cannot say that you are really considering the future of agriculture. Otherwise, you would have altered and amended both those factors.

You must be able to take things like the geopolitical changes into consideration. Fertiliser is going up in price because of what is happening in the middle east and, as Sir Geoffrey says, you are adding an additional burden on to farmers. Farmers on Exmoor in my constituency, who are some of most resilient in the country, are absolutely on their knees. The SFI thing was just a disgrace.
Okay; you have got the flavour of the Committee.

I have got the flavour of the Committee. I just want to say what I am accountable for and what I am not. I am not accountable for tax policy, because I am not accountable for policy, and I am not accountable for tax—that sits with the Treasury.
Let me stop you there. I was thinking that, but did you make any representations to the Treasury to delay this tax?

I obviously cannot talk about what representations we might make within Government between different Departments, but suffice to say, whether it is about fertiliser, the fuel costs that have gone up or any of the other things that happened when the middle east crisis hit—some of the witnesses in your session earlier in the week were talking about that—our Ministers are involved in cross-Government conversations about how we could spend taxpayers’ money to support different sectors. We are always involved in those conversations. There are difficult judgments that Ministers have to reach within them. I cannot get into the detail of individual sectors. I am not here to respond to questions on tax policy; that is not what I am here to do. I am happy to respond on the SFI.

Q75 Okay, let’s leave the tax, but the SFI is certainly a fact. Some of the environmental benefit that this country has had for 20 or 30 years from taxpayer subsidies is now going to be completely destroyed because that land will ploughed up. That is surely not a very sensible continuous long-term policy, is it?

I agree with you; that worries me. I am not here to try to put a positive gloss on the SFI. I absolutely appreciate the level of frustration and indeed anger that is out there, and so do our Ministers. I am simply trying to explain the cause of that. The budget available to my Department is not sufficient to pay all the farmers who wish now to do environmental land actions. If the Committee has a suggestion as to what I do about that, I am all ears, but I have to administer the budget I have. It has always been administered on a first come, first served basis. That has been the approach taken through multiple SFIs. Inherently, that is not an unfair way of doing it. When you get into the scenario we are now in, where the demand for SFI so far exceeds the potential budget, it is right that we look again at whether there is a different way of doing that. Ministers have signalled that that is their intention. The fundamental challenge we have is that I can only administer the budget I have.

Q76 I understand that. Just as a comment rather than a question on the SFI issue, to my mind and the farming industry’s view it was entirely predictable, because of the economic situation that farmers now find themselves in. It was entirely predictable, and therefore I think you should have been able to think about it and do something different rather than have the chaos that ensued.

I think we did. We increased the budget by 40% in the final weeks before. We found every bit of money we could to put into that budget. That is probably the most effective thing we could have done. We capped payments as well, so that we could stretch the available money to more farmers. Previously, a quarter of all SFI funding went to just 4% of farmers. That is why we introduced a cap, so that the money could be spread across more farmers than was previously the case.

We supported farmers as far as we possibly could by providing much more simple guidance in the run-in to the window, so that people were prepared. We actually reduced the number of actions available in order to simplify it. We took numerous actions and then we ran a first window, so that small farms and those who were not in ELM schemes could access it. That was a very orderly window. We took a number of actions for exactly the reasons you are suggesting, in anticipation of the excess demand. There are only a certain amount of actions that we can take to smooth that out.
Thank you for that. I am sure the industry will want to reflect on that reply, so thank you very much. Let us move on to Clive Betts, my excellent deputy.

Q77 The supply chain is clearly very important, but it is a very complicated chain with lots of businesses. Engagement with those businesses and involving them in the process and preparedness is really important. The feedback in the Report is that it got quite good during covid, where there was a real need for that to happen, and then it has sort of dropped off since. There has not been as much engagement, and the various committees and working groups that were set up do not meet as often as they did. Do you recognise the need for improvement in that?

This was probably the one bit of the Report where I did not quite recognise the critique. I know it is not coming from the NAO; it is coming from stakeholders. Either way, we would take very seriously the idea that in some way we have stepped back from engagement with the sector.

There is a specific question about one forum that we used to run during covid, which was very highly regarded: the food resilience industry forum. That was set up with, I think, over 150 organisations to help manage the crisis. To Mr Lowe’s point, it was a co-ordination mechanism. The leadership was coming from businesses. They were the ones solving the problems, but they were coming to the Government and saying, “If you could fix this issue—road haulier hours or an issue in the Competition Act—it will help us.” We were in a convening and response role. That was very popular with the industry. We shut it down because it was a response mechanism to a particular crisis. In effect, it still exists. We can stand it up very quickly. It is all there ready to be stood up if we need it. Thankfully, we have not needed to, so it is a sort of success factor.

We have a whole range of different fora that we usually run on a quarterly basis. Some of those are run by officials and some of them are ministerial-chaired, including the food strategy advisory board and the farming and food partnership board. I attended a number of the ones that Ministers run. They will talk about issues of resilience, but they will not necessarily be specifically focused—they are not resilience forums, if that makes sense. If you are talking at the farming and food partnership board about opportunities for sector growth, you are talking about the resilience of the farming sector, but you are not necessarily having the kind of conversation that the NAO invites around specific events.

We have set up a new forum to address that, which is the food readiness group that I referenced earlier. That brings together people from right across the food chain and adds in local resilience forums, the voluntary sector and other Government Departments, with a view to developing a plan. That is both forward-looking, rather than reactive, and specifically focused on resilience.

Q78 You have plans and structures in place and then you look at the issue of disruption and how you might respond to it. The complaint identified in the Report was that businesses have not been involved in preparing those plans. Is that a fair comment?

This goes back to the question the Chair raised earlier, which I think was specifically about the playbook, our internal manual. We have a set of playbooks on how DEFRA works internally, but it is absolutely fair to say that we do not have a single overarching framework or plan that sets out the roles and responsibilities for every part of the system. That is the piece of work that we have begun, and we will use the food readiness group to help us develop that. We will work on that over the coming months.

Q79 Will that also look at the exercises you do to test resilience? Again, businesses have said that they have not really been involved in those exercises. If the exercises are going to be meaningful, clearly it is absolutely key that those who will be at the sharp end of responding to any crises should be engaged in them.

I totally agree. I will bring Helen in to say a bit more, but I think that over the last four years the food resilience team has been engaged with about seven different exercises—four around cyber-security, and three others. We definitely take the approach that exercising is absolutely critical to testing the plans that we have. That is very much policy across the whole of Government. It is right that industry have not always been involved, but they have been involved in some. The farming industry have been involved in a few more than is suggested in the Report, which is about the food sector, if that makes sense. We also learn from actual ongoing crises. Over the summer, we have obviously been dealing with the middle east, droughts, wildfires and so on, so we do lessons learned around that. I do not know if Helen wants to add a bit more on exercising.

Absolutely. As Paul says, over recent years, we have done seven exercises. One of them was really notable; one of the cyber exercises was about a cyber-incident in retail, and we invited retailers in to join that exercise. How we do that has always been incredibly challenging, because they are all in competition with each other, so we cannot all sit around the same table and have a discussion about how one retailer would respond in front of the other retailer without getting into those blurry lines around competition law and what their approaches would be. In this one we found a fantastic format that worked, where they had their own space to discuss within their own business what they would be doing, and we could come together as a group to discuss the bits that were appropriate to discuss together.

Direct involvement is not the only way that this happens. We have engaged with industry ahead of some exercises to say, “This is the scenario. How would you approach this? What do you think you would be doing?”, so that we can feed that into the exercise. It is important to note that actually dealing with incidents is also how we learn, and that can be just as powerful as exercises themselves—of course, industry is involved with those.
Q80 Is that an improvement on what we were told in the Report?

The exercise that I referred to, where the retailers were involved, is the one that is mentioned in the Report as the key one where the food sector were involved. We were already discussing with industry ahead of exercises without involving them in the actual exercises, and we completely acknowledge the suggestion in the NAO Report that we need to do this more.

The food group that met last week did a workshop on a national power outage scenario, where we did quite a desk-based exercise of “What could we be doing? How can we tackle the problems in this particular scenario?” Th at is something we will also be taking forward . We will involv e that group in proper exercising, but also do desk-based scenarios with them.
Is that an improvement on what was referred to in the Report?
Yes, absolutely.

Q81 Let us move on to lessons learned from elsewhere. We tend to take the very narrow view that we can do it all and learn all our lessons, but other countries obviously have similar problems. You came on to the issue of the food supply chain and supermarkets, and the problems they had in France the other day. How far are you learning from what other countries do? Are there examples where they are already doing it better , from which we can learn?

I might come to you, Helen, to answer in more detail, but overall we do learn quite a bit from other countries. We are part of a NATO panel in this area, so we discuss regularly with allies their approaches to food security and resilience. It is fair to say that, as we develop the new framework that I have been describing through this food preparedness group, we will want to look at different international examples we might be able to learn from.

A couple of examples that come up quite a lot are perhaps worth talking about. One is stockpiling. It is sometimes asked why the Government do not have a central food or grain stockpile . We used to as a country, but I think we ceased to sometime in the 1990s. There is no in-principle objection to the UK Government having stockpiles; indeed, we have them in certain other areas, such as critical minerals or medical supplies.

It basically comes down to a value-for-money judgment. Ministers across Government and within DEFRA thinking about the food system will have a range of options for spending taxpayers’ money to try to improve its resilience, and it is not clear that a national food stockpile would be the most value-for-money way of doing so. That is not to rule it out for all time, but it is not clear that it would represent value for money for the UK in the way that it does for some countries because of their particular circumstances and geography.

The other thing that people sometimes point to, where I am more sympathetic to learning the lessons, is household readiness, where there is a greater focus on communication and perhaps a different social norm and culture around being prepared for different events. We are working with the Cabinet Office on a new readiness campaign that I expect will be rolled out in due course, asking people to take sensible step s like having bottled water and non-perishable food in the house so that they can cope, particularly in the more catastrophic events we are talking about — which hopefully will never happen — such as a national power outage. Do you have enough food in the house to get you through a few days? Things like that. Other countries tend to have more deliberate approaches than we have had traditionally. We do have an approach in the Prepare website , but we know that awareness and use of it is very low.

Q82 We will come to tha t later , but let me pick up on it for a second since you raised it . H ow do you deal with families who are wondering how they will pay for tomorrow’s food, let alone how they will store food for two or three weeks in an emergency?

It is a really important question. There are a couple of things. One is that not all the ways households can prepare require cost. Some advice that I think will come out is already on the Prepare website: cost-free things, such as knowing where your torch is if you have one and bringing those things together. I lived in New Zealand for a few years, and it was absolutely common for everybody to have a grab bag in case of an earthquake or a tsunami. Luckily, we do not face those kinds of things, but there is something about having a culture where people just know where things are. When it comes to food and water, the message really is, “Do it if you can.” For those who can afford it, it is a good thing to do for everybody else, because if there is some kind of event , you can look after yourself for a few days, allowing emergency responders to respond to those who cannot.

Q83 When you are talking to households and pitching a scenario to them, will you also be talking to organisations such as food banks, particularly the national ones, about how they can help in th o se situations?

Absolutely. We did a bit of a workshop last week on a national power outage, and we talked to a national charity with a reach into some 8,000 communities and organisations about exactly this question: how do you get food to people in the event of catastrophic failure ? Going back to one of the lessons we learned from covid, the existing private sector system is incredibly effective at responding to acute crises and getting food to the community level, but it is not as strong in knowing how to get it to the final mile . W e can get it to stores , bu t how do you get it to households? T hat is where the Government did play a role supporting voluntary and community groups and others to make sure that food got to households at that level. I t is very much part of the conversation we want to have through this group.

Q84 You mentioned that there is perhaps more awareness in other sectors, such as energy, of the need to have a resilience plan . Are y ou learning any lessons from them about how they go about it? We recognis e that they are much more regulated and perhaps there are more powers with the regulator to organise the industry than there is in food.

One thing that the Cobra unit does at the Cabinet Office is bring together lessons across the different 13 critical national infrastructures. One thing we find in those lessons to some degree is that food is a bit of an outlier because it is, unusually for a CNI, all essentially within the private sector and is very dispersed across a large number of organisations. That creates a bit of a challenge for us sometimes in docking into the Cobra systems. That is reflected in one of the comments that the NAO picks up in the Report from our own self-assessment around our CNI capabilities.

However, that does not stop us looking at those lessons. On your question about regulatory powers, in essence, we, as the Government, do not hold a set of resilience powers over the food sector. There are various regulations that the food sector has to respond to, around everything from health and safety and labour laws to food standards and so on, but there are not a set of resilience standards in the way that there are for the energy or water sector and so on. That is one of the questions that the NAO Report raises: is that right and should there be standards? Should there be a set of powers that Government hold over the food sector if there is a catastrophic event?

Our sense of that is that, as we have gone through quite a series of acute events, we have not felt the need to reach for a particular lever. There are things that we have done through the legal system that have provided additional flexibilities in those circumstances, as I mentioned earlier. However, it is not inconceivable that you could have an event so catastrophic that the Government would need to reach for a lever. It is at least sensible for us to be looking at that.
