I just think that we need to make sure we can advise Ministers when the time comes. We have got to set a reasonably high bar for a new regulatory imposition on the food sector. It has to be justified by whatever the event is that we are looking at. Last time I was before the Committee, I was being held to account for how much we regulate and whether we can simplify and lighten regulations. There is a constant challenge to get that right.
Q85 Would you be looking for a regulation that you could bring in as and when it is needed, rather than one that applied all the time?

P otentially . I do not want to speculate too much on what are essentially policy options, which ultimately would be a decision for Parliament, let alone Ministers. I do not think that, when we look at the recent history of the food sector going through various events, we have felt “Y ou know what, if we had the following big regulatory lever, we would have used it .” B usinesses have responded brilliantly to these changing circumstances.

However, you could imagine a world where , in a national power outage, Government intervention needed to be far greater for some reason, a nd we would want to know that we had the legal basis for doing that. We always have the backstop of the Civil Contingencies Act. I f we were in a n extreme circumstance , that A ct would probably give us —as the NAO R eport touches on — the legislative framework that we needed.

Q86 I want to follow up on an earlier question with you, Helen . W e need to consider the food sector as a holistic whole. We ha ve spent a lot of time today talking about farming as t he primary producers. You then go on to how you transport goods from the farm and within the food chain sector and then to processing in one form or another, be it mills, slaughterhouses and so on . T hat i s a problem in itself in that more and more of our food processing is being done outside this country, which is a systemic risk. T hen you go on to the retailers. When you consult with industry, will you be sure to consult with all those different parts?

Absolutely. I t has been important in the setting up of this food group to make sure that we have representation from end to end. I t goes all the way from farming through to hospitality. We want the group to be able to have really strong operational conversations , so we did not want it to be too big, which has been an incredible challenge because of the size of the sector. Trade associations can represent their part of the supply chain, but they represent the entire supply chain. I completely agree with you; everything has to work together.
Just to add, we had the NFU, the cold chain, logistics, retailers, the voluntary sector and LRFs in the room.

Q87 To follow up on your emergency legislation, during covid Parliament obtained pretty strong powers pretty quickly from the Civil Contingencies Act 2004. If you needed any particular powers, you could use that mechanism, which would be more specific to the individual risk, as it was with the Coronavirus Act 2020, rather than having blanket legislation now that may not fit the individual emergency.
Yes.
Good—we are in agreement!

Q88 Are you now saying that your playbook has the right amount of operational detail to respond to a severe food supply disruption? That was not the suggestion of the NAO Report. Are you now saying categorically that you have the operational detail?
No, we are talking about slightly different things. It is worth setting the playbook to one side. The playbook is just an internal DEFRA document.
You said that earlier.

What we are talking about developing is the sort of plan the NAO is suggesting that we develop. That will set out the operational detail and the roles and responsibilities of different parts of the sector in order that we can respond to different scenarios that may play out, if that makes sense.

The short answer is no. We would not sit here and say that we have all that detail laid out. When I talk to people who were involved in the pandemic response within DEFRA, which I was not, they say, “It worked really well, but we could do with codifying some of it. We were making it up as we went along. We are pretty confident we’d be able to do it again, but can we write it down so that we are all really clear what we are doing?” That does not feel beyond the realms of possibility to me.
You don’t want to reinvent the wheel. If the wheel is already there, you use the wheel again.
Correct.

Q89 You are now talking about having done a detailed national plan for food supply in the event of a national power outages, or at least having a discussion about one. You were urged to do that in 2023. Are you now saying that you have done that, or is it part of an ongoing plan of action?

It is part of ongoing work. We have done quite a lot of work since the Mighty Oak exercise a couple of years ago. We are focusing our efforts in three areas within DEFRA. The first is household preparedness. We talked about that issue earlier. It is one of the most effective things to build resilience not just in the food system, but nationally within communities. The second is how we would get food to the most vulnerable, which picks up Mr Betts’ point as well. The third is recovery after a power outage and how we get the food chain up and running as quickly and as close to normal as possible. We are taking a fairly proportionate, focused approach in the work. Those are our three priorities at the moment.

Q90 Has the work you are doing on the plan been independently assured? Has somebody been asked to have a look and say, “That’s really good,” “No, you’ve forgotten this,” or, “You haven’t put that in”?

That is in our plan; we are going to have it independently assured. We are going to get somebody external—probably more than one person—to test it. We will also run the actual process of doing it by various parts of industry and the local tier to test it, but there will be an official external independent assurance process.
Q91 To go back to the point the Chairman just made , will that independent assurance take into account the numerous sectors that need to be there to assure?

Absolutely. A key part of our programme of work is recognising that we need a whole-of-society approach to deal with these issues. No one part of the sector, nor Government alone, can deal with this. It needs to be a whole-of-society approach.
Q92 Will the Government’s database of critical national infrastructure assets include key food supply chain assets?

The short answer is yes. At the moment, the food system, as a system, is on the database that you are referring to—the Cabinet Office knowledge base of critical national infrastructure. This comes back to my earlier point that some of the ways in which we think about critical national infrastructure across Government do not fit brilliantly with a food system that is so dispersed.

As a starting point, the system, at system level, is on there. We have learned a huge amount about different aspects of the supply chain over recent years, partly because you go through these events and you have to learn pretty fast. We are now trying to identify individual assets from within the food supply chain that would go into the knowledge base as individual assets. I am not allowed to talk about what those assets are because they are tentative.
Q93 Okay. So you have not done it yet but you are doing it.
We are part-way through it.
So you have learned your lesson from previous events and you are using that information and knowledge to make things better in future.
Correct.
Q94 Is there a timescale?

There are different phases to the work. There are some easier parts where there are obvious assets that will need to go on there. We should have completed that in about the next four months. Then there is a longer piece of work, because of the complexity of the supply chain. We are looking at a set of products that you would still want to be available in extreme crisis, and we are tracking them through the supply chains to work out what parts need to be on the database in order to make that true. That is a much longer piece of work, as it is incredibly complex. For that, we are aiming for March 2028.
So it will be completed by March 2028.
Yes, and then it will need to be constantly kept up to date.
Obviously. So in 18 months’ time, you will have nailed it.
Yes.

Q95 Perhaps we will have you back then to see how you are getting on. Interestingly, I see there is currently an urgent question on the sustainable farming incentive. It will be interesting to see whether your Minister says the same thing as you said, permanent secretary.
It will be interesting for both of us.
To be fair, she has already indicated that she will look at how they do the payments, so I am holding her to account.
Excellent. I am going to take a short break now. The clock is at 11.02 am. Please be back by 11.10 sharp, because I will try to finish around midday if we possibly can.
Sitting suspended.
On resuming—
We will recommence with Clive Betts.

Q96 Permanent secretary, I want to follow on with the issue of families who are strapped for cash, and how they would deal with getting themselves resilient for any significant disruption in their food supplies.

When I asked you before, we talked about poorer families, and particularly their reliance on food banks and what you could do there. Some research has indicated that, to have a resilient package of food in the house, families would have to spend about £500, which is more than many spend on a month’s supply of food and not something they can go out and buy tomorrow at the supermarket.

Have you got a plan whereby you can fund food banks and get food to them in a crisis, probably with the help of supermarkets, to help the poorest families, who will otherwise have no food at all and cannot put those stocks in place in advance?
To clarify, I do not think I was suggesting that we would expect people to rely on food banks in that scenario. I am not sure if that is what you were saying to me.

We are working with the voluntary sector, and we had an initial conversation at the food preparedness group last week—a bit of a workshop on how we would get food to vulnerable groups, which may well include those on lower incomes. We do not have a clear plan in place at the moment on that, but that is the work we are trying to do through the food preparedness group. It is a work in progress.

Does the Government expect low-income families to spend a lot of money buying food? In essence, no. The ask is that those who can should build up their food, and indeed bottled water, because that helps the wider societal response.

Q97 Who would co-ordinate that at local level? One of the lessons we learned from covid was that organising at a local level is a lot better than national telephone banks and things that often did not work.

I completely agree. I might ask Helen to come in again, but I have a couple of thoughts. The first is that one of the principles in the Amber Book, which is the Government’s overall approach to responding to emergencies, is subsidiarity: responses are better done at the local level where possible.

One of the issues raised in the NAO Report is about LRFs, which, as we know, vary in terms of capacity and capability and have not necessarily had a strong focus on food supply issues historically. That is one of the reasons we have brought them into this new group to help us develop the plan. It is definitely an area that we need to strengthen for exactly the reasons you are suggesting. I don’t know if Helen wants to add to that.

I would add that in a lot of the resilience world and looking at CNI sectors, the local response would be quite reliant on the local resilience forums. For food, we think it goes much broader than that. Particularly during covid, we saw fantastic networks popping up in local areas, with communities looking after each other, many of which have remained in place. We want to work across those—across the national charities that look at food and across the food banks—to see how we can join up all these fantastic community organisations, who are the people who really understand where the vulnerable people are, and make sure that they have access to sufficient food, including during the most challenging of situations like a national power outage. That will all form part of this plan that we are going to write, helping communities and those sorts of organisations understand what is out there to help them get to that point.
Q98 Who would be responsible at a local level? Is there a clearly identified responsible organisation?

The local resilience forum would co-ordinate, and they are usually chaired by a chief constable. One of the things we want to do in our plan is set out responsibilities at national, local and industry level.
So it would be clearly identified. I think the general assumption is that if no one is responsible, in the end everyone gets a bit of responsibility and it falls apart.

I agree. The experience in covid was that we did get food to people, but we were, to some degree, making it up as we went along. It comes back to codifying what we know works and going into any crisis with much greater clarity on who is responsible for what. That is what the plan would intend to do.

Q99 Paul and Emily, I don’t mind which of you answers this. There was a lot of good work done, as you have just indicated, permanent secretary, during covid, and a lot of good databases were built up—certainly in my authority, and I am sure in authorities up and down the country. I would be very keen, under local government reorganisation, for that information not to be lost so that we can build on it in a future emergency. I wonder if you could look at that.
Of course.
Thank you. Sarah Hall, you have been waiting very patiently.

Q100 Thank you. I want to continue along the theme of the LRFs. The NAO has identified significant weaknesses in local preparedness for food supply disruptions. Some of that relates to the uncertainty about the role and what is expected of them during a major food disruption. I suppose I want to know how DEFRA, MHCLG and other stakeholders are working together to strengthen that LRF preparedness and response capability. Is there now clear guidance, and are there defined expectations for LRFs? What practical measures are being taken?

I will turn to Helen, but I will just make a point on why I think there is a bit of a lack of clarity about the role of LRFs when it comes to food supply. LRFs tend to work off the national risk register, which provides around 95 different risks. Each one of those has a reasonable worst-case scenario, which we effectively ask local resilience forums to plan for. There isn’t a specific risk on food supply in the national risk register. There isn’t one of those 95 risks that is a reasonable worst-case scenario around food supply. Food supply is, though, identified in around half the risks as an impact of that thing happening. In a sense, the questions around food supply are all over the national risk register when you read it, but there is not a specific reasonable worst-case scenario on food supply.

Q101 Is that likely to be a change or addition? It is great that it is included in a range of things, but it is quite a pressing issue, particularly as we have seen what is happening in France and what you were talking about with cyber-security and so on.

It is a question that is raised in the NAO Report and one that we will want to look at. In the meantime, the food system is a critical national infrastructure—one of 13. It is also identified as one of our national response capabilities. It is all over the national security infrastructure, as it were. There is just a very particular thing that then feeds through to LRFs, which I think creates this lack of clarity.

We are aware of and would agree with the findings of the NAO Report that a lot more work needs doing in this area. Capacity is quite an issue for the LRFs, so we need to work within what they are able to do. We are using the resilience structures across Government to do that, working closely with MHCLG and across wider structures. We are setting up some forums, and others are already in place, where we can speak in detail with the LRFs. In fact, I have been talking to MHCLG in the last couple of weeks about setting up a very specific forum on this, which I hope we will be able to do soon.

Q102 Why is it taking so long to deliver? During covid, there was obviously quite a run on shops and a rush to get food supplies. That was in 2020, so why has it taken so long to get to this point, where we are only just talking about having something and have not actually started it yet?

In 2020, we and the NAO found that industry was able to plug that gap. Yes, we had a run on shops, particularly in the beginning, but industry was very quickly able to address that. What we recognise now is that there are broader, bigger issues on the threat landscape, which we need a whole-of-society approach to. That is why we are now focusing effort here.
Q103 Okey-dokey. Obviously, this is quite pressing, so when do you expect it to come to fruition?

This is all part of the plan that we have been talking about. We are aiming to publish it as soon as we can. We are actively working with all the players who need to be involved to develop the plan and get us to a point where we can publish something.
Q104 How soon do you think that could be?

I would like to aim for the end of next year. I say that with slight jeopardy because I do not know whether we can achieve that, and until we get into the detailed work with the range of stakeholders we have been talking about, I will not have confidence in exactly what the right timescale is. We might be able to do some aspects of it sooner, so I do not want to commit to a particular timescale, but that is the kind of timeline we are working on.
It is always good to have that aim.
Yes, and these are groups that we intend to meet every couple of months, and we will keep the work going.
Q105 How will you assess whether it has improved? Will it be a moveable feast, with you reviewing it time and again?

I think it will be a constant review process. Helen answered a question earlier about getting an external review to stress-test and red-team whether the plan works. To some degree, you get to test these plans in real time because events happen. You also get to test them through exercising, and we will have a programme of exercising.
I call Anna Dixon; welcome.

Q106 I apologise for being late, Chair. It has been an interesting hearing. In terms of identifying vulnerable people, Paul, can you explain what work is being done to share data nationally—say, around DWP or the NHS—so we can understand where there are people with disabilities who may be particularly vulnerable or housebound and respond more quickly to those who are likely to need support?

Again, I am going to go to Helen because she is the expert in this area, but overall, we have to bear in mind that, as you know, there is not a single definition of vulnerable people. The circumstances of individual people within different scenarios, whether it is a national power outage or a cyber-attack or whatever, mean different groups become vulnerable.

It is not always the groups that you would naturally assume are vulnerable. We talked earlier about people who are on low incomes and may struggle to have a small stock of food in their house. In certain scenarios, infants under the age of six months who are solely fed on baby infant formula, even if they are in quite wealthy households, could become vulnerable in certain circumstances. We have to map out what vulnerability looks like in each scenario.

Absolutely, and I would extend that a bit to look at how vulnerability changes. In something like a national power outage, if you have somebody living in a studio flat in London who buys their dinner on the way home every night, they are immediately very vulnerable, when they might not have been on anybody’s radar at all before that.

Recognising how vulnerability changes depending on the scenario is really important. It is the first thing that happens in my team. When something happens and we realise we need to respond, the first conversation is, “Who is vulnerable? Who is going to be at the most risk in this situation and how can we focus our response on them?” Often, that involves talking to the likes of DWP, DHSC, MHCLG and perhaps those Departments responsible for public sector settings to make sure we have got a really full understanding. But it can change in each scenario.

Some brilliant things were done during covid, which I think are replicable. For example, there were five charities—I am not going to be able to name all of them—including the Royal National Institute of Blind People, which was able to nominate people to say, “This is a vulnerable person; they need priority access to online delivery slots.” We have things like that that can be replicated, and as Paul has said a few times, that is where we need to codify things. That is an automatic thing that happens and we know exactly how to do that, rather than laying the track in front of us as was being done with covid.
May I add one thing? There is also a priority services register, so if you are concerned, you can sign up and then utilities companies will have you on their list.

Q107 We had a hearing. I do appreciate and am glad that you are defining vulnerability by circumstance; it is a long-standing point that I make to most Departments about not just assuming that people are vulnerable.

I want to push slightly on the data linkage, because we know that during covid, local authorities and the NHS found ways to join up their data and identify people that had been struggling for decades to do it. All the barriers were swept away during covid. We do not want to wait for the next crisis to do that again, so I want to understand, particularly on data sharing and linkage to make us more resilient as a society, whether there was any progress on that. I think you are saying that, in the circumstances, you will talk to the right people, but I would have liked to hear a bit more about looking and planning ahead with that data sharing so that, in the eventuality that you need to identify certain groups, the data can be accessed.
I think you are raising a really important point, and it is something we should add into the programme of work we have as we develop the new framework.
It is also something we should do as we review powers.
Yes, if you need or have new powers.

Q108 I just had a message from my team, who have been listening to the SFI statement from the Under-Secretary in Parliament. He basically blamed the SFI debacle on the mess that the Government inherited from the previous Government. He is refusing to apologise to farmers, and apparently, from listening to the debate, the Government are accepting no accountability for what I would describe as a complete farce. I genuinely think that the public and MPs like me—I represent farmers in Great Yarmouth—have had enough of this buck-passing and blaming of everybody else.

I do not know what experience you have in farming, Paul, but listening to your answers today, you seemed very confident that DEFRA was fit for purpose, which I would totally disagree with. When are we going to get some honesty about the crisis that is now facing the farming and retailing industries—the agricultural merchants, the machinery dealers? It is a crisis that is about to come and haunt you, and I think you would do well to have a good look into it. Are you a farmer? Have you had experience of food production? It did not look like it from your CV.
I live in a farming community.
Right, but do you farm?
No, I do not farm.
Do you have experience of farming?
Not directly—I picked potatoes in fields when I was growing up in a rural community.

Q109 When do you think we are going to get some honesty? I do not even know how many members of staff at DEFRA have any farming experience. When are you going to start listening to the farmers in industry rather than believing your own narrative?

We do not have our own narrative, we have a narrative that is informed by exactly what you are describing: endless engagement with lots of stakeholders, including many farmers. I go out and visit lots of farms and people across the food industry more generally. I was sat at the table with a potato farmer the other day who was telling me in no uncertain terms what he thought about SFI and the challenges he was facing; he was desperate to try to build a reservoir on his farmland. That is what we need to hear in the Department. We have lots of people—not just me—out across the country having those conversations. Our understanding of farming is informed by conversations with farmers.

I have given you a very honest account today of the degree to which we understand the challenges that are going on in farming right now. They are challenges that are not necessarily of our making—they are challenges of the weather, which sadly we do not control, of high input costs as a result of global events, and of lower output costs as a result of global markets. We absolutely recognise that context. We face into it, we have conversations with farmers and we work out how we can support them, but we try to support them toward the long-term resilience of farming through environmental land management and greater productivity and innovation.

Q110 Can you tell the Committee when you are going to have a scheme for those farmers who missed out on SFI because of what I would describe as extremely bad management and not having a planned window to allow people to plan long term? When are you going to come forward with something that tells the 60%-plus of farmers who did not get into SFI when they are going to have a plan for their land? To Geoffrey’s point, when do they decide to plough up all the stuff that they have done in the past?
Just to be clear, more than half of farmers are in ELM contracts. More than half of farmers—
Sixty per cent got in; 40% did not.
But they are the cohort of farmers who were eligible to apply for that single window. There are multiple windows, and there are farmers who have multiple-year contracts already.
Q111 When is the next window?
The next one is SFI27. That will be launched as soon as possible.
It is not until next year, is it?
It is SFI27, so it will not be until next year.
Q112 So what are farmers supposed to do between now and then?

Twenty thousand farmers are now in three-year contracts as a result of SFI26. That is one in five farmers. That is almost £1 billion over the next three years. That is from windows 1 and 2 of SFI26. SFI27 will be the next opportunity for farmers to apply for SFI funding; we are lear ning the lessons that you are encouraging us to learn from SFI window 2, and we will launch it as soon as we can.
Q113 Do you think that is an ideal situation for those people trying to plan a long-term business?

No, I do not think it is ideal, but I work in Government; we do not deal in ideals. We have to be very practical about what we can do with the resources we have available. That is what I am trying to explain. I have a finite budget. Ministers have a finite budget. They have to make difficult decisions.

As you know, if you have greater levels of demand than the supply of funding, you have to make quite difficult decisions about what is fair and just, and how you get that money to as many farmers as possible. The Minister has made a number of decisions to make sure that the money went to as many farmers as possible, capping the amount of money that went to some of the larger farmers. We now have more farmers than ever before in ELM schemes, and we will continue to work on that as we go into SFI27.

Q114 You are telling me what I already know. Ultimately, when are we going to get some honesty from people running the industry? You are running the industry. There is far too much Government throughout the entire economy. The state accounts for far too much of GDP. When are you going to own up to the fact that you are responsible? When is the buck-passing going to stop? How much longer do the Government have to be in power before they accept responsibility for things that go wrong?
I am not passing any bucks. I am giving you an entirely honest account of how we have run the SFI scheme, the challenges that we are facing and the things we have to lean into as we go into SFI27.
I am going to run a poll on my social media to see whether the farmers agree with me or you. I will let you know the outcome.
I can probably guess.
Does anybody have any more questions?
Can I ask one thing?
Of course. We have time.
Q115 I accept what you said about the budget being upped by £40 million relatively last minute.
It was upped by 40%—by about £70 million.

So will the lesson be learned for next year that the system needs to be changed so that we do not have the scramble we had this year? The application system needs to be changed, but at the end of the day, the scheme needs to have more money in it to meet the demand. Isn’t that just the basic fact?
The more money there is, the easier it would be to run an SFI scheme to meet as much demand as possible. I do not have control over that. I have a set budget.

We also have to meet the environmental goals that are set out in statute by Parliament; I have an obligation to meet those as well. As we are trying to work out how to spend our finite money, we want to do it in a way that supports food production, supports farmers to move to more resilient agricultural approaches and delivers our environmental targets, which we are required to do that by Parliament. That is how I have to try and support Ministers in using our finite budget.

We will continue to do that as best as we can—to stretch the money to as many farmers as we possibly can to support that transition. Obviously, I would like SFI27 to be much more orderly than the second window of SFI26. We will absolutely be learning the lessons with Ministers on what we can do.

I cannot guarantee that there will not be challenges. That is because the mismatch between the number of farmers who are coming forward wanting to take environmental land management actions, and the budget available to pay for them, continues.
Q116 Thank you for that, Rachel. At the beginning, I said you had underspent your critical agricultural budget by £350 million. Do you disagree with that?
I did not recognise that number. I am not disagreeing. It is just not a number I am familiar with.
Q117 Can the Committee know whether you have underspent your budget over consecutive years? I think you have. In fact, I know you have, so perhaps you can confirm.
Over the last two years we have spent just under £5 billion through the farming budget.
That is not the issue. You have opened and closed an SFI window, and you have added £40 million, but you still underspent your budget, so it is not a matter of being short of money, is it?
I am happy to write to the Committee on that.
Yes, if you would clarify that, it would be really helpful. Thank you, permanent secretary.

Q118 Given that we have moved on to the subject of SFI and I was not able to be in for the statement, I thought I might take the opportunity to talk about the experience of my smaller farmers. One of the challenges is that some of the very large landholders seem to have been better able to access some of the funding opportunities. Am I right that efforts were made to create a separate window of opportunity for the smallest farms to apply for some funding? Would you look at revising that as we move into the ’27 round, to recognise that there are some that fall above that very smallest farm but who we need to distinguish from the largest farms to make sure the scheme recognises the size, scale and variety of farms we have across the country?
I think we have covered that point, but do you want to recapitulate it?

Very briefly. You are right: there were a few things we did to make sure that small farmers had better access to SFI this time around than previously. One of those was that we inserted a cap of £100,000 as the maximum amount any individual farm could have. Previously about 25% of the SFI budget went to just 4% of farmers, so we inserted a cap in order to be able to spread the money more broadly.

We had an initial window that ran in a very successful and orderly fashion, getting money—I think about £70 million—out to either smaller farmers or to those who had not been in an ELM scheme previously. You are right: there is always a question about the definition of small farms. We can no doubt look again at that definition. Sorry, please do not take that as a hint that we might change it; I have absolutely no idea, but there is always a reasonable question about how we define small farming.
On behalf of my farmers, I appreciate you taking that feedback.
Mine too. We can help you define what a small farm is because I have loads of them.

I thank you all very much. I reiterate that there is a lot of worry out there in the farming community. People have been farming for generations, wondering if the next generation is going to be able to carry on. If farmers cannot make a profit, they will not be there to grow food, and the country will ultimately face a disadvantage to that effect. I think that your Ministry needs to recognise the despair out there in the farming industry and do all it can to reassure farmers that there is a future. I am not actually sure that I have heard this morning that there is a future for some of the farmers in my patch who live on pretty poor soils and who are deeply concerned about their future. I leave you with that message; it is a serious message. If you want to hear how my farmers are getting on, you are very welcome to come to one of my quarterly meetings to hear directly from them. I can even take you round some of those farms. I extend that invitation to you.
You are going to be visiting a lot of farms.
I visit a lot of farms already, but I am very happy to visit more in your constituencies.

I thank all three of you very much. An uncorrected version of the transcript will be available in the coming days. We will produce a report, no doubt on the whole of the food and farming resilience week that we have had, with recommendations. I hope that you will study those carefully. We look forward to seeing you again in the future to see how you have progressed with some of the things you have said today.

segs.tx: Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee
Oral evidence: Tourism , HC 143
Tuesday 13 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 13 October 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Dame Caroline Dinenage (Chair); Mr Bayo Alaba; Nigel Huddleston; Dr Rupa Huq; and Jeff Smith.
Questions 1 to 86
Witnesses
I : Chris Haslam, Chief Travel Writer, The Sunday Times ; and Vicky Philpott, t ravel b logger and c ontent c reator.
II : Jamie Christon DL, Chief Executive, Chester Zoo ; and Alex Polizzi, h otelier, b usinesswoman and t elevision p resenter.
Examination of witness es
Witnesses: Chris Haslam and Vicky Philpott .

Q1 Welcome to this meeting of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Select Committee. Today we have the first session of our inquiry into tourism. The first panel is Chris Haslam, the Chief Travel Writer of T he Sunday Times , and Vicky Philpott, also known as VickyFlipFlop, who is a travel blogger and content creator. You are both very welcome. Thank you so much for joining us today. Before we begin, I remind members to declare any interests at the point that you ask your questions.
I will kick us off, starting with Chris. Do you think that tourists’ expectations and priorities have changed very much in recent years?
Generally speaking, all kinds of tourists, globally or jus t in the UK?
The UK.

Habits have changed. The 14-night holidays are a thing of the past. The average length of a holiday now is about 9.6 days. We are seeing people trading down. Expenditure and duration have been falling away ever since 2021 when tourism peaked post-pandemic. People are trading down — either spending less time in destinations or less time and staying in cheaper properties in destinations.

We have seen a move , across Europe and in the UK, from traditional accommodation — hotels, guesthouses, B&Bs — into short-term rentals, known as STRs, the Airbnb type thing. Within a very short time, that has grown to take probably 20% to 25% of the market. Hotels and traditional accommodation is now around 40% to 45% .

Let me just look at my notes to see what else has changed in the past few years. I have said about downsizing and shifting away. Funnily enough, something across Europe now that gives you an indication of how tight spending is and how little disposable income people have—it is not just the UK; I heard it in Spain as well—is people self-catering in hotels. Cleaning staff go into hotel rooms and find supermarket bags in the UK, in Spain , and last week I heard about it in Switzerland as well.

The general indication is that there is much less money around but the joke is that people, particularly the British, will put the holiday before the kidney replacement. They will always prioritise travel but they are having to cut their cloth to suit their budgets.

Q2 Vicky, what are you seeing? Are you noticing th at people’s priorities for their travel are changing? Do they prioritise experiences over destinations? What are people prioritising when they go on their holiday s ?

I think that as a priority they want a new experience that they can maybe put on their social media and they can talk about, something they have never done before. It is not really going to somewhere known and just lying on the beach. They want to be out doing things, entertaining the children with whatever they can, going to the coolest cafes and more interesting, adventurous travel.
Q3 To what extent do you think the UK destinations have responded to these changing priorities and, to Chris’s point, the changing finances?

A lot of attractions and places are making them more visually interesting and having activations there where you can take Instagram photos and tag them, ways to share the experience easily and things that you have to do when you go to a destination. I think they are trying to add to the experiences there by creating Instagramable-visual things to do there.

Q4 Chris, expanding on what you said earlier about the pressures on finances and the changing patterns of how people are spending their money, how successfully do you think UK destinations have adapted to these changes?

I don’t think they have really adapted to it at all. They do n o t know whether this is a permanent change or a temporary change. Everyone is hoping for the best that people will choose more. Adding to what I said about changing habits, my area of expertise is the British coast, the UK seaside, and overnight stays in the British seaside have dropped by 18% in the past 10 years. Not only that , but the average duration of short breaks has gone from 3.3 days down to 2.9 days. I just wanted to add that in answer to your previous question.

On the industry’s preparedness for shorter durations, shorter stays, they are not ready for it , but I want to make clear that this is not uniquely British. This is exactly the same across Europe. There is an article in the Spanish trade press this morning talking about how hotels have been hit by the fact that people are spending so little money in hotels. They are not going to restaurants and spas. They are not buying all those extra things. They are not doing it in the UK either. The problem is if you are going to offer spas and 24-hour dining, you have to have the staff there, so you are not taking the money but you are still spending on the provision.
Q5 That sounds unsustainable in the long term. Good news for you : at least two Committee members represent coastal potential tourist destinations, Bayo and me, so we can liaise with you later.

Vicky, quite a lot of what you do talks about how families can still go away even though they might have financial constraints as the cost of living pressures are mounting up on them. What do you see that families prioritise when they are deciding whether a holiday offers good value for money?

I think it is the overall experience and the cost of the overall experience. As Chris said, people are prioritising self-catering because obviously that can save a lot of money. Then there is a whole movement online of travel hacks and money - saving travel hacks, like booking a hotel room and making meals with your hotel kettle, and just ways that people can save on things like that so that they can spend it on experiences and getting out.
Thank you. Let me turn to my fellow coastal MP.
Q6 Good morning to you both. My first question is to both of you. What determines whether UK residents will choose domestic holiday destinations rather than overseas locations?

I will tell you what the facts are, what the statistics show. The average British family—and that is husband, wife and two kids—takes about three to four holidays a year. The re will be the big summer trip, almost always the southern Med or maybe Florida or the US, but it is generally an overseas trip. They will also take another trip during the year, possibly at half - term, which is either going to be short-haul Europe or the UK coast. They will then take one or two further breaks during the year, which could be a weekend away in the UK or a city break. That is the general model at the moment. The average spend for all that, according to things like GfK and ABT A data, is about £7,500. I don’t believe that. I think it is a lot more than that now.

Going back to your question about what makes them choose, the one driver with the British holidaymaker is value : the money, the cost. The permanent constant problem with UK holidays is the high cost. For example, if you wanted to go away to a famous four star hotel in Cornwall at May half-term next year, that will cost you £1,020 per person B&B. You can have a week all - inclusive in the Algarve for £960 or a week all - inclusive in the Costa de Almer í a in Spain for £678. It is not competitive.

Bear in mind that I just said that was £1,020 per person B&B. If you add a modest £30 a day per person for lunch, dinner, drinks, ice creams, things like that, that takes the full price up to £1,200, so it is twice the price of going to Spain. That is one of the biggest drivers and it increasingly makes the glamorous side of the British coast, the north Cornish coast, the south Devon coast, more and more a middle - class destination.
You did n o t mention the Essex coast, but we will come to that in a second.
I can talk about that.
Q7 Vicky, would you like to add to that?

I think the cost of holidays in school holidays is escalating out of control. A holiday point I was looking at was £700 for four nights at the start of May but then in the May half-term it was three and a half times as much at £2,386 . T hat is just for basic lodging, no food or anything like that. That is making it totally prohibitive for people to go on holiday.

Q8 I represent Southend, a beautiful part of the country, very historic, but, as you mentioned, over a generation or so it has lost out to international travel. You mentioned that your experience and speciality is coastal communities. What should communities like Southend do to increase their appeal to the tourism market?

I am going to make a position statement here. I have travelled almost everywhere. I can’t tell you how many countries I have been to in my job, so I am in a position of authority when I say that the British coast is the most beautiful on earth, without doubt the most beautiful, and I have seen almost everywhere. I have not been to Chechnya but I do n o t think they have a coast.

The other thing you need to bear in mind is that the great British seaside is almost a figment of our imagination. If you look at the history of the British seaside, it was developed for short-term gain. You need a lot of money to maintain those massive Victorian buildings with all that wrought iron, all that decoration and grandeur . T hat money is not there and it never was there during the 12-week season. The season is longer now than it was at the height of the British seaside. It was never built to last and the idea that we go back to what we had is ludicrous .

T hat said, what can Southend do? I think there are two very different towns to look at : Bude in north Cornwall and Great Yarmouth in Norfolk. Great Yarmouth was a moribund classic Victorian resort with piers and all the attractions that you would expect, winter gardens, in a state of decay , near collapse. It was not quite up to H M O level but it was getting there. Bude, on the other hand, is a little country town on the north coast of Cornwall.

Great Yarmouth has benefited from external funding. First off, its council has gone for every grant it can get from the Government — the small town scheme, the community trust scheme, heritage funding. It has gone for everything , but it also has a big income stream from offshore energy, renewables. It has a lot of money and it is transforming that place. It is astonishing how it has grown in the past two years. That is one way that you can change fortune.

The cheaper way to change fortune is to engage the community , and Bude is the exemplar of that. If you have ever been on a British beach and seen the # 2MinuteBeachClean stand, there will be a litter picker and some bags. That was an idea that came out of Bude. Bude is the only place, apart from South Shields—it is one of the two places in the country — that has a coastal parliament made up of citizens who make decisions about what their town needs to survive and thrive. That is all community engagement. It is almost the polar opposite to the Great Yarmouth model using external funding. It is from within and it has succeeded. I write The Sunday Times beach guide and it won beach of the year this year, and that is a tough competition that Southend ha s never won.

Q9 Yes, it is interesting. Southend is definitely one of the fastest growing seaside towns for day visitors but not overnight, which is something that we have touched on. This takes me to my question. Vicky, you were talking about the experience being very important , and that is quite big for my constituency of Southend because of its growing day visitor base. What should UK destinations do to increase the experience? You spoke about the visual elements. What else should they be doing to attract families?

I have lived in Portsmouth for the last nine years. I moved there to be by the sea, because I am from the m idlands. Something that Portsmouth does really well is to have so many events every weekend, especially through the summer . P eople are coming down to join in the music festivals, food festivals, car festivals. There is all sorts going on throughout the summer and I think that helps to bring in people. One of our main festivals is Victorious , and a lot of people come and are so impressed by Southsea and Portsmouth that they come back. I have evidence of this.

Events like that are important to bring people in because they might not necessarily have thought of Portsmouth or they might think of it in years gone by when it was not the most attractive place to go, but now they have done a lot work on the seafront and it is looking good. There is a lot to do there. The Portsmouth marine dockyard is the biggest attraction but then it is nice just being there. It is a very arty place, coffee shops, so people want to come back. After they have been to these festivals, they want to come back and see more.
And then pop over to Gosport, of course.

Q10 The Government are quite keen for regional mayors to have more say. There is talk about overnight visitor levies. What is your view, your position , on visitor levies for coastal communities, or even for any tourist attraction area?

I think if you can directly see that it is benefiting where you are staying , then great, but if the money just disappears—maybe if there was a way for it to pay for something tangible that you can see and say, “This is what we got from the levy” rather than just saying it was distributed.

I don’t think I ever seen any evidence of tourism levies making the slightest difference to visitor intent. They come anyway. No one is not going to go to St Ives because they have to pay £5 extra a night. They will still go. If anything, tourism levies are way too low to make any differenc e and I think they could go a lot higher. Y ou could probably start charging people to get into museums as well, because they are coming.

Q11 My last question is : if there was an opportunity for communities to have package offers—train, hotel accommodation and so on, maybe even into one or two attractions—is that something that communities or towns or cities could do to support their local communities? I know how that is administered could be a challenge but is it something that communities should be thinking about?

It is an interesting idea. Every large city has something like the London P ass, so maybe they could work together and create something, maybe offer vouchers to help consumers. I think that would work.

I am interested that you say that because the systemic challenge faced by domestic travel in the UK is that it is up against a mature, efficient, highly polished industry that takes people, puts them on planes and delivers them by bus to the door of a hotel with a water park in it and it is all inclusive. That is the outbound travel agent, but if you look in the window of any travel agency in the UK and see how many UK offers are there , t here might be a coach trip to go and see “Mamma Mia” but there is no equivalent. UK domestic is up against this huge machine of the travel industry. It does not have the equivalent.

That is the same in other countries , but in Spain, for example, Turespaña has been massively successful at promoting Spain to Spanish people. It created the España Verde campaign, which completely transformed Galicia, Asturias and the Basque Country and turned that into a massive tourist attraction. That is the equivalent of finding a new Cornwall in the UK. Andalucía is always popular with everybody but it had a campaign called Andalucía te quiere, bringing people from all over Spain.

I do n o t know if it is VisitEngland or VisitBritain — I do n o t know what they do . I do n o t hear from them ever, and I am in the industry. I think it is about stronger representation—if it is not going to come from the private sector, it will have to come from the public sector—of British tourism attractions to the British people, something like the English Tourist Board. That is my answer.

In answer to packages, yes, definitely. There is only one all-inclusive hotel in the UK. It is on the Norfolk coast or Suffolk coast, called Hopton ’ s , near Lowestoft . Packages is a very good idea. I do n o t know how it would work , though.

Q12 Good morning. Before I ask my questions, I was very interested in what you said, Chris, about the Bude and Great Yarmouth examples. Are there others that we can look at where they have managed the transition from the traditional pier arcade?

Amble in Northumberland was a derelict former coal port and the community took the harbour over and turned it into a fabulous tourist attraction. It started with a coffee shop and it is great now. If you get hold of old pictures of Amble from maybe 20 years ago and look at the high street going down to the harbour and now look at the way prosperity has radiated back up the high street, you see that it has gone from being pound shops to boutiques and there is a deli. It is almost like Southwold. Amble is a good one. Hastings is another good one. It turned a huge derelict department store into a community art centre. It puts on gigs there and there are craft breweries. Again, it is the community.

Bournemouth ’s south beach is also a very good example. It was a neglected beach at the far end. Bournemouth is one of the most beautiful beaches in Europe if treated properly by those who look after it, the council. South beach renovated a patch of neglected beach. They put a double-decker bus down there and turned it into a café. They were holding classes for children , for veterans, for the lonely, for widows. It became a proper community asset, used by the whole community, and brought tourists into the beach.

Now the lease has run out and the council is saying, “You have to go. We are going to give someone else the job.” They do n o t mind that. They do n o t mind going if someone else comes straight in but it could take two years, at which time south beach just collapses again.
Q13 Does any organisation bring all these coastal resorts together and learn from each other’s experience?
No.
Q14 Thank you. The questions I was going to ask you are about how people discover the places they choose to go on holiday. What has the biggest influence on a tourist’s choice of destination?

I think it will be what they have seen on social media, places going viral. It used to be the Lonely Planet effect where Lonely Planet would mention something but now if it has gone on TikTok, everyone else starts going.

Definitely social media, definitely TikTok, also traditional media. Some 24% of our unique views on The Sunday Times are for UK destinations, which is extraordinary because we cover the entire world. There is a lot of interest from that, particularly in new hotels.

Q15 That is quite a change in just the very recent years from traditional travel journalism and official tourism promotion to social media. S hould the UK, VisitBritain , just get loads of influencers in to promote the UK destinations?

I think a lot of TikTok and Instagram is what has come naturally, not necessarily the tourist boards putting their information out. It is organic posts that randomly do really well rather than a targeted thing, but obviously they should do that as well. They do include influencers and invite influencers on trips and invite them to try new places out, but I think it is quite hard to make something go viral.
Q16 It seems that everything now is influenced by AI. Have you seen any influence from AI in the travel industry?
I think it is quite negative.
How does it work?

I will give you a very quick example. A guy at the WTM two years ago told me to choose a random travel video from YouTube , and it turned out to be a German having a long weekend in London. We put that URL into an AI travel agent called Mindtrip and it scanned it and came back with exactly the same itinerary, where to stay, where to go, “ Tower Bridge ? T his is the time to get there. ” Not only that, going through the user’s Google records to find out what shops he goes to, what food he buys , it recommended restaurants and hotels. It was absolutely personalised.

That was terrifying to see but , that said, travel agents talk about it all the time. At every conference you go to, there is a module on AI : is it going to steal our jobs? They have either got their heads in the sand or they are being extremely sanguine but they are saying no because you are always going to need humans behind AI. They are seeing it as a tool that travel agents can use rather than something that would make travel agents redundant.
Q17 Do you think it is the latter?

When I first started in this industry 29 years ago, I was told to write an article called “The travel brochure is dead” and you still get travel brochures. They are still making the glossy brochures. No, I don’t think it will put travel agents out of business but I think they will have to adapt.
Q18 Vicky, do you use it? You probably use it in your writing.

I have used it for research , but I am of the stance that people will always want people. I think that is why social media is so influential because people see actual people like them doing the trips that they want to do and then they can recreate it rather than just typing it in and an AI avatar telling you what to do. I would not follow that information. I would want a real person.
Q19 Do either of you know of any examples in other countries where they have successfully harnessed social media to promote their destinations?
Dubai . R emember during the pandemic? That backfired a little bit because no one else could travel. Malaysia is good at it. I do n o t think anyone else is good.
That is helpful. Thank you.

Q20 Chris, given the rise of creator-led content on travel, is there still a place for travel journalism and travel journalists like you? What do you bring to the table that would not be there otherwise?

We see a lot of suspicion and fatigue in our readers of the whole notion of influencers and of a certain amount of travel writing as well. It is basically you have a free holiday and write something nice about it, so there is a lack of critical analysis . W hat we can bring to it is critical analysis. If we think something is rubbish, we will say it is rubbish. That has changed. In the past, not so much at my newspaper but in other traditional media, there was the idea that if you can’t say anything nice about it, don’t write it, but that has changed now because the public need it.
Yes, you tell it like it is.
You have to tell it like it is.

Q21 I still like using Rough Guides and Lonely Planet guides. Do you think they are on their way out as an influence or do they for that reason, the honesty and the rigour, maintain their market share?

I think people still like them and it is just a different way of giving the information and a different way for people to receive it. One of my friends has just written the Cornwall guide but she is also a travel influencer. I think it is seeing it from those two different perspectives, from the influencing and maybe getting free things to make the video , whereas with Lonely Planet she is not allowed to get anything at all. It is interesting to see the different approaches.

Q22 These are really interesting answers. They remind me of that Morrissey song “Every Day Is Like Sunday ”— I think it is about Blackpool, the seaside town they forgot to shut down. Some of the things you are describing are a bit sad, the infrastructure not being up to scratch in some of the regional destinations.

I used to get my trip to the seaside with party conferences — Bournemouth, Blackpool. I remember seeing Tony Blair at Blackpool. I think they have stopped using those because, as you have said, they just can’t cope any more. We are doing a trip to Blackpool, aren’t we? Is the onus going away from these regional seaside towns to cities? They used to be conference venues. The N U S conference used to be in Blackpool twice a year I remember.

I can no t remember the statistic but the vast majority of—as I said, the seaside has dropped off 18% in the past 10 years but overall overnight trips have also dropped off. They have dropped by 12% since 2021 for the time people are spending away from home in the UK.

Event tourism is big now. You will fill this city up for Taylor Swift or you will fill Manchester up for Oasis. They are not playing in the seaside ; they are playing in the cities because that is where you can get the crowds in and where the infrastructure exists to get that many people into a venue and out. The truth is that many of our seaside towns are in a terrible state of decline. Blackpool is one — Eastbourne, Bognor Regis.

Q23 Could they be brought up to scratch? The party conference s, Neil Kinnock falling over in the sand — that used to be part of the thing, when the faithful would get a trip away, whereas now going to—
Is that why they did it? I did not realise it was so that—
Do you remember? Am I the only one of my generation who remembers any of it?

If I can come in there, o ne of the things is the capacity. I was party chair for a while and we were looking into these. We need for both of the big conferences, Labour and Conservative, 6,000 to 10,000 rooms . T he harsh reality is that Blackpool just cannot cope with that now.
Even Brighton we have stopped using. Has Brighton gone forever? It is too small?
It is not just numbers; it is security and things like that , t housands of room s for police.
Q24 We talk ed about events . I see coming up on my feed things like Butlin ’ s 19 80s night, Butlin ’ s ska night, Britpop night. Is that the way forward for these venues?
I think that saved Butlin ’ s, moving into those big weekenders. It is a mini festival every weekend.
Q25 Is it still struggling?
I do not know, but I know that those weekends are very popular and they cross pretty much every genre.
Q26 You were asked about travel . A re people from overseas coming to our seasides?

We get 43 million visits from overseas here every year and they spend £33 billion, but they are mainly from the US, then from the EU, then from Asia-Pacific, then from Middle East. They spend an average of eight nights here, but they go to, in order: London, Edinburgh, Cambridge, Oxford , and recently Manchester is popular. T hey do not go to the seaside.
Q27 Is England not aggressively marketed? A n aggressive marketing campaign would not be enough because the stuff is not up to scratch?

You are right : it is not quite up to scratch. It is very seasonal. A lot of our seaside towns are beautiful on a summer’s day, but as soon as the sun goes in in wintertime, they are just ghastly. We have an issue with the British seaside in that because it declined as an industry from the late 19 60s onwards due to the rise of the package holiday, many of our seaside towns have become retirement homes because the property was cheap and people could move to the seaside ; t he British dream to retire to the seaside.

However, there is no youth there. The young people have had to move away to the cities. Bude is different because people always come back to Bude, but that is what makes it unique. Most places they leave, they do not come back. So you have a place that is effectively a retirement colony. The season is only 12 weeks long . T he industry is all focused on making as much money as you can in the season and not investing.

If you think of those huge Victorian properties along the seafront in Bognor or Eastbourne : the cost of maintaining those is staggering. Who is going to take on a great big building and open it as a seaside hotel? In Cromer, Norfolk, we have the Hotel de Paris, opened in 1888 by a Parisian hotelier who swore the future was in the British seaside. It is now almost derelict.

T he southern Med ha s serious issues going forward. L ook at any climate science you like, but if you take World Weather Attribution or CRS, the prediction is that by the middle of this century one in two summers will be detrimental to health. We will have blisteringly hot summers detrimental to health, with a 50% frequency. It is supposed to be one in 10 now, although it is not.

W e have already seen something called coolcation s ; e veryone talks about coolcations now. They do not really exist in the UK yet, but the idea is that people flee the summer heat to the northern climes, to get away from the heat and enjoy it. We talk about people going to Finland, Lapland, but the UK is in the perfect position to grasp that opportunity and to profit from it. We have the seaside resorts; we have properties within the seaside resorts. When we see the migration of people from the south, people from Spain, Italy and Greece will be coming on holiday in the UK, Ireland, Netherlands, Scandinavia.
Q28 When was this?
This would be by the middle of this century. This is the prediction.
A long time to go.
Well , it is only 20 years away.

Q29 Vicky, you are a blogger . I just wondered how far TripAdvisor ratings affect where people go, and how manipulable are they? I am an academic and I remember people used to review each other’s books and, say, give it 10 out of 10. C ould you muck about with those things?

I think reviews are very controversial because anyone can leave them and you can be really annoyed at something—you see reviews where people are moaning that a mountain was too windy and things like that. It is not a science ; it can just be an opinion in that moment. A one-star review can totally drag them down, and competitors can do it. I used to work at a company called Hostel Bookers and competitors of the hostels would book a one-night stay, so they would only have to pay the deposit, and they would drag each other down with the reviews.
Okay, I am being told to shut up.
We are just trying to keep to time. Thank you very much . L et ’s move on to Nigel.

Q30 I refer hon. Members to my entry in the register of M ember’s interests and declare that I previously worked in the tourism sector, was a tourism M inister and shadow M inister, and I have taken hospitality from players in this sector previously.

Chris and Vicky, thank you. There is so much that you have already mentioned. One area that I would like to look into is how can, and should, our tourist destinations or individual attractions or hotels differentiate themselves? Chris, you have alluded to this a little bit. I magine two touris t resort s that are similarly beautiful with similar beach es: what makes the difference in terms of controllable things that either a local authority or an individual hotel can do?

Vicky, you are probably familiar with this. What I am thinking here is things like cleanliness, basic customer service, access to toilets — those practical things that can differentiate one place versus another and make something stand out or , indeed , people complain. I will come to you first , Vicky.

There are a lot of things that you can do to add value to a destination or attraction. If we are already paying all the money that it costs —and some people would deem some attractions too expensive — yo u can add value by being kind, the place being clean , by people helping you and having maybe more things to do there, especially for the kids . If there is an app or even just some activities for the kids to do while they are there, I think you can add value in that way . I t is not necessarily all about what they are directly doing.

There are different ways they can make it a better attraction and more appealing to people, and make people want to tell their friends about it as well , so that it can either come in from word of mouth or through them sharing it on social media.

If you speak to anyone who has been to Disneyworld in the US, the one thing they always say is it is so clean. We have seen real big problems in the west of this country where councils have stopped emptying bins, closed public toilets and depended on the private sector to provide toilets, and the private sector charges 50p to use it. That causes distress. It is very simple. Divesting car parking to ANPR — people are furious about that. If you do not buy your ticket within three minutes, £60 fine in the post, rapidly becoming £200.

That is what gets people’s goat. It is a very easy fix, if you have the money for the local council to keep it clean, keep the facilities open, make sure the toilets are clean, make sure the bins are emptied and make sure the car parking is fair.

Q31 Following the pandemic, we had a staycation boom, and lots of people were saying, “First time I have had a domestic holiday in ages; it is great, really enjoy ed it”. Chris, you have come up with some quite alarming figures about numbers declining recently . Y ou have mentioned value for money in the prices and that it is very expensive in the UK. Is that the killer? Is it all about the money and the cost?

It is and it isn ’ t. Yes, it is, but it is the same everywhere. I looked at the top complaints in the German, Spanish and French media, and it is exactly the same. Top of it is cost of living, the price. The other thing that I thought was uniquely British was the service window : t he fact that you walk into almost any British pub at 8 o’clock in the evening and the kitchen is closed, “Sorry, you can’t eat”. You end up with families sitting in cars eating fish and chips. It is t he same argument in Germany, France and Spain. I do not think that our travel industry is as bad as we sometimes think it is. In many ways, it is better than other countries ’ .

I just want to say that one of the biggest things in the UK is the state of the waters , e verything that Surfers Against Sewage is doing . T he amount of sewage getting pumped in is huge with the decline in coastal accommodation and holidays, because it is not as fun to go in the sea any more. Even if they say it is a clean sea, you still have it in your head that it is where they pump sewage in.

There is a place in Portsmouth by the pier that is probably one of the most populated parts of Portsmouth — everyone is coming to the beach . Y ou are not meant to swim in that bit year round, it is condemned, but people still do. That is shown around England. I was recently in Northumberland on a beautiful beach, and there was toilet roll everywhere. I check on the app and it says that there has just been a sewage discharge there. I think that is a huge part of what is affecting coastal tourism in the UK.

Can I add to that? The difference is that we have DEFRA doing samples on bathing water throughout the season; 20 samples throughout the season every year. They then rate the beaches, but when you go to a beach, say Cromer beach, next year, you will be looking at last year’s ratings . I t had three stars, so it was good last summer. The peril on the British beaches is the CSO discharges, the c ombined s ew er overflow discharges , which can happen at any time. As Vicky has said, we are now depend e nt on private sector apps to find that out: Surfers Against Sewage, Safer Seas & Rivers Service. That is a massive turn - off for the British coast now .

Q32 That concern of the British public, and indeed overseas visitors, for the impact of their tourism on the environment and sustainable tourism has been going round for a while, but do we need to worry in the UK about overtourism, or is that fabricated?

That is Cornwall, everyone going to Cornwall when there are so many beautiful places. This year, in the heatwaves, I went up to Northumberland and on the beaches there was barely anyone about. I had come from Portsmouth where the roads were blocked , and everyone is going to Cornwall and Dorset. There are definitely areas, like Cornwall, where everyone is going, but there are many beautiful parts of the UK that people are not. It is a problem.

Q33 How do we deal with that? We talked earlier on about the tourism tax, which I am personally dead against because I think we are already very expensive and should not be taxing the sector more. However, there is an argument about it . I t looks like it is being brought in. One logic of the tourism tax is to inhibit overtourism, such as Venice and so on.
No, it is not.
Well, some of the argument for that is.
We disagree on this one.
Yes. Well, the logic overseas is, is the point I am saying. I s that part of something we should do here in the UK?
Tourism tax?
Yes, as a tool to depress tourism numbers?
I do not think we want to stunt them, do we?
No.
Right, okay. I am a bit leading there.

Q34 You have seen in areas like Barcelona and Venice there have been objections by local residents to the volume of tourists coming in, and you do begin to sense that a little now in some parts of Cornwall, where the resident population is completely overwhelmed in the height of summer by this huge ingress of visitors.

It is a double-edged sword, because these are areas whose economy entirely relies on the visitor economy, but equally they can sometimes become swamped in the summer months, making it unbearable for those who live there all year round. Is there a balance where the taxation could be used to try to find a happy medium to that?

I would need to think about that more because, as you say, these places want all those people but at the same time it is a problem, like in the Cotswolds and the Lake District where people are parking on people’s gardens . I am not sure how a tourist tax would help those people.

It would need to be a significant tourist tax to deter anyone. As I said, £5 extra is not going to stop anyone going to Porthmeor Beach in Saint Ives. More to the point is looking at seasonality and extending the season. At the moment, all the traffic is happening within three or four months, when everyone is piling into the British seaside. The g ood resorts are working to extend seasonality . T hat is an initiative within the private sector and the public sector.
Q35 To what extent is that dictated by school holiday times rather than just weather?

If we go back to the model at the beginning, the way the British travel on their big holiday is almost always overseas, so a package holiday to the Med in general. They would not be coming to the UK in the summer months anyway. They would not be spending July in Cornwall, although some people are. The issue is to spread it out more across the year. If we are taking four holidays in the year, if there was something that would attract us down to, say, Cornwall, or the Gower Peninsula, or the Llŷn Peninsula, in October.

One thing that has transformed the British seaside is neoprene, because now you put the kids in a wetsuit and it does not matter if it is raining, 12 degrees; they will have fun all day. That has been transformative o n the UK coast. It is not that we only go to the seaside in the summer, when it is sunny.

Q36 This is one of the points that we will be looking at very carefully here, because you have hit the nail on the head: seasonality is the key to the success of British tourism. It will help with productivity, all the problems with people getting a job in the summer and then being un employed for six months, all that kind of thing. If we can extend the seasonality, that is the magic thing, but how do we do that in the UK, recognising the challenges of the weather?
There is a lso school holidays. You get charged to take the children out, so there is no way that parents of school - aged children can do that.
There is a lso the 3 million people who work in the tourism sector who cannot have a holiday with their own families because they are working in the peak season.
You can obviously extend it for people without school - aged children, but some have no option.

Q37 There is l ots to cover, yes. Chris can I just challenge you again on the tourism ? I know what you are saying £5 probably would not make a difference, but £50 would. Given what you said earlier on about people coming to a caravan and then the first thing they do is the Lidl shop rather than go to the pub, bar or restaurant nearby , I think you are right that a few pounds here would not make a difference . However, there is that magic point at which the tourism tax, if levied in an appropriate way, could make the difference in people’s decision to go. Do you think that might be the case?

Yes, it would. A per person tax, suppose you made it £10 per person for a caravan park in Lincolnshire, that is £40 extra for a family. They are going to say, “No, we w ill not go there”. T hen, going back to your thing about overtourism, they go, “W here can we go that has not got a tourist tax? ”
Q38 So the way that the tourism tax is implemented, and the dynamics and one region versus another , is also important here? Yes.

We could also just develop the UK as a low-volume, high-price destination. That would be another option. Rwanda and Bhutan have done it; Botswana has done it fantastically. The Balearic Islands are trying to do it, clamping down on STR — short-term rentals — and all-inclusive properties, trying to basically get people to come and spend more money. Fewer people, but spending more money.

Q39 Finally, is that one of the key things? We have been obsessed in the UK with domestic tourism or inbound tourism numbers, volume, as in 43 million or 100 million overnight stays. Do you think that is the wrong thing? You alluded earlier on that it is the length of stay and how much they are spending that is key.
I do not know, I am not an economist — but you think do we pile it high and sell it cheap or do we go for high-spending, low volume?

That is something that has been seen on the Isle of Wight, where they have had fewer visitors but they are all spending more money because it is the people who go to Cowes Week and other yachting things. T hey are seeing fewer people but they are spending more.
Remember the argument against that is we cannot make travel a pursuit for the elite, although “ elite ” is the wrong word. I mean the rich.
Q40 Just on that, how could we do the pile it high, sell it cheap, without the guarantee of good weather?
That is one of the troubles with the UK. It is unreliable weather, unreliable transport.
The weather is changing at the moment.
Yes, 40 degrees is not unusual any more.

No. That is something to look at in development of policy going forward: how can we profit from climate change rather than suffer? All those Spanish people are going to want to go on holiday somewhere.
Q41 On the fewer people and more money, what markets are we looking at? Are we looking at the Middle East or US?

The US already are spending a lot of money here. They stay for eight days and they spend a fortune. Their biggest complaint , though, the one thing you could do to change, is to bring back VAT - free shopping — tax - free shopping in the UK. That is the biggest complaint of all the foreign markets coming to the UK. They are going to Madrid; London’s loss is Madrid’s gain.
This Committee did recommend that we do that.

Q42 Yes, we did, a couple of times. I have a couple of extra questions . Y ou mentioned how areas like Galicia have been successful at attracting tourists away from your mainstream Spanish destinations. What could the UK learn from them? How did they do that? As you say, we have some amazing coastal locations, not all of them are right there in the heartlands of the tourist destinations, so what could we learn from areas like that?

What comes straight to mind when you ask that is do you remember those great railway posters for the seaside? Even now, you see those posters and you think, “Wow, I actually do want to go to Grimsby”— or wherever it is, Scarborough—“ I t i s so bracing”.
Skegness.

Skegness, yes, “ I t i s so bracing”. It is as simple as that. It is just to remind people—and it is not going to be the private sector because the travel industry does not deal with the UK ; it would have to be public sector somehow , reminding people how beautiful the UK is and what they are missing. We do it in our newspaper all the time.
Q43 How did the Spanish do it? How did they attract people to go to Galicia?

Turespaña, the Spanish national tourist board, but working i n conjunction with DMOs in the regions, said , “Let ’s promote your region; what have you got?” I t has worked so well, so much so there was an anti-tourism protest in Asturias two years ago. There is no definition of overtourism. It is like Father Christmas; if you think you have overtourism, then you have overtourism, but it is not defined. The increase in visitors had gone up by 0.02% .
