segs.tx: Transport Committee
Oral evidence: Scrutiny of the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement , HC 482
Tuesday 13 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 13 October 2026.
Watch the meeting
Members present: Ruth Cadbury (Chair); Steff Aquarone; Dr Scott Arthur; Jacob Collier; Daniel Francis; Olly Glover; Alex Mayer.
Environmental Audit Committee member present: Chris Hinchliff.
Questions 438 – 474
Witnesses
II : Professor Piers Forster CBE, Member , Climate Change Committee ; Dr James Richardson, Chief Analyst, Climate Change Committee.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Professor Piers Forster CBE and Dr James Richardson .
Q438 Good afternoon, could I ask you both to introduce yourselves?

Good afternoon. I am a member of the Climate Change Committee. I have been on the Committee since 2018, and I am one of the two aviation champions. I am also a climate scientist who has done particular work on aviation.
I am the chief analyst of the Climate Change Committee.

Q439 Excellent. The first question is on the draft HENPS climate test. In order to pass the climate test, the Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement states that any proposed scheme must not have a “ m aterial impact on the UK’s legally binding carbon emissions.” However, the draft NPS does not define the term “ m aterial impact.” How would you define it?

Inevitably the courts are going to end up defining the terms, but what we have said is that you have to look at the impact not just on the carbon budgets but on 2050 net zero, and the full impact when Heathrow is fully expanded. That could be after 2050, but you cannot just say the problem has gone away if it is later than 2050. You have to have a way of balancing any additional emissions from Heathrow within those targets. For 2050, if there is a plus from Heathrow expansion, there has to be an equivalent minus to get you back to net zero. On current policies that would not be achieved, but there are alternative policies that could be put in place before granting a DCO that would achieve that.
Q440 We will come to that. Would you expect material impact to be defined quantitatively or qualitatively?

It is bound to be a decision in the round to some extent because you have to look at what other parts of the economy could do, particularly engineered removals , because really you are not going to be able to deal with 2050 from other sectors such as buildings or surface transport. You have to be a little wary of putting a fixed number on it because that might encourage slightly heroic modelling assumptions to push you to one side or the other. However, if you say, “Look, actually, you have to show how this is compliant with the net zero target,” you are pushing people to really explain everything.

Q441 Your advice does not specify the volume of emissions caused by Heathrow expansion that would make it unviable. Do you think there should be a higher-end emissions threshold that means if it reached that, you would fail the climate test? If so, what should it be?

Again, the point really is that if Heathrow expansion leads to an increase in emissions, you have to have an offsetting equivalent amount to get you back to that net zero because it is a zero target. That could be from greater use of sustainable aviation fuels, it could be from engineered removals, but you have to get back to zero. You cannot rely on other parts of the economy to do the job for you because aviation is just too big.
Q442 Some witnesses have said to us that they do not feel there is a way that you can fail the climate test at the moment. Would you agree with that assessment?

If you made the amendments to it that we are proposing—to include the 2050 target, to include the full scope of full expansion—then there definitely would be a way of failing that. Indeed, we would say that under the current policy you would fail that test.
Q443 You have just spoken about your four recommended changes. What practical difference do you think those would make to the decision making?

The key thing here really is being clear on the face of the document that it is not just about the carbon budgets, which only run through to the early 2040s when the airport would not be fully open. It has to include that 2050 net zero target. It has to look beyond that as well so that the full scope of Heathrow expansion, which might come after 2050, is included. It must recognise that hitting net zero in 2050, you still have to do that or better in 2051, 2052 and so on. You cannot just say, “Well, the problem doesn’t arise if it’s after 2050.”
Q444 If those four changes that you suggest are not made, do you think that the whole document should be rejected?
You have to be clear about what the approach is. A test that does not include the net zero target is no test at all.
Q445 Thanks for coming, nice to meet you. You seem to be saying that we cannot rely on carbon savings elsewhere to offset the additional emissions from Heathrow Airport.

That is correct to the first order. The point of the Climate Change Act 2008 and the carbon budget framework we have is that they give the Government flexibility about which parts of the economy ought to be decarbonising. If you look at the reality of the aviation industry at that 2045 to 2050 timeframe, there are not a lot of alternatives there, basically.

If you are talking about other ways to compensate for carbon dioxide, you have the choice only between decarbonising aviation directly through sustainable aviation fuels and efficiencies, or potentially building up your removals. If there is a trade-off, it is a trade-off between those two components. It is a trade-off between direct action on the aviation industry and alternatively trying to build up a removal industry. If you look at our advice, we are quite clear that the aviation industry should be paying for the removals.

Q446 It is difficult to argue with the notion that the aviation industry . should pay for the removals, is it not? However, if the Government were to look elsewhere for emissions savings, you are saying that they cannot be found anywhere in the economy. It is not just the transport sector, you are saying anywhere in the economy. The Transport Secretary said that she thought the emissions could be offset holistically elsewhere.

To give the Transport Secretary some credit, it is explicitly allowed for within the Act to do that, but it becomes quite difficult in the case of aviation. The other factor to consider is that if you look at the residual emissions we have in the 2050 timeframe, the others come from agriculture and waste, for example, but that is in methane emissions predominantly. That is a short-lived greenhouse gas, which cannot really compensate for the climate effect of carbon dioxide.

Looking at it from a climate science point of view, you have to look for compensation in carbon dioxide. If you are looking at that, you actually cannot really take it from other bits of the economy. It is just the trade-off between aviation and the removals. Perhaps the Secretary of State could have been thinking of the Department for Transport, which has the responsibility for aviation, compared with DESNZ, which has the responsibility for the removals. Perhaps she is talking about a conversation between two Secretaries of State.

Q447 Okay. I do not want to put words in your mouth, but if the Government were to choose to focus more on agriculture to offset some emissions—the example you gave—while Heathrow is not going to use Government money, it is unlikely that the agricultural sector could accelerate reducing its emissions without Government support.
Yes, absolutely. Those emissions from agriculture are very difficult to get rid of. You would almost have to get rid of our livestock animals completely.

Q448 Some of our vegetarian friends maybe would not feel bad, but yes, let us leave it for another day. Is there an ethical issue here where we are saying “Actually, Heathrow is so important that we are going to ringfence those emissions and allow them, while other sectors have to make that sacrifice”? I was speaking to people today about reducing carbon emissions from road transport and how challenging that is right now. It seems unfair to people in that sector if Heathrow has some kind of special status. That is another leading question for you.

Yes. If you have a look at the sectors of the economy, practically all those other sectors will have completely decarbonised by that time. It is almost impossible to find any degree of compensation. You can look at one of our reports that outlines those compensations.

Q449 In terms of SAF and engineered removals, which have been mentioned, realistically, if you are investing your pension or your savings, are these products going to deliver over the time period required? Do we have confidence in that yet? SAF is nowhere near what we thought it was going to be two years ago. Can we have confidence that these things will come online at the time required?

We certainly do not have confidence currently. If you look at our advice, we are very, very clear that the investment and the policies really need to come in today to be able to deliver the technology by this timeframe. We want to see the Government policy put in, and we want to see significant investment that goes into aircraft efficiency, sustainable aviation fuel for the next generation and removals.

Q450 I do not expect you to have watched it but we previously discussed HS2. One of the criticisms was that HS2 would have worked if technology had been invented to allow it to work. Is there not that danger here , actually? Should we be cautious about approving expanding the airport before we have more certainty about engineered removals and SAF?

That is correct in some way, but the way out of it is to try to get airlines to pay for the cost of their carbon currently. It could then be up to the Government to decide what to do with that cost of carbon in some way. They could invest it in trying to scale up the technologies to make them more economical, for example. If they were to do that, that would also benefit other industries that also potentially rely on carbon capture and storage.

The challenge is affordability, which we will hear about tomorrow. What you are suggesting is just going to add to affordability, which just undermines further the business case. I am putting words in your mouth; maybe I should hand back to the Chair now.

Q451 We have moved on to SAF, which is fine, but I just want to go back to a clarification question on carbon budgets. Obviously, your overall regular reports cover aviation as a whole and in relationship to other sectors, but just in terms of this report on Heathrow, could you confirm which airport expansion projects are included within your Seventh Carbon Budget modelling? Does that include Gatwick, which only relatively recently passed its final hurdles? We have some other airport expansions that have growth in air traffic movements.
It includes all approved expansions within the modelling, including Gatwick.
Thank you, that is useful.

Q452 Just to pick up on Scott’s questions there about SAF and engineered removals, are there any implications for the wider sector of aviation on needing to rely very heavily on both SAF and engineered removals that you can foresee?

When we talk about the timeframe we are considering, we are talking about the second and third generation type of SAF here, particularly power-to-liquid. This does not necessarily have the same restrictions to it as some competition in the current SAF that are being produced with bio energy and pre-production. Of course, the next generation will be more expensive, and they also require a lot of renewable energy to produce them. There are not necessarily material restrictions, but there are certainly these financial ones.

Q453 The Government are relying on more SAF and engineered removals if this expansion goes ahead. How much more do you think is going to be needed on top of what is already required for the industry to decarbonise overall?
The estimate that we have is 4.5 million tonnes annually to compensate for the extra Heathrow expansion. The total removal in our net zero pathway is about 36 million tonnes, as far as I remember.
Q454 How much is being produced at the moment?
Zero.
Q455 You are not confident at the moment?
No.
Over to Chris, who will ask about polluter pays and carbon pricing. We have touched on that already.

Q456 I will try to go quickly, Chair. In your advice to the Government on Heathrow Airport expansion, you say that Government should legislate policies that require the aviation sector to abate 100% of its emissions before a development consent order for Heathrow. Can you provide a bit more detail about what timelines parliamentarians should be looking at for that legislation and what you would expect to see in that legislation, in order for us to feel comfortable that we have done our job scrutinising a DCO?

The key policy moment in this would be the revised jet zero strategy that the Government have committed to for next year. There are a number of mechanisms by which you could do this. We are not trying to specify exactly how you would do that. You could do it through the emissions trading scheme, through expanding the SAF mandate, or through creating an additional removals mandate. There are other ways. The key thing is it has to add up to 100% of removals by 2050. We would hope to see that through that jet zero strategy. That would then create enough time before the timescale—as we understand it, I know these things keep moving around—for a DCO at the end of 2029.

Q457 Thank you, that is very helpful. Picking up on that for my second question, following on from what my colleague was just getting to, there seems to be a fundamental issue that is difficult to reconcile at the heart of this. The DFT figures for carbon emissions associated with Heathrow expansion assume that—let me get this right—74% of Heathrow’s additional passengers come from other London airports.

If you assume that the airport expansions that are cumulatively going on all want to see passenger increase, then the additional carbon emissions are enormous. I understand that you as a Committee say, “Well, that could be offset by additional investment in SAFs. Make the aviation sector pay for that.” Does that not bring us to the point where the cost becomes so high that the whole thing becomes self-defeating, and the demand would not exist to justify the expansion in the first place?

There are a lot of things there. Let me try to unpack our position. First, what we are saying is that the growth in demand would be lower; it is not lower relative to today’s demand. In our pathway, the growth in demand relative to today is about 21%. In the Government’s, including Heathrow, it would be 64%. There is a big difference there in terms of demand growth. It is the growth in demand rather than the level of demand.

Then there is the question of how many airports do you want? Do you allow a competitive market? Do you centrally plan that? Those are issues for the Government, not for us. We assume in our modelling that there is displacement. If you expand Heathrow, there are fewer flights from other airports. I would not want to put any particular emphasis on which airports it would be. Airports would compete. The most successful would get them and others would not.

We are clear that the risk in this expansion should sit with the developers. It should not sit with the taxpayers or the flying public. If you own an airport and you choose to expand it and there is no demand, that risk should sit with the developers. Therefore, it is really important that it is clear to the developers what the policy pathway is and that they are not working on an assumption that we will never solve emissions but think, “Actually, we have to do that,” so the developers know whether there is actually going to be the demand or not.

That is another point about getting the Government to set out a viable pathway for the sector to net zero. Developers can then make their decisions. Obviously, those questions: is it one airport, two airports, or hubs are not for us. Those are for Government and the developers.
Q458 Does your demand modelling obviously include the carbon price?
Yes.
Q459 Does it include the construction cost: £35 billion divided by the passengers?
We have not specifically included that. There is obviously a question about how that would flow through, which is quite complicated.
Q460 That goes back to the point that was just being established earlier. Have you finished?
I have for now.
Let us get through this quickly and then there might be time for you to come back.

Q461 Your advice states that Government should be prepared to implement contingency measures if aviation emissions exceed the trajectory required for net zero. What specific measures do you have in mind to achieve that?

The big thing is we need to see the industry begin to pay for the cost of the carbon basically. There are lots of different ways of potentially doing that. From our scenario, it will make the cost of taking flights a bit more expensive. By doing that investment, they can potentially invest in the technology. That is also a way to suppress the increase in demand. It is required to suppress that increase in demand until these technologies become widely available because we have to also hit the interim carbon budget. If you look at the trajectory currently, we are not on course to hit the sixth carbon budget because of the increase in emissions that come from aviation.
Q462 Do you think Heathrow should be subject to ongoing climate performance tests if consent is granted? What is your view on how that should be looked at?

The key thing that James talked about before is that this revised jet zero strategy, when it comes out, will have to illustrate the way the Government plan to achieve this net zero aviation industry. That should be the key test to deciding whether expanding Heathrow Airport is compatible with our net zero policies. In terms of the ongoing checks on delivery, there ought to be ongoing checks of course that the jet zero strategy approach of the Government is delivering.

Q463 I would just like to follow on from what Daniel was saying. When Gatwick got the go-ahead to expand, some future growth is tied into meeting various environmental requirements but that is not in this Heathrow document. Would you be more comfortable if it was?
In a sense, it is the point we have made already in terms of being clear in the planning framework that any expansion has to be consistent with net zero.

Q464 Professor Forster, you mentioned earlier about the need for co-ordination between the DFT and DESNZ in relation to carbon budgets and the upcoming revision of the jet zero strategy. Where do you believe the ultimate accountability should lie if the expansion results in overshooting carbon budgets?

It is not my job to run the Government, but if I was the Secretary of State taking the decision, I would want a very frank conversation with DESNZ. If you look at the jet zero strategy of the Government, that ought to be across the Government Departments to deliver on.
Q465 You said that the Secretary of State for DESNZ should play a defined role in Heathrow expansion. In what way? How would you define it? How would you envisage that that would work?

The Secretary of State for DESNZ is responsible for the policies that will increase the removals, so they need to show that they can deliver these engineered removals. This is not just the 36 million tonnes; it is the extra that comes from the Heathrow expansion.

Q466 Let us move on to non-CO 2 emissions. If the non-CO 2 effects are not properly assessed, there is a level of risk that the overall climate impact of Heathrow will be underestimated or overestimated. The Committee appears to disagree with the Government as to whether the non-CO 2 effects can be quantified robustly enough to inform decision-making. Where is the difference of opinion on this?
This is my area of expertise. I am really pleased to talk about it.
Q467 Have you submitted on this basis?

Yes. We are very pleased that the HENPS document talks about non-CO 2 directly, but it could go a bit further than that. There is enough evidence to quantify the impact of non-CO 2 despite its uncertainty. There is a different way to do it. It is not necessary to include it within the carbon budget calculation, but that does not mean it should not be accounted for quantitatively in some way.
Q468 Do you have a methodology or evidence base that you feel could be used to give confidence in the non-CO 2 impacts?

We have one proposal in our Seventh Carbon Budget work, which is to have no more warming from non-CO 2 after 2050. That is what we proposed. That is the same sort of thing that could be considered with this.

Q469 Okay, we will dig that out from the Seventh Carbon Budget. I have just a final question on this issue. Is the risk sufficiently high that the decision whether to approve Heathrow expansion should be paused until an agreed method of quantifying non-CO 2 emissions is arrived at between your Committee and the Department?

There is still a lot more work that needs to be done to understand the exact role of non-CO 2 components and to try to look at ways we can reduce the non-CO 2 impacts. What we recommend is really that there are opportunities to put in trials and things, for example. If Heathrow were to get the go-ahead, it could do trials of reducing the non-CO 2 effects over the north Atlantic corridor, for example, where we expect the effect to be particularly pronounced.
Q470 Sorry, which corridor?
The north Atlantic corridor. There are a lot of contrails that develop when you fly between the UK and the States.
Q471 Is it possible for changes to the draft Heathrow Expansion NPS, as opposed to changes in other Government policy, to allay your concerns about the climate impact of Heathrow expansion?

We need the two. James talked about how the most important document is the revised jet zero strategy. That is the one that will give our Committee confidence that net zero aviation is a serious commitment from the Government and that they can introduce the policies to deliver a net zero aviation industry. As a Committee, we would like to see two documents. We would like to see that revised jet zero strategy and a reinforced HENPS.

Q472 On my Committee we have discussed multiple times the need to have contingency measures if we get off track, as we have already discussed. We have reached the point where in your advice on Heathrow you say that even before Heathrow Airport expansion, we do not have enough policy in place to decarbonise aviation. In your 2026 p rogress r eport you said that only 32% of aviation emission reductions in the Sixth Carbon Budget are supported by credible plans. We have the World Meteorological Organisation now expecting global average temperatures to breach 1.5°C by 2029, which previously we had not expected to be passed until 2045 when the Paris Agreement was being signed.

After the summer we have just had, my final question is, are we not in emergency time now? Is it not time to start applying the more stringent approach and firmer measures now, rather than continuing down a path of saying, “This is a risk, but we’ll have contingency to fall back to”?

We absolutely agree as a Committee that aviation is not currently on track to deliver the reduction required for the Sixth Carbon Budget. We need to see additional policies from the Government. The Government should absolutely prepare these contingencies and should be prepared to introduce them. As we said before, the industry needs to start paying for the cost of its pollution and the cost of carbon.

Q473 I just want to pick up a question from earlier on carbon pricing and affordability. Airlines have said to us in open session that affordability—in fact it is a Government consideration as well—should be a key consideration in Heathrow expansion. A third runway should only be provided if the costs to airlines, and therefore passengers, are not excessive and do not result in demand dropping. Is there any way to square that with the polluter pays principle?

There is no getting away from the fact that emissions are a cost. At the moment we are all facing that cost through blisteringly hot summers, droughts and floods. We are saying that the cost of tackling that should be addressed by the aviation industry. That will have an effect on the cost of flying. We are quite clear about that.

It is important to put that in context. We have said that a flight to Spain would add about £150 by 2050, but that should be phased in. You are looking at a few pounds a year. The impact of that will have an impact on overall demand. That is why our figures for overall demand are lower than the Government’s current policy figures, because of that cost. That is enough to address all this. It is still only a relatively small fraction of what is expected as the growth in household incomes over that period.

I appreciate that right now, with households suffering from the cost of the second fossil fuel shock in five years, the idea that anything might become more expensive is pretty hard to accept. However, over that period with things phased in gradually, that is a pretty small percentage of the total increase in people’s income. It is enough to address the costs of tackling the emissions from aviation.
It is more appropriate to put the cost on those people who take aeroplane flights, because it is still the majority who do not take flights at all.

Q474 Finally, unless anybody indicates, in terms of the draft NPS, does the climate test make sense to you as a test for the promoter to meet, rather than something for the Government as a whole to address?

It is a bit of both, but in many ways it is more about Government policy. That is why we have emphasised the actions we think the Government need to take before the Government could award a DCO. Clearly, it matters that the aviation industry is on board with that. There are things that any developer can do. Partly that is about airside emissions and smaller parts that are within their direct control; partly it is about supporting the development of SAF. It is predominantly a question for the Government because it has to address the whole of the aviation industry, not just the Heathrow expansion slice of it.

Thank you. That brings us to the end. The bell has not yet gone. Thank you very much for your written evidence, the time you spent preparing to talk to us today and for your time today. If there is anything you feel you did not have a chance to cover or cover adequately, feel free to email us ASAP. That concludes today’s meeting. We will continue our oral evidence on the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy statement tomorrow morning.

segs.tx: Transport Committee
Oral evidence: Scrutiny of the draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement , HC 482
Tuesday 13 October 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 13 October 2026.
Watch the meeting
Members present: Ruth Cadbury (Chair); Steff Aquarone; Dr Scott Arthur; Jacob Collier; Daniel Francis; Olly Glover; Alex Mayer.
Environmental Audit Committee member present: Chris Hinchliff.
Questions 390 – 4 37
Witnesses

I : Christian Hughes, Chairman, Longford Residents Association; Deborah Petty, Member, Molesey Residents Association; Mike Fawcett, Member, Putney Society; Stewart Pomeroy, Managing Agent, Colne Valley Regional Park Trust; Parmjit Dhanda, Executive Director, Back Heathrow.
Written evidence from witnesses:
– Longford Residents Association
– Putney Society
– Colne Valley Regional Park Trust
– Back Heathrow
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Christian Hughes, Deborah Petty, Mike Fawcett, Stewart Pomeroy and Parmjit Dhanda.

Q390 Welcome to this afternoon’s evidence session, the fifth session of our scrutiny of the Government’s draft Heathrow Expansion National Policy Statement. We welcome Chris Hinchliff MP, joining us as a guest from the Environmental Audit Committee.

We will be hosting two panels this afternoon. During our first panel we will be hearing from a community campaign supportive of the expansion plans and leaders of residents ’ associations in the Heathrow area that have a variety of views. On our second panel we will be hearing from representatives of the Climate Change Committee that recently published its formal advice to Government on the proposed expansion of Heathrow Airport.

Could I also remind members of the Committee to introduce yourselves before directing questions to the witnesses ? I recognise many people sitting in the public gallery who will already know this but speaking from the public gallery is unfortunately not permitted during C ommittee proceedings. Could I ask our first panel of witnesses to introduce themselves ?

I am from Back Heathrow. We are a campaign of 105,000 people who live predominantly close to Heathrow ; o ver half live within 8 miles of the airport. We would like to see the growth and opportunities that come with a new runway.

I am representing the Putney Society — the civic society of people living in Putney and Roehampton — where one of the chief concerns is noise from planes flying overhead, not least those that wake people up in the early hours of the morning.

I am from Longford Residen ts’ Association and am involved with H ASRA and HVF, two other associations covering the local villages. We have lived with Heathrow collectively as a neighbour for hundreds of years among residents. Many of us are highly opposed and would obviously like our views represented here today.

Since 2019 I have sat on the Noise and Airspace Community Forum at Heathrow representing the M o l e sey Residents Association but also with a wider responsibility to keep Elmbridge Council informed of forum matters.
I am from the Colne Valley Regional Park, the first large area of countryside to the west of London providing accessible green space for 10 million people who live within 15 km of it.
Q391 Can I just establish the status of your organisation s ? Stewart, you are a charity funded to protect the Colne Valley Park , and that is what pays you.
At its core, yes.
Q392 Deborah, Christian and Mike, are you s tandard r esidents a ssociation s and here as volunteers ?
Yes, we are here as unpaid volunteers.
Yes.
Q393 Y ou r members may or may not pay to join , is that right?
Yes, it is about £3 a year or something.
Q394 Parmjit, Back Heathrow is mainly funded by Heathrow Airport, is that right?
Heathrow Airport set it up during the Davies Commission.
Q395 Your 100,000-plus members do not necessarily have to pay ; t here is no membership fee , is that right?

No . They largely joined up when they felt the threat of the airport being closed during the Davi e s Commission when there was a proposal to shut it down by the leader of the host authority at the time in Hillingdon and move it to the Thames Gateway.
Q396 Was that the Boris Johnson estuary?
Yes.
Q397 Your website says you campaigned for a better and bigger Heathrow. What were you campaigning on two or three years prior to Rachel Reeves’ statement in 2025?
We have been around since 201 3 .
I know .

The airport discovered that the 1 05,000 supporters are very representative of the boroughs that they live in. The boroughs are 70% non-white in Hounslow, Ealing and Hillingdon. Very many of our meetings — town hall-like events —are held in all the constituencies and boroughs. They found it a useful mechanism to connect with them and be challenged by them. It ha s kept moving and survived even through covid. Now here we are again looking at a third runway at Heathrow Airport some 20 years after the last.
Q398 As you say, here we are again. Would it be fair to say that most of your individual members either work or used to work at Heathrow and t he business members are in the supply chain?

Ye s, they are local businesses, trade unions, the business community and an awful lot of individual residents — many in your own host borough — from a very diverse background and 80,000 people actually work on site. There are a lot of employees in the airport.

I have 70 ,000 in my head , but okay. That is useful to just understand the different roles your organisations have. Stewart, I am afraid quite a lot of our questions will be to the other four but we have some specific questions for you as well.
I l ook forward to it.

Q399 In the draft Heathrow e xpansion NPS, the Government set out four tests that must be met before expansion can proceed. Are these the right tests from the perspective of communities that are or would be affected by expansion? Is the threshold clear and set at the right level for determining whether each test has been met?

I reread the HENPS yesterday and have to say it was a thoroughly depressing read from a community perspective. It is the only potential protection that communities have f rom a permanent change to how they live and what they experience in terms of noise , particulates and pollution. I feel the HENPS falls woefully short. It is quite a partial document. The language is quite woolly , as other people have said, which gives room for manoeuvre.

We are very concerned that communities are potentially going to get thrown under the bus because of the n ational g rowth i nfrastructure designation . At every turn in the document, the Secretary of State could just give it the green light anyway if it is in the overriding public interest .

There are six quick points I would like to make. F irst , it is completely toothless. There are few hard and fast targets and absolutely no sanctions or penalties for failing to meet them. Secondly, it needs to have stronger independent assessments and oversight. When I first read it I thought, “Gosh , the promoters are being allowed to both report on and mark their own homework too much. ” When I reread it yesterday I thought, “Blimey , they ’ re actually setting their own homework .” The parameters with how things are described , “Take reasonable steps, ” “As much as reasonably practicable ” , “t ry to , ” essentially allow the promoters to say what they can do and get measured against that , and that is not acceptable.

There are very few specific targets. There is one on mode share, the 5,000 apprenticeships and the three-year subsidy for five new domestic routes. If the main purpose is growth and jobs , there are no metrics on those . It has a very fragmented and confusing oversight structure and there needs to be a much better delivery body that communities should be represented on.
As far as emissions — combining air quality and climate for speed — other more expert people have outlined that there are few protections on the particulates.
We have heard from them.

PM2s and UFPs in particular are not covered , but j ust because they are not measured does not mean the harm is not there. In fact you could argue that everybody around Heathrow is going to be subjected to a long-term medical experiment that they have not signed up to because we do not sufficiently know what the harms of ultrafine particles are at the moment.

The unaccounted carbon cost for us is a scandal. From a community and local business point of view — all the people paying ULEZ and congestion charges and sharing the pain of transitioning to green vehicles — for aviation to be given a green light to just say, “Knock yourselves out, ” and undo all that good work at the stroke of a pen for minimal if any GDP gain is really not acceptable.
Moving on to noise, there is much to be said , so I hope we can return to that.
We will.

The big thing that is missing from the HE N PS is noise change metrics. There is absolutely nothing that limits the amount of noise change that people can be subject to and nothing about the intensity with which routes can be flown or the number of noise events. In the 2014 events of the trial on the concentrated flight path, the change was what brought people out waving placards. That is what makes people really sit up and take notice.

The communities deserve that the best data is used in the HENPS . At the moment the ANAS and AN NE studies have been delayed and therefore excluded. If they are taken into account , the inconvenient truth is that the airport has a much larger impact on noise. Rather than 400,000 people it is 4.65 million. In freedom of information requests to the DFT, 1.9 million are set to see their noise increase by 25 % to 100% or more. Some 400,000 people could potentially see their noise increase by 100% or more.
Q400 What is the source of those figures?

DFT, freedom of information request. It could be from a low base of noise exposure or an already high base exposure to something catastrophic. People have a right to know what they are in for. There is no protection in the HENPS for that.

Quickly on growth, for minimal GDP growth t here are not enough protections on the financial viability of it. There is nothing that says there needs to be any debt control or liquidity buffers or anything like that. If the cost is as it is now, say for the Heathrow promoter scheme, the airlines have already said they will not use it ; i t is too expensive. Nigel Wicking was talking about £5 to £6 per person that they could weather on top of the current passenger charges. There is a genuine risk that we end up building a hugely expensive white elephant at great expense and disruption.
Q401 You have actually answered several later questions. Thank you for that very comprehensive answer. Just to remind everybody we are looking at the NPS, not the pros and cons of a third runway.
The safety of how the airways are used is not adequately covered in the HENPS either.

I would agree with Deborah on all the points that she raised. There is a lack of a joined-up approach on these things. We have a planning schedule and a follow-on airspace schedule. Again, the promoter is able to dismiss and set things if they are too expensive in terms of mitigation , which should not be the case.

We have particular health problems that are not really mentioned anywhere in the HENPS , which I would like to come back to at some point. There have been huge impacts on mental health across all the local villages and t he statistics are really quite devastating. We would like to see a tightening, especially around noise, vibration and UFP monitoring, and baselines taken in surrounding areas. They talk about future change ; y ou cannot have future change if you are only working on model data. You need a baseline from the start.

As the closest village, Longford — 240 metres from the northern runway —for three years we have been asking for noise data , vibration data and access to UFP monitoring data, which we know they have 10 years’ worth of. We have offered sites and so on ; n othing has been forthcoming. They are just reluctant to do it and w e would like to know why.
Q402 You brought in two other elements in addition to the four tests, which are mental health and safety.

I very much agree with what Debbie and Christian have both said. The HENPS has a general lack of teeth and precision and a poor evidence base. We have been particularly concerned about noise because that is what most worries people in Putney and other areas underneath the flight paths. Regarding t he noise appraisal, the people who have done it have done the best they could but i t is all on the basis of an indicative set of flight paths . We d o not yet know where the flight paths are going to go because the airspace redesign has hardly started.
Although surely below 3,000 or 4,000 feet the final approach and the vast majority of the departures are a given.
Yes, indeed.
It is a wider area.

The fate of the people who live closest to the airport is absolutely clear although the HENPS does not make that very clear either. It is when you get further out that there is more uncertainty. I hesitate to use the word “ test ” in terms of noise because it does not actually have any effect. It says that on a couple of metrics, noise should be no worse in future than it was in 2024.

There are three problems with that. One is that in 2024 the noise was already horrendous, affecting 4.65 million people on the Government’s own appraisal . Of those about half a million were, “Highly annoyed ,” which are the precise words in the appraisal. Just maintaining that level of harm really is not good enough. In our view t he Government ought to be seeking to reduce the amount of harm that Londoners and people living to the west of the airport are suffering.

It is also a rather theoretical metric. It is measuring the average noise. I guess what it is really measuring is that — on average — planes are gradually getting quieter , but i t is a very, very gradual process. Airlines do not suddenly introduce a whole new fleet of quieter aircraft. Most people will not even notice it is happening.

As Debbie said it is the changes when it gets worse that are going to be much more dramatic. When the third runway opens, all the people living under the approach paths and departure routes to that runway are going to really notice that — whereas previously they might never have heard aircraft noise — they are going to have planes flying over about every two minutes for three quarters of the day. As we understand it t hey will only get respite for a quarter of the time on average. Similarly people living underneath the approaches to the southern runway will only have respite for a quarter of the day, whereas for decades we have had respite for nine hours each day. That is going to be a huge change.
To be fair nobody has done any modelling recently on how alternation will work.
There are undoubtedly various options for how alternation will work.
Q403 Is that not part of the Government’s consultation ?

No, the consultation ha s a vague warning that respite periods might have to be reduced but it does not spell it out. When you read the noise annex to the appraisal of sustainability it explains that at any given time there will be two streams of approaching aircraft and two streams of departing aircraft. That is f our streams of aircraft on three runways. The way it will work is that one runway will take purely arriving aircraft, one will take purely departing aircraft, and the third will take a mixture of both arrivals and departures, what they call mixed mode.

What the noise appraisal also reveals is that the runway in the middle — the existing northern runway — will not operate in mixed mode for safety reasons. That means that the southern runway will be operating in mixed mode for half the time and then have a quarter of the time on arrivals and a quarter of the time on departures, and similarly the new third runway. In total there will be arrivals on the southern runway for three quarters of the time and on the new runway for three quarters of the time. That is our deduction.

Q404 Thank you for those ful l answers . Parmjit, I will give you a chance. Ha ve the Government set out the right four tests from the perspective of communities and is the threshold clear and set at the right levels for determining whether each test has been met?

I will try to stick firmly to the question. On all those in our response we said yes . They are demanding targets. There is no guarantee that Heathrow is going to meet them ; it is going to have to work very hard to do it . We have already heard in your own discussions around this table that some people think that it cannot or will not , but it is absolutely right that it is challenging.

I am going to agree with something Deborah said. Last time around there was a lot of talk about independence and an independen t noise regulator. When it comes to the DCO process I hope they have a look at that again ; t hat would be helpful.

On the subject of noise, I have to say that for so many local people who m we represent, that is not the lived experience they have. I do not know why that is. The airport has been there for 80 years and I suppose s ome genuinely have zoned out. It is normal to them. There is a fellow called Shafi ck Emmambokus , you might know him, who lives in Cranford. He claims to be the closest person to the runway ; I do not know whether that is true.
Probably . Is it B erke ley Avenue ?
I do not have his address but it is in Cranford and very close. The constituency MP is aware of him.
John C hatt , former leader of the council, lived there .

Shafi ck ’s view is that he does not lose a night’s sleep and i f anybody should be affected by noise it should be him. I meet people like him all the time and i t affects different people in different ways. That is a fair comment.

Q405 That is true . Many of my constituents are slightly further east of him ; he is in Seema’s constituency. Those people who live under what would be the approach path of the third runway — in n orth Cranford, n orth Heston, Osterley, n orth Brentford and n orth Chiswick — do not experience that. There would be a very significant increase in noise for them, would you agree? For the people under the existing two approach paths that has been the case for 70-plus years , but not for those to the north who have relatively little noise. How many of your members who live in that area underneath what w ould be the approach path —
There will be thousands of them.
How many of them know what the approach and departure paths that are in the DFT documentation would be ?
You are right , and part of the problem has already been mentioned. We do not know exactly what the new flight path is going to be .
Q406 We know what the below 4,000 feet will be.
There need s to be far more information out there.
But i t is out there.

I have family members who live in Harlington, for example, and would be in the WPO area. We need more clarity on compensation as well. We need to make sure that if this is to happen there is an adequate insulation scheme, which I know is something that has been debated in some meetings as well. It is crucial to get all those things right but t here is a balance to be had here as well, which is the economic benefits. I know we have had a discussion about whether you include trade or inward investment in that. Jobs are very important.

May I just interject very briefly on the below 4,000 feet bit? Once performance-based navigation is in, the airports or the UCAVs will set the co-ordinates that every single plane has to follow. There will be a much greater level of route concentration than now, where there are about three or four international coding houses that different airlines use. There is a degree of spread within the 3 km noise-preferred route.
Yes but not between central London and the end of the runway ; t hey are very concentrated.

Can I come in with one sentence about the four tests? Just to quickly say it seems really odd that there is no natural environment test or that it is not more included in one of the other tests given the huge and unprecedented impact on the rivers. In answer to the test question , there is something missing.

I just wanted to pick up the effective independent noise regulator. Parmjit made a v ery good point : i t is very, very weak at the moment as we — as MPs in the current noise insulation scheme — are finding with the RAB model mitigating against extending the noise insulation scheme to those who are eligible for it as you probably know.

Q407 My question is for Parmjit. I represent the other side of London : Bexley heath and Cra y ford. You described the draft HENPS as a clear and robust framework. What is it within the draft HENPS that gives you assurances that local communities will be genuine beneficiaries, particularly in relation to long-term employment opportunities?
Sorry, would you like to know what is germane to them in terms of long-term employment ?
What is it that gives you assurance that they will be genuine beneficiaries?

As you have seen the airport grow over the decades you have seen the number of jobs grow for local people. If you are from the diaspora, let us say the Indian subcontinent, which very many people in the local boroughs are, you cannot go to any of the home boroughs — whatever your background — without actually having a relative , neighbour or someone you know well working at the airport. Those of us who have grown up in the area have seen the benefits .

The idea of having a growing airport with a supply chain sounds a little absurd; the supply chain is probably well over 100,000 workers. That probably also relates to the fact that if you look at the S avanta poll from June it said there is something like 68% support overall and in e very single constituency there are more people supporting a third runway than opposing it.

There is a silent majority out there. A lot of those people are people who get up early in the morning, go to work and come bac k, and v ery many of them are in the supply chain. Our experience is that there are an awful lot of workers who actually work at Heathrow. We know there are 80,000 on site but there are so many more in the supply chain in places such as trading estates, for example Park Royal, which is the biggest trading estate in Europe. The leader of Brent Council was with me just the other day talking out the importance of that and saying that a new runway can be absolutely crucial for opportunities for boroughs slightly further afield such as his.

Q408 Obviously we have heard evidence about changes that may be needed such as moving the M25 and different flight paths as we have discussed. What level of engagement have you undertaken locally on the proposed subject ?

We run regular surveys. We have an email tree of about 30,000 people and w e s t ay closely in touch with them. We have regular town hall-style events. As I said at the outset and you have asked the question quite rightly, why ha s Heathrow continued to support Back Heathrow over the years? We are the rough and ready, raw end of the stick I suppose. You can turn up at a meeting , whether it is in Hounslow, Hillingdon , Windsor , Surrey or Buckinghamshire , and w e have had lots of supporters turn out to our meetings. There was a meeting a little while ago in Slough where they came out and talked about things such as the Great Western Rail way and actually g a ve Heathrow quite a hard time about it. “ Where is the funding? When’s it going to happen? We ’ ve heard about this so many times. ”

Overall I have found — doing these meetings for some years now — there is a level of pent-up frustration among local people saying, “ I thought this was meant to happen years ago. We thought this was going to happen. How much longer is it going to take? How many more delays are there going to be? Is it going to end up back in court again? ” That is a problem. People start to lose trust in processes when they see Parliament vote for something with a majority of 296 and years later it is still no closer to happening. Hopefully this time it will be different.

Q409 Parmjit, at one of our earlier sessions, we asked Perry Phillips , a representative of the GMB, “If r unway three does not go ahead are people worried about their jobs? ” He said yes and I said, “Where’ s the evidence for that? ” He did not have any. Is there any evidence?

Yes. From the conversations we have locally there is a feeling that if it does not happen here at our only hub airport — you have had a lot of conversations in this room about the importance of hubs — then what happens next? There is the idea of trade , jobs and opportunity moving to S c hiphol ; Schiphol tends to get mentioned more than the others —
Q410 I am well aware of the emotional response , because they are my constituents too. Where is the factual evidence to sustain that emotional response?
I do not think anybody ha s run a survey to say specifically, “Are you worried? What are the things that worry you?”
Q411 Not , “Are you worried? ” Obviously that goes with the territory.
We get that in conversation.
Q412 Has anyone coldly assessed that as a risk?

Statistically that is the sort of thing we should be asking someone such as David Blunkett in the role that he has in terms of the economic forecasting for the future , working to ensure that there are jobs for the future and to get that analysis from local people in terms of what they are thinking. Maybe that is something he c ould look at. It is fair enough to ask the question , but I know what the answer would be. I am pretty confident the answer would be , “We are concerned because we want jobs for the next generation. ”

Q413 I get the, “We are concerned ,” bit ; i t was about the factual stuff. The second question is about Slough , and I cannot remember if it was Hillingdon and/or the local authority grouping that made a proposal that as Heathrow is a massive generator of jobs and economy t here should be an enterprise zone. There should be a much bigger investment in the link between the local area and investment in and around Heathrow. We do not have anything like that at the moment. Is anybody doing any work on that? Are you proposing that?
I am at those local meetings. Actually quite a lot of stuff gets suggested like that including better work with local schools. Some good things have come out of that on an individual basis.
Q414 Is that because people feel that Heathrow Airport Ltd is not doing that at the moment?
Generally people think it is doing a great job in providing jobs, opportunities and apprenticeships .
Q415 There are always vacancies at Heathrow.

The re are . There are a lot of opportunities there but o bviously t he current generation that are working there want more. My parents’ generation wanted much more for their kids. Tha t is a normal thing.
Q416 We noted that deprivation is increasing in the areas around Heathrow as well.
The local boroughs — not least your own — suffered very badly during covid. You will know, partly because so many of your own people work at Heathrow.
It still has not picked up.
There were 30,000 people furloughed at the time .
That is a fair point.
May I just say one thing?
Very briefly, yes .

The claims that Heathrow ha s made about 108,000 jobs are not in the public domain in any detail and have not been substantiated. They are not broken down. The only thing we know for sure is 5,000 apprenticeships because that is a metric that is set. One of your earlier panels said that the net gain in jobs could be as little as 7,000 because of displacement , substitution and so on .
Q417 Is that after construction ?

After construction. T5 was a classic example. It promised 6,000 permanent jobs, threatened that 9,000 to 16,000 or something would be lost if it did not go ahead and then said there would be 6,000 construction jobs for that. The airport ha s been really coy about what has been delivered. I had a meeting with Elmbridge Borough Council recently where I asked , “Do you know how many people in the borough are employed by the airport and whether any of the promises made previously were honoured? ” T he answer was no.
Steff, is there anything you wanted to pick up on?
It has been pretty well covered.
Q418 Could I just ask Christian , because your area is the only one represented : y our area benefit s from the noise mitigation schemes , h ow is it going?

It is varied. It took a long time coming. To put it in context, the closest property in Longford v illage is 240 metres from the n orthern r unway and the furthest is about 480 metres, so there is a very close concentration. I personally am about 400 metres. Despite that, I have been fighting with Heathrow in excess of 20 years for replacement windows and have been told that I was the wrong side of a contour line and therefore did not qualify. Only because it was part of the noise plan was it rolled out very quickly.
Q419 Am I right that people are still waiting for what they had expected to have after Terminal 5?
That is correct, yes.
We will now go on to air pollution.

Q420 How well does the draft HENPS address the concerns about air pollution impacts resulting from the airport expansion? Are you confident that air pollution will be properly monitored and managed over the longer term?
T here is no need to repeat what you have already said, it is on the record.
I have to say that in Putney, 9 miles , 10 miles from the airport, noise is our greatest concern , so we have not looked at air quality issues.

I know that ultrafine particles are not on the Government’s radar in terms of planning controls right now, but there is increasing evidence that ultrafines contribute to things such as dementia, heart and lung issues, and so on. I cannot emphasise enough that there needs to be a precautionary principle included in the HENPS; there is nothing in there about ultrafines at this point. I have a copy of a document here actually written by Brian Stacey, the head of air quality at Heathrow, that outlines that it has been known for the last decade that ultrafine particles are up to 14.5 times the World Health O rgani z ation recommended exposure level on a regular basis. That is with two runways. T here is nothing in the HENPS that means that monitoring has to be done. There is obviously European legislation coming in where by super sites will need to be monitored from December , but t here is no mention of that in the HENPS.

We would like to see really stringent controls and have visibility of the data that it has . Three years ago we specifically asked for the equivalent monitoring that it has in LHR2, which is the station closest to the northern runway: at the Cranford end it is 170 metres away. We asked for equivalent monitoring equipment to be put in Green Gates, which is in the middle of our village. It has basically come up with a budget version of that, with sensors that are cheaper to maintain, and we still do not have visibility.

We might have nice new windows and insulation to protect from noise but, to go back a step, if easterly alternation comes in—the step before the third runway—which is what it wants to do starting with mixed mode, we will not be able to go out into our gardens and enjoy the summer or sleep with our windows open during that supposed respite.

It needs tightening. UFPs need to be taken into account. We need to have access to that data and proper modelling across local boroughs so that there is a baseline. I keep coming back to that : w e need to have a baseline, not only for ultrafines but for other particulates as well. It has been remiss, and we need to get better at it.
Deborah covered that point very well.

I agree with those points. The local authorities need to be supported financially if they are going to have the burden of monitoring put on them. We need more and accurate monitors, both for particulates and for noise.
That is a useful point, thank you. We will now turn to access.

Q421 D oes the draft HENPS sufficiently address the transport impacts of Heathrow expansion on local communities? Do you think the mitigation measures are clear and robust enough to prevent additional traffic from overburdening local roads?

The short answer is no. An additional 60,000—at best—vehicles on the road daily is untenable. I quite often go to meetings at the airport, and as the crow flies I live about 10 km away. My record is one hour 45 minutes back to home, with current traffics and stuff. Other people have talked about the M25 being turned into a potential car park; I do not think that is a cost that has been actually modelled either. That means that things get pushed on to the local infrastructure.

Even if Heathrow is going to insist on using green vehicles to try to minimise emissions, they are heavier and they damage the local roads more. You are going to have more interruptions from potential roadworks and things to try to keep the road network going.

If the s outhern and w estern r ail, which is not factored into any of the costs properly at the moment, does not happen, you cannot attempt to get the mode share targets that it is after anywhere. The danger is that most people will fall back on vehicles, which have their own emission issues. For people just going about their daily lives, getting anywhere is a real problem.
We have had a couple of sessions on that.
Q422 If you did have s outhern and w estern r ail, do you think the targets are achievable in that scenario? What impact or benefit would that have to local people?

It depends on where they genuinely hook up to and how good those services are. Some rail infrastructure people were saying that you need to build it in advance to try to change people’s behaviour before the airport comes on-stream. That is a massive investment to make that also has its own impact in terms of the build going on. It would help, but personally I do not think that people who live within a certain radius of the airport are ever going to move away from vehicles. It makes no sense to go to hubs further out to then go back further in. From where I live I would never take the train to the airport. None of the proposals for s outhern or w estern r ail would actually affect people who are in my borough to make them change their behaviour.
We will turn to environmental monitoring; at last Stewart gets a question.

Q423 Mr Pomeroy, the Government have said that Heathrow expansion does not need to come at the expense of the green belt . Do you think the national policy statement as currently drafted is set out to achieve that?

I do not see how you can do that without affecting the green belt . There is something like 1,200 hectares of green belt to be lost, plus all the knock-on impacts that are not considered as part of this because cumulative impact does not seem to be being addressed. Those businesses that are being displaced : hotels, BA headquarters, the Grundon Incinerator industrial estates, plus the houses —
Harmondsworth i mmigration c entre.

Stewart Pomeroy: Yes, exactly, plus the new business that will be attracted by a bigger airport, this is going to have an immense impact on the green belt . I cannot see at all how it is possible to state that it can be done without an impact on the green belt .

We have to remember that the areas of the Colne Valley Regional Park provide that attractive place for people to use. I have already mentioned the 10 million people who live within 15 km. There are the people who currently live near the airport and people who will move in as other people move out. They all need access to attractive and useful green space. We need some joined-up thinking and a co-ordinated approach to this rather than this piecemeal, bite-by-bite section without the cumulative impact being considered. I have not even mentioned data centres and everything else that is proposed in this area.

Q424 Thinking ahead to a parliamentary C ommittee report on the national policy statement, is there any recommendation that you would have in terms of how the policy statement could be improved or strengthened in order to result in better outcomes for the green belt , compared to how it is currently drafted?

That comes back to that missing test about the natural environment and the impact on the rivers ; I hope we can come to rivers in a bit more detail in a few minutes. We need that master plan for it to pick up on some of the points we have heard. It is not just public transport ; you also have the opportunity for active travel to get around the local area. Currently you could argue the first taste of England for our international visitors is, in places, a national disgrace. We need to restore the landscape to provide something we can all be proud of. We hear from Government about win-wins for growth and nature; we need to see them.

Q425 Just very briefly on that, what would your response be to someone who would say that biodiversity net gain requirements will automatically require that improvement in the natural environment as a result of this development?

We also need that joined-up approach in the way that the landscape and the rivers work, and we need those internationally protected sites. We need to ensure they are connected across the landscape and that we do not carry on with this unco - ordinated piecemeal bites approach. We need to ensure there is connectivity for people and wildlife.

Q426 Following on from what we have just heard from yourself, Mr Pomeroy, and from many of the other guests today, it brings me back to something that Ms Petty referred to very early on : the draft HENPS designates the development as critical national growth infrastructure. If the draft is approved with that policy in place, does that not effectively have the potential to outweigh the concerns that you have set out in relation to air pollution, noise pollution, traffic, and environmental impacts on the landscape as well?

Thinking about what changes, if any, ought to be made to the draft policy statement, would any of you have confidence that the supposed growth would be effectively balanced against your concerns with the draft as it currently is, or does that critical national growth infrastructure need to be amended in order for your concerns to be taken seriously?

I would say it need s to be amended to take our concerns seriously. We are absolutely worried that we are going to be stuffed by it, basically. That they will just say, “This trumps everything, and therefore we are going to do it,” in the face of any evidence to the contrary, which is a big concern.

On the growth argument I would also say that the DfT needs to do some more work on looking at whether the airlines would actually follow through with what they threaten. If it is too expensive, they have basically said they are going to take their planes somewhere else. If they do that not only do you have a white elephant, you have one that is potentially going to start eating into the mother elephant next door. The actual profitability of the extant airport could be compromised by out-of-control expense and cost on the extension. I do not think anybody has modelled that. At the moment it is contributing £23 billion to the GDP. The supposed extension is meant to deliver between £0.03 billion and £0.05 billion, which is a tenth of what was previously advised to MPs when it was first mooted.

There is a real danger, particularly if the promoters are on a knife edge financially, as they are. Standard & Poor has rated it as potentially credit negative now, as well as sensitive. Anybody who invests in it is going to want to have their share of interest for something risky. Heathrow is a potential promoter that has been paying dividends, not husbanding its own cash to put into it, so it is looking to the debt and bond markets to pick that up and it is going to be on very fine margins. Nobody believes that Heathrow can fulfil what even it has proposed as a massively expensive scheme for the costs it has proposed. It is even at the lower end of its own internal estimates. If its cost overruns it is going to be completely unaffordable, and therefore the extant profitability of the existing airport could be damaged.

Q427 For the other members of the panel, notwithstanding the fact that the growth figures have been very heavily criticised during this process, would any of you like to comment on whether that designation of critical national growth infrastructure impacts on the possibility of taking a reasoned approach to balancing the concerns that you have made?

It feels very unbalanced. I would say that critical national growth infrastructure cannot and should not remove the need to demonstrate that unacceptable impacts are avoided, mitigated, and controlled. We have to get the balance right and it feels that that status has unbalanced everything.

Yes, I very much agree with that, and this is a very important question that you have raised. Taking the noise test as an example, the actual test is set at a level that the Government’s own forecasts suggest will easily be met even if there is no effort whatsoever from Heathrow, the airlines or the Government, just because planes will gradually get quieter. It does not reflect real-world impacts, but that test would be met. Due to the designation as critical national growth infrastructure there is absolutely no incentive for Heathrow, when it submit s its DCO application, to come up with anything better.

I will let Parmjit come in, but we are on a 10-minute warning and I still have three more questions we are covering. I am sorry, but we have done critical national growth infrastructure at previous sessions so if I can I want to keep it to the community impacts this session.

In terms of how the DfT do es its stats or whether it include s investment or trade in that , which it really should , it is nearer £17 billion than 0.05%, which is 10% of that. Either way, is it critical? From the view of local people it is pretty critical because they have seen the levels of local support, they work there and they want it. They see the polling, they see Parliament, and a parliamentary C ommittee supported it back in 2012, or whenever it was. They have seen it go to the courts: the appeal court and the Supreme Court gave it the green light. We are just waiting. Even when we go through this process there is the DCO to go through as well, which is where a lot of this detailed discussion with Ministers, quite rightly, is still to come.

Q428 The parameters have changed. The economic modelling and our climate change commitments have changed. We have three residents groups here and many more who wrote in who are not on the same page as Back Heathrow. Their evidence has either been neutral or a modest expansion.
Not every group has the number of members that we have and represents the communities that we do across those boroughs as well .
Yes, that is a point you have already made , but thank you.

Q429 Would anyone on the panel like to comment on whether the draft policy statement is drafted adequately in relation to compensation, perhaps particularly picking up on the points that you referred to about air pollution and the potential health impacts?
Sorry, what we meant by compensation was mainly about compensation for the loss of property value, and that is mainly for Christian.

Compensation is a difficult topic. Those that want to go want to go now , and the only way they can do that is through a blight process. What we have seen over the last 20 to 30 years is a systematic undermining of the fabric of our communities because of Heathrow. It is an attractive employer, as Parmjit references, but that has driven more people into the community. We have gone from around 14,500 residents in 2021 up to about 18,000 now. A lot of that influx is not because of new properties being built, it is because the fabric of our community is being undermined with predatory investors turning family homes into HMOs. It is useful for people who want to just put their head down somewhere and have easy access to the airport. Those people will probably be the ones worst affected come the development, if it goes ahead. A tenant ’s compensation is far lower than if you are a property owner in situ living in your primary property.

There has also been a huge softening over the years. When Heathrow first launched its consultation over a decade ago it said, “We will give 125% of the unblighted value of homes.” We have seen a softening in the more recent documentation that basically says, “It is now 125% of the unaffected value.” What is the difference? From our perspective we need to see some really hard and fast rules, it is supposed to be there.
You said that in your submission, thank you. I am sorry, I need to move on because I want to get the last two questions out.

Q430 How well does the draft HENPS capture potential impacts on communities beyond Heathrow’s immediate development boundary, including on connectivity, local amenity, construction disruption, and access to services?
C ould I come in on that ?
If you have not already answered that question.

On connectivity, building a new airport the size of Gatwick on top of five rivers affects connectivity between the internationally rare chalk streams of the Chilterns and the Thames. That covers a catchment of 1,000 square kilometres, taking us way up into Buckinghamshire and Hertfordshire. There is a huge connectivity impact that building on top of those rivers has.
Can you just repeat the last bit of your question?
Q431 Connectivity, local amenity, construction, disruption, and access to services : a ny views on how well the draft HENPS captures those potential impacts?

I would really like to jump in on access to services. The south of the borough in Hillingdon has had very little in terms of health services for decades. We have been fighting for them for as long as I can remember and some of the villages have no dentist, no GP and no pharmacy. From a practical perspective we have engaged with Heathrow and with local authorities to try to get these things funded, but nothing has been happening and there is this consistent pattern.

Coming back to the surface access , we have issues with AVAs that are still unresolved that could be solved very easily if people sat around a table . T here is no obligation for Heathrow to do so and actually properly engage with communities to resolve issues that are very clearly of its making.

I want to mention a really quick point ; it is in the evidence already but I want you to be aware. We have about 18,000 residents. Pre-covid, for 300,000 residents in Hillingdon, there were about 1,200 referrals to MIND, the local mental health charity. Post-covid, specifically with people’s inability to understand where they are going to be living moving forward, Hillingdon MIND has had 7,500 referrals in the last year—2025—and 69% of those are within that 18,000 population that is the Heathrow villages. That is the level of uncertainty that we are dealing with, and in terms of community engagement that is what we are having to face.

I am slightly further out, but the construction of this is going to suck in building resource and skills particularly that could and should be being used in other areas to provide housing and cladding remediation. It is prioritising this project over the really vital provision of homes, both close to the airport but also potentially further out; we are not going to be able to just magic up those construction people from nowhere. That cannibalisation effect of how much it is going to suck into itself and therefore affect everywhere further out is something that needs to be considered. In terms of travel it will inevitably have an impact on people just trying to get anywhere around the M25 to find alternative routes through for local connectivity.
Some 17,000 people who will be displaced will have to go slightly further afield to the new boundary, where the rents will be higher and they may not be able to afford to work at Heathrow anymore.

I agree with Christian and what he said about certainty. People locally have felt an awful lot of uncertainty over the years. Particularly around those blighted communities they need to be able to access that money sooner rather than later. I also agree in terms of surface access ; this is a great opportunity locally to have better surface access.
Q432 Does that need to be added, or improved , in the draft HENPS?
I would be all for improving it and driving it through quicker, if possible.
Q433 Okay, and there is the local free bus, which has not come back and is not going to.

Absolutely. It quite happily paid out £500 million in dividends—or whatever it was—and said, “When we return to profitability we will bring the bus back for the free travel zone.” Ha s it ? No, of course it has not.
No, and it is not likely to either.
It is just a catalogue of broken promises.
There is also, Christian, actually an issue around buses at nighttime for workers as well ; something that the unions are very keen to keep, as you are probably aware, Chair.
We are, thank you .

Q434 Moving on to heritage, finally. Obviously nobody likes it if the village that they live in is knocked down. I completely understand that. If we get to a situation whereby certain places are demolished, is there enough in the document that provides recompense for that? Would we be losing anything genuinely unique? Is there anything in the document that goes further than a standard planning practice?

Absolutely nothing. There is a 600-year-old barn, the oldest barn that we have in Europe , with no vibration or noise monitoring in place. We are talking about a new runway that will be probably within 50 metres of that structure, which is a grade 1 listed building. We have been asking for vibration monitoring in Longford Village, as I say, for three years now, and nothing has been forthcoming. We have recently been offered an appointment but it does not want to do seismic monitoring, it only want s to do airborne noise monitoring.
Q435 Sorry, but that is what is happening at the moment. Do you think there should be anything specific in this document?

Absolutely. As we have sa id all along, we need to have a rigid structure that says, “You must put in place this monitoring,” and it must be done beforehand so that there is a baseline and it cannot be any worse afterwards.

I have read that specific chapter quite closely in the HENPS. What it says as a framework works in terms of, “Find alternative solutions if you can,” if there is an impact on some kind of habitats in some way, and, “Ensure, if necessary, compensation is in place.” It also talks about, “Reasons of overriding public interest.” I am not talking about the barn here, but on some occasions I suspect jobs and local communities may well be within that. The next stage in this really is the detail. That has to be at the DCO process, where you can actually talk about these individual things and find solutions for them.
In our opinion there is too much being left to the DCO stage.
The DCO stage, yes.

That is the problem. We need these things finite in advance and not left up to Heathrow and its huge budgets to promote. I t is having 200 or 300 meetings with civil servants this year, if not more; there is a very clear engagement with communities that Heathrow is ignoring.
A lthough Heathrow Airport L td may well have a consultation.
In that case we are 100% agreed ; get to DCO quickly.

Does everybody agree that if this is not sorted out in the national policy statement it should be in the DCO, and too much is being left? J ust for the record, I saw nodding from Mike and Deborah that too much is being left to the DCO .

We need to sort it at this stage in the national policy statement. I particularly wanted to mention the issue of mitigation and affordability ; if the whole scheme is not affordable, then why cut the mitigation? Is it the right scheme?
Others have said that too.

Yes, too much is being left to the DCO because this is not going to be a normal DCO application. It is going to be one where the promoter knows that the project is going to get approved. It completely changes the whole dynamics.

Q436 Thank you very much for all your evidence, written and oral. If there is something that you feel was not included or you did not have a chance to say, within reason and if it is brief, we may accept some more evidence. Quickly, Christian?
