First, it doesn’t stop us doing things now, it does not stop us doing things next year and it does not stop us planning, with some assumptions that defence spending will continue to rise. I do not think it needs to slow us down or stop us from doing anything. I do not know when the spending review is going to be.
Q23 Are you going to be spending money you have not got, then?
No, because we know what we have got for this year. We know what we will get for the next year—

You are missing the point. The spending review may be in autumn, although it could be spring; let us say that is in the autumn. You are telling us that you will not know exactly what you have got to spend up to 2030 until then.
The Budget will set out—
Q24 Is it acceptable to wait for nearly a year for that decision to be taken? It is a simple question. Yes or no?

I think we can live with that. We can absolutely live with that. We have got the resources we need for this year. The Budget will set out next year, and we can make some confident assumptions that defence spending will continue to rise, and plan on that basis, which gives me the confidence to do what we need to do to be ready.

Q25 But Secretary of State, I think what Mr Twigg is saying is that the threats are here and now. It seems palpable to many of us that we are not meeting the moment, and that is why there is a sense of exasperation. I highlighted to the previous Prime Minister the fact that it was he himself who stated that we needed to be able to deter, or a NATO nation may well be attacked by Russia by 2030, and that is not what is being done. Even the new Prime Minister has not charted out the path to reach 3% by 2030. As Mr Twigg has already stated, you cannot spend money that has not been allocated to you.

You have also stated that the funding that you are looking for will be given in due course, but it needs to be allocated now for you to make preparations. Don’t you think that there is a lack of urgency with respect to defence spending?

No, I don’t, because we have already got the biggest sustained increase in defence spending since the end of the cold war—in the space of not even two-and-a-half years, from 2.3% when we came in, to 2.7% next year. We have a stated commitment from the Chancellor to give us—
Q26 It is 2.7% by the end of the Parliament. I don’t think it is 2.7% by next year.
No, in 2027-28, we will be spending 2.7%.
By the end of 2028.
That is all we are committed to—2.7%. Not 3%.

Sure, and I understand. I think where we are at odds is that there is nothing to stop us making reasonable planning assumptions on the basis that the spending review will chart a further increase in defence spending because the Chancellor has told us that is what he intends to do.

Q27 But Secretary of State, how can we can go about taking reasonable steps when the funding is not there? You also intimated that we have to wait until the spending review. The spending review has now been kicked into the long grass again, until next autumn.

Let us also remind ourselves that the previous Prime Minister, Sir Keir Starmer, came into the Chamber—you may well have been there for that statement, as was I—and overnight we went to a 0.2% increase, without the need for a CSR or a Budget. He simply came in, made a statement that we were increasing defence spending by 0.2% by taking the funding from international development. He did not wait around for a Budget or a spending review. Do you not think, given the urgency, that we can make a statement and that that is exactly what the Prime Minister and Chancellor should be doing?
But crucially, Tan, what Prime Minister Keir Starmer did when he made that choice was to set out the increase in defence funding and how it was going to be paid for simultaneously—
Without a spending review.

Outside a major fiscal event, but still explaining how it would be paid for. We have had very bitter recent experience of a former Prime Minister making unfunded commitments to spend more, tax less and borrow more, all simultaneously, and it led to enormous loss of confidence and people’s mortgages going up, and a level of fundamental loss of confidence in Britain among investors that this country is still recovering from.
That was done at a fiscal event, in a Budget.

Where I would absolutely defend the Chancellor is that he wants to spend more on defence —we know this. He says he will do more at the Budget. He says he will do more at the spending review. He also has to show how he pays for it.

Our debt-to-GDP ratio is somewhere around 100%. The amount we are spending as a state just on servicing debt interest is about one in every 10 taxpayer pound s. If we go out making unfunded commitments, and the markets choose to price that risk in, the cost of borrowing goes up and we have less to spend on our priorities, before we have even done anything.

Q28 I don’t think the Defence Committee is advocating for unfunded spending commitments, but the Committee was recently in Denmark which has gone, amazingly, from a 1.3% spend of GDP on defence to 4.99% within four years. Germany is saying it is going to have the largest conventional land force in the continent. Within four years they will be spending the same as the UK and France. And here we are, just kind of trundling along.

And in those cases, Chair, look at the cost of borrowing in those countries. We are not comparing like with like. I wish we were, but that is one of the reasons why they have got a bit more headroom than us to make those choices. Given the constraints we are operating under, I would just say—and believe me I am not remotely complacent about this; I cheered John Healey on when he made his principled resignation, I felt just as uncomfortable as he did about where we were on defence spending, and I would not have accepted the Prime Minister’s offer to take on this role if I did not believe he was also committed to funding—that we have got to make sure we understand the economic and fiscal context we are in and give the Chancellor the time and space he needs to give us what we need while showing how to pay for it.

Today’s IMF numbers are particularly encouraging—relatively as well—but they do not show the benign conditions we want to be in. We have a responsibility collectively, Parliament and Government, to think about that context, otherwise our taxpayers, our citizens, our constituents and the state pay a heavy price if we are not disciplined with the finances.
We look forward to your confidence being rewarded.

Q29 Secretary of State, you said you wanted a defence pact with this Committee—that we would advocate for higher defence expenditure. No doubt you will be aware that this Committee has been calling for 3% by 2030 for quite some time. You also said that you wanted the public to be calling for that.

In the strategic defence review, there was a call for the beginning of a national conversation. When the Committee was in Norway, we heard that their Prime Minister, regardless of what speech he is making, will always refer to the threat that his country is under. We here are not having that conversation nationally and the Prime Minister rather foolishly said that national security cannot come at the expense of social security, a position I was happy to hear him row back on yesterday. Do you see part of your role as an advocate for defence to be louder in that conversation at a national level, so that the public come to realise just how much money we need to spend on defence and potentially some of the difficult trade-offs that we are going to have to make?

Yes. One of the reasons why the Prime Minister asked me to take on this responsibility is to make sure that we communicate effectively the kind of threat environment we are in, and to ensure that we have a country that is alert but not alarmed. In terms of the Prime Minister’s position, he has, on multiple occasions since he took office, talked about the kind of threat environment we are operating in, and in a number of ways—from hosting President Zelensky down in Portsmouth through to the two-and-a-half hours he spent on the Floor of the House of Commons yesterday talking about some of the hybrid threats that we are experiencing as a country. In the spirit of hope and optimism that the Prime Minister is bringing and for which I think the country is crying out, there is an absolute recognition from the Prime Minister down, throughout the entire Government, that hope is built on the bedrock of security.

If you have hope and opportunity on one hand and security on the other— as Defence Secretary I am very much into the security part of the argument, but I also think that, through the way we invest in defence, we can show how we are strengthening opportunity in this country and building hope through growth in every postcode and defence industry and so on. I think that will be part of maintaining public support—showing we’re backing Britain by buying British and the other ways in which we can demonstrate real impact for our country.

Q30 To pick up on a point you just raised, Secretary of State, hope is not a strategy. Hope is not based on security; confidence is based on security. That is what we are seeking from you. It was a great disappointment that the last Prime Minister talked about the need for a national conversation and then did nothing to promote one. Anything you and the current Prime Minister can do will be welcome.

When you said that you have confidence in the Chancellor and the Prime Minister, you also said that you are taking decisions now, at the MOD, that reflect that confidence—that is to say that you are anticipating future spending increases in the plans you are making now. Could you elaborate a little bit more on that, because obviously that is quite an important defence to the idea that you only e ver spend money when you get formal authorisation from the Treasury ?

On one level , just by the nature of what we do in defence we commit to a lot of programmes that are long-term. That demonstrates that just because we operate in annual budget and three-year spending review cycles does not mean that we do not have a view on the longer term. We see that reflected in everything—
Q31 Right, but you are doing more as a result of your increased confidence in the Chancellor and the Prime Minister in respect of getting from 2.7% to 3%. That is the key point.
Well, we live within our means for now, but we plan in the context of the SDR and the DIP for the future.
On 3%.
I will not be drawn on any specific percentages.

Q32 Secretary of S tate , I am not going to ask you h ow much money defence has to spend, but about an element of spending more within your control . In one of your previous responses you mentioned buying British , which ties into the agenda you have laid out this afternoon around using defence as an engine for growth. I think it is fair to say that t here has been a somewhat confused position from the Government in recent years, which clearly predates you taking up this role , so it would be interesting to hear your thoughts on the direction you intend to take the D epartment.

For context , in the Labour manifesto, which you and I stood on, we said we wanted to buy British. We said that over and over again , but then the language slightly changed within the MOD, during the previous A dministration . For example , earlier in 2026, one of your junior Ministers made a pre-prepared speech to the whole defence industry— not an offhand comment —and said , “F or avoidance of doubt, if you’ve got a British postcode, you are a British company." I was very confused by that . We have new leadership , with a new P rime Minister and a new Secretary of State for D efence. Could you clarify what you think of as a British company, how you would tell industry what British means to you , and how you are going to take this forward ?

I did a good session with the Lords industry Committee t his morning and this came up. T he legal definition of a British business is as simple as having an address in this country . I think we would all agree that that is not sufficient and would not constitute buying British in so far as the spirit of the manifesto we stood on . I suspect that spirit is shared across this entire Committee, regardless of political party.

There are a number of ways in which we can measure impact in Britain —jobs, growth, where the IP is held. Ownership can be one of those. For me, fundamentally , over and above everything else, in terms of backing Britain and buying British it is about the impact on jobs, opportunities and growth in this country. T here are plenty of examples of companies we procure from that are American , Italian or from other countries, and that are creating jobs here in Britain, and I would consider that to be backing Britain by buying British.

Q33 I nevitabl y, a balance needs to be struck between wanting Government D epartments to buy from British companies and support British IP , as most people would probably like , and, as you have alluded to, making sure that Government D epartments are efficient and getting the best value for taxpayer money. R ealistically, that will not always be British. Previous questions have alluded to the urgent sense of needing to make sure we are ready for any action that needs to be taken. H ow do you see that q uite difficult balance? I do n’t think there are any easy answers, but I just wanted to hear what you think.

There are going to be questions of judgment in all this; it is not as simple as just running things through a spreadsheet and getting a mathematical answer. There are a whole range of factors we will want to take into account at various points. Timing might matter. Where those jobs are created might matter, even when we are talking about competition within the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

Our starting point as the MOD is really good: the overwhelming majority of defence spending stays here at home. In terms of our footprint and the Prime Minister’s ambitions for growth in every postcode, other Government Departments see our starting point as way beyond their wildest dreams compared with theirs, so we start from a good place.

But I was saying to the Lords this morning that we cannot be complacent. For example, defence spending per head in the north-east of England versus in the south-east of England is wildly different. We could be doing better in Wales. Northern Ireland, despite its defence industrial heritage, is still much lower. There is no room for complacency.

You draw out some of the tensions we’ve got, because the whole argument for competition is that you inspire innovation, you force down prices and people have to have that competitive edge, so it is good for industry. In a world in which I am regularly lobbied to do direct awards or UK-only competitions in the spirit of buying British, I have to weigh up some of the risks as well and make sure that we see these things in balance, rather than simply as black-and-white choices. We are not doing too badly so far—we have a good starting point—but we do take into account some of those wider issues.

Should I say a little bit about some of the work we have under way to really cement this policy? The first thing we are doing is working with industry right now to come up with a practical and transparent definition that does exactly what the Defence Secretary has said, so it is focused not just on the address but on the benefits, the jobs and the impact on the defence industrial base that comes from that.

Secondly, we are also undertaking the detailed mapping of different capabilities across the country, so that we have really good knowledge in the Department. We will all agree that having a strong industrial base does not run against military capability but actually cements it. It is essential for national security, and events of the last couple of years have really shown that for all of us. We need to grow that industrial base for our national security.
Thirdly, this will then relay into the decisions we make as we implement the defence investment plan. We have begun, but there is a lot more to do over the next couple of years.

Finally, as you have alluded to, it may not always be right to buy British, and we need to be open to that possibility, although I note that in the last available numbers 86% of our defence spending with industry was for work taking place in the UK. The significant majority is UK-based, but it will not be all. We are also refreshing our offsets policy, so that when we need to buy from abroad we are also building the industrial base in this country.

Q34 Secretary of State, you have obviously followed defence for a long time, but you have been very plugged into health in opposition and then in government for quite a few years. Speaking of buying British, what has been your impression of British industry and the British defence technology innovators you have had the chance to meet in the last three months since taking up the role?

I think we start from a position of relative strength. I do not just mean in terms of our primes; some of the biggest opportunities for this country are some of the SMEs that are pushing the frontier of defence innovation. We should actively try to keep those companies and scale them here in Britain.

We have a general problem across the economy: we are really good at start-ups, but often when it comes to scaling up the investment environment means that people ship out, often to the United States. That plays directly into the conversation on AI that we are having across Government and wider society.

If I look at Brakestop, for example, and the way in which that programme operated— the number of companies that expressed an interest, the numbers that made it into the active competition and those that made it through to the final—that is an outstanding SME success story, even for those companies that did not ultimately prevail. Everyone learned something through that process, and those companies will be back in the future.

We talk ourselves down as Britain a bit too much at the moment , and that applies beyond defence as well. We are second only to the US and China when it comes to AI, for example. We have to make sure that we continue to punch above our weight in the world , and draw on that innovation in the defence context.

Q35 This morning I was on the phone to a contractor who lost out on a bid to one from overseas. They were going to manufacture in the UK ; the overseas bid was 53% cheaper. I do not know where in the world that is, but I would be sceptical of the quality you are going to get if it is 53% cheaper. How can British businesses compete in that landscape?

This is why we are currently in the process of updating our social value guidelines . It is not just about measuring the economic and social impact of buying British on jobs, opportunities and growth here in Britain; it is also about casting our beady eye over supply chain ethics and making sure that we have fair competition. I do not know the details of th e particular procurement you mention, but my instincts are immediately to be sceptical about which country and what that is.

Q36 In the tendering process, it seems cost wins a lot of the time over sovereignty . You talk a good talk on backing British, but when push comes to shove , cost wins over and over again. How are you going to embed sovereignty into the tender documents?

Th is is where having an ally in the Chancellor is really important. If you take the Pro ject Euston announcement that the Chancellor and I made during the Labour party conference week, we chose a UK-only procurement for that . That was because it was of such an order of magnitude—probably worth around £6 billion in the end—that being agnostic about that amount of taxpayer money going overseas did not feel right to me. Conventionally—I do not cast any aspersions on previous Chancellors—the Treasury institutional view would certainly have been, “What are you playing at ? B ig procurement ? Then g o to global competition.” P olitical leadership really matters in that sort of space.

The final thing I would say about sovereignty is that we are going to have to have quite a nuanced focus on sovereign capability , s overeignty full stop, and control, particularly in the world of AI and where some of the most powerful frontier models are not British and w e are going to rely on other countries . I n a defence context , t here are obviously enormous opportunities with AI, but there are enormous risks. Whether it is AI or other forms of technology, we need to make sure that we have control over our capability and that we are not dependent on others. Working , partnering and procuring with others is all great — we do a lot of that, and long may that continue —but th e se concepts of sovereignty, sovereign capability and control are going to become more relevant in the coming years.

T o follow up on that very important point , Secretary of State, you rightly stressed the importance of supply chains. Ultimately, at some level, war is always a contest between supply chains. When you evaluate domestic capability a ccording to the perm sec’s new rules, do you evaluate it in the context of scenario planning? Of course, we discovered in the financial crisis that if something hits the whole system, it just seizes up. We have got to have some mechanism by which we know, when we pull the ripcord, on key technologies, key capabilities or key munitions—whatever it might be—we can develop what we need, fast.

I 100% agree. I was reassured that we do some of the wargaming and exercising we do in the Ministry of Defence with industry as well. That is really good practice, but we have to go a bit further. Just as we need to think about broadening and deepening our defence industrial base to make sure that we have warfighting capacity and capability within the defence industry, we also need to look across the whole of the economy and, from a national resilience point of view, across public services.

For example, as Defence Secretary I do not feel remotely agnostic about the future of Britain’s steel industry, the automotive industry and a whole bunch of other industries whose day-to-day work now might have nothing to do with defence but, should this country find itself at war, we would want them to switch production from civilian everyday use into defence production and warfighting. If we start to look at our wider industrial base through that lens, it lends itself to different strategic choices. We need to do the same exercise with NATO allies. If we start to think more in those sorts of terms, we will be in a better place.

Finally, there were obviously CBRN threats that concerned me when I was the Health and Social Care Secretary, and I was sighted on things at a higher classification in that role. One of the best innovations in that area was the resilience committee of the National Security Council, which allowed domestic Government Departments that would not normally find themselves around the Cobra table to have that conversation. We should be thinking about warfighting in 2030 through an NHS lens, through a logistics lens and so on—look at Ukraine.
Q37 To pick up on the theme of procurement and industry, what changes do you want to bring about to the way we procure kit?

The MOD does not have a great reputation on this, but even I was shocked when I saw how long it takes to get from the design, and what it is you want to buy, to contracting. For major platforms that takes six years. For systems like sensors, radars and so on, it takes three years. That is an extraordinary length of time just to get a contract agreed. It makes some of the worst bits of my last job look remarkably efficient.
What are you going to do that is different, though?

The NAD group is already beginning to make a real impact. In terms of the impact of that reform, we have now gone down to just under five years on major platforms, and that is just since the SDR. For pace-setting modular upgrades—the systems I mentioned—the time has gone from three years to one year, and we want to be able to do off-the-shelf within three months. With the introduction of the NAD group, the system is now wired to do precisely that.
The NAD group is still fairly nascent—was it January this year that it was stood up?
Jeremy Pocklington indicated assent.

Rupert Pearce has been in as the National Armaments Director for a year now, but it is my job to keep my beady eye on it, to make sure it is working in practice and to give Rupert the backing that he needs with Jeremy. I have to say—I think you all know this through your previous engagements—in terms of ministerial leadership, Luke Pollard is outstanding and has driven a lot of the focus on this.

If I may add to what the Secretary of State said, first of all it is about segmenting procurement more effectively. That is one of the overwhelming lessons from Ukraine: you do not need to procure drones—low-value kit—in the same way that you procure ships and planes, so we need to have different systems that enable us to go after things more quickly.

The second thing is to clarify accountabilities in d efence. It is a large and complex enterprise, so the thing about defence reform is that it clarifies and simplifies accountability. Simplicity has been my mantra as we have moved to implementation.

The third thing to highlight is the shift in responsibility for the invest budget from MSHQ to the National Armaments Director, with a system of problem statements, whereby we now have the armed forces setting out clearly the problem statement, their capabilities and the gap they have, and that enables the NAD group to engage industry to identify more innovative solutions to the problem statement.

It is a bit about how you square that circle. In that environment where you are doing more buying British, and being more open to things like direct awards or UK-only competitions, by having the approach of setting out problem statements for industry to get its teeth into, you start to inspire a bit of competition, and also some collaboration. You really drive innovation at that stage, which is part of mitigating against the risk of driving up costs.

Q38 There has been progress, definitely, and that is great to see, but six years to five years is—you know? What would you like to see? Will you continue to drive those timescales down? Are they going to get better? In a year’s time, what do you want those timescales to be?

I am hesitant about setting new targets unilaterally in front of a Committee, but we want to continue to accelerate. Ultimately, we want to get that from six years to two years, recognising that for major platforms it is complicated, so we have to be realistic.
Let us now delve into the defence investment plan.

Q39 Welcome to Defence, from one 10-year plan to the next. Lord Robertson, on the SDR, said: “ we built the strategic defence review based on an assessment of 10 years—that was our assessment at the time of when a peer opponent might challenge the United Kingdom. That timeframe has clearly now been accelerated. Quite simply, we are running out of years. ” He said that moving from the SDR to the DIP “dismayed” the UK’s allies. General Barrons said that the delay in its production had “depleted the industrial base” and dismayed our allies. Our concern is with that criticism—with that critique—by two of the reviewers of the SDR. How will you rebuild confidence in UK defence?

Crucially, I absolutely accept the wrangling over the DIP taking far too long, and that that has caused wider uncertainty and concern among industry and allies. I think that we now have greater certainty about the level of ambition and intent of this Government and Chancellor. Since taking office, from the conversations that I have been having with allies, whether in NATO, the United States, across Europe or further afield, I think that people can see the seriousness of our intent. That is important, particularly in the context of the push for higher spending, sometimes being perceived by the public as being driven by Washington.

It is absolutely true that President Trump and his Administration have urged Britain and our European allies to do more and to take greater responsibility for our own defence and the defence of our continent—they are right to do so, and it is in our national self-interest to do so—but I do not feel that we are doing what we are doing because of external pressure; we are doing it because it is the right thing to do. I think it is for Britain and Europe to be out of this defensive crouch about defence spending and to lean in actively to spending more, to doing more and to strengthening European NATO. That is the message that I will be conveying. I speak and engage fairly regularly with my US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, and that is the message I will be able to relay directly when I visit Washington this week.

Q40 The DIP says that the MOD will be required to provide an annual delivery update to Parliament each summer, with the first of those expected in July 2027. What can we expect to see in the first report to Parliament?

This is a good time for you to help to shape it—it will be the first one. In terms of how you want us to set out that reporting to Parliament, there is a good opportunity for the Defence Committee to shape with us the contents, so that we provide useful, transparent information and accountability to Parliament. That is important from two perspectives: to show the impact that we are having and also to demonstrate what more needs to be done. Making the case for greater defence spending is an ongoing process. Public support is high, but we cannot take it for granted.

Q41 Effective parliamentary scrutiny relies on transparency, yet the DIP omits much of the detail that was routinely shared in the old equipment plan. The equipment plan set out a 10-year strategic view and forward spending. Obviously, as Mike alluded to earlier, the DIP goes only to the next three or four years. How can it be justified that we are not seeing the actual detail and costings like we did in the old equipment plan?

There is a balance to be struck in this area, for reasons I know the Committee is sympathetic to, of being accountable to Parliament and open with the public, but also not providing information voluntarily and avoidably that is useful to those who would do us harm.

Back to the spirit of my first answer, we might want to think through what the public report to Parliament looks like, but also what the briefings to this Committee and the Public Accounts Committee look like so that we get the balance right between being as open and transparent with Parliament and the public as it is responsible to be, and also making sure that, where we cannot show as much as everyone might like, we can provide assurance to the Committee, on their behalf, and give you space to scrutinise and challenge in a way that is constructive and helpful without publishing information we would not want to be in the public domain.

There is a balance between giving certainty to the armed forces and industry about our direction, and also retaining some flexibility, particularly in the later years, to respond to the evolving threat landscape and changes in technology.

One reason why we made a very conscious decision not to reproduce the old equipment plan is because the pace of change is faster than it has ever been historically. Setting out now in detail exactly what we need to spend our money on in years seven, eight, nine and 10 would not be sensible. The pace of change is so fast.

No one in this room knows what types of drones will be the most appropriate ones to buy. What we need to do now is to build the market, the industrial base and the innovation system so that we can move quickly as the years progress. There is a balance to be struck between providing certainty where we can, but taking a different approach.

Finally, in comparison to the old equipment plans, we also made a very conscious decision to look across the whole of the defence budget in the investment plan. The equipment plan did not do that. We are trying to set out a more holistic picture across the entirety of our budget, recognising that all parts of the enterprise need to work together to support the war fighter.
Q42 Maybe this question is for both of you—
Feel free to pick on Tim as well.

Guest commentary from RUSI said that the DIP should be “judged not only by whether it allocates enough money, but also by whether it helps Parliament, the Treasury, the services and the public see how money becomes capacity—and whether that capacity becomes military power.” How do you think the DIP should be judged, and do you agree with the commentary that we received from RUSI?

I think that is a good summary . In some ways it bridges between the argument for more money and the argument I have been making about making sure that that money is well spent. Spending more money badly on defence is not what any of us want to see; it would not be virtuous. It does need to translate into warfighting capability. Sometimes that has meant choices have not always gone down as well as we would have liked, but that is because we have got to keep that focus on capability.
Q43 Can you confirm whether you made a decision recently to take money—over a billion quid—from the defence housing budget?

My predecessor took that decision. The amount being spent on defence housing is unchanged, but I concede that the profile of that spend—back to Mr Twigg’s earlier question—is more backloaded than it would have been. That is not stopping us from making a big difference on defence housing. Is it as fast as we would all like to see? No. You cannot pretend that, by backloading, you are still able to deliver the same as you would have done earlier on. It will improve year on year, but a choice was made to focus on capability over housing at that point in the process.

Q44 I would say, Secretary of State, that our personnel are the best capability that we can have. As someone with a large garrison in their constituency, with poor defence housing in some areas, I think that is a priority that you should revisit. You have no capability without the personnel to operate it.

I absolutely take that on the chin. I think a lot about the responsibility that I personally, and we as the state, have to people who serve, their families and people who have served previously. When I see the condition of some of our defence housing, it is up there with some of my worst constituency casework. I expect a lot better for those families who make enormous sacrifices and experience a lot of disruption for what they do. I am not comfortable with that choice, and I am not going to add insult to injury by pretending that rephasing does not mean that we will not be able to do as much as we would otherwise have done on the previous phasing.

There will be year-on-year improvement, and already, since coming in, we have brought 36,000 military homes back into public ownership, delivering significant upgrades. I am keen to see what more we can do to leverage in investment in that area, because I understand the choice, but I do not think any of us ought to be comfortable with it.

It was a very difficult decision in the final stages of the defence investment plan that the Secretary of State’s predecessor had to take. I would emphasise that we are still getting on and delivering. We are going to refurbish 1,000 homes this year and move another 1,000 homes from void unavailable to void available. It is a technical change, but it will release more homes through the hard work of the Defence Infrastructure Organisation. Obviously we would all like to get on with this as quickly as we can.

Q45 Secretary of State, you have talked rightly about the importance of boosting the defence industrial base. Are you aware of the yawning gap that still exists between the speed of procurement through Kindred and the speed of procurement through MOD, often for similar kinds of weapons systems? What is the way of getting past that? We really need to move the entire procurement process, for systems that we can, much more towards a Kindred-type system.
I do not disagree. There is definitely more to do.

Q46 Could you elaborate a little on that possibly? What are the kinds of things you would like to do, or the kinds of systems you would like to see brought under a Kindred approach? What do you do about tens of thousands of people thinking about alternative ways of procuring?
What would you prioritise?

Well, you ask the MP for Hereford what he would prioritise. Let us talk about that for a second. I would prioritise technologies that we know are going to be essential, even if we do not know exactly what. We are talking about munitions, drones and systems of delivery that fall short of platforms. I would be looking for a 300% acceleration in the speed at which we deliver those. I think that is absolutely doable for many of these systems. I would be looking for a further investment in the way in which we finance these things. At the moment, we provide inadequate domestic demand for these systems, and then we are surprised when these players go to Norway, Scandi, America and the Gulf. We do not have enough patient capital, so we force them into the hands of VCs, who are often very demanding. They get hooked on cash and then cannot build fast enough, and that puts them on a treadmill. There is a whole series of things—this is a bigger conversation.

I do not disagree with what you said about the investment environment. We have a defence investment summit coming up before Christmas—it will take place on 1 December. The intention is to make sure that, ready for that, we have an order book of investible propositions and that the right people—domestic and international investors—are gathered so that we can look at what more we can do to leverage in the support that we need. It would be worth our having a longer conversation ahead of that.
Q47 I would be grateful for that. Maybe the perm sec can talk a bit about patient capital, which is the other part of the equation.

I was not actually going to come in on that point. The thing I was going to highlight, in terms of learning the lessons from Kindred, which I think we would very strongly agree on, is that we think that UK Defence Innovation is going to have an important role in being able to procure very quickly right at the edge of innovation, with the ringfenced budget of £400 million that we will be establishing. That will enable it to move quickly and be free of controls. It will be many of the same people—people with the skills and experience from Kindred—working in that part of the Department to make sure we really are learning the lessons. We can move very quickly in certain circumstances, and we need to expand the range of circumstances in which we are able to do that.

Q48 Right, but the obvious further pushback is that if you are constantly buying through a farmers’ market of competitions, you are not necessarily growing domestic in-depth capability. Put it this way: if we were car manufacturing, we might decide that we want a Mercedes-Benz and a BMW of drones. We are not doing that at the moment. Why not?

Ultimately, what the right industrial strategy is around the drone sector is a really important question. My own view is that I am not sure the market is developed enough to reach a very clear view on that. We need to do more to continue to develop the excellent companies that we have. We obviously have the Uncrewed Systems Centre in Swindon, which will be able to play a leading role in this.

On your wider point about financing, we also need to ensure that we have adequate financing for the supply chain into these companies. There is obviously a role for different forms of capital, and there may also be a role for the state in that to make sure we are building that ecosystem so that we can really build a sector that can innovate and has sufficient agility.
Q49 Secretary of State, what is the timing for the Type 45 replacement?
I believe it is early 2030s. Is that right, Tim?

I can speak to that. As you know, the Type 45s are due to start going out of service from 2035. At the moment, we have started investment in a hybrid Navy alternative for that. You probably heard the First Sea Lord talking quite passionately about his vision for a hybrid Navy. The early investment that we are doing is to get those projects up and running so that, by the time the Type 45 starts going out of service, we have a hybrid replacement for that capability coming into service.
So a hybrid Navy by the early 2030s is what you are saying. Is that right?
There will be a hybrid Navy solution that comes in over time, and that will begin to come in in the 2030s as the Type 45 goes out of service.
Q50 Will you extend the life of the current Type 45s?

We don’t want to extend the Type 45. Rather than extending older platforms that cost a lot of money to run, we would rather spend the money focusing on new technology. That is what the First Sea Lord wants, and that is what we are aiming to do.
Q51 What is your estimate of the amount of money that has been saved by taking this approach to be deployed on the hybrid Navy?
Saved in comparison with—
In comparison with the previous regime, which was Type 45 and its successor platforms.
It is undoubtedly a more cost-effective approach, but that is not why the First Sea Lord is pursuing it—
Sure. I just wonder how much you think is available to be spent on it.

The defence investment plan sets out our initial investment. There will be more money to follow after that initial spending period. We have £1.5 billion in this Parliament set aside for initiating hybrid Navy projects, and that project team is standing up now.
Q52 But there is a possibility of a shortfall of capability before the hybrid Navy is fully established, right?

We have almost 10 years to get the Type 45 replacement up and running. We are in a world where we are seeing innovation moving quickly and the market being disrupted by start-ups and new tech companies. We were just talking about how we reduce the procurement timelines. The sorts of companies that are coming on to the market now are not offering us procurement timelines that go on for decades; they are offering us far quicker turnaround timelines in order to bring new capability in.
Q53 The Type 45 was a well-established air defence platform. I just want you to give me some reassurance that we will have adequate capability to cover that gap and more by the time it is retired.
We will.
You are saying that we will.
We will have air defence capability for maritime—
Comparable or better?

It should be better, because new technology will come online, and the aim is to do that in a more effective way. As to when the transition happens in detail, that is what we are working through at the moment. We do not want to extend Type 45. It is clearly an option, but it is not part of our plan. We want to focus our money on investing in new technology and bringing that online as soon as possible.
Q54 Secretary of State, it will not surprise you to hear that I want to come on to defence finance, but I want to pick up on another case study first.

Evolve Dynamics is a drone manufacturer that is not in my constituency, but it employs people from my patch. It has been making small surveillance drones that were part of the battlegroup ISR programme. It won that work and delivered 245 drones successfully in August. It was told that the Army loved the product, and was told to ramp up because they wanted up to another 1,000 of these products.

Going into the DIP, everything was good. They were told to grow their business and work out how they could deliver up to 1,000. Two weeks after the DIP, they were told that the programme was frozen and were then left to work things out, because of budget constraints. Do you recognise how difficult it is for a British company to have gone through the process of ramping up and then been told to stop?

Yes. I spent a lot of time this morning in front of the House of Lords Committee talking about the importance of this being a partnership with business and industry. What you just described is not an example of us being a good partner. It is bad enough when we, or our partners on the other side of the equation for that matter, shift timescales, rephase and all the rest of it, but it is a different order of challenge if you are one of our primes making that adjustment, or one of our SMEs. We have to be a better customer and partner, particularly to the SME sector.

There is another thing that Luke and I in particular feel strongly about, but it is true across the Defence team, particularly for Lord Coaker with the international engagement he does. I also want to make sure that we are a champion for exports, and that we support with exporting. I would be grateful if you could send me further details of that particular case study.

Q55 Your office has the details. My frustration is particularly because the Army wants these products. This is not a case of the Army or MOD not liking the product; the Army is asking for it, but they have been told to freeze. These guys have employed extra people and worked out how to produce this stuff, and suddenly those people do not have jobs. I would be really grateful if you could look into that case study and see if there is anything you can do.

I will now come on to defence finance and the defence, security and resilience bank. You obviously joined my campaign to advocate for the UK to join the defence, security and resilience bank. What was it about the case for the DSRB that made you want to give it your public support?
An excellent way to put that question in the middle of the Chancellor’s live decision-making process on this issue.

The DSRB offers a number of opportunities in terms of supporting access to finance for the defence sector, particularly if, in terms of the rate of borrowing, it can be lower cost. It is interesting in terms of the geopolitics of the offer and Mark Carney’s leadership as well, which we very much respect.

This was not your question, but I can sense where the next question will go. I am working closely with the Chancellor on this and caught up with him only last night in anticipation of your question, which I knew would come without you telling me.

The Chancellor is keen to see whether we can get the DSRB and the multilateral defence mechanism in alignment and working together, and whether that would be of greater benefit to the UK, our partners in the MDM and to the DSRB initiative. But that is very much a live conversation that is led by the Chancellor.

Q56 I slightly regret that we cannot just have a conversation about the merits of the DSRB without it always being drawn back to the MDM. We finally got the Treasury to acknowledge that these are very different products; they do different things. I believe there are some really quick wins when it comes to defence finance. Ultimately, as much as we are having this debate about percentages of GDP, from an industrial capacity perspective we will not be able to spend that money unless, for example, the SMEs in my patch can actually get money from the banks to increase their capacity to answer that call. What is it about this MDM-DSRB conversation? The joint procurement piece is a very complicated thing to do in practice. How do you think that is all going to play out?

From the Chancellor’s perspective—I am taking the risk of speaking for the Chancellor, which is potentially career ending if you get it wrong—I think what he is trying to explore is whether the whole could be greater than the sum of its parts in relation to both the DSRB initiative and the MDM, and how that plays into the wider strategic strength of NATO itself.

When he was Defence Secretary, the Chancellor was a big champion of the principle of NATO first. In the spirit of what I said in my opening remarks about trying to make sure that healthy competition among friends does not become self-defeating protectionism, the more we can align a shared economic outlook and shared approach to financing and procurement as allies—as well as on military co-operation—the stronger we will be on military co-operation, and the stronger our deterrence, capability and collective defence industrial base will be.

There is potentially a big prize if those things could be brought together and cohered. But obviously it is not entirely straightforward because they are different initiatives and slightly different configurations of countries are involved in those conversations. They are not decisions that are owned solely by Canada in the case of the DSRB or the MDM in the case of the UK, so that is very much a live conversation. You will have seen what the Chancellor said publicly about his conversations with his Canadian counterpart.
Q57 On NATO first, have you looked at the NATO Support and Procurement Agency? Do you see any benefit in the fact that we could use that more fully?

My sense is that we are not making great use of it at the moment. In common with what we are doing across the rest of procurement and the integrated force model we are building, and how that then translates into the problem statement rather than the status quo that we have had on procurement, I am keen to make sure we are playing the NATO procurement route into that too.

There is another thing I am struck by, which I feel particularly acutely in the work I do with and on behalf of Ukraine to try to meet its requirements. It is a live case study of how we are often fishing in the same pool for the same stuff, and if we are not careful, we are going to end up driving up costs and not broadening our industrial base, individually and collectively, in the way that we need to. The more we can have a coherent approach as NATO members to understanding our requirements and procuring together more effectively, the more that will also help us to send the right demand signals into industry, now and for the longer term.

Q58 But also, through the NSPA, you can procure things without doing joint procurement. You can procure single source, and you do not pay VAT. In terms of a quick win, that is taking 20% off the cost of a product. I have never got the MOD to really give me an answer on why they do not do that.
Jeremy, do you want to say anything about what has happened historically?

Single source has an important role to play. It is regulated, and about half our spend comes through that. However, historically, there has been a desire to use competition where possible. I think we are looking afresh at the boundary and at exactly how to get this right, so we are seeking to be more open-minded than we have been historically on this issue.

Q59 On the hybrid Navy, you mentioned that £1.5 billion has been allocated to the development of that concept, which is really vital because it will replace our Destroyers by 2030. As we have discussed, beyond 2030 we will be relying on the new spending round. Do you think that £1.5 billion is enough to effectively do the early stages of bringing into work five classes of ship?

It is a start, but it is not going to be the limit of our investment in the hybrid Navy. I go back to the point I was making earlier on: the market has been completely disrupted by the kinds of company, industry and technology that we are seeing come online.

As we stand up the team to look at the hybrid Navy, which we are doing now, and as we look at the detail and engage with industry, the kind of investment we need to make will become far clearer, and that will be a matter for how we prioritise our future spend. It is a start, but I do not think we see it, by any means, as the limit of our investment. It is what we decided and judged was enough to get us going.

We are already almost on contract for an uncrewed surface vessel; the competition is in the final stages, and the results of that will be announced soon. That vessel will be in the water next year, so we are getting on with it.

We will learn more about how these technologies are fielded. We are at the cutting edge of this, and we are seeing an explosion of industrial energy around it. It is about harnessing how industry are engaging with this, as well as the new levels of competition and, frankly, the appetite for private investment in this area, such as research and so on. As we learn more over the coming months about how that is coming together, we will know more about how we will then need to prioritise our funding going forward.

May I emphasise that this is on top of the fact that we are still investing and constructing two different classes of frigate in this country and three classes of submarine right now? This is in addition to the huge investment that is under way. Obviously, we would all like it to be quicker.
Q60 It is a new concept, and it is the first time we have done it. Would you consider it a risk, Secretary of State?

Innovation always involves some degree of risk. One of the things I said to the House of Lords Committee this morning was that, politically, we need to be more comfortable than we sometimes are with carrying risk.

In any successful innovation, there are a whole bunch of stories of failure before you get to the success. What we actually need to do is go much more quickly through those rounds of failure before getting to success. Politically, we must then own that and be comfortable with it. In politics, we do not always lend ourselves to leaning into that culture of innovation, so we become risk averse, drive up cost and reduce capability.

In that spirit, what the First Sea Lord is championing in the hybrid Navy concept is—I am sometimes in danger of over-claiming—genuinely world-leading. I have been struck in the last few months by the number of conversations that I have had with counterparts who are actively interested in tracking what we are doing because they see the potential benefits , so if we get this right — I think there are grounds for confidence —we will not only have a novel and groundbreaking capability here in Britain ; we will have a great export opportunity as well.

I note that we have less than half an hour left and there is still quite a lot of ground to cover, so I ask M embers to keep their questions as concise as possible , and could the responses be likewise concise?

Q61 I have a question, Secretary of State, about defence reform. You have come into a live process . You have earned a reputation , from running the H ealth D epartment , as someone who is a fairly radical reformer yourself , given your success there. But you have come into D efence and there is already something under way , which you alluded to earlier. You mentioned wanting to cohere a bit more. Can you give us a sense of your view of defence reform , what kind of tweaks you might make during your leadership and what you see as the likely delivered benefits of it in the coming years ?

I think my job is to get it motoring and to make sure that we are using the new structures and new ways of working to deliver the outcomes that we want to see. There is still a bit, at this stage in the process , in some places, of the worst of all worlds — still doing the old way of working and shoehorning it into the new model. That is not really going to work. And there are some cultural challenges.

If I think about the combination between the integrated force model approach that MSHQ is driving and how that relates to the NAD group in terms of problem statements and going out to industry on that basis , that is not just an operational change. It is a big cultural change that not everyone will be comfortable with, because there will be a lot of people who are used to specifying what they want and sticking with the tried and trusted and will find themselves instead having to present their requirements in a different way. So it is a big change operationally and culturally.

I do think that overall it is the right change. Of all the features of defence reform, the one that I am probably keeping my eye on most closely is the NAD group , j ust because of the size and scale and the opportunity of it. I think it ’s really exciting, but we have to pull it off and it has to deliver tangible results.

If you look back at the Lords Committee hearing this morning, I think you will see that we have the right leadership in place , but we also have to make sure that carries down throughout . I certainly feel that , across the leadership of the D epartment and the leadership of our armed forces , people are bought into this , b ut that has to cascade right the way down through the four branches —

Q62 It always concerns me greatly when I see how much time S ecretaries of S tate have to spend in Parliament giving evidence to millions of different Committees. You mentioned your counterpart , Pete Hegseth , earlier. I wonder how much time he has to spend in Congress giving this kind of —
I will ask him on Thursday .

Yes, be sure to ask him . I just have another quick question , on culture. A lot of defence reform is structural changes , but you have alluded to the cultural shift that that is trying to get after. We had in front of this Committee the previous CD S , Admiral Tony Radakin —a very impressive and hugely respected character, and quite rightly —and he spoke to us about defence reform at some length and about cultural shifts. He then moved on from the role , and for his first speech promptly gives a very frank and honest speech where he says , in his own language, “I failed to shift the culture . We couldn’t do enough. ” And he had years to attempt it , so there is something very deeply ingrained that need s shifting. Have you noticed that yourself? What is your sense of that?
With any part of Whitehall, you will find lots of people admiring the problems, but feeling unable to bring about the change that they want to see.

When I was driving the modernisation and reform that we were doing at Health, I felt that we were at the head of the pack, actually. The NHS England decision was very big, very visible and very radical. I came into the Ministry of Defence acutely aware that John Healey had started defence reform a year earlier and that it is a lot further down the track. I have inherited something that is at more of an advanced stage than what the Health Secretary has inherited from me.

I think that is a great opportunity for defence, but it is now sitting in a wider Government programme, which the First Secretary has been setting out, of changing the way that the Government take decisions, strengthening democratic control and accountability, and stripping back layers of Whitehall bureaucracy, arm’s length bodies and opportunities for pointless judicial reviews that just cost time and money, and make lawyers wealthier. I feel that we are now swimming with the tide rather than against it.

On the point about culture, though, I think that we have to be more adventurous and be prepared to take some risks. We definitely need to speed up decision making, and try to short-circuit clearance processes as best we can.

The final thing I would say on culture, which is markedly different from that of the Department of State that I led before and the public services that it was responsible for, is that I am acutely aware that I am working in a far more male environment than I did in Health and Social Care.

There are some real strengths in terms of the chain of command and the professionalism that the military bring, and co-locating the military and civilian personnel on civil servants has strengthened the Department of State. However, there are also real behavioural challenges in terms of sexism, misogyny and the wider issues that we face, which we need to grip and take seriously, and not see as a box-ticking exercise.
Thank you very much. We will come back to that later.

Q63 Secretary of State, I really welcomed your words earlier about more accurately naming the grey zone or hybrid threats as state-sponsored terrorism. With Russia escalating its attacks throughout Europe, I just wondered how the MOD is prioritising and assessing the future threats, and its reactions to them.

It is a major focus of the Department of State, of defence intelligence, of our intelligence and security services, and of the work we are doing across our armed forces to anticipate potential threats, and to deter, to detect and, should deterrence fail, to be ready to defeat. We are not doing this on our own—that is one of the other things that I feel extremely assured of when I have been with international counterparts, either bilaterally or in formats such as JEF. We are all confronting the same challenges. We have the same picture of the nature of the threat, and we have the same resolve. And the collective security in the principle as well as the practice of article 5, which underpins NATO, remains absolutely unshakeable.
Q64 Specifically, what is your assessment of the threat around drones for our national infrastructure and our airbases, and obviously I will mention the shipyards as well?

We cannot be remotely complacent. We are putting £790 million into integrated air and missile defence to modernise some of our older systems—obviously, we have to take a layered approach—but as we have seen in the war in Ukraine, drone technology presents a new threat. Those are relatively low-cost, high-impact devices; I am sure that my Russian counterpart could convey far more powerfully the impact that fairly low-cost Ukrainian drones, for example, have had on very expensive platforms. It is in that context that we—not just as the UK, but with our allies—are actively working on developing effective defences against drone warfare.
Q65 To touch on ballistic missiles, we have heard a lot about iron domes or shields in the media recently.
I think Luke Pollard called it an iron sieve.

Yes. The Committee heard that it would cost £1 billion per city to cover what we need to. I am interested to hear it reported that Faslane is getting ballistic shelters. Are you looking at rolling that out in other areas?
There is a danger of my being dragged into a level of operational security detail that I would not want to share in this format.
It is public knowledge. It is in the UK Defence Journal .

There is a difference between what others report and what we are willing to say. Given the spirit in which we engage with this Committee, first, I would always be happy to try to share with the Committee in a closed format as much as we can of that which we would not want to share in an open session. Given your constituency interest in this, I can reassure you that the security of our nuclear deterrent and the enterprise that underpins it is obviously of the highest importance to us. I would be very happy to make sure that we properly brief you as the Member of Parliament for Barrow.

Q66 We are going to switch targets, Secretary of State, to focus on the letter about the Northern Ireland troubles Bill amendments that you sent to the Chair yesterday, in which you referenced the fact that inquests and inquiries will be prohibited unless they are viewed as “essential”. The joint framework explicitly guarantees that the nine inquests that were previously put on pause, including Loughgall, will be automatically restarted. Does what you have written in these amendments trump that, or will the interpretation of “essential” be, “Well yes, because we have committed to it in the framework”?

In terms of those particular inquests, there is just not a way of circumventing that particular issue that is consistent with our treaty obligations. With the amendments we have laid, we have got to a place where it deals with some of the fundamental concerns that I as a Member of Parliament, let alone colleagues, had. We are in a much stronger place, to the extent that Sinn Féin have condemned the amendments and the Bill as a “Veterans Charter”. As far as I am concerned, that is the highest plaudit possible, and I am absolutely delighted that that is where we have got to.

We have worked intensively with the Northern Ireland Secretary and his team to get the Bill to a much better place where it deals with what I think is my personal moral obligation to people who have served: to make sure that we are not constantly rinsing and repeating, that they are not lying awake with anxiety about hearing a knock at the door or a telephone call, that the actions of the British military who served in Op Banner are not in any way considered equivalent to the terrorist activity of paramilitaries, that people are given the right to seek anonymity and that the presumption is that veterans will not be called to Northern Ireland to give evidence, but can do so at home. That, as well as compelling new evidence, provides the most robust protections possible.

The final thing I would say in relation to the treaty obligations we are under is that we should not see this as a one-way benefit, as it were. Obviously, the Irish Government have a particular political perspective, and those who are republican in their political outlook have a particular interest, but the interest I have in this is also about making sure that victims have answers and recognising that many of those victims were British service personnel and their families, and they deserve answers. That sometimes gets lost because some of the other voices are louder.

I am not saying this to be ingratiating or party political about it, but I want to place on record that I am genuinely thankful to Chris Bryant for the way he has approached this as Northern Ireland Secretary. He has a range of considerations to balance. The way I approached this with Calvin Bailey was to see my job as being solely to champion the interests of our veterans and their families and think through the consequences of the choices we make as Members of Parliament today for the future for people who are serving today and people who serve in the future and giving them the certainty that, as they have our backs as a country, their Government have their backs now and in the future. That is the spirit in which I approached it as Defence Secretary.

Q67 We will have more time to debate these things next week. It still hangs on a very subjective judgment of what is essential and in whose view, but we will leave that one there. On Lord Justice Haddon-Cave’s inquiry, he said recently that a number of the SAS operators who have been called to give evidence have exercised their right to silence. Given what has happened in Northern Ireland, can you really blame them?

No. That is their right and I am not going to criticise anyone who exercises that right. More generally, what is my impression? I do not want to prejudge what the inquiry is going to say. It was commissioned by one of my predecessors and concerns some very serious allegations of wrongdoing. In the conversations I have had—with special forces specifically, but it applies right across our armed forces —first, no one seeks immunity. Everyone agrees that we should hold ourselves and each other to the highest standards and that people ought to bring ethics, professional integrity and the highest level of professionalism to these roles, and people seek to do that. Where people are guilty of illegal action in whatever theatre, no one is asking for immunity.

I think where the concern lies, and I would echo that concern, is the risk that the actions of a few are used to smear the integrity and the honour of the many. Special forces do not ask for special treatment. What they do expect is that Governments who send them into difficult operations to act in the interests of this country stand with them and not leave them exposed. That is the responsibility I feel today—to stand up not just for the people I send into operations, but for those who went into operations on behalf of my predecessors.

Q68 Yes, but you have also said that you will not stop the automaticity of the Loughgall inquest. That is exactly what you have just said: you could not guarantee that Loughgall will not go ahead. Having the back of the special forces who did that, however many years ago that was, has been played out at Haddon-Cave.

I am not going to pretend that the amendments do things that they do not. It is a Northern Ireland Bill, but it is hugely consequential for the framework we think about for the future. I genuinely think it offers better protections than the status quo. It is a significant improvement on where we are today. If it were not, I would not support it.
No doubt this will be debated at considerable length in the main Chamber as well.
Q69 Can you tell us about the timeframe and contents of the defence readiness Bill, which we were meant to have in this Parliament, but disappointingly was not in the King’s Speech?

It was obviously one of the recommendations of the strategic defence review. It is one that the Government accept and we are actively working on. I have to be a bit careful what I say, because we never ever make announcements on behalf of His Majesty about what is in his Speech, and almost as terrifying as falling foul of the Palace is falling foul of business managers. Recognising that I have to work with and through colleagues, I can tell you that we are actively working on the defence readiness Bill. I think it is an important piece of legislation that we will need to pass, not least given the threat environment that we face, and I would want that to be introduced to Parliament as soon as possible.
Q70 What is in it?

In the spirit of readiness, it does not take us, and will not take us, as far as the legal framework we would need to be in, in the event that we are at war, but it is everything leading up to it. One of the things I anticipate that the Committee will be interested in is the role the Committee can play. I am keen to try to provide an opportunity for scrutiny of measures in the Bill sooner rather than later. It is something we are actively working on, so people are free to make representations to the Department any time they like—
Q71 Pre-legislative scrutiny?

That is definitely something that is for business managers to decide with us, but I can tell you that I am instinctively in favour of pre-legislative scrutiny, as long as it does not slow up getting the Bill through. I actually think that pre-legislative scrutiny would be really beneficial in terms of helping both Houses to understand why we might need to put certain measures in the Bill, but I think it is a massive opportunity in the context of the national conversation. I am instinctively in favour, but I recognise that business managers have a really difficult job to do in balancing all the competing demands for Bills, and pre-legislative scrutiny feeds into that. Hopefully that public acknowledgment of the fiendish dilemmas they face will make them more amenable to my request for a Bill.

Q72 Secretary of State, you will know that this Committee takes the issue of women in the armed forces extremely seriously, whether through the groundbreaking 2021 Committee inquiry report that was published or our regular sessions within the Committee. You know that we have exchanged correspondence on this where you have acknowledged that your initial impression is that culture and behaviour remain a major challenge in our armed forces .

You will also be aware of the BBC reporting by Sima Kotecha and the team of some very harrowing testimonies from our youngest female soldiers at AFC Harrogate—the Committee also recently visited there. You will also be aware that the Armed Forces Commissioner has stated that she would like to conduct an investigation. However, many victims might not be as confident or as willing to be as open with another serving member of the military. Given that we are dealing with young people, do you think that sort of investigation is sufficient? Should we not have an independent inquiry on this?

First, as I outlined to the Committee—in the interests of time, I will not repeat it all, because it is stuff I have already shared and you already know—there is a lot of work being done on raising our standards and a particular focus on sexism and misogyny, but there is more to do. I definitely want to bring in some external scrutiny of the programme of work that is under way. I have a plan in the pipeline and hope to make an announcement on this in the not-too-distant future, because we need some independent assurance that the things we are doing are right and are having real impact, and that we are walking the talk when it comes to this.

On AFC Harrogate—I welcome the fact that the Committee has visited—the tragedy is that you have an institution that provides enormous opportunity and makes transformational difference to the life chances of young people from a wide range of backgrounds, particularly under-represented working-class backgrounds. That should be a transformational experience, and for the vast majority of young people who go through it is, but that cannot be used as an excuse to tolerate the sorts of experiences that have been reported—
And the misogyny and the sexual violence.

Wes Streeting —which I find profoundly shocking. More than that, all who have taken an interest in this issue for a long time know that what is reported is often only a fraction of the reality. To your point, Chair, about taboo or not wanting to come forward, often it is the victim that feels this burden of responsibility and thinks that if she—often, it is she—comes forward, that can have devastating consequences. Often, the victim is put into this position of feeling like they are the one with responsibility to the perpetrator, rather than being in an environment where they can come forward and be supported, and it can be addressed and dealt with.
Q73 Given that context, would an independent inquiry not be more appropriate, rather than merely an investigation by the Armed Forces Commissioner? That is the key point.

I am looking at what more we can do on external scrutiny. I will come back to you on that. We have commissioned a whole-force safeguarding review, which includes subject matter experts as well as people who have military experience. I will come back to you specifically on external challenge.
Thank you very much; I look forward to that correspondence.

Q74 On the previous question, when we visited, I am afraid that I left fairly unconvinced that they had a grip of the actual issue. When you are talking about the different backgrounds coming in, there seemed to be an awful lot of weight put on that as part of the problem, yet we find that a lot of the investigations focused on people higher up the ranks rather than fellow cadets in there. The culture needs addressing, as you said earlier. I was pleased to hear those words, but my concern is that it is not being taken seriously enough, and that some of those things were being brushed off and dismissed as a cultural problem within society rather than a problem within the academy itself.

Speaking as someone who comes from a very working-class background, despite appearances and accent today, we cannot tolerate this tyranny of low expectations that says because someone is from a working-class background or they have hardships in life, somehow we accept lower standards. If we are serious about transforming the life chances and opportunities of these young people coming through, that is of course about their literacy, numeracy, how they present and the career opportunities we can provide, but it is also about behaviour and how people interact with each other. If you think about the sorts of roles we might ask them to take on if they have a successful career in the military or the wider defence industry, they carry great responsibility, where they are working in close proximity to others and they have to have each other’s backs.

For me, this is fundamentally a moral issue about how we treat people in our society and make sure that we have consistent standards for everyone, but this is also about the performance of our military and having strong, coherent teams that can operate in the most challenging contexts and environments. If you cannot keep your hands to yourself, and if you cannot take responsibility for your actions at this stage in your life and career, we cannot take the risk of putting you into a far more challenging and dangerous environment.

I have a lot of love for the mission of AFC Harrogate, and I want to see that mission replicated elsewhere, but that has got to come with some tough love. I am all up for the armed forces transforming life opportunities for people—and we do. We can tell that story much more effectively about the guys who come in unable to write or add up and whose lives are completely transformed by careers in the military. It is remarkable and we should be really proud of it, but we must not allow the tyranny of low expectations just because of where someone has come from.
Q75 My concern was more about the leaders rather than the people coming through at a younger age.

We have to take that seriously as well. If I may say, I know it is not always comfortable for people, and people might point to a whole range of impressive things that people have done in their careers, but high-profile examples of people being held to account for their conduct is really important—because culture is set from the top.

You may well be highly decorated, and you may well have served this country tremendously in a whole range of avenues, but if your conduct has fallen short of the standards that we expect, it is no use complaining about it or expecting special treatment. We have to have consistent standards and that has to be set at the top.

Q76 The Prime Minister said yesterday that when he met President Trump, he discussed the Falkland Islands with him. Do we know whether the Prime Minister discussed the Chagos islands with him? If he did, what was said? Now that you have been inducted into the c osa n ostra at the MOD, have you been able to work out what the hell the National Security Adviser is up to trying to get rid of it?
First, I don’t think it is a fair characterisation of the poor National Security Adviser that he is trying to get rid of the Chagos islands—quite the opposite.

As someone who sat around the Cabinet table as Health Secretary, and so was part of the conversation on Chagos from that perspective, I came into this role being immediately read far more into the detail on what is going on and what is driving it.

I can assure you that, in the first cross-Government meeting I attended on this, I was as difficult and uncompromising and as big an—I won’t use unparliamentary language—as I could possibly be, to interrogate all of the arguments we often have in the Chamber and in public about why we are engaged in this negotiation.

I can absolutely assure you that I have come to the same conclusion as Boris Johnson, Liz Truss, Rishi Sunak, Keir Starmer and now Andy Burnham, which is that the unique and extremely valuable capability that our base at Diego Garcia provides us and the United States is of such high value that the legal uncertainty around the Chagos islands is not worth carrying. It is therefore in our national interest, as well as the interest of our collective security with the United States, to have a settled legal position through negotiation.
