Indeed, when oil went from $45 a barrel to $100 in 2007- 0 8—how good is your memory?—world food prices went up absolutely in tandem. That shook the Treasury and DEFRA at the time. A food review went on loosely in Government, led by DEFRA. People like me were involved in that, and it concluded, after two years of very large consultations, that we needed to have a new food strategy . I t was called “ Food 2030 ” and it was launched in early 2010. With a change of Government , that was all swept away. Basically, w e have had nothing since. To get something, to answer your question, Mr Lowe, was a lot better.
That was not my question.

It was not your question, but I am giving the good news. Is it adequate? No, because of the enormity, for British politics, of which you are a part, and for policy making, of realising we have a different food system. There are different crises coming down the track, and indeed already here, and a different policy framework is needed. That is a very big shift for a Department—let me be very clear, as a DEFRA watcher—which is weak, small and lacking much high-level political support. One of the many things I appreciated the NAO R eport for was that it gently, and in very low-key, genial NAO language, put it very firmly that there is not the attention. We have not got high-level attention.

If I can digress for a moment, Neil and I and about 35 other academic colleagues, and many from civil society, sent a letter to the Prime Minister and the First Secretary of State, Louise Haigh, last week, on 5 October, to urge them that in the c ivil c ontingencies r eview — not the a gricultural r eview — food should feature very highly. I was a signatory to a coalition of food industry and civil society calling for a new food Bill three months ago. We all think that there is this empty hole at the heart of Government—they are not taking food seriously.

That is not something to point-score with this Government, but is actually looking back to say that British culture has been really bad politically. I, as a citizen, can blame all of you politically for not getting this high enough up the agenda. In that sense, there has been a little movement and—as I am sure you know—it is accelerating at the moment, because of the events that Neil described. I agree with him: events are making food security and food resilience higher profile.

I think we should push Government very hard, hold them to account to do more, on a bigger scale. The present Government are pouring out little initiatives, trying to fill the space, but actually the food system is so enormous that little projects here and there ain’t going to do it. It is big league change that we need to do, and to argue that, over the next 20 years, we have to go in a different direction from what we have done for the past 70 years. That is the conclusion of my “Just in Case” report and, if you really want to take climate change seriously, it is what Neil’s report, “The Roadmap for Resilience”, says.

In particular, I was looking at the public—at whether the public or food consumer culture is prepared—and I was very critical of DEFRA for being silent on that. You could just take “food” out of its title and call it DERA again, because that captures what the reality has been. That is why, in the letter that Neil and I sent last week—I was the lead person on that—we even suggested that the Prime Minister rename DEFRA as the Department for Environment and Food Security. That would hold it to account for what it is it doing for food security—the answer at the moment is not enough but a little more than it has been doing for the past 15 years. That is my honest answer.
Neil, do you want to add to that?

To quote the strategy directly, “ It has become increasingly apparent that the food system is driving negative impacts on our health, environment, and resilience that undermine our food security. ” It is quite something for a Government strategy document to admit that, so there is a sense in which that document is quite a bold step in acknowledging some problems. But I think it is then, “Well, what is to be done about it? What is the long-term vision? What do we aspire to in, say, 2050?” That is where we are left with quite a lot of questions still.

It has also felt a little quiet on the strategy. It was as if there were an announcement some months ago, or 18 months ago, and there does not seem to be a lot of profile around what is happening. One has to work quite hard to find out what work is going on with that strategy. Some are concerned that it is not an open enough conversation. We have a lot of very good and very committed groups on food system reform, beyond the food companies themselves, and I think a concern is that the conversation might be happening just between Government and the food industry, without that wider set of voices.

It is always a challenge with DEFRA. It was interesting: I was working in the Cabinet Office about the time that the previous Labour Government were worrying about what to do with the Ministry of Agriculture, Fisheries and Food. I worked on proposals for a Department of Rural Affairs, which was the proposal in the 2001 general election. DEFRA is actually quite an accident of history. It was not meant to be like this; it was meant to be a Department for rural development. I think Tim is right, however: you get more purchase and more traction sometimes when you pin food system reform to health or to economy and growth agendas that are outwith DEFRA, because it is quite difficult for a Department of that size and type—
Q46 It is encouraging that they have accepted their weaknesses. That is half the equation. Now we wait for more actually to deal with the problem.
To echo Neil, and to accelerate it, we want detail. What can they do precisely—
Farmers need that detail.

Both Neil and I know, and I am sure you know, that farmers are getting into groups that do really imaginative things, rechanging joint land ownership into landscape management in a really imaginative way, but it is not about food production or about feeding the people in a crisis. That is my hard assessment. The creativity is there, but it is not being harnessed. It could be facilitated by DEFRA a lot more than it is at the moment. I want them to be bold, to have confidence to say that the public does want to be fed. They keep on saying that the public wants British food and isn’t getting it.

Q47 Given your answer, we ascertained in the previous session that during covid, a lot of the private sector operators, particularly the food retailers, helped us to get over the short-term problem and did an incredibly good job. Are you worried that there is a slight conflict of interest between the retailers and the producers of our food? Arguably, they are wearing two hats: obviously, they want to see the country do well, but, equally, they have shareholders to whom they report, and they need to make profits. Do you think that is the right formula: to effectively be relying on those private sector food retailers so much, as we clearly did during covid?

I dealt with that at some length in my “Just in Case” report for the National Preparedness Commission. The danger is the food retailers are so powerful: they are the gatekeepers, and they are also the choke point—they are the risk and the most vulnerable spot. In an earlier answer, Neil talked about public engagement. The public—this is my language—need to be involved in that process much more. If you look at DEFRA’s committees, such as the food strategy committee, there are no consumers on it. If you look at one of the others, there is one. It is as though the British policy reflex is just to say, “We are only concerned about supply, not about the people.” The other bit of the equation is demand. What do they want, and how? I am not even sure that “supply and demand” is the right language for dealing with resilience.
Q48 But supply will not happen if the supermarkets are taking all the margin and leaving nothing to the producer, which is what tends to happen. As you say, they are very powerful.
It is, but they would say, and with some justification, that their returns on the capital employed are actually quite small for the vast turnover that they have.
Q49 It is more than the farmers.
It is a lot more than for farmers, but they have not got the assets. The farmer has the assets, and that is the key difference. It is what keeps people on the land.

Q50 My final question—I hate asking this, because I personally do not think there are any areas where Government actually improves things—is whether there are any areas where you think that the Government should be taking a more active role to ensure food supply resilience?

Economists in the Treasury and elsewhere have an orthodoxy for where Government should be getting involved in things. Market failure and public goods are the sorts of concepts that they use. The world is not actually as simple as that, but it helps to think that way if you are an economist. The resilience of the food system is a public good, so I think that there is a legitimate case. The private sector will not necessarily just sort that out by itself, because it is driven by profit. It just will not do that. So you need some Government intervention there and a Government vision. You need to be able to have resilient targets and planning that brings citizens, food poverty groups, distributors and producers together. You need someone to convene the meetings. I think that there is a role for Government as well in agricultural policy and protecting public goods.
Q51 Historically there has been.
I saw you nodding when the farmer was saying on the previous panel that we need more Government support and help.

To answer your question in a different way, although I agree with what Neil said, the role of Government in this is to be the framework and to facilitate asking what we want from that total food system. At the moment, we have—dare I say it—almost ruthless self-interest of different sectors, land being one along, and retailing as well. Another is the logistics industry, although it is actually not being taken seriously enough, yet it is the lifeblood that moves everything. I do not know why logistics is not the key industry. It should be.
It is in the US.
Yes, it is in the US. One in five trucks on British roads is food. When there is a crisis in the diesel market, wow, everything falls apart.

Following Neil, I think that the role of Government is about facilitating, being clear, banging heads together and saying that the public interest is in—to take the answer from my report—feeding people in good times and bad. It is very simple, actually. Around that , we have to do some hard stuff. We must be very clear about defending food systems—literally hard defence. Misinformation and disinformation is huge; I have just come from a huge meeting talking about that. Disinformation as a risk to food systems is a completely new phenomenon in changing food markets. So w e want Government to frame. That does not mean the old arguments of nannies —call them parents , and everyone is in favour of them. It is about frameworks , facilitation and, as Neil said, calling the meeting.

G oing back to the previous answer to Mr Lowe, it is about not just saying there are problems here but saying, “Here is what we want to do about it. Are you up for it or are you not?” It is about unlocking investment. There are walls of cash in the City that are being held back from making the food system more resilient. I was at a huge meeting in the City two weeks ago where th at was discussed, and I was a speaker at it. We were discussing how big insurance companies and banks are awash with money, which is not being applied to developing new infrastructure for the food system to make it more resilient. Why not? I think o nly Government can bring that discussion together.

May I come in on the role of Government? W e need quite a transformational set of changes over the next 25 years. We have had big food system transformations in living memory, in the 1940s, 50s and 60s. We raised our productivity immensely. There was huge technological change and there were changes in cropping practices. That change did not happen just as a result of spontaneous activity by companies. It was orchestrated and convened through a partnership between the state, farmers and agribusiness, all working together around a unity of purpose.

We live in a different world now, but there is a lot to learn from that experience of the 1940s and 50s, when the UK drove a lot of agricultural and food system change quite successfully on its own terms. We should be thinking , “How did that work, and what made that work so well?” because we need change of that magnitude over the next 25 years to cope with the need for resilience to climate change.
I agree with that completely. There is a case for imagination in Governmen t.

Q52 Is there a sense that, in the 1940s and 50s, the memories of the s econd w orld w ar were very fresh? People could remember almost running out of food, whereas now they think we have got food running out of our ears, which is not necessarily the case.

Consumer culture assumes that food is there 364 days a year, 24 hours a day. Look at resilience planning , the sort of meetings I have just been in — twice this week —and the shock when phones go down. One of the points my report made was that we do not know how a culture that thinks food is available in that way will respond if there is major disruption.

There is a bit of complacency about saying, “ W e were great in c ovid, weren't we?” Actually, Government w ere terrible in c ovid. They closed the hospitality sector when it was close to where people are. It needed to be better organised and used. It was people from outside Government who went to the then Government and said, “ Don’t you think we ought to actually be looking at food, because you are closing down some of the workers who are in the food system?” That is why the Food Industry Resilience Forum was set up, and it was closed down. No notes were even taken about how it should be resurrected. That is complacency, to be hard about it.

We need that direction to deal with crises in the short term , but the long-term change that Neil and I am referring to requires a bit of political courage : “Dear British public, we are now in a new era. Things aren’t going to be the same. Here ’s the options for what we could do.” The food industry broadly thinks like this. Talk to people privately and the stories will come out about how close things are to being completely broken up.

Q53 Isn’t part of the answer to your question about why the City is not investing in food security and farming is that successive Governments keep changing the policy ? I nvestors need stability and certainty, and they are not getting that from their Governments.

If that is true for the supply side, think how true that is for the demand side. Consumers want to have security. At one level, they have it—through their phones, or through walking in and seeing full shelves—but that is very easy to knock. We know—indeed, the food industry tells me of its experiences—how easily disrupted that is, and people go from confidence to panic very quickly.

I do not think we can turn to DEFRA to do that sort of work, but there are some of us in academia who are interested in it. To be nice to Government, having been quite critical, there is actually a really interesting bubbling up in the Resilience Academy in the Cabinet Office, as well as the two units now in DEFRA itself, where they are realising that the public are not that myth from world war two—the compliant, knowledgeable, skilled and thrifty shopper. That is not the modern shopper.

Q54 Our previous panel suggested that you would be able to provide some good answers to this question, so I am looking forward to them. Can you give us some examples of other countries that have a really good approach to food resilience? What can we learn from them?

I will get in first and then Tim can expand, because he will have more to say on this than me. For a start, it is really good that people are asking this question, because a lot of discussions about agricultural policy and food policy in the UK are quite parochial. It is really useful to be thinking, “What can we learn from elsewhere?”

Finland comes up very prominently, so I would suggest you look at Finland. There is all sorts of interesting institutional architecture there, but I think it is largely a function of the geography of that country and the Russian threat in the north. Singapore, the Netherlands, Japan and Israel—there are lots of countries that have active and assertive approaches to the resilience of their food systems. They have different types of concerns, and they will have different complexions to their strategies, but there is plenty to be learned from other countries. I am sure Tim will be able to say much more.

I think you have given that breadth. Different countries have different strategies, and their motivations are different. If you go to the Netherlands, which I did for my report, it is a small country that had experience of famine in world war two. Welfare and health policy are really important in the Netherlands because of the 1944-45 famine, and you can still measure the life expectancy of Dutch women by the preconceptual care of their grandmothers—it is quite extraordinary. The threat of famine has had a very big impact, and a bit like how Finland decided to specialise in ceramics and glass, post second world war, the Netherlands chose to invest in those very fertile soils beneath the sea level. It built a culture within Government of taking food production very seriously, while Britain’s approach has been much more about avoidance.

I agree that Finland is also very good. In my experience, the closer to Russia you get, the more seriously they take this. I agree that Singapore is interesting as a city state, because it has decided to double its own production, even though it is a city state, not a big landed sovereignty. I was personally very impressed in France by how—not in the name of resilience, but in the name of rebuilding urban-rural connections—they had done some very interesting work to diversify food systems in the name of agri-food regionalism. Now that work has been of great interest and support to the French Government in the name of resilience.

At the sub-national level, I was particularly taken by the French-speaking part of Belgium: Wallonie or Wallonia , depending on what your language is. There is a city called Liège —it is like Sheffield, because it is a deindustrialised coal and steel town—and 15 years ago they essentially started to say, “What is the point of Liège ?” They said, “Well, let’s run with food as a purpose. People in Liège eat food,” and they basically built a new culture. They have a big annual food festival, and they have started a new programme of regional horticultural enterprises around it.

What I did in my report was look at countries, which is why Neil was turning to me, and there are lessons we can learn from them. For me, the No. 1 is actually Sweden, which I was hinting at earlier. It has done the most astute national review of resilience and what it want s from its land . Norway is doing something very similar , so I think we can learn from the Baltics. Latvia was very interesting to me. It looked at, “ What do we do if Russia rides all over us? Well, probably the Government will have collapsed , so we need to go down the levels and think about hyper - local community food resilience. ” My answer to your question is : don’t just look at national Governments. We need to look below national Governments at the regional —or the sub - national , to be pompous —and at cities down to the very local.

To go back to the question Sir Geoffrey asked a quarter of an hour ago , one reason why I think Neil and I were both saying that you do need the Government to set new frameworks is that one weakness of DEFRA and the British Government system is that they do not apply food and environment strategies to the sub - national. It is all assumed to be done from Whitehall , until you go to Wales.

In Wales, there is a really interesting movement going on. It has created and appointed a food security adviser and a food strategy adviser , but it also has 22 local food partnerships covering the whole of Wales. County councils are doing interesting things in Wales. It is much more multi - level. Do not just look at what we can learn from other countries ; we need to look at who is dealing with the multi - level - ness of food security resilience well . The short answer to that is , no one is doing it perfectly , but there are wonderful lessons we can draw for different levels from different countries.

To wrap that up and to try to be practical , one of the things my report suggested was that English mayors get powers . The Devolution Act needs to do for England what it has done rather unequally and differently for Scotland and Wales. We need to unleash imagination and change to be a more resilient food system . Giving mayors and unitary authorities responsibilities and powers— people like me have been arguing that that needs to come but for resilience . If you are just planning for bombs going off , shocks , disasters , floods and droughts, you in voke the Civil Contingencies Act . Call it a “ resilience Act ”; you would want food to be in there, in which case we need to be giving powers to different levels for different capacities. I think the metro mayors would be up for that in England, and certainly the devolved Administrations in Wales and Scotland would; Northern Ireland is slightly different.

To answer your question in one sentence, there is lots that we can learn from lots of other people, but no one has it perfect because we are all having to rethink what we have done in the last 70 years. We have created a more vulnerable food system that is more prone to shocks . We are now all having to think, what do we want for the next 30 years? We will need to look at that multi-level -ness very seriously.
Tim, thank you. We are up against the clock now. We want to finish by 6 pm .
It was a big question—forgive me.
I want short questions and short answers, please.

Q55 Tim, you just mentioned the issue of critical national infrastructure and the database, from which food is of course missing at present. I think you just said to us that that is an issue in itself , but that a lot more can be done as well. Should the food supply chains be part of the critical national infrastructure database , and should more be done in addition ?

Clive, I am going to answer you frankly: is the Pope a Catholic? Of course. It is absurd . If we make food a critical national infrastructure — which we have , and rightly so —then come a shock , within three days , you need some food. Well, actually, you can do without food for 30 days — it depends where you are —but you need water. We have things like water, electricity and food as CNIs . It clearly ought to be in the database. The NAO—I defer to your colleagues here with you, the NAO team—has that excellent bit of the Report saying that DEFRA has the database , has a benchmark and has dashboards , but they are weak ; they are not enough. But should they be there? Absolutely. That is why we need clearer guidance from the Government about what we want from the food system—or, as I put it, “What’s food for?”
That would then lead on to what elements should be in the database.

Precisely. As I put it very clearly in my “Just in Case” report, I would like that to be not just supply or targets for production; it has to be availability, confidence and trust measures—consumer-ish measures. Again, that takes me back to the thinking behind the food Bill proposal; it is all about that. Keeping the confidence of consumers is a key indicator.

I would just add a point—which is inspired by Tim’s work, actually. I do not know whether this is because of the rules, but a lot of the discussion about critical national infrastructure seems to focus on distribution centres and the cold chain—the hard, technical kit, the science and the big capital stuff. You were also told about the NFU list, which talked about abattoirs as well, which you could add, but there is institutional infrastructure as well.

There are local food groups and food partnerships; Tim mentioned 22 local food partnerships in Wales. There are organisations where people come together regularly to talk and think about this stuff. That is part of the critical national infrastructure for food. It is the institutions and food partnerships that help to distribute food, and promote growing food as well, that will play a part in the resilience of the food system in a crisis.
They are kept out of it at the moment. They are operating as civil society, but they need to be in the overarching framework.

Q56 Is there a responsibility, presumably for the Government, to start educating the public so that they understand some of these challenges and difficulties, and the fact that food is not just going to be there automatically? We do see some national politicians questioning whether climate change is actually a problem that needs addressing; perhaps that sometimes confuses the public on social media, when these are big issues that ought to be part of any understanding.

They are. As you will probably remember, Clive, on the day that the election was called, 22 May 2024, the Government of the day launched the Prepare website . People like me were glad that it had been launched, but it is weak. Telling the 20% of the population who cannot afford to eat well, or even adequately, that they now have to spend about 500 quid preparing for shocks was not helpful. We can do better.

Shortly, the Government will launch a revision to the Prepare website. I think that is good, and we should encourage that, but just having a website is not engaging with the public. It is not—going back to Neil’s point an hour ago—involving the public or representatives of the public in DEFRA committees. We need more public involvement at the heart of what DEFRA is trying to do, or not do, with food.

It is a big question, but Neil is right: it is partly an institutional failure. We do not have a council of food and national food security; we should do. If we had something equivalent to the Climate Change Committee , we would have something giving clear, strategic, central advice to the Government. We have a few bolt-on committees that come along one moment and seem to fade a bit, but we need something put on a better footing. When you look at other countries—to go back to the earlier question—the ones that are doing interesting things for resilience and security have better institutional structures. Ours are out of date.

One of the recommendations in “ The Roadmap for Resilience ” is that we have a co-ordinating board or committee that sits above DEFRA, perhaps through the Cabinet Office and reporting to the Prime Minister. It is easy to make these sorts of machinery of government recommendations in these sorts of reports, but I think this is a case where you have a major and complex challenge that crosses Government Departments and does not really get the co-ordinated focus that it warrants. This is an occasion where it would be quite good to have a bit of machinery of government change.
Or else why have food as one of 13 CNIs? I mean, we either take it seriously or we don’t. The public take it very seriously—they want their food; but it might be different food in crises.

Q57 This is the last question. Both of you have previously touched on elements of what I am about to ask. You just said, and I think you are right, that a Government setting up a website saying this, that and the other is not enough; you are not drilling down as much as you need to, whether that is into local resilience forums or otherwise. And out of that falls another question: how can you ensure that vulnerable people would have access to food during a severe disruption? And out of that then falls another question: how much should be left to individual households, in terms of preparedness? So there are three tiers, if you could wrap it up, please.

I am glad that Mr Turmaine pressed my button pressed earlier about different levels. This applies to consumer confidence. One of the big holes—the NAO Report did not go into this for whatever reason—is storage.

If you look at the Prepare website and, I think, from the hints that we are getting, at the replacement that will be announced shortly—Get Ready, or Play Your Part, or whatever it is called—we know that the onus is going to be on households to protect themselves. But when we interview consumers, we know that it is actually about neighbourliness and community. If we go to the community level, we know that we need something slightly bigger than that.

That is why, in answer to Mr Turmaine, I pointed to the Swedish report. The Swedes were very Swedish and said, “We cannot just say to consumers any more than, ‘Well, it is all just up to the central state to have storage.’” You have got to have different levels of storage, of different things and at different levels if you want to be serious about maintaining trust and confidence that the food will be there.

It is back to this challenge of multi-levelness and encouraging the creativity of the British public. They are amazing; British civil society is fantastic. However, as Neil was alluding to earlier, it does not have the support or indeed recognition. It is not being included enough in central Government thinking about what we want from food. That is where they told me loud and clear, for my report: “Look, we are doing sticking plaster work in food banks. What would it take for them to become community food stores?” What a thought!

What would it take for cities or towns to have town plans for which neighbourhoods can help each other? What skills would we need to spread in the population to enable better access to land? I speak to those of you who are farmers. At what point would you allow 10 acres to become an allotment? Seriously. I talked to landowners who said, “We are up for that. Why not?”
Q58 Why not, Rupes?
There you go; you can have this internal discussion.
I don’t think they’d grow very much—

I talked to very big landowners who said, “We’d be up for that.” We need better access. You look at other cultures, to go back to Mr Turmaine’s question to me, such as the Netherlands, Sweden or France, and you see that access to land is totally different. Go to Russia—old-style Russia—and the allotments kept people alive.

The “Roadmap for Resilience” report talks about three core transformations in making production more resilient, particularly to climate change but also to shocks, and to be smarter about land use. That is my point about better mapping the productive capacity of our agricultural resource to our needs better, and making healthy food more accessible and affordable. You have to do those three things together.

I do not think that we do the accessible and affordable very well, irrespective of the resilience challenge. However, if thinking about the resilience of the food system is becoming more high-profile and more prominent, that might be a way in which we can start to get a food system that delivers more broadly across the population. The Food Foundation has done really interesting work. It shows that to afford a healthy diet among the poorest families takes up 85% of their total income, just on food.

We have a problem around access to healthy food among a part of the population. Community initiatives around food—these local food partnerships—can be a vehicle to bring in all sorts of other social wellbeing improvements and deal with a range of social problems beyond the food system. It is really important to think about people on more modest incomes and more vulnerable groups.

Q59 It strikes me, as somebody who represents very strong communities, that we don’t have to just talk about food resilience; you can talk about communities in terms of resilience generally. I very often say our community will probably be the last thing we have.

In my report, the Treasury very kindly gave me the figures on how little money is spent on the British population for civil defence. I was interested—following the Sweden, Latvia and Finland example—in getting the population engaged in general food resilience. I asked them to show me. They said in Britain we spend less than £1 per person on civil defence, out of £55 billion for the MOD.

Apply that to DEFRA’s thinking and you can say there is no civil food defence. If we put a hard, military lens into our glasses, you would say, “Well, you would want more than that.” You would want some serious money to go into helping people to protect themselves to protect the nation, if you took that framework.
The NAO Report went into that in a roundabout way, on the question of how much money we are prepared to spend on that sort of infrastructure. At the moment it is not much.

It is quite interesting because it is very comfortable for people to say that the first function of a Government should be defence of the people—you hear people say that—and no one challenges it and says, “Hang on a minute, I think there should be less government.” That is very comfortable, but having a well-fed population ought to be pretty close to that.

That is where I called it; I said we have to dust down the 1930s notion of food defence. It changes the whole discourse. If you start looking at the complexity of the food systems that Neil and I and many colleagues have worked on for the last 30 or 40 years, these are acutely vulnerable chokepoints from very big powerful industries. They are vulnerable to attack.

How can we protect them? The answer is to create a slightly different food system. You go from single supplies to networks. That requires a very different economics. The notion of civil food defence is really interesting, and it is being applied by some groups in Wales now as part of the movement that is going on—with the approval of the county council. What would we do at a community level to protect ourselves?

Q60 I want to finish on that theme. I have a question for Neil. I want to quote paragraph 25 of your evidence back to you: “Responsibility for resilience should sit at the lowest effective level, while responsibility for systemic risks should sit at the national level. Major disruption exposed the limits of purely commercial approaches. Resilience should therefore be treated as a public good requiring a long-term partnership between Government, industry and civil society.” What did you actually have in mind there?

I have done a lot of work on trying to make sense of how we have the agriculture and food system and land use system that we have. We take for granted its current pattern and structure, but it has actually evolved quite a lot. You can look over 200 years and there have been huge shifts, but in living memory—since the second world war—it has been through quite a profound set of changes. The changes were relatively highly planned and orchestrated by the national state, with an architecture of county agricultural committees that oversaw what constituted good farming practice in different counties. Farmers could be told to pull their socks up and sort out the rabbits, the nettles or whatever— [Interruption.] And plough more, yes. And they were graded A, B, C—it was quite interventionist.

But in that period it was a partnership between the farmers and the state and the agribusiness companies and science and technology interests in the agribusiness companies. I think we need to revisit that idea of a national system—it could even be thought of as a patriotic mission around making our food system secure and resilient. I think we need the scale of ambition for change that was evident in the post-war period.

The “public good” terminology is to appeal to the very doctrinaire economic orthodoxy about the limits of government, but I do believe that the resilience of the food system is a public good. You can’t get away from that.
I agree.
Good. I was going to give you 10 seconds, but as you agree—
Geoffrey, can I just—

No, time is up. I thank our witnesses very much indeed. You are both very busy people, and we have benefited a lot from your evidence this afternoon. We will be having officials in on Thursday and we will no doubt use some of the information and knowledge that you have given us to further probe their intentions, so thank you very much indeed.

sessions.iT: Dunkelflaute and the risks of electricity intermittency
sessions.w: Jon Saltmarsh (Energy Systems Catapult); Professor Keith Bell (University of Strathclyde); Dr Emily Wallace (Met Office)

segs.tx: Environment and Climate Change Committee
Uncorrected oral evidence: Dunkelflaute and the risks of electricity intermittency
Wednesday 16 September 2026
10 am
Watch the meeting
Members present: Baroness Sheehan (The Chair); Baroness Coffey; Lord Jay of Ewelme; Lord Krebs; Baroness McIntosh of Pickering; Lord Redwood; Lord Rooker; Earl Russell; Lord Trees; Baroness Whitaker.
Evidence Session No. 1 Heard in Public Questions 1 - 2 1
Witnesses

Jon Saltmarsh, Chief Technology Officer, Energy Systems Catapult; Professor Keith Bell, Electronic and Electrical Engineering, University of Strathclyde; Dr Emily Wallace, Fellow in Weather and Climate Extremes and Impact, Met Office.
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Jon Saltmarsh, Professor Keith Bell and Dr Emily Wallace .

Q1 Good morning and welcome to the Lords Committee on the Environment and Climate Change. Today we will be holding the first session of our new inquiry into whether the Government have a firm handle on how to fill the renewables energy gap when the wind does not blow and the sun does not shine, a weather phenomenon often referred to as Dunkelflaute .

Before we start, I remind everyone that the session will be webcast live and that a transcript will be taken and made public. Witnesses will have an opportunity to review the transcript and, if necessary, make very minor amendments. Members are reminded that they should declare any relevant interests the first time they speak, and this applies equally to all witnesses. I will take the opportunity here to say that I am a director of Peers for the Planet.

We are very grateful to our panel of expert witnesses for making the time to be with us today. Dr Emily Wallace is not quite with us, but we hope that she will be very shortly. I will ask each of our witnesses present to briefly introduce themselves. Can I start with you, Jon Saltmarsh?

Hello, everyone. I am chief technology officer at the Energy Systems Catapult. I have been there for about four years, and before that I had about 10 years in what is now DESNZ, responsible for innovation, research and engineering. I am an engineer by background.
Excellent. Can I ask you to move your chair right in front of the microphone? It is quite sensitive directionally, so that would be helpful to us.

Good morning. I hold the ScottishPower chair in Future Power Systems at the University of Strathclyde. I am also a co-director of the UK Energy Research Centre, where I lead the research theme on energy infrastructure transitions.

Q2 Thank you both again very much for making the time to be with us today. The purpose of today’s session is to understand the impact of wind and sun intermittency and how potential gaps in energy delivery from renewables could be filled. Let me start by asking the first question: what is Dunkelflaute? When you address this, could you do so from a meteorological perspective and an energy sector perspective? I would be interested to know whether it is quantifiable. How is it measured and how is it defined? Lastly, how useful do you think the term Dunkelflaute is for modelling and preparing for the risk of energy shortfalls from renewables? Professor Bell, I will come to you first.

Yes, certainly. I will have to leave it to Dr Wallace. Hopefully Emily will get here soon to address the meteorological phenomena behind it, for example, how long it might last and how you can forecast it. From an energy system perspective, there is no set definition.
Briefly, from your knowledge, what is Dunkelflaute?

When we want to make use of energy from renewable sources to meet demand—wind and solar in particular—we are subject to the variability of wind and solar. When it is not so windy or not so sunny, we have to meet the energy demand from somewhere else, at least the demand for electricity. We can see periods of time when the total available power from renewables is low. That suggests a bigger need for meeting the electricity demand from somewhere else. We could quantify this in terms of residual demand. At any moment in time, what is the demand for electricity and what is available from wind and solar? That residual demand, if you like, is the gap. If that persists over some period of time, that is clearly a bigger amount of energy that we need to find from somewhere else. That is what we can quantify and we can use modelling to do that.

We can look over different periods of time. For example, what is that gap over the worst-case day or week , two weeks or four weeks? Of course that will be subject to weather variability as well. We might be able to model weather patterns over a multi-decade period, over 30 or 40 years, depending on what the data is that we have available. Then we can look at something like the 95th or 99th percentile of that gap over those different periods of time. From there, we have to understand what the risk is of not meeting that gap. What would the consequences be? In the first instance, you would hope that demand would reduce. In that period of time, the cost of meeting that electricity demand from other sources will become increasingly high. You would expect that that would be an incentive to try to reduce your use. For example, a few winters ago, at the beginning of the Ukraine war when gas prices went sky high, we saw some industrial users of gas just stopped using it, just stopped production. Therefore , there is that element, which is not ideal, but it would be a feature of how economics works in terms of supply and demand.

Flexing to move when you use energy is possible. For a day, that is totally possible across all sectors, but for a period like five days or a week or more for the domestic sector, especially depending on electricity for heat or for transport, you cannot rely on that demand flexibility, so that gap still remains to meet that demand from somewhere else. I should also say that as a last resort you might have to rely on rationing access to electricity, such as rota electricity disconnections. The last time we did that in the UK was in the early 1970s when fossil fuel supplies were disrupted, so it is a thing that can happen.

Excellent, thank you very much indeed. Dr Emily Wallace is with us now from the Met Office. Dr Wallace, please introduce yourself — but first I will put the first question to you , then you can go straight into the question. What is Dunkelflaute from a meteorological point of view from your perspective , and from an energy sector perspective? We would like to try to understand how it is measured and defined, and whether it is quantifiable. Lastly, how useful a term is it for modelling and preparing for the risk of energy shortfalls from renewables?
Thank you, and apologies for my late arrival. Unfortunately , Paddington was not playing ball this morning.
Thank you very much for taking the time to be with us.

It is my pleasure. I am a fellow in weather and climate extremes at the Met Office and I am seconded to the National Energy System Operator as a meteorological adviser there. Finally, I am a visiting professor at the University of Strathclyde. Today I am speaking on behalf of the Met Office , an executive agency of the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade. While we are best known for our UK weather forecasting service, we are also a world-renowned climate research organisation. It is from that point of view that I am talking this morning.

Dunkelflaute—Keith may well have already covered it—literally means doldrums. That is referring to a lack of wind and a lack of sunshine. The meteorological cause of this is anti - cyclones or high pressure sitting over the UK and Europe. When we think about the weather, it is useful to think in large spatial terms because that is how our weather manifests. What we are talking about in a Dunkelflaute situation is a high-pressure system sitting over the UK. Often that will be sitting over northern Europe at the same time. These are large-scale phenomen a , and they often stay in place for long periods of time. High pressure means we have descending air , and that is what traps the moisture at the earth’s surface, which why we tend to get drizzle or low cloud associated with these high-pressure systems.

The Met Office refers to th at as anti - cyclonic gloom. There was one last year that was long enough and dull enough for us all that the Met Office wrote a blog about when it w ould end. A typical feel for a Dunkelflaute event is that we are all feeling a bit tedious — and of course it has implications for the energy sector as well. The other feature that you can get with a Dunkelflaute event is cold conditions. In that case it would have more impact on the energy system. I have talked about wind, I have talked about lack of sunshine and I have talked about temperature. All of those have implications for energy systems. Obviously , the wind and the sunshine—or the lack of—will reduce the amount of generation from wind and PV on a large scale and on what we call embedded generation on our houses.
Sorry, what was that term you used?

Embedded generation, embedded PV panels on people’s roofs, which means that they are suppressing the demand. If they are operating, they are suppressing the demand from those households, as opposed to allowing the whole demand to be seen by the transmission system. The temperature relates quite strongly already to demand for electricity and demand for gas. In that sense, they are very important for our energy system. I suspect Keith may have covered this already. There is no single definition for Dunkelflaute. It is usually focused on the winter months only when we think about Dunkelflaute, which is because we have shorter sunshine hours and tend to see lower sunshine strength radiation in the winter months. For that reason, it is often thought about as a wintertime condition and that descending air trapping cloud is a wintertime phenomenon. We do not tend to see that in the summer months so much.

Meteorologically, it can be defined in a number of different ways. We can define it, as the name suggests, using wind and sunshine amounts, perhaps choosing some particular locations in the UK where we know that there is generation and looking for periods of time where both sunshine and wind are low, the 20th percentile of what is normal at that location. We can define it with just wind. On our current energy system, Dunkelflaute events are primarily controlled by the amount of wind. That is the larger factor within the Dunkelflaute, so just defining on wind is an option. The other alternative is thinking about the cold Dunkelflaute , which is arguably the more important type of Dunkelflaute because that will be increasing the demand at the same time as the wind and solar generation is depressed, so that omits sunshine from the equation.

The final meteorological way of thinking about the problem would be through pressure patterns, and looking for that high pressure. There are a number of different ways of doing that, some using AI approaches to match pressure to predefined pictures. The other would be via something like the North Atlantic Oscillation, which is a measure of the tendency for winds to come from the west or for that prevalence of westerly winds to be reduced at two ends of the spectrum. In terms of defining on energy, some of the common ways of defining Dunkelflaute would be just on generation, either observed generation from wind and solar or modelled generation taken from a meteorological condition. There are a number of translations between what the wind is doing, what the sunshine is doing and what the temperature is doing towards generation.

The other approach is through demand net renewables. This is taking again either observed or modelled demand, what we expect the demand to be, and subtracting the amount of renewable generation. High-demand net renewables mean that we have a lot of demand to be met with not so much in the way of renewables to meet that demand. It probably means that we are using gas or interconnectors at the moment. If we have low-demand net renewables or indeed negative, that means that we will not be using so much gas. That is the opposite of a Dunkelflaute .

The final way—Keith and Jon may be able to step in to describe some of the mechanics of this more than I can—would be to use something called capacity expansion models. These models are energy system models. One of the uses of them is to chart out potential pathways to meet particular conditions — for example, net zero 2050. A capacity expansion model takes , or can take, year-by-year weather conditions and build out the technologies that are required to meet demand for those weather conditions day by day. A way of defining Dunkelflaute or these conditions is something called system-defining occurrences within that modelling process, where there is a big step change in the technology that is required to meet a particular weather condition, perhaps because in the time series something as bad has not been met before. There may be some additional details that fellow panel members can add in there.

In terms of definition, the best-practice approach is take a cumulative view of Dunkelflaute , because one of the things that can be particularly taxing is if it is going on day after day. A very severe Dunkelflaute may be less important, depending on the energy system, than one that is perhaps less deep but goes on for a number of days. As I say, intensity is important. There is no specific definition for Dunkelflaute, but we do have models and data. There is a lot of rich information on what we can expect to experience today and what we can expect to experience in decades to come coming out of climate simulations.

It is that rich information combined with understanding of energy systems or energy system modelling that we can use to understand whether or not our system is resilient or what it takes for our systems to be resilient. The important part is that collaboration between the rich information coming out of climate modelling and how we apply that to energy systems. It is advocating for that data-driven evidence approach, because what matters is that it is system dependent, it is situation dependent and it is application dependent — so that rich approach is needed.

How useful a term is it? It is useful for communicating compound risk. I described that picture of the large scale and the long term, the combination that means that you might get cold at the same time. It is a term that helps us to communicate that compound aspect, so it supports having a conversation. However, it lacks the meteorological and engineering precision that we need to say whether we are resilient to a Dunkelflaute. It is not a question you can answer — it comes back to the genuine collaboration between the rich information we have about the climate and what it could do and how we build our energy system.
Q3 Thank you very much. Jon Saltmarsh, over to you. Could you keep your remarks brief? We have several more questions.

I will be very brief because my two colleagues have covered this in immense detail. I absolutely agree that it is a useful shorthand, but if you try to focus down on what we mean in terms of whether it is two weeks, one week or 24 hours, that does not help. The second point to think about is that it is not just about the supply of energy. You need to think about demand as well. Within the Catapult’s modelling, we talk about gaps rather than a Dunkelflaute, because it is not just a Dunkelflaute. You mentioned the cold weather and cold weather drives up demand. It is the gap between supply and demand that is an important bit.

It is also broader than the single event. Generally , it is defining the amount of storage that you want as far as your energy system is concerned. However, there are two ways to deplete storage, one of which is to have a long period with slightly below average wind or renewables or generation, whatever you are particularly measuring. The other is to have an intense period. In a lot of the scenarios, we see that it is not the intense period of a two-week Dunkelflaute that is the problem but the 100 days of 5% below average wind. That is important from a planning basis. You very much need to state what you mean by a Dunkelflaute and how you are measuring it. Clearly the amount of storage that you require varies dramatically , depending on your mix of renewables and firm generation. Most of our modelling would recommend a balance between renewables and nuclear. Generally , the more nuclear you put in, the higher the costs are of the overall generation, but the less storage.
We can come on to specific technologies later.
That covers all the extra points that I wanted to make.

Excellent, thank you. Before we move on to Baroness McIntosh’s question, I want to go back to the question of a definition. We understand that some sources define a Dunkelflaut; is it Dunkelflaut or Dunkelflaute?
I am afraid I am not a German speaker. I am the wrong person to ask.
That is how I have been referring to it, but I was interested to understand whether the industry refers to it as Dunkelflaut. Anyway, we will stick to Dunkelflaute.

Some sources define a Dunkelflaute as a period of at least 10 consecutive hours in which wind and solar generation falls below 10% of installed capacity. It seems to me that a baseline definition would be useful. Is this something that you think could be useful as a baseline definition?

Leading off Jon’s comment, the 10 hours would be a relatively short period to be worrying about. Some calculations done by a Met Office colleague, Gillian Kay, some time ago defined a less extreme version of a 20% wind capacity, effectively. She found that up to five weeks was possible, unlikely but possible. The one-in-40 event would be three consecutive weeks of suppressed wind at around the 20% mark. That is not that very severe—
Has that scenario happened?
That is coming out of simulations — the worst scenario that was found in the historical record of that nature.
We will come on to that and talk about trends. Professor Bell, do you have anything to add to that?

Yes. I would favour looking at things from an energy system perspective, because that is what we are trying to deliver — reliable supplies of energy. What Emily called demand net renewables I call residual demand. We need to be able to quantify that and we can do that using the models. We can look at that and the risk over different periods of time, given the variability of the weather over long periods. We might define it in a 24-hour sense or one week, four weeks, or indeed—as Jon suggested—even 100 days and look at a particular infrastructure mix of where we are getting the energy from, what the demand is and the different options of that, how much we want to build and what storage capacity and so on. We can run through the models to assess the one-day, one-week, four-week or 100-day risks that we are exposed to. However, in the end we still need to make a judgment about what is an acceptable level of risk, because we cannot eliminate it completely.

Q4 For that reason, no wonder we get the doldrums in autumn. Could I declare my interests? I have small shareholdings in National Grid, BP and Shell, well below the registrable amount of shares. Dr Wallace, you touched on this as a phenomenon across northern Europe. Being half-Danish, I follow the DMI, the Danish Meteorological Institute. Do you co-operate with the Danes and Norwegians, who probably have had renewables for far longer than we have, to learn from their experience?

Yes, meteorology is very much a global collaboration. I am not aware of specifics, but no doubt there will be links into the D MI . In terms of the energy, it is not something that I have had specific links with before. I know that there is a lot of international collaboration in the energy sector as well, learning from other organisations.
We will come on to further international collaboration later on. Baroness McIntosh, let us go back to your question.

Mr Jon Saltmarsh, your organisation did a joint report not so long ago on the frequency, duration and severity conditions. Could you share the conclusions with the committee so that we can get that as evidence today? How effectively do you think these events can be predicted? You looked at a period of roughly every eight years ; presumably from what we have heard already it is largely unpredictable, but it would help us to understand.

We look backwards rather than trying to predict forwards. Probably the best data for this comes from a Royal Society report that Sir Chris Llewellyn Smith did a couple of years ago on large-scale electric storage, where he looked back over 37 years, from 1980 to 2016. He analysed the gaps in lots of different ways, identifying 22-hour gaps, which was one of the peaks of short-duration gaps, up to how many of those months we saw 20% below normal. What it identified was three years, 1997, 2007 and 2013, where there was a whole month where wind and solar output was 65% below average, and that was one of its forcing functions. We have done similar : w e ended up identifying a two-week period as probably the worst situation that we saw in the eight years that we were looking at. The model that we had for generation and the mix of generation resulted in a 15 terawatt-hour gap that needed to be plugged with some form of long-duration storage, if that answers the question.
That is very helpful. Does it help us predict these situations going forward?
I would turn to Emily on whether past history is a forecast of the future. I do not know how climate change is likely to impact that.
We will be coming on to that, so we can park that.
Professor Bell, do you have anything to add?

Yes, a couple of quick things. We can model what would happen if weather conditions from the past were reproduced. To the extent that future weather patterns are similar to past weather patterns, which we know they are not because climate change is happening, we could say that a particular condition could arise. I expect that it is more difficult to say exactly when it will arise. In some of our modelling, we used 34 years of past weather, put it through a representation of a 2030 electricity system and found similar results to what Jon mentioned in terms of the scale of the gap of 10 to 15 terawatt hours.

The other thing I will quickly mention is you talked about Norway and Denmark. In a sense, Norway especially has faced these questions for a very long time, because it makes use of a lot of hydropower. It has a lot of electricity demand and most of that is met from hydropower. It has a plan for how much water it will get, what the weather will deliver in snow and rain, and plans its reservoir sizes on that basis to manage the possibility of not having enough. This issue has been a live question for it for a very long time, so when you mention collaboration, that is a useful place to look. However, I understand from talking to colleagues that there is still a lot of debate about quite how you model and assess the risk associated with this.
That is very helpful, thank you.

Q5 Good morning. Thank you very much for being with us today. Dr Emily Wallace, how is the Met Office working with NESO and other key stakeholders in the energy sector to understand the Dunkelflaute risk? You have given us a long introduction in your first piece, which was very useful, about different ways of defining the interaction of weather systems and building of the energy transition and different conditions. We could have a long slow decline or we could have a deep period of no wind or no wind plus cold weather. Could you say more about how you are working with the energy sector to understand, manage and predict some of these risks? For the sake of clarity, the next question will be on climate change.

The energy security energy sector is extremely important to the Met Office. The thing that I say a lot is that weather is the fuel of our future system and it is no less important a vector than any other. On that basis, the Met Office has had a formal agreement with the National Energy System Operator to build a partnership to support it to have the best forecast information, the best planning information and the best information to support resilience from a meteorological point of view, and that expertise as well. On a daily basis we send observations to support demand calculations of forecasts to support generation demand forecasting at the National Energy System Operator. We have worked with the teams there, which are already using 10,000 simulations of weather to inform its winter outlook. That is the margins of electricity that we expect to see over the coming months. We have now built in some predictability information into that from innovative approaches coming out of the Met Office Hadley Centre. Beyond that, there is already use of data going much further ahead. We will come to projections in a moment, so I will not dwell on that one.

The Met Office was involved in the Royal Society report to pull the conclusions about long-duration storage beyond the historical record. One of the things we know, particularly in the case of wind, is that it is very variable and we have only been observing it for about 50 years. Therefore , we have not seen some of the combinations of weather that can be thrown at us. We have been using an approach called UNSEEN, which helps to simulate beyond what we have already seen, and that was involved in the Royal Society report. We have worked alongside the National Infrastructure Commission and the Climate Change Committee to support the calculation of adverse weather scenarios for exactly this purpose, what some of the worst conditions are that we can see for stress-testing of future energy systems.

We are also working closely with the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero. We have a channel of work there on energy security as well as the climate change work, which has been going on longer, and have a relationship with International Gas and much of the rest of the industry and the Energy Networks Association. I t is a very important area for us at the Met Office.

If I could summarise, there is very close collaboration, drawing on historical records, the latest technology and AI for future predictions, but risk is at the heart of what you are doing in the collaboration between yourself and NESO and the energy sector in terms of understanding weather impacts on our transition and our ability to generate.

That is it. We are moving towards having the very best information from the weather side as it develops, as we get new innovation plugged into those energy system models at those critical organisations that are responsible for the resilience of our system.
Do Jon Saltmarsh or Professor Bell have anything to add on this question?
I do not think so. The point is that it is about risk and we need to think about it in those terms. We cannot be definitive.

Q6 You have talked about the difficulty of prediction, which all of us entirely understand. However, one question that is often asked—at least I find is often asked—is whether the frequency, duration or severity of Dunkelflaute conditions will be or might be affected by climate change. I know that is a very broad question, but what do you think about that?

As we have described, the definition is not very tight, so I will break down the components of it. We know that the variability in wind speeds will continue, so it is highly variable. That variability is much larger than any climate change signal in wind speeds. That is the first point; the variability will continue. There is not a very substantial signal for changes to wind speeds. Similarly, there is not a very substantial signal in changes to sunshine amounts. Last year was the sunniest on record for some time, but that is just natural variability. Temperature, however, which is an important part of this question, is set to rise. Through the winter, on average we will see warmer temperatures than historically. That is not to say that we will not experience cold conditions from time to time.
Do you think that that will increase the chances of Dunkelflaute conditions?
That would indicate that the chance of the Dunkelflaute conditions will not increase.
Does anybody disagree with that assessment?

I would not disagree with the assessment. The reality will be though that we will need a significant amount of long-duration storage, in the terawatt hours. At the moment we have nothing like that, and whether it increases a bit or decreases a bit will not change the overall direction to where we are trying to get to.

My two colleagues have summarised it very well. The important thing—and we have touched on this already—is the correlations between these different factors. Demand for electricity for heat in the future will be a big part of it. If a day is warmer, that demand is lower. If that day happens to be one where it is a bit dull, that is not so bad because the demand is lower. However, these periods where it could still be cold and you have these dark, still conditions, that is the thing that we would worry about. Jon made the point very well: from where we are now, there is still a lot to do.

Following on from that, what other risks could lead to or amplify Dunkelflaute? We talked a bit about cold weather or hot weather or low renewables across interconnected countries or gas supply disruption. There is a tendency when talking about this always to talk about Britain, but of course the climate is not insular. Are we likely to see the same conditions in other European countries that will affect us or might we find ourselves in some way protected from Dunkelflaute when other countries suffer from it? What is your view on that?

My understanding is that these weather effects would affect the whole of northern Europe, and that if we are suffering from this problem, you will probably find that our nearest neighbours, which are where we get our electricity from over interconnectors, will be in exactly the same position.
The safest assumption to make is that we are not just talking about Britain, we are talking about northern Europe, however you define northern Europe.

You need to look at interconnectors on the continental scale, taking energy from the far east of Europe over to the western side and vice versa to get a balancing out of weather effects around the country and around the continent.

The precise meteorological conditions and how they spread across a certain geographical area is something that Emily and her colleagues will be able to look at in detail and that is what their models already do. It is certainly true that we have to take proper account of those correlations across space as well as across time.

Yes, that is beautifully summarised. As I described at the beginning, high-pressure systems tend to be very large scale. You could draw a big circle of that high-pressure system that could easily incorporate the UK and much of northern Europe. However, there is a lot of subtlety in there, which is why I am advocating for that rich data approach to the problem. To find the very worst conditions, it will be very system dependent and situation dependent. Exactly where the winds happen to be blowing will have subtleties to it , as well as that very large-scale picture.
I have Earl Russell, Lord Krebs, Lord Trees and Lord Redwood for short supplementaries.

Q7 Yes, a very short supplementary from me. I want to ask for a comment on changed winter wind under climate models. Are there any signals that we might get more periods of either 20% less wind over longer periods or periods of very low wind? Obviously our climate is changing and we have defined Dunkelflaute on past climatic conditions. Are there any other particular types of climatic conditions that could cause problems for our renewable energy sector? I am thinking about still wind and very high summer temperatures as an example.

There is not a strong signal for changes to wind speeds. In that case, yes, we might see something worse than we have ever seen before, but that is not because of a strong climate change signal. There are some models that say higher, some that say lower, but generally the variability eclipses it. On other weather conditions, absolutely, yes, there is a lot of weather that stresses our energy system. Heatwaves are a great example because that will be in conjunction potentially with a lack of water, wildfires, infrastructure problems and risks. In these high-pressure systems we also often get worse air quality, because again we have that descending air and stagnant air underneath, so air quality can be a problem. I have already mentioned cold going alongside the Dunkelflaute. If you think about the health impacts as a result of that cold, you get different compounding aspects.
Q8 I should declare an interest. I used to be an adviser to Drax, the energy company. I stopped doing that last year.

This is a question to Emily. Tim Palmer has recently written an article in The Economist in which he alludes to—in addition to the thermodynamic impact of climate change, which is what you talked about—another impact there could be, which is that it changes the circulatory systems themselves, for example, altering the jet streams, and therefore it might be that there eventually is a tipping point in which the climate system, including the regional weather system, moves into a new model or new mode. Does that have widespread acceptance in the climate modelling community or is it an outlying view?
It is not something that I can comment on today. I suggest that we go to our colleagues at the Met Office and provide a written response balancing all of the views at the Met Office on that one.
That would be very helpful.
Absolutely, yes, please do ensure that reaches us.

Q9 Thanks very much for coming. I am not an electrical engineer and we are trying to concentrate on Dunkelflaute in this inquiry, but I would like you to confirm what is emerging from what you have said — taking wind first of all — that the amount of electricity generated by a turbine will be related to the speed of the turbine and ergo the speed of the wind. Therefore , there is a variable continuum. Dunkelflaute is the extreme of a continuum ; there are varying degrees of necessity to augment that supply. Does that also apply to solar? The intensity of radiation will affect the output of given solar capacity. It is important for us to understand that when thinking about solutions.

Building on that, a lot of it is predictable. Certainly with solar we have very good models , and across the country we have an idea of how much cloud cover there is likely to be, so we can make very good predictions. Similarly, the prediction for wind is getting much better. We have ways of dealing with this for the short term with batteries and other short-term storage. The Dunkelflaute issue, as far as we were concerned, was very much more on the long-duration storage bit and how we deal with that element of it.

Q10 I would like to ask a question that bridges into the next group of questions, but arises directly out of the fascinating testimony by Professor Bell , who told us that when there are these problems of windless and sunless days and weeks, the first thing would be dearer electricity. If that did not shake enough demand off, you would need to go to rationing. He reminded us of the 1970s model. As a very young man I experienced that — it was called the three-day week. It was the first time that I had a very profound disagreement with the so-called Conservative Prime Minister who imposed this on the country and discovered that it was not popular and he promptly lost a general election caused by the issue. I would like to explore with Professor Bell how practical this idea is, that in order to deal with windless and sunless periods you either make sure that only the rich can carry on buying power at crucial times or you ration us all.

In the end, this is a policy decision about how much risk we are willing to take, and policymakers making that decision on behalf of the whole of society. The particular economic model for how you recover the cost of that is something for policymakers to decide. Whether it is a progressive policy or a regressive one, that is a decision to be made. The key point of course is that energy is a crucial part of modern society and reliable supplies of it are therefore important. It is also worth noting the importance of energy supplies for various aspects of critical national infrastructure, things like health services, transport, water treatment and so on. Of course this has to be taken very seriously, regardless of where you get your energy from, and there are risks associated with all forms of energy supply. What is n otable about the 1970s is that it was a fossil fuel-based energy system.
And nuclear.

It had some nuclear power, yes, and nuclear power has a value. I know that Energy Systems Catapult has been an advocate of nuclear power for a very long time. It has its advantages, although the costs are stubbornly refusing to come down. It is all part of that decision and risk-taking or risk-judgment context.

Q11 Absolutely, and we will certainly be asking Government about that when they are before us. Before we move on to Lord Krebs’s question on technologies that could fill the gap, I want to go back to how we quantify and measure the problem and whether it is important for parliamentarians in terms of accountability for the system. We need to be able to grab hold of some data, some baseline and so on, to say, “This is not right. What did you do to meet this foreseeable problem?” From publicly available information, it is not clear what parameters NESO has chosen to assess the risk of Dunkelflaute events. We have heard of some of the difficulties in looking at these parameters, but nevertheless it behoves experts to be able to define some of those parameters and give us some indication of the guidelines to which they should be working. What parameters, in your view, should NESO use to assess the risk of Dunkelflaute events? I know that that is a tough question, but it is something that we need to try to get to the bottom of. Professor Bell, would you like to start us off?

I would suggest something that I mentioned earlier, which is an assessment of the risk in terms of that energy gap, that residual demand over different periods of time, given the long-term variability of weather. It is something that has to be done using modelling, and that is a thing that has to be looked at carefully, what the credibility of your model is, where you are getting the data from and so on.
Whose job is it to do that, Professor Bell?

NESO has this responsibility, being a strategic energy planning adviser to Government, so NESO would be the first party that I would look to. However, there is no harm in others having a separate assessment so that we can compare that with what NESO is saying. Perhaps we can get things out more quickly than NESO seems to be doing. We can be open about the modelling methods and be happy to have those methods critiqued, to understand where we can improve the methodology or where it seems to be all pushing in the same direction and we can be confident in the results. Energy Systems Catapult, as Jon has already talked about, has done some of its modelling. My group at the University of Strathclyde has done some as well. Various consultancies have done some. The Climate Change Committee commissioned work from a consultancy called A3. All of this is helping to inform us , but it needs to be done sufficiently, robustly and transparently, giving the full picture of information. I am not sure that the full picture is always there. For example, in my group a lot of our funding is a bit piecemeal. We do bits and pieces and improve the model, but to properly inform all of this debate there is more that can be done.

I just add that from a modelling perspective, a model is just that. It is not a perfect representation of the real world and you have to make compromises to make the models run and be meaningful. People make different compromises and they end up with a different set of assumptions. The only way that you can test this for real is to compare results of different models and have, as Keith says, full transparency of what assumptions and what modelling approaches are being taken. It is more than simply defining what a Dunkelflaute is and everyone will be happy. It is much more about how you are using that information.

Q12 I want to pick up on a couple of points that Professor Bell made. It is an important point that that transparency is there, not just in relation to Dunkelflaute but across the whole of the energy sector, and that different forms of energy have different risks and different profiles associated with them. Do you think that there is more to be done in terms of the whole of the energy mix and some of the rationale and risk profiles associated in making that more publicly available so that there is opportunity for greater parliamentary scrutiny on the energy mix that is being created and the risk profiles associated with the different sectors?

Yes, I think that there is more that could be done. Some of these models are difficult to set up and time-consuming, especially in management of the data. They are sometimes also very long to run. That means that people can take a while to get around to publishing their results. I will confess that my group is a bit the same. We have some stuff that we could get out there, but for academics we are pushed towards doing, quite rightly, peer-reviewed journal publications, which take forever, frankly. I think that there is value in quicker, dirtier analyses that illustrate the nature of the problem and the dimensions of the problem and can help inform that debate, with the slight caveat, as Jon said, that there are always approximations or assumptions that are made. The quick, dirty models will have some things that are a bit rough around the edges, but they can help, as you say, as an assessment of the various options.

I do get a bit frustrated sometimes that NESO is so cautious in what it puts out and that everything seems to be very slow. It has delivered just a week or two ago six different possible pathways for its strategic spatial energy plan, delivered to the Secretary of State. However, it has not told anyone else what they are and what the dimensions are. I am not sure that that is okay. The Secretary of State wants to be able to make a judgment.
