He has a role in Government and the Secretary of State has that degree of authority, but the public debate about what the right options are and understanding the different risks is important.

To quickly summarise that, there are of strands of very useful information lying with various stakeholders. The body currently responsible for bringing those strands together is NESO, but we do not know what NESO is doing, and its work and workings are not in the public domain and you would like them to be. Is that a good summary?

Some of what it does and some of its working is in the public domain—it tries to be transparent—but in other aspects of the work it seems to be not at that position. Maybe I am putting words in its mouth. Maybe it is not yet completely confident about the methods that it has developed and wants to wait before it puts it out in the public domain. In respect of the strategic spatial energy plan, the way of proceeding with these six scenarios and presenting it first to the Secretary of State is something that it agreed with Government, in my understanding.

Q13 I would like to move on to the potential technologies or approaches for addressing periods of intermittency in renewable supply, as illustrated when there is a Dunkelflaute. I would like to distinguish between long term in days to weeks rather than short term, which would be hours or within a day. Could each of you say what potential technologies you think are in the running for both long and short-term energy storage, what the timescales for their deployment are and what scale is feasible for them?

I am very happy to start off on that. You are absolutely right to look at what we can do in less than a day, within-day balancing, and how we deal with the much longer term. There are two ends to that, and within a day your primary solution will be batteries and moving demand around, which in a lot of cases is batteries. When you choose to charge your car, for example, that is still making use of a battery. That is the within-day bit. However, at the end of that day all those batteries and forms of energy, for example, if you are overheating your house and letting it cool down a bit, will only last for a short period of time and you need to return those batteries or the house temperature to what it was at the beginning of the last day by the beginning of the next day. Those are the ones that are about flexibility and moving stuff around short term.

At the other end, you need technologies that are very long term. From an Energy Systems Catapult perspective, we believe that that will almost certainly be molecular storage in some sense, so broadly storing gas, whether that gas is biomethane, whether that gas is methane or whether that gas is hydrogen, but you need the storage to be able to run your generators for periods of days or weeks. The interesting bit comes in the perhaps two days, up to five or 10 days. That is a place that hydro is operating to a degree at the moment and there are a lot of other technologies being developed there, such as compressed air storage, some forms of thermal storage and so on. The debate is whether they have a role in their own right or whether you will see batteries that will become increasingly less expensive and starting to encroach into the one day, two day . Batteries are always talked about as one hour. Suddenly we are now talking about batteries as four hours, eight hours or even 10 hours and that can continue to expand.

From the other end, your molecular storage, be that hydrogen or whatever, will that start encroaching from the top and do you end up with a squeezed middle? Is there a role for some of these technologies in the middle? I do not think that anyone has a clear answer to that at the moment. It very much depends on the price of those technologies and their round-trip efficiency. There are two prices there, the price of the entity that is storing it and the price of volume of storage. If you are talking about hydrogen, you have a very cheap price for the volume of storage, but it is quite expensive to generate it and produce power. Batteries, on the other hand, cost a huge amount to store energy but they can put it out very cheaply and have a very high round-trip efficiency. There are horses for courses. What I cannot tell you is who the winners in the middle will be.

Before I move to Emily and Keith, can you say a few words about the timescales to deployment—you mentioned various technologies like molecular storage, compressed air and so on—and the potential scale at which they could be deployed? For instance, Chris Llewellyn Smith concluded in his report that we needed north of 100 terawatt hours of long-duration energy storage. When I was on the S&T Committee and we looked into it, we thought that was pretty extreme and more like 10 to 20 terawatt hours would be a no-regrets level. Can you comment on scale and magnitude and timescale?

That is very important. In terms of technology readiness, which is in many ways your timescales, batteries are here today. They have a technology readiness of nine and we are seeing them deployed at scale. That is not the case for hydrogen, which is probably at a technology readiness of eight. It is not being deployed at scale for a number of reasons. We are probably talking about five years before we would see a significant amount of it, even if we were to start today and move forward with some of the projects that seem to be stalled at the moment. In terms of scale, at the moment we have something like 18 gigawatt hours of batteries and we have something like 12 gigawatt hours of pumped hydro storage, hydropower. To put that into context, if we move to 30 million electric vehicles, that would increase the total amount of battery storage to 2 terawatt hours. That is still not getting anywhere close to the 10 or 20 terawatt hours that people are saying is probably the likely amount of long-duration storage.

On the gaseous storage at the moment, if you look at Rough, which is the main gas storage plant—it is a disused oil field in the North Sea— that stores something like 16 to 18 terawatt hours of energy today. Therefore there is a three orders of magnitude difference between what we are likely to see with batteries and what we are likely to see with molecular storage. Even if you were to convert Rough into hydrogen storage—there are some big challenges with doing that, not least that we have not done that before—that would reduce the amount of storage, perhaps 8 terawatt hours of hydrogen, but it is still massive compared with what we are getting from batteries. Does that answer the question?
It does, thank you very much. Emily, is there anything you would like to add?

No, I think you are better off with Keith and Jon for the technology questions. What I would add is the importance of thinking about—as well as the average conditions that storage is operating in—what other potential compounding hazards might need to be considered at the same time. Water resources would be an obvious one, where there is a signal amount of rainfall we are expecting to see in future and where that is relevant to storage, for example. It would be worth thinking about that sort of compound picture of what else is going on as well as us charging and discharging storage.
Climate resilience.
Climate resilience . There are other hazards as well, but clearly I am here with a climate resilience hat on.
Keith, do you want to add anything to what Jon has talked about, on scale and time to deployment and alternative technologies?

I think Jon has summed it up very well. With t hat kind of importance, at that scale of tens of terawatt hours, molecular-based storage seems to be the way to go. Another important point that Jon made was about the cost : the cost of converting and the rate of converting energy from one form to another , so the cost per megawatt compared with the cost in terms of the total volume over a perio d of time , the cost per megawatt hour. That is a trade-off, depending on what you want to do with the storage. At the moment lithium-ion batteries are playing very well in giving a rapid response to things to smooth out variations on the electricity system, but the cost per megawatt hour of those batteries might not be competitive with other options.

In terms of moving the things along and how quickly, Lord Krebs, you will recall in the Science and Technology Committee hearing evidence from some of the people involved on the geological storage side that there is work to be done to evaluate the different options , to establish that a particular geological resource that you think is suitable really is suitable and then to get it available. Then it is the conversion to and from hydrogen . W e keep being told by the big gas turbine manufacturers that “Yes, we are ready . W e can do it ”. T hen there are the buyers . It is like a standoff , saying, “W ell, we will buy one when you have proven the price and the performance ” and the manufacturers say, “W ell, we will prove the price and performance when you place an order ”. We have to somehow break that logjam.
The Chair : Thank you. I have a series of supplementaries from Baroness Whitaker, Earl Russell, Baroness McIntosh, and Lord Redwood. Baroness Whitaker.

Q14 T hank you for your evidence. You have explored various things that are very expensive, particularly battery storage. I do not know whether it is in your particular areas of expertise, but there are other technologies outside. As far as households are concerned, there is thermal energy. You cannot dig it out of the ground everywhere, but you could do it much more than it is done. It is already in use. Also , as far as the grid is concerned, there is at least marine energy. Tidal is already almost there. There is tidal stream and there is wave energy. These are obviously long term , they are a few years away, but they would cope with intermittency extremely well because — I do not need to say it— the tide is every day, twice a day, and the waves are all the time.

Two separate points there. I am glad you mentioned thermal because it is something I forgot about in my list. Thermal storage is a cheap way of storing energy for short - ish periods of time. There are a number of companies in the UK, some very innovative, that are producing heat batteries, for example, which can provide the energy to your house for a period of a day. You can charge it up overnight and then use that heat during the day. Thermal storage is a great way of looking at it .

In terms of your firming up generation, which is what you are proposing to do with tidal, wave and some of these other technologies, yes, you can do that and they are good approaches. In m ost of our modelling at the moment — and this is perhaps E nergy S ystem C atapult — the way we price these technologies compared to nuclear , we tend to firm up our renewables with nuclear and that proves to be the most cost-effective solution. We build into our modelling prices for tidal, prices for wave technology, but at the moment the data we are seeing says that those prices need to come down a long way before they are attractive .
They do.
A bsolutely they are a good solution, but only if we can make them at an affordable price.

If I could briefly add to that, yes, a great point about thermal energy storage over short periods of time is that it is really cheap. People have been exploring using, for example, disused mines to store heat down there . You could store for a longer period of time and then extract the heat later on — maybe you are using a heat pump or something —so it is not always very cheap by the time you get the heat in and out, but it has potential.

I n respect of marine energy sources, idle stream, the turbines are quite similar . I suppose it is on a different scale to th e sort of thing we see quite commonly as the design of wind turbines , but of course you have this different environment under the water and the different stresses on the machinery , s o that is still to be proven in terms of the reliability of it. T idal b arrage is expensive, very high capital and has environmental impacts, but you can store a lot of energy and access a lot of energy. As Jon said, it depends what assumptions you make about these relative costs as to how some kind of optimal design would come out from your big energy system model. I am not an expert on this stuff at all , so I would have to defer to the experts, but wave energy comes from the wind as well , so t he best way of harnessing the wind energy — I think we already have technologies that are well proven in doing that.

Q15 I am slightly baffled as to why all the evidence you have given us is focused on storage. My understanding is that renewables in any event rely a lot on household subsidies and other subsidies. Baroness Whitaker has given a number of variations. I am quite taken by energy from waste, and of course Drax used to take quick-growing willow coppice trees from local farmers across Yorkshire , so it had a double effect. Are these not proper alternatives? Why are we so obsessed with very costly storage?
Because we have always had storage.
It has not been a success, carbon capture and storage.

If we go back to the coal age, when most of our power stations were coal-powered, we had huge amounts of energy stored in piles of coal beside power stations. We now have huge amounts of energy stored first in the North Sea in the fossil fuels, the gas reserves, and in the gas network itself and in our storage. T his storage has been intrinsically part of our system in the past and by moving to a world where we are using more renewables, that does not come with this sort of inbuilt storage. It is something that we have taken for granted up to now and when we move to renewables, it is not there to be taken for granted. We need to address the fact of the gap there.

Just humour me for a moment. If we relied on energy from waste, which serves two purposes —it is getting rid of residual household waste and it is creating an energy stream , which is working very successfully in n orth Yorkshire , but it is going into the national grid —it could be used locally, which is a whole separate question , b ut you seem to discount it.

I am not discounting it, but it is a matter of scale. If you burn ed all the waste that we have , it would not come anywhere near enough. I could write to you with the exact numbers ; I do not have them off the top of my head .
Please do.

It would come to a very small percentage of the overall demand for electricity or the overall demand for energy that we have. We are not discounting any of these other technologies and saying that they do not have a role , but let us look at the big numbers. We will write to you on that one.

V ery quickly , bioenergy does have a role to play . To the extent that you can store the wood pellets or whatever, it is a storable source and it is replenishable because you can grow more biomass. However, we need to be careful about the provenance of the biomass and whether it is genuinely sustainable and what impact it has relative to other potential uses of land . Energy from waste has carbon emissions . I think 40% - ish o f waste is biogenic , so it counts as biomass, if you like. T he rest of it — a lot of that tends to be fossi l- based — has emissions , so energy from waste is not zero carbon. I think that is the thing to be to be cautious about.
Lord Redwood and Earl Russell , and we do need to speed up a bit, colleagues.

I would like an update on the Swansea tidal barrage scheme , b ecause my understanding was the public sector scheme did not have numbers that added up and that part of the problem was the design life of the barrier. I thought the private sector had now extended the life to 125 years and had found potential industrial interest in co-development and in co-contracts and they thought that was now economically viable. Do our experts have an update on that?
I do not .
I do not either , I am afraid. I am sorry. I am not on top of the latest numbers.
I think in two weeks w e will have the relevant experts in place to be able to answer that. H opefully they are hearing this session as we speak and will write in to us with their suggestions.

Q16 V ery briefly, Jon Saltmarsh, I want to go back to the fascinating comments you made earlier about this time s- three order of magnitude of lack of long - duration energy storage. As you rightly said, every energy system has had its need for storage . W hatever type of energy you are using, you need a store of it. My basic question to you, just for brief comment, is that we have this huge gap and we are not managing to fill it. Do you think technology will develop to fill it in time? W hy do we continue to transition our energy system and continue to have this gap in long - duration energy storage? And a comment : obviously energy from waste is the most polluting form of energy we generate.

A t the moment we do not need it because we have lots of gas - generating plants and we can use those when the wind is not blowing. We put them in in the 19 80s and 19 90s in the dash for gas. The problem comes in over the 2030s, when a lot of those reach the end of their life and get taken out of commission. It is not a burning issue today. As it stands at the moment, the technologies to burn hydrogen or to create hydrogen in the first place and then burn it, or to use carbon capture and storage and store the carbon dioxide you produce, will be more expensive than simply burning and pumping the carbon dioxide into the atmosphere as we do today. T here is not an economic business case for anyone to develop one as it stands at the moment . If you want to generate it, that requires government policy to recognise the difference in costs and pay for that.
As a kind of interregnum.
The Chair : We need to move on. This is something we can explore further in another session. Lord Rooker, your question.

Q17 Good morning. Do not laugh, but I am a non-paid director of the Ludlow Hydro, which is a small Archimedes screw on the R iver Teme. I have to say that because there are some nit - pickers out there. It supplies 4,000 houses when the river is running , but we need rain in Wales to run the river.

I want to ask about gas and using retained gas power . Dr Wallace, you said this , and it was on the first three questions, but it overloads all of what we have been talking about. At the time of the conditions of no wind and no sun , I am assuming the interconnectors are out because you made it clear it is across northern Europe , so we have to take into account that the interconnectors are not available. That is the way I have looked at the conversation so far .

I want to ask you about the G overnment ’ s clean power 2030 target, the 5% coming from retained gas . What do you see are the trade-offs between retaining gas beyond the early 2030s and investing in alternative technologies, some of which of course are completely unproved , such as carbon capture and storage?

I will make a comment on the scale of the high pressure just to start off the conversation and then I will probably pass it on . T he worst situations might be where the high pressure sits over n orthern Europe as well and b ecause of the scale of it, that is something that will happen from time to time. Often the high pressure will be offset, so we will have renewable generation from the c ontinent. It is also true to say that that would not be the only source of electricity generation on the c ontinent , so whether or not the interconnectors are flowing would be a much more complex question than whether or not the wind was blowing . However, there is a relationship there, and thinking about a large-scale lack of wind is certainly a scenario that we should be considering , yes. Now I will pass to my colleagues.

It is an interesting question that you should ask some of the other people that come to give evidence : do their models assume that interconnectors will be flowing at the times when we have peak stress ? I t does make a huge difference to the overall cost of the system and the overall amount that you need. Y ou are probably always going to end up with some unabated gas being burn ed for short periods because it is your cheapest fallback. If you are dealing with something that happens once every 10 or 20 years, do you want to put a huge carbon capture and storage plant on the end of that or is it just better to accept that every 10 or 20 years we will have to burn a bit of gas and we will absorb it in some other way? I think it is not unabated gas or carbon capture and storage. There is a spectrum between those . As time goes on, the less you are using these plants and having them for backup, the less important the carbon emissions be come and it is much more important that you do your backup in the cheapest way possible.

Adding to what my esteemed colleagues have said, I think Emily is quite right . T here are nuances and subtleties around what is happening on a c ontinent scale. It is not always that it will still be absolutely everywhere. As it happens, the model of the electricity system that we have in my group does model the whole of Europe, s o we do try to do that. On nuclear power or hydropower , some of it is available, but there might be a lot of demand for it. Our interconnector that we already have between Britain and Norway offers a very nice complementing of resources. When it is windy here, we can export electricity to Norway. They can leave more water in the reservoir while still meeting demand in Norway. When it is less windy here, we can make use of the water that they have saved in the meantime. There is a spatial dimension to it ; there is a choice about where they need to be if you have the ability to move energy across space.

On Jon’ s point about what the volumes are , with a small amount of unabated gas, the emissions associated with that are small, but we have to understand how small and how much we need to capture . If we do have some of those emissions, that is part of our carbon budget. If we have more emissions in one sector, we maybe have to reduce emissions in another sector , but it is important to get that sense of scale , of quite how much and how often we would end up using any backup unabated gas capacity.

I have one final question. I know we will have other witnesses, but I could not help but recall , Dr Wallace, that you were involved with NES O. Y ou are here talking for the Met Office, but were you involved with NES O when the c lean p ower 2030 report was published?
I joined the organisation and started my second ment about a year ago . No, that was before I was in the organisation.

You are not responsible for this rubbish — that is what it is been described as by some other people : the list of items to get to c lean p ower 2030 . There are about 10 items , all of which have to be delivered at maximum capacity simultaneousl y . T here does not seem to be a shred of evidence that that will happen. I obviously cannot ask you about that because you are not responsible, but I warn N ESO that it will be asked about it. Thank you very much.
Yes, I cannot comment on that one.

To be slightly fair to N ESO , I think the question it was given was : what would need to happen in order to meet this target ? I think there are caveats in the report about this that are highly challenging . C ertainly when I have spoken privately to the people involved in some of that work, they have been very keen to highlight how challenging a lot of these things are to deliver in the timescales outlined.

Q18 Just one question following from what Professor Bell was saying when we talked about the interconnector . Y ou talked about how the interconnector between Britain and Norway is fine when there is wind in Britain and no wind in Norway and vice versa. What happens if there is no wind in either? Does the interconnector work there?
The interconnector still works and they still have water in Norway, provided they have not already used it.
T hat is not a problem then.

It is the water resource in Norway that is so fantastic . A lso, as we were discussing earlier, they still have to manage the risk associated with that , the possibility of having a relatively dry winter so there is not as much snow . T hey depend on the snow melting in spring to fill up their reservoirs. They have to size their reservoirs appropriately to manage the same kind of weather variability in the end that we have been talking about. It is a choice about how much money we need to spend on making the reservoirs bigger, given what we think the variability is, both of the water inflow and of the demand for electricity.

Q19 My question to some extent you have answered . What challenges exist for gas power with carbon capture and storage ? Is there anything more you want to add to what you have said so far? P articularly though , what chance is there of a realistic, scalable, commercially viable system being in place in the timeframe we need?

It depends what timeframe you are looking at. By 2050 almost certainly, yes. There is always the question about what you mean by “ commercially viable ”, because it will always be cheaper to use the atmosphere as a sewer than to store the carbon dioxide , so you will have to have some mechanism as far as that is concerned.
Environmentally acceptable , then.

Fine . From a technology perspective, we will have to do some carbon capture and storage at some point because we will almost certainly overshoot our carbon targets and have to do some sort of amelioration . C arbon capture and storage is one way of doing that. I think it needs to work. We have proven that you can pump carbon dioxide into the ground. It is been used for decades for enhanced oil recovery. It is pumping it into the ground and keeping it there with a commercial business model that makes sense that appears to be the biggest problem.

I fully support what Jon has just said. There has been an ongoing debate about how you get the business model right to get some of this deployment of carbon capture and storage at scale. My understanding is that the Teesside i ndustrial c luster has a dispatchable power agreement that is supposed to be delivering some decent - sized scale plant by around 2028 , but that is something you may want to follow up with other witnesses who are closer to the detail.

Thank you. Before we move on to Baroness Whittaker ’ s questions, just a quick follow - up from what Lord Trees was asking about. Many gas plants will be approaching retirement by the early 2030s. Alternatives will take many years to deliver. With h ydrogen storage, for example, it says here “ seven to 10 years ” . Jon, I think you mentioned five years at the moment, but you also said it was stalled, the development of hydrogen storage. Can you say a little bit about why it ha s stalled? Given that what we are looking at is how we deliver decarbonised electricity and fill it with low - carbon options, hydrogen seems to be a good contender. Professor Bell was talking about molecular storage being a possible way forward for the longer periods when we needed to fill the gap. W hat is the problem with hydrogen storage?

Technically , there is no problem. We have had hydrogen salt caverns in the past in the UK. Most of them have been converted to methane now . Y ou can convert one back again ; y ou can produce new salt caverns. T echnically , that is doable. The reason that it appears to be stalled is because of the cost of doing it. We have been very good at funding innovation . You can do an awful lot of innovation for £ 10 million . When you come to, “We want an end-to-end plant that will electrolyse power, produce hydrogen, store it in the ground and then put a gas turbine on the end of it at a scale that is useful for grid generation ” then you are talking £ 500 million upwards , £1 billion that needs to come from somewhere . T he simple answer is that I do not think the G overnment ha ve had the money to do that and that is predominantly why it has stalled. It is very difficult to do that without putting money into it , because at the moment it is cheaper to do that with a simple unabated gas turbine. It broadly comes down to money.
The Chair : I will park that there and move on to Baroness Whitaker. Lord Redwood, if we have time to come back for your supplementary, I will do so.

Q20 Thank you. We return to intermittency. The majority of the new capacity set out in the G overnment ’ s Clean Power 2030 Action Plan and the Clean Flexibility Roadmap is set to be delivered between 2030 and 2050. D o you think that that level of progress is right? If not, in what areas ought there to be further progress particularly?
Are you talking about the whole programme here or the storage bit?
I think we are talking about anything that is relevant to addressing Dunkelflaute intermittency.

I am not sure how to answer this one. The starting point is that the more variable renewables you add on to the system, the more you are going to make this a problem that you need to be solving. Clearly, we have a plan at the moment that is moving to significant amounts of wind for the future , so that problem becomes increasingly an issue. It is driven as much as anything at the moment by when the gas plants are going to go offline. As we have discussed o n the previous point, we are not moving fast enough with replacements for those gas turbines . Even if you were to replace them like for like, there is a huge waiting list for gas turbines at the moment. It is not as if you can turn around and say, “R ight, we will just do more gas ” and expect that to appear within two years or some such. It will be longer than that , so there is a looming problem as far as this is concerned . We will almost certainly solve it by running these gas plants on for longer , but running something on beyond its lifetime ends up with the costs going up because you end up with more maintenance et cetera . I do not feel I got to the heart of your question.

T here are other things. NESO said in July 2025 that this will require investment in new low - carbon generation , but I would also like to turn your attention to the market mechanisms at the moment for getting all these new technologies on to the market. It s eems to me that you could say there is a market failure at the moment from the lack of investment in scaling up new technologies. We do have the contracts for difference system a nd tidal energy has got a little way with that , but, as you pointed out, the other marine things are very expensive. That is because they are still at the prototype stag e—but, you know, private sector , come in on this !

This has always been the way . Y ou need the first of a kind funding et cetera to come from somewhere other than the private sector . The private sector does not like taking those first risks . The cost of borrowing associated with first of a kind is absolutely enormous compared to what the G overnment can borrow a t , s o it makes a lot of sense for the G overnment to be funding things like this. It then comes down to priorities. The other point to note with how we prepare for D u nkel fl aute and events that happen very rarely is whether it is ever going to be sensible to have contract s for difference that will pay you once every 20 years .

I think there will be an argument in the future about this. Should Governments be saying that this is a strategic asset we need to buy and that we should not put the risk of when it will be used on the private sector , because we will pay through the nose for that risk when actually it is the G overnment who are ensuring against that risk ? C ontracts for difference has been very successful for what it has done to enable wind. It should not be the only tool in the toolbox.

There are other reasons for addressing intermittency apart from Dunkelflaute. It is not our concern , but could Dunkelflaute be an incidental gain from the general approach to dealing with intermittency ?

Absolutely, but as we discussed earlie r, you have these two solutions, one for the short-term problems, within day, and one for the longer ones. If you solve the short ones and you solve the long ones, you probably deal with the bit in the middle. If you just go for the bit in the middle, you will leave the extremes to fend for themselves and that will not necessarily work.
Thank you. Anything to add?

Just a comment on how the processes in place at N E SO are already taking account of this intermittency problem. I have already described the short term . C hecking the resilience against D unkelflaute and other intermittency in the winter ahead is taken care of in the winter outlook , where they use the 10,000 simulations. The resampling of weather years is making its way into calculations around the capacity market and also resource adequacy out to 2040. The simulations to understand the problem are making it into those assessments. But the policy questions are not for me.
I know we are running out of time, have run out of time almost —
The Chair : Indeed, so before you say anything, we realise we are a little bit over time. Is it okay if we overrun by a couple of minutes? Excellent, thank you. Professor Bell.

Yes, so I will chip in a couple of quick things. For the short-term variability, the market mechanisms do seem to be working. On b attery deployment, grid-scale batteries are being installed and used. There is a new mechanism, the cap-and-floor mechanism , which is trying to encourage further investment, in particular pumped hydro storage , t o help manage the investment risk. It is a kind of sharing of risk between consumers and the investors.

We have talked about the scale of this long-duration, longer-term storage, and we are maybe being a bit scary —I am a bit scared — by the scale of tens of terawatt hours. On the other hand, however, we have to start somewhere. It cannot all be delivered overnight s o we have to start doing things. It inevitably gets developed in stages , so there are opportunities for learning by doing when we get going . B ut , as noted, these things are of expensive.

There are a few things and we have to see how effective they are : the dispatchable power agreement and the hydrogen transport business model that the G overnment ha ve put forward. Are they going to deliver? W e can maybe also say something about the choices on the storage of energy. Jon has already noted that we have made use of the storability of fossil fuels for ever . Of course it is a one-way store ; we will not turn it back into fossil fuel. The point about wind and solar and its variability is that, although there are periods when this residual demand is large and has to be filled from somewhere else, there will be periods when that is negative and t here is a surplus that can be used. That represents an opportunity to make a form of energy that can be stored for a long duration and then extracted from the store when needed.
The Chair : Excellent , t hank you very much. Before we finish, I will come to Lord Redwood and then Lord Jay.

Q21 Briefly, I think it would be very helpful to the c ommittee if we could have in evidence w hat the current gas dispatchable capacity is that we rely on to keep the lights on . Also, what is the current view in the system about how much dispatchable gas we will still need in 2030 , when there will be even more unreliable renewables on the system?
I think N E SO ’ s publications do give some information on that.
I know where to find it, but I thought it would be helpful for somebody to put it into the record.
Yes, of course it would, but this is in the absence of any further action that the G overnment or N E SO and the energy generat ors take to fill the gap. Is that right?
Yes, but my main concern is keeping the lights on.

The Chair : Indeed , we all want to make sure that that happens. That is one of the reasons for carrying out this i nquiry . We want to make sure that the G overnment are thinking ahead as to how we are going to plug that gap. Lord Jay.
Just one interest that I should have declared . I used to be a member of the main board of EDF in Paris.

Excellent , t hank you very much. Colleagues, thank you all very much and thanks to our panel of expert witnesses for being with us today. W e look forward to receiving the bits of supplementary evidence that you have undertaken to send to us. With that, I call an end to the public part of this session. Thank you.

Oral evidence: Armed f orces housing and Annington Homes , HC 98
Thursday 10 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 10 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown (Chair); Chris Kane; Rupert Lowe; Tristan Osborne; Blake Stephenson; Matt Turmaine .
Gareth Davies, Comptroller and Auditor General, National Audit Office, and Marnya Jain, Alternate Tr easury Officer of Accounts , were in attendance.
Questions 1 - 59
Witnesses

I : Jeremy Pocklington CB, Permanent Secretary, Ministry of Defence; Aneen Blackmore, Director General, Finance, Ministry of Defence; Mike Green, Chief Executive, Defence Infrastructure Organisation; David Brewer, Chief Operating Officer, Defence Infrastructure Organisation ; Rupert Pearce, National Armaments Director.
Written evidence from witnesses:
– [Add names of witnesses and hyperlink to submissions]
Report by the Comptroller and Auditor General
The repurchase of the service family accommodation estate (HC 29)
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Jeremy Pocklington, Aneen Blackmore , Mike Green, David Brewer and Rupert Pearce .

Welcome to this session of the Public Accounts Committee on Thursday 10 September 2026. Today we are examining armed forces housing and the Ministry of Defence’s repurchase of service family accommodation from Annington Homes. In 1996, the MOD sold around 55,000 houses to Annington Homes for £1.7 billion. The NAO estimates that by 2024 the deal had left the Government £14.5 billion worse off.

The MOD has bought back more than 36,000 homes at a cost of £6 billion, ending an expensive arrangement, but not undoing nearly three decades of poor value and weakened control over a vital part of the defence estate. The repurchase and the MOD’s proposed £9 billion defence housing strategy offer a major opportunity to repair and refurbish service family accommodation, but success will critically depend on the MOD building capacity and expertise to achieve that. This morning we will examine how the MOD plans to use this opportunity to improve military housing, and what lessons Government must learn before selling public assets for short-term gain.
We have a very senior cast this morning and I am very grateful to everybody for sparing time to come to see us. W ould you like to introduce yoursel ves ?
I am Jeremy Pocklington, the permanent secretary at the Ministry of Defence.
You are very welcome again.

Good morning. I am Rupert Pearce. I am the National Armaments Director, responsible for the National Armaments Director Group, in which is located in the Defence Infrastructure Organisation , run by Mike. It will be the place where we locate the Defence Housing Service.
Good morning. My name is Mike Green. I am the chief executive of the Defence Infrastructure Organisation and the director general of infrastructure in the MOD.
Aneen , you have been before the Committee many times before ; w elcome back. Would you like to introduce yourself?
Aneen Blackmore: Good morning. I am Aneen Blackmore, director general of finance at the Ministry of Defence.
And finally, but by no means least, David.
Good morning. Working for Mike, I was the MOD lead official on the Annington buy-back deal and on the work we have been doing to prepare for the Defence Housing Service.
It is very good to see you.

Q1 The defence of our country is the most critical responsibility of Government. Our troops serve for our country, potentially putting their lives on the line. That is deep in our country’s mindset and we have a profound sense of responsibility for those people. This deal, in my view, has let those people down, not only by its outcomes in terms of the financial liabilities, but by the state of the housing they were put in. My questions are about how we ended up in that deal in the first place and the lessons we need to learn. My colleagues will follow up on it.

I have read the 2018 NAO Report and recent Government announcements around poor value for money. The original contract was signed with that homes company backed by Terra Firma Capital Partners and other financial institutions. How did we end up with such a poor contract, which left such a liability on the taxpayer and let down our troops?

I want to draw an important distinction between what you are talking about, which is the 1996 deal, and the repurchase deal, which is the focus of the 2026 Report and which I think is a good deal. The Department is praised in that Report and I begin by thanking all the civil servants and public servants involved in the repurchase of the homes. It is a very significant success. There is a lot to do to learn lessons from it for the future, for the Defence Housing Service.

I strongly agree with you on the importance of housing. Housing matters because every service family deserves a safe, secure and well-maintained home. I entirely agree. Our armed forces face unique challenges, such as frequent redeployments. My colleagues, Mike and David, can talk more about that. We in the Department deal with 15,000 moves a year. Obviously, our troops are also frequently deployed, so there are periods of separation and school changes. Defence has unique characteristics, and we need to ensure that housing supports life, rather than creating stress. That will improve our military capability, and I completely agree with that.

The 1996 deal was not a good deal, and it is not a deal that the Department would make today. Looking back 30 years is not straightforward, and my focus has been on the repurchase and the future, but it is really important to emphasise to the Committee that the Department would not approach this issue in the same way now.

Judging the 1996 deal is exceptionally hard. One thing the Report is clear on is the fact that the objectives of that deal were different and reflected the priorities of the Government at the time. Yes, it was partly about securing funds for the upgrade, but in truth, only a fraction or small amount of the proceeds were used for that. It was a sale-and-leaseback deal to secure value through a competitive process. I think that was the primary objective, and a lot of things flow from that.

I apologise for the length of this opening answer, but I think the most important lesson is the importance of Government taking a long-term view of the stewardship of a national asset. That is how I feel, and I know it is how the Defence Secretary feels about this issue. That needs to be the most important thing, rather than short-term pressures.

Colleagues can reflect on the details, but there is something about really understanding the value of what you are selling and the assumptions underlying it. The world looked very different in 1996 from how it looks today; the focus then would have been on the peace dividend. Looking back, I also reflect that it is really important to think about human behaviours and the incentives created by the deal. It is very hard to judge these things 30 years later—obviously, everyone involved has long since moved on. My focus has been on understanding the lessons from the repurchase and the future.

Q2 I appreciate that response, but part of understanding how we have ended up losing such huge sums of public money is understanding the original deal and what lessons can be learned. I appreciate that you have given some answer to that, but fundamentally, there has been a delay in us coming back to the original contract and looking again at this issue. The 2018 NAO Report was produced almost 22 years after the original deal, for instance.

Who negotiated the original contract? At the time, did this long 999-year lease not seem unreasonable? I appreciate that some might have considered that to be unreasonable even at the time, so who was involved in the original contract negotiations? How have we ended up with this liability, meaning that we now have to go through, in effect, a nationalisation of this asset?
It was a long-term sale and leaseback. I completely agree that it was a poor deal undertaken by the Ministry of Defence, and it is not a deal that we would undertake today.

What would be my other reflections? The sorts of financial appraisal, the skills and the approach that are brought to these things are very different today from in 1996. I joined the civil service in 1997, but you are looking at a world in 1996 where you did not have expert advice across Government from UK Government Investments; it was before the Shareholder Executive was created, and before the Major Projects Authority—now NISTA—and Infrastructure UK were created. Approaches to financial appraisal were very different then.

Your next question is why we could not get after this sooner. Part of the answer is that there was a contract that needed to be managed. The R eport sets out very clearly —my colleagues know this in a lot of detail—that the Department had to turn quite a weak contractual position into a favourable position. That was the process from 2019 through to 2024, so it was relatively soon after the Report you referred to was published. The key elements are about strengthening the position through the cases of enfranchisement and the negotiation on rent. The original contract, in theory, was a return to market rent after 25 years.

Thirdly—and crucially; this made a real difference—was the change in lease accounting rules through IFRS 16. For those who are sceptical that accounting is important and drives decisions—I know this Committee is not sceptical of that—this repurchase deal is living proof of the importance of good accounting rules. They shifted the contractual position, and a more complete reflection of our future liabilities was on our balance sheets—and ultimately hit public sector net debt, as I understand it. That meant that the repurchase did not increase sector net debt by the full amount.

My colleagues can talk more about enfranchisement and the shift in rent. Unfortunately, in my career, I have spent a lot of time on accounting rules and fiscal rules, so I can see the benefit of that as well. The situation changed. My impression is that quite skilful work was done, but I say that as someone who was not involved. They were using advisers, there was good work from civil servants and public servants, and strong support from Ministers in successive Administrations. The now Chancellor played a leading role when he was in the Department and provided the political direction that is needed to drive progress.

The shift from 2019 to about 2024 was key in turning that quite weak position under the contract to a very favourable position, and key to unlocking the deal and driving value—the value that is recorded in the Report. Ultimately, we acquired homes for £6 billion that were valued on Annington’s balance sheet at £10.1 billion. You have read the Report.

Q3 I will ask one final question and then pass it on. The 2018 NAO Report highlighted that there was a lot to learn about that contract. The head of the National Audit Office at the time said that, “ This has cost the public sector a great deal in capital growth ”. Subsequent to that, the MOD agreed to take on responsibility for the cost of maintenance.

You agreed a contract previously which the NAO subsequently highlighted as being poor in terms of stewardship, but then you took on additional responsibility for revenue maintenance of the estate, and the benefit went to Annington Homes. What consideration process led to that decision, given that at that point and just prior we knew some of the liability we were getting as taxpayers from a potentially poor contract arrangement?
I think maintenance was always in there, so I don’t think that is the case. I think the original deal had that in.
That is why the rental level is below market, to reflect the ongoing role of MOD in maintenance. But that created the reverse incentive that caused some of the toxicity in the deal.

Q4 Can I just push back? P aragraph 1.7 of the NAO Report says “The value of any investment that the MoD made to improve the standard of accommodation would pass to Annington in the form of either increased rents or increased value”. Can you clarify whether that happened?

If we do up a house, it is a better house and they charge us more rent for it. There are some anomalies in the detail of the deal that are just not good; you are correct. There was the hand-back situation, which was not good. There was the situation where we didn’t own the house yet we were responsible for maintenance, which is unusual.

There were assumptions around the increase in value each year of the houses, which is the big problem in losing value, being around 1% or less. I Googled it on the way in this morning. House prices are rising between 6% and 9% every year. There are some huge modelling assumptions in your questioning that could not be made today, because the Macpherson review after the west coast main line set out how civil servants are to model things—independent peer review, openness and all those kinds of things. It would not happen today.

Just to clarify, my understanding is that the “arrangements” in paragraph 1.7 of the NAO Report refers to the arrangements established in the original 1996 deal rather than a change in 2018. That may be the cause of the confusion.
Okay, that’ s fine.
That is my understanding, too, P ermanent S ecretary. To correct one thing you said there, Mike, house prices do not always go up continuously—look at the present situation.
Over time!

Q5 Jeremy, this Committee is often very critical of a lot of things, not least your Ministry. Where your Ministry has got it right is this repurchase deal, which is a good deal. I reran the numbers last night—it is a good deal—so everybody who was involved deserves to be congratulated.
Thank you.

Q6 I concur. Jeremy, I know that 1996 was a long time ago—it was before you were there—but you have the role that of ensuring that the lessons we have learned are baked in. You said that approaches to financial appraisal were very different then, but then you referred to the toxicity of the deal, so even by 1996 standards, it feels like this deal was particularly bad. Are you confident that you have got under the skin of that very different line of approaches to financial appraisal? Have you learned the lessons of that specific deal? Can the Committee be confident that what specifically went wrong here has minimised the opportunities and chances of it going wrong in the future?

The sophistication of the analysis and use of expert advisers is different from in 1996. I have already indicated some examples of that. It is about understanding the value of assets and understanding underlying assumptions and sometimes hidden assumptions in a deal. It is also about doing more to model uncertainty. Ensuring checks and balances in the system of government enables richer discussion and conversation. Often, Government is accused of being slow, but sometimes that is because it is making time for those discussions. Often experts are brought in from the outside—Mr Lowe is here , for example . These external experts are about having people with relevant expertise to help us to assess these deals. I will be honest with the Committee and admit that I have not read the advice from 1996, and I am wary of looking into it too far. To some extent, how bad it looks is how it looks now.

Q7 The military is very good at looking to history to learn lessons for the future, and it can look very far into history to learn lessons. It is perhaps a fair challenge to you that the MOD can do that.
I think I have already indicated several lessons.

Q8 Can we talk about the time it took—from 1996 until 2019—for the MOD to start looking at how to improve the terms of the deal? We will look at that going forward, but it is important to spend a little more time looking at a couple aspects of the period then. Why did it take so long—nearly 25 years?

I reflected on that question when preparing for this hearing. It is obviously a deal we would not do now—I have indicated some lessons. Overall the period from 2019, following the 2018 Report, was handled exceptionally well. We can talk about that and debate that. The question I have is whether more could have been done before 2019, and it is quite hard to judge that—a lot of other things were happening at the time. The key difference, though, is that the accounting rule changes really unlock this in government—the shift to IFRS really does unlock this. The other thing I would say—we have already alluded to this fact—is that we were in a weaker negotiating position before 2019. One of my colleagues might want to add to that, because it is a good question.

It takes two people to negotiate, and if the answer is in how to bring Annington Homes to the table, there are several key things. First, on enfranchisement, we went to court a couple of times and did well. Going forward, we could have been locked in legalese for years—these are big sums of money and no one would want to lose. What the court case, the changes in IFRS 16 and the renegotiation of the rent did over that period you describe were to give us the opportunity to bring Annington Homes to the table for a proper conversation about the way forward, so that is why we did what we did then.

Q9 That means that at some point after 1996, the Department was aware that it was a bad deal and it started to look for ways to pick at and challenge it. It would be important for the Committee to know whether that started happening in 1997 and it took 20 years to find a way through, or not until summer 2018 did someone say, “Oh my God, this is terrible. How did we get to this?”

The two previous NAO Reports are clear, the first more gently and the second much clearer that there is work to be done. I was not around at the time—to be clear—but I do not see that the negotiating position would have been strong enough to bring people to the table before. An alignment of the three things enabled us to have a great conversation and sort this out.

Q10 Jeremy, one of the things that you said earlier to Tris was that one of the lessons is that taking a long-term view is important, but you followed that up by saying, “But it is very hard to look 30 years into the future.” That inherent tension between the two statements, which I agree with, is very difficult to deal with. You have the responsibility of dealing with it, but I think you can look towards one side of what you said or the other. If you look towards, “It is very hard to look 30 years into the future”, and your predecessor 30 years ago was saying that, that might explain how we got into this; but if you say that we should take a long-term view, with all that that involves—

We should absolutely take a long-term view. I think I was trying to say that it is hard to look into the mind of the decision taker 30 years in the past; I was not saying that today we should not be looking 30 years into the future—of course we should—
Q11 Your assessment is that he was not taking a long-term view.

I think that the objectives that were set essentially led to a more short-term approach than should have been taken. That is partly driven by the objectives that were set, so there is another lesson there. Again, these things often come to the Committee, but our job is to maximise value for money and the outcomes for the objectives that have been set, and there is another really important lesson here around this. I think that a long-term objective that is focused on stewardship of national assets is important.

I echo what the Chair said, that it is important that we are about to start talking about a good contract—what looks like a good contract, so I hope that does not come back to bite me in 30 years’ time when people are sitting in this Committee then—and I know you take this lesson-learning piece seriously. It can be easy to be defensive when we are asking these questions, but that does seem particularly bad, which is what I think the Committee is reflecting on. That is just a comment from me.

Q12 I appreciate your answers about the 2019 position. The assets that we acquired as part of this deal were in quite a poor state—as referred to in paragraph 14 of the Report—partly because essential maintenance was only conducted to a safe and legal standard. I also appreciate that we celebrate that the deal had us purchasing the asset at a significantly reduced valuation compared with what the seller was looking for. There are two parts to my question. We paid a significant amount of money on the original contract to this private provider, and the asset that we have now had to repurchase on behalf of the state is in a suboptimal condition, hence the reason why we have to improve it, so why has it taken till 2024 for the M O D to exit the deal?
I am not sure that I have very much more to answer on that, I am afraid—
I think it has already been answered.
I feel it has been asked and answered to the best of my ability, but maybe David has something to add.
Unless anybody has anything to add, there is no point repeating what we have already said.

There are a couple of points. One is the way the deal was structured, and you are both right that the commercial consequences are a consequence of the detail of how it was drafted, how it worked and how the various clauses worked together. The way it is structured, the level of losses was increasing exponentially. You can see, if you track through the various NAO Reports, that the scale of loss was increasing really rapidly in a relatively short period of time. In real terms, it went up from about a £5.5 billion loss in 2018; six years later, they were talking about the equivalent figure being an £8.5 billion loss. You can see that that was really ratcheting up, and as we rolled forward into the future, the losses as a consequence of the deal were continuing on a really steep upward trajectory, so there was a real imperative to act at the point in time that we did.

Then, as colleagues have said, in order to secure a decent deal when we were buying it back, we had to create commercial leverage. That commercial leverage did not exist earlier; it was a consequence of a series of really carefully calculated steps that created the conditions where a buy-back was deliverable. If we had not done that, we would have been buying these homes back at many billions of pounds more, with a much stronger counterparty, and we would have been sat in front of this Committee with you saying, “Well, why did you pay twice as much as you should have done to buy these homes back in 2018?”.

Q13 Matt Turmaine : Moving on to the condition of the accommodation, Mr Pocklington, can I ask what you are doing to resolve the MoD’s negligent approach to maintenance and upkeep of the military homes that we have seen over the past 30 years?

It is a priority. That is one of the reasons why we are creating the Defence Housing Service: to ensure that we provide the quality of homes that our service personnel rightly expect from the Department. The thing I would say is that work is already underway. Last year, we refurbished and decorated 1,250 homes. The quality of the service we are offering has already improved. One thing that struck me while preparing for the Committee was the number of active complaints that we have regarding the quality of homes. On 1 July there were 60 or 66—in the 60s—active complaints; in November 2022, there were 4,200 complaints, so the service has improved.

The other thing I would point to is survey data on satisfaction with military homes. That has increased by 12 percentage points over the past year to 75% of families now saying that they are satisfied, and that is across the entirety of housing provided by the Department. That is actually higher than the national average for civilian landlords by four percentage points. Obviously, I would like it to be higher still, and I expect higher standards for our service personnel, but we are getting after this. There is more that we need to do, but it is a priority for the Department because when it is not good enough, it is not good enough. We have all seen examples of housing that is not yet of the standard we need, and that is why we need this long-term plan to get after it.

I joined in 2022 and was surprised at the condition of the forces housing and what we were doing. I think we have had a previous hearing on this with the Defence Committee. It is fair to say that we were not in control of the things we were taking care of. We had a non-compliance issue and a damp and mould issue—we were issuing houses with damp and mould. We changed all that. We have turned all that around. I think, at worst, we had just over 4,000 cases of houses with severe damp and mould. All that is gone; we have dealt with that. We have dealt with the compliance issues.

The few non-compliance issues that we have now tend to be failure to get access into a house. We have worked really hard on that. We have got to a position where the remaining houses are not resistant to modern life . We have single-brick or single-pane windows, so damp and mould are generated a lot. Our houses generate probably between six and eight calls per house per year to our help desk, whereas for an equivalent housing association it is probably three. I am generalising, but that is the scale of change that we are looking at. The only way now to fix it is for our houses to get a boost, which is the point of creating the Defence Housing Service to deal with it.

If you think about how people use the houses and the price of energy, nobody opens the windows and people dry their clothes in the houses. Understanding the use of the house and making houses properly to resist the way they will be used going forward is what we need to do now. That is the point of the Defence Housing Service.

I would quickly add one other point, which is a philosophical one. This is about moving from a reactive approach to a proactive long-term mindset, which is a very different approach. It allows us to engage in the structured, thoughtful steps that Mike has just talked about. That is why making this part of a 10-year programme in the DIP is so important. I think one of the problems we have had in the past is that we did not maintain something until it failed. That, by definition, is a reactive and often costly approach to life. I think we can move forward in a more efficient and effective way by having this long-term programme and putting specialist skills to work in that programme.

Q14 Matt Turmaine : The three of you have communicated points that touch on my other questions. That “fix on fail” point, or however the Report describes it, is not a great approach. I appreciate that progress is being made and that things have got better. I have a constituent who has an example of this. There are a couple of points that I would like to come back to. On the satisfaction levels, Mr Pocklington, the supporting material that has been provided by the NAO shows that we have satisfaction levels currently at 52% with regard to the SFA, which is not amazing. Equally, in terms of the response to requests for maintenance for the current accommodation, satisfaction levels are 39% versus 45% for dissatisfied. For the quality of the repair work being done, there are dissatisfied rates of 49% and satisfaction of just 33%. There is clearly some way still to go, isn’t there, to get to an acceptable level?

The simple answer is yes. We are on a journey. We have fixed the big things in front of us. We are working with lots of people to get better, but the core component of the houses that we own are not great. We go out to them a lot and we fix them a lot to drive the things that you are talking about. The D efence H ousing S ervice thing that we need to carry out over 10 years is to put ourselves in a different position for the next 50 years or however long it is. I am a great believer in doing it efficiently, which is what we are planning to do. I am a great believer in doing it properly. When you look at the housing stock and find things like vents that do not lead anywhere, single brick walls and no cavity insulation, I am not surprised that our houses need a lot of love. We have under-invested in them for the best part of 40 or 50 years, and that needs to change. It comes back to the effect on the family, because it does affect families, and I am sure we would agree that our wonderful service personnel deserve better. That is the intention.

Q15 Matt Turmaine : I acknowledge that progress is being made and things are improving. What is your assessment of the overall quality of the estate now? There are examples where things have been improved, but where are you on the estate as a whole?

We know that nine out of 10 houses need some serious attention. Near enough all—90% or something—meet a decent homes standard, but that standard is perhaps not as aspirational as you or I would like, to be frank. The plan is to sort out the building blocks of what we use to house our service personnel , and hopefully to turn them from tolerable to aspirational.

I can add a little colour to that. On the estate overall, most of these houses were built either immediately post war or through into the early 1970s, so their inherent build quality standards—the inherent design and the inherent construction—are of their age. As we know, they have also not been particularly well maintained subsequently. Well over half of the estate is below an EPC standard of D in energy efficiency.

If you compare this estate with, for example, most regulated housing providers, we are starting from an inherently worse place. We end up doing about 250,000 reactive repair tasks across the estate in a year, as that poor quality of housing and its condition drives a huge amount of reactive work. Every single example of a reactive repair is disruption to a service family just trying to get on and enjoy their homes peacefully.

That is why we need this sustained, long-term programme to address the fundamentals and the underlying quality of the properties. While we are getting on with that, we must also get much better at dealing with the reactive repairs and the service for people in those homes. We are tackling both of those things in parallel.

There is a “lessons learned” thing here, which we touched on earlier. If you look back to the original deal and think about the human behaviour that followed, doing up someone else’s house to their benefit is inherently not what you would want to do, so we have neglected these houses. As I said, we have put right the things in front of us, but there is now a major thing to do to sort out the building blocks.

Q16 Matt Turmaine : That is great. I do not want to keep dragging us back to 1996, but how much of this is a legacy of that 1996 arrangement, in which the responsibility for maintenance was taken on by the M O D?

It is difficult to say. I think a lot of it, but I have no idea how the M O D budgeted money for housing over the subsequent 30 years. It could be that we have spent a lot of money on the houses and did them up well, but there is an inherent behaviour not to do that. Running through the whole military estate, not just housing, is the fact that our infrastructure is in poor condition.
Q17 Matt Turmaine : A last question from me for the time being. When would we expect service personnel and families to be able to move into the refurbished properties?

It is a 10-year programme to get the whole estate up to standard. We are actually doing two things with that programme: we are trying to not only fix the condition of the homes but make sure that we have the right homes in the right locations. One of the other consequences of the Annington deal was that we ended up not being able to move our homes around, so we could not sell and buy homes where we needed them. There is a big mismatch between where we need houses of certain sizes, and where we have houses. That is another important factor unlocked by the deal.

We will see people moving into better quality homes progressively throughout the period of 10 years. The Defence Housing Service will publish the plan to do that in its first year of operation, and we are doing quite a lot of the planning and analysis that sits behind that now.

At the same time as we are doing those fundamental repairs, much more quickly than that everybody will be seeing an improvement in the standard of the repair service, as well as the standard that we prepare homes to when families move in. We have between 10,000 and 15,000 families moving home each year, and we are trying to ratchet up the standards. People will feel a benefit quickly, but really tackling the underlying problems will take the whole of that 10-year period.

Q18 Mike, I do not want to be unkind, but you have been in place since 2022. The Committee has been very critical of these housing survey figures for many years, and it is not good enough. If we want to recruit and retain our service personnel, I would suggest to you, David, that we need to do something about this much quicker than in 10 years.

When we went to Marham, for example, to look at the F-35s, we found that people who had been on Operation Highmast to Japan came back and were immediately sent off to the Gulf. We saw that in some cases their families were living in substandard houses. Modern families will not put up with that length of tour and that level of housing.

To give you an example, Matt has cited the worst figures , but the figures on how people regard the current service family accommodation are worse today than they were in 2012: 52% are satisfied, compared with 56% in 2012, and 33% are dissatisfied, compared with 29% in 2012. If I ran a business and over half my customers were dissatisfied with my product, I would not be in business very long. I think, P ermanent S ecretary and Mike, that there is a degree of complacency about the condition of this housing. Why can the MOD not produce a published minimum standard for single living accommodation? You have to do that for social housing.

You are right: I have been in place since 2022. I walked into quite a storm around damp and mould, compliance and all those things. We have fixed all those things. We have bought back Annington Homes. We have put together a plan to launch the Defence Housing Service, financed it and got money to do it. I understand your point about the 10 years. We are effectively rebuilding 50,000 houses, and at the same time hope to develop some others. I wish I could tell you there is a quick fix.

It is not that we have not been doing anything. Last year we tackled the worst 1,000 houses. We will do something similar this year. We have largely fixed the service. I used to work in retail construction, and I really like to view these people as our customers. That was not the case before. We are working really hard to change that.

I actually think it has changed significantly. The conditions now allow us to fix it, which has not been the case for 40 or 50 years. I hear what you say, and that’s fine, but it is my intention to fix this over the next 10 years for the following 50, which we have failed to do for the previous 50.

Q19 I suppose some of this revolves around money, so perhaps we could sort out the money aspect of it. As I understand it, Aneen , the deal to repurchase the Annington houses at £6 billion was granted to you by the Treasury on the condition that £9 billion was spent on refurbishment and repair over 10 years. If that is the case, how much is going to be spent in this Parliament?

Aneen Blackmore: We touched on this when we were last in front of the Committee. You are absolutely right to refer to our £9.2 billion commitment for service family accommodation over 10 years. As we talked about, that was absolutely protected through the DIP process. It is a core priority for us for all the reasons we have set out today, which the Committee is familiar with. As part of the DIP process, we considered a variety of priorities and critical capabilities to ensure that we had a balanced plan, and we needed to reprofile around £800 million from this Parliament into next Parliament.

I can assure the Committee that alongside that we were really clear that we wanted to prioritise a real-terms increase so that we were really getting after the immediate problems and supporting defence housing services. Our plan for this year is a real-terms increase on last year. The plan for next year is another real-terms increase. The plan for the year after that is another real-terms increase. We are really not complacent. We know how important this is to our service personnel and more broadly so that we can optimise our estate and drive even greater value for money for it, but we needed to balance it in the wider plan.

Q20 Can you clear up a bit of confusion over the figures? As I understand it, the original allocation was £1.5 million to be spent in this Parliament. You have deferred £0.8 billion. I think that figure is in the public domain, but I am not sure about the £1.5 billion in this Parliament. That means you are only going to spend £0.7 billion in this Parliament. It sounds as though you are a long way short of getting anywhere near the £9.2 billion in 10 years.

Aneen Blackmore: I think there is a risk of confusion between the service family accommodation budget and the single living accommodation budget. The £1.5 billion relates to the additional increase that we were looking to spend. We set out in the DIP that we are planning to spend £2.7 billion on service family accommodation over the next four years. That already include s some of the reprofiling that we needed to do to ensure that we balanced the broader programme, given the pressures that we have in defence, but, as I said, we absolutely were protecting the £9.2 billion over the 10 years—we need to do that; we will continue to do that—and we were absolutely ensuring that, alongside that, we were continuing to drive real-terms increases, so that we continue to make the progress that we wanted to make.

Q21 Sorry, I am being confused by sophistry. How much are you going to spend in this Parliament, full stop, on all defence housing accommodation? Is that £2.7 billion over four years? This Parliament only has another three years to run, so how much will you be spending in this Parliament?

Aneen Blackmore: On housing in totality , I would need to write to the Committee , because that gets into the single living accommodation figures , which I do not have in front of me. I would need to write to confirm that . On the service family accommodation, for the four years going forward , it is £ 2.7 billion. Obviously, this Parliament includes a prior year on that as well.
You have had two years of it.
Aneen Blackmore: Yes; that is only looking forward. But I can confirm that we are continuing to build in real - terms increases.

Q22 It should be relatively simple. How much are we going to spend , in this financial year , on defence housing ? If you are deferring £0. 8 billion , how much are you actually going to spend in this financial year? It will come out in the accounts eventually , so how much are you proposing to spend? You must have a budget.

Aneen Blackmore: W e absolutely do have a budget . B ecause housing is much broader than the service family accommodation , I would need to write to give you a full set of what we would include. That includes single living accommodation and it would include some of our defence optimisation budget as well.

Sir Geoffrey, you wrote to me about two days ago , asking for this information and for a reply later this month. We will write ; w e will reply. You have asked the question , and it is a perfectly fair question. It is in different places in our budgets in the D epartment , because you are including single living accommodation as well as service famil y accommodation , so I will reply on the deadline that you have asked me to.

Q23 Rupert, g ood morning. We have not heard from you this morning , s o now is your opportunity. How is it that if this was not defence housing, there would be a social housing standard ? Why should n’t defence housing have the same standard?

I do not disagree with that in principle. What we have to do is deliver standards that are going to attract and retain our top - quality armed forces and also recognise, as Jeremy said very eloquently earlier, the very unusual nature of service life — the peripatetic nature of it and the fact that families are separated , sometimes for long periods of time. P hilosophically , where standards will need to flex and differ is where they have to reflect the operational necessities of life in the armed forces. But absent that, it is obviously our intention to offer people the same standards they could get in commercial life — in normal life ; o therwise, how are we going to attract people into the armed forces?

Q24 But if we take David ’s point that you have a 10-year programme, is n’t that too long? You want to recruit people and retain them . We are in a desperate state at the moment with needing to recruit more people. Housing is integrally linked with that. Isn ’t 10 years far too long?

Well, you could say that about the DIP as a whole, about investment across the reinvigoration of our armed forces ’ capabilities, and about our broader infrastructure , which Mike has talked about and is also not in a state we would like. Housing is part of that. I t is a question of balancing all those priorities, Sir Geoffrey. It is not an easy task, and we do n’t have a lot of time to get after it , either.
F orgive me if I gave the impression that we were waiting for 10 years before this would be fixed.
No, didn’t get that impression; I got that you were having a 10- year programme . I am just saying that you need to think about that , because I think it is too long.

There are a few bits that go with that . W e are prioritising improving condition over capacity , so we are bringing in the condition improvements as early as possible in that programme. We are improving all the houses as we go through and improving the service throughout the whole of that period of time . As we have touched on, we are targeting the worst properties first. So the scale of the problem that we are challenging will be eaten into progressively through that period , and we will see significant improvements across the estate much earlier than in 10 years.

It is a combination of factors as well. Ultimately, our ambition is gated by the 24 hours in the day and the amount of money that we can put to work, particularly at the front end of this process, to get ahead of events. That is part of a resource allocation in terms of the overall pot and what we prioritise.

Obviously, at one level we want to have the best possible service family accommodation and single living accommodation for the brave men and women in our armed forces, and we need to get to “good” as quickly as possible.
