It is like doing a PhD. The first time you put together a programme—that process—even if people tell you you are doing a good job, you do not believe it. When doing a PhD, you do not believe it until you are all the way through the process, so you have to be resilient.

Nobody comes to ARIA or to DARPA with all of those skills, which is probably not surprising given the list of things I have just told you. Therefore, you also have to be able to take feedback well, because if you do not take feedback, the time it takes to learn all those skills is too long because you only have a three-year appointment plus one or two years of renewal. People who are able to learn on the job faster by listening to people who are working hard to coach you to get up to that set faster will make a bigger difference faster. Those are the set of skills that we are looking for. We found them in the first two cohorts and I am convinced that we will find them in this cohort as well.

On some of the learnings, the first cohort was heavily academic and the second cohort was heavily entrepreneurial. We are looking in the third cohort for a balance of both academic and entrepreneurial. In the first cohort we allowed people to be 80% time, to accommodate academics. The second cohort we made 100% time at ARIA. The third cohort will go back to letting people be 80% time to allow people to be academics. That is partly because academics often have PhD students who they do not want to abandon. I have seen at DARPA that it is definitely doable to be an academic on 80% time and be effective as an ARIA or a DARPA programme manager.

The Chair: To intervene for a second, on the 1,200 applicants who you have just mentioned, do you have, off the top of your head, what proportion of those would be academics and what proportion would be from outside academia?
I do not know. I am sure that there is a healthy mix, but I can get you statistics.
Lord Winston: It would be useful to know.
The Chair: Yes, it would be helpful to know.
Lord Winston: Is that possible?

We can get you the statistics. Maybe wait until the 28 September deadline so that we can get you the statistics of the full pool. We have been going on a tour around the world and the UK to highlight the positions and to explain working with ARIA.
Lord Patel: Does it matter for your programme whether it is academics or those who come from industry?

The people matter a huge amount. I think that both academics and industry people can be hugely successful as programme directors. Having a mix in the cohort is valuable because a bonding happens between the programme directors. They talk to each other a lot, so having some of each is a good combination. At this point we have a good mix of academics and entrepreneurs across the two cohorts. We would like to see that replicated within the third cohort.

Lord Winston: Could I come back with my last question? Your previous CEO suggested to us that the ideal projects were the ones where there was violent disagreement, where half the people looking at it thought that it was a fantastic project and the other half thought that it was complete rubbish. What do you feel about that? Do you feel that you can make those decisions to find the projects where there is very considerable disagreement in the panel that is looking at it?

I do not know that I would be as strong as Ilan was, that what you are shooting for is 50:50. I think that zero people is a bad sign and 100% is a bad sign—it is somewhere in between. I do not think that you should be going for 100% of people who think that this is a good idea. If you are there, it is probably too settled and probably a case where the field is already going to go there. If nobody thinks that it is a good idea, you probably should not be doing it either.
Lord Winston: That is a pretty sane answer. Thank you very much.
The Chair: Lord Willis, would you like to come in online? Oh, I am sorry, we are not getting Lord Willis; we cannot hear you. Lord Winston, would you like to ask the question for Lord Willis?

Q5 Very quickly, because it follows up on what we have been discussing already. Programme directors retain a great deal of autonomy. How do they allocate their funding with that autonomy, what approaches have been taken to allocate that funding and what is your view of how the research is best performed?
I did not hear the last part of your question. Can you repeat it?
Lord Winston: What approach have your directors of projects taken to allocate the funding that they get? What is your view as to where the research is best performed?

There are lots of different programme structures that can work and the right programme structure depends on what the programme is trying to accomplish. One structure is that you allocate all of the money up front and you then actively manage as the programme goes along, cutting the teams that are not effective. Sometimes you overallocate at the beginning because you assume that you will cut certain teams. The programmable plants programme, for example, took the first strategy there because plants, it turns out, grow really slowly, so they anticipated that, no matter what, it would take a long time for the plants to grow and doing something faster was not going to be helpful.

In the enduring atmospheric platforms programme, where the teams have a relatively expensive cost to send various vehicles up into the stratosphere to set up communications, the programme director wanted to take the approach where we invest in a whole bunch of different approaches, overcommitting at the beginning and then cutting the teams—the ones that show the least promise—which allows you to put more shots on goal. That is an advantage of that approach but it means that the teams know that they are actively competing against each other for a smaller pot, so they will not be working with each other because they know that they will get cut. Some of them will have to get cut because the programme does not have enough budget to continue all of them forward.

The forecasting tipping points programme set up a structure where they were not sure what approaches would work. Therefore, they set up a two-phase programme where they ran the first phase for 18 months and they will send out a second solicitation in the next month or two to set up the second phase of the programme. That was appropriate because they knew that they would be able to iterate and get information in the first 18 months that would dramatically affect what they wanted to do in the second part of the programme.

The trust everything, everywhere programme that Alex is running is running a competition because he wanted to see what was out there. That space is moving so fast and there are so many players and it did not seem that he would be able to get all of the people on contract that he wanted to be able to try out. By running a competition, you can throw it out there and see who will come to play. The challenge of a competition is that it is extremely challenging to get the rules exactly right so that you are rewarding what you want to be measuring and not inadvertently rewarding something else. You need to be very careful about setting it up so that the players cannot cheat in a way that you do not want them to be cheating. Those are all interesting different structures.

We recently hired a chief science and technology officer, who comes from spending significant time at DARPA and has had a large amount of his career working on different programme structures, to help particularly cohort 3 be very sophisticated in programme structures. One thing that he will be particularly looking at is setting up; I talked about phased structure and funding structure. Another interesting structure is the technical area structure. ARIA has done quite a bit on a social impact structure and an adoption structure of how this technology will be received, which has been interesting.

Another technical area that is very common at DARPA is an evaluation team, because often how you evaluate cutting-edge science is itself a research area and it provides programme directors with an interesting lever arm. If you are creating challenge problems, you can make challenge problems more or less difficult and you can choose challenge problems to facilitate translation or adoption. Having a separate technical area that is responsible for managing evaluation gives the programme director another lever arm to move. The new chief science and technology officer, who will be starting on 1 October, has deep expertise in these structure choices and he will be working with cohort 3 in those choices.

Q6 Good morning, Dr Fisher. My questions will focus on ARIA’s approach to bringing economic benefit specifically to the United Kingdom. When we spoke to Matt Clifford, he said that ARIA has been designed very explicitly as a value-creation mechanism rather than a value-capture one. However, ARIA has a mandate that says it needs to bring economic benefit to the UK specifically. How is ARIA doing that?

Thank you for the question. I appreciate that ARIA has indeed a mandate to bring economic benefit to the UK. I think that ARIA is a value-creation agency primarily, but it also has a value-capture role. ARIA’s value-creation mechanism by itself will bring tremendous economic benefit to the UK. For example, the precision neurotechnologies effort that Jacques Carolan is bringing is working on creating technology to address neurological disorders and neuropsychiatric disorders that currently afflict one in six citizens of the UK and cost the National Health Service £4.1 billion a year. If that programme delivers technology that could treat those patients in a much more economic way, that will deliver enormous economic benefit to the UK without having any profit associated with it. Therefore, value creation can be economically impactful by not costing the NHS an enormous amount of money and by returning the people who are currently suffering from those ailments to the productive workforce.

That said, I agree that value capture is also an important part of what we are doing. That is part of the reason why we created the chief translation officer, whose job is to work with programme directors to identify what the impact path is. Every time we create a programme, we also think about what the path is for translation of this programme, what the path is for social or economic impact. Some of them are things like climate change, but some of them are creating companies and driving those companies to cross the valley of death and commercialisation and how they can deliver that benefit to the UK.

Our IP terms are designed to maximise that. We have chosen not to take intellectual property. We think that the best way to drive economic benefit for the UK is to have the creator themselves maintain the IP rights so that when the creator goes to start a company, their cap table is clean and they have the best terms to go to the venture capital companies and get funding. They will be maximally incentivised to go and do that process. We have, with multiple activation partners, worked to create a climate to incentivise an entrepreneurial spirit to go and drive the commercialisation through those mechanisms. I can say more, but I will stop there for now.

Lord Drayson: Your example, Dr Fisher, is a great example of how the programme would bring economic and societal benefit to the UK, but not specifically to the UK. Those issues that you highlighted are common globally. It is the economic benefit to the UK specifically that I want to drill down into, rather than a spreading of progress globally. When we spoke to ARIA’s leadership back in 2024, they very clearly expressed the view that any attempt to capture value for the UK specifically could jeopardise the success of the project attracting investment. Do you agree with that?

Crossing the valley of death is really hard and crossing it successfully needs to be the first priority . If we can successfully cross the valley of death, we need to think about how to make sure we cross it in a way that maximises benefit to the UK. ARIA is working to create an environment that makes crossing the valley of death in the UK as maximally attractive as possible. That is why we are doing things like the venture café with the activation partner in London, Manchester and Edinburgh to create a climate where entrepreneurs know that they are not alone—that there are tons of entrepreneurs in the UK.

One of the things that I have been asked by creators who are thinking about becoming an entrepreneur is, “What if I create a start-up and it fails?” with the implicit notion that having a failed start-up is like a kiss of death and your career is over, versus the mindset in Silicon Valley where a failed start-up is a perfectly good thing to have on your resumé. It gives you credibility to start another start-up. The creator communities, the Venture Café , are creating the mindset that if you do not try, that is a failure. Trying and failing is a perfectly reasonable thing to do. It is why we have the activation partner, Fifty Years, which is one of the world’s best deep-tech venture capital companies, working with us to run the 50 50 partner, to work with scientists on how to create a pitch deck and how to be an entrepreneur—to create a population who will become entrepreneurs who decide that they want to create a great company and want to stay in the UK and do value capture here.

Lord Drayson: Dr Fisher, you have highlighted the important role of activation partners in crossing the valley of death, as you describe it. Why are some of your activation partners not based in the United Kingdom?

When we made the agreements with the world-class, deep-tech investors who know how to convert science into world-class companies, the terms of the agreement required them to establish UK operations and to invest all of the money in the UK. Yes, they are US companies, but they are focusing these efforts on the UK. That is a good thing for the UK because they are bringing their expertise. They know how to do this but they are bringing them to the UK.

Lord Drayson: Yes, but as multiple inquiries have shown, the UK does not have a problem in attracting investment. The UK has a problem in commercialising the breakthroughs that are made here in the UK to generate economic growth from the UK. Is there a case to be made, when it comes to selecting investors to help commercialise ARIA’s discoveries, that ARIA should prefer UK investment partners?

ARIA’s role is producing companies that have world-class technology and world-class teams and want to stay in the UK. If there are UK investment organisations that want at that point to fund the organisations, that would be fantastic. If there are not UK investment companies at that point that want to invest and there are US investment companies that want to invest and keep the company in the UK, that would be fantastic. The most important thing is that the company decides that it wants to stay in the UK, whether the funding comes from the US or the UK. The most important thing is that the company does not die.

Lord Drayson: Unfortunately, Dr Fisher, from this committee’s previous inquiry, in our Bleeding to Death report we have catalogued thoroughly the tendency of promising UK technology start-ups to leave the UK. Therefore, my concern is the risk that the activation partners become acquisition partners facilitating the cream of ARIA’s IP to ultimately benefit global investors outside of the UK rather than creating wealth and economic growth in the UK. Do you see this as a risk? If you do, what will you do about it?

I do not see that as a huge risk. I see the huge upside of leveraging their knowledge and expertise to produce world-class companies that maximise the chance of crossing the valley of death, and therefore getting the benefits of the value creation no matter what, and maximising the chance of having companies that will in the long run decide to stay. It is not only ARIA’s responsibility to make it so that these organisations decide they want to stay in the UK. Our remit is producing the selection of companies and, as an entire ecosystem, we have the opportunity to create the conditions in which they will want to stay. We are doing our part to contribute to that ecosystem to make it attractive for those companies to want to stay.

Lord Drayson: You have already in your earlier answer touched on the issue of intellectual property. ARIA is unusual in that ARIA projects do not have the IP generated retained by ARIA. There was some explanation by Ilan Gur and Matt Clifford in their previous evidence to us that there are some royalty payment arrangements that come back to the UK, but you will be aware of the significant concern that has been raised on this issue. Have you considered or are you considering changing ARIA’s approach to intellectual property to help ensure that these breakthroughs do stay in the UK and do generate economic growth here?
We are always reviewing our policies, and if we come across a policy that we think would serve ARIA’s mission better, we would be happy to adopt it.
Lord Drayson: I am afraid, Dr Fisher, that that is a very politician-like answer, a bit surprising from the CEO of ARIA.
It happens to be true.
Lord Drayson: Are you reviewing this policy now?

We are constantly—we are looking at our IP policies, but our current assessment is that the policy that Ilan talked about last year is the correct policy. ARIA’s best way of making the world and the UK a better place and producing economic return for the UK is through value creation. To do that value creation, we have to cross the valley of death, and that means getting the technology out. Our analysis to date is that the best way to do that is to put the IP in the hands of the creators. Most of the creators are in the UK and that intellectual property is, therefore, in the UK. If the intellectual property is licensed or assigned or sold outside of the UK, there is a royalty fee due to the UK. They are the same conditions that Ilan talked about last year. If we come across a better policy, we will implement a better policy. However, again our primary goal is the value creation and crossing the valley of death.
Lord Drayson: I think I understand that you are saying that you have everything under constant review, but you have not considered changing ARIA’s approach to IP.
We have talked about changing ARIA’s approach to IP, but those conversations to date have concluded that our current policy is the best policy for accomplishing ARIA’s mission.
Lord Drayson: Thank you for that clarity. Thanks very much.

Q7 Thank you for your time today. I am following on from Lord Drayson’s questioning about economic benefit to the UK. As someone who spent most of my time in the private sector, I am very supportive of collaboration between industry and government when we are at the cutting edge of science and technology. There was an announcement last week where the chair of ARIA, who has resigned now, was moving on to a global US firm, Anthropic, but was going to retain his position as chair of ARIA. That led to quite a bit of dismay in the UK, as we are talking about UK economic benefit and UK businesses—particularly now in the AI industry, where growth, development and investment is such a hotbed and we are competing in that global race. There was confusion that somebody who had been so close to the UK’s AI strategy, not only the AI Safety Institute and the AI action plan but the architect of the AI action plan, would remain in position as chair of ARIA and take up such a critical role. I say this, I should declare, as a co-founder of the Business AI Alliance, which has several hundred UK AI start-ups in it, as vice-chair of the AI APPG and an adviser to some UK AI businesses. I heard this and it was felt and it was in the press, and there was a genuine anger and I think that it united the political spectrum as well as industry in questioning how this decision had come about. I know that yesterday Matt Clifford announced that he was resigning as chair, but I would like to understand what the thinking was within ARIA before that resignation in allowing that role to continue.
It was not ARIA’s decision. It was up to BIST to decide on the mitigations in place. ARIA did not have a role in that decision.
Lord Ranger of Northwood: Did the executive team and you not have any consideration about how that may impact ARIA’s perception, the people involved in ARIA or the broader industry?
It was a conversation between Matt and BIST. The appointment of the chair of the board is under BIST not under ARIA’s purview. Therefore, no, we were not involved in that conversation.
Lord Ranger of Northwood: Did you receive any feedback once that announcement came out about how it was being received?
Yes.
Lord Ranger of Northwood: Would you like to share what feedback that was, without any—
The feedback that I received was much along the lines of what you have reported.
Lord Ranger of Northwood: What was your view on that? How would you communicate a response to that feedback?
The decisions and so on were conversations between BIST and Matt, and it is up to them to decide what they needed to do.

Lord Ranger of Northwood: The reason I am asking this, as I think you will understand, is about confidence in UK AI businesses and the relationship between such a significant funding body that is so strategically critical to decisions that the UK will take and its relationship with large international businesses such as Anthropic, and this was seen as a huge conflict. The concern is there that, yes, okay, the decision may sit with BIST, but what was ARIA itself thinking and what was its executive team thinking as this decision was being made? That has raised a lot of concern in the industry. Do you accept that point?
I understand the concern, and ARIA was not consulted.

Lord Patel: Following on from that, do you think that there are lessons learned from this episode that occurred—that it is important that the future chair of ARIA does not have conflict of interests that may in some way end up not harming necessarily but impeding the work of ARIA in any way?

I think that it is essential that the chair of ARIA does not have conflict of interests that impede the agency. It is important to acknowledge that we choose board members for their expertise in science and technology and translation. It is not uncommon that board members have interests that overlap with ARIA. Board members declare their interests and those interests are published on the website and are routinely monitored and updated, and we have mitigations that are put in place. ARIA has a code of conduct that is in line with the code of conduct for board members of public bodies and we monitor and put in place those mitigations regularly. You do not want board members who know nothing about the industry or the topics, so there is a judgment call about the expertise and the experience and the degree of conflicts.
The Chair: The point you are making is one of 100% transparency.
Indeed.
The Chair: We understand. Thank you.

Q8 Good morning, Dr Fisher. My question will come as no surprise in that I am calling in from my home in Cornwall. ARIA has been criticised in the past for the percentage of funding that goes on projects in the golden triangle of London, the east of England and greater south-east. In 2025 your corporate plan said that you would set diversity metrics based on gender and geography to drive a more diverse discovery process. However, in 2025-26, 67% of ARIA funding was spent in the golden triangle, and that was much unchanged from the previous year at 66%. Given the Government’s focus on regional economic development through research and development, what steps is ARIA taking that funds opportunity across the United Kingdom?

I have talked about how ARIA’s mission is to make the UK and the world a better place through scientific breakthroughs. That mission on a per-programme basis requires a science miracle and then a crossing the valley of death miracle. That is a daunting mission and it requires working with the absolute best scientists. We know that the best scientists are spread out across the entire UK. I have talked about Oshen, which is in Plymouth. I have talked about Amodo Design, which is not a creator but an activation partner, in Sheffield. I have not mentioned Touchpoint, which is a small company that is on our robot dexterity programme in Sheffield. [2] I mentioned the creator I talked to in Newcastle the other day. We have worked with fantastic creators.

Those are just four that I have mentioned not across the golden triangle, but we are not where we want to be. The golden triangle has a dense concentration of world-class scientists, so it is not surprising that they are well represented in our portfolio. However, as I said, we are not where we want to be. That is why we have put in place the requirement that our programme directors must do their discovery process. When a programme director sets up a programme, they kick the tyres on their thesis by going and talking to scientists all over the world, not just the UK. We now have a process of taking their programme thesis and identifying the science and technology that underlies that, cross-referencing that with the scientists across the countries and regions of the UK and figuring out where they are and requiring the programme directors to talk to a representative sample across all the countries and regions of the UK.

I just got back from meeting with the DCSA [3] of Scotland and the DCSA of Northern Ireland, and I am scheduled to go to meet with the same in Wales. The DCSA of Scotland and the DCSA of Northern Ireland agreed to work with ARIA to make sure that in that process they would help us identify the scientists in Northern Ireland and Scotland that we should be talking to. Part of the challenge is that the way ARIA works is very distinct from the way the traditional funding agencies work. We do not have a call that comes out on a fixed deadline; for example, it is November, so the deadline comes out now. Our calls come out when the programme director has finished the discovery process and there is a relatively short period to when the proposals are due. The people who are in the know have been following the thesis publication or the discovery process to know that the proposal is coming and have already been talking to the programme director.

That is why I went to Newcastle a few weeks ago, Scotland two weeks ago and Northern Ireland last week to meet with faculty at University of Strathclyde, University of Glasgow, Edinburgh University, Ulster University and so on to communicate this. This is so that people across all the countries and regions of the UK know how to work with us so that we can pick the best scientists across all the countries and regions of the UK and at the same time distribute the funding more equitably across the countries and regions.

The programme directors are required to do this discovery across the UK and in proportion to the scientists in the areas of their programme. They cannot get the programme approved until they have demonstrated that they have done so. We had one programme director a couple of months ago say, “I got all but one”. “Okay, well, we will delay your programme approval meeting until you are done.” Then they say okay and get that one scheduled. We are taking that seriously. It is important for ARIA to deliver on our mission, and the best way of doing that is reaching the best talent throughout the entire UK, and we are committed to doing so. The same thing applies with gender as well.

Baroness Jones of Whitchurch: I am listening intently to what you are saying, and it is good to hear that you are doing that regional engagement. The reality is that the consequences of this are not having a great deal of impact. The statistics are not changing. The money is still going to the golden triangle, the south-east, and so on. It is all very well talking to people, but that is very different from putting your money where your mouth is and funding the projects with a much broader distribution. You will know that the new incoming Government are focused on regional development, and I am sure that there will be pressure on you to be able to demonstrate in practical terms how that distribution of investment is happening on a broader scale. Do you recognise that there is a lot more work to be done here? Engagement is one thing, but you need to go out and find new talent in places that you would not normally find it to bring it into your funding structure. Please reassure me that that is happening, because otherwise you will talk to lots of people, but the bids for the projects will still come from the usual suspects.

That is what the engagement has set out to do—to find those people. Another thing we are doing is refining our data collection. Right now our data collection is only at the prime level. The primes are the people who have contracts directly with ARIA. In fact, primes have contracts with subs that are spread out, so prime contracts do not do a very good job of tracking where ARIA’s funding is going. We are working on refining our data collection so that we have a much better sense of where ARIA’s funding is actually going, tracking not just the people who receive ARIA funding but the people who apply for ARIA funding, at both the prime and the sub level, so that we can get a better sense of whether the problem is people not applying or people not getting funding.

When I went to the meeting in Newcastle, one of the comments that I heard in the audience was that they are serious about wanting to work with us. Part of the challenge is people not believing that ARIA wants to work with people outside of the golden triangle. Some of the engagement is extremely important from the point of view that we do not just care about the usual suspects; we care about working with the best people wherever they are. ARIA’s funding model of covering 100% of the costs and not just 80% means that universities do not have to pony up some of their own money and universities that are not so well funded are not at a disadvantage in applying for ARIA’s funding. The messaging is an important part of delivering in the long term. I want to try those mechanisms as the next step, which is a significant step up from what we have been doing, because I do not want to sacrifice ARIA’s prime mission, which is super important for the UK and the world.

Baroness Jones of Whitchurch: Going back to the discussion that we were having earlier, the latest stats show that 15% of your investment goes outside of the UK. Is that being reviewed? To what extent can we focus it? Fifteen percent is more than some of our regions, for example. Therefore, we are putting more money outside of the UK than in some of the regions that could have and do have very good research capacity. Are you reviewing that?

We definitely think about that, but the freedom to invest there is important. When we choose to start a programme, we kick the tyres on whether the science hypothesis is plausible. Is it at a place where it has the potential of a breakthrough? If the science breakthrough comes, is the potential for societal impact enormous? If ARIA does not do this, is it unlikely to happen? Those are some of the questions. Another key question that we ask is: does the UK have enormous scientific potential in this area? If we put out the funding call, will we get really strong proposals so that we can run the majority of the science and research with UK technology? It is unlikely that all the science and technology capability to give the programme the maximum chance of succeeding exists in the UK.

We reserve the potential to fund up to 20% of the research outside of the UK. When we get the proposals in, every proposal that gets funded outside of the UK has to cross a high bar—that this is a capability that is not in the UK and will enormously contribute to the likelihood that the UK part of the programme will succeed and cross the threshold, the scientific barrier, the valley of death, do that value creation and produce the promise of the North Star of the programme. All the non-UK funding has to cross a much higher bar and have a case that it will add enormous value. Sometimes non-UK contracts cause the non-UK companies to relocate to the UK. For example, Normal Computing, one of the creators on the Nature Computes Better programme, moved to London and subsequently invested 150% of their ARIA funding because the talent it has found in the UK and London has been so strong. There are sometimes upsides to that non-UK funding as well.

Q9 Thank you very much for coming and for your very thoughtful answers. I want to take forward some of the discussion that has already begun on your understanding of and relationship with the research landscape across the UK. We have just discussed the regional part of that, so I will not ask you to repeat that. In response to Baroness Willis, you emphasised that if nobody is doing something, there may be a reason for that, and that may not be a good place for you to do your ploughing, as it were. If everybody is doing that, maybe you are not needed, and you did not want to stick with a number in the middle but somewhere in that spectrum, which will depend presumably on the subject matter.

Could you say something more about how your programme directors understand that research landscape? You have said that you are out there and you are trying to convince people that you are serious, and it sounds as if they are responding to that. This has to be done at a fairly granular level and the programme director has to understand what is going on where in quite a detailed way. How do they go about doing that?

The programme director has some initial idea about what they are interested in doing. They read a lot of literature, and they use AI a ton, which is common practice these days. They then talk to a ton of people. It turns out, as with DARPA, if you are an ARIA programme director and you call people, they answer the phone or the email and spend time. I was talking to a programme director the other day and, “Wow, fancy, people answer the phone when you talk to them”. They talk to various people to refine the hypothesis. They go on what we call discovery tours. Ivan, who is the programme director for the materials science programme, went to talk to people in every country and region of the UK. In the process, they refine the programme thesis.

At some point, when they have kicked the tyres to their satisfaction, they publish the programme thesis, which is both a short statement and a multi-page document, outlining their beliefs and observations and what they think that says, to get open feedback. This statement is informed by all the conversations that they have had. At some point, either before or after the workshop—it depends a little on the programme; some have done it before and some after—they run a workshop, which is by invitation. They invite people who they have talked to or who have been named in the process. In this discovery process, you talk to one person and ask who else you should talk to, and that goes on. One of the termination criteria mentioned by a programme director was when that process does not discover any more names, they feel they have reached the conclusion.

The discovery workshop often ends up with three or four different scientific disciplines that do not normally talk to each other, and they are facilitated so that you get those people talking to each other and finding out what you can discover if you apply this technology to that problem. Often one of the other programme directors in the precision mitochondria programme was talking about how at the beginning they wondered, “Why am I here? Why are they here?”, and then on the morning of the second day, they realised, “Oh my God, we can do this, and we can do that”—a discovery process. After ingesting that information from the discovery process, publishing the thesis and getting open comments from the workshop, the programme director writes a programme approval document, which is presented to a panel at ARIA, including the chief technical officer, the chief translation officer, the CEO and outside experts for approval.
Lord Stern of Brentford: Those workshops would include also people from outside the UK, and their view of what is going on in the UK is of real value.

Yes, for sure. The workshops often include the world’s experts on certain topics. There are many people from the UK, but the workshops vary in size depending on the programme. Some have multiple smaller workshops and some have a larger workshop, but there are many people from the UK and there are also people from outside the UK.
Lord Stern of Brentford: On tipping points, which is a subject that concerns a number of us in this group, you would obviously want to bring in people like the Potsdam Institute, PIK, and so on.
There are definitely world experts on the panel. It is not just people in the UK.

Q10 Very good. Thank you very much for that. I would like to ask now about how you compare ARIA and DARPA. You are particularly well placed to answer that question. You have brought DARPA examples up during this discussion. Could you give us a broad-picture view of how you see ARIA and DARPA as similar or different, and how ARIA learns from DARPA, can learn from DARPA and so on?

They are both high-risk, high-reward, programme director-driven, project-based agencies. The mission is different. DARPA’s mission is national security; ARIA’s mission is making the UK and the world a better place through breakthrough science. DARPA does a lot of classified work, which adds a ton of friction that ARIA does not have to deal with. DARPA’s budget is a lot bigger. DARPA is a lot older and has a proven track record that means it does not have to prove its existence, while ARIA still has to prove its existence.

DARPA has the Department of Defense as a customer and I think it is overblown that people talk about how DARPA has a built-in customer. Having been the director of the Information Innovation Office, DARPA’s computer science office that just got renamed IPTO, there was nobody in the Pentagon who was eagerly awaiting the products of IPTO or I2O. I spent a lot of my time as the director of I2O strategising about how to take the results of our successful programme and subversively getting them to be translated into the Pentagon. I think that translates very well into ARIA, where we have to figure out how to engineer translation.

I mentioned earlier about the hiring process, how DARPA hires on a one-off basis, and ARIA hires more in cohorts. ARIA will still have to hire sometimes in individual cases; I had a lot of experience of hiring individual programme managers at DARPA, which will be helpful in the cases where we have to hire programme directors at ARIA individually. DARPA has another level of hierarchy that ARIA does not have because the scale of ARIA is smaller. The scale of ARIA is roughly the size of the office that I managed at DARPA. ARIA’s scope is all of science, roughly the way that DARPA’s scale is all of science, but the financial size of the office and the number of programme directors at ARIA is roughly the size of the office that I managed at DARPA, so a significantly smaller budget.

Lord Stern of Brentford: Thank you very much. I want to follow up on the public procurement side, because DARPA, being associated with national security, would have a customer in defence for a lot of what it did, although perhaps not the stuff that you were doing. The public procurement issue is still important for the UK because crossing the valley of death, as you have emphasised a number of times, depends on the market and potential customers—that is the first question in crossing the valley of death. Do you think there is scope for a more active link between public procurement in the UK and what ARIA does? If so, how could that happen?

There definitely is, and I have talked to our chief translation officer about this. Every programme director has what we call an impact mechanisation plan: assuming your science pans out, what is your strategy for crossing the valley of death; or, as not every programme is doing commercialisation as their strategy, what is your strategy for impact? Some programmes have a strategy in place, but the science is very early, so they are mostly thinking about what they would do if the science panned out. Others are further along and may have an entrepreneur in residence working with the creators to put together business cases and teaching them that a pitch deck for a VC is not 17 slides about how cool the science is and one slide for “Give me money”; it is more like 17 slides on what the market is and one slide on “Give me money”. If they get further than that, it is all hands on deck. On some of the cases may need us to create a market, so how do we create a market, and how do we co‑ordinate with government to do that?

Advance market commitments could be very helpful in creating a market. For example, the Scaling Inference Lab, a programme in the AI hardware space, started with creating novel hardware because of the end of Moore’s law and Dennard scaling. Perhaps the end of Moore’s law is overblown, but we are now having to create more unusual kinds of hardware and co‑ordinate different kinds of hardware to be able to continue producing more and faster hardware. That programme funded the creation of different kinds of hardware, which has been very successful so far: “This piece of funky hardware is doing things much faster”. But the end user does not care about funky pieces of individual hardware; you have to put them together into a system that delivers overall system performance. Therefore, we stood up the Scaling Inference Lab, which is actual rack compute that delivers performance an end user can measure, and we are partnering with the Government; they are providing a commitment to buy it.

That is an example of ARIA doing exactly what you were talking about, and that is what our chief translation officer works on with programme directors when they reach the point where they need all hands on deck, all parts of the Government who might be potentially helpful in doing that kind of translation.

Q11 Clearly, you need the other side of the partnership. To push the question a little bit further, do you think BIST and the Treasury should do more to encourage government departments to have a closer relationship with ARIA so that these possibilities of procurement are explored as early as possible? That also would, of course, be a way of responding in part to the question that Lord Drayson was emphasising about benefit in the UK.

It depends on a programme-by-programme basis. So far when we have reached out we have met with partners across the Government who have been very enthusiastic and helpful in working with us on what is needed for the particular programme in a way that continues to preserve ARIA’s independence. I would welcome those continued kinds of engagement across the Government as we get particular programmes in particular locations in particular stages where that kind of engagement would be helpful.

Lord Stern of Brentford: I want to go on to something else, but to remark on that, it is one thing you reaching out to them; it is another for them to have an active role in getting all parts of Government to reach out to you.

Indeed, and it is tricky because before we are ready, we do not want premature engagement but when we are ready, we absolutely want to be actively engaged with the appropriate parts of the Government.

Q12 My last question is about UKRI and the way in which the UK research and innovation landscape is changing—and it is changing for good reason. In that process, do you think there are major lessons from ARIA that can help inform the strategies being followed to recast those structures?

I will start by saying that a healthy UKRI ecosystem is absolutely essential for ARIA to be able to do its job well. Part of the discovery process that I was talking about, or the basis of confidence for whether the science in a given area is mature enough or is at a point where an ARIA investment makes sense, relies on there being a science and technology base that is suitable for ARIA to build on top of. Part of the reason why I was excited to come to ARIA as a CEO is because in many indices about research and engineering in the world, the UK is around third, and per capita it is number one in the world. That is on the back of UKRI’s investment. You cannot have an agency like ARIA if there is no agency like UKRI doing the blue-sky research.

The funding for the long-term scientific infrastructure that ARIA pulls upon comes from UKRI. ARIA does projects; we go in and we do three-to-five-year funding, or maybe we do it for a long time, in successive funding chunks. We do not do the long-term commitment that UKRI does that sustains a healthy ecosystem of scientists. You cannot have a healthy ARIA if you do not have a healthy UKRI. It is extremely important for ARIA that there is a healthy long-term agency like UKRI.

The way ARIA funds is programme-based. We go in and we do a sprint in a particular area to say we think we can accelerate the progress in that area. UKRI does the important work of building the path forward, brick by brick. They are very complementary models. I think before ARIA was established, the UK was missing an important modality of doing research. With ARIA’s establishment, it has become an ecosystem that has a lot more promise.

I am not sure that I have a lot to say on lessons learned because I am not an expert in the UKRI. I was a researcher for many years. I was a professor for seven years, department chair for five in the NSF ecosystem in the US, which is only somewhat analogous to the UKRI analysis. I do not want to overstep my areas of expertise.

Lord Stern of Brentford: Is that something you would bear in mind? You are learning a lot about how to get research done and about the research environment in the UK. Do you see openings or value added in sharing that in a direct way with UKRI?

Sure. I have already met with Ian Chapman multiple times, and I have met with the heads of all the UKRI organisations multiple times as well. We have a lot to learn from talking to each other, and certainly at the scientific level, there are many things to learn.

Lord Stern of Brentford: Before I hand back to Baroness Willis, I cannot resist just one observation, which is that—and I say this as a university professor—the UK’s deep strengths in science come from, in large measure, a few hundred years of first-class universities before UKRI came along. Our strengths, I hope, and we all hope, are enhanced by UKRI, but there is a deeper source there, which is, as many of us know, under some threat at the moment on the financial side. That is not a question; that is an observation. It is prompted by not overdoing the link between the strength of the UK science base and UKRI, although we all hope and encourage UKRI to do its best to make the most of that.
I appreciate the information regarding both UKRI and the universities.

Q13 One more question, coming back to how you ensure there is not overlap in the subject areas that you are working on compared to those being funded by other trusts and foundations. I have sat in workshops—I am not going to name the foundations but they are not in this country—for the very role that you mentioned of having international experts come in. I found in the two that I have done in the last couple of years that I was the lone voice in there; the rest of the people were scientists from that country with incredible levels of self-interest regarding what the areas should be going forwards. In some ways, that plays against the blue-sky nature, because you want the expertise but there is a balance in there.

Is there another way, with all your background and expertise from DARPA and your AI knowledge, that we should be moving away from workshops? What is your view on this? Are there alternative ways to work out what the new areas of research are? My second question is: how do you manage to avoid overlap? One criticism I have heard of ARIA is that some of the programmes directly overlap those being funded by other large trusts and foundations in other countries.

We are experimenting with using AI extensively. This was the summer of AI, and “everyone is a dev” was one of the projects this summer. We have been experimenting extensively with using cutting-edge AI to kick the tyres and read the literature and challenge our assumptions. I personally have been using AI a lot, certainly not for making decisions, but it is incredibly good at reading a large volume of literature. I have an AI Gem, or whatever they are called—and I actually use multiple of them—and I have told it to not be sycophantic at all. I do not need it to suck up to me at all. I want it to challenge the assumptions, kick the tyres and always give me the sources to go back to. The programme directors do the same thing and are very sceptical of all these things. These are the kinds of tools that the programme directors and the leadership at ARIA are hungry for. We use those tools to supplement the workshops.

The workshops and the discovery are helpful, not just for being sceptical. I appreciate your point that there is a little bit of a conflict of interest because the people in the workshops are also possible funding recipients. The workshops are also mechanisms to recruit the creator base, so you need to do them as advertising but you also need to do them to gather information. The people who serve as experts on the review panels are expressly conflicted from ever receiving any funding in the programme, so they do not have a conflict of interest. We are doing our best to get unbiased opinions throughout the pipeline, even if the workshop feedback is not always unbiased.

On the point about other foundations potentially funding the same thing: we do ask the question about being differentiated among the experts who are on the panels and are conflicted from receiving funding, and we weigh that consideration strongly. Sometimes it may seem similar but not be that similar when you pull up the hood—the digital olfaction programme that we just approved is a good example. There was an article, maybe in Wired , about digital olfaction that came out shortly after the announcement. If you dig into the article, it was very much about specialised olfaction for a particular application, as opposed to a general-purpose e-nose. The question becomes whether you want 15 different electronic noses or one, and the game-changing nature of having one versus 15 or 70 as you go on. When I asked the programme director about the particular article , she had already talked to all the people quoted in the article. If we discover something that contradicts a particular part of the thesis, or the whole thesis, we pivot and shut down part of the programme or all of it.

Baroness Willis of Summertown: Taking the olfaction example, how would you react in your capacity as CEO if you found that the Gates Foundation, for example, had an almost identical call coming out at the same time?

We would talk to them, and in fact we have been talking to the Gates Foundation, so I am comfortable on that particular point . We would talk to them and do a deeper discovery to figure out how much they overlap, who the creators being funded are, how much technical risk there is in that area, and how much creator population there is. It could be that funding two efforts in parallel might be perfectly reasonable, or it might be that there is not that much depth and it would be the same people involved, so double funding would not be appropriate. We would need to look at it and figure out the appropriate response.
Baroness Willis of Summertown: There is a network of other foundations, such as the Simonian Foundation, that talk to each other.
Yes.

Q14 My question is slightly tangential, but maybe it is part of it. ARIA seems to be focused mostly on technological advances that may occur. One of the key pillars of UK economic activity or economic growth is the life sciences sector, which is quite strong. Part of the government plans now are that UK life sciences are the engine, and the fuel is the huge amount of NHS data, dirty and fragmented in most part. The challenge is—and the UK is now beginning to invest in it—to streamline this data and curate the data in a format that is accessible, the NHS being a cradle-to-grave organisation. Do you have a view about where you think ARIA may focus on this area or be able to help? There has also been a criticism that because it is data, if it is given to outside organisations, it could be—how should I say?— put to different kinds of usage.

Indeed. ARIA does have life science programmes. We have the precision neurotechnologies opportunity space, with two programmes in that area looking at neurological and neuropsychological disorders, with more than £100 million invested. We also have the programmable physiology opportunity space, which has a programme on viral resistance and a programme on precision mitochondria, amounting to roughly a £100 million investment. ARIA does do things in the life sciences. That said, ARIA has £ 1.2 billion to invest across all of science in the spending review period. Although £ 1.2 billion sounds like a huge amount of money, when spread across all of science, it is not very much, and ARIA can only do things where we have programme directors. The unit of energy or deployment is programme directors.

I experienced this viscerally at DARPA, where I wanted to do a programme on shutting down rogue AI—which seems extremely relevant these days—but I could not find a programme manager to hire who had the expertise and wanted to work in that space. It took me two years to recruit a programme manager for it. For ARIA to do work in a particular space, you have to hire a programme director in that space. The question of data and the protections around data is always important, and you have to be careful about who has the data and who has access to data. We take that very seriously. We always have the ethics, social responsibility and the normal procedures and practices about how you ethically and responsibly do work in a particular area. If we stood up a programme dealing with big data in a medical area, we would follow those practices and potentially conduct research on how to do that work even better.

Q15 Dr Fisher, you have very helpfully answered many of our questions. I have just two final questions for you. You mentioned, and it is very welcome news, that ARIA has been funded through the recent spending review, so you will have, we hope, quite a long time to go as CEO. What will be your top priorities for ARIA during your tenure and what would you most like to look back on and say you have achieved with ARIA?

My top priorities are delivering on many of the things I have talked to you about: the science miracles, the translation miracles and the shining beacon of hope. What I most want to accomplish is delivering on those things. ARIA’s long-term success is creating one of those breakthrough technologies, along the lines of the internet for DARPA, that establishes ARIA firmly in the minds of the UK and the world. That will take a while, and it is unpredictable when that might actually happen . In the meantime, we will deliver a steady progress of important breakthroughs and meaningful translation that will benefit the UK, both through value creation and value capture.

Another important contribution will be ARIA’s growth from a small start-up to a well-run organisation that is at full capacity, where programmes are ending at the same rate that programmes are being born. We are not quite at steady state at this point, but we are almost there. An organisation of 10 people who all fit around a table at the British Library operates very differently from one where everybody no longer fits around a table. Getting through that growth period is another important contribution.

ARIA is a place where people love to come, and I want to maintain that. I want people to come not because it is the new shiny thing but because it is a place where people know they can make a tremendous difference in the world and have a massive lever arm to change it for the better. Building and maintaining that is important. The people are critically important. I highlight that the people ARIA has attracted across the board are fantastic, and that is true of the operational teams, the communications teams, the finance team and the procurement team, in addition to the programme directors and their support staff.

Let me highlight one of the programme directors, Brian Wang, who, before coming to ARIA, started a company to create medication in advance of the next pandemic—hopefully not in the immediate future. He came to ARIA with the idea of new technology to address the same challenge, leveraging the innate immune system instead of the adaptive immune system. The challenge with the adaptive immune system is that vaccines have to be specially crafted for the particular virus , which is why we have to get a flu vaccine every year and why it does not always work. You have to predict what the particular manifestation of the flu will be, and if that prediction is not exactly right, the vaccine does not work. A little while ago, however, our understanding of the innate immune system advanced, and it is now possible that we might be able to sculpt and control the innate immune system more effectively.

One of the advantages of the innate immune system is that it is more general purpose, so it would be able to respond to all variations of the flu and not just be targeted to a specific version. Brian Wang’s goal is for that protection to last approximately three months at a time. That is what he came to ARIA to do, and that is the North Star goal of his particular programme . If successful, it would have enormous economic benefit. Among other things, it would finally provide a cure for the common cold, so that parents would not have to miss work when their kids are sick and we would not miss work when we were sick. We would, of course, want to commercialise that in a way that benefited the UK financially, not just in value creation but value capture. If it is successful, it would also provide an off-the-shelf treatment, most likely for the next pandemic, and so would have a national security application as well, delivering on ARIA’s mission of making the UK and the world a better place through breakthrough science.
The Chair: A cure for the common cold is a great ambition.
Of course, it is high risk, high reward. It most likely will not work exactly as envisioned, but no matter what, it will advance science.

The Chair: Indeed. Dr Fisher, thank you very much. You have answered our many questions and have been very helpful and informative. We wish you every success in your tenure as CEO of ARIA, and we will keep in constant touch with what ARIA is doing. Thank you very much for coming to talk to us this morning. That concludes this session.
[1] The witness has clarified that this refers to 35 projects across 25 Creator teams.
[2] This should refer to Touchlab in Edinburgh.
[3] Devolved Administration Chief Scientific Adviser.

Watch the meeting

Members present: Baroness Sheehan (The Chair) ; Baroness Coffey; Lord Jay of Ewelme; Baroness McIntosh of Pickering; Baroness Rafferty; Lord Redwood; Lord Rooker; Earl Russell; Lord Trees; Baroness Whitaker.
Evidence Session No. 1 Heard in Public Questions 1 – 17
Witnesses
Dame Helen Ghosh, Chair, Office for Environmental Protection; Natalie Prosser, CEO, Office for Environmental Protection .
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Dame Helen Ghosh and Natalie Prosser .

Q1 ​​ The Chair: ​ Good morning and welcome to the Lords Committee on the Environment and Climate Change. For this morning ’ s session , w e will be hearing from the O ffice for Environmental Protection . I am delighted to have with us Dame Helen Ghosh, the newly appointed chair of the O EP , and its CEO, Natalie Prosser . W e look forward to hearing your evidence.

Before we start, I remind everyone that the session will be webcast live on Parliament TV and that a transcript will be taken and made public. Witnesses will have an opportunity to review the transcript and, if necessary, make very minor amendments. Members are reminded that they should declare any relevant interest s the first time they speak . This , of course, applies equally to all witnesses, which may not be so relevant in today’s case. I take the opportunity here to say that I am a director of Peers for the P lanet. Dame Helen, perhaps you could now introduce yourself .

​ Dame Helen Ghosh: ​ Thank you very much. I became chair of the O ffice for Environmental Protection on 1 June this year. My previous career was 30 years in the C ivil S ervice in a variety of departments, latterly as P ermanent S ecretary at Defra and then at the Home Office. I moved from there into the NGO sector and became the d irector g eneral of the National Trust for almost six years . From there , I moved to my immediately previous role as M aster of Balliol College at Oxford University. In all these roles, in various ways, I had contact with the environmental and natural resource issues that concern the O ffice for Environmental Protection . T herefore , it is a delight to be in this role in this organisation, which I think has already had , and can continue to have , a real and measurable impact on the outcomes for the natural environment and resources. It has been a pleasure. I have to say that my first two months have reinforced my view that it is a great privilege to be carrying out the role.
T he Chair: ​ Thank you very much. Natalie, perhaps you could introduce yourself.
​ Natalie Prosser: ​ Good morning. I am the chief executive at the OEP , and I ha ve been chief executive here for about five years.

Q2 ​ The Chair: . Thank you. We will kick off with the first question . Dame Helen, g iven that you are so new to the role, what are your plans and priorities as the new chair of the O EP? I will ask a follow - up later.

D ame Helen Ghosh: ​ My initial impressions of the O EP are all very positive. As your Lordships will know from your previous hearings with representatives, it was set up very effectively. It i s an efficient, impactful organisation. I find a number of highly committed staff , an excellent senior team and—saving her presence here today —an outstanding chief executive .

I pay tribute to Glenys Stacey, my predecessor, for the work she did to make the OEP such a going concern, one might say. W e now have a challenge, following the experience of the last four years or so . In particular , we face a resource challenge for the future three years —the current year and two future year s. W e have been given flat cash as our settlement for our activities in both England and Northern Ireland. T hat is a real challenge since it is , in effect , a real - terms cut. W e are having to go through a process — as we do every year and have done every year in the past —and be very clear about what our priorities should be . We are focusing on the things that really make a difference, that are most salient to the Government achieving their environmental improvement plan targets — but more broadly so that , in England and Northern Ireland , the environment is both protected and improved.

T hat process of prioritisation is extremely important to us. The staff have begun the process , b ut the board will be looking at the new draft strategy for the organisation. Every three years w e have to renew our strategy . That will be an opportunity for us to think about priorities , organisational shape and so on. In fact, this appearance is timely since the views of members of the c ommittee will be very useful in feeding into that strategy review process.

T he Chair: ​ Thank you very much. On your appointment, you said that you will be focusing on areas and actions that will make the most difference. Can you outline some of those areas that you think deserve priority attention?

D ame Helen Ghosh: Indeed . I entirely support the statement made by the outgoing chair and acting chair when they were reporting on the most recent EIP , EIP 23 . T hey said that the most important thing in achieving the Government’s ambitions is to get nature - friendly farming r ight. As this c ommittee is aware, that has many aspects, in relation to support systems, protected areas , regulation and so on. So I think that is an area that we will be focusing on , and it is a focus for our work i n this current year .

W e are also engaging ourselves in the issues around reform . Reform of the water industry, which is in process at the moment following the Cunliffe review , is of great interest to us . A mong other things, we need to make sure that the mistakes of the past are not repeated in the future when it comes to the areas of regulation that our public authorities are responsible for . We will also be monitoring very carefully what one might describe as the unfolding issues around planning.

If we look at our priorities for this coming year, marine is also a very significant area for us. W e have a major investigation ongoing , on the issue of good environmental status and the continuing failure of that to be achieved. N ature - friendly farming , keeping our eye on and playing a positive and perhaps innovative part in some of the developments on water reform , a nd marine —those would be our priorities for the next couple of years .

I n Northern Ireland , t he absolutely central and important issue is managing the nutrients produced by livestock farming, as well as sewage outflows. O ur team there are working very hard on that in various aspects — investigations, for example, but also in relation to nutrient action plans and regulations. So , in Northern Ireland , n utrients is front and centre of our work.

Q3 ​ The Chair: Excellent. Thank you. Before I come on to members who have indicated th at th ey would like to ask a supplementary question, I have something else to ask . This may be more for you, Natalie, but I will leave it for you both to decide who is best placed to answer. The c ommittee has finished an inquiry on pet parasite medications . We found that some of the chemicals, the ones that are used traditionally — imidacloprid and fipronil — because they are so harmful to the environment are being phased out in favour of isoxazolines and related compounds whose impact on the environment is not so well documented and researched.

My question is not really about the impact on the environment . T he c ommittee found that we could not get a handle on how many of these chemicals were in the environment, because that sales data was not available to us due to commercial sensitivity, we were told. Y et we know that in similar circumstances — for example, for antibiotics — that sales data is available. G iven that the OEP has a remit to apply environmental law, I wonder whether that is something that you could help us r ationalise.
To get hold of the data?
Yes. W e will be debating this report in the Chamber, so it would be really useful to understand where we stand on getting the data that we need to quantify the problem.
I think that is for Natalie rather than for me.
I thought it was a bit left- field , but it is important that we ask the OEP these questions.

I am not sure that I can assist with that specific question, but I think I mentioned last time that I was before you that we have an ongoing concern about how we regulate chemicals more generally in this country , and that we have identified that as a potential very serious threat. T he c ommittee’s work illustrates that in relation to a very specific chemical. We have a small amount of work looking at the chemicals regime in the round, and that is so that we can identify areas to sharpen our focus on. We do not have a great deal of resource to attend to that, but I recognise that chemicals present a very material threat to our environment, whether they are pesticides or pet treatments, and we are concerned that our overall regulatory system may not be adequate for dealing with that. I am afraid I cannot answer your specific question, but I recognis e the salience of the issue and that it does warrant further attention.

I wonder whether you could write. The reason I ask is because I know it is your remit to monitor and report on the implementation of environmental law. I wonder whether there is anything in the environmental law that says that data should be made available where the chemicals involved have been shown to be so harmful to the environment. I will leave that there.

Q4 You mentioned resources a nd enforcement. Y ou are not the only body enforcing regulations concerned with the environment , so I wondered, first of all, how you liaise with other enforcers as to who does what. Also, do you have any thoughts yet about how you ought to prioritise enforcement? I t can be very expensive.

Yes. Clearly one of the outstanding features of the O ffice for Environmental Protection is that it has very clear purposes and a very clear role and legislation , and the board of the office has very particular powers in relation to its functions. I t is not true to say that we are the regulator of regulators, but of course the public authorities that we are regulating —N atural England , Ofwat, the Environment Agency in particular and of course Defra itself —a re , to some extent , partners in achieving outcomes , and also often the object of our investigation s . A gain, this is something that I am exploring. Clearly , we have close connections with the regulators that are themselves responsible for administering various aspects of environmental regulation ; Natalie has many years of experience doing this. We have to remain close to them in terms of understanding them and , when things get tricky in an investigation, being able to negotiate a satisfactory outcome for our purposes and for theirs.

I n that sense, yes, we liaise with them on a continuous basis, but sometimes life gets tough and we have to use some of our more po werful tools, either to get information out of them through an information notice or by requiring them to carry out what we regard as the appropriate steps to resolve a poor environmental outcome . A s it happens, I know a number of the heads of the key regulatory bodies , including Natural England and the Environment Agency . B ecause of my past career, I understand quite a lot about the organisations, but we have to be both close and distant.

Of course , the other partner we have — in a fundamental sense given the future of the country’s natural environment —is the Climate Change Committee. V ery clear lines were drawn up in the A ct as to what the committee does and what we do. T here is a memorandum of understanding about its role and our role. However , particularly on adaptation, we have to understand its view on the pressures from the sadly inevitable increase in temperatures and the impact it will have on nature and the natural environment.

F or example, Baroness Brown came to our most recent board meeting with the chief executive, Emma Pinchbeck, and talked to us about its latest report, which we will now be able to absorb, as it were, into our thinking. We operate in at least four dimensions : the three dimensions and then time. W hen one thinks about the length of both the interim targets and the longer targets that we are collectively trying to achieve, the impact of climate change —which has been vividly illustrated this summer — is something we have to have in our minds all the time.
Thank you. Lord Redwood has a short question, I hope, on plans and priorities before we move on to Baroness McIntosh .

Q5 Dame Helen, you described three very general areas as aims, which I would have thought would have had policy work led by accountable Ministers from a range of departments and policed by independent regulators. It would be helpful to the c ommittee if you could give us one example of a recent unique intervention by your body that has done some good and has been taken up , with a headline of its costs and benefits.

There are a number of such outcomes ; f or example, our investigation into combine d sewage outflows. That is a matter of both environmental concern and great public concern. In that instance, our investigation showed that there was , in essence, confusion between Defra , the Environment Agency and Ofwat as to what the regulations meant and what the standards of implementation should be. O ur clarification of what the current law — including some important court cases — actually meant has changed the operational practice of all the relevant bodies to good effect.

M onitoring is very important to us. I imagine that we may get on to the subject of waste later in the hearing. F or example, the most recent report on waste inspections found, as you know, all sorts of failures in both the statement of achievement and the process and outcomes. We are very conscious that what will now have to happen , when the response from the Government is formally agreed , is that the things that were promised to be done are really done .

On combined sewage outflows, the data on monitoring is available —going back to the data issu e. W e will us e the existing datasets to do our monitoring and then feed that back into our assessment reports .

Q6 I will try to ask short, sharp questions, but you are both very welcome ; it is lovely to see you here before us. You are on the record in 2025 as saying that progress towards improving the environment has slowed and that the Government are still largely off track in achieving their legal environmental commitments. I n January, we heard that the revised environmental plan was a little too early to form an assessment. Are you in a position to form a more general assessment as to where the Government are on achieving these? I will give a specific example: the failure to give legally binding species targets is quite a gap.

As you say, in relation to EIP23, which of course is not the most recent EIP, our report found they were off track on 21 out of 43 targets, I think. We advised on how we thought the structure and approach of EIP25, published by the Labour Government, could be improved, and it is improved in a number of areas, particularly around implementation. This is a persistent failure in many elements of both Government and other public authorities. There should be clear delivery plans and measurable outcomes. EIP25 is better on that, although it is not ideal.

We will be producing our report on the Government’s progress report in January. That will obviously deal with, as it were, two halves; the 25-26 year , part of which is covered by EIP25 and partly still by EIP23; and then we will give our opinion on progress in that year. I do not think we have any reason to think that there will be a significant change. We have got this wonderful infographic, which sadly has a great deal of red and a little bit of amber and tiny numbers of green against the dartboard of achievement. I do not think we are expecting anything to have changed significantly, but EIP25 gives us a basis, if the measures in it are implemented, for at least better delivery plans and better KPIs.
On the question of species and specific figures, I turn to my chief executive. Do you know?
I am not sure.
We can write on that.

You mentioned reform of the water sector. When we were part of the European Union, there was a very effective enforcement regime where water companies were brought to book. That is one of the reasons why we have now got cleaner water than we had in the 1980s. Do you believe that the current regime is as effective? I ask in particular: what work might you be doing on the water framework directive and where? I am slightly concerned that the clean water Bill seems to have been delayed to next year. The water framework directive has been a key part of the water regime in this country. They have obviously moved on in the EU to a different phase. Do you have any ongoing work in that regard?

We do. We are currently carrying out one of our investigations into the water framework directive implementation and outcomes. It is well known, not least from the Court of Appeal, that the Government is failing to achieve its water framework directive targets, so in that sense it is already known that the law is being broken, which is, of course, one of the things that our investigation will highlight. That investigation will conclude this year, I assume, and therefore we will be making our findings on that public.

We know that the Government, as part of its water Bill, is thinking of adjusting the measures in the water framework directive, in so far as in the current legislative arrangements that is possible. That is of course of interest/concern to us. We have already started to have some discussions of an informal kind with Defra officials, the Environment Agency and others who will be involved in that. That is an issue which is very salient and current for us.

I have just one last question, if I may. The Government are reluctant to implement, for example, Schedule 3 to the Floods and Water Management Act to make SUDS mandatory. They say that the planning regime covers this. There has been an appeal which has driven a coach and horses through this; I think it was Gladman, and they literally just said, “No, you do not need to worry about this. Just build where you like”. Do you share my concern about there not being these mandatory statutory targets? Without SUDS you are going to have sewage spills, potentially into existing houses and certainly into watercourses, because water companies are not statutory consultees, are not going to be statutory consultees, and are not given the tools to prevent the sewage spilling in this way. Do you share that concern?
I can entirely see the problem that you outline very clearly there. I assume that this is one of the issues that should be picked up by the Bill in due course.

One would hope, but of course planning is under the housing department and I get the impression that Defra are keen to have mandatory targets. The housing department, not wanting to upset the planners, are less keen.
I will hand over to my colleague, who may well know the more detailed answer to your question. I think one of the most interesting things—
Actually, can we just park that there, because on the next question we will be looking at BNG in far greater detail, so it can be addressed there?
Can I just have a quick answer, though?
Do we have a quick answer?
Just on this one issue, then.

Not specifically on SUDS, but there are some serious dysfunctionalities in the current system. One of the reasons we have focused on water framework directive compliance and implementation is that we think part of the root cause of why we have not managed to grip pollution in rivers is because of the lack of engaging with why pollution is getting into the rivers in the first place, which the framework is meant to prevent.
