Today’s announcement, however, will have caused significant uncertainty, after councils have invested scarce public money and countless hours in the government’s LGR programme. ” This is clearly going to be met with dismay. I indicated to you earlier what I think people in Gloucestershire will be saying about it, because I know how many meetings I have had with them and how much work has gone into all of this.

The Secretary of State was very clear about that in her statement to the House. We do not underestimate the blood, sweat and tears that have gone into getting us this far, and how difficult it has been. I am aware of that from my own engagement with councils up and down the land. That is taken as a given. We take that incredibly seriously. That is why we want to do this piece of work quickly and get back and tell the House the conclusions of our review.

It does not come as a surprise to me—I know just how much effort has gone into it. None the less, Ministers of this new Administration have wanted to satisfy themselves that the current arrangements are the right ones, hence us taking the decision to pause and review. But I empathise and understand that comment.

Q90 I understand that the Government needed to take powers to do this reorganisation in February. If you don’t get it sorted out by then, is that legislation likely to be put back? If so, what effect will that have on the elections next year?
The elections next year will go ahead as planned. I don’t think we need new powers per se to implement local government reorganisation.
Q91 Does it not require secondary legislation? An implementation order?

The make-up of the new councils will require secondary legislation, as we have done in Surrey, but we are not asking Parliament for a new power. We will be laying secondary legislation—I forget whether that is affirmative or not—for the final make-up of councils, but we are well used to doing that. We do not need primary legislation or something like that to give us the ability to lay those orders.

Q92 I would like to ask a couple of questions about local accountability. “Rewiring the State” commits to a clear role for MPs in local accountability. What do you think the role of local MPs will be? I direct that to Cat, Will G and Melissa initially.
I will ask Will to start, and I will add to his reply.

To be honest, I don’t think we have a fixed view on this. It is something we want to engage with Parliament on. In a sense, we are not the best people to say how the experience of MPs should be utilised. You see it there in black and white—the commitment that Members of Parliament have to be involved, in terms of both accountability and decision making. Ministers will want to engage with Members of Parliament over the coming weeks and months, so we can set out a plan in conjunction with Members of Parliament. There is not in my bottom drawer a kind of “This is the best way to engage with Parliament” plan, because I think we need to ask Parliament.

Q93 That is interesting. It would be interesting to hear about any ideas you have, because it can be quite challenging for MPs to engage on a scrutinising level with their local authorities as they exist at the moment. I appreciate that they are going through a stage of transformation, and there will be something new when this is envisaged to happen. With your experience, any pointers?

One thing that is in the pipeline—it is not being lived yet, because we are doing the regulations for local scrutiny committees—is that once those committees are up and running, MPs will be able to make submissions to their local scrutiny committees where they have concerns regarding the operation of the MSA, or lines of inquiry that they would like the local scrutiny committee to follow. That will be a new route into the strengthened local scrutiny committee.

I would also flag that we are thinking about the role of local accounting officers; like Will said, the options are quite broad and we genuinely want to engage and understand the best route. Different models can be applied in relation to this sort of committee and the way that mayors are called before them, so we are looking at those as well.
Q94 Do you think that local public accounts committees would be an effective way of doing that?

The model of the local scrutiny committee is akin to a local public accounts committee. Where it does not match up to the model that some people talk about is in so far as the scope of public spending currently within the purview of a local scrutiny committee is limited to that which flows through the mayoral strategic authority and associated bodies, like development corporations. As we go further with devolution and more powers come within the remit of the strategic authority, that will naturally make the local scrutiny committee more of a true LPAC model, where you see a fuller gamut of public spending falling within the scope of that Committee. I think we will move towards it the further we go down the devolution journey.

Let me add one point to that directly . You see in the Cabinet statement, with the reference to the NAO, that we are conscious of just how important the support you get from the NAO is to this Committee’s ability to effectively scrutinise Government Departments, and how, of course, hearings are preceded by r eports. We are thinking about how the right support will be provided to local scrutiny committees, so they have a similar sense of infrastructure and support to enable them to scrutinise effectively. That cannot mean suddenly asking the NAO to replicate its function directly for those authorities; that would not work, but that is precisely the discussion that the Cabinet statement indicates we want to have with the NAO, and it is indeed the conversation that we are picking up with Gareth and colleagues.

The Local Audit Office is an obvious organisation that could take on some of that work of looking at the value for money of spend and supporting scrutiny committees as the NAO supports this Committee. That would be one option open to Ministers.
Thank you. That is very interesting. Thank you for your contribution. I am sure Gareth would like to see an expansion of that responsibility at some point. [ Laughter. ]

Q95 On that point, I gather that there is literally one person at the Local Audit Office at the moment, and this is coming on like a tidal wave. What is being done to, very rapidly, scale up the local offices?

As you know, we needed primary legislation to establish the Local Audit Office because the previous architecture was dismantled. We got Royal Assent in April. We lay the secondary legislation to establish it in July. As you know, we have appointed Bill Butler as the chair. We are making executive appointments over the course of this year, and seconding in people from the Department to get it up and running. But you are right about the danger of asking the Local Audit Office to do more when our priority for them is the accounts and we must not lose focus on that. But I think over time there is an option—it would be good to discuss this and get input and views from this Committee—of asking them to take a wider role and look at the value for money of spending in the West Midlands combined authority, for example.

Q96 To go back to what you were saying, this Committee knows more than anyone else the value of scrutiny of central Government spending. The way that we are lucky enough to be able to do that is, first, we have the resources of the NAO behind us to provide us with the information, and secondly, the Committee is independent; it has to be chaired by a Member of His Majesty’s Opposition. Will these strategic authority settlements provide enough resources to be able to do that properly? If you are going to hand down billions—£15 billion over the next four years—it is essential that is properly scrutinised.

Hopefully, you can take comfort from the way the Cabinet statement, even within those first two weeks, recognised the importance of capacity and capability to this system as a whole if it is to operate at the deeper level the Government envisage. That is in part of course about the capacity and capability of MSAs themselves. There is a huge discrepancy already, because of the time periods over which different MSAs have developed—take for example the capacity and capability of Greater Manchester versus some of the more nascent and recent MSAs—so part of what Government will need to do is make sure the funding is there for capacity and capability of the MSAs.

You are completely right that, for the system to function in the way we have been discussing, Government must ensure there is the right funding and resource for the organisations that are going to support it. The Local Audit Office is key to that. So I think for now the answer to your question is, yes, we completely recognise that, and we are determined to make sure that what is needed for the system to work is there. That is the direction Ministers have set us. Our expectation is that we able to say more about how that will work at the Budget.

I said right at the top of the session that this has large implications for central Government and for the resources we have. The really interesting question is if that resource is being moved in financial terms, the capability and capacity of central Government must also flow to local level. That is why we are seconding people directly from central Government into MSAs. We have a whole programme of options for how we build capability. I think the National School of Government will play a really important role in building capability across the whole of the public sector. The civil service has to become smaller and much more strategic and deft in our ability to move that capability across the United Kingdom.

Q97 I am compelled to ask you all a question. We talk about the Westminster blob. Having sat around this table, I do not agree with you, Will: there is still a lot of work to be done on accounts being filed on time and work being qualified.
Oh, I agree. I did not say I meant otherwise.
Q98 I have seen some pretty bad stuff. Is there not a danger that we just devolve the Westminster blob into a series of unaccountable regional blobs?

Obviously, I would not characterise the centre of Government quite as you have done. Fundamentally, by the nature of what we do on behalf of the state, we have some of the country’s most senior and capable experts in commercial finance transformation. In our work, we run a very high-risk set of systems on behalf of the taxpayer. Of course, there are things that we have to do better. On our capability, with the 6,000 commercial professionals that I run through the Cabinet Office, I absolutely expect us to be sharing that capacity and capability across the whole of the United Kingdom. We also have to get better at being more porous with the private sector and building capability for the whole economy.

Q99 I am glad that you are proposing cutting central Government as you increase devolved local government; that is essential. In the summary, the NAO says that it found tension between MSAs’ expectations of autonomy and the accountability requirements of funding Departments. Are you happy that we can create a framework through which we can effectively hold to account the people who have been given this money to spend? After this, I will talk about MPs, because that is a very important point.

It is a work in progress, as I have tried to illustrate. Let us take in what is there: how do we do accountability at the moment? Currently, Steve Rotheram or Paul Bristow would say, “I feel accountable to my electorate,” although you may or may not agree with that. They also have to get their budgets and all their plans through their local authorities, which, apart from in London, are combined authorities. That is a second element.

Also, as we have discussed, if you are in receipt of the integrated settlement, you have to try to hit a number of outcomes. We have 12 to 14 at the moment—cue the debate on whether there are too many: is it too hot, too cold or just right? If you do not hit your outcomes, we have a matrix of interventions ranging from doing a bit more monitoring to intervening and ultimately clawing back money.

Then, we have the new local scrutiny committees that Melissa spoke to, which have more teeth than any other form of local accountability that we have had thus far. Then, in the Cabinet statement we said that we still do not think that this is enough and want to set out plans to go further. That is where we are now. I recognise that views will differ on whether that is the right level of accountability or whether it is too much or too little, but that is the circle that we are trying to square.

Q100 Fine, but it is essential that we do have that. Coming on to MPs, it is important that they are included, because ultimately they are the elected representatives of the people. You have done me a favour, James, because you raised the issue of the overnight levy, which I was going to use as an example. My constituency, for instance, is coastal, so an overnight levy would have a greater direct effect on my constituency than on other constituencies. We need to ensure that MPs are included, not just in the scrutiny but in the decision making.

I have seen suggestions of a £5 or £10 overnight levy charge, but I have also seen polling that suggests it would put a lot of people off holidaying here; they would go abroad. At a time when our tourism, our entertainment and our pubs are declining massively, it is important that MPs are included, and I am slightly concerned that, based on the answer you gave, there is no plan to do that at the moment—it is a matter of discussion. It is essential that we get that right; otherwise, we will end up with an even more confused electorate, because the mayors will grab the power and the MPs will appear irrelevant.

It is worth saying a little about the overnight levy. The Government will set out the framework through which you can do that. On why this is in place, w e are the only G7 country without that, so in terms of your competition point, lots of other countries do have that. The key to whether it is a good idea, or whether it should proceed, is about a couple of things. First, there is no compulsion, so you do not have to have an overnight levy. You can decide not to go ahead with one. Secondly, there is a requirement for an authority, if it wishes to have a levy, to consult. That is probably the time when everyone can get engaged, including local MPs.
Q101 This is why it is important that MPs are involved.
Yes.

To add to what Will said, we absolutely agree with you. We are engaging with MPs. We are engaging with the NAO and with this Committee. We are looking at other models as well, because we are moving fast. We are going to set out exactly how we are going to do this as part of the White Paper, and we are going to be taking action.

Q102 But Cat, to Geoffrey’s point, we are discussing things that keep changing. We really need a sitting target, so that we can actually judge whether it is going to work or not. At the moment, you say it is work in progress. We have not got a firm idea. We are talking about this, and we are talking about that. My constituency is in Norfolk, so as of this afternoon we are going have a borough council election next year because it is back to normal. All these things are changing, and it is extremely destabilising. If we cannot even basically set out what we are going to do because we have not reached a conclusion on that, that is when things go wrong and mistakes are made, because it is all being done in a hurry and it is not being thought about.

For us, this is how good policy development works. We want to engage; we want to iterate. That is why the White Paper will be coming out fairly shortly once we have undertaken a good policy development process. To your point, you do not want to rush into it; equally, we want to make sure the ambitions are reflected and we get this right.
Q103 A lot of change has happened before the White Paper, hasn’t it?
Indeed. Change is constant.
Thank you. We will move on to Sarah Olney. I pinched one of your questions, Sarah. I’m sorry; I did not do it on purpose. You can do the next question.

Q104 That is quite all right, Chair. Will G, we have talked a little bit already about scrutiny and audit, but when will the local external audit system be in a fit state to allow Departments to reduce their monitoring of mayoral strategic authorities?

If you mean when do the 12 to 14 indicators that we have for the integrated settlement fall away, I cannot give you a straight answer because we still have to make that decision. We have talked about how they can be useful for scrutiny and accountability. We have said that 12 to 14 is far fewer than we have ever had previously. Ministers announced an intention to streamline them, but I cannot tell you what decision will be made over the coming months as to when there will be fewer, or how many there will be, because we have not made that decision yet. Ministers have not taken it yet.
Q105 Do you not have a deadline for the establishment of the permanent audit overview?
Are you talking about monitoring outcomes via the integrated settlement, or is your question about the Local Audit Office and the establishment of decent accounts in local government?
Q106 Establishing the Local Audit Office.

The Local Audit Office is now established. It is a body, thanks to the regulations that Parliament approved in July. We have been out to advert for a chief executive. We have appointed a chair. We want it up and running early next year.

We are not waiting for the LAO to be in operation to tackle the crisis in local authority accounts. As I said earlier, we have upped from 1% to about 90% in terms of accounts published on time. Just for the avoidance of doubt, Mr Lowe, I am in no way complacent that this problem is fixed, not least given the number of disqualified opinions. I am simply pointing to a trajectory that is improving on quite a challenging timeframe.
Q107 Presumably the end state of the trajectory that is improving is a full y up-and-running Local Audit Office. When will that happen?
Yes. Our target is for 100% of audit opinions to be published on time by 2027-28.
Q108 On the establishment of the Local Audit Office, you were talking about recruiting. When will that be fully up and running and taking on all of the audit responsibilities?

It will be fully up and running early next year. It is legally established now. We have appointed a chair. We are in the process of making executive team appointments over the next few months, but we needed a legal body to recruit them to, if you see what I mean. I am slightly at the mercy of Parliament.
Q109 W hat role will that play in providing strengthened local accountability?

The first job of the local audit office is to fix the unacceptable state of local authority accounts. That is the thing it must focus on beyond anything else, because we cannot have a system where James and I return every year and the whole of Government accounts are disqualified . F rankly, this Government ’ s view is that the decision to abolish the Audit Commission was a mistake , and provision was not made to replace it. That damage is being undone; that is the view of Ministers now. T hat is the primary thing the local audit office must get right, and nothing must take its focus off that .

The thing we have explored this afternoon —it is tentative, but hinted at in the Cabinet statement — is, in order to support scrutiny locally, what the best way of doing that is. We have discussed how this Committee benefits from the expertise of the NAO, and the Comptroller and Auditor General and I are meeting tomorrow to discuss how we might do more on th at .

One option we will want to discuss with Ministers, although no decisions have been made, is whether to ask the local audit office to play a role in assessing value for money of the integrated settlement in the West of England combined authority. That is an option open to Ministers; it is not something we have decided on, but it would be an additional ask beyond fixing the accounts, which is the No. 1, primary job. Does that answer your question?
It does; thank you very much.

Q110 Following on about local scrutiny , I have many good things to say about local government; I am very supportive of it. One thing that has never really worked very well is scrutiny committees. If you talk to most councillors, they have concerns and reservations, particularly when the scrutiny committee sits and the officers advising them on scrutiny come from the same departments being scrutinised . That happens regularly. When billions are being spent and scrutinised, how will we get that degree of independence, both in the advice and the process of scrutiny?

L ocal scrutiny committees, which we have legislated for — forgive the slightly duplicative language — replace the mayoral o verview and s crutiny c ommittees . It is a deliberate attempt to have a regime with more teeth . T he ability to have up to 40% of the committee who are independent s and experts is a good innovation, as is the ability to insist that the mayor attends and, if they consistently do not , they are out of a job—a different change to ratchet up the pressure. As I say, t hat policy was written before this A dministration came into being, so as the transfer of power happens, there is clearly more to do.

Q111 Okay, t hat is helpful. Just as we have the NAO to give us technical professional advice, we also have our excellent Committee staff to advise and assist us . L ocal scrutiny committees do not have that—they have good staff, but they are not independent of the areas being scrutinised.

One of the changes we are moving towards is partial independence : independent membership alongside representatives from the constituent authorities. We are also designing a mechanism whereby the local scrutiny committee must take advice from a panel of independent experts, focused around the different areas of competence for which the mayoral strategic authority is responsible. We are trying to build in that level of independence . W e are also working closely with the Centre for Governance and Scrutiny on how it can offer training and provide support to upskill local scrutiny committees and their associated officers as they come on stream.
Q112 Getting independent advice all the way through is key to this.
I agree. J ust to repeat, our improvements to local scrutiny committees predate this A dministration. T here is more to come .
Okay, right. We hear you; watch this space and see if it gets —
Indeed.
Q113 Okay. Let me come back to the programme board, which is the effective monitor at national level to ensure that everyone is doing the right thing in the right way . It’s a bit clunky, isn’t it?
Well, I chair it, and I try to make my views— [ Laughter . ] I will say that it is no more than an hour and a half.
It is a triumph.

There is a tension, right? On the one hand, it is clunky. There are too many outcomes. You guys are micromanaging these people—I get that. On the other hand, how are you ensuring consistency, value for money, accountability and so on? People can say that we are too light, too little or not enough. We are trying to get it right, but I appreciate that there will be a range of views.
Q114 This is a tension for all.
Yes.
Q115 What Government want to do and what strategic authorities might want to do won’t always be the same.

No. I mean, that is devolution, right? I am just exposing that there is a trade-off. This Administration and this set of Ministers are very clearly up for more devolution. If that brings different priorities in different areas, they are more relaxed about that than the previous Administration, so we will respond accordingly.
Q116 The outcomes programme board will monitor against four authorities. It is going to be agreed in the first place with the authorities that they are the outcomes—

Yes. The outcomes that we have with the integrated settlement are proposed by Departments and agreed by mayoral strategic authorities, with the Minister and I in the middle trying to reconcile the competing demands, which we do to the best of our ability.

The one thing I would say about the programme board is that I agree with the point about tension. You must have in the checks and balances—as you as a Committee do so well, and the NAO, too—a check on delivery, so that you are not just doing announcement and target; you are actually getting in and looking at delivery and implementation. All the learning that we have had over the public sector in all its guises is that you need that delivery check.

Q117 Will, I am just wondering how you are going to cope with all this. Are you going to work 24 hours a day? As you get more strategic authorities wanting to participate in these strategic boards, how will you actually cope?

That is kind of you, Chair. I am confident that we can cope. When I look at what local government is doing under significant resource pressure and what the new mayoral strategic authorities are achieving, my bigger worry is this: are they set up for success, not the Department? Whitehall—central Government—will be fine. I think we cope by ensuring that our partners in places are properly resourced, and that they have enough capacity funding to recruit staff and bring expertise into the organisation.

I am not saying that this is quite what you are saying, but the wrong response to this would be, “Devolution is now a massive thing. Let’s hugely increase the number of staff in MHCLG.” Instead, as with the rest of the civil service, we should look to reduce the number of staff in MHCLG and to transfer at least some of the administration budgets to new and emerging combined authorities, so that they are our decent partners.

Q118 I am coming on to that in a minute. First, I just want to talk about when things go wrong. The rubbish is building up on the streets of Birmingham. At the moment, you have a fairly quick mechanism. You can put that authority into strategic measures and you can send in the commissioners on the ground, who can do something about it quite quickly.

I am looking at figure 9 in the NAO Report, which is gradated into “minor” things that might go wrong and “moderate” things that might go wrong, and then it goes on to “major” things that might go wrong. I am still wondering whether the commissioners’ option—the strategic measures—is still there, because if something really major goes wrong, you need to do something about it quickly.

The answer is yes, they are. The best value regime that the Department runs applies as equally to local authorities as it does to mayoral strategic authorities. We have the same—I sometimes call it climbing a ladder, but my team correct me and say that it is a climbing frame, because you do not need to go from one stage to the other. So there is a best value notice, a best value inspection and then sending in commissioners. Those options exist in a mayoral strategic authority, as they do in a local authority.

We have had two mayoral strategic authorities that have received best value notices in the past, which have now had quite a useful bit of engagement with the Department about improvements. Those are Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, and the West of England. Those now have established status and are due to receive an integrated settlement at the next spending review. So we have intervened in combined authorities in the past and we are prepared to do so again.

Q119 Thank you; that is helpful. On mayoral strategic authorities building up capacity, I will quote two little bits of paragraph 2.17 of the NAO Report. “They”—the strategic authorities—“will not always hold all relevant expertise themselves and may need to draw on the capacity of constituent authorities and other local partners”, and this is the important bit: “MSAs may grow faster than their capacity to deliver, particularly in newer MSAs still putting core systems, staff and processes in place.” How will you make sure that these authorities are going to be able to grow capacity at the speed required for the devolution of functions to them?

I think this is one of the most important things for this bit of the Department over the next six months. We are acutely conscious that we are building new institutions and that takes time, effort and resource. The first thing we are doing is putting a bit more money in—that is a straight answer. Administration funding needs to go up a bit. Most of the combined authorities have, even as a proportion of their budgets, less administration spend than Whitehall Departments.

Cat has talked about the immediate actions that we are taking: secondments to MSAs from the civil service, opening up the civil service future leaders scheme, the national school of government, and the LGA peer support and review. Those are all immediate things and low-hanging fruit. That is necessary but not sufficient for the scale of transformation that is needed. We said in the Cabinet statement that we want to publish a blueprint of what a good strategic authority would look like. We will do that in partnership with our colleagues who actually run those institutions. We will set out what we think is needed and, critically, the gap between what exists today and what is needed, as well as plans to fill that gap. All that detail is coming in the autumn.

Q120 I am glad that you recognise the scale of the problem, because it is starkly revealed in the Local Government Chronicle of 5 August. I quote the second paragraph of its article: “ Staffing levels ranged from 5.9 full time equivalent (FTE) staff at Devon & Torbay CCA to over 1,500 at the Greater London Authority and nearly 1,000 at both the West Yorkshire and West Midlands CAs. ” There is a really big job to be done here if some of these are going to be ready to become mayoral strategic authorities.

Often, those large staffing numbers are where the combined authority comes from an existing transport authority. Transport authorities predate mayors in many circumstances. If you go to the north-east, for example, they have had a transport authority for longer than they have had a mayoral combined authority, so they have more of a history of working together, via the transport authority, and have an infrastructure to build on. We are acutely conscious that in other parts of the country there is not that existing infrastructure, and that is a priority for us to get right over the coming weeks and months.

I think we have covered the subject fairly well. As the Committee have no more questions, I will draw us to a close. I thank you all; you are very busy people. We are very pleased to have with us no fewer than three permanent secretaries. That has been very useful because this is a big, important and diverse subject. An uncorrected version of the transcript will be available in the next few days, following which we will produce a report, maybe with recommendations, which I hope you will study carefully. We look forward very much to seeing how it goes.
Finally, please do try to clear up what is being done today as quickly as possible because people out there will be in despair tonight, I think.
That is very well understood, Chair.
I thank you all again.

segs.tx: Housing, Communities and Local Government Committee
Oral evidence: Modernising Elections , HC 43
Wednesday 9 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 9 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Mr Gagan Mohindra (Chair); Andrew Cooper; Mr Lee Dillon; Mr Will Forster; Sarah Smith .
Questions 149 - 192
Witnesses
Robert Nicol, Vice Convenor, Electoral Management Board for Scotland; Sandra Matthews, Electoral Services Manager and Deputy Returning Officer, Powys County Council.
I I : Leigh Middleton OBE, Chief Executive Officer, National Youth Agency; Dr Christine Huebner, University of Sheffield; Helen Blachford, Chair of ACT Trustees, Association for Citizenship Teaching.
Examination of w itnesses
Witnesses: Robert Nicol and Sandra Matthews.

Q149 Good morning and w elcome to the Housing, Communities and Local Government Select Committee. Before I go on to the formal request to introduce the witnesses, can I first put on record my thanks to Florence Eshalomi, as the former chair of our Select Committee, who has now rightly been promoted to Minister ? With the permission of the Committee, we will send a letter to congratulate her before we grill her at a future meeting. Can I ask the witnesses to introduce themselves, please?
I am Sandra Matthews from Powys County Council.
I am Robert Nicol . I am ERO for the council areas of Inverclyde, East Renfrewshire and Renfrewshire and a depute convenor of the Electoral Management Board for Scotland.
Can I welcome you both to this morning ’ s Select Committee ? Could I ask my colleagues to introduce themselves?
I am Lee Dillon , Member of Parliament for Newbury.
I am Will Forster, MP for Woking.
I am Gagan Mohindra, Conservative Member of Parliament for South West Hertfordshire and acting Chair.
I am Sarah Smith, the Member of Parliament in Hyndburn.
I am Andrew Cooper, the Member of Parliament for Mid Cheshire.

Q150 Votes at 16 have been in place for devolved elections in Scotland and Wales for some time. What are the key lessons from implementing this change that colleagues in England and Northern Ireland should know?

We had quite a long lead-in in Wales. Registration went live for young people on 1 June 2020 and their first election was then the following year, for the Senedd on 1 May 2021. That allowed a good period of time for registration, raising awareness and general engagement activity.

This phased approach led to quite good success. We had a whole annual canvass in which to raise awareness that the franchise had changed and that 14 and 15 - year-olds could now register to vote and anyone at the age of 16 or over could vote at the elections coming up the following year. While, unfortunately, a lot of the engagement activity was curtailed because of covid, we still managed to get that message across during the annual canvass .

There was a national leaflet that was developed and used across all of Wales . That was followed up the following spring with a household notification letter, which reinforced the messaging that the franchise had changed and a new, younger voter was in being. That second communication helped because we now know that, in recent years, voter registration has become more and more event - led . That messaging in January and February led into the May Senedd elections. That is something that certainly was useful.

Unfortunately, because of covid, all that engagement work was not as impactful as we would have liked. Further work was done that following canvass . There was really good practice. There was extra funding for an engagement officer in electoral services teams, which perhaps had not been the case the previous year. There was a network working group that was managed with Welsh Government support and involved civic societies as well. That proved to be invaluable.

We saw huge jumps in registration from the Senedd elections in 2021 to the local government elections in 2022. In some cases — the extremes — that was a 35% increase in some where like Ynys Môn. Swansea, I think, had a 75% jump in registrations. In Powys, we had 80%, so that was a huge impact in th e second summer of engagement. I t was not just about encouraging people to register ; it was about raising awareness of the importance of their role, how they could use their voice, methods of voting and what to expect in the polling station. It was a much more comprehensive programme than just, “ You can now register to vote . ”

In Scotland, it started off with what was known as the young people ’ s register, which was used for the independence referendum in 2014. The registration landscape was vastly different at that point in time. We had not had the Elections Act, the extension of the franchise within Scotland for foreign nationals, canvass reform or IER, which came into force at midnight on the day of the referendum.

At that point in time, registration was very much paper - based. There were not the same identity checks as there are now. The Act that came into force allowed the registration officers to do a slightly delayed canvass from October of 2013, so 11 months before the referendum, through to March of 2014. That involved sending out what at that point in time was a normal annual canvass form , along with a young voter registration form , to each household.

Where no form was returned but the ERO did not believe that there was somebody living there, because the ERO also had education data to check against, that non-return was not a problem. It did not need to be pursued. Where there was a non- return but we believed there was an individual there, reminders would be sent out. Thereafter, from March of 2014 through to the final date for registration for the election, there were the normal monthly updates of that particular register .

One lesson was that a major electoral event focused the mind. It got a lot of publicity about , “ This will be the first time that under-18s are able to vote . ” There was a build-up within the media about it, which all helped. The Electoral Commission, along with the EMB and electoral registration officers, engaged with education authorities and created education programmes and suchlike . I went out to schools myself. I had a full head of hair at that point in time and I did not have a beard. W e engaged with the young people at that point in time.

If you have not already done so, I would direct you to have a look at the EC report into the referendum. It say s that , even given that period of time for the canvass, the Royal Assent to the Act was only two months before the start of the canvass. The EC report suggested that it should have been at least six months to allow registration officers to plan and direct. There was engagement beforehand with G overnment, so we were not starting from ground zero , a nd indeed that is happening just now with MHCLG.

T he lesson out of that is that it need s time to embed. A big bang , in terms of saying that somebody i s registered in one day so you can vote i n the next immediate election , is going to be difficult. I n many ways you miss the opportunity of saying , “ Here is where this will start . ” I f you end up with a small local election somewhere being the first place with under-16s, you miss out on that natural free publicity that would happen in the lead - up to try to get voters engaged there.

Shortly after the referendum, there was a further A ct to embed the franchise change for local government elections from 2015 onwards. While those regulations and that A ct happened in 2015, I think it was from the elections from 2016 onwards that it was there. I f there were by-elections during that period, under-16s were not able to vote . It was at that next big election event from there.

F rom a registration point of view, the lesson to be learned is that each elector is an individual. Each elector has their own lifestyle and quirks and we need to have a system that can take that into account . A lso , it is important to ensure not only that they get registered, but that they are able to exercise their vote in the manner they want to, with a full range of options that are open to other electors such as postal and proxy .
Q151 Sandra, you were talking about what to expect when young people first go in to vote. What media and channels were used to push that out to young people?

Quite a few local authorities filmed videos showing somebody walking into the polling station, approaching the voting desk and asking for their ballot papers. It took away the unknown for these young people. There is a little bit of apprehension as a young person going in to vote for the first time and not knowing what to expect. There are quite a few adults who feel like that as well. Certainly in the initial year, because it was covid, a lot of that was remote. It was just video and film.

In the following year, when there was a much more inclusive engagement programme with the engagement officers, there was a lot more outreach with youth groups. Civil society groups got involved and fixed that barrier between what they have been told or understand and actually going in and voting themselves, what it means for them to use their voice and the impact that that could have on their local and national communities.
Q152 Was any analysis done of the impact of that campaign to see whether young people were actually clicking on it?

For a couple of projects that took place in Swansea, I know feedback from some of the young people who took part in a couple of the working groups or projects that they had w as very positive. The young people ’ s feedback was that they felt far better informed about the process and what it actually meant .

Swansea also had a great project of vote ambassadors that it introduced. Two students from each of the high school areas in that local authority were designated as vote ambassadors. They helped engage and promoted registration and participation, so influenced their peers. From both perspectives , feedback from that project was very positive.

I know that a couple of other authorities in Wales have taken that on under different names, for example with democracy champions in Pembrokeshire. I always thought that it was a bit of a shame that there was not a national programme for those vote ambassadors, because it is something that could have given schools the support network that they needed to roll it out. For the ambassadors themselves, it gave them great life skills, influence and public speaking skills that they could take forward in future careers, maybe.

Q153 Sandra, on that last point, the Representation of the People Bill will introduce consistency of the voting age across all elections. Given your previous answer, presumably you welcom e that consistency?

Yes. My colleague Robert and I were just discussing that outside before the session. We think that it will have a very positive impact on registration rates and clarity of messaging. At the moment people do not always understand that you can vote in this particular election or this type of election, but not this level. I think it is going to have a positive impact on our ability to engage with young people and encourage them to register, because that message is not diluted. It is not, “ W e think you are okay to vote for this, but not that .” I think their understanding will be clearer of how different levels of government engage when knowing that they can vote in all elections .

Q154 I had some questions around lead-in time, but you covered off quite a lot of that in your initial response. More for clarity, Sandra, you spoke about an 11-month run-in time—I think June to May—in Wales. Robert, you mentioned the two months to six months. In your professional opinion, what would be the minimum lead-in period needed to implement the votes at 16 successfully for a UK parliamentary election?

On the two to six months, the two months was between Royal Assent and the actual registration window opening up . The first time that it was used within an election was around about a year later. The Electoral Commission suggested six months within its report.

I am slightly risk - averse in this kind of thing, in as much as, if this goes wrong, it goes wrong for the public and could potentially destroy confidence in the process. There were instances of things not going well in Scotland in the past. We had the Gould report and the Gould principle of , “D o not change the law within six months of the electoral event ,” albeit there are caveats and exceptions to that. There is always a guiding principle in as much as , if you are going to move away from that, you need to know why you are moving away from that. You need to be certain . T he first thing I think the Electoral Commission will ask you if things go wrong is , “W hy did you ignore Gould? ” As I say, there m ight well be good reasons for that, but that has to be a conscious decision rather than just sleepwalking into it.
Q155 You are saying six months is the minimum .
Certainly that would be the minimum that would cover your back. There may well be logistic s reasons where you may want slightly longer, but that is an absolute minimum, yes.
Q156 Ob viously without a fixed-term Parliament Act, for example, we have no gift of when a general election will be.
Yes , and that is where the tricky part falls . If you were to prescribe, say, a fixed date, so elections held on or after a particular date, that may prey on politicians ’ minds.
Q157 Can you talk a little bit more about the barriers that young people have faced to voting at 16 in both Scotland and Wales?

The first barrier is obviously to get registered. Votes at 16, you need to remember, is actually registration from 14 onwards. For many 14 - year-olds, their parents or guardians play quite a prominent role in gatekeeping their interactions with Government and suc h like. That is in many ways the role of a parent. Some of them can do it in a way that is positive in terms of registration and some people can do it in a way that is negative.

We sometimes come across the positions whereby, for example, a parent may say, “I do not think my child or my young person is mature enough to be on the register. They are still too young .” The information does not get to them via that kind of channel, which is where education and suchlike is important. The registration is voluntary, but it is important that everybody who is eligible has the opportunity to make that decision around registration. That is certainly one of the barriers.

Some young people themselves do not think that they are ready for it, and again that is where education and engagement comes in. In many ways, the solutions to these kinds of problems are not sitting this side of the desk. It is within our communities and within trusted voices who are giving accurate information. People want to be part of the process if they are given something that they feel is meaningful. We saw that with the likes of the independence referendum, where it was a binary choice but there was engagement. Then you look at some of the more recent council or local government elections, where turnout is a lot lower. It is about the whole process, not just the barriers within it, but actually getting engagement within it . I think that is the case.

Q158 Do you want to say anything about the potential impact of voter ID? It was not a factor, as I understand it, in the elections in Scotland and Wales, but now would be. How might that impact on younger voters in particular , Sandra, particularly building on what you said before about examples of where you have been able to overcome some of those barriers for young people, even if they are about their own belief and their ability to contribute to that process? Where might there be learning?

With regards to voter ID, this reinforces the need for an even longer lead-in, because we need to engage with young people if they do not have readily available access to ID. We need that period to not just reinforce the message that they need to be registered, methods of voting as well as just attending the polling station, but also that, if they want to go to the polling station, they need to have an additional identification, whether that is a voter authority certificate or something else . It is joined up with their actual registration process.

Depending on what changes may happen with voter ID in the future, that may make it easier for them to have access to some suitable forms of ID. That may be something that you will want to consider: are there some forms of ID that young people have that might extend that list?

It reinforces that there is a lot of preparation. People do not just show up at the polling stations to vote because we tell them to and they have been registered. We took part in automatic voter registration pilots in Wales. While that was the easy part, possibly, of identifying people who were not registered and getting them on the register, it is still about getting them out to vote.

You all have been candidates at one time or another. It is important to build trust. People do not just show up and vote because we have told them to. You have to engage with them, whether it is your side of the desk or ours. They have to have an understanding of what is required of them, the importance of their voice and the impact it makes. Without giving us sufficient time to administer that process or for schools and civic societies to build that experience and knowledge for the young people, we might lose them completely. They will just turn off the whole process because of lack of trust.

Q159 Building on this point around the lead-in time and registration, we know from data from the Electoral Commission that there is a huge differential between rates of registration among younger people and older people. For the lowest age group, it is around 60% and for the upper age group it is more like 95% or 96%, or something along those lines. What learnings can you share on getting 16 or 17 - year-olds registered to vote ahead of their first election? Which groups of young people were the hardest to reach and what can you tell us about that?

Young people are not just a blob or a single grouping. You have young people of all nationalities, who speak different languages or who have disabilities, just like you have throughout the whole range. The way in which we currently register young people is that the ERO will get information from, within Scotland, the local council ’ s education records, which will be a name, address and date of birth. We will write out to them to request that they submit their application.

That data is reasonably good, but it varies throughout the time of the year. It is better at the start of the term, because during term time sometimes people move and do not necessarily tell the school. It is about using the information that you have and making sure that that information is both current and accurate to try to engage and contact them.

We also look at civic society groups. The Electoral Commission run s the excellent W elcome to Y our V ote w eek, which mostly involves empowering educationalists, mainly in schools, to engage with their pupils for a particular week of the year, going through the process and trying to educate them around why it is important and what actual difference being registered can make.

I do not know if necessarily there are any particular groups that are harder than the general public , but we need to be wary about creating a system that works really well for, if you like, linear lifestyles. Where perhaps young people have more than one home, where they register can become a bone of contention between their parents and guardians. Even that kind of thing can cause problems and put people off registering. There is a wide variety of groups that can be difficult to engage with in general and young people are included within that grouping.

Q160 You mentioned at the beginning that young people are not a homogenous blob. You talked about disabled people and people of different ethnic origins. Did you do any specific work with any of those groups to try to reach those groups directly through charities, community groups or churches?

A variety of different things happened around 2014 and 2015. Some of these are not necessarily as sustained as they would be. That is why you get the benefit of the big bang of, “This is the election that 16 - year-olds are able to vote in .” That embeds within the psyche of society that this is there, rather than just a small aspect. There is ongoing work, but we need to be realistic that it is not something that is happening every single day within every single office there.

One of the premises that was put earlier on was , “W hat can we learn from Scotland and Wales? ” I am viewing the extension of the franchise for the parliamentary register as an opportunity in Scotland to try to get better. It has been in place for 10 or 12 years. There have been a variety of different changes in the legislation since then . H ow can I benefit to help the electors within my area in this franchise? That is what I a m looking to try and benefit from.

As Robert said, one size does not fit all. We find that, where parents are already engaged, they do a lot of the legwork. They register their children or encourage them to register, so they make our job easier. Unfortunately, we then have other households that are not quite so engaged and are even disconnected from the issues. Young people feel that politics maybe does not have a particular impact on their lives. They cannot see that link . It can be quite difficult for us to get through that barrier.

S omething we experienced last year with automatic registration pilots, where we identified up to 3,000 young people between the ages of 14 and 18 and wrote out to them , was that we did not hear from one young person with regards to that mailout. It was their parents who rang us to opt them out or discuss issues surrounding that process. I t is sometimes quite difficult, unless you have an engagement officer and proper resources within your local authority , so r eaching schools, youth groups or other groups within the communities , for us to get through those barriers .
Q161 Could you tell us more about that? You worked on the automatic voter registration pilot in Wales.
Yes , Powys was one of the three local authorities.

Q162 In the evaluation with the Electoral Commission, it was noted that using education datasets was particularly valuable. Can you explain a bit more about how that process worked and how you did it?

The automatic registration pilots allowed us to use local authority datasets to register people where we were convinced and assured that they were accurate. With regards to young people, education data was deemed of high value and with confidence it was secure. That allowed us to data mine our education records, identify anyone who was not registered and write out, so send them a notification of automatic registration. As I said, we sent just over 3,000 to that group.

On the feedback, there was a lot of concern from parents where they felt very strongly that they did not want their child showing up on the register or registering at such a young age, because we included the high 14 - year-olds. Quite a number of parents phoned. They were concerned about their child ’ s name showing on a public register. Once we alleviated that concern, they were okay.

We received quite a few emails also regarding how the child was going to know how to vote when the time came, which showed to me that parents, even where they are engaged, registered and vote themselves, perhaps lack confidence in their ability to educate their child about that process. It was quite interesting for us to hear from the parents about their concerns about how they could involve, help and support their child.

I am not sure whether, with the pilot process, it was completely joined up with other wider engagement work. That was probably a weakness. The engagement work ahead of the Senedd was provided by the Senedd Commission, which visited high schools just ahead of Christmas, so there was a bit of a gap there. Turnout was not unduly affected during the Senedd, even though we managed to register quite a few—I think it was over 5,000—on top of an electorate of 106,000 in Powys.

It was effective. T iming may have had some impact on the numbers just because we did it before the normal annual canvas s , but it was effective in identifying young people and taking the burden out of registering them and their need to do anything. It concern s me somewhat if they believe that that is always going to happen for them, so that is something we need to consider.

It almost reflects a lesson we learned back in the autumn of 2021, ahead of the local elections in 2022. One engagement project was to identify any young person who was not registered and directly send them an ITR —an invitation to register. During the autumn of 2021 into 2022, that direct mail, along with other outreach and engagement work by our engagement officers, really bore fruit . I gave you the stats of some of the increase s in registration. That shows the impact that a joined-up approach can have and the time and resource that is necessary in electoral services teams, because we are quite small in most cases.

Q163 Yes , I was just going to ask you about resource. Did you receive any additional resources to help with the pilot? Based on your experience of the workload to conduct automatic voter registration, do you have any concerns that you would have sufficient resources to do that on an ongoing basis?

On resource, using local data was an interesting process. The amount of work to data cle a nse, to check the quality and content of other data sources that we do not have responsibility for, took quite some time, so the preparation work that was needed was a lot more than I anticipated. Once we got into the data matching and mining, that was fairly similar to what we are used to with the canvass. However, it identified that, as a team, we probably need some better skills with regards to data cleansing and data. That is possibly a skill that needs developing further within electoral services teams.

With regards to the individuals that we identified and could automatically register, because we had found them on two, three or four different datasets within the council, we wrote out. We had a flurry of phone calls. There was a very low opt-out rate — only 0.5% , I think . I recall that it was 28 out of just over 5,000.

W here the work began was, because we had thrown quite a lot of data into our systems, we identified quite a few people who may not have been registered with one piece of information. The duty on the ERO is to then follow that up, write out and find out whether that data was accurate. That is where the work and the cost came, and that was not insignificant.

The term “automatic” might sound easy from the electors ’ perspective, but I can certainly assure you that, from the administrators ’ perspective, or even a cost perspective, it was not insignificant. Robert referred to the “big bang” of any sort of project. As a pilot area, I am hoping that the bulk of that work was done last year and that, once we go through that process again this year with much smaller datasets, because we will only take anything that has happened and changed since last year, and it perhaps embeds into a process, it becomes more business as usual.

Q164 I see. There is a year- one cost, but not necessarily ongoing. I am curious. You are never going to get away from the need to have those data - cleansing skills within your team doing this. I wonder whether your experience of it, and perhaps your influence within the council, might drive other departments within the council to improve their data quality in the first place. If they know that it is going to be used for this important civic duty, might that encourage some of those skills to be built up in other teams within the council, so the data that you are receiving is better in the first place?

It is funny you should mention that. Only a month ago we had a consultancy firm in our council where we were looking at corporate performance, where AI could possibly help us and actual corporate quality data. Unique property reference numbers was a big challenge for us. Our council tax does not contain that. Whenever you data mine, you want to be sure that, if you are looking for an elector, you are looking against the right property. Otherwise you could inadvertently create somebody who has never had a link to that property.

How all our council departments need to look at a corporate standard and improve was something that has come up quite recently. For example, we looked at Blue Badge data, but it did not actually have a full name or a full address, because they do not need it for their records. As you have said , a lot of other departments will help develop that .
It might drive storing the UPRN and all those other datasets and help you join it all up at the end. I could talk about data cleansing all day.
Q165 Have either of you seen evidence that allowing 16 and 17 - year-olds to vote has changed an impact of an election?

We are looking at each other. That is quite difficult. I am not sure with regards to our Senedd elections. I am not sure that it has had any distinct impact on turnout, for example. It is quite difficult to say whether it has changed any results, certainly at this current time. The political world has changed in recent years. I am not sure I am qualified to give a full view on that.

Likewise, I think that that is outside my wheelhouse. I am keen to ensure that everybody who is eligible to vote is registered and has that opportunity to cast their vote . There is more than enough in that sphere to keep me going. I am sure there are other experts who could give a better - qualified opinion.

Q166 If you have not seen evidence that it has changed an outcome, it either has not or it is very difficult to pin it down. In a way, that is reassuring . A lso, in a way, the change of allowing 16 and 17-year-olds is a radical decision, which is both positive and negative in terms of the potential change.

Sandra, when researchers described votes at 16 when they were brought in in Wales—because they were brought in in the 2021 elections—I think they used the word s “ false start ” , because it was during the pandemic, which was a very difficult time. Is there evidence that it has become more successful in the post-pandemic Sen edd elections in 2026?

The false start was probably because—let ’ s be honest—everyone had other priorities during covid. Our engagement and registration rates were probably not as high as we would have liked them to have been going into that first Senedd election. I think that education has embedded the processes a little more , but, like anything, it is time and people ’ s understanding.

We still get people phoning us saying, “I did not realise that people could vote at 16 in Wales .” It is about a general awareness. I guess that, if you do not have young people in your household, it is perhaps not something that you generally concern yourself with. You get your poll card and show up and vote if you so wish.

Q167 This is a question to both of you. Do you think lowering the voting age has reduced inequalities in participation to ensure that 16 and 17 - year-olds do not feel disadvantaged, or has it mainly just enfranchised young people who are already quite politically switched on in the first place?

The most recent Electoral Commission report into the registers had around about 60% of 16 and 17 - year-olds within Scotland on the register. That started off at the mid to high 60s and it has dropped down very slightly, hence the reason I am saying that I want to use this as an opportunity to expand.

I am not convinced necessarily that a direct percentage of those who are actively engaged within the process are active in terms of politics. I do not know whether you can necessarily link the two things directly. From the experience that I had going into schools, which is about 10 years old and was limited to the particular schools that I was in, more often than not you got good engagement with the people. There were a few who just did not want to be involved in any way at all. There were others who were hyper-involved, if I can put it that way.

Looking at what mattered to them at that point in time, it was political things. It was around, at that point in time obviously, independence, but also access to public transport and cost of car insurance for young people — all things within which the politics thing actually matters . You can see that they could make linkages within that.
Q168 Can I thank you both for attending this morning ’ s panel ? Before I formally ask you to switch out, is there anything else you wish to raise following our discussion this morning?

Can I perhaps touch on something? Voter ID was mentioned. It is easy to think of voter ID as the polling station part, but there are so many different parts of ID checks within the process now, whether it is at registration or if somebody applies for a postal vote , for example. We also need to look at those areas to make sure that our young voters are being served in the same way as other electors are, in terms of the availability of IDs that they can utilise.

For example, to apply for a postal vote at the moment , if your ID check fails with DWP—and for around about 5% of electors it does —you are supplying either a passport or a driving licence. If you cannot supply that, it is two of a birth certificate, a firearm certificate and two or three others, or four from the next table down, which is things like utility bills. I am not certain that that is fit for purpose in terms of for those who fail, albeit they can then go down the attestation route.
Q169 On that, a council can provide a photo ID card as well if you do not have any forms of photo ID to be able to vote. What ID do you need to get for the council to issue you with that photo ID?

We can issue voter authority certificates, but that is different from the process for actually approving a postal vote application, which is unlike registration, where we can look at local data to match against somebody . F or example , if a young person applies to register, I can check their education data and say , “Y es, that is that person ,” and put them through registration. I cannot do that for a postal vote application . There is a prescribed list of documents that you need if you fail that ID check. Most pass the ID check, but there is a significant chunk who fail.
Q170 Sandra , is there anything that you wanted to add ?

To reinforce what Robert said, there is more to do in registration if we want those young people to be able to vote when the time comes. There is other work that needs to happen. Sometimes the existing processes might be a bit of a barrier for them in a way that they are not a barrier for those over 18.

I guess that the challenge and risk for a general election is sheer volume. We probably were both very lucky in Scotland and in Wales that the numbers were from a low starting point. A huge event such as a general election could break a very fragile new process within local authorities and electoral registration offices. That needs to be considered.

Equally, for young people, we are telling them, “Oh yes, you can vote at 16 .” If they have not been able to be registered in time or if they have applied for a postal vote but we have not been able to approve that postal vote, they might not actually be able to vote. That would undermine any trust in the system that they may have. That needs to be considered in any roll-out. As I said, both Robert and I were lamenting the possibilities and positive impact in Wales and Scotland of having a whole franchise, but there are considerations of issues that we did not have.

Q171 Sandra, the request is that 16 and 17 - year-olds are allowed to vote, but we have a set of local elections in—hypothetically—2028, where local authorities work out what the challenges are and the capacity and young people start to understand the system a bit. Then it goes to the general election the year after. If 16 and 17-year-olds get the vote for the first time just before a general election, you worry that something will go wrong.

If we knew when that general election was, that would help enormously, but it is not specifically about that election or what election it is. There needs to be proper time, not just to get people registered, but to give young people the knowledge to make that decision and choice when the time comes. Equally, there is quite a lot of administration with voter ID and applying for a postal vote that we did not necessarily experience to the same extent.

Q172 The Committee met yesterday with a lot of young people and it became apparent that there needs to be an education or support programme. I am more interested in the practicalities from a returning officer management point of view. You think that there needs to be a time window for the legislation to pass and then for 16 and 17-year-olds to vote in an election. For the infrastructure to build up, how long do you think that could be, should be or needs to be?

I think that Robert mentioned it earlier . It depend s how risk - averse we all are. Gould has mentioned six months for any changes and for anything to embed. In an ideal world, we would like to have a canvass. I think that my colleagues in England would like to have an electoral registration canvass. Then any engagement work could be built on that, leading into elections the following May, potentially.

Time needs to be considered, so how our natural registration process happens and when the best time to identify these young people and get them on the register is. For the school system or engagement work, we know, as I mentioned earlier, that registration is event - led. As with any marketing campaign, if it is le ading into a specific event it helps that engagement and knowledge building.
That is helpful. Thank you.
Thank you both very much for today.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Leigh Middleton, Dr Christine Huebner and Helen Blachford.
Q173 Can I ask our panel to introduce themselves?
My name is Christine Huebner . I am a lecturer and a researcher of youth democratic engagement at the University of Sheffield.

Hello. I am Helen Blachford . I am the chair of trustees for the Association for Citizenship Teaching. Liz Mo o rse, our CEO, was unable to be here today . She is on annual leave and sends apologies. I a m also director of personal development across the Bohunt Education Trust and head of citizenship at a school in Portsmouth .
I a m Leigh Middleton. I am chief executive of the National Youth Agency, the national body for youth work in England.

Q174 Can I first welcome you all this morning and thank you for attending? Polling shows that the majority of the public are unsupportive of lowering the voting age to 16. Do you think now is the right time to lower the age of voting?

If not now, when? It has been a key topic for young people for a very long time. The UK Youth Parliament voted nearly 10 years in a row, I think, to place votes for 16 and 17-year-olds as its No. 1 campaign topic. I have worked with young people for 30 - odd years . I have been talking to young people for 30 - odd years, it feels , about this topic, since I was much younger .

P olitics affects so much of our lives and so much of young people ’ s lives . C ertainly with social media and the education young people have today, they are feeling that . T hey understand that politics has an impact . T hey do not necessarily understand all the details, but they understand that politics affects everything they do. The chairs we are sitting on are affected by politics, literally. I f not now, when?

I would concur with that. I have worked with young people in the classroom for over 30 years now. Young people, over all that time, have been willing, able and wanting to take part in elections and have a say. The decisions that politicians are making are going to affect them for the longest time , so they ought to have that opportunity to take part in elections themselves and be able to express their voice and opinions through that. Absolutely, yes.

I agree. As a researcher, I can add that we do a lot of research on public opinion . Public opinion, particularly in terms of attitudes to what the right voting age is , can shift quite significantly in a short time. In Scotland, we have seen a major shift in public attitudes after the voting age was lowered and the population saw that actually nothing bad happens. Now we have a majority of voters in Scotland who are in favour of a lower voting age. I would assume that the same would happen in Wales, England and Northern Ireland too.
Q175 On public opinion, critics argue that 16 and 17 - year-olds may lack the knowledge and maturity to vote. What are your views on that?

I can again add some empirical evidence to that. Colleagues in different countries where the voting age is already 16 or similar reforms are being debated have done quite a lot of research. There are multiple tests that you can give to 16 and 17 - year-olds, as to the rest of the population, including how well they can select, for example, a political party that would represent their interests, how well they can select a candidate who would best represent their interests and how well their interests are matched to the political party they would vote for. On all these tests, we find no significant difference between 14, 15, 16 and 17 - year-olds and the rest of the population. You can say that, empirically, young people are just as good or bad at selecting a political candidate who represents their views as the rest of the population.

I would say that it is about your own engagement activity with young people, the work that ACT does with young people and the Electoral Commission and the surveys that they have done with young people, and probably the young people that you met yesterday. If the general population were able to hear from those young people themselves, I think they would very much realise that our young people are mature enough to take part in the political system. I would absolutely concur with what you are saying and the evidence that you would raise.

I would agree. No other part of the electorate is put to the same test. DVLA will say, “You are over a certain age. You cannot drive if your eyesight has failed .” We do not apply the same test to any other member of the electorate and that does not feel fair or appropriate.

The key here is to give young people the tools and the understanding to make good decisions and to understand what they are voting for. We hear consistently from young people that politics, political parties and manifestos are not aimed at or do not talk to young people. They are aimed at older generations typically, because they tend to vote more. That is the challenge. Get the narrative right, get the education and get the communication to young people correct , and they will make really smart decisions.

Q176 We heard from the previous panel of election officials in Wales and Scotland about their experience introducing votes at 16. In your opinion, what lesson should we draw from the Scottish and Welsh experiences?

For me, it is the education programme that is in place. Our young people need access to high-quality citizenship education. I am really encouraged by the CAR—the curriculum and assessment review—which brings in statutory education for citizenship from primary age. It should not, as we have heard this morning, start from pre-registration and getting our young people to register to vote. They should have that opportunity to have democratic education right through from primary schools and right through secondary.

If we have that high-quality citizenship education for all our young people, that supports them in developing their political literacy and enabling them to be ready to vote at 16. It is learning about democracy, but also through democracy and those practical activities. Even before the franchise and before they are able to vote, learning about that through practical activities and supporting their development of skills is really important for me. That is backed up by what we have heard from Wales and Scotland this morning, from my point of view.

I have led the evaluation of the lowering of the voting age in Wales and been involved in research in Scotland as well. I know that you have heard in the previous session that some of my colleagues call the implementation in Wales a false start, but even there we have not seen any headlines about significant decreases of trust in democracy or depressed turnout. The main conclusion that we can take from Scotland and Wales, but also from a number of other countries in Europe and around the world that already have 16 as the voting age, is that nothing bad happens.

On the contrary, there are real opportunities to increase trust in democracy and engagement, especially among the youngest cohorts, if the lowering of the voting age is implemented in conjunction with measures that really help young people engage with political representatives and political parties. S ome of the things would be statutory and high - quality civic education, trustworthy information to build and grow political opinions, safe spaces for debates of political issues in schools and youth work settings , and engagement with young people from political candidates, political parties and the media.

Talking to colleagues across borders, the key things seem to be that the support needs to be provided before, during and after. We might be used to thinking, “The election is out of the way. We do not worry about it anymore .” What were young people ’ s experiences? How do we improve citizenship education? How do we improve their experience for the next generation and going into their next election? If you have a bad experience the first time, you are not going to come back in a hurry. It is certainly one for us to get right.

For us, it is experience of the process and understanding what that process is and what you are going to go through. I remember being 18 , going through that polling booth for the first time and being not quite clear what I do and where I put the thing in which box. Mock examples are really good . We run the UK Youth Parliament programme and millions of young people vote for their local Me mber of the Y outh P arliament by going into a polling booth and putting it in the box and having done that w e know that they are really confident they know what they are doing. They have been to hustings and seen what candidates are saying. They are making those positive choices. Giving young people the experience of it before they go and do it formally sets us up for success in that sense.

We also have to focus on access. Who will struggle to access? This is the same for adults as it is for young people. It is no different. Those with special needs or those with additional support needs may feel more excluded. How do we get those who do not feel politics talks to them effectively engaged? How do we keep them part of that process? Tackling access before, during and after is key.

Q177 This will touch a little on what we have just covered. I want to be specific around the national curriculum and the changes around citizenship. In your opinions, what would be your main asks to make that a success?

I could talk all day about that. The strengthening of citizenship in secondary schools, with that statutory requirement that it goes from primary right through, is really a key for us. Alongside that, we want investment in teacher training. We have evidence that, if we have discrete citizenship lessons taught by specialists, it is no surprise that outcomes are stronger. Young people are able to have access to that high-quality education.
