Real investment in teacher training is needed, not only for new teachers, so teachers coming into the profession and wanting to be citizenship teachers, so financial bursaries potentially for new teachers, but also for those teachers existing in schools about the changes to the curriculum and changes in things like pedagogies and new knowledge, potentially, from those additions to that national curriculum that we are going to be seeing from what we have seen in the CAR.

I should say that ACT is writing the new national curriculum, so it is under an NDA with the DfE, but we can talk to what the CAR recommendations are, knowing that they are accepted. It is about high-quality teacher training for existing teachers, but also for new teachers into the profession, and more citizenship teachers with expertise.

Alongside that are the new measures around Progress 8, which will have an impact in secondary schools. Moving citizenship into the humanities bucket with geography, history and RE will raise its status in secondary education. That would help with some of our schools being given an incentive to teach, and offer not only core citizenship but also GCSE citizenship, which has been deprioritised over perhaps the last 10 years or so. We are starting to see growth in that area, and that is a real opportunity within our secondary education as well.

Greater access to a qualification in citizenship for our secondary colleagues would be really helpful , as well as CPD for teachers and that strengthening of the curriculum, and also holding schools to account for teaching that curriculum through our Ofsted process. I know that Polly Haste, the Ofsted lead inspector for citizenship and PSHE, is doing a lot of work with inspectors about how we inspect citizenship, particularly as a national curriculum subject. Holding schools accountable would also be really important .

Q178 Yesterday we were talking to students, and there were teachers there as well. There was a bit of a pushback in terms of where in the timetable all of that fits . You talked about putting it in the same basket as humanities, but would it be your opinion that you could also embed it in maths and physics? When you are doing a maths question, it could start , “If 70% of the population vote...”, and so you are starting to get it embedded throughout the curriculum as live examples.

There are certainly areas for embedding in other subjects, but it is a discrete subject that I would want to see in schools. It becomes distilled if we see it across the curriculum, which takes away from the importance of our aims within citizenship education in its own right . I plan my school and my trust’s curriculum, and I do lean into other subjects, but that is in a very planned, co-ordinated way, because I have an opportunity to affect all of the nine secondary schools in my multi-academy trust. I write a core curriculum, and I do that in conjunction with directors of maths and history, where there are elements where there is crossover, but I would definitely be advocating for discrete provision as well.

Schools are important, but young people spend 85% of their waking hours outside of school, which is where the youth sector is active and operating. We should also not forget that 18% to 27%, depending on age groups, are persistently absent from school, and so just focusing everything through schools misses a huge audience. I am going back to access and equality of access for young people, making sure that everyone has that right.

Q179 In fairness, Leigh, this particular question was about the national curriculum. I absolutely accept that you have a point, and we might come on to that, but, just on the national curriculum, what would you like to see?

There is also a national curriculum for informal learning for the youth work sector. The two should join up and cross over. We cross over as national bodies and agencies, so we are doing that joining up of the dots. For me, it would be that it is consistent and practical. How can young people apply what they are learning and understand that application?

Whether it is the mock process, as I touched on earlier, it has to be relevant to their lives and what they are doing. When young people are learning things, even in the classroom, if they cannot see how they are going to use it in the real world, it will not stick as much. If they can say, “I can really understand how that lesson that you have brilliantly planned is going to make a difference to my life ,” they will absolutely take it forward.

Q180 My daughter was standing for school council, and I said to her, “Did you vote for yourself?” She said, “Last year, we were not allowed to ,” and I said, “But the rules might have changed this year, so make sure you check the rules for each election .” That is that lived example coming to life through a classroom.
It really is, absolutely. It is so important.

Helen made the point about teacher training, and there is a different way of looking at this as well from young people’s perspective. I believe that your report on work with schools and young people has shown that what they really lack and request are spaces for debate and being able to form political opinions in safe spaces in schools. That requires well-educated teachers, and teachers to have guidance on how to create those safe spaces. If I were to ask for one thing, it would be guidelines for teachers and a right to deliver civic education that is politically neutral and non-partisan but allows young people to form political opinions and discuss real-life issues.

There are international examples of this. Germany and Austria have guidelines for teachers in schools—not only for citizenship teachers, but for all teachers—on how to talk about political issues. That is a right that teachers can rely on and use to create those safe spaces. Estonia has a really difficult problem with lots of ethnic minorities, both Russian and Estonian-speaking . It had a fantastic process, where it worked with the Ministry of Justice and youth representatives , discussing and developing guidelines that are nationally binding. That can be used by students as a right to civic education, and by teachers as a way to guide their teaching.

Q181 From the research in Wales and some of the conversations that we had yesterday with young people, the connection between parental engagement and your likelihood to register to vote as a 16 or 17-year-old is quite high. Does this potentially pose a risk in terms of expanding the socioeconomic gap in terms of who is exercising that right? Are there ways to overcome that, particularly by engaging with more disadvantaged pupils and moving on to the role that youth workers can play in trying to tackle that? It would be great to hear more on that from any of you.

Youth workers are the backbone of that 85% when young people are not in school. We are connected to young people outside of the home in that space with their peer groups, and we can have those debates and create those spaces for young people to have that learning, as well as to unpick their views and opinions.

The risk that you talk about is genuine and a real concern. We know that many generations do not engage with the state, and that could be perpetuated. We also know that the key to that is education. We know that the key to that is giving young people the experience of doing it differently and understanding what different can look like. That is where youth workers will run mock activities or set things up, such as workshops or conversations, to challenge that.

What youth workers are also brilliant at doing and often do not get recognised for is working intergenerationally. We work with mum and dad, and grandma and granddad, and try to change their views of these things up and down the line.

It goes back to the point that, as long as young people understand what difference voting would make, they will do it and lean in on it. If they are frustrated that their experience of school has not been great, but, by voting for different things or whatever, that might change in the future for the next generation, young people are motivated to see that change, just like every other adult is. We can create that space, but it has to be consistent and we have to give them the time to do so.

Britain is one of the most unequal electorates in a European context in terms of who participates in voting. Of course, I share that concern that enfranchising 16 and 17-year-olds just perpetuates that inequality that we already see in society. On the other hand, it also provides a huge opportunity to change that, because, at age 16 and 17, young people are still in educational institutions, and that is statutory in most parts of Britain, so we have a huge opportunity to reach young people at an age where lots of them are able to be reached. That is not the case at age 18 or 20, when you are voting for the first time.

In Scotland, for example, we have seen that, among 16 and 17-year-olds, the inequality between young people from different social backgrounds is lower. We see young people from marginalised backgrounds participate in higher numbers at age 16 and 17. We do not quite know why that is the case, but it is a real opportunity whereby, if joined-up work is happening and young people are reached at scale, some of those inequalities can be mitigated.

I was going to use that word, “opportunity”, as well. It is a risk but it is a massive opportunity. We are at a really historic moment, whe n we have votes at age 16 potentially coming in, alongside a new national curriculum with reinvigorated citizenship education. It should not be a postcode lottery in terms of where students go to school whether they get that high-quality citizenship education from primary school right through that is going to prepare them and give them those opportunities, working in conjunction with those outside of education settings as well.

We run parallel elections in my own trust, through resources that ACT has produced. When the general election happens, we use our local constituencies. All of our young people then get to look at manifestos and take part in hustings. We had podcasts of all the different political parties produced. There was a real buzz around the school. We produced our own parallel election results, and then compared them and did the statistical analysis alongside the real election results. Students really engaged with that; it was fantastic.

Eighty of my students took part in this Committee’s inquiry in terms of putting forward evidence. That is a real opportunity to have their voice heard. That was 80 students, from those who are disadvantaged to higher prior attainers, because my citizenship GCSE students are option students. They come from the whole gamut of ability range, and they all took part in the request for information and would have loved to be here today, sitting there, but unfortunately were not allowed. They are really keen to get engaged.

Those opportunities to have real decision-making are so important, regardless of age—so at key stages 3 and 4—leading up to that opportunity, when they do get that franchise, so that they have had real-life opportunities to discuss, take part and deliberate in those classrooms, in those safe spaces, and have those views sometimes challenged, but challenged respectfully in a classroom situation with skilled teachers who are doing that.

It is probably worth noting for the record that what is definitely recognisable is the number of young people who have come to listen today, which is not normally the group of people we see sat behind the panel—
I thought that it was to test my chairmanship skills.
—so full credit to all of you for coming in and getting engaged with this whole agenda. We really appreciate you coming in and being part of this as well.

Q182 We have seen research by Ofcom and the Electoral Commission that shows that younger people are more likely to encounter political misinformation online. Separately, Internet Matters says that only around half of young people aged 13 to 17 feel confident in determining whether information that they see online is true or false. We have heard from young people that they would like to feel more confident navigating the online information environment. Does lowering the voting age to 16 increase the importance of media literacy education?

I should say that this is not my particular area of research expertise. It is important to note that misinformation and disinformation online is a whole-society problem. Young people see it more often, as you cite the evidence, but that is also probably because they are more often online and more savvy in recognising that kind of information as untrustworthy.

The situation that we need to contend with is that young people are probably most aware that the information that they come across is not entirely trustworthy. One thing that I would like to see is trustworthy information sources for young people that they know they can turn to in that kind of space.

Media literacy education is obviously important, but we also need to think about those 20 to 70-plus-year-olds who are not going to get that kind of education any more . They are just as affected by it.

Q183 That is interesting. You are contending that it may not be the case that they are more likely to encounter political misinformation online. It is just that they are better able to recognise it as misinformation.
Yes.
That is interesting.

First of all, I am really pleased to see that media literacy is going to be a core part of citizenship education in the national curriculum. I could talk all day about media literacy. It is one of my real passions with the young people who I teach, and it is a core part of our offer across the trust as well. All of our students take part in media literacy education throughout their five years of core citizenship education as part of the curriculum that I design.

Our young people need the knowledge, skills and resilience to be able to assess information and recognise trustworthy sources, and check whether it is reliable and accurate. Also, our teachers and parents need that to be able to work with those young people. ACT already supports teachers in this area. I would urge you all to go on to its website and maybe take part in the Media Matters course, where you will see me again, because I helped it to design and run that course, alongside another citizenship teacher. We already offer that wider programme of CPD for teachers, because we recognise how important it is.

In fact, with one of my year 11s this week, we were talking about some of the news stories over the summer. We talked about the Clacton by-election. She said, “I have read this information, but, before I tell you what I have read, Miss, I just want to let you know that I read it on Reddit, and I have not had a chance to go through and assess the information and check its reliability. I am just going to put it out there, and maybe we could have a look at whether it is reliable .” That is what I want to see my young people do.

My students regularly say to me, “Where did you get that from?” If I put up a news headline and I have not said where it is from, that is what I want my young people to do. It is sometimes a little annoying, because then I have to go back and say, “Look, it is from here ,” but I absolutely want young people to be doing that and to have the skills and the confidence to be able to do that.

I know that my young people are getting their information from Instagram or TikTok. They are often not getting it from BBC News. Just reiterating that message, we use The Day , which is an online newspaper for young people . We reference a range of sources when I am teaching, so that we are giving students the opportunity to look at news stories from different viewpoints and recognise fact, opinion and bias across time. In media literacy, you cannot look at just one article and say, “This organisation or this news outlet is biased .” We need to look at that over time and think critically about that.

I could talk all day, and I apologise, but I am so passionate about citizenship, and particularly media literacy within that. It is a fundamental part of the work that we need to be doing in schools with our young people, with our teachers and, ultimately, with parents, to support them with that.
Q184 On that theme, what change would you like to see in the revised citizenship curriculum to ensure that media literacy is given sufficient prominence?

It is in there now as part of the curriculum and assessment review recommendations. That definitely needs to be a strength within that curriculum. Again, we come back to ensuring that teachers have that training themselves to be able to deliver that high-quality education. It is really important for citizenship teachers to do that, but I also do training with all of the teachers in my trust.

It is really fundamental for all teachers to have high-quality media literacy education, because they are all dealing with information. They are likely to come into conversations with young people on a daily basis who have watched something in the news. They will have seen what has been happening in Portsmouth, so we are dealing with really high-profile national news at the moment, which is unusual for us in Portsmouth, but not unusual in terms of the same skills to be able to allow our teachers to have those sensitive, challenging conversations in a politically impartial way. I do that training with all of my teachers, and particularly our citizenship colleagues as well.
Q185 You have recognised that your colleagues need that support to deliver that media literacy education.
Yes, absolutely.
Q186 In your experience, is that widespread across other multi-academy trusts? Do you think that something more formal should be put in place to provide that support nationwide?

I would say that it is not widespread. I do know of other multi-academy trusts that I work with through ACT, which have requested for us to deliver some of that training. I do know that it is happening, but I would say that it is not consistent across multi-academy trusts, so it does need to be more formal and recognised. We would do safeguarding training every year with our teachers in schools, which I go through every September, and rightly so. This is also so important to enable our teachers to have those safe spaces that we are talking about with our young people.
Q187 That is as part of their continuous professional development.

Yes, absolutely. I deliver to citizenship teachers at UCL. As part of their course, I go in and do media literacy training with them. That is something that could be embedded into initial teacher training, as well as for teachers in schools who are teaching these areas already.

I would echo most of that. I would agree with the comment that young people are probably ahead of other generations. They are digital natives. They have grown up with iPads and digital screens pretty much their whole lives, so they have learnt to read and digest information quite quickly and then drop and dump what is not relevant and focus in.

To stretch your thinking for your wider review, though, there are broader challenges in this space. The Online Safety Act is not working for young people. They all have VPNs on their phones. My nephew’s phone is in the UK but is VPN-ed to America, so his social media feed is just filled up with American content, which is different from the UK’s , and the context is different. He comes to me all the time going, “What about this? What about that? What is going on? I do not understand this ,” and I say, “That is rubbish, because that is New York ,” or wherever.

The other part of this is the rise of the use of AI bots and chat functions, where young people are asking them questions: “Who should I vote for? What do you think of this policy?” They are having a conversation with a bot that is filled in by Grok or other companies. That information is presented as so factual and accurate, but it is not accurate. It is presented in a way that makes them think, “That is truth ,” but it is not. The problem is that the technology is moving at such a pace that teachers, youth workers, the system and the state cannot keep up with it.

It is a real challenge to our society and democracy, because there are big organisations investing and undermining the narrative that our young people are getting. The scale of this is colossal. Please do not think that this is just a few young people. The majority of young people’s social media feeds are full of nonsense.

The social media ban is another factor, which, when that comes in—or whatever version of that comes in, and how that is applied—could also restrict young people’s access to certain information and may open up others, or they will all use VPNs, we will never know about it and we are pushing them in a further direction. We do not favour the social media ban for that very reason. It will push young people into darker parts of the internet, or other parts of it that are not public or available. That is a challenge to our democracy as we go forward.

The point of media literacy is that it is so important, because it is about equipping young people with the tools to analyse and understand what they are being presented with and to ask questions. The fact that my nephew comes to me and asks those questions is amazing. Does every young person have an adult with whom they can go and do that? We know that the answer to that is no.

Q188 You broaden that out beyond media, but also considering AI chatbots as media. I do not know, Christine, whether you know the answer to this, but what data is there around the use of AI chatbots to answer questions such as who I should vote for and the extent to which the companies behind the biases within the large language models are directing people towards sites where they can answer those kinds of questions for themselves, or whether it is steering them in a particular direction? I am just wondering what the evidence is on that, if, indeed, it is part of your area of research.

I am not aware of any evidence on this. Part of the problem, as Leigh has mentioned, is that this technology is moving very quickly, and research is often on the back foot when it comes to monitoring these kinds of things.

The other thing that I should add is that it is incredibly difficult to do empirically rigorous research with these kinds of small groups of 16 and 17-year-olds to get valid results. That holds for political attitudes, but also for how they use AI chatbots. It is a wider society issue that we need to address.

There are two final questions from me to conclude. What can political parties do to engage young people in the electoral process? Do you have any really good examples? Do you have any really bad examples? I think that votes for 16 and 17-year-olds are good, but we certainly need some education support around that.
That is not a unified view of the Committee.

Q189 I did slightly look at the Chair when I said that. We clearly need an education programme around this. Do you think that teachers are equipped to do this? Do you think that teachers have the confidence to do it? Do you think that the public would accept teachers talking about politics? Talking to young people yesterday when we had our Committee inquiry, they feel that they learn about government and about how law is made, but not about the party politics side. If we are going to correct this, we need to put politics in the classroom in an appropriate way.

You have asked about teachers, but, if I could talk about youth workers first, we can then move on to teachers. Youth workers are very well placed to have these conversations with young people. They are trusted within the community to have those conversations. I would say that confidence around party politics is an area that needs proper guidelines and structure to make sure that we are not imposing youth workers’ bias on young people, and that young people are given critical thinking skills and the opportunity to ask those questions and to go and investigate, learn and bring all that back. We can create that.

We are about to publish new guidance to the youth sector around all of this. It will be democratic education guidance to youth workers in the youth sector to give them that framework in which they can operate effectively and safely, and also , if challenged, to be able to say, “I am using this framework. I am not just a rogue operative. I am doing it in this way .” That is really important .

There are good examples of how good political education participation can be done. Local youth councils are an amazing opportunity for young people to get involved in. I mentioned the UK Youth Parliament, which is fundamental, because it is how young people get their first experience of the electoral system in a practical application, not just in terms of standing but also voting and electing, and going to hustings, as well as interrogating candidates’ manifestos in a really safe and more enjoyable way than in big-scale politics.
There are real challenges for parties. I see very little from the parties’ comms machinery that is aiming messaging at young people and putting it into language that young people use.

Going back to the previous question, we see the use of influencers quite a lot to influence young people. Those influences may be positive; they may not be positive. It depends on your politics and your view of the topic, or whatever is going on. We see that party machineries are not using the channels or the communication methods to get those messages to young people, who do not know what parties typically stand for. They do not know what your policies are and what you are aiming for. Therefore, they are not convinced of or do not understand what they would be voting for in that sense, so they might choose not to.

If I was advising parties, it is an open door to engage young people, invite them in, educate them and explain what you are doing, but you have to be on their level, which is a horrible phrase, but on the platforms that they are on, when they are on them, and communicating in the visuals and the language, with more video content. All those sorts of things are really needed.

Two weeks ago, I ran three days at the UK Youth Parliament conference. 250 young people were together for three days, and we were talking about these topics. They were like, “I do not know what the different parties stand for. I do not know what their manifestos are. I do not know what they are trying to achieve. I see them fight at the Dispatch Box at PMQs ,” but we all know that that is not how politics works. There is a lot more cohesiveness and engagement behind the scenes. There is a job there for MPs and parties to connect and engage with young people, and you are not doing it well.

On the politicians’ side, before I give Helen the floor for teachers, I absolutely concur with what Leigh said. Political parties, candidates and representatives must do a better job and must be held to account to address young voters with relevant information, in ways that are relevant to young people. There are multiple ways of how that can happen.

One important guideline is that it should be continuous, not just ahead of elections. It should be with specific measures around election time, such as manifestos in understandable language. I do not like the words “youth manifesto”, but young people in your own inquiry have complained that the language is impenetrable. These kinds of measures help not just young people. They make your programmes and political issues more accessible to all of the population, as well as to young people.

Young people often like to feel listened to. Your own inquiry has shown that, and certainly a lot of my and colleagues’ research has shown that. The key barrier is that they do not feel that it is worth engaging with politics because no one listens anyway. Key measures would be to listen and to then report back on what kinds of measures have been taken, based on what has been told.

There are ways of doing that. It is important to think about scale. You can think a little bit about candidates or representatives going into schools. If every MP engaged with a school group every other week, that would engage almost half of 16 and 17-year-olds in an average constituency over just one academic year. You can really do a lot of work there.

You can think about engaging young people in the way that messaging is constructed. We have run pilots in Germany, where young people were placed in parliamentary offices and were helping make the reels on Instagram and the communication that goes out to young people.

Closing the feedback loop, one of the most effective ways for politicians to raise the quality of interactions is to take action and then report back on what has been happening. Again, that could be in an asynchronous way with online sources, but it is really important that young people hear what has happened with what they have told politicians.

If I pick up on politicians first and then look at education, I am very fortunate that my local MP is highly engaged with my school. He is an ex-student, which does help. Stephen Morgan, Portsmouth South’s MP, is regularly in school. He works with my citizenship students. They go down to his office and talk to him about their concerns and things that they are taking action on or would like action on. He comes in twice a year to do assemblies, but also then comes in at other points during the year. Meeting with students, listening and engaging with them, and hearing what they have to say is really important , so I would urge you to get into schools and go meet those young people, and meet them where they are at.

We also engage online. We do things such as Learn with the Lords with our young people. We can engage online, which means that we have access to those opportunities even if we cannot get up to Parliament, or politicians cannot get in. We have done online meetings with them and had the opportunity to do a Q&A with those peers, as well as with politicians from the House of Commons.

Also, you have lots of young people working in local youth council groups and the Youth Parliament. We have the Council of Portsmouth Students. You could meet with students from across the city who will bring views from those individual schools as well. Those opportunities are really important .

In terms of education, you asked whether teachers are equipped. In my multi-academy trust and among the teachers who I work with, I would say yes, because they have me. I am in there doing the training. I work with the teachers. I help and support them, and answer their queries. I deliver training around controversial issues, how to run deliberation in their classrooms and political impartiality. I would deliver that CPD on all of those with them.

I would say that teachers who I work with are well prepared, confident and engaged. They want to be involved in it. I do not think that that is the same in every school and every multi-academy trust, and that is probably something that we need to look at as part of your work leading up to those votes at 16 to ensure that it is part of the training for all of our teachers.

It is also about working with and talking to parents, and opening up opportunities for conversations with parents who may be concerned about teachers delivering political education. We have political impartiality guidelines, quite rightly, to keep ourselves and our young people safe, but we absolutely should be talking and teaching about political parties’ role in democracy. That is something that we recognise, but we would also value ACT maybe leading the way in delivering that political impartiality training for everybody as well.
Q190 If I could ask you to keep your answer really tight , because we are running short on time, can votes at 16 succeed if it is not accompanied by automatic voter registration?
Short answers are preferable.
Yes.
Yes.
Yes.
Q191 If you were to recommend one practical reform to maximise participation among newly enfranchised young people, what would it be?
It would be running mock processes so that they know what they are going through and what they are going to experience.
It would be access to high-quality citizenship education, which includes those opportunities, and training teachers as well.
Q192 Can you recommend somebody who might be able to help?
I think I could help, alongside ACT.
It would be assisted voter registration while we wait for AVR.
Thank you all for attending today.

sessions.iT: National Planning Policy Statement on Nuclear Fusion
sessions.w: Michael Shanks MP (Department for Energy Security and Net Zero); David Sandford (Department for Energy Security and Net Zero)

segs.tx: Energy Security and Net Zero Committee
Oral evidence: National Planning Policy Statement on Nuclear Fusion , HC 571
Wednesday 9 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 9 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Bill Esterson (Chair); Sir Christopher Chope; Wera Hobhouse; Melanie Onn; Mike Reader; Claire Young.
Questions 1 - 96
Witnesses
I : Paul Methven CB , CEO, UK Fusion Energy Ltd, UKAEA Group ; Tris Denton , UK Director, Fusion Industry Association ; and Jo Nettleton , Chief Regulator, Environment Agency .
II : Michael Shanks MP , Minister for Energy, Department for Energy Security and Net Zero ; and David Sandford, Deputy Director, Department for Energy Security and Net Zero .
Examination of witness es
Witnesses: Paul Methven , Tris Denton and Jo Nettleton.

Q1 W elcome to the Energy Security and Net Zero Committee and our inquiry into the nuclear fusion national policy statement. Welcome to our first panel. If you could introduce yourselves , starting on my left , please .
Good morning. Tris Denton, UK d irector of the Fusion Industry Association. FIA is the global trade association for the fusion sector.

Good morning. Paul Methven . I am chief executive of UK Fusion Energy Ltd, which is the Government-owned company running the STEP programme, trying to make fusion energy a global strategic success for the UK.
Good morning, everybody. Jo Nettleton . I am chief regulator at the Environment Agency and I lead our regulation of nuclear and radioactive substances.

Q2 Thank you, and thank you very much for hosting my visit a couple of weeks ago, along with the s enior Clerk, which gave us a very good sense of what happens at Culham and the exciting opportunities there, which I am sure you will tell us all about in the next 45 minutes or so.

I will start with a question about the impact of nuclear on the community . We know that nuclear fission development is better received in areas that have historically already hosted it. Do you think that we will have a similar approach for fusion, in that it is likely to go to the areas that have already hosted fission?

I think it is going to go better than that. I have one really good data point for that, which is what has happened so far in West Burton. We selected that site for the Government ’s STEP programme in October 2022. That was a volunteer process, where sites put themselves forward to host a fusion plant. Of course there had been no fission plant there before, but what there had been was an incredible legacy of energy generation up and down the Trent v alley. There was a community used to big infrastructure and doing something that matters for the nation , and w hen we came along with the fusion programme, they really embraced it. That has continued and we have had a great relationship with the local public , and increasingly with the important regional stakeholders coalesced by the East Midlands Combined Authority and the Greater Lincolnshire Combined Authority. So our experience so far is that it is even better , and I think that is because people understand that although the processes are nuclear , the hazards are very different.

Q3 In our report “Gridlock or growth? Avoiding energy planning chaos” we identified the problem s of a lack of effective consultation in placing energy infrastructure. You have talked about the success you have had already at West Burton. What are the lessons from West Burton for community engagement?

We are learning them as we go , but I absolutely echo your point that early engagement and sustained engagement is critical. I think we have done that. Our first non-statutory phase of consultation for our development consent order, which is going into the formal process next year, shows that people really welcome the opportunity to get engaged. We do too. This is not just about a smokescreen of consultation ; it is critical to hear what people have to say. They all have brilliant ideas locally. Our experience is that it is essential and, having done it, that it works . P eople should not be afraid of that early consultation and engagement. It is a really good thing to make your programme better.

Q4 How would you encourage the rest of the nuclear industry , and infrastructure developers more widely , to adopt your approach ? Do you think it is relevant and do you think there are lessons that they can apply?

I hope most developers are doing this , but it is actually really simple to say, “Be open , b e honest , b e completely transparent . ” If you do not take your community with you , then you are going to have a very difficult time , and t hat is going to drive up schedule , drive up costs and reduce benefits. If you take the communities with you on the journey and listen to what they have to say , you will be much more likely to have a success. I would hope that is a natural approach from developers . I t certainly should be , in my view.
Q5 Do you think developing fusion power will be easier than it has been to develop fission power? If so, what are you doing differently that demonstrates confidence in that happening?

Technically, no. T he evidence is just there : w e have been working on this—albeit that things are really accelerating now—for some 70 or so years. I should say, by the way, that AI has been in gestation for 70 or so years and has only recently had its inflection point , so it is not new that technologies take a while. L ook, this is fiendishly difficult technically, but the prize at the end of it is so huge in terms of what you can do for an energy source —
Q6 What about in planning terms, which is the essence of our conversation today?

In planning terms, as I say, what we are doing early is getting in place the relationships with regulators. We have a very strong relationship with both regulators in fusion. That reduces surprises on both sides and allows us to design. We also have an e arly relationship with the public and early consideration of all the consents and permissions that are going to be required. T he lessons are not unique for fusion ; they are how you make any major infrastructure and technology development work properly.
Q7 Jo, do you agree with what Paul has been saying?

Jo Nettleton : Yes . I think the policy statement is absolutely spot on in that it puts fusion on the same basis as other energy infrastructure, including fission. It gives that element of clarity and certainty to developers and their ability to make decisions. Obviously planning is just that first step. Our regulation—we can talk about it during this session—and the regulation of the Health and Safety Executive is absolutely designed to ensure that we are proportionate and robust in relation to the hazards presented by fusion, both the actual technology and the radioactive side of things , but also the wider environmental impacts. You talked earlier about the views of the community. Obviously , things that matter to the community include water resources and impact on habitat , so we have that wider perspective as well as the atoms.

Q8 You say that you have to take communities with you. Does that mean that it is purely voluntary , or is there a coercive element of that? There is a big distinction between people saying, “I will voluntarily sign up to that” and the Government, through their regulator s , saying basically, “You have to sign up to it . ”

For sure. We would aim for people absolutely wanting the development there. O ur experience in West Burton is that what we can provide in terms of jobs growth and renewal in the region could be so transformative that that is the bit they welcome.

T here are clearly concerns. The majority of those, as with a lot of developments, focus on transport movements. The consultation process we have been going through gives us some really good ideas from the public about how to manage those pressure points that are inevitably going to come.

W here possible, we say this is actually taking input from the public, which gives us a better approach to the project. In the final analysis, yes, if the Government ha ve a policy and decide that something has to go somewhere , you could get to that sort of definitive stage at the end, but you are on track for a much better development if you can take people with you.
Q9 In the latter example you gave — the Government forcing it — that could be counterproductive , because it means you do not have the consent of the local people .

I think it would be counterproductive if it happened too early and if it was clearly in the face of a large amount of public opposition. We don’t think we are going to face that particular situation here , but yes, you could. L argely you want to avoid those sorts of situations, and I do not think we need to get into that territory.
Q10 How environmentally friendly do you think fusion energy is?

We think, o nce developed, that it will be. There are a couple of dimensions to that . I nherently , this is zero carbon at the point of generation. Our fuel source is lithium-producing tritium and deuterium , an isotope of hydrogen from seawater. Clearly it is a major piece of infrastructure, so there are carbon impacts and environmental impacts more broadly in the development and construction itself. U sing modern methods of construction, working effectively with the local regions and local public, we can reduce those impacts , as with any major development. I nherently , I think this is a low-carbon solution and can be done in a very environmentally positive way.

I will give o ne quick example . A t West Burton we are utilising the site of an old coal-fired power station —w e are reusing a brownfield site that was focused on energy generation to do exactly the same — and , as part of that , we are looking to reutilise a large proportion of the old waste pulverised fuel ash, probably to produce concrete for the plant construction. W e think we can do these things in a way that is as environmentally positive as possible , and of course in the big game around climate change is definitely the right thing to do.
Q11 How does it compare with traditional nuclear, for example? Do you think it is more environmentally friendly?

I would say yes, broadly, and probably slightly better , in the sense that large-scale infrastructure is roughly on a par in terms of the scope and scale of these projects , but once we get operating , we are in a better position in terms of the net environmental impact because of the fuel source and the waste products.

I support that. This is fusion ; i t does not rely on criticality, so the environmental risks from something going wrong are really different than for fission reactors. I t is a developing technology. The conditions in the fusion system are really challenging and will result , potentially, in some novel wastes —both radioactive material and hazardous materials that need to be used for that environment —that we still need to develop the appropriate routes for. However, that waste will not be of the same type as th e very long-lived waste that comes from nuclear fission. A gain, we are looking at a different type of impact and, I agree, a lesser impact generally.

Of course, as Paul says, the wider environmental impacts — impacts on water and transport systems, and impacts of building and combustion — are exactly the same way as for any large infrastructure. However, we do believe that fission absolutely is a key part of the energy mix as we move towards net zero.
Q12 You refer to large infrastructure , but isn’t one of the arguments that this is small construction—
This is a prototype.
W hich can be put in lots of different places — perhaps not quite as much as solar panels , but compared with nuclear power stations ?

Paul can talk in more detail on this. The particular STEP programme is around 100 MW . That is a prototype to demonstrate that we can get energy out of a fusion system. Fusion will be scalable. We might have smaller sites ; we might have larger, more complex sites. Similarly with nuclear fission, there is a range of technologies looking at different sizes of reactor and different types of reactor , some of which can be placed to power industry and some of which are the large, multiscale reactors that we have at Hinkley Point C, for example. Fusion , in the same way as a technology or a set of technologies, will be scalable.

I t is too early to say whether there is an equivalent of the small modular reactor as there is in the fission space. I n the public sector, with the Atomic Energy Authority and UK Fusion Energy, our view is it is probably biased towards large-scale energy generation , big baseload provision and juxtaposition with major industry , and that it is difficult to get to a small version. But, look, there could be some private providers internationally who have some ideas we have not thought of that do unlock the smaller end of the spectrum.
Q13 You mentioned water. There is a big concern about the water requirements. What can you say about that?

We will obviously take into account the impacts of the water for fusion in combination with other impacts. At the Trent Supercluster there are a number of developments there, including some small modular reactors , the large reservoir , datacentres. In terms of this particular site—again, Paul can give you better information—our expectation is that the water need will be much less than for Hinkley Point C. We are looking at around the order of magnitude of the coal-fired power station . Again, it is developing , isn’t it?
Yes.

Q14 You seem rather vague about the water requirements , but obviously , at a time when people are saying, “We need to build a lot more reservoirs , ” t his will put a lot more demand upon the water supply.

At t his particular site itself, the water demand is not insignificant , but it is in no way of the order of magnitude of a large new fission reactor. We will look at the impacts across the whole of that cluster and consider this in combination with the datacentres and the reservoirs in our approach to water regulation.

O ne of the important things about the national policy statement is that it makes it clear that developers have to take into account the requirement to compute what their water usage is likely to be. Of course that is for cooling , so the water is returned ; it is the temperature difference it is returned at that is the issue we have to manage. It is not a net consumption, if you like. The onus to address these things— and this is why we need the clarity of the national policy statement — is explicitly on the developers. We did that at an early stage, before selection of the site, but every developer in fusion will have to look at that issue.
Q15 So t he Environment Agency is going to be in charge of all this .

We are joint regulator with the Health and Safety Executive. We are the environmental regulator ; the Health and Safety Executive is the safety regulator. As we are not talking about nuclear fission, it is appropriate for us to regulate , rather than the Office for Nuclear Regulation. As I say, we have a lot of experience. We have been regulating Culham for many years and w e understand how to develop the skills around fusion regulation.
I thought the idea was to have a primary regulator , and I thought you were going to be the primary regulator.
We are the primary environment regulator. We work really closely with the Health and Safety Executive, which is the safety regulator.
Q16 I see. So the simplification of regulation promised by the Fingleton r eview is not yet going to result in a single regulator .

We work really closely. The Fingleton r eview is in relation mostly to nuclear fission. We are developing a lead nuclear regulator model that will bring together co-ordination of regulators much more closely. In the case of d efence, I think the d efence nuclear regulator will move into ONR. But generally across the nuclear fission regulation landscape , we are developing that lead nuclear regulator model and a regulatory commission. Th is is much simpler—regulation in terms of the landscape for fusion is much simpler than for fission— hence ourselves and the Health and Safety Executive are working very closely.
Q17 What percentage of your workload do you expect this to represent in the future?

Again, it is difficult to predict exactly. We spend about 20 days a year with our technical team regulating Culham. We think it will be larger for the STEP site , but again, as Paul said, the size and complexity will vary for different developments. We think at the moment our regulation for STEP will be around 60,000 a year to the developer.

Q18 I n our consideration of EN - 7, our Committee recommended that greater use of conditional commencement mechanisms should be used. Do you see that as something that might be useful in delivering fusion generation?

Within the conditions, within policy statements and development consent orders, that does offer a potential to ensure that any uncertainties are addressed as things develop. For us , though, the key is early engagement.
Q19 So y ou do think it is useful .
I don’t know the answer to that. We will need to come back to you generally around the policy statement.
Q20 Mr Methven, do you want to say anything about that?

At one end of the spectrum , developers do not want conditions because they just get in the way of delivery. However, I think there are circumstances bespoke to projects where conditions are really helpful because they drive certainty. I t is better to have a condition that is clear for a developer than the absence of a condition , which means there is a huge uncertainty to carry forward.

One example is c onditionality around apprenticeships or skills development in a region , which could be something that the local populus really want s and the developer really want s and is mutually reinforcing. Overly restrictive conditions are clearly unhelpful in terms of realising benefit , so I think it is horses for courses.

An example where we have asked for strengthening within EN - 8 is flood risk. We support t he open siting criteria , because of the lack of certainty in this space, but we do think there are risks around the length of the life cycle of developments and the potential for flood risks to change.

B ack to the comment about early engagement, I absolutely think that how we address that is to be talking early to developers about what the length of the full life cycle of the site might look like and what the changes to flood risk might be through that period , and to make sure that is built in to the plans early.
Q21 Why is regulation simpler for fusion than fission? You said it was much simpler.

The regulatory landscape is simpler . It is ourselves and the Health and Safety Executive. As Paul said, the technology itself is very complex and developing. There are s ome of the same challenges as for nuclear fission regulation : in the advanced nuclear technology world , things are changing , and developers’ plans change , so that is the same —

Q22 Why is it simpler? Is it because, as yet, all those additional bits of regulation—we had a private session with a spaghetti bowl full of organisations that have involvement in delivery of nuclear— are just not in volved yet? Will it get more complicated over time as this becomes a commercial reality?

I do n’t think so , because the basic physics is different. We are not talking about a system where you have the potential for a nuclear explosion, which is where a lot of the addition comes in around nuclear fission regulation. This is a different set of physics. There are risks associated with it . We do have large amounts of tritium, radioactive materials , and t here are risks associated with the waste. However, again, we do not have that really long-term waste profile that we do for nuclear fission , so all that makes it easier.
Q23 Tris, Paul said it was net zero. Is it really?

Yes. This is zero carbon at the point of generation. All energy technologies, all activities, have an embedded carbon element , but w e represent around 50 companies looking at different ways of doing this , and a ll of them are zero carbon at the point of generation. They are large scale ; they are variable. There is a range of models—you can have small, you can have large—all at different stages of maturity. But t he overwhelming consensus is that companies expect to be delivering commercial plants in the mid-2030s with zero carbon at the point of output.
Q24 Those raw materials that have to be mined, transported and produced , are t hey are all net zero too? Are t hey net zero mined , net zero—

No , t o be clear, it is zero carbon at the point of generation. It is low-carbon life cycle, just like fission, just like offshore wind. It is absolutely in that bucket. All energy technologies have baked-in carbon.
Q25 So only a t the point those materials come through the door does it become a net zero operation . A ll the things that power the operation are not included in that statement that it is net zero .

Let me be clear ; a pologies if I was unclear. This is a low - carbon technology, just like fission, just like offshore wind. There is no carbon released at the point of generation. But a s I thought I said—apologies if not—with all energy technologies there is baked - in carbon , and we should be clear about that.
Q26 Why are fusion reactors going to be planned separately and in a different way from fission?

B ecause they are just fundamentally different technologies being developed by very different industries. The Planning Act 2008 was a fundamental enabler of a range of things, including fission development , but f or fusion we are looking at this and you have an international community that is coming forward to deliver plants at pace. When we look at the UK as a deployment market—it is absolutely in the lead as one of the best deployment markets , and as a British taxpayer I am delighted about that—there is a range of things the Government are putting in place to make it an attractive place to come and do business. One of those is clarity on the regulatory landscape. One of those is the forthcoming work on market structures. But EN - 8 gives absolute clarity , and t here is a bespoke and very applicable set of arrangements for deployment through consenting.

A lot of infrastructure sectors see consenting as a challenging area. I think this is a very good national policy statement. I think it gives great confidence to technology companies and their investors and their developers. That means we can hopefully see the UK in the first wave of fusion build .

Q27 Paul, is there not a bit of smoke and mirrors here in terms of the scale of opportunit y ? We heard in inquiries on nuclear and SMR that SMR could be anywhere ; it wa s going to be this technology that was going to transform things. Then we look ed into EN - 7 and it start ed to narrow down around needing a workforce , space , existing grid capacity and everything else, and you get down to, “Oh, we’ll just put it on the existing nuclear site s. ” W hy do n’t we just have EN - 7 applying to this and have it all in the same place , where there is the skills, the capacity, the land and the water you will need and the existing local consensus on large-scale power?

I think we are having a really UK-centric discussion here that is completely missing the opportunity for the UK. The big opportunity for the country here is that fusion is a global technology in which the UK is currently the world leader in the science. The opportunity is to convert that into a world leader in commercialisation.

Y es, we are going to need some fusion plant in the UK , but not just for UK domestic energy production. We can, frankly — as a small, windy island with a shallow seabed — produce a lot of wind. The s olar is a bit less , but we can do that and we are doing that successfully, and we have a fission programme. But t his is about global energy. This is the export opportunity. The reason we need this in the UK , more than anything else , is to lead the world in the export of a technology that really ha s a transformative opportunity.

As far as the UK hosting is concerned, as Tris said, the physics is literally 180 degrees from the physics of fission , if I am not mixing my scientific metaphors there . T he hazard profile is different , so we do not need to restrict ourselves and we can open up those opportunities. Y es, we could put fusion plant on old fission sites , but why not keep th ose for fission programmes and open up the massive development opportunity , as we are doing in the east midlands ?
Q28 Is this NPS as much a signal to investors as it is an actual planning document, given we are a long way away from commercial delivery?

It is both, but we are not a long way away from investment. W e see development consent as pretty much in our critical path for delivery of the STEP plant. If the critical path for delivery of fusion plant is consenting, we have got this stratospherically wrong ; i t should be development of the technology, so we need to get these things off the critical path. But i n doing so, yes, it does enable growth, development and international competition , and I don’t think we should shy away from that. In fact, we should embrace it.

I think we are really close to commercial delivery. There has been a level of progress in the last six or seven years that was just unseeable in 2018 / 2019. There are companies globally selecting sites for their first commercial power stations now. We saw just a month ago the UK Infinity c onsortium, a commercial entity, selecting the UK as a deployment market for a power station . W e are seeing companies right now choosing their sites , and i t is incredibly helpful to them to have a very clear planning regime as they choose those sites.

I also think it is useful for communities. When West Burton was being selected, 15 communities came forward and 15 communities were engaged. There were open conversations, town hall events and all that good stuff. There was a whole range of conversation about, “Is this fission? Is this fusion? What ’ s the difference?” Being able to demonstrate that it is under a separate planning regime is another demonstration to those communities of what they are dealing with and it avoids conflation. It avoids communities feeling that you might be consenting a different technology by the back door. I think it is great for investors, developers and communities.
Q29 I understand that the tritium currently need ed would need to be imported . I s that correct?
The initial charge, yes —
Q30 I just wanted to confirm that . I s it an omission that the NPS says nothing about use, storage and transportation of that radioactive material?

There is a set of existing regulations that cover all that. Just to be clear on this, our intent as far as the technology is concerned is that once we have the plant s operating , they self-generate tritium , so o ur base fuel is lithium , and the amount you use in a fusion plant is very small proportionally. So w e self-generate. We do need an initial charge to get going on that, which is import ed . We already do import much smaller quantities from Canada , so w e know how to do this.
Yes, and tritium is absolutely something that we are familiar with. We understand tritium. We know how to regulate tritium .

Q31 Why should it not be in this statement to guide developers , that they have to consider this when they are considering developing these schemes? We have talked about wanting to strengthen other elements of the NPS in terms of water . There are e xisting regulations on water and flood risk , so could we take that out of the NPS? Are we doubling up on regulation in some areas and then in other areas , such as radioactive material, we don’t seem to have any coverage at all?

My understanding—and we can confirm this— is that the policy statement does include tritium when it talks about radioactive substances generally, because tritium is just another radioactive substance.

To go a bit further on that , under the Energy Act 2023 the EA and the HSE regulate the production of fusion energy. The transportation of radioactive substances is regulated by the Office for Nuclear Regulation, so there are an existing set of regulations around that transport. I t is not that it is not covered ; it is just already dealt with in the regulatory firmament.
That is our third regulator now. We are starting to make a small spaghetti bowl of regulation.
It is the same for any transport of radioactive materials.
Q32 You have talked about novel waste and there are some quite unique processes here. Does the NPS fail to address the unique radioactive concerns about this technology?
Not in my view.

No . Again, the development consent order is just the first stage. Our permitting regulation and HSE’s regulation of the safety are the absolute ly vital elements there. As I say, w e are developing, along with the technology, the skills around what those novel wastes might look like. DESNZ fund s us to develop our capability and capacity as the technology changes and becomes more complex.

It is important to understand that, as Jo says, this deals with development consent. We still have to produce a safe design and get that design approved through the regulators . In doing that , the onus is on us as a developer or any other developer to demonstrate that all the hazards have been managed to the position of being as low as reasonably practicable. That is entrenched in UK legislation , in the regulatory model for the UK, so that is covered. It is not that it is absent.
Q33 When things go wrong—if things go wrong—who w ill bear the radiological third-party liability, and how w ill parties affected be compensated?

There is still work to do on that. In the fission regime there is a mature market for insurance and in certain instances there are indemnities. There is work to do , which the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero is leading on , to look at what is an appropriate set of regimes to enable the development of a vibrant fusion market , what the Government’s role in that should be and how we stimulate an insurance market, which is helpful. Of course we lead in the UK, having international nuclear plants that are insured from the UK. The risk profile is very different, we should remember, so it should be possible to get there. I think w e all start from the position that the developer pays , but when you are starting up an industry you will need to look at whether there are some changes just to get it off the ground.

I agree with everything Paul says. I t is worth noting we have already seen bespoke fusion-focused insurance funds launched. There was one launched earlier this year in the UK. It is an area that the DESNZ f usion s trategy draws out as a potential economic opportunity for the country. We do lead in fission; we should lead in fusion. All the companies we deal with believe this is a private sector insurable product.
Q34 If something went wrong at West Burton today , you are insured and you are all covered, just for the record .
T his is a G overnment project , so the answer is yes.
I think Sir Christopher is horrified by that.
I am , too.
He is not denying it.
Q35 Tris, you mentioned that you think the technology is near to commercialisation. What does that mean in terms of cost per megawatt - hour compared with other technologies?

T his is something I was talking to our member companies about , because clearly we are relying on their data. The publicly cited numbers in US companies are between 5 and 10 cents per kilowatt - hour. E xtrapolate that out and it is £35 to £75-ish per megawatt - hour electric. That will not be for first of a kind , but that is their nth-of-a-kind target. What you are talking about is a technology very comparable to the better end of low - carbon generation at the moment.

Q36 We are going to put in £2.5 billion over the next five years, which is only a fraction of what other countries are putting in. China and the US are doing probably double that over the same period. The rapidity of it , and the delivery, to come in at such a low point seems quite remarkable.

Yes, t o do that just on the UK contribution would be remarkable. Look, f irst , I would credit the UK. The UK Government spends more as a percentage of GDP on fusion than anyone else and I think the sector is grateful for that.
That is because we are small. We do not have the same population as China.

The Industry globally has had about $ 15 billion of private investment across the last five years or so . T here is a very significant amount of capital flowing into private fusion companies , and those are the companies that are targeting those kinds of numbers. There have also been PPAs signed with companies like Google and Microsoft, so globally we are seeing a very credible ecosystem emerging around the fusion off-take environment.

What all fusion companies are clear on is that if they are not economically competitive, no matter how strategically secure or environmentally beneficial they may be, they will struggle. Making sure they are designing very competitive products is absolutely front and centre of what these companies are doing.
Q37 Tris, can you repeat the figures you were quoting there for price ?

Yes, sure. The numbers quoted by FIA members vary , but between 5 and 10 US cents per - kilowatt hour — so , pulled through , £35 to £75 per megawatt - hour — are the kind of numbers that our member companies are talking about. They are the kind of numbers they are targeting for nth-of-a-kind plants.

I completely accept the point : i f we could do that for £2.5 billion of public investment , that would be wonderful and we would all be delighted, but it would be incredible. But t his is a global effort . W e talk about the other countries developing this: the Germans have a fantastic programme, the Japanese have , the US have, and Canadians are doing loads. It is that international effort that will drive this forward.
Q38 And t hat is at West Burton that you are expecting that?
No, that is private fusion companies — private companies with private plants.
Q39 Thank you for clarifying that. Paul ?
We don’t know. That is the short answer.
Q40 So Tris is saying £35 to £75 and you are saying you don’t know .

I am saying we don’t know. W e absolutely need the ambition that is demonstrated in the private sector. From a public sector point of view—we are utilising the £2.5 billion over five years, £1.3 billion of i t currently for the STEP programme, which will obviously expand—our starting point is very different. It is to say: w e have to get this to a position of competitiveness, not just technologically working but commercially working . F rankly speaking , the benchmark is large - scale civil nuclear. If we can be broadly on a par with that as we enter commercial generation we think we are in the right space , b ecause the hazard profile is lower, it is more globally deployable and therefore from an export potential that is the thing to go after.

You are right to mention China, by the way . It is going the proverbial gangbusters on this. There is genuine opportunity for the UK internationally and economically here. We have to grasp it and sustain it. I am glad to say that is what is happening at the moment , but we need to keep at it.

Q41 W hat are the key drivers to make sure we retain the international lead that you say we have in this technology? When we spoke a couple of weeks ago , we talked about the fact that we have a long list of technologies where we led and we threw those away. How do we avoid that happening again? What are the key ways of retaining that lead?

Thank you for that question. The first thing is sustained Government support. The planning environment is critical. This NPS is really important , but it is not just that ; we have to really push forward on a much more pragmatic implementation of planning policy i n a wider sense. It was g reat to hear the Chancellor’s commitment to that on Monday. We need a really good regulatory system that gives confidence to developers and the public, and they both feed off each other.

We have to have a sustained technical effort . Y ou really need a sustained, credible fusion laboratory, which we have in UKAEA. We sa w what happened in the fission programme when we let that go some decades ago , and we are trying to rebuild it, so we need to keep that going. We need a really ambitious public sector - led programme to bridge that investment valley of death. That is the STEP programme and we need to keep at it. We need a market mechanism—which the Government are committed to producing—to allow private developers to start working out what that economic delivery will be.

There are a few things. One thing that does not cost much is sustained vocal commitment : getting this into the region and talking about it internationally and making the UK the best place to do this. I am delighted to say that we have the UK - US global fusion summit coming up on Monday.

Yes, and you are being broadcast on BBC Parliament , so you have the opportunity to do exactly what you have just said is important. I hope lots of people are watching, hear your words and take them to heart.

Q42 Following on from what has just been said about being a leader in something, it is rare , isn’t it, for all parts of a technology to be sourced from one country ? I s there something that we as a country should particularly focus on that we are best at, where we can easily be a leader?

That is a superb question. The answer is yes, we do not want to try to do it all. There are elements of this technology , when you have a full plant , that we just need to have best in class from international suppliers , but there are some things that the UK can genuinely lead in. The first of those is the integrated design and development. The experience we have in the UK from the operation of the JET plant for the last 40 years means that we can do that in a way that I think very few other people can. That is exactly what STEP is about.

Underneath that you have the tritium fuel cycle, which is a huge opportunity for the UK, again building on that JET experience. We have robotics; we are absolutely world-leading in complex robotics at Culham. That is an opportunity that the UK should pursue. There is w hat we call breeding blanket, so how you get that tritium out of the lithium — n obody has done that internationally yet. We have some amazing engineering capability in the UK and we should be all over getting that front and centre. There are a number of other supporting technologies and materials development as well. So n ot everything, but there are some really important things for the UK to go after and lead in, and lead globally.

I agree. This is a global sector and the UK has a tremendous offering. We have a nice balance of capability in the national lab in the public sector. We also have some wonderful private companies doing things like HTS magnets, inertial confinement targets, and looking at things like robotics. There is a real press for the UK to make sure we are getting the maximum collaboration between the public sector and the private companies so that we commercialise those capabilities and ensure that we do not lose out on this national opportunity.

W e have seen sustained political support across multiple Governments and multiple Ministers over many years now, which has enabled global industry to have confidence in the UK and enabled UK companies to have confidence in our own operating environment. I think that will see us forward. Within that, the DESNZ s trategy published this March was widely welcomed by industry because it laid out specific tier 2 sectors where we could really lead and it laid out a pathway to develop them.

Looking across all sectors, when we are in a position where Government policy is stable, there is a strong pipeline of investment and industry is very well aligned to that, it is a great opportunity to sustain it and deliver together what the Government laid out in that strategy.
Q43 But should the Government focus on delivering test reactors or just on clearing the way for the private sector to deliver?

The Government are absolutely clearing the way. Everyone will see this long term being a private sector enterprise. There are lots of companies coming forward and I don’t think many people would want to see the entire sector owned and run by Government , but that does not mean the Government ha ve —
Q44 What about t est?

The Government ha ve done fantastic projects on test. If you look at Culham and everything that is down there, the legacy of JET, what is going on in the materials research facility, the robotics facility, there are really great Government capabilities , but it is now about that really difficult transition of those into private industry, and as much of that private industry as possible being in the UK. Whether that is UK exports or foreign direct investment—likely a combination of the two—that is the sort of hard yards of the next five years or so to put the UK in the best possible position.

We have talked about China, which is clearly spending a lot on this and trying to drive a programme forward. There has to be absolutely lockstep collaboration with partners in Europe, North America and beyond to make sure that we , as a whole , can develop the technology.

Q45 Turning to skills, which you have already touched on , w e understand that over - regulating the whole sector is not what you are advocating for. Is there a different way to give private developers confidence in the ambition for the UK Government with respect to fusion energy?
In terms of skills?
Yes.

I would say—and it builds off the last answer—the Government are taking and do have a stimulus role here. We have to start from the position that axiomatically there is no fusion market today ; it is starting, and so the Government’s role here is market making. There is a market failure, if you want to put it in economic s terms. We have to stimulate that through some demand, and what that does in skills terms is have that pull through the supply chain. So, h ere we are going to build that initial demonstration plant that pulls through critical suppliers — temperature superconducting tape , for example. That allows them to invest with confidence to build their skills base. It allows us to work with the universities to produce the right educational programmes. It also allows us to work with the regions to say the whole panopl y of skills that are going to be needed.

Without that pull through the system from the full - scale plant down through all elements of the supply chain, you will not have that critical mass , which we definitely don’t have in fusion technology, but we need it. If you put it this way in terms of skills, we need that pull through to generate it . That is where the stimulus role—
Q46 Is there a significant overlap with f ission or other energy technology?

There is a partial overlap. There are some areas — material s science, for example — where there is quite close parity. There are other elements , such as robotics , where I would say that fusion is leading and fission could probably take some lessons from what goes on in fusion. There are other areas , like plasma physics, that are completely different and unique. Then there are other generic technologies, such as application of AI, which offer huge potential for both sectors but in slightly different ways. There are some overlaps, including some supply base overlaps , but there are also some entirely different elements.
Q47 How nimble and quick off your feet are you to go into colleges, universities and schools to—

We are a lready doing it. I n the West Burton area , we have probably been engaged with about 16,000 people directly, including thousands of schoolkids , in pitching with our outreach team to the region. T here is a long - standing relationship between UK Atomic Energy Authority and universities across the country , and graduate programmes and so forth. This is already building.

Q48 What lessons have you learned from other technologies that have failed to put people and skills at the forefront of the planning of their new technology? What are you implementing to ensure that the same failures do not happen , and that you are not retrospectively scrabbl ing to try to find a workforce?

Trying to look ahead is the big issue , and it is difficult. It is quite easy—and I have almost just done it— to focus on the very deep technical skills, but what tends to be your chokepoint is broader - based skills. At the moment , we are probably screaming hardest in commercial expertise and project management expertise. At some point that will become, “What is the construction pinch point?” On the flip side, there is a huge opportunity for apprentice development and keeping jobs in the regions where these plants are developed.

It is really about trying to plot your skills demand signal to a degree of fidelity way ahead and then working with regional providers. The No. 1 thing is that the more certain and confident you can be that you are going to do it, the easier it is for industry to plan ahead and put the mechanisms in place.

It goes b ack to the discussion we had at the start about what it means for local communities . By s tarting at that grassroots level and h aving good engagement from the early days, bring ing communities in to listen to their concerns and what it means for their local community , you begin to bring people into the vision—whether it is this technology or other technologies—and grow th e desire for young people to go into STEM , with a view that they might have a career in fusion or fission or in regulation of those things . Engagement really is the key.

This is a people industry. The vast majority of work being done in the private fusion sector at the moment is people working to develop their products. It is not a steel - cutting industry . T hat is not where most of the money goes; it is in people. The overriding thing I have experienced when I talk to people joining fusion companies and those in fusion companies is certainty in the pipeline. We talked about universities. The UK has the most incredible university base to support this. There is a phenomenal breadth and depth of capability.
