T he underlying problem with the HE NPS is that it is based on the j et z ero strategy, which assumes that it is fine for the aviation sector to just hugely expand and that technology will come along and deal with it. There is no requirement at all on the sector as a whole, or any actor within it— any airport that is seeking expansion — to have demonstrated that th e se technologies are deliverable and affordable and can be resourced within the rest of the economy before expansion is permitted.
Thank you. Those we re very ful l answers and may have covered answers to some of our other questions .

Q114 I think that has largely covered what I was going to ask. I was going to ask whether the climate test was a tick-box exercise. Playing devil’s advocate, though, if the development can fit within a carbon budget that works, and can fit within the jet zero strategy, which was working, surely that is good enough?
Technically, yes, but—
Well, that’s okay, then!

Our perspective is that we should have a discussion, as an economy and a society, about what activities we think should be allowed to consume that ever-shrinking amount of carbon. If we are going to stick to our climate targets, we have to do that. If you look at what is happening in other sectors that are decarbonising, I can imagine they will be quite annoyed that aviation has basically been given, as was said, a “get out of jail free” card to keep expanding while other sectors are having to reduce.

It will mean that we have to speed up the roll-out of heat pumps and electric vehicles, electric blast furnaces, and other things in other parts of the economy. We at AEF think that we need a discussion as society about whether we want to grant those remaining, residual emissions to one sector that is, in many ways, a luxury sector with a lot of leisure travel. Maybe if people understood the nature of the carbon budgets, it would be technically, feasibly, mathematically possible, but the moral case is possibly not as strong.

Q115 I was going to ask what you think the test should be. I do not want to put words in your mouth, but you seem to be saying that we should be looking at all these big carbon uses and developing some kind of hierarchy. Maybe it will be that blast furnaces are easier to decarbonise than an expanded Heathrow, but we don’t know that yet. Well, let’s not put words in your mouth. What should the test be?

What we are doing here is assuming that the blast furnaces and other things will have to be done first. I do not think we have had a discussion about that. If you look at what we were trying to say about how complicated it all is, at the moment the test appears to be meeting carbon budget 7, which is the only one we have legislated for. It is not meeting carbon budget 8, because we have not legislated for that yet, and it is not meeting anything after 2050. If you stick only with the very narrow definition of the carbon budgets, you miss huge amounts of the carbon impact of the test.

I think it needs to be showing that there is a demonstrable reduction in aviation emissions happening across the board before it is given the go-ahead. That isn’t something that is pie in the sky, because if you believe the aviation industry, things like SAF and greenhouse gas removal are going to deliver, and zero emission aviation is going to come online. We are not going to say that isn’t true. It may well be true in the future, but the problem is that if you let that happen now, it is a risk, and I think it is a society-level decision to let that risk. We would want to see measurable targets of reductions in emissions before it goes ahead.
I am guessing the other two witnesses would broadly agree—okay. It sounds like we need blast furnace people before the Committee, Chair, so we can really explore this.
Yes. Obviously, these debates are true whenever we talk about carbon budgets and net zero by 2050, which seems to be rapidly coming towards us.

Q116 You have answered quite a few of the questions on carbon budgets and emissions projections, but I wonder if I could ask a specific question about the Climate Change Committee’s estimates. The Department for Transport’s own emissions forecasts are quite a lot higher than the CCC says they need to be. Specifically on the reductions required or the technology used, do you have any comments on what that says to us about the Department for Transport’s views on what the Climate Change Committee has perhaps assumed—or maybe they know something we don’t—about technology advances that are to come?

The CCC’s projections on the scale of technological developments, and consequently the space within the emissions budget for aviation expansion, is much more realistic than the Department for Transport’s. The CCC’s assumptions are also in some ways quite generous, but even with quite optimistic assumptions about technology, the CCC is really clear that there is just no space at all for net aviation expansion, at least into the medium term.

The DFT just seems to assume that you will have this absolutely massive, unprecedented scale-up of these very expensive, very resource-intensive technologies; that SAF will be delivered at an unprecedented scale. On the resource requirements for that alone, the Royal Society report found it would need 68% of the UK’s agricultural land. That is completely ridiculous. The impact on food prices, the whole economy and the cost of living would be completely ridiculous.

It is also a huge problem that DFT does not have any costed or resourced plan to deliver the carbon removals that underlie the whole jet zero strategy. It does not have anything approaching a plan to mitigate the non-CO 2 impacts, so that is two thirds of warming unaddressed. The DFT really has it the wrong way round. They just assume that aviation has to grow and aviation can grow, and that technology will come along to deliver it and somehow, across the economy, that will be dealt with. It is just a completely un-evidence-based approach.
Q117 Maybe they think we will eat a lot more chips than we currently are, or something like that. Any other comments on that?

One thing I wanted to say at the beginning of this session is that the DFT has released its aviation forecasts, which include emissions forecasts, and as part of the work we did for this report we looked at which of those were actually within our seventh carbon budget. Even before Heathrow expansion, every single scenario took us well over what aviation’s share is. That has to be a key framing when we are talking about this: Heathrow is not expanding in a world that has room to expand; it is expanding in a world where we are already significantly over. In the central case the DFT put forward, which is current trends for behaviour and flying, even in the best-case scenario, where sustainable aviation fuel meets the mandate that has been put in place—there are serious questions about whether that technology will arrive at the scale and pace that we need—it was still 30 megatonnes over the budget. That is the equivalent of taking something like one in 10 cars off the road for five years—it is a really high amount. I just wanted to make it clear that that is what we are talking about.

I know you are concerned about environmental mitigations, so I will add quickly that there is nothing in the HENPS document that makes sure that any of this stuff is actually delivered. We talked about the displacement; that is a modelling assumption. We talked about the terminal capacity being small, so that even if the third runway is built, it will not fill up immediately because the terminal is not available; that is also an assumption. None of it is written into the HENPS to say, “This has to happen.” The only way that they could get it to look like the emissions impact would not happen until later was to have these modelling assumptions, and there is nothing in it to say that they have to happen.

Q118 Let us turn to non-carbon emissions. Aviation, I think more than any other sector, produces emissions beyond the carbon emissions that have significant climate impacts. The draft HENPS says that applicants will have to provide only a qualitative assessment of the impact of non-carbon dioxide emissions, not a quantitative one. Do you agree with the reasoning behind that? If they are not required to quantify the non-CO 2 emissions, to what extent can the climate impacts of expansion be accounted for?

It is a serious flaw in the HENPS that it does not require the non-CO 2 impacts to be quantified. Again, that is echoed in the jet zero strategy, which also fails to do that. The DFT’s reasoning seems to be that there is too much scientific uncertainty, but that is just ridiculous. There is very clear scientific consensus that the non-CO 2 impacts of aviation are two thirds of the total, so two times the carbon impacts.

The even bigger underlying problem is that there is not really any effective mitigation pathway for those non-CO 2 impacts. Even if the SAF is delivered as planned, even if you get 19 million tonnes of carbon removals coming online by 2050, and the cost, resources and all that work, you are still mitigating only around a third of the impacts. It is such a huge problem. The DFT says it is too uncertain. It is not uncertain, but even if it was, the precautionary principle suggests that they should take that more seriously, not just ignore it.
Q119 In terms of the changes you would make, do you all believe that those quantifiable measures are there and could be inserted?
They definitely should be, and that should go along with some kind of plan to mitigate those measures.

DESNZ has a published recommended multiplier of 1.9 times. There is a bit of debate about whether it is 1.9 or 2, but DESNZ has a figure, which is used when it is doing other assessments. When companies are reporting their corporate emissions under SBTI targets, they use the multiplier to show the impact of non-CO 2 emissions. It does not make any sense to us that another Government Department says that you can quantify this, but that has not been used at all, even to assess it. As Ali said, they are not even assessing it, let alone mitigating it. This is a problem.

Things will change. As you know, in the EU they are now monitoring contrails, and there is an MRV going on at the moment. The science is coming all the time, and it is likely that that will develop into some kind of policy in the future, but again, there is nothing in the HENPS that says that you have to take account of that, even if the science does become clearer—and we agree that the science is clear enough. We do not see the reason for than when you have another Government Department that publishes a figure.

Q120 Ms Warrington, I am not clear about the figures for SAF that you quoted. I thought that CB7’s balanced pathway said that 38% of liquid fuels would be SAF by 2050, meaning that the majority of flights from an expanded Heathrow would still be running on fossil fuel after 2050. I think you used a figure that suggested that the majority would be running on SAF, but that is not the case, is it?

I was referring to the jet zero strategy, and I think the DFT has more optimistic assumptions about the level of SAF deployment, but I definitely agree that even the slightly lower levels that the CCC suggests are reasonable are still incredibly optimistic. That is still a really high level of SAF to get.
Q121 Just for clarity, I was quoting the Committee on Climate Change’s figures and you were quoting the Department’s figures.
Yes.
Thank you; that is helpful. We will now go back to net zero policies and economics.

Q122 As you have recognised, aviation is a huge contributor to our carbon emissions. How do you think zero emission flying technologies, airspace modernisation and improved aircraft efficiency will help to deliver the emissions reductions required to support Heathrow expansion, if at all?

I think they will have a relatively minimal impact. Zero emission propulsion technologies—hydrogen and electric planes—are going to be incredibly difficult. Even the Department for Transport, which is very techno-optimistic, recognises that the proportion of emissions reductions by 2050 will be just a few per cent. They are very, very far away.

The DFT relies more on efficiencies but, again, there are marginal gains at this point. Jet engines are already very efficient. The industry is already financially incentivised to optimise for efficiency. The Government talk a lot about airspace modernisation, but a key goal of that is to get more planes into the sky. I think the emissions reductions from all of those will be relatively minimal.

Since the jet zero strategy came out, the Department has reduced its level of optimism. Zero emission aircraft are assumed not to arrive at all within the periods that have been forecasted, whereas in the jet zero strategy in 2022, they were assumed to come online sometime in the 2030s. Similarly, the efficiency assumptions have also been downgraded by the Department, even in the four years since the jet zero strategy. The evidence is showing that we cannot rely on these technologies to arrive at the pace and scale that we need.

You only need to look at the aviation forecasts to see that the Government have had to go back and start remodelling that. They have already announced that they will be redoing the jet zero strategy in early 2027. We have quite a big problem with that, because Parliament has been asked to decide whether this HENPS is adequate before that remodelling has been done. It has just been announced in the aviation forecast that it is falling behind schedule. I can only imagine that that situation might not get better by next year, by which point it has been baked into the HENPS that we can go ahead with this thing. That is a real problem for us. You really have to go into the modelling of it, but there are some quite significant changes on airspace modernisation and efficiency gains that will be remodelled.
Q123 We have touched on sustainable aviation fuels. How important are those to the case that Heathrow expansion will meet climate targets?

As I said, if we are talking about a sector that is already massively over its budget, the question about sustainable aviation fuel is, how much can it limit the damage? Even if SAF arrives at the mandate level within the carbon budget 7 period, we are still expecting it to bring us tens of megatonnes over the budget. The only scenario we modelled that kept us within our carbon budget was if SAF arrives at the mandate level, but demand is held completely flat from this point onwards and does not increase. If SAF does not arrive, our emissions will go over our budget. It is critical, but we cannot rely on it.

Ali mentioned the precautionary approach. If we look at the SAF plants that have been funded and the SAF plants that have been built, and bearing in mind that every single economy around the world is now looking to use SAF because they want to decarbonise their own aviation, we cannot rely on importing it from anywhere. The amount of SAF that is forecast to be produced in the UK does not look very promising after about 2030. I can follow up with the exact figures.

The fundamental problem is that there is a very limited amount of alternative feedstocks available. There is not a huge alternative source on the scale of the aviation industry’s demand for kerosene. There is not the available agricultural land, the available waste or the available biomass. The more the aviation industry tries to take from other sources, the more we will potentially see problems elsewhere. We are already seeing that the sector is trying to lobby to reduce the sustainability requirements so that it could use fuels from crops. If they try to scale that up, it could have a gigantic impact on food security and deforestation, so there needs to be a lot of caution about SAF.
Q124 I guess from what you say that you don’t believe the UK is going to meet its SAF mandate.
It is already not meeting it at a very small scale. There is no sign that it will find it easier to deliver at a larger scale.

We were quite surprised that the importance of SAF was not drawn out as much as we thought it would be. When the Heathrow expansion plan was unveiled in January 2025, it was assumed that SAF would be the golden bullet. We have discussed this internally, and we think one of the reasons is because the DFT have looked at the figures and said, “Not quite sure we’re going to get there.”

If you look again at the aviation forecasts—I am sorry; I spent the summer looking through thousands of pages of tables and spreadsheets, so I just need to get this off my chest—the SAF assumptions have dropped from 50% in 2050 to 30% in 2050. W e think that SAF is maybe not playing the role that we thought it would because they are looking at the numbers and it does not make sense.

W e are not quite sure what happens post 2030. Things look okay now on delivery, but that is because it is mostly HEFA SAF . For example, I think Heathrow attracts some 17% , or even more than that , of the world ’ s global SAF suppl y. That is coming to Heathrow at the moment because they are paying huge incentives for airlines to uplift SAF from Heathrow but, o bviously , that will change . A s people have mentioned, oth er economies are doing that.

Beyond 2030, we really don ’ t know. The Government is doing some great work on the revenue certainty mechanism, trying to encourage second - generation fuel producers to build plants in this country. They a re small scale, but they will make a difference. But we are behind schedule with that as well : w e were expecting contracts to come this year , and i t looks like they will not come till the end of 2028. Y ou can see already that we are getting a couple of years behind where we need to be. I think that is why the assumptions have been revised down.
Do you want to come in, Barry?
Very briefly.
For the record, Barry is from the Environmental Audit Committee, which produced a very extensive report last year—or was it earlier this year?—on aviation and the environmental impacts.

Q125 Dr Pennington, I believe you were the lead author on the Tyndall Centre’s report. In that you spoke about the infrastructure for large-scale SAF production and how greenhouse gas removals should be operational prior to the infrastructure to expand the aviation sector. Is one of your main beefs with the HENPS that they have put the cart before the horse? That is fine if you can show you are going to do it, but don’t assume you are until you actually have the infrastructure in place to do it.

Yes. Beef, I suppose, is the word. Yes, that is the main point that we wanted to get across. I started working in this sector in 2020. I remember writing a review of all of the plants that were meant to come online by the time I had finished my PhD, and now it is six years later and none of them has. They have been delayed and closed around Europe, or the websites have gone dark. Again, based on the precautionary approach, we should make sure that we have the technology in place ready to operate before we even consider expanding. That was in the CCC’s advice on the sixth carbon budget—that we should not expand our aviation infrastructure until the sector is well ahead of its carbon targets, which we can say it is categorically not. It is behind.
Q126 You have already expressed a degree of scepticism about greenhouse gas removals. What level of them would be needed to compensate for a third runway at Heathrow?

I keep going back to the same point, but again, there is a slightly different question, because we are already projected to be over. We would already need additional removals to compensate for how much it is going over before the third runway, and then on top of that as well. When we talk about the carbon budgets, it is worth bearing in mind that at least when you look at carbon budget 7, they already have the removals baked in. Aviation’s sub-budget of around 146 megatonnes already relies on there being around 21 megatonnes of carbon removals throughout the period, 60% of which goes to aviation. A really large share of that is going to remove aviation’s so-called residual emissions.

At the moment, the global capacity for greenhouse gas removals is only 2 megatonnes per year in the whole world. Getting from that to 21 megatonnes just to meet carbon budget 7, plus whatever else we go over in the aviation sector—30 or 40 megatonnes—is just an astronomical amount.

The simple answer is that it would be effectively 41 megatonnes, because when you get to 2050 and you have 41 megatonnes of unabated emissions, we have nothing other than greenhouse gas removals to address those residual emissions. The difficulty in understanding the impact of Heathrow is in what we were saying about how the carbon budgets are measured, and because greenhouse gas removals are not accounted for under the aviation sector, so it starts to get a little complicated. We estimated that it is around 3.5 megatonnes extra per year from the Heathrow runway from 2050 onwards, so you have 41 megatonnes, possibly plus 3.5 megatonnes, depending on how you look at the modelling. Anyway, it is a big number, as Lois said, compared with what we have today.

It is worth adding that there is no plan for DFT on how that will be delivered, who will pay for it, what the technologies will be, the resource impact or the electricity requirements. There is currently one plant in the world doing even remotely large-scale carbon removals, and that is in a very specific location where it has access to geothermal power and underground storage. The idea that we could replicate that at the scale needed for this one sector—for this one airport—seems very based in fantasy, really.
Q127 Are carbon pricing and emissions trading part of the solution?
Well, yes—
Ah! I found it.

Can it be the solution? Again, going back to the aviation forecasts, one thing the eagle-eyed among you will have noticed is that the carbon price used under the jet zero high-ambition scenario was—I will just check my figures here—£432 per tonne. One of the reasons why the emissions have shot up under the jet zero scenario is that DESNZ has now come up with a much more reliable way of calculating what the emissions trading price will be in the future.

Previously, jet zero said it needs to be £432 per tonne, and that is how we will get to 19 megatonnes in our high-ambition scenario. DESNZ now says that it will be more like £125 per tonne, which is why the emissions have shot up so much. It is about £40 a tonne today, so there is still quite a long way to go until it actually reaches that level. The other thing is that there is no mechanism to ensure that the carbon price rises to meet what we need it to do—in effect, dampen demand by making it more expensive to fly. There is no mechanism at all available for that.

The other problem with emissions trading is that only about 25% of flights at the moment are facing a carbon price, because it covers flights only between the EU and the UK at the moment. The EU is trying to extend it, just marginally, but is avoiding going to America so that the Americans do not get angry about carbon pricing and taxing. Basically, 75% of the emissions are long haul, and they are not being priced.

On top of that, the long-haul flights are the ones more likely to create contrails, and we have also missed out the contrail warming impact. The ETS could have much more potential if the price was higher and there was a mechanism of guaranteeing a higher price, but there isn’t—sorry.

Carbon pricing is not our area, but price signals have not historically had much impact on demand itself. When you look at the group of people who are flying the most, 50% of flights are taken by the highest earning 10% of society. Those frequent flyers are not the people who would necessarily be put off by higher prices.

It is quite a blunt mechanism. It definitely has a role to play, and it needs to go up, but it does not necessarily seem fair that the cost of a tonne of carbon emitted by someone taking their first flight in two years is the same as the cost of a tonne of carbon emitted by a millionaire flying on a private jet. You would also want to make sure that it does not have a distorting effect across the economy. We need a much higher carbon price for aviation emissions, but you would not want that to, for example, make food or people’s daily essentials more expensive.

Q128 Someone in the Government said that we all have a right to go on holiday in the summertime. That is an interesting perspective given the wealth inequalities that you are talking about. Is the projected carbon price not incentive enough for change, in terms of trying to change the emissions profile? The numbers are moving around a little bit.

Last time, when we had the ANPS in 2018, they used indicative carbon modelling prices, which honestly blew my mind because either it costs a thing or it does not cost a thing. Apparently, it was just an assumed value that DESNZ used to appraise what the price of the carbon would be to keep the demand at a level where it would not exceed the carbon budget. Since then, there have been big developments at DESNZ in terms of working out what the carbon price is actually going to be as opposed to what it should be.

In the last round of jet zero , in the high-ambition scenario, they had to crank the carbon price up to £432 a tonne to keep the demand at the level they needed so that it met the trajectory. I am sure we will talk about demand management, but—you might remember I said this at the Environmental Audit Committee—carbon pricing is a form of demand management. Basically, you increase the cost of flying so that you reduce the amount of people who can afford to fly.

Obviously, if it is just a number you can stick in a spreadsheet, you can put anything in there. When you actually start thinking, “What does that £125 mean on your average family summer holiday ticket and what now does DESNZ think the price will be?”, it starts to be more real. Again, if you need £432 to deliver 19 megatonnes of residual emissions, and it is actually going to cost almost a quarter of that, you are not going to have the same dampening of demand. It is really complicated; this is the trauma of it.

Q129 On the point you are making about demand management , I was thinking, “Well, is this still really meeting the climate targets if all they are doing is buying these credits?” But you are saying it could reduce the demand to use Heathrow and therefore reduce emissions. Then the question is, why are we upgrading the airport only to throttle the demand because of emissions?
You have just had a “ Eureka! ” moment .
Thank you—you facilitated it!

Lois can probably answer this better than me, but that is broadly what the Climate Change Committee said in its advice last time round. So it said instead of demand management being through capacity constraint, which is basically what we currently have at Heathrow—demand is not exploding everywhere because it is constrained—we will stop doing that because we do not want to say that you cannot expand airports, and we will say that carbon pricing is effectively the demand management, but we will call it carbon pricing; we are not calling it demand management. Lois probably has plenty to say on that.

No, that was it. In their modelling, the CCC have used an assumption that it will become too expensive to fly because the aviation industry is bearing the cost of decarbonisation, whether through technologies or carbon pricing.

And the airlines will say they are also having to bear the capital cost of the infrastructure, so there are two sets of potential costs. If they are passed on to passengers, which came into some of the modelling, they will reduce the demand such that we might ask whether there is a need for a third runway.

Q130 Is that not then regressive? Instead of the demand being a constraint on the flights going out at a lower price, you are bumping up the price in order to get the same level of constraints. That means that the poorer people will be cut out of their family holiday, whereas the wealthier people will not. It is actually a regressive way of doing it.
Yes.
Yes.

Q131 While we are on this topic, some organisations have advocated for frequent flyer levies as a more progressive form of demand management, because the bulk of Brits who fly at all go once a year, and a small proportion—15% of British people—generate 70% of passenger demand. To what extend could a frequent flyer levy play a part in demand management in this context?

The problems with the technological solutions are really severe. It is not just that they are not working yet; they are never going to work at the scale needed. That means that demand management has to play a role. In order for this to be fair and acceptable to the public, it has to take into account how incredibly unequal access to flying is. As you say, most people fly rarely, if at all, and most people in the UK fly once a year or not at all in any given year. The more you go into people who are wealthy or extremely wealthy, the more you get higher levels of aviation—you get frequent flying up to the very luxury end with things like private jet use.

Something like a frequent flyer levy could really help to constrain demand. We produced a report with the New Economics Foundation last year that looked at a very administratively simple way to do that and target the 3% of people who take 30% of all the flights. That kind of policy would be really fair and popular, and it would increase tax take from the sector, which is incredibly undertaxed. It also really needs to include a tax on the fuel burned. Something like that could relatively painlessly take out a huge chunk of aviation demand, completely undo any perceived case for Heathrow expansion and increase tax take.

It would also take the strain off the technological solutions, because delivering a smaller scale of alternative fuels and carbon reductions would be easier. Most people would be unaffected, and it would avoid the kind of situation where any increases in prices that will have to come as a result of things like airport expansion and the costs of decarbonisation technologies are levied in an unfair way. Even airlines are saying that Heathrow expansion will hugely increase costs, so a sensible solution is to not have airport expansion. Tax the frequent flyers and protect access to occasional flights for ordinary people.
Q132 Can I ask the question the other way round? Is it realistic to expect aviation emissions to reduce without some kind of demand management?

It is completely unrealistic. The level of technology deployment is completely fantasy-based. Demand reduction would make the technological lift so much easier—it would be a safety/insurance policy. If at some point the aviation industry is exceeding its expectations and it has delivered all these amazing technologies and everything is fantastic, there is nothing to stop them expanding at that point, but that is so far from where are right now.

Yes. Emissions have to be capped. When we look at the technology solutions being so far behind, the only lever that remains is looking at demand. It does not have to be an either/or. If demand is capped or limited, technological solutions will come—they are coming—but it is about the timing. What can we do now to reduce emissions as we know we need to? That is about looking at demand, and then, when you get into the future, once the technology is there, that is when you can start to look at making more space.

Demand management is in the HENPS forecast. If you look at what I said earlier about the terminal capacity coming online, there is a modelling assumption in there that the third runway has been built by around 2035, but it does not fill up for three years because the terminal that goes with it to allow the passengers to use it has not been built. That is during carbon budget 6—even during that time, it will not fill up because there will be terminal capacity constraint. That thinking is in the modelling already. You basically cannot just let all the airports expand and all the passengers come, which goes back to the point about displacement.
Q133 If the key decarbonisation assumptions are not met, what do you think the contingency plan should be?

The Government need to think really seriously about constraining the total amount of flights, whether that is constraining demand or capacity, or putting maximum limits on emissions. To some extent, there is a contingency plan expressed in the jet zero strategy in terms of the five-yearly reviews. We think that every five years is not often enough; it would ideally be yearly. Also, we are at the point now where the technological solutions are demonstrably failing to be delivered, and face huge barriers to delivery, so the Government should be putting in contingency plans until the aviation sector is actually delivering decarbonised flights.
Q134 You have just said that the climate targets should be reviewed every year. Are the other panellists in agreement with that?

The progression towards the targets should be looked at every year, o r if, for example, a major sustainable aviation fuel plan or greenhouse gas plan is cancelled , t hat should be reviewed as well , because we have seen quite a few large-scale cancellations in the last few years that will have a significant impact on the quantity of SAF.

Yes, i f you look at the technology development scenario in the aviation forecast, even in the “ techno-optimistic ” scenario, which is equivalent to the jet zero high-ambition one , it is now 28 megatonnes, whereas it was 19 megatonnes in 2022. Even in four years, we have gone from 19 to 28, and that is now that the SAF policy has come online. If you leave it five years, we are likely to find then that we are actually 35 megatonnes behind, so I think there need to be earlier revie ws .
Q135 Thinking about the wider economic impacts of Heathrow expansion , a re there particular risks to l ocal biodiversity and broader biodiversity that you think we should be aware of?

Obviously, there will be local harmful impacts , with things such as protected areas, rivers, woodland and green space being lost. There will also be an increase in noise and air pollution over London. More broadly, there are the climate impacts that we are already seeing. Over the past year, there have been floods, wildfires and extreme temperatures. Allowing Heathrow’s emissions to push the UK over its carbon budgets would have a serious impact.

Going back to the broader economic point, the HE NPS analysis also made it clear that the overall economic impact of the third runway would be really harmful, with up to £62 billion in overall negatives. Of course, w ith the UK’s aviation sector, w hen increased capacity comes online, it very much goes to the people who already fly most often, who then tak e more outbound flights and export more tourism spend.

There is just not anything even vaguely resembling a convincing economic case for why this should go ahead. If we want jobs, we could get a lot more jobs for much lower emissions elsewhere , supporting the UK’s domestic economy rather than taking resources out of it . Given the risk to the climate, the lack of an economic case and all the local impacts, it is very difficult to see any convincing argument at all about why this is worth it. T he HE NPS does not provide enough of a safeguard against that.

I do not want to prejudge what is coming in the next session, but I believe that the health impacts of PM 2.5 are not monetised in the WebTAG assessment. We also think that they did not monetise the noise impacts identified by the ANNE and ANAS studies, which came out in the summer and basically showed that annoyance from aircraft noise occurs at much lower levels than previously thought. For us, th ose are big omissions: the emissions of PM 2.5 a nd the ANNE and ANAS noise levels . B y the way, those are both WHO-recommended levels, and they have just been left out of this. But, a gain, I know that you will probably talk about that in the next session.
Q136 Dr Pennington, is there anything in particular on biodiversity that we should know about?

I would just underline the effect that we know climate change is already having on biodiversity. Of course, there are the local impacts of Heathrow on the wildlife there, and there is a significant amount of infrastructure and construction that would need to be done , b ut, as the world is heat ing up, we are seeing a devastating impact on biodiversity worldwide, so that should 100% be accounted for as well.

Q137 On the biodiversity side, I am looking at the main obligation on SAF, which rises from 2% to 10% and then up to 22% in 2040 . I wonder whether you could talk about HEFAs—hydrogenated esters and fatty acids—because that is the most successful, yet it is being reduced over the period. Can you comment on what that is going to do, and the transition to what they are calling the third level of SAF?

On the HEFA side, as Al i already mentioned, there was a great Royal Society report that looked at the fact that this is a very finite resource. We also use HEFA to make biodiesel, which of course is being used in other transport sectors to decarbonise, so it is under a lot of competition. For that reason, there is a cap in the mandate as to how much of it can be HEFA, and it reduces, like you say.

The transition to these advanced sustainable aviation fuels—called power-to-liquid or eSAF—basically relies on high amounts of electricity, and they are very expensive to run. Looking at the future of the whole economy and the way it is going as we decarbonise, we are becoming very reliant on electricity—transport and other sectors are becoming electrified. That is where the risk comes. That does not mean that we should increase the HEFA cap, but that we should be realistic about what the technologies are and what scale they are going to arrive on. The power-to-liquid eSAF is looking very dry.

Q138 If I can tease out what this means, we are moving to a future of SAF that is as yet untested and extremely expensive. The reason that we are decreasing the amount of HEFAs is the impact on the wider economy. But is it not also because of the impact on food production, because we need that land for food production, and therefore, there are wider biodiversity and sustainability impacts here? I want to be clear on how this teases out in different ways.

In the SAF mandate in the UK , crop-based biofuels are not eligible to be used, so in that sense, it will not have an impact. On waste oils and fats, most of which are imported, it becomes a bit harder to verify when we are importing them from abroad.

Q139 So your point earlier about the future being one where everybody is trying to get their own SAF means that that supply will be reducing, and in the UK we are not allowed, because of the impact on farming, to switch over to producing it that way ourselves?
Yes. Crop-based biofuels would not be eligible under the mandate, so I cannot imagine a world where they would use them.

I will just point out that the DFT did a call for evidence earlier in the year about what the impact would be on food and land security if they did include crop-based biofuels. Our interpretation of why they did that was because they knew that the HEFA cap was coming in and that the HEFA supply was constrained. You cannot increase the amount of used cooking oil in the world—you just cannot do it to the extent that we need. In the absence of PtL coming online in those requirements, they were considering other options and one of them would be crop-based biofuels. We have not heard any update on it yet, but it has been discussed at least.

Thank you. That brings this panel to an end. I would like to thank you all very much for the evidence and the time you spent preparing for today. As I said, if you feel that there was something else you would like to add, please do write to us.

sessions.iT: A new Syria: assessing UK strategy in a transitional state
sessions.w: H.E. Hind Kabawat (the Syrian Government)

segs.tx: Foreign Affairs Committee
Oral evidence: A new Syria : assessing UK strategy in a transitional state , HC 578
Monday 7 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 7 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Emily Thornberry (Chair); Fleur Anderson; Richard Foord; Abtisam Mohamed; Edward Morello; Emily Thornberry; Sir John Whittingdale.
Questions 1- 6 8
Witnesses
I : Dr Reem Turkmani, Assistant Professor, London School and Economics Middle East Centre; Dr Neil Quilliam, Associate Fellow, Middle East and North Africa Programme, Chatham House .

I I : Charlotte Leslie, Director of the Conservative Middle East Council; Jon Wilks, Adviser to the Syria Britain Business Centre, Associate Fellow, Middle East and North Africa Programme, Chatham House, and f ormer Ambassador to Qatar, Iraq, Oman and Yemen and Syria Envoy .
I I I : H.E. Hind Kabawat, Minister of Social and Labour Affairs in the Syrian Government .
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Dr Reem Turkmani and Dr Neil Quilliam.
Q1 The Foreign Affairs Committee is beginning its formal inquiry into Syria. We are very grateful to have our witnesses before us—will you introduce yourselves?

My name is Reem Turkmani. I am an assistant professorial fellow at the London School of Economics and Political Science. I run a research programme about Syria, which has been running for more than 20 years.
I am Neil Quilliam. I am an associate fellow at Chatham House in the middle east and north Africa programme. I have run various Syria projects over the years.

Q2 As we come into the beginning of September, many of us become increasingly mindful of the 9/11 anniversary, the terrible deaths, and never forgetting the pictures of the aeroplanes going into the twin towers and the impacts on international politics. It is important for the Committee to officially mark that awful anniversary once more.

Let us move on to what has been happening to Syria. It has had a decade of conflict, huge displacement, the collapse of institutions and terrible human rights abuses. Given all that, I wonder whether our witnesses could begin by helping us to understand how much Syria may have changed recently, whether that can be seen as positive change and whether it is moving in a more democratic and inclusive direction. Dr Turkmani, do you mind beginning?

Sure. Thank you very much. Getting rid of the Assad regime is a very positive change, and the transition, despite all the challenges, has been smoother than anticipated, but I cannot say that right now we are moving towards democratic governance. While the transition created a big power vacuum, with the overnight change, the new authorities do not have all the tools to control the public space that were there before.

We have citizens pushing for more participation, more democratic institutions and more inclusive governance, and an authority that is trying to control the space, but we have a lot of space to occupy that no one has occupied before. I want to say that there is an opportunity—an opportunity to come up with new institutions, different ones that are more accountable, in which citizens really feel that they belong. That is an area where I think external help, particularly UK help, could be very important.

I have just come back from a five-week visit to Syria. I went all around the country. It is my sixth visit since the change and I can see that security has improved, but serious concerns about security—in some areas of the country, not every part—remain. There are concerns about the economy and about the collapse of the environment, which I would like to come back to in a later intervention.
Please do, but let us hear from Dr Quilliam first.

Basically, I echo what Reem has said. As a long-term analyst of Syria—I wrote my PhD on Syria centuries ago, and have studied the country for centuries—I find myself very much torn. That is because, as Reem said, there has been tremendous progress in the past couple of years. The country has made big strides, internationally in particular, and I think a lot of the successes—if we may use that term—have been quite surprising, so there are lots of positive stories to tell. Against that backdrop, however, as Reem described it, there is a big space that needs filling. There are lots of troubles, lots of obstacles and lots of concerns. That should not be a surprise, given that Syria has just gone through a very painful war, and it is not going to walk away in a very short space of time.

Q3 Certain obvious things are measurable, and the composition of Parliament is an obvious one. As I understand it, a third of Parliament is going to be appointed by the President. Do we have any idea of what the composition now is and how inclusive that might be? I do not think that anything is publicly available, or if there is, we have missed it.

Having just interviewed several Members of the Parliament, let me answer that. We have 210 Members of Parliament, and one third of them were appointed by the President and one third through semi-election from a college that was selected—
What about the other third?

O ne third of Members were appointed by the President and two thirds were elected. Every area had an electoral college from which to choose, so 400 or 500 people elected a certain number of people. However, if you want to look at representation, let us start with women—only 10% are women. There are also huge gaps in representing certain parts of the country, especially in the north-east, in Suweida and in other areas. However, I would not read the Parliament as—
Q4 The north-east being who?

The Kurds particularly. They have questions and do not feel that they are part of the central institutions. Even the Kurds who are there are not seen as people who come from that area, who represent the people who chose them; rather, they are seen as people appointed by the Government to represent them.
Q5 You talked about Suweida , too ; w ill you spell that out?

Suweida is almost politically cut out of the Parliament and central institutions. The Government are appointing some people from a Druze background to fill this gap, but if you go to Suweida , people there will not see these people as representative.
Q6 Again, for people who are watching and may not know, Suweida is an area that is particularly dominated by Druze.
It is absolutely dominated by Druze right now, and there is a huge rift with the central Government following the massacres in July of last year.
Q7 Are there minority groups that are well represented?

I would no t even say the majority feel represented. I have to stress that a Parliament post conflict cannot be fully representative. Even if you run elections, the results will not be really representative. The question is this: is that Parliament able to handle the transition? Does it have the tools and powers needed? The answer is no, because its power, as provisioned in the constitution, is limited. Its ability to make the Government accountable is very limited. Also, its byelaws, which have just been drafted, give a lot of power to the—

Q8 You are saying a lot there, so may I reel you back just a little ? I just want to understand . I hear the criticisms , but in the Parliament itself are Christians represented ? Are Alawites represented? Even if the team that has been put together cannot do as much as some people might think it should, is there a team that is widely representative of the peoples of Syria?

T here are Christians and Alawites in the n ew People ’s Assembly. Even the deputy head of the A ssembly is a lady from a Christian background. But I would not take that to say that the Alawites, for example, feel represented.
Q9 And you were saying that that institution nevertheless does not have the sort of power and authority that ideally it should do.

Exactly. It is much better than where we were in the Assad era, whe n the Parliament hardly played any role. It is an improvement , b ut the powers, particularly the ability of the Parliament to make the Government accountable , are limited. T he M embers of the Parliament —I have spoken to many of them — are not exactly totally loyalist when it comes to the central Government. They are not exactly O pposition, but they are saying , “W e are not there for them ; we want to serve the country, ” and they are willing to use the existing rules , as much as they can , to make the Government accountable and to play their role in drafting the whole new legal infrastructure that is needed for the transition.

Q10 I think we will go into this in a bit more detail, but do you mind just giving us an example of a lever that the new Parliament might have ? If there is a bit of power that they might be able to exercise , what is that? You say that they have very limited powers when it comes to keeping the Government —

They have the power to invite the members of the Government to listen to them about their plans, but there is nothing to make them accountable. But the Members of the Parliament have said they want to use th o se hearing sessions to press the Government. Most importantly, where they have more power is in drafting new legislation . So they want to learn more , because they still do not have the learning or the knowledge needed about how to draft new laws to ensure that we come up with accountable governance and accountable institution s that are really fit for a country under transition.

Q11 Th at leads us on to the next question . In what way do the Syrians want help , and in what way can Britain help? I was struck to hear that President a l- S haraa was talking about wanting to follow the Rwandan model, which was not very encouraging — I just wondered where we were. A re there things that Britain is doing or could do , or that they would want us to do? What are we talking about? I include D r Quilliam in this .

T here are lots of areas where the UK can support. Again, to echo what Reem said, there is a Parliament that does have some capacity and has the byelaws in place, but there needs to be training and an exchange of experiences between different Parliaments to embed the institution. Generally, across the board, the institutions that have been filled—both the pre-existing ones and the new one that are being put into place—need serious and significant capacity building.
Sir John is very keen on us having joint hearings of Select Committees; perhaps we should have a joint hearing with a Syrian Select Committee.
That may be a little premature.

There is a dearth of capacity within the state institutions, and that is really where the UK can support. We can identify and talk about the different institutions, but a lot of this is new—as Reem said, what you have in terms of a Parliament is very different from what you had under Bashar al-Assad.

Looking more broadly, there are very few democratic Houses or Parliaments in the region—for example, Saudi Arabia has the Shura Council, but that is 100% appointed—so Syria has the chance and the opportunity to develop and embed that. The fact that we have a partially elected Parliament is very positive, but parliamentarians, and the institution itself, need support, and the breadth of experience that the UK can bring to bear.
Q12 Could you give us some examples of the sort of thing that Britain should be doing, to bring it to life?

For example, at the moment, there will be a Foreign Affairs Committee established by the byelaw. It is about co-ordinating and working with that new Foreign Affairs Committee, and sharing the experience that you have directly.
There we go .
Go for it!
That is very real and tangible.

There are constraints around some of the byelaws. The extent to which Ministers will be called before Committees to be held to account is not clear to me—that is a very grey area—but this FAC could certainly teach the new one and perhaps share its experience of what that looks like, how it might shape up and all the procedures behind it.
And get some ideas for how to do it better.
T his is a new institution , effectively .

There is a great willingness to learn; for example, some Members of the Parliament went to Jordan to learn from the Jordanian experience. I think they would very much welcome the idea of visiting here to see how the Committees and hearings work, and to go into the Chamber—that would be beneficial. Certainly, a visit by Members of the UK Parliament to Syria would be very beneficial.

To add something else about what the UK could do, one area where the UK is already doing very well is moving from humanitarian support towards economic recovery by supporting the agriculture sector, which is the key economic sector in Syria. However, there is a gap there. Right now, Syria is facing tremendous environmental issues. That is not just an environmental and economic issue, but a security threat. A few days ago, a Member of this Parliament, Adrian Ramsay, said in a UK Select Committee meeting that environmental collapse in the UK should be seen as a national security threat. That is in the UK. Imagine the case in Syria, a country that relies on agriculture, but where the temperature is rising at twice the international average rate. Most of the industries in the country depend on the agriculture sector—
Q13 Sorry, the temperature is rising at twice the international average rate?
It is , in the whole of the middle east.
Q14 What was the next bit you said?

In recent research we conducted on the value chain in the industrial sector, it came out that all the industries start from agricultural products, so any collapse of that sector would have a cascading effect on the economy and on livelihoods.

Also, the research that we conducted recently into worldwide conflict drivers, with support from the Foreign Office, shows that climate change is increasingly becoming one of the accelerators of conflicts worldwide. It does not cause conflict on its own, but it overlaps with other issues. Especially in areas like Syria, where we have weak capacity, weak governance and an inability to adapt, it intensifies conflicts and the chances of displacement, migration and so forth.

Although the UK currently has an element about climate adaptation in its support under the agricultural sector, I think that climate adaptation should become a whole new line in the UK’s support to Syria. That would increase its ability to adapt and mitigate, help it to produce its own knowledge about this, rather not just using imported knowledge, and help us to see this as a climate justice issue. Syria contributed very little to the international climate crisis and it is unfair to leave it to face the consequences on its own.
Q15 That is a really important point, but is there another problem when it comes to access to agriculture? Is there a problem with unexploded ordinance or that sort of thing?

Absolutely, there is in some areas, especially in the northern countryside of Homs, where there are still many mines and we still hear stories about farmers being killed by them. There is a lot of work that would certainly help to regain lots of those areas.

There are also important areas where we have water. One of the consequences of climate change is that droughts are becoming more frequent and longer. Competition over water resources is intensifying, and some of the water is on land where there are lots of mines.

Q16 Before I open this up, I have an important question—I do not know if it is answerable or not. It is important for the international community to have some way of measuring progress. How can we measure the transitional Government? Is it being successful in building robust institutions while being representative? At the moment, in these early stages, it is great—"It’s not Assad; it’s great!” But in the next stage, how do we move beyond—to use a fashionable phrase at the moment—the vibes to something that can be measured? Is there an answer to that?

That takes my mind to those horrible things, KPIs. You need to have some massive tracking document with KPIs that are being hit. Everything at the moment is very much ad hoc and based on different testimonies.

How do you see the balance across the piece? The word uneven always comes to mind; it is one of those horrible words, but progress is clearly very uneven. One would have to devise, probably using AI, a very complex set of measures and then you would have to feed into it on a regular basis.

I would also add that, right now, there seems to be a tendency to measure the progress based first on traditional security measures, but also on what you see written on the papers and the official statements made. We need to go beyond that.

We should see progress in terms of the citizen-state relationship. Is it improving, and do the citizens feel that it is a state they belong to or are part of? Are they contributing to the making of a state that they can belong to? That is where long-term stability lies. In some areas—take the north-east, where the Kurdish majority reside right now—that is not how they feel.

It is important to continue to talk to people to understand the change and how superficial it is and really go beyond what you hear in the statements, especially about inclusion. Ask people how they feel, not what the Government say they are providing.

Q17 We met some Syrian refugees when we were in Lebanon, and we asked some women, “What would help you to go back?” They said, “We want to be safe, and we want education for our children. There are no schools functioning at the moment, and if we went back home, we would not be safe.” That is quite an interesting perspective, and it is very different from the way the Government are talking about Syria and the importance of progress.

It is very easy to be seduced by all the international successes that we read about. That is where a lot of attention and focus is, for example Sharaa attending a G7 meeting. All those things are really well broadcast, but we need a much better understanding of what is happening at a much more local level.
T hat leads to another important point: the way to know what people feel is to be there, so I would argue for a stronger UK presence inside Syria and I would think about opening the embassy again.

I am being warned that we will run out of time if we are so expansive, although it is very interesting—I am sure this will come up again. We ought to move on to Abtisam; I think her questions follow on from what we have been talking about.
Q18 Dr Reem, you mentioned that 10% of the composition of Parliament are women. We know that one was previously appointed by the President, but were the remaining elected into position?
Five were elected and seven were appointed by the President.
Q19 So that is less than 10%. Do any of those women have responsibilities in the current Parliament?

Yes; one is the deputy head. I think the other responsibilities are still emerging. They seem to be very serious about their role. They see their success as the opening for more women to come in the future. They want to be seen as successful not because they are women, but because they are bringing a substantive, meaningful contribution to the Parliament.

Q20 Following on from that point, what specific actions or opportunities are available to encourage more participation—not just the numerical aspect in the Parliament, but the grassroots involvement of women getting engaged in politics in Syria?

We need to support the women who made it to the Parliament and build their capacity, including their media presence, but also protect the overall space for women stepping into politics in Syria, particularly the virtual one. It is being used to attack them. My friend Rola Roukbi just gave a speech, for example, at the Security Council, in which she was critical of the Government, and vicious attacks came not from the Government, but from the populists on social media who made threats to her life. How we control that space to make it safe for Syrian women is a big question right now.

Q21 We spoke to a number of women in Lebanon as well, and they said very similar things. They were not entirely confident about the process and what it would mean for their involvement. They saw it as an opportunity, but they were very worried about what it could mean for them to speak up against the Government or challenge any different ideals. We spoke earlier about the UK perhaps helping Syria. Is there any support we could offer in terms of gender involvement and becoming more inclusive in the political landscape?

Absolutely. To stress meaningful gender inclusion, I would put three lines under “meaningful”, and not just have women appointed. In the north-east, there has been a lot of gain, and now it is being lost in the recent integration. For every position, they used to have two men and a woman. Now, because they are being integrated in the central Government, it is mainly men who are taken on board, so we are making losses. I mentioned the north-east because that is an area where the UK have some influence and they can use that right now to say, “No, we cannot go back on the gains that were made on women’s participation, and we hope that that would present a model that can be replicated in other parts of the country.”

Q22 Thank you so much for seeing us today. We have many Syrian refugees in my area of London whom I know well—I am sure they will be listening in. I want to talk about wider peace in the region and the role of Israel at the moment. The Syrian Observatory has documented 53 Israeli attacks inside Syria during 2026, 49 of which were carried out by ground forces, and there were some incursions in established positions beyond the 1974 ceasefire line. I will come to you first, Dr Quilliam: what are Israel’s objectives in Syria, and how have they evolved since the fall of the Assad regime?

I think we have to look at Israel in a new light since the fall of the Assad regime. I don’t think we need to think about it prior to that. It has made very clear its opposition to the Sharaa Government and its support for the Druze community. It wants to extend its influence inside the country. Initially, after the fall of Assad, it made military interventions to downgrade weapon stocks—that was a very clear goal.

I think Israel wants to keep Syria in a state of—I am using very nice words—flux and disorganisation. It has a goal to undermine the authority of the state and stop the state from extending its authority right across the territory. In the interim, for the time being and I guess going forward, Israel will want to hold on to the additional territories that it took very early on in this new phase of Syria.

Personally, I see Israel as a destabilising force. When one looks at Syria, nearly every country in the region wants it to work and has come in with what I would describe as a bear hug—trying to make it work. There are two countries that are not doing that: one is Iran and one is Israel. I do not think Israel sees a unitary, strong, together Syria as something that serves its interests.

Q23 You mentioned the Druze community. Israel are saying that they need to be there for protection of the Druze community. Are they using that as an excuse for their actions more widely? Do the Druze community see them as a protector? Is it a valid and useful position that they are taking there?

Syria has been permeable and highly penetrated since prior to the civil war, but certainly during the civil war. Israel has traditionally in different countries backed specific, individual groups. It has its own Druze community, which places pressure on the Government. We cannot just use the word “Druze” to refer to everyone; it is like using the word “Briton”—we are all very different. There are components and elements within the Druze community that are receiving support from Israel and do so because they want to build out either their own federal structure or a much stronger autonomous structure, but that is a small component.

To answer your question, yes, Israel is using this as leverage. I do not think that it would necessarily need to use it if it did not want to. It can still hold on to and occupy part of the Golan and beyond, going up to Hermon. As we saw a couple of weeks ago, it carried out attacks against an airfield in Idlib. I do not think it needs an excuse, but it certainly gives it an anchor through which it can purport its support.

To follow up on this, which I fully support, there are two things that the UK could do. That attack on the airbase was one that Turkey wanted to use, so, in a way, Syria is becoming an area where Turkey and Israel are testing each other’s red lines and confronting each other. That is very dangerous for the whole region, and that is where the UK can come and play a deconflicting role. Secondly, given all that Israel is doing—continuing to occupy the Golan heights and now going and taking even more Syrian land—the current ban on trade with settlements that the UK Government are considering should also extend to the settlements in the Golan heights.

Q24 What situation is the Syria-Israel security agreement in now? What are the likely pressures from the international community—maybe neighbouring countries or others, like the UK? What are the main barriers to having that agreement?

The two Governments held their meeting a couple of weeks ago. The file very much sits in the hands of the US. It depends whether the US puts the pressure, makes them come together and makes them work. The Syrian position has been fairly clear from early on that a security agreement or a security framework is very much in its interests. The lack of interest or the paucity in wanting to push forward with that sits with Israel. The way through that is that yes, the international community and the UK can support and encourage both sides to work together, but I really think that sits within the purview of the US President and his team.
Q25 Is there pressure from within Israel? Do the population want to see this agreement? Is it discussed or talked about within Israel?
I do not think it is a big issue. There are other, bigger issues that are on the minds of Israelis. It is not prominent.
Q26 I am going to ask a few questions about Türkiye. What do you think Türkiye sees as its role in shaping Syria’s security agreements?

Turkey clearly feels a strong alignment of interests with Syria. It is very close to this current Government and so will want to match and mirror its security framework—its security co-operation. There was concern in the early phases—if we discount Israel in this part of the conversation—that there would be competition between Turkey and some of the Gulf states, particularly the UAE or Saudia Arabia, but there has been some alignment and clear interest there. Turkey sees Syria as falling within its purview, but that is not to say that Syria is not an independent state that wants to have an independent position and will want to hedge and balance out that relationship.

I would support that, but I would like to add how Turkey is shaping the internal security scene inside Syria, particularly with it backing the battles against some of the Kurdish factions in the last six or seven months. That played a role in the calculations made by the recent Kurdish leaders when they settled the agreement with Damascus last week. The agreement is seen as very unequal. It appoints General Mazloum Abdi , the leader of the Syrian Democratic Forces, as an adviser to the President. People are asking, “What is the power of an adviser? After 14 years and all that has happened, that is what you get?” They do not have a legally protected presence in the Government in any shape or form.

When we asked them about their calculations and why they accepted that compromise, Turkey came up. They said, “We knew that if we went into a battle, it would not just be a battle with the Syrian forces. It would also be with Turkey. Could we afford that?” The whole Syrian scene is being influenced. It is good progress that they reached an agreement on security—on how to integrate the Syrian Democratic Forces into the Syrian security scene—but it is not matched with political integration. Turkey needs to know that if the Kurds are not meaningfully integrated politically in Syria, in central Damascus but also in other areas, there will be no long-term security, because so many Kurds resent the current arrangements.
Q27 What is the political representation of Kurdish communities, aside from that adviser role to the President?

Hardly anything. There are no roles in Government. In the previous Government that was put together, the Minister of Education came from a Kurdish background, but he was not somebody that the north-east Kurdish community nominated. They have nothing legally protecting them. They have only some cultural rights now being protected, such as the Kurdish language, the right to teach it and so on. That was the only advancement they made—nothing further than that. They feel excluded from the decision-making power inside Damascus.
Q28 Thinking about the peace process between the PKK and the Government in Türkiye, do you feel that those developments in Syria can help ease the tension between the PKK and the Turkish Government?

I think they do, but there is a fear among the Syrian Kurds that Turkey does not want them to make political gains that then become precedent for the Kurds inside Turkey. They will create a new model and then have to replicate it. That is why they would rather keep them excluded. Other than that, there has been confusion among the Kurds I spoke to about what is going on within Turkey or even in Syria, because we still do not know the details even of the agreement in Syria. That raises even more questions about the content.

I might flip that, though. I think that the progress made between the PKK and the Turkish Government has had a bearing on what we have just seen taking place with the SDF and Mazloum Abdi —that absorption. That is a part consequence coming from Turkey itself.
Q29 But the absorption does not include women fighters, as we hear in the media.
That is right.

Q30 I am sure that other people have already got this, but there is this issue about women fighters, which is the sort of thing that hits the media. You are also saying that there was equal representation in the democratic structures among Kurds in Syria, because each post had a man and a woman doing it.
Yes. In every seat, they would have two co-chairs: one woman and one man.
Q31 In each seat?

For chairing any office. Even for the leadership of the Syrian Democratic Council, the co-chairs were chosen so that it was one female and one male, and they replicated that model in many of the top positions they had.
That is very interesting; thank you.

Q32 Can I ask about Russia’s position? Russia was obviously the primary backer of Bashar Assad and has the two bases in Syria. We understand that an agreement has been reached and Syrians will, to some extent, take over those bases. To what extent do you think Russia still has influence in Syria, and how important is it that it retains a military capacity, particularly at the naval base for access to the Mediterranean?

It does. There were those negotiations and agreements yesterday, and it retains some military capacity and capability in the country. It is clearly not what it was prior to the collapse of the Assad regime, but Sharaa has been quite adroit at hedging as best as he can and managing that relationship. In the early days after the fall of Assad, there was a lot of speculation that Russian influence would vanish overnight, as would Iranian influence, but they have long, deep ties to the country that are still present, so they still have degrees of influence.
Q33 So will Russian naval vessels still be able to operate from Syria?
Yes, they will.
Q34 Does the presence of Assad in Moscow affect the relationship, or do the Syrians just accept that that is the way it is?

I think that the Syrians just want to move forward. Assad is not the central point right now. Russia has far more leverage over Syria because of the wheat; Syria still imports a lot of wheat and oil from Russia.
Q35 So to some extent there is an economic necessity to maintain that relationship.
Yes, they heavily depend on it.
Q36 Although Syria used to be the breadbasket; Syria used to grow wheat.
Exactly. We used to export wheat. We still grow wheat, but we used to export it, and right now we have to import it. Ukraine and Russia are still two of the main sources.

Q37 One of the reasons Russia always gave for its support for Assad was that, if it was not Assad, it would be Islamic extremism. It cited ISIS very much as the alternative. We have clearly moved on a long way since then, but to what extent is ISIS still a threat in Syria?

It is still a threat; it still has a presence. We have seen a series of attacks over the past year, and some well - timed—or poorly timed—attacks during Macron’s visit, so it still has some capabilities. It obviously does not hold territory or have the same organisational structure from before it was struck.

As Reem said, this is a big canvas and a big space. The Government will do what they can to extend their authority and influence into those areas. We have to remember that Syria is, to a large extent, still very fractured. The Government do have reach, but there are groups that are beholden to them and were fighting with them that have just disappeared and gone into the ether, and they have differing loyalties that are not to the Syrian state or the Syrian people. I think we will continue to see sporadic ISIS attacks. They announced back in May, I think, that they are going to begin a new campaign, so they will be ever-present, waiting to puncture any security vulnerabilities that they can identify.
Q38 Without US support, do you think the Syrian regime is capable of resisting and preventing that?

This is where it really needs to draw upon the experience of the SDF. It really depends on how those forces are brought into the central armed forces, how they are deployed, and whether they draw on the extremely valuable experience that they have gained.
Can I add to that? ISIS thrives on recruiting people who feel very bitterly excluded, so the more that we help to build inclusive governance, the less of a threat there is from ISIS in Syria.

Q39 You talked earlier about Israel’s incursions indirectly into Syria. Obviously, one of the broader regional geopolitical issues is the Israel-Iran conflict. What is your feeling of the impact of that conflict on Syria? Syria has sought to stay neutral. Has it been successful in that? Do you have any view on whether that is sustainable in the long term, or is it just background noise to what is going on internally?

It is not a very big issue right now for Syria. It is rather neutral. Syria is trying to be rather neutral—more anti-Iran, let’s say. It does not want a confrontation with Iran, but Iran’s presence inside Syria has been weakened dramatically. Its only role now is what it is doing in Lebanon—that is the indirect way—but inside Syria it is much weaker than it was before.

I would second that. It is more background noise. Project Syria is huge and is consuming a lot of time and energy but, as Reem said, Syria is trying to chart a neutral course, focusing very much on the domestic side of things. The strange twist of fate is that it looks like one of the most stable countries in the region at the moment.

Q40 Obviously the Israel-Iran conflict and US involvement have impacted quite a lot of the GCC countries. You mentioned the bear hug that neighbouring countries were giving Syria. GCC countries are reprioritising money internally into their own rebuilding of damaged infrastructure and improving defence. Is that likely to have any impact on their commitment to sending money to, rebuilding or investing in Syria?

The instinctive answer is yes. A lot of commitments have been made, and a lot of MOUs have been signed, but we have not seen that materialise in any meaningful way. There are contracts. There is quite a lot of port development , and some infrastructure development. As we saw with Syria during the years of its war, there are a lot of pledges, but they have not materialised. Clearly, the Gulf states have to reprioritise. The issue of Hormuz is structural, so they are putting their money in other areas. That will have a diminishing impact on how they can support Syria.

Q41 Dr Turkmani, the Chair mentioned that Syria used to be the breadbasket of the middle east—it was a great exporter of grain. As Syria looks to rebuild and, I assume, hopes to become a regional power, as all countries do, what are the sectors that it has an opportunity to emerge in? You mentioned the importance of agriculture, but are there any other potential markets in which Syria could be a regional leader?

Certainly, restoring agriculture, because it relates to many of the industries that are the signature of Syrian products, which you can buy even here in the UK, in London supermarkets. They are excellent food products.

There is also an opportunity in that the Syrian desert is the closest desert linked by land to Europe. It could be a place where you build massive solar power plants to generate energy that arrives in Europe by cable over land, rather than undersea. You can compare it with the project that you had with Morocco, which was meant to feed 8% of UK energy. That was meant to be through very expensive undersea cables. With Syria’s desert it could be done all over land, so it would be much cheaper. That is a huge area where we can make use out of empty land, which can help to recover the economy and, if you use the right technology, can also help to recover the Syrian economy as well. That can be the right alternative to Hormuz. Rather than saying, “Let’s use Syria as a transit for pipelines for oil and gas,” which Europe is already transitioning out of, you can say, “Let’s use Syria as a source of clean energy.”

I would also look at tourism, which used to be one of the major sectors. Of course, we need increased security for that, but I just came back from a five-week trip to Syria with my family, including my son, who is sitting behind me today. We went through the whole country. I asked him at the end of the visit, “Did you at any point feel unsafe?” , and he said, “No.” So it is improving.

One point that I would really like to stress is that we need a UK presence inside Syria in order to know all this and to really understand what the people want, what they feel towards the state, and to be influential during this extremely important phase of Syria’s history. It is a critical juncture, and these two institutions that are going to emerge are going to last for some time. It is an important time for the UK to be present on the ground, through an embassy. Already, Denmark and Germany have established their presence; why cannot the UK follow, when it has opened embassies in other countries where the security situation is difficult, such as in Tripoli, Mogadishu and Baghdad?
