We do not know. I say that on purpose because I am really cross about it. What is the mechanism? The tech companies, supposedly, have written risk assessments for Ofcom. There is not an outcomes measure. They are completely not transparent. As the most senior safeguarding person in this country for children, I have asked Ofcom to see those risk assessments, and it has said no. I have threatened to use my data powers. I have statutory powers to get them, and it has said that it will attempt to stop me getting them.

One thing that I did want to ask this committee was for your assistance in this matter because I am planning to use my powers. If we cannot even see the risk assessments that may well have put these mechanisms into place—they may not have; we do not know—how on earth can we judge the efficacy of the Act? I will leave that one with you, but I am pretty furious about that.

Q4 I am sure we will have noted that plea for help, if nothing else, getting the legislative power to have access to those risk assessments. Can a regime of risk assessments, safe harbours and those sorts of things ever work effectively or do we need to legislate further to do better?
We need a couple of things. We need Ofcom to use its teeth. It has a lot of power. It needs to use its teeth. We need Ministers to encourage it and give it the air cover to do that.
We will come back to those in a minute. I am more interested in the structure of the regulatory regime.
Are you interested in any bit in particular?
I suppose I am, t o an extent, distracted by the Meta settlement in the United States. The US courts look like they have achieved a settlement that goes further than our legislation does.
Indeed, yes.

I am interested in your reflection on that. If it were possible to get that set of measures to apply to the UK and to apply to other social media companies, as well as the Meta ones, would that be an improvement on what we have through legislation?

I gave you a description pre-Online Safety Act of what children were seeing. I have been out repeating the porn work and I have literally got 625,000 responses from children. I have talked to children right across the country. We will be publishing in February. They are concerned about different things — things that the Meta settlement covers. They are concerned about functionality. They are concerned about being online for too long, not being able to cut down, strangers coming into their games and talking to them, what AI means for them and how it is affecting their lives. We saw that with nudifying apps.

We had hoped that the scope of the Act would be able to change and evolve to the new world that our children are living in. Believe me, it is new and different. As Children’s Commissioner over five years, I cannot tell you how different 2021 is from now. The concerns from children around the country are very different.

Yes, we should be looking at functionality in gaming, time online and curfews. We should be looking at all of these things. Why? It is interesting. Up here in Westminster, we have been having this debate about banning or not banning social media. It is a Westminster debate, and it is everyone doing their best. We will come to a decision. When I ask children, “Do you want a social media ban?”, their answer to me is always n o. I changed the conversation. This is right across the country, from Preston to Birmingham to Bournemouth. I have been everywhere this year asking this question. When I say to them, “Do you have any worries?” they talk about the terrible things that they have seen online. They talk about issues with gaming. They talk about addiction, needing to cut down. They talk about algorithms. I say, “Do you want the adults to protect you?” and they say yes. When I say, “Should the adults say that any company that does not keep you safe should not be allowed to have access to you?”, their answer is yes.

We need to be very careful about our language. There is an opportunity to engage with young people. Banning or not banning is just so simplistic. In terms of the Online Safety Act and banning social media, most children will think it is funny and irrelevant. The right conversation really does elicit a cri de coeur and a response of, “Please help”.

Q5 My final question, before opening up to others, follows that up. Should we prioritise the systems that the tech companies use, the algorithms, the use of addictive by design and the lack of design for age over banning? Is banning just a political win that is easy? Is there a more sophisticated and effective thing that children will buy into?

I have been challenged in one of these rooms before on whether I would ban. My answer always is, “If it is a simple binary and there is nothing else , at the moment with the levels of danger— ” .T hat is what people in this place are doing. They are trying to be responsible and protect children. Having looked closely and talked to my Australian counterparts, it is not a magic wand.

We absolutely need to prioritise systems. We need to look at children up until the age of 18 as well. I was in youth prison last week sitting with boys, and they were telling me about the radicalisation into violence that they experienced online at 17. They need protecting. We need to protect children, full stop.

Q6 Just to go back slightly, you have done extensive work on consulting with children. You have all that input. Are there particular groups of children for whom significant gaps in protection still remain ? With the Online Safety Act, are there groups that are outside of its scope?

I would say 17 and 18 year-olds . We have only talked about 16s and under. Just because you get tall does not mean you are not still a very young person. I would say the under-18s. Some of the most awful things I see are things such as c om sites, where children who might have mental health problems or be very vulnerable are persuaded into self-harming in front of other children online. They are often sucked in through TikTok. They are our most vulnerable.

Another group that I highlighted recently in my report on the Prevent duty is children who have been pulled into non-ideological extreme violence and obsession with violence. It is a small but important group. That is the group that is worrying our anti-terrorism police and others the most. It is where vulnerability intersects with childhood. That is where we need to look.

I still worry about girls. I know we are strong in our language up here about protecting women and girls, but there is not a place I go where I do not have a queue of girls talking about dieting material, comparing themselves online and algorithms. That is not going away. The boys will quietly tell you after. We looked at the selling of beauty and health products recently. I did a piece of research on this. Something like 45% of black children that we spoke to have been targeted with skin-whitening products.

Children are being targeted with health products. It starts with health products. For girls, it is, “Change your eyes”, “Get Botox”, and “Get fillers”. What 15 year-old needs that? With boys, it is often health products through to steroids. It is completely not allowed; it is illegal to be selling anything to under-16s. If you speak to an under-16, they will tell you that they are targeted all the time with products. I have done a piece of work. I am sorry. It is not very pleasant. What I am really saying to you is that there are vulnerable groups, but it is everyone.

Q7 You already mentioned that Ofcom has teeth and that the Government need to encourage Ofcom to use its teeth more. How effective has Ofcom’s implementation and enforcement of the Online Safety Act been in driving services to make the changes that they need to make to protect children? Do the services fear Ofcom or not?

We have some examples where Ofcom has been very effective after the fact. It is finally getting involved with nudifying apps—the Grok issue—and it is working on age verification with pornography companies. I am really pleased that it has asked me to provide a group of young people to help it as an advisory board. There is an openness there.

I have a couple of concerns. One is that, if Ofcom is going to be the vehicle to protect our children through the implementation of the Act, we need them to be getting ahead of the harms. I do not think it has. When I talk to children around the country, what is worrying them are things around AI. It was the nudifying apps. There are new harms, and we need Ofcom to be getting ahead of those. I do not think it is.

We all had hopes, but when government changed in the States, it felt like there was almost a pulling back here. I can only say it felt like that; I do not know. What I need for children is for Ofcom to be incredibly robust and not pull back. I do not just want to criticise it because, frankly, it is Ministers who drive and give the air cover for Ofcom to be strong. We need our Ministers to be really strong in asking Ofcom to protect children. How effective do I think it has been? It has not been effective enough.

It is interesting that you speak about the States, because we are watching with great interest the TAKE IT DOWN Act and how the US will use the Federal Trade Commission to implement fines should there be breaches. Will that strengthen Ofcom’s hand or encourage it to go further and faster, if we start seeing those fines being issued, if you are saying that we are being influenced by the US?

I hope so. I led a roundtable at UCLA just last year and I was talking to people who are involved, as we are. I do feel sometimes that where they go, we follow. There is the opportunity. Ofcom should be fining. It should be more robust. When I read the children’s code, I was so disappointed. It felt like it was a technical document written for the companies, not a document written to every child in this country about how Ofcom was going to try to keep them safe. That is what it should have been.

Yes, I want it to use all its powers. I would like to see some big fines and I would like to see it be ahead of the cases and ahead of things as well, because it knows. It will need the air cover of Ministers. We know we have had turbulence. I am on my seventh Prime Minister and multiple Ministers. We need some really focused ministerial energy on keeping children safe.
Has Ofcom been cautious because it does not believe it has cover from Ministers?
I do not know. How would I know? I do not know. We have had lots of change politically and Ofcom just has not used its teeth.
Q8 Do you have any comment about the potential role of the ICO? I was interested to hear that it is contacting Meta about the outcome of the case. Does it have a significant role to play here?
Do you mean the Information Commissioner?
Yes. Might it have teeth that Ofcom is not using?

It is good when the Information Commissioner does things; it is good when the Children’s Commissioner does things. We need Ofcom, which is the regulator whose job it is, to make sure this is implemented.
I am not wanting to let Ofcom off the hook. I am just wondering whether there is a multi-faceted approach to this.

I would like to see the new Prime Minister really commit to keeping children safe and making sure that the ministerial team does that. Whether it sits here or there, we need someone in charge to give proper air cover to Ofcom and to demand that Ofcom does their job and gets ahead of it. If we are going to use Ofcom as our means of implementation and keeping children safe, it has to do better.

Q9 You have given us such interesting answers. Thank you very much indeed, Dame Rachel. I just want to look at some specifics. I have read your response to the codes that have been published and you have just said that the code seems to concentrate more on the companies and not on the children. You have said that Ofcom seems to be more worried about the cost to business of enforcing the Act and it gives that disproportionate weight.

You have called for children’s voices to be part of the process in the enforcement of the Act. How would that work? You have gone around and listened to thousands of children. How would you like Ofcom to move the balance in favour of children and create this process?

There are so many ways, but a simple straightforward thing that I have offered the last three Ministers and Ofcom is to write to every child in the country to explain the children’s code. I write to children. I speak to everyone. Just do it. I have said, “I will do it for you”. We will write to them, tell them that the children’s code is meant to keep them safe and then go back every year and ask, “Do you feel safer?” It is a simple, straightforward thing that Ofcom could ask my office to do or could do themselves. I could help them. We do not need to overthink it. Getting an advisory board was a good start.

We do not need to do everything that children tell us they want. We need to listen to them, but we are the adults and we need to try to make good decisions. It is that listening piece about their genuine experiences. The children’s code was a massive lost opportunity. At the time, I said to the Minister, “The children’s code should be for children. Write to them and explain it to them. I can get you a letter that will go into every single child’s pigeonhole in this country”. That is a simple straightforward one.

Q10 We have talked already about the American judgment against Meta and addictiveness. In your response to the code, you said that Ofcom must reconsider its decision not to include persuasive design features in order to try to limit the amount of time that children spend online. From that comment, you obviously do think that Ofcom does have the power to be able to affect addictiveness. How should that be enforced?

When the Online Safety Bill was being drafted, redrafted or redrafted—it went through many iterations—I tried to get some of these things in. The response I got was, “No, this will be a Bill that can adapt, grow and change to what is needed”. I took that in good faith and hence my response. Children’s experience is here and now. Children’s negative experience is online. It is not just the content. It is the features. It is the addictive features. It is the length of time that they are spending on there. It is the algorithms. It is those things. Ofcom should absolutely have those powers.
Ofcom has come before us and said that the Act does not give it the power to look at addictiveness. Do you agree with it on that?

It might have some particular legal argument. I do not know. I have not looked at it. At the inception of the Bill, we were told that we could go back for amendments and make changes. That is what I want to see, if Ofcom does not have that now. It is all to play for, frankly. We were promised an Act that could evolve, develop and change to children’s needs. That is the important point.

Q11 When it comes to categories, there has been a lot of concern that Ofcom has concentrated on the size of the companies and not on the risk that they pose. We know perfectly well that smaller companies can be just as risky as larger companies. Is that a problem in the Act or is it a problem in Ofcom’s enforcement of the Act?

I would say it is Ofcom’s enforcement of the Act. I am sure it would have an argument against that, but the scope of the Act ought to cover that. If we are going to keep children safe, we cannot say, “You have to be a multi-billion-pound tech company to be covered by this”. Ofcom’s argument was about the burden on the company, was it not, but what burden to keep children safe?

Q12 Lord Tarassenko : I am going to declare a conflict of interest, not a financial one but one that is relevant especially to my second question, which is that I am working with the Raspberry Pi Foundation to introduce a level 3 qualification in schools to teach children about data science and AI. We start our first pilot of an EPQ in about a fortnight’s time.

I want to discuss with you the pace of change of AI versus the pace of change in legislation. You have been quite vocal about this yourself. The House of Lords has tried in the Crime and Policing Act to introduce new offences. Likewise, in the then Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Bill Baroness Kidron had an amendment on AI chatbots, which is an issue that you highlighted in June. Unfortunately, it was defeated.

Is it possible to have an evolution of the legislation or maybe the children’s code? You must have thought about it because you spoke up about AI chatbots. How can we ensure that children are aware of the dangers of AI chatbots in terms of becoming over-dependent on them as companions and so on? They are not being protected at the moment . Can you see a way of doing that?

I would like to see, if necessary, amendments to the Online Safety Act to enable it to stretch to cover harms related to this. As I said, I am out asking every child at the moment . They are doing a survey for me called The Big Future. We are asking them about AI. We have already got 625,000 responses and we will have more. Before we went out, we did a bit of polling of all the children who would be of an age to vote in the next election, so 14 to 19 year-olds . We asked them what their biggest concerns were. I have to say that AI came down very low.

The kids see the double-sided nature of it. When I am talking to them around the country, they are all using it. They are all using it to mark their homework. They can see its efficiency. They think it is going to change their lives. It is exciting. They want to know about it. At the same time, they are saying to me, “I applied for 100 jobs and all I got was an AI message back from each of them”. They are seeing it as limiting their experience. They talk to me about their friends who think the AI is their friend and talk to it and all the rest.

There is a role here for a modernised Online Safety Act and some amendments that would really help. There is also a big education piece here. That is for families as well. It is incumbent on all of us to educate our children and help them through the difficulties as well as seeing the positives.

Q13 Lord Tarassenko : You mentioned part of the solution that I wanted to follow up on in my second question, which is about education. What should be the top three priorities for AI literacy in schools? Would you allow school children to use ChatGPT in school? If not, what kind of AI tools should they be allowed to use?
In February, I will tell you what a million children in this country think about the answer to that question —w e are asking them that — which would probably be a more interesting answer than mine.

The fact is that they are using them. They are using AI in school already. Many of them are using AI in their classrooms. Many of them can see great potential in using AI. There is no question that teaching and learning both at school and at university level is going to change. Examinations are going to change. Kids are absolutely aware of the transformation that is afoot and they are ahead of us on it. Like I say, most of them see that as incredibly positive, but there are problems too. I think I would like to come back to you with what the children of this country think in response to that.
Lord Tarassenko : Which AI tool are you going to use to analyse the million responses?
Ask the team. I have a very good research team.

Q14 Lord Kirkhope of Harrogate: I had the dubious honour of being involved in preparing the GDPR when I was in Brussels. We knew at the time that legislation and regulation in the field of data—I am following on from Lord Tarassenko’s question—can never keep up with technological development. There is a big flaw in the legislative system both in Europe and here in this country. I find it very frustrating.

We are looking here at all the different elements that feed in to give you the powers to take action appropriately to protect children. You have everything, really. You have various pieces of legislation. You have the regulator, which seems to be totally inadequate to deal with this matter or indeed to pursue regulation. What I would ask you is this. I have been suggesting this in other fields, particularly in AI. Would it be more helpful if we could really concentrate on codifying all these pieces and bits — in other words , bringing them all together — so that there is, if you like, a menu available that can be used for the circumstances as they develop? You have touched on that. Lord Tarassenko touched on it in his question too.

We are moving at such a pace. It is not just children trying to get around something. It is the platforms trying to get around it. Therefore, as legislators, we cannot be adequate. We do not have a third form of legislation. We have primary; we have secondary. We need to have some kind of third element of faster-moving legislation. You said you could stretch the Act or you could add some amendments and so on. By the time that is done through our processes, it is out of date. Would you prefer to have this codification that we can move faster on to sort out the problems that you envisage?

We always have to take the time to think of the unintended consequences of any such proposal. We absolutely can demand more of our regulator. Any bringing together of an offer is a good idea, but it would need some really careful thinking through. That is not to try to pour cold water on your idea, but we need to think. We are clear about our legislative process and our regulatory processes. If we start free-forming, I worry about unintended consequences. Come up with a great idea, but what we can do today is demand more of those who are meant to be giving more.
I have a couple of members who want to raise points, but, Baroness Owen, you wanted to raise your declaration, did you not?

In my enthusiasm to ask my question, I forgot to declare my interest. I am now going to do that. I receive pro bono legal advice from Mishcon de Reya on image-based sexual abuse and I sit on the advisory board of A raya Ventures, a venture capital company that may invest in AI technology.

Q15 I was just going to ask a small supplementary about Ofcom. The scale of the task is large and grows ever larger. A regulator that previously was dealing with the media industry and a small number of companies is now having to deal with multiples of that. Those multiples will grow and the areas that we want them to regulate will grow. It is an organisational question, really. Is Ofcom the right body? Does there need to be another body? Does it need to be more than one body? It is a hard question to answer, but do you feel Ofcom is underpowered? Is it about will or is it about will and power and resource?

I think about my office. It is a tiny office. We have 30 members of staff. The NAO says that we have the biggest impact of any small office. It is amazing what a small group of people can do if they are genuinely committed. It sounds simple, but, in my experience—I have 20 years as an educator connected to Westminster and six years in this role—with the right ministerial air cover and the right passion and desire to get the job done, it can be done. It is good to have children’s experts and things like that—I would always support Ofcom with that, if it needed more—but it is amazing what you can get done.
Thank you. That is very helpful.

Q16 Thank you for your answers so far, Dame Rachel. You have described your frustration and you have said you are cross. That is all well said and understood. In terms of the Act itself, are you more frustrated and cross with the Act as enacted or with what has happened since in terms of how it has been used and how the provisions within it have been relied upon?

We are really fortunate to have the Online Safety Act. Although it is not perfect and although we went through many years of getting it to where it was—I am just talking about the children’s bit now—it is strong. I want amendments. I want it to be able to change and to do the thing that it said on the tin, but my frustration is how it is now being used or not used to hold tech companies and others to account.

That is incredibly helpful and an incredibly insightful point for what we are trying to get at here, because it goes to the heart of what legislation can do. You have said that there is a lot in what has been enacted, but how it has been used is where your frustration lies.
Q17 First of all, I am sorry I missed you when you came to Southampton and Winchester. You had a good time.
It was a lovely visit. Thank you. I was going to thank you for that. It was excellent.
Not at all.
Your young people were brilliant.

Thank you. That is good. Thank you so much for, well, doing your job and , in particular, taking such a child-centred and child-focused approach to all this. I have a simple question. In your view, what would need to change in children’s experiences for you to judge the UK’s online safety regime to be a success? I will give you my supplementary now. It is the “Desert Island Discs” question: which of the eight would you have? If you could make one recommendation to the Government, Ofcom or Parliament to help achieve that outcome, what would it be?

I am going to go back to my conversation with Lord Knight. It is the risky features and the addictive nature of the systems. If we dealt with that, we could make children a lot safer — if I only get one.
Yes, you only get one. Let me come back to the substantive question, then. What would need to change in children’s experiences more broadly?

I will tell you some of my biggest worries. I can think of all their little faces. When I am talking to five, six and seven year-olds , I say, “What did you do last weekend?” They say, “I gamed”. I say, “Was that all weekend ?” They say, “Yes, all weekend”. I ask, “What do you enjoy doing?” They say, “Gaming or whatever”. They do hours and hours and hours and hours of it. They are not going to the park; they are not going to see friends. There is a completely different experience qualitatively to sitting down with a group of pals and playing a competitive game and then going out and doing something else to spending hours and hours in this doom-thing of social media and tech.

For me, what needs to change the most, apart from obviously safety first, is we need to be giving children equally compelling experiences off this blessed stuff, so that, when they do use it, it can be wonderful and instructive, but it is not their whole life.

That is excellent. Thank you. That is a really good point for us to end on today, so thank you. Thank you for opening our inquiry in the way that you have done today, with such rich experience that you have from working with children across the country. It is very worth while , the job that you and your office do, with, as you said, such a small team and so successfully. Thank you.
Thank you. It is great to be here.

sessions.iT: New Towns: Bricks and Mortar
sessions.w: Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government; Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government

segs.tx: Built Environment Committee
C orrected oral evidence: New towns: bricks and mortar
Tuesday 1 September 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Gascoigne (Chair); Baroness Andrews; Lord Bailey of Paddington; Baroness Barran; Lord Bassam of Brighton; Baroness Griffin of Princethorpe; Baroness Janke; Baroness Lawrence of Clarendon; Baroness Miller of Chilthorne Domer; Lord Porter of Spalding; Lord Ravensdale.
Evidence Session No. 6 Heard in Public Questions 58 - 7 3
Witnesses

Rt Hon Matthew Pennycook MP, Minister of Housing and Planning, Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government; Lise-Anne Boissiere, Co-Director for New Towns, Infrastructure and Housing Delivery, Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government .
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Matthew Pennycook and Lise-Anne Boissiere .

Q58 Welcome to the House of Lords Built Environment Committee. It is the first day back after the Summer Recess, but, as everyone knows, we have been talking about new towns. We are bringing that work to a conclusion, and there is no better way to do that than by having our special guest before us. I am delighted to welcome the Minister to talk to us—the man who is going to drive this through. He is a bit like Gandalf, if I may say so. He is back but he is even more powerful, because now he also attends Cabinet and is able to bash heads together, as we have asked for. I am delighted that the Prime Minister has acted on one of our recommendations from a previous report. In all seriousness, Minister, we are delighted to have you here. Congratulations on being reappointed—power to your elbow, as they say. We are also delighted to welcome back Lise-Anne from the department. Thank you; I know how busy you are.

With that in mind, I suggest that we go straight into it. I think that you know we will focus mainly on new towns. First, while I appreciate that the new Prime Minister is only 40 days in, can you make any comparison, or comment, having served under Prime Minister Starmer, versus what it is like now under Prime Minister Burnham? How are things going to change? For you, personally, now that you attend Cabinet—and I appreciate that it is 40 days in—how do you see that position as being able to strengthen your hand in driving this and the 1.5 million homes through?

Thanks for that opening question. I would say a couple of things. One is that having the Housing and Planning Minister attending Cabinet alongside the Secretary of State is an indication of the importance that the new Prime Minister places on housing. It is of real importance to him. He has strong views on the subject. He has delivered in Greater Manchester. He has learned some lessons about what works and what does not in Greater Manchester, which he is keen to bring in and ensure that they are hard-wired into the Government’s approach. The Cabinet position gives the department as a whole some extra tools, and the ability to have more of those direct conversations, in particular with individual Secretaries of State, where we need to co-ordinate across government to deliver.

On the 40 days of evidence, I think you have seen the change of priority. We have slightly altered some of the announcements that we have made in recent weeks, as a result of the new Prime Minister’s refreshed priorities. A good example is the social and affordable homes programme. We announced just last week the first wave of funding out of that programme. We have left back more of the funding, to be allocated to councils to do direct delivery of council housebuilding. I think that that is an example of how we have pragmatically adapted the programmes to ensure that we keep pace and keep delivery going, but have slightly tweaked them, to reflect the new Prime Minister’s priorities.

Thank you. I am very grateful that you wrote to me over the summer about the NPPF, which is another thing you announced. More broadly, it is welcomed by the sector as pro-growth and as trying to move development on. When I looked at the NPPF—I checked again last night—there is no reference to new towns. There is talk about well-connected stations. There are two questions I want to ask about that. First, will the list of those well-connected stations be announced? I know that the criteria are in there, but is there a list so that we can see exactly what those locations are? Related to that, is there any correlation at all between the well-connected stations in those areas and the new towns programme? Forgive me for not knowing, but DfT will have a big interest in making sure that the capacity on those stations works. Is it plugged into that? Is there any conflict or competition between the well-connected stations and new towns?

I do not believe so. Let me say a couple of things on that point, and specifically on the travel to work areas. We certainly published the 60 travel to work areas alongside the draft NPPF that we consulted on. I can ensure that the committee gets the full 80 travel to work areas, so that it can see where we are talking about. On well-connected stations, we obviously tied minimum density requirements to different service frequencies at different well-connected stations to reflect the capacity on the line. The DfT—you are absolutely right—will be looking for projections and where it needs to put capacity.

On the new towns programme specifically, what I come back to relates to the consultation that we have undertaken since I was last in front of you. We published a draft new towns planning policy statement to go out to consultation. We will publish a final new towns planning policy statement alongside the final programme. That will relate to the NPPF. The NPPF remains a material consideration in planning decisions, but we will have a bespoke planning policy setting out all the parameters that need to apply to how new towns are delivered—placemaking principles. I am sure we will speak about some of these issues in more detail, but the two will be in alignment.
When do you think that that document will be published?

If you give me a chance to set out where we have got to, in the round, when I last spoke to you in July 2025, we had not even published the initial government response. We did that in September. The former Secretary of State was before you after that response, prior to our going out to consultation. In March we went out to consult on the programme as a whole—not on individual sites or the detailed delivery of those—and the SEA. That is the statutory requirement of the strategic environmental assessment regulations, as you know. We sought views on that and on the assessed cumulative impacts of the programme on the environment, and practical methods of mitigation and monitoring how we deliver. We received nearly 3,000 responses—some of them incredibly detailed. The consultation closed on 19 May. We are working through all that feedback with a view to publishing a government response in due course, and publishing the environmental assessments at least before the end of the year. At that point, we will have final locations to announce.
This year.
This year, yes.
Okay. Thank you.

Q59 It is very good to see you again, and terrific to know that you are in Cabinet and really showing the flag for housing. There is a lot to follow up there, because in a way our starting point as a committee was taking a lot of evidence, as you know, and there has been a sort of unanimous chorus from people who are responsible for delivering, who say, “We have the delivery capacity”—these are people involved in skills, or materials or design and development, and so on. “We want to do this—we believe in the new towns programme. We have had to mothball a lot, because it has been a protracted business and we are not entirely certain where we are”. You, Minister, said that several things are now happening: there will be a planning statement specifically on the new towns, which will be the planning guidance with all the requirements of design, so there will be a blueprint for the new towns when it is published. Is that due to be published at the end of the year, as well?
We have published the draft planning policy statement.
That is out for consultation now.
That was out for consultation up to 19 May. We will publish the final one.
Then there are the SEA consultations that you are working through, which will be published separately; so there will be a suite of documents that developers and investors will have to hand.
Absolutely. In short, yes.

One problem has been that we have had a raft of announcements. We have had good news on social housing. We have had the NPPF. We have had the interesting stuff on where we are developing—growth areas and so on and so forth. You used the term “pragmatic”. Do you think that there has been a problem because you have not made a statement about the continuing importance of new towns as a programme in itself? Do you think there has been a sense of loss of momentum because the narrative has been lost a little in recent months, because all these other things have happened?

No. With all due respect, I do not think that would be fair. The Government are going through a transition with a new Prime Minister. We have had a variety of announcements that were slightly set back, where we have had to recalibrate. I gave the example of the social and affordable homes programme. We remain committed to the manifesto commitments in respect of the new towns programme. At the point when we publish that suite of documents, with the final response, you will see exactly what we intend to do. I would not say there has been any loss of momentum as we work through the consultation response.

There is a general point worth making: we are talking, here, in some cases, about sites that will deliver tens of thousands of homes over multiple decades. If we had published a consultation response two weeks after the consultation closed, you would all be asking me why it was all so quick and we had not given due consideration to all the feedback we received. We will take the time to go through things—belt and braces. This is too important to get wrong.
I think that is a perfectly respectable position to hold. You are saying that the final sites will be announced at the end of the year. Do you expect changes to the final sites?

That is one thing that we are working through from the consultation responses. We proposed seven sites, and three priority sites. The consultation seeks feedback on the programme as a whole and, in particular, the environmental assessment of those sites. I have had no chance to say this, and it is worth saying: the SEA is important because development at the scale that we propose needs to be mitigated. At the point where we confirm final sites, take the programme forward and publish the final planning policy statement, we need to show how, through good planning, upfront investment and high-quality design and placemaking, we are achieving that mitigation. The process is important, but it is one of various things we are working through in the consultation responses.

It is also important to be clear about how policies integrate, is it not? Following on from the Chair’s question about this very good idea in the NPPF that railway station location brings connectivity, and therefore it is a quick win if you can get development around it, how do you see that being integrated as a modus operandi, in a way, with your thinking on new towns? That will be integrated into it. Might it alter some of the locations?

I think it is quite difficult to compare the two. There is a slight apples and pears situation, in the sense that the National Planning Policy Framework is obviously a document to guide plan making and decision-making across the country. The Government have been clear about the fact that we want more development around train stations and well-connected train stations outside urban settlements. These are some of the most sustainable locations on which to bring forward development. That is slightly separate in my mind from the new towns programme, in the sense that the task force has identified a series of sites that meet all our objectives and criteria, one of which is to be sustainable and well connected.

I will give you an example of one of the three priority sites—Tempsford on the east coast main line and intersection with East West Rail. By its very nature, if we take that new town forward, it will build out on the intersection of two railway lines in a highly sustainable location. The NPPF would be a material consideration in those decisions in terms of the minimum densities that the new NPPF is asking for; but we will overlay and ensure that aligned with that is a bespoke new towns planning policy statement that will really get into some of the detail about how we deliver on the placemaking principles that the task force recommended. So it is bespoke to the programme itself, but, as I said, the two will be complementary.

One last question: the Prime Minister is very clear about placemaking and what it can bring and optimise. Do you think that will make a difference to the approach to the new towns, in the sense that there is a new and slightly more powerful narrative around the notion of those places?

I think, from memory, that I was questioned on this at my last appearance, but it is worth taking the opportunity to re-emphasise the importance of the placemaking principles that the task force recommended and the Government absolutely agree with. The new towns programme, in a sense, is a chance for us to boost innovation, quality and competition in housebuilding, but also to show, in terms of design and placemaking, what can be exemplary and how other large sites across the country outside the programme can adopt the approach that we are taking in it, and deliver really high outcomes. We want these, at the end of the day, to be great places for people to live, as well as making a contribution to housing need, economic growth and the other objectives we set out.
Thank you.

Q60 Good afternoon, Minister. So far, you have answered many questions that I needed to ask you. You talked about the consultation that started in March, the feedback in May, and that you are looking to have a report on the draft this year. Overall, a lot of work seems to have progressed step by step, rather than waiting for things to happen; you are moving forward with those. Part of my concern is about spades in the ground and how far we are with that. How far have we moved forward with Manchester Victoria North and Thamesmead as part of linkage to the new towns?

There are two things I would say, although Lise-Anne might want to come in. One is to emphasise again that, despite the change of Prime Minister, the Government remain absolutely committed to the programme and to delivering our manifesto commitments in respect of it, and the commitments that we have already given, one of which is that we will have spades in the ground on at least three—I emphasise “at least” because there is a good chance it will be more—in this Parliament. When looking at the programme, it is really important—we have a bit more clarity now than when I last came before you, in the sense that we have seven sites we can talk specifically about—that some of the sites already have development under way. They are sites that we are adding to and that we will furnish with the new towns approach on top of what is already taking place. There is development at the site in Thamesmead, which is in my borough, although not in my constituency. It can do far more, particularly with the DLR transport intervention that was confirmed at the last Budget.

There is work under way on some of the sites. When we confirm final locations—and this is an important point because the Commons Select Committee put it to me that we have only this one point of consultation, but there will be other chances for input—those final locations have to go out and become much more granular about what they will deliver. We have done that in Greater Cambridge, where we have now established a centrally led urban development corporation. What is the red line? What is the proposed delivery vehicle? What is the approach to plan making? There will be other chances to input, including, obviously, by the local communities, and a series of events and direct engagement that we will undertake as part of it.

So there are at least three, and we are progressing as many as we can and going as fast as we can after we have confirmed final locations. It is worth saying that some already have development activity on them. That speaks, I think, to a question that I am sure you will ask me: what are the delivery vehicles? The delivery vehicles and the approach to each site will be very site specific. They are all at different states of maturity. They are all different propositions. They will inevitably need to be taken forward with different delivery vehicles. Again, once we have confirmed locations for each of the final sites, we will be much clearer about our proposed approach to how we want to take them forward.

One thing that has been said is that you are hoping to complete at least three in this Parliament. On the news this morning, there was talk about the new Prime Minister and the manifesto that was set not being his. It may seem, if people think he is doing a really good job, that he might call an early election. How would that sit?
I have already said, “Nice try”. It is entirely a decision for the Prime Minister, and I cannot tell you what his thinking is on the subject, I am afraid.
Yes, but what would be the impact on what you are trying to do now?

Again, respectfully, that impact is entirely hypothetical. The Prime Minister has said that, much as he wants to put a different emphasis on what the Government are doing, he remains committed to the manifesto that we stood on, and were elected on, and that includes with respect to a new generation of new towns.
There is a question, but I will come back to it, if I may, Chair.
Okay. Thank you very much.

Q61 Thank you, Minister, for coming in. I want to ask you a few questions about skills in the sector, and start, in a way, with a very open question about how you judge the skills situation. We heard quite conflicting evidence. Some suggested that huge numbers of jobs need to be filled, both because of an ageing workforce and new projects between now and 2035. There was also a sense that in reality there have always been worries about skills but we kind of get through. Then there are big dropout rates from colleges and early in a career. It feels curious, in an employment market that is not as buoyant as we would all wish it to be, that people are not flocking to these jobs that are decently paid and skilful, and that we are seeing this unsatisfactory situation. I wondered what your take on it was—both the severity of the problem, and what is behind the two types of dropout rate: college and professional.

There is a lot in there, so let me unpack it. Your inquiry is obviously about the new towns programme, so let me link it to that directly. There is no specific skills and workforce challenge in respect of the new towns programme. There is a general challenge across the country. Opportunities come with the new towns programme, in terms of employment and innovative methods of housebuilding. We might come on to MMC, but I think one reason why category 1 MMC, at least, has failed to take off is that there has not been the certainty of pipeline. A new towns programme can give that certainty. There is no doubt that there are quite serious pressures on the construction workforce. We said, from the moment we were elected, that we have to do more to expand and upskill that workforce, and diversify it. I think that MMC, again, gives a chance to do that.

As to the reasons why the industry does not attract more young people, I think that is a good question, because some of these jobs are extremely well paid now. We could, I am sure, deliberate at length on what the reasons might be. To a certain extent, I think there is an image problem about what working on a development site entails, and all the rest of it. The important thing is that we have acted to try to address those workforce constraints, with £625 million investment in a construction skills package. That includes £100 million for skills bootcamps; £98 million for industry placements; £100 million to establish 10 construction technical excellence colleges; a £90 million uplift for 16-to-19 courses and £75 million for adult retraining. The private sector is doing a huge amount, as well, through the Construction Leadership Council, which the Construction Minister sits on and co-chairs. The private sector is alive to the issue as well. We recognise it, and we have acted.

In terms of the new towns programme, as I said, some sites will take many decades to build out. We can use the programme to align with our general push on getting skills and capacity into the industry in a way that is really beneficial; but, on the central point, yes, there are pressures. Those pressures are partly how we recruit young people. There are other issues. I have seen this in my constituency, where there is a lot of previously developed land that is ripe there for building. We relied heavily, until we exited the European Union, on EU labour. That does not come over in the same volume it did. Despite visa adjustments and all the rest of it, we have not, in some senses, filled that drop-off. We have to do more, and it is right that we do more, to get young people in our own workforce—particularly NEETs—into this industry. As you have said, it can be a lucrative job and a rewarding career. The last point that I make is that it is not just in construction but in the whole built environment and everything that comes with it—the planning side of the new towns—where people can get highly skilled, well-paid jobs.

Obviously, the investment that the Government have made is incredibly helpful, but when we met with Skills England it did not seem—perhaps, speaking for myself, I asked the wrong questions—that there was depth of understanding about the dropout rates. As you know better than I, lots of young people go to college to do construction-related courses, but drop out very quickly. Some go on, and then drop out. If we just take the college bit, it felt like there could be something to learn either from looking at it regionally, or by individual colleges. Is there a dispersion, so that some colleges have great retention and others do not? We did not get much insight into that. Maybe there are better ways of thinking about it, but we did not hear a depth of understanding as to what might change it. You are putting a lot of money in, but you need to make sure we get the results that everybody wants.

Skills in local areas and engagement in a lot of priority projects, schemes and sites is obviously an agenda in which the mayors are also incredibly interested. They know that they have young people who want to get involved, and I think they will want to engage with this issue, with all of us. It is an area that people are alive to and will want to collaborate on—how best to try to address the attrition rate. It is important for everyone that we grow that workforce.
Yes, and beyond the money are there other tangible things that you can talk about that you are approaching differently, to try to address those issues?

There is the investment in skills. There is the work being undertaken by DfE. There is this broader push to deepen devolution much further, and there is a live conversation about what skills and education mean. We are going to publish a construction jobs plan later this year. That will set out a far more comprehensive package of support from the Government and what the industry is doing, as well, to address shortages. The investment has been the main and most important intervention.

From the feedback that I have had on things like technical excellence colleges and some of the stuff that has been undertaken by the private sector—homebuilding hubs that have been on large-scale sites that we have visited, and for which the Government provide support—they are making a difference. There is a rewarding career there, but I do not have any more information to hand on the DfE side and the attrition rates that you speak about.

Q62 You already know I am an ex-bricklayer. I have not laid a brick in anger for ages, thankfully, but a good brickie earns £100,000 a year. It is weird how, as parents and grandparents, we force our kids to put a suit on to earn £40,000 a year and think they come home better citizens. I am guilty as sin of doing that. I pushed my kids and grandkids to uni, when secretly I am saying, “Learn a skill as well”, because AI is going to put anybody in a suit, almost certainly, at job risk. It is never going to threaten anybody with a bucket of tools. Somehow we need to get more social acceptance of the good skilled people and that kind of responsibleness. Has anyone thought from a government perspective about government information films, with a bit of light-heartedness, getting decent people with a bit of attitude to show how good it is to do construction for a living, and how entertaining it is? Admittedly, the winters are a bit rubbish, but in the summers you cannot get a better job than being out on a building site earning quite a few quid with the sun on your back. It is a good place for young people to be.

On Poland, and eastern Europeans, forget it: we will be sending bricklayers to Poland, and we will certainly be sending them to Ukraine, because the money they will earn in Europe will be far better than we get over here now. We will end up with a reversal of roles. Poland is a tiger. It is racing away at the moment. You will never get a Polish bricklayer coming to England. They are always going to be over there, and of course the Polish people are quite happy to have the Polish people, where the English were not always so happy to have them, in some places, with some people, unfortunately.

I will take that as a sort of prompt to my comms department to get us out there and do more. I would say—again, coming back to the Chair’s initial question—that the Prime Minister has put a lot of focus in these early weeks on things that matter to him and interventions that can make a difference. One of those is improving the status and attractiveness of technical education vis-à-vis other routes. It is something that is important to the Government. I think we need to be cognisant of the fact that for a lot of people for whom construction might not be an obvious career, if the thought of a building site puts them off, things like modern methods of construction can make a real difference. Factory-based construction methods are a different prospect and perhaps to some people a more attractive prospect, so it is about getting innovation going in the sector as well.

Q63 I have a quick question. I am delighted that you are in the Cabinet. It is great news. We had Steph Peacock here, and she talked very convincingly about good ways of engaging with children and young people. I was delighted to hear you talk about placemaking, homes, sense of community and it not just being about building houses. As you know, we examined how you consult with children and young people. Lise-Anne, we have not met before, but looking at your biog and your background in health and social impacts, I wonder how we knit all this together to get the best outcomes that we can for new towns and the people who live in them.

What is there that I can helpfully say on that? Let us bring it back to a hypothetical new town. At the point we confirm a location, confirm the red line and the delivery vehicle, and we have a tangible sense about what a development proposition means in a given area, if you are a young person in that area, you could reasonably look at one of these larger sites and say, “Do you know what? There is a job for life on that new town if I want it. Also, I can have pride in what is being built because we are going to ensure that it is infrastructure-led and that it has great amenities and infrastructure”. Then you can do all those things around it with that certainty of the delivery pipeline on placemaking and on other social objectives that you are trying to take forward.

I can see this really being knit together, in some cases led by mayors if it is a mayoral development corporation, and in some cases local authorities. It might be a joint venture. There will be a range of delivery vehicles. But there is a way you can knit an awful lot together through the approach that we are taking. We are essentially doing much more efficient land assembly, master planning, and design and placemaking, and showing what can be done on other large sites. You can tick any number of boxes through that approach in the way that you cannot with conventional private housebuilding.

Different locations will want to engage in different ways. As we have already referenced, these are multi-decade initiatives. The types of engagement that you do in terms of very young people, older people, the facilities and the amenities that they want will happen, I would imagine, over time as you phase different elements of buildout. Depending on where you are in the first instance, some of the work is going to be all underground and not necessarily the most inspiring stuff for people to be interacting with. But, as you go forward, you start thinking about the different amenities, hubs and other things that will bring people together, how people will move around and the impact of AI in how this will be shaped. You already see how active travel is changing how people live in spaces. The important thing—and we have reflected on this a lot in learning the history of previous new towns—is that you cannot plan now for what the future will look like. You have to give yourself that flexibility because none of us has perfect foresight. The people who are interacting in the space will keep interacting with it, and they will want to shape it. They will see the things that need to evolve with it, and we need to ensure that in how we get these things up and running we are not restricting that, so that people can engage in different ways and give their feedback.
Who holds the ring in terms of working across governmental departments in this and then working with stakeholders and mayors and local authorities?
I am the lead Minister.
Marvellous.

We have a new towns delivery unit, which is a partnership between ourselves and Homes England, which essentially is to operate as a front door for the programme for anyone participating. Then we have a commitment from every department in government to prioritise the work that is required—transport interventions, whatever it might be—to ensure that these places are delivered.

Q64 I would like to bring us on to supply chains, particularly around construction materials and products. We have the new towns and the 1.5 million homes. There is all the steel, cement, bricks and timber that are needed to produce all those homes. As well as thinking about sourcing those materials, there is a more strategic question about where we get those materials from. We heard quite a bit from witnesses on this, and part of what we heard was around confidence in that we have seen a reduction in demand in recent years across the built environment sector. Some facilities have been mothballed or closed down, and there is not that confidence within supply chains at the moment on the path to ramping up and delivering for these new towns. What steps can the Government take to inspire confidence within supply chains to ensure that they are really ready to deliver for new towns, but more broadly as well?

All that government can do is give certainty over policy and the direction of travel, and we will do that on new towns when we come to issue the government response, the final planning policy statement and the final locations. We have provided certainty in a range of other areas. All the feedback that I get from the sector is that it very much welcomes that. A finalised National Planning Policy Framework, a 10-year rent settlement and a 10-year social and affordable homes grant programme—all these things—give the sector lots of certainty going forward. That then interacts with the fact that—there are no two ways about it—housebuilders are going through a really tough time at the moment, partly due to things completely outside the Government’s control. A good example is construction build costs. They have gone up by about 40% since 2020 across the market. The current conflict in the Middle East is adding pressure to those costs. These are the sorts of things that housebuilders are struggling with in terms of where they can get their supplies.

What can the Government do to help with those supply chains? The first really important thing to say—I have referenced it already—is that we have a Construction Leadership Council co-chaired by industry and the DBT Construction Minister. That supports the construction industry to work collaboratively with their supply chains, and to look at the potential for market volatility, forecasting and communicating their requirements early to suppliers, distributors and builders’ merchants, so that they are looking as the sector, with the government voice there, at pricing, production planning and delivery. There is no silver bullet when it comes to those cost pressures that I talked about. The Government have done lots on the circular economy. We are streamlining product regulations. We are looking at what more we can do in terms of domestic manufacturing. You have seen the intervention that we have made on steel. MMC is another asset to that. There are various ways that we are looking to try to alleviate the pressures, but those pressures are there and they are somewhat outside the Government’s control to the extent that they are global pressures.

It is really good to hear about that work that you are doing with the sector. You mentioned the points outside the Government’s control, such as the conflicts and so on, that are driving up energy costs. As you know, industrial energy costs in the UK are much higher than our peer competitors. There is a risk that we are driving a lot of this business abroad. Cement manufacture comes to mind. There are various initiatives going on, of course, but is there any work going on within government to join that up across departments to ask what we can do to look at this more strategically and what we can do for our UK businesses to help them deliver for these programmes, notwithstanding the constraints that they are facing with energy?

There is cross-government work on all these issues. When we look at the new towns programme when it comes to energy capacity and water capacity, we are working with other government departments. On the specific issue of industrial electricity prices, I am afraid you will have to have the DESNZ Minister in front of you to set out what that department is doing specifically on this issue. As I said in reference to a previous question, one really important commitment that we have from those other government departments is to do what is necessary to prioritise within their spending reviews the investment necessary to ensure that the programme can be delivered as a whole-of-government endeavour.

Q65 Hello, Minister. I am very pleased to be able to have this conversation. I would like to turn to the matter of innovation. You have mentioned it a couple of times this afternoon already with reference to MMC. As you said, this programme is going to be decades long. What might seem innovative now will not seem very innovative in 40 years’ time, probably. We had quite a lot of evidence on innovation and what is holding it back. First, do you see the new towns as a real platform for innovation?

Yes, very simply. This helpfully relates to my previous question. We have asked departments to look at new towns through the lens of what innovative policies they want to deliver in their department. A good example might be that, if the Department of Health and Social Care is looking to pilot innovative approaches to public health, is a new town a good place to trial those policies? How do we factor in the cutting-edge thinking from each department in how we design infrastructure and amenities? So, yes.

That is very encouraging. The evidence we heard is that there is possibly a lot of consumer resistance in terms of the new materials. People think of homes traditionally as bricks and mortar and so on. How do you see getting over that issue when it comes to people being happy with the home that they are getting or buying because of the construction materials? How can we make innovation more exciting?

You have put me on the spot in a sense. I am not sure that we need to make it exciting. We absolutely need to make it beneficial in terms of people’s wallets: more energy-efficient homes and homes that are cheaper to deliver. That is where modern methods of construction have the potential to accelerate delivery and improve productivity with those workforce benefits. They can have benefits for the home buyer. Bills are a great example. We are seeing real innovation across the country with, in some cases, zero-bill homes. People will be led in some ways by their wallet, but people are interested in innovation.

As to what the Government are doing, we have already taken a number of steps to support the rollout of MMC, which it is worth saying has not completely faltered. In some cases, particularly cat 1, we saw lots of big sites being mothballed. Category 2 MMC is doing quite well. Timber frame is doing quite well. In terms of what support Government can give, we have published PAS 8700. It brings clarity to the insurance and warranties market. We have a joint venture with Vistry Group to deliver more homes with MMC. We are working with over 20 local authorities to develop a pattern book of standard house designs that we think could be rolled out. Lots of the local authorities that are participating are really enthusiastic about the value that can add. There are lots that we are doing in that space to encourage innovation and lots of benefits for the consumer, certainly with the examples that I have seen across the country.
Thank you. I think you have just answered my question on the issue that we heard evidence on about insurance. The Government intend to make sure that that is not an inhibitor of innovation.
No, not when it comes to MMC. PAS 8700 should have the required impact in that space. People will let us know, I am sure, if there are ongoing issues with it.

On new products coming to market, have you noticed any issues caused by the suspension of BBA from UKAS? If a new product does not have an agrément board certificate on it, it cannot be used on a building site, because nobody will touch it. UKAS suspended BBA’s accreditation at the beginning of the year. My understanding is that as of last week it was still suspended. It might be worth having a look to find out what has gone on there and to see how much of a bottleneck of clever new products are out there but just cannot get over that last accreditation line.
As ever with these things, I am sure the department is aware even if I am not.
Yes, I am definitely sure somewhere down in the detail. It is one of those things where there could be a bottleneck of good stuff sitting out there waiting to be released.

Q66 Thank you very much for being here. I am finding this very encouraging. Sorry, Lise-Anne and Minister, but some of our questions will now converge slightly, which I think is healthy. I am delighted to hear you talk about energy efficiency, because the cheapest fuel is obviously the fuel that you do not use at all, and the opportunities within this to combat energy poverty, pricing and to combine energy efficiency with fire safety not just in installation of materials used but inspection, which is crucial. You will know, Minister, from your background that in European legislation we married energy efficiency legislation with fire safety after Grenfell, and that quite a lot of work is being done on this issue, but that is slightly an aside.

To come back to what Daniel said, would it not be great if we decoupled gas and electricity prices? As we say, that is not really the remit of this committee, but there we go. Obviously, demands for energy and water in this country are rising, not only in terms of new towns but in what is happening with data centres and so on. How does all this work towards net zero and national resilience? As you say, Lise-Anne, this is a long-term project. How do we learn what it is that we are not doing well and how to mitigate that on an ongoing basis? We have seen quite a lot of examples of that, sadly, this summer. How are utilities involved right from the beginning as part of infrastructure as opposed to being an add-on? As a local councillor in the north-west, it used to drive me to distraction when you saw the same street over a period of three years dug up separately because the utilities did not have a way of working together. It is energy and water. How can we preserve net zero and be resilient? It is the whole picture, really. Thank you.
Just a general comment on all of that?
Yes; some hows would be great.
It takes me well outside the remit of the new towns programme, but I will try to comment.

It does very much, though, get to the heart of the strategic environmental assessment process. That is why we have to do all these important assessments at the outset in terms of understanding the implications to inform the decisions that get taken on the shape of the programme. All the departments have been involved and we have published a consultation so that people can respond to that draft strategic environmental assessment. On the water side, the Environment Agency and Natural England are fully engaged. The benefits, in a sense, of doing this very planned approach are that you should be surfacing where you have tensions and issues arising as we move forward. Therefore, you do not have that issue of people constantly digging things back up, because we all know exactly what we are doing. That is the intent.

I do not think there is much that I would add to that. Lise-Anne is right that that is the heart of the SEA process, to understand what the pressures are and how they would be mitigated. The Government are doing lots of other things in other areas. Speaking about water constraints, we have not built a reservoir since the early 1990s. We now have nine in development. We have two being actively taken forward, in East Anglia and Lincolnshire. Some of the infrastructure is coming through. Through the changes that we made to the planning system, we are ensuring that reservoirs can be taken forward as nationally significant infrastructure projects. Importantly—it goes back to the innovation point—where we are trialling innovative approaches to water efficiency in Cambridge, these are lessons that we are taking forward and we will ensure they are hard-wired into the new towns programme so that what we are building is as future-proofed as we can get it in terms of what we can foresee.

Q67 Minister and Lise-Anne, you mentioned the SEA. One of the things that we heard about, particularly from a new town perspective, if it is a new town or an expanded settlement, is getting the utility companies in early as part of the discussion so that they can at least appreciate and understand the potential demand, be it 10,000 at the beginning up to 50,000, or whatever it may be. Is that happening there? I heard you mention the SEA. Is that part of the same conversation, or is that more the resilience side?

On the SEA aspect of it, we have gone out to public consultation. The point at which you start getting utility companies in and all the rest of it—because all the different sites are at different levels of maturity—is when you have confirmed which locations you are taking forward as part of the programme.
They will be brought in quite early. From memory, the concern that we heard was that they were not being brought in.

They will definitely be brought in earlier. That goes to the point of what the SEA is. It is an assessment of the whole programme and broad locations for growth. To get hypothetical, because we have not confirmed locations, at the point you say location X is confirmed and is in the programme, we will get much more granular about the exact red line, the exact proposed delivery and how everything is going to work. That is where I am tempted in my mind to bring it back to the real-world examples that we have. Greater Cambridge is a great example where we went out to consult on a defined red line and a definitive delivery vehicle. We have now established that. That is not exactly the same but a very good illustration of how each of the finally confirmed sites will be taken forward, with much more specific assessments relating to those sites. At the moment, we are assessing the programme as a whole. We have in those broad locations for growth identified the tasks, and we have taken forward the pressures and the potential mitigations that need to be brought forward.

There is a separate thing that it is worth saying for the committee’s clarity. Alongside the SEA, we have also been progressing a habitats regulations assessment for the programme. That is a requirement of the habitats directive, similarly, to examine the effects of the programme on national network sites and to identify mitigation measures to avoid or lessen the effects on those sites. We intend to publish that alongside that final suite of documents that we have been taking forward.

Q68 Forgive me if I feel my way through this question. How do you start thinking about future situations that we cannot always comprehend because there are too many unknowns when you have a set of national priorities such as data? How do we think about the capacity for data in the future and try to marry that up with the local decisions that will have to be made by these sites, which are governed by development corporations of whatever nature? Who, in the end, will adjudicate if there is a conflict of interest between what is needed or what is possible locally in terms of the character of the local site, given that they will have followed the NPPF and so on and so forth? It ought to marry up with the NPPF and so on. There are very likely to be some conflicts of interest, are there not, between what we see in the national interest and what may be in the specific regional and local interests on that side between the utilities? Water is a particularly difficult example because of the specific challenges now. Who will make that decision? Who holds the ring on that?

Again, I bring it back to a real-world example. Let us say that hypothetical site X that is confirmed is taken forward through a development corporation, whether it be mayoral or centrally led. There is a clear accountability for a centrally led development corporation such as with the Secretary of State and with the board in the case of Greater Cambridge, where we have been at pains—and the same principle would apply to the new towns programme and any sites that are taken forward—to have local representation on those boards. Ultimately, those boards are accountable to the Secretary of State in that instance, who is responsible for plan making eventually. We want to get the local plan in place, but eventually there are plan-making and decision-making powers over certain thresholds, bringing a spatial plan forward. It would be looking to be making decisions about what goes where in accordance with the NPPF and the final planning policy statement that we will publish.

There is a bigger question outside the new towns programme. The Government after the coalition, in my view, took us to a hyper-localist position where all decisions are very local, to put in a real hierarchy of plan making. We have reintroduced spatial development strategies and subregional plans aligned with devolution geographies, and they really should be, in due course, the high-level frameworks for housing growth and infrastructure provision. In my mind, a good SDS would be looking at how much data centre capacity we require in this region and the appropriate locations where it might be sited, and it is much more plan led. I suppose I come back to a fundamental point that we have not had. At the point we came into government, we inherited a planning system predicated on local plans being in place but less than a third up-to-date coverage. We cannot have a plan-led system unless we have far higher coverage, and we are boosting that coverage. In SDSs and local plans, new towns with the red line that they draw will be assembling land and master planning for the specific locations.

I entirely agree with you about spatial planning. We lost years when that was diluted and lost. If you take that a step further in terms of a national spatial plan or a national resilience strategy, do you think that is where we are heading? Is that the way to try to flatten out and make these fairer and ultimately more efficient decisions, where you minimise conflicts of interest between local and national resources?

That is a really good question. On that point, again, I have a memory of answering it before either to this committee or to the committee in the other place. In opposition, we did quite a lot of thinking about this, or I did at least and others did. Is it in our interest to go into a process where we look to bring forward a national spatial plan? Doing so would have been quite a slow and cumbersome process. Various ideas were put to us in opposition: a royal commission, or whatever it might be. We have taken a slightly more pragmatic approach, which is that across government a number of strategies or plans are spatial in nature that are being taken forward: the industrial strategy, the land use framework, and the new towns programme. What the Government have tried to do and need to continue to do to ensure that everything works and is in alignment is to knit all those strategies together to ensure that they are complementary. Rather than pause everything and say that we are going to take three, four or five years to do a big national spatial plan, we are getting to the same point. When a new town is created, it needs economic purpose. Is the industrial strategy factored in? Our explicit remit and the terms of reference of the task force were to look at all these strategies and to factor them into their thinking when recommending locations for the sites.

Q69 I would like a few clarifications. In your previous answer, Minister, you talked about the habitats regulations assessments that you said you were doing for a number of the sites. Will that have the benefit of the updated guidance that has been produced by Defra and was out for consultation in May this year? The reason I ask that is because that was aimed at a more straightforward path through the habitats regulations and a more proportionate approach. Secondly, you talked about the NSIP process and some of the supporting infrastructure to new towns, but has there been any discussion of new towns themselves going into the NSIP process?

On the habitats regulations assessment, that is not for individual sites; it is for sites within the programme as a whole. That is important to say. I am not quite clear in my mind whether you are talking about that or environmental assessment more generally.
No, the habitats specifically. Some new guidance is being produced for the habitats regulations.
We have been working hand in glove with Defra colleagues on it all. I am assuming that they have given us the best possible advice.

To give to the HRA. Then there is a related point in terms of the SEA, but also the EIA is more generally on site-specific projects. The Government are committed to replacing those. These are EU legacy assessments. We are committed to taking forward environmental outcomes reports. We think they are a better way to approach things. That is a fairly complex process to take forward. We have made clear we want them in place, though, by the end of 2027 as a replacement environmental assessment regime.
