I t was really pleasing to see retention incentives for heads in disadvantaged areas come through as one of the proposals. However, i n terms of how that is being delivered, it is unfortunate that it is not being done via the pay framework . I agree with what James said about how it is not about the financial aspect— but then it sort of is in a way. Again, if the distribution of funding were such that there was sufficient in those particular areas for the trust board or the governing board to be able to make good decisions about retaining its leaders so that it can develop those leadership skills over time , that would be better . T hat is what is not happening at the moment. I think that would be a way, at least, of contributing to getting some sustainable leadership in those areas which w e need so badly.

Just before Manuela continues, we are at the point where we are going to have to pick up the pace quite a lot in order to ask you about all of the topics that we would like to get your views on. I ask witnesses to be concise and members of the Committee—and I am also guilty — to limit your supplementary questions as well . W e will then get through as much as we can by about 4 . 30 pm.

Q23 My next question is about the move to a trust-led system. The Government have said that they want all schools to either join or form high-quality school trusts to put collaboration at the heart of the system. What is your view on those proposals?

The first thing to say is that collaboration does not require academisation. We as a union obviously strongly believe in schools working together, sharing their expertise and accepting collective responsibility for every child in their community, but there is no evidence at all that converting every school into an academy is the best or only route to achieving that.

I agree with a lot of what Daniel said. We have members who work in multi-academy trusts who think they are fantastic; they really enjoy being a part of that partnership, and it works well for them. Equally, we have school leaders working in local authorities where they collaborate and have local clusters, and that works incredibly well for them.

The point the Government really need to consider is that, when I speak to school leaders and schools who work in a local authority and that works well for them, they say, “There is no compelling reason for me to move. The outcomes for children are good, and we are working well with the local authority. I like the relationship: they are supportive, but they hold me to account. The school is performing well: I have a good Ofsted rating, and I have good numbers on roll .” Given everything we said earlier about the cumulative load, their priority will not be rethinking governance structures and joining a MAT. That is not to say, “MATs bad and LAs good”—we have members working across both—but a lot of our members who are not in MATs say, “With everything else going on, if it’s not broken, don’t start meddling.”

There is no evidence that they raise standards. A lot of the Government’s policy agenda is about collaboration, but that will have to take place by looking over the walls of the MAT where there are different structures in place, and at how you can get collaboration between different schools when one of the key foci of collaboration between schools is the MAT system.

There are absolutely MATs that are doing an excellent job, and there are staff in them who are also doing a good job, but one of the key issues is the lack of transparency in some multi-academy trusts about how decisions are taken. In some multi-academy trusts, there is an awful lot of power and not very much accountability. There is a school funding formula that is focused on individual schools, and we see some individual MATs collecting all that money and distributing it as they see fit, and they are not accountable for those decisions. Accountability and transparency are key weaknesses in much of the multi-academy trust system we have today.

ASCL are supportive of schools working in strong collaborative groups. One of the key points that has come from our members in looking at this policy is the importance of clarity of role between schools, trusts and local authorities, which could also create their own trusts. An additional point is that our members have said that it looks as if collaboration will be a central mechanism in delivering some of the expectations from the White Paper—maybe not explicitly, but implicitly, thinking about SEND reforms and system leadership. If we pursue this, it is incumbent on Government to think really carefully about how those collaborative structures are co-constructed.

I would like to add that I think the workforce evidence should make the Committee quite cautious about moving to a more trust-led system. Our analysis of the school workforce census and freedom of information data found that one in five teachers left their jobs in some of the largest multi-academy trusts in a single year, compared with one in seven for maintained schools. In some of the really large trusts, more than a quarter of teachers left in a single year. If you had a system running like that, where a quarter of teachers were leaving a school, it would completely grind to a halt.
Q24 Having considered the White Paper, what measures are needed to close the disadvantage gap? That is a short question, but the answer is huge, so I would appreciate your brevity and precision.

These are deeply entrenched issues, so we would say that there will not be a quick fix. In terms of some of the place-based proposals , that will allow policy to specifically support schools and leaders in those particular geographical areas—that might be, for example, delaying the school’s inspection window to give time for training and support to embed in a school.

I will focus a bit on funding, if that is alright, because that is my area of expertise within the organisation. We think that there are some very blunt instruments at the moment around supporting disadvantage. Therefore, if we were to look more broadly at how we funded schools to support disadvantage, that would perhaps then enable them to be the masters of their own success in terms of the disadvantage gap. Geography makes a difference, but within that, there will be areas of high deprivation, which will lead to the disadvantage gap being perhaps broader in some of those areas. There are funding things that we can do.

There is a lot of talk about reviewing the pupil premium strategy, and proposals around interventions on the pupil premium strategy where schools are not performing as well as they might be. I think we have got to be really careful about that. We are urging caution in that. We would welcome support, but schools would need to be really clear that interventions being put in place were an opportunity and not a punitive action, because we think that is counterproductive to closing the gap.

The best way in which we can stop disadvantage impacting adversely on children and young people’s life chances is to have fewer children facing poverty and disadvantage in the first place, and that is about the Government’s economic, social and welfare policy, which are complex issues.

One feature of effective practice that we have seen in policy in the past was the team around the child, which I think was lost between 2010 and 2024. If we have children who have vulnerabilities and susceptibility, school has an important role to play, but it is also about joining up with those other services—they also face challenges in terms of investment—such as health services, social care services, youth and community services, and having structures that allow those services to collaborate and work together. We know from policies such as Sure Start under the previous Labour Government in the 2000s that those policies can have a positive impact on disadvantaged children and young people.
May I include support staff in schools as well?
Absolutely, yes.
I absolutely support that. Tackling child poverty and focusing on the early years is probably one of the nearest things we have to a silver bullet in this.

The other nearest thing to a silver bullet is the quality of teaching and learning that goes on. That is the thing that has the biggest impact in terms of closing that disadvantage gap in school—having that brilliant teacher in school. What we therefore need to do is to allow schools to focus on that.

To go back to my earlier comment, I am worried that what we are about to ask schools to do is to focus on developing an enrichment programme, and on an engagement programme, and on this. That’s nice, but we have to be really careful that we are not asking schools to focus on so many things that they can’t focus on the core teaching and learning.
Q25 My question is about impacting on the disadvantage gap.
You do that through high-quality teaching and learning. All the evidence says that the best way you close that gap is to have brilliant teaching—high-quality teaching and learning going on.
We need to allow schools to focus on that, because that is what the evidence says closes the gap—
Q26 Okay. Would you say that that is possible with the current curriculum and assessments?

The curriculum is overloaded at the moment. In terms of the curriculum, my big plea would be that we look a bit more boldly and ambitiously in terms of reducing curriculum content. We talked about how the curriculum and assessment review said let’s reduce a little bit. I am slightly worried that it has not gone far enough. We are about to load more in, aren’t we, because we are about to load citizenship in.
I would like this Government to have another look at the content of the curriculum, because you are right: an over-stuffed curriculum is part of the problem.

To go back to my previous point on getting brilliant teaching and learning going on if we want to close the disadvantage gap, we also need to make sure that the best leaders and the best teachers go and work in those schools serving disadvantaged communities. As I said earlier, the system doesn’t encourage that at the moment.

I have a little anecdote. I was speaking to two people over the summer—one of them was working in a school serving a really disadvantaged community. They advertised for maths teachers; they couldn’t get them. They were struggling. They were trying to get overseas teachers. I am not saying that was poor quality, but they were really struggling to get them. And I was speaking to a school about half an hour away; it was a different sort of community. They had a queue of people wanting that job.

We need to flip that. We need to make it so that teachers are desperate to go and work in those schools , and that they come into the profession because they want to work with those pupils. We want to close that disadvantage gap. Let’s get the best teachers working with those pupils, but let’s not penalise them for doing so. Let us make that the right choice.

Q27 I am not sure how quickly you will be able to answer this: what changes would you wish to see in how disadvantage funding is distributed? We know there is quite a discrepancy in funding between areas. I will start with you, Daniel.

I would like to see reform to the national funding formula. More weight should be placed on additional need and deprivation, but that needs to be achieved through additional investment, not by taking money from one underfunded school to give to another. Our aspiration should be to level up all children and not redistribute scarcity

I would agree with that. It is not about rearranging existing money so that we have winners and losers. It is about investing more in those schools and disadvantaged communities. Look at the pupil premium. I would credit this Government with increasing the pupil premium in the last few years, but that was after a 10-year freeze in pupil premium where it moved by about £2 in the space of eight or nine years. We are still catching up with that. We should look at things like pupil premium, ensure there are genuine real-terms increases, and target the money at disadvantaged children and not rob Peter to pay Paul, moving it around the system.
Q28 It is about how you measure disadvantage, isn’t it? Some disadvantage is hidden. You say that areas do not get the money that they require because the disadvantage is averaged out.
But then we should transition how we measure disadvantage. It is not solely on free school meal eligibility, but parental income.

You can understand why that has been used in the funding formula in the past, because it is straightforward as a proxy and there is some merit to it, but it does distort and, as was mentioned in the previous session, there are lots of families living in genuine poverty whose circumstances are not captured by that current framework.

Moving to a different system is complex. This is riven with trade-offs—of course it is. But that fundamental point that we should not focus disproportionately on the funding formula without thinking about the overall level of investment in the education system is a good point. How the system distributes funding according to the levels of disadvantage it identifies is of course legitimate, and there is probably a good case for looking, as Daniel says, at maybe moving away from a strict free school meals indicator.

I would agree with moving away from free school meals and looking at things like persistent absence, low prior attainment, which is already being looked at, as well as adverse child experience and family experience. Our members tell us that often it is the teacher in the classroom that has the best understanding of those things. So if you have to move to a system where you look towards school-based disadvantage funding rather than being heavily pupil-led, it gives a little more flexibility for those that have the best experience of the need to deliver it. But I completely agree it needs to be additional and not moving the existing pot about.

Q29 The new Government have proposed strengthening technical education pathways alongside greater devolution, increased work experience and stronger ties with local employers. What is your response to those announcements?

A good case was made for looking at the role that technical education plays in the education system, particularly in the school system, so we need to look at that. The thing I was struck by was the lack of detail, so we need to see more detail about what is proposed. The last time something like this was genuinely attempted was following the publication of the Tomlinson review in 2004. The Government did not accept all of Tomlinson, but got to the same place by a different route. It lost the election in 2010, so it could not pursue that policy. It was incredibly complex . To try and achieve those worthwhile objectives that we think the Government wants to achieve was not something that could be done just by tinkering with a performance indicator for schools and maybe moving a little bit of the curriculum here and there. It was a fundamental reform that that last Labour Government planned and then began to implement, so this is really complex stuff.

One theme across many of the answers we have given here today is that that cannot be done on the cheap. You have a system that is already struggling. It is about to face a curriculum and assessment review—which, by the way, was done with no reference to this announcement at all, so how are those two things going to join up? Yes, it is worth while, but yes, it takes time. It needs a plan, and it also needs to be built upon the voices of those teachers, leaders and young people who learn in that system and work in that system, so it is a big task, and it is not as straightforward as perhaps it has sometimes been portrayed.

I would just echo that point. Broadly, it seems like a good idea, but the lack of detail is the tricky thing at the moment. We are largely working effectively off a press release, and we need to get to that detail. For me, the big thing around that is workforce; the workforce implications are huge, and that will take time. I think there is a link to the White Paper there again, around workforce, but “What does that need in terms of people to deliver it, and what does that look like?” is going to be a big part of that question.

We have real questions around workforce—who is going to teach?—but there is also a question around parity in terms of how vocational qualifications are measured. Unless they are put on an equal footing to academic ones, then regardless of what speeches say, they will be treated as second class.

We absolutely back the ambition for parity of qualification. We need more detail; we would like to see more detail, although it is very early days. The real test for us at this point will be some safeguards or guardrails across the system, so that it does not become a postcode lottery—so that your local offer, if you like, is not determined by where you live.

Just to pick up and reinforce a point that a colleague on the earlier panel made, we all need to be really careful that the conversations around English and maths resits and the 14 to 19 curriculum do not become conflated in the public consciousness, because one is not to solve the other. I think that is something we all need to be mindful of.

Q30 The White Paper places emphasis on enrichment for all pupils. From the perspective of your members, what measures are needed to make this enrichment a reality? I think I know what Daniel might say, but we will start with Julia.
Are you sure you do not want to start with James? No, I am very happy to take this.

Obviously, all our members are absolutely for enrichment; nobody needs convincing on that. Where we have serious concerns about the proposals is where they become statutory, and without significant investment to enable them to happen. While we can see why changing non-statutory guidance or adjustments would be really helpful, we are worried that this becomes a sort of accountability by the back door—or not even by the back door, really.

One additional point, which again came up in the earlier session and I think was well made, was that yes, you can hold schools to account for their enrichment offers, but you have to make sure you are investing in it. We are kind of in a position now where it is not really being invested in, but schools are being held accountable, in terms of the inclusion of enrichment in the Ofsted inspection framework and also this tendency we increasingly see in government—not just this Government, but its predecessor—towards government by expectation.

What the Government has said about the enrichment framework it has published is, “We expect you to implement it. We are not telling you to implement it; we are expecting you to implement it.” That is ambiguous, and in most schools, it is being interpreted as “You are telling us to do this, and if we do not do it, adverse consequences for us will follow.” Not only do we not have the investment, we also have the investment aligned with accountability that I think schools are really worried about.

What we really have to hold on to here is that we have to distinguish between enrichment during the school day and extracurricular enrichment. I think that is so central to this. If we are talking about enrichment during the school day, I am reasonably relaxed, in the sense that schools up and down the country already do outdoor learning, author visits, trips to the theatre, creative arts days, days off timetable—the list is as long as your arm in terms of enrichment. If we want to talk a bit more about trying to do that a bit more systematically , I don’t mind that conversation; I think that’s an interesting one.

When we are talking, though, about providing a programme of after-school, out-of-school enrichment, that is a completely different kettle of fish, because you need someone to organise that; you need people to turn up and put that on. Who is going to do that? After school, teachers have staff meetings ; leaders have parent meetings. They cannot do it, nor can we expect them to do it contractually. The answer might be, “W ell, we ’ll get partners, we’ll get clubs, to do it,” but someone still has to organise that. If the ambition is genuinely wrap around enrichment , after school, which I do not disagree with—it is a great ambition — you have to resource it. We go back to the extended schools era of many years ago. You have to have people to co - ordinate that . You have to have people on the ground to run the clubs and what have you. I know this is a recurring theme, but you can not do that for free ; s omeone is going to want to be paid to do that. We can not expect existing school staff to do that. That would be a huge extension of their job.
Q31 Do you think there is a question about how, for the purposes of accountability and Ofsted, enrichment is captured and looked at?
Yes.

Q32 I can think of local authority primary schools in deprived areas of my constituency that have an absolutely brilliant programme . One in particular has an absolutely brilliant program me of enrichment that runs throughout the school day and throughout the school year. For a whole year, e very child gets to swim ; e very child gets to play an instrument. All these opportunities are delivered within the curtilage of the school day and within resources that are at least as stretched as they are in any other school in a deprived urban area of the country.

That begs the question : are we talking about extending this and making sure that what happens in the best places at the moment happens everywhere , or are we talking about an over and above requirement — something that schools are not currently required to do at all but that the Government are now going to be requiring them to do? There is a difference between those two things.

I will t ry to answer that quickly. It’s a “Yes, but”. Broadly speaking, yes, I have no problem with inspectors saying to school leaders and their st a ff, “W hat do you do to enrich your curriculum ?”, and school leaders talking about stuff: “A ctually, every child learns a musical instrument here .” That is a healthy conversation about how you bring your curriculum to life, how you enrich it . I think that is fine.

The “but” is that we have to recognise that not all schools have the same resources —for all sorts of reasons . Expecting the school that you described earlier , with just 12 kids, to put on the same provision as the big school that has 500 children is unfair , so we have to be mindful of context and budget . And a bsolutely n o to Ofsted judging your extracurricular stuff — coming in and saying, “W ell, you can ’t be at the expected standard , because you are running only five after - school clubs and they are running seven after - school clubs. ” For me, that goes way beyond what is acceptable and reasonable.

I agree with lots of what ha s been said. First, I do n’t think there is anybody —I have never met a teacher or support staff person, a colleague , who opposes the idea of enrichment. Everybody in this room, I am sure, wants young people to have access to culture, music and so on. We all want that. But the reality at the minute is that two thirds of our members are telling us that their schools are having to fundraise to supplement their budgets. So what you are going to end up with —I think this is where James ’s point about Ofsted is really important — is schools in the affluent areas , which can do fundraising off fairly affluent parents , having a better offer than schools in the deprived areas. And Ofsted are going to be measuring schools on it this month. If it is going to be part of the accountability measure, it has to come with the appropriate funding , and frankly that is not happening at the moment.
Q33 The Government ha ve said that they want to ensure that all pupils feel a sense of belonging at school. How do you build that sense of belonging , and if it is missing, how do you create it?

I do n’t think belonging is something that is vague, but I also am not sure it can be created by another framework. For me, belonging is a staffing question , if we’re being honest . It means that there are enough adults in the school , who know every child, that class sizes are small enough for people to notice when something changes and that teachers and support staff remain there beyond one year to sustain lasting, trusted relationships. This is a really important question because pupils who said that they felt that they did not belong in school went on to achieve, I think, roughly a grade lower at GCSE. Again, I think it relates to investment, appropriate staffing levels and appropriate support for schools.

I would not add too much to that . This is about relationships , isn’t it? Those of us who had a positive school experience will probably think about a teacher or teachers who m we had a really close relationship with — someone who looked out for us, who was there for our entire schooling, who had the time to talk with us after school. That relationship is absolutely at the heart of it.

I suspect one thing that will worry teachers and leaders, notwithstanding how important they know belonging to be , is that something as complex as a concept of belonging and what that means is going to be reduced to two or three quantitative performance indicators against which you will be judged. We know what that leads to. It leads to all kinds of pressures to do certain things and not do other things in order to meet those expectations. B elonging is really important , b ut we need real caution about how we think we are going to measure that.
Yes. Please no belonging league tables . That would drive the wrong behaviour .

It is about looking at it in the round , isn’t it? B elonging , engagement and attendance are inextricably linked. If we are looking at a system where by schools have good support around them , so that s chools have confidence that families are being supported —to go back to one of the points I made earlier , workload pressures are quite often driven by diminished local services. I think there is something about rewinding that , and that having a positive impact on belonging , attendance and engagement.

Thank you very much. I know there are topics that we have not been able to cover today. We have had a good , detailed look at some things ; we have had a canter through some of the topics. I know that all of you have access to really rich seams of information through your members , so if there are things that we have not been able to cover, please do write to us afterwards . We would very much welcome that as we get goin g; this is the first session in what is quite a significant inquiry for us th is autumn. Thank you all very much indeed for being with us today.

sessions.w: Social Mobility Commission; The Education Policy Institute (EPI); Centre for Social Justice (CSJ)

Oral evidence: ‘ Every Child Achieving and Thriving ’ White Paper , HC 430
Tuesday 1 September 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 1 September 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Helen Hayes (Chair); Jess Asato; Sureena Brackenridge; Manuela Perteghella; Mark Sewards; Peter Swallow; Caroline Voaden.
Questions 1-3 3
Witnesses
I : Alun Francis OBE, Chair, Social Mobility Commission , Daniel Lilley, Head of Youth, Centre for Social Justice and Julie McCulloch, Chief Executive, The Education Policy Institute .

II : James Bowen, Assistant General Secretary, National Association of Head Teachers , Mrs Julia Harnden, Deputy Director of Policy, Association of School and College Leaders , Daniel Kebede, General Secretary, The National Education Union and Darren Northcott, National Official, NASUWT .
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Alun Francis, Daniel Lille y and J ulie McCulloch.

I welcome everybody to this oral evidence session of the Education Committee, and I welcome colleagues back from summer recess. This is the first evidence session in our new inquiry in which we are scrutinising the Government’s White Paper entitled “Every child achieving and thriving” ahead of what we believe will be legislation coming forward later in the autumn or early in the new year. We are also scrutinising the White Paper in the light of some subsequent policy announcements that the new Administration has been making over the summer.
I would like to thank our witnesses for joining us today. I will invite each of you to introduce yourselves, but before I do, I invite Committee members to make any declarations of interest.

I declare that I am the chair of the all-party parliamentary group for schools, learning and assessment, the secretariat of which is the NEU. We have just produced a report on votes at 16, which might be relevant today.
I declare that I am a former member of ASCL.
Now we will go to introductions from our witnesses.
My name is Daniel Lilley. I am the head of youth at the Centre for Social Justice.
Good afternoon, everyone. I am Julie McCulloch, chief executive of the Education Policy Institute. Thank you very much for enabling me to join this session remotely.

Hello, everybody, and thank you very much for also allowing me to join remotely. My name is Alun Francis. I am the chair of the Social Mobility Commission and I am the chief executive of Blackpool and The Fylde College, which also includes Furness College in Barrow.

Q1 I will lead off our questioning with a question about some of the changes in policy. We have the White Paper, which is the Government’s formal statement of current policy, but over the summer the new Prime Minister announced further changes to policy specifically around technical pathways and the delivery of technical and vocational education in secondary schools, as well as plans for devolution. I would like to ask, first, for your understanding of how the new announcements have an impact on the existing White Paper and the impact that they will have on schools seeking to navigate one policy change and then a further evolution and iteration of the policy that has come subsequently.

My opening comment is that it is probably not entirely clear yet how much of the White Paper the new Prime Minister and Secretary of State remain entirely committed to and how much they want to change or align with different priorities. So this is my best understanding as things stand.

In terms of the new changes that we are expecting, our view as an organisation is that there is a lot to admire about England’s education, but we think there continue to be some significant challenges. We think it is a system that works very well for some children and young people in some ways but much less well for those from disadvantaged backgrounds, which is one of our major areas of focus, and those with SEND, and also in promoting pupil engagement and strong mental health for all children and young people. So we definitely think there is a case for delivering on many of the proposals that are in the White Paper as it stands but also for thinking whether there is more that we can do in those areas.

We think there are things that need to change. We definitely think that improved technical education, as the Prime Minister is now proposing, should be one of those changes. It feels to us as if the system is still very much one in which the default assumption is that young people will follow an academic pathway, with options for those who want to follow a more technical or vocational pathway being both fewer and much more complicated to navigate. We are pleased to see those changes, but the challenge—as you are alluding to in this question, Chair—is how the system can navigate and understand both the direction of travel set out in the White Paper and what changes we might see now.

In terms of those newer changes, it is important that they are done carefully, drawing on relevant evidence and not undermining the academic improvements that we have seen over the past decade, and that they recognise many of the reasons for the disadvantage gap and the shocking number of young people not in education, employment or training. Many of the ways that we tackle those challenges sit within education, but many more sit outside it, in the labour market, health, social care and welfare. In summary, we are warm to the changes in the White Paper and to those that the new Administration is hoping to bring in, but there is a lot of devil in the detail in how those two slightly separate visions at the moment are brought together and how we make sure that both are delivered in a really clear and evidence-informed way.

That was a really coherent summary of some of the areas where we are clear and not clear. To pick up first on the technical pathways, obviously that is my specialism and my day job, and something we in the Social Mobility Commission are keen on. We have been keen to see a much stronger technical pathway alongside the university pathway. It is clearly the case that over a long period of time, one has had much more attention and funding than the other.

I will make a couple of observations about the whole academic or technical debate, though. The first point to make is that everybody has some of both at some point in their career. We all start off with general academic education, in primary and most of secondary. There is then a question mark about when we move over to some more technical training. Some people do that at 16, particularly things like craft trades, construction and so forth. Others do it at 18, particularly higher and degree apprenticeships, which now allow you to start your degree a little bit earlier, in the workplace. Others start their technical vocational training after they have completed their degree—the typical examples would be medicine, law and teaching—so I think we have to be careful not to set them up as opposites. They are very much complementary and have a large degree of overlap.

That leads me to a second point, which is that we must not confuse technical education as an alternative to academic learning, because actually there is so much overlap between them. The best technical education requires really strong academic skills. You can see that in the way that, for example, T-levels have been constructed, and in apprenticeships, which frequently require good English and good maths. We must avoid the idea that they are somehow alternatives to each other.

That being said, there is a great deal about attraction. Some people find the applied learning of an apprenticeship or a technical course more appealing and motivating than they find academic study. I do not think that is necessarily reflective of academic ability; I just think it is about motivation and interest. The question we then have to ask ourselves is, at what point do we allow people to make that transition? The notion of having clearer pathways from 14 is a really good one in the sense that it is very helpful for young people—this comes out of the research on NEETs and various other sources—to have a clear line of sight to work, to understand how the qualifications they are studying can help them to move in the direction of the career that they want to go into. Whether that means that we need to start to think about a 14-to-16 technical curriculum in schools involves some really hard questions that we have to ask.

The first point to make is that, when we taught technical education in schools before, we did it really badly. We ended up devaluing the qualifications and actually encouraging young people to take courses that schools were very keen for them to take, because they improved league table performance, but in all honesty, the young people would arrive at college not ready for the workplace or to progress, and they would have to resit quite a bit of work that they had done. That was the work that the Wolf review challenged in vocational qualifications becoming less valuable.

We will also need to think about whether young people are ready, at 14, to make those choices, which can be quite weighty. As you probably know, in Europe the system works differently—but it is the whole system that works differently, as well as the labour market. We need to bear that in mind. That being said, my college currently delivers a 14-to-16 programme for a group of local schools; under the right circumstances, with the right, skilled tutors, the right kit and equipment, and the right facilities, such programmes can be powerful additions to the general curriculum.

My final point is that there is potentially a role for strategic authorities and mayors to think about how they can broker that kind of provision, as long as it is of high quality and an actual choice for the student that sits alongside their other choices, and as long as students have a clear line of sight to work and it is not presented as, “Well, we just want to get you out of class and into something else because we do not know what to do with you.”

If the provision is brokered in that way, groups of schools working with colleges could be productive in thinking what a 14-to-16 pathway might look like. The broader Manchester baccalaureate philosophy—thinking about careers and groups of choices that lead to careers—definitely does not always mean changing the curriculum; it just means helping young people to get the right work experience and so on. There are some really productive ideas to be brought in that regard. I will stop there.

A lot of ground was covered there, so I will just make two short comments. The first interesting thing is that the White Paper—broadly speaking and zooming out—emphasised continuity in synthesising what had come before. It is not yet clear that the implication of this announcement has been that it will emphasise discontinuity from what has come before.

At the Centre for Social Justice, we are cautiously optimistic about the idea of technical education at 14. We have advocated for it and worked with the now Prime Minister on it while he was Mayor of Greater Manchester. But we really think that it should sit within the continuity framework of the White Paper. Some things will need relitigating in terms of how we look at the EBacc, Attainment 8 and Progress 8. If the policy is to function well and not look second rate, those things have to be relitigated. But in general we would really like it to be integrated within that continuity document, which we think synthesises a lot of really good work.

Q2 There is some concern, based on past experience in this country, about technical education; as Alun said, it has not always been delivered very well. The concern is about the risk of a technical pathway from 14 resulting essentially in a limitation of the academic aspirations of some children and proving to be a constraint on social mobility for children from some backgrounds.

Briefly, what policies, mechanisms and checks and balances need to be built into the new system—each of you has broadly welcomed the intention—that would guard against the risk of its becoming a limiting factor on some children’s aspirations, rather than a broadening of aspirations and outcomes?

There are three points in particular. The first is about what the policy is seeking to achieve. It will go wrong if it is designed as something for children who are failing in education; that would be incompatible with parity of esteem. There has to be an aim for high-performing children to be taking this technical pathway. What problem are we trying to fix? I think it is a lack of technical excellence in the system.

The second thing to make the policy work is that it needs to latch on to something at 16. Look at the issues with T-levels—in many ways, the children who have done them have been very successful, but T-levels have had very low take-up because they have been somewhat incongruous; there has not been a runway up to them. This is an opportunity for embedding such a runway into the system.

The third thing somewhat repeats my previous answer. The policy needs to be integrated into the accountability frameworks. For it to have the same esteem, it needs to have the same rules and sharp edges as the academic framework. It needs to sit in things like Attainment 8 and Progress 8, and potentially even some sort of EBacc/TBacc-style thing.

I agree with all of those comments. I would also add that I think it needs to be a high-quality qualification. It needs to be a clear choice that involves the young person and their parents so that it does not become an option that is imposed on people. Where young people are struggling with their English and maths, in particular, it has to be a condition that the English and maths continue to be a high priority because we cannot ignore those challenges.

I also think it needs to be carefully managed in the relationship between schools, colleges and strategic authorities, as the scale of this for employers could be overwhelming because of the number of people looking for work placements and so forth. That is where the brokerage role of the strategic authorities could be quite productive. Keeping that balance between the school and the college on expertise is, I think, very important.

I also agree with both of those points, so I will just add a couple of extra thoughts. One is about teachers. I take on board Alun’s really good points about how we can have schools and colleges working together more closely, but to deliver this vision we will have to look at the skills, knowledge, backgrounds and expertise of teachers in schools as well as colleges, particularly if we are looking to extend some slightly different options down to 14. We need to look really closely at what we need from the teaching workforce to deliver that.

The other point that I would make is that we need to be really cautious—I do not think that this is where we are, but there is a danger that we could go there—about thinking that this solves all the issues, particularly those around disengagement and disadvantage. We know that whatever route children and young people take, disadvantaged students need more focused support than many of their peers and than is often currently possible in our tightly funded schools and colleges, whatever route they take.

Let’s make sure that we are looking really carefully at having the right teachers in place and the right wider support to sit alongside the broadening of the curriculum that I think we are looking at.

Q3 I think we have covered this extensively, but I want to ask one brief question, perhaps to Julie. There is sometimes a risk in having this conversation that we fall into the trap of thinking that vocational subjects are the only place where students develop skills, whereas the reality is that skills are taught across the curriculum. Are you concerned about that and what do we need to do to ensure that the academic side of the curriculum is also better at delivering and articulating the skills that it is teaching our young people?

That is absolutely right. Too often, as a system, we have fallen into that slightly tiresome debate between knowledge and skills. We know that both knowledge and skills are essential and both are developed through a range of different pathways, approaches and routes that children and young people take.

What is really important, and what is implied in your question, is that we should essentially make sure that the policy pendulum does not swing too far away from the significant benefits we have seen in academic knowledge and skills over the past few years. There is no reason why it should or why it needs to; with intelligent policy design we can keep what has been beneficial about that focus on academic skills, particularly for disadvantaged children, that we have seen recently while recognising some of the challenges of that to curriculum breadth, engagement and opening up different routes. It is about ensuring that we do that at a national policy design level and about how, as this plays out in individual schools and colleges, we do it in a really mindful way and recognise the potential benefits and the challenges.

Q4 The Government’s White Paper sets several ambitions, and I want to ask about one. It says that, on average, by 2040 children will leave school achieving a grade 5 or higher across their GCSEs. There was obviously a slight fall this year, but there are 14 years to go yet. In your view, what steps need to be taken to achieve the necessary changes within the timeframe set out? It would be helpful if you could touch on whether you think any changes need to be made to the curriculum and assessment.
Could I confirm whether you are asking about the specific ambition for achievements in English and maths?
The ambition is that, on average, “children will leave school achieving a grade 5 or higher across their GCSEs”, so not just in English and Maths.

Okay. The great strength of an ambition like that is also the great weakness of it—it is a bit like GDP. It compresses and condenses so much information and so many different factors into something that gives you a really clear sense of system health in one number. That is extremely helpful for understanding what is going on in the education system, but very difficult for understanding what specifically contributes to it and what specifically is causing different movements that we see in the number, which then makes your question very difficult to answer. That is one of the cautions that we have to exercise when we chase the really big numbers, as it were. It is the same with halving the disadvantage gap—the same thing would be true.
I will come on to that.

To try to give a specific answer, the strategy has to match the metric, and it has to be a broader system health strategy, as opposed to something specific. Attendance would be a different example, where you have a very specific number that you can then have a specific strategy for, whereas this is a very general number that compresses lots. Really, the strategy should be, “Make the system function as well as you can”, and that number should move.
Thank you—I appreciate that.

It is hard to disaggregate an answer to the question about the attainment ambition and the ambition on closing the gap, but I will try to focus on attainment and then perhaps we will come on to the disadvantage gap afterwards. It feels absolutely like those two are both the right ambitions. Having those as parallel ambitions is really important, because there is a danger that they can fight against each other. It is easier to close the gap by focusing on children who are more likely to achieve a higher target, so it is really important that those are both there.

When I look at the work that the Education Policy Institute does, particularly around the latest version of our annual report, which looks at attainment and gaps—again, it is quite hard to disaggregate—we are seeing that the socioeconomic disadvantage gaps remain wider than before the pandemic at every stage. The recovery we had started to see has either stalled or reversed at all stages of education. So keeping that attainment target, as well as the gap target, is hugely important.

In terms of what changes we need to see to achieve that, the answer comes from looking at which groups of children do not currently achieve in a way that would enable us to meet that target. Those are particularly pupils with special educational needs and children from certain ethnic backgrounds. There is a huge geographical piece to this as well, which we might come on to later when we talk about the missions.

Looking at changes focusing on which groups of young people are not achieving what we need and making sure that our policies are focused on supporting those groups will enable us to close that gap. Some of those might sit within the curriculum and assessment review, but most of those changes are probably outside of curriculum. They are more in the space of funding, focus and structures, which we might come to in other questions.
That is really helpful. Alun, although I did not mention the disadvantage gap in my question, feel free to refer to it, as both Daniel and Julie have.

I will try to stick to three points, which I think will complement the points that have been made already. The first point I would make about the next 14 years is that it worries me that if you take the 20 worst-performing local authorities in the year 2000 and compare them with now, they are pretty much the same, with the exception of London. London has bucked the trend considerably. If you look across the other areas, they are pretty much all post-industrial towns or coastal areas, with one or two rural areas in there. What concerns me about that is how deep rooted the problem is around the attainment gap and around the geography of that, and we must recognise how important place is in understanding what is happening. That is my first point.

My second point, which is slightly more controversial, is that we have a problem where, whenever we see anybody improving outcomes, it becomes instantly very political— I know you are all politicians, so I am saying this to you all, not any single one of you—but that is actually very unhelpful. When we have schools that are apparently high-achieving, we need to understand properly why that is the case. What happens, generally speaking, is that it becomes a bit of a political football, and we never get to the bottom of what they are doing that is working, if it is working.

That is very important for another reason, which is that we can see a whole set of schools and social circumstances in London that may explain the improvement in outcomes for children. Some of them appear to be demographic changes and others appear to be educational changes. If we want the rest of the country to start to learn the lessons of that, we need to understand what sits behind it. We need to start to think systematically about how we can extend across the country what we know works, and that is the part we are not very good at. We still have those areas I have described that are not doing that well.

There is a second point, which I will come back to later if anybody wants to. The Social Mobility Commission has recently been doing a qualitative piece of research into NEETs in Blackpool. One of the things that has come out of that research and has stuck in my mind and that of the commissioners is that, for all the range of factors that we can look at—and there are many; there is always a complex range of factors in any of these situations—one of the things that stands out that we do not have a tight grip on is what we have called—we have not invented this term; we borrowed it—the psychosocial aspect of underachievement and underperformance.

We know quite a lot about what it takes for students to perform well, and many schools can describe what that process will look like in terms of teaching, learning and assessment. But we also have a huge body of research around what we might loosely call disengagement. Why do some people disengage from learning? What is it that is taking place that leads to that? They point to things like issues with planning, goal setting, thinking ahead and emotional control, but there are also things about the experience of failure if you are the one who always tends to come last, and how that impacts on your engagement with learning. You do not have the same sense of expectation and anticipation. Learning becomes something that you feel ashamed of, or you don’t want to engage with because you find it painful.

I do not think there is any single easy explanation for this. What troubles me about the whole debate about improving outcomes is that although we are absolutely right to focus on the outcomes of those who are not doing so well, and to focus on belonging and the importance of getting a system that works well for them, I just do not think we have a clear educational theory about what it is we need to do in learning to help them to overcome those obstacles. I know I have opened up a big issue in saying that, but it is an important debate. Do we really know what needs to happen for those most disengaged learners to be more successful?

Q5 That’s right. I am sorry to cut you off but we have eight more questions and 30 minutes, so I am going to ditch one of my questions and just ask this. We have talked about the disadvantage gap—you were quite right to bring it up in your answers, because you cannot tackle one without talking about the other. The Government’s ambition or target on the disadvantage gap primarily focuses on the performance of pupils who have been eligible for free school meals for six years, and those who have been in care at some point. Is that too narrow? Does it need to be broadened? I am very keen to hear your answers on that, starting with Daniel.

One of our founding principles at the Centre for Social Justice was that the way we look at poverty in this country is reductive. Obviously, the issue with that is that it becomes very difficult practically to define poverty if you define it in a deeper way. In that vein, if we moved in either direction in terms of specificity, we would do better.

On the one hand, we could strip back the focus and say we are going to isolate children who are falling behind in school. We do educating, schools are the home of opportunity—we are going to focus on those falling behind and catch them up. We do not then get into the question of exactly how we define disadvantage and hardship, and just focus on those falling behind.

The other option is to go in the other direction and say that we need to look at family structure, debt and addiction. We need to look at the security of their housing. We need to see whether they are in an inter-generationally workless household. We to need to properly understand the context of this child and what, outside of school, is stopping them achieving. When you do that process, you can properly identify challenges and focus areas. Either of those would be better than what we currently do.

Free school meals is a very helpful proxy—it has enabled lots of analysis over many years—but we do think that a move towards a more income-based measure would be more helpful and would be useful to do at this point, for a number of reasons. One is that many children in poverty are not currently captured in the free school meal measure, and that varies across different pupil characteristics, geography and time. It is felt particularly acutely in the early years and the first years of primary school, where there are many children whose families have not registered as being eligible for free school meals but who could be. A move towards a more income-based measure that captures that and moves away from requiring families to self-declare would be really helpful. It would mean that more of the children who would benefit from the additional funding that comes from that identification would be helped.

It is really important that any threshold that is used to identify disadvantage and provide additional funding is reviewed regularly and adjusted in line with inflation, the cost of living and so on. We are also interested in how geography—area-based measures of disadvantage—sits alongside that, as well as measures of persistent disadvantage, which we think need much more focus.

I will keep it brief, because I agree with both previous contributors’ comments. I think that disadvantage is much broader than income or free school meals. I will give a couple of examples from my own experience. One is that in areas like Blackpool the impact of private sector housing and the instability of housing is a much bigger issue for some young people than anyone can imagine. Daniel picked out a really good example.

The second thing I have noticed is a very strong correlation between family size and structure, and which families are in the poorest parts of town. The students who are on the entry level 1 courses at college at 16 will predominantly come from families who are much bigger, often with only one parent, and you can imagine the stresses and circumstances that go with that. If we only focus on things like free school meals, there is a spectrum of people, and if we want to really change the outcomes for the most disadvantaged, we have to be much more searching in the questions we ask, in ways that are not stigmatising but that try to get us to focus on improving outcomes for the very truly disadvantaged.
Thank you very much Alun. I will leave it there.

Q6 My question closely follows what you have been discussing, and is about the new model for targeting disadvantage funding through the national funding formula. Julie, you mentioned widening it to look more broadly at income; should the funding focus on other areas? We heard from Alun that housing should be a factor, but there is a range of ideas out there about what else you might focus the money on. Would you like to add anything further?

There is a range of options. I think there is also a danger that this becomes too complex to administer, both centrally and for individual schools. There is an argument for making broader funding streams to schools as helpful as they can be in recognising the different circumstances in which those schools are operating, but keeping the pupil premium—that very focused funding for disadvantaged children—as straightforward as it can be. It is helpful to look at those two things slightly differently.

In terms of the pupil premium itself, we welcome the interest in looking slightly differently at how it is targeted and particularly, as I started to say at the end of my last answer, in looking at how we offer as much support as we possibly can to children in persistent disadvantage. We use the measure of children who have been living in poverty for at least 80% of their time at school so far. Those children do much worse than most other groups of children , and we are seeing no improvement in closing the gap between their attainment and others. So a focus on persistent disadvantage is hugely important, but it needs to be done in a way that keeps things as straightforward as possible.

We would like to see more focus on persistent disadvantage, and we would also like to see the pupil premium extended beyond the age of 16. At the moment it stops at 16, just at the point where young people are moving into post-16 education, when they—particularly those from more disadvantaged backgrounds—often most need additional support. It has long been our position that there needs to be an equivalent of the pupil premium in the 16-to-19 phase.

I do not have a huge amount to add. The problem with formulas is that they are formulas and there is never a perfect way of designing a formula that applies in every case. It is about how you get the general rules right and sufficient to say, “Actually, there is a lot of judgment to be made in individual cases as to where schools and colleges provide the individual support that people need.”

I do not think there is ever a perfect way, but it is about looking beyond free school meals and taking into account wider factors. Julie’s point about making it administratively simple is right, or we will all tie ourselves in knots. I do not envy the person who has to sort the policy out.

I have a short observation on what seems to be the direction of travel, which I think is interesting. To build somewhat on Julie’s comments, the direction is towards isolating persistent disadvantage in a smaller cohort of more persistently disadvantaged children and then having more missions on areas, and having place-based capturing of the nuance—“There’s a problem here and a problem here. We will take from the pot that we will essentially save from having a more direct focus and build missions across the country.” That seems to be the direction of travel. I can follow up in a briefing to provide comment on that, but I do think it is an interesting change.

Q7 The good news is that my next question is literally about those missions. The Government have launched Mission North East and Mission Coastal—as a coastal MP, I am very excited about that. What lessons can be learned from similar place-based policies, such as the London Challenge and opportunity areas?

That is an excellent question, and it somewhat builds on Alun’s earlier comments about the London Challenge. The London Challenge is an extremely helpful case study and proof of concept from which to work, but it also has its uniquenesses, and we have to be careful as to what extent we can apply it. For example, the issues that the north-east faces are quite different from the issues that London faced in that context. One of the things that was so brilliant about the London Challenge was that there was a synergy of lots of different things going on at the same time that seemed to build on one another. The leadership of the London Challenge captured that momentum but did not act alone in it. It was very much a lightning rod in a context where you had Teach First, academisation, demographic change and other moving parts.

This weekend, we published a piece of research looking at the NEETs crisis in the north-east. One thing we have seen, which is very similar to what Alun commented on, is that the north-east does quite well until the end of primary school. Year-on-year data obviously varies, but as of last year it was the second highest performing region at the end of year 6, but then comfortably last by age 16—a large fall-off in that environment. On the one hand that is encouraging, because the secondary school-based mission has a real opportunity, as there is a platform from which to grow. On the other hand, it suggests that things outside of school are the main factors in that fall-off and that there is a lack of aspiration.

We obviously have a very high NEETs rate in the north-east, and have done for 20 years. We have not had economic growth in the north-east for coming on 40 years. There is a broader question there as well. My one concern for Mission North East would be that if every secondary school was brilliant, how much would the problem be fixed?

I strongly agree with Daniel’s points. Just to add a little more detail, a lot of our research looks at the variable disadvantage gap across different regions. Looking at the latest data on that, I think the focus—the proposed focus, at least, as it was in the White Paper on the north-east and on coastal areas—is absolutely right. That is consistent with evidence of where some of the gaps are. I would add the south-west to that. That is the other region where we see significant challenges in terms of closing the gap. That is important and powerful, and I hope it will continue.

I would add a couple of other points. One is that there are a lot of differences when you look at sub-regions—at individual local authorities as well as regions as a whole. If you look at the difference between the highest performing and the lowest performing local authorities in terms of the disadvantage gap, that equates to almost two years of learning. It can be too broad brush sometimes to look at a regional level without really drilling down into the details.

To completely reinforce something that Daniel said as well, I should say that when you look at the reasons for the challenges in those areas, you see that they need a cross-governmental, cross-societal approach to solve them. If we continue with that mission-led Government, which I really hope we do, thinking about those challenges across all those areas that affect children, young people and their families will be really important when addressing those challenges.

Those comments are absolutely excellent. I have a few brief comments. No. 1 is that we have had dozens of place-based approaches, and I am not sure we all know what we have learned from those. Think back to Excellence in Cities and education action zones: one of the things that worries me sometimes about those approaches—this was alluded to in earlier comments—is that improving the institutions and the institutional measures is not necessarily improving the outcomes for the children. There are certainly experiences and examples that we can point to—yes, you could say at the end that schools look like they are better, but are the outcomes for everybody who goes there better?

The point about the wider issues is really important. Let me refer again to some of our recent research. When young people talk about moving to employment, one of the things they talk about is how difficult it is for their families to help them; their families might be broadly supportive but just don’t have any experience of work and or of the occupations that young people want to choose. That is more difficult in areas where there is less work or less well-paid work, and where you meet fewer people who have those higher-level occupations.

To that broader issue of a cross-governmental approach, thinking about improving educational outcomes in the broader context of improving the economy and broadening opportunities are all important. That is why the devolution agenda is as important to this as the missions themselves.

Q8 My question is for Julie. A third of all pupils do not currently achieve grade 4 in GCSE English and Maths, and those pupils are more at risk of ending up not being in education, employment or training. In your view, what is the best way for the school system to support those pupils who are currently struggling at key stage 4?
That is a big question. I will try to offer some immediate thoughts, and then some of them may come up through the later discussion as well.

I won’t labour the point, but at the risk of repeating myself again, the cross-Government approach to looking at the challenges of those young people not reaching grade 4—the forgotten third, as we often call them—is hugely important. I would absolutely reiterate that point.

To add a couple of others, we need to look really closely at the attendance of those children and young people. We may talk a bit more about attendance later, so I will give a bit more detail then, but according to our research the really crucial importance of attendance, and the even greater importance of attendance for children from more disadvantaged backgrounds, comes through time and again.

The Government have had a really helpful focus on attendance so far. Continuing that, thinking beyond attendance targets for schools and really thinking about what support schools, families and communities need to help with those attendance figures, which are starting to improve a little bit post pandemic, will really help.

The other point is that we need to look closely at what we are measuring with that statistic. It is based on the attainment of students in English and maths GCSEs. It is a really important statistic, but it is worth looking under the bonnet at what those qualifications are measuring. Are they really the best measure of the literacy and numeracy knowledge and skills that young people need to be successful? I would argue that they are not. They are important qualifications, but it is worth looking at what is actually being measured through them and what that tells us.

Linked to that, what happens next to young people who have not achieved a grade 4? At the moment, they go into a resit mill, where many of them really struggle to achieve those qualifications at another sitting, and often another sitting again. We need to think carefully about how we can help young people who have not got to those grades in the first place to be more successful as they go into their post-16 education and support schools, and colleges in particular, to do that.

Q9 That comes to my next question. The panel has mentioned the issue of GCSE resits in English and maths, a process that can be quite demoralising and demotivating for our young people. The Government have announced that pupils attaining below grade 2 at GCSE in English and maths will take a separate stepping-stone qualification. Do you support that proposal? Should that type of qualification be a high-quality alternative to GCSE English and maths rather than a stepping stone?

I am sure that Alun will also have views on this from working in his institutions. The stepping-stone qualification is an interesting idea. Within the current system, it is certainly worth looking at. Anything that can help to break through the demoralising cycle of resits and offer an alternative route for young people who have not got those qualifications in the first place is worth looking at.

A better answer, though, as I alluded to in my previous answer, is to look at what we are asking of children and young people in the first place in those GCSE qualifications. I would prefer as a first step to look at English and maths GCSEs themselves and think about whether there is a better way of identifying proficiency in literacy and numeracy than those qualifications currently enable. That is not easy to do. I recognise that there are challenges in moving away from that GCSE basis for those subjects. If that proves too challenging, I think the stepping-stone approach is a useful one alongside considering other aspects of the resits policy.

I don’t know where to begin. I could talk all day about this, probably not satisfactorily. If I am honest, I am not a fan of the stepping stone. The first point I would make is that we need to improve English and maths outcomes before students get to 16. I think we can say that and park it. Once they have not got it at 16, it is incredibly important that we put a lot of effort into making sure that as many 19-year-olds as possible do.

I do not think the stepping stone will necessarily help for these reasons. If you are going to do the stepping-stone qualification and you do not pass it, what happens then? Do you do it again in year 2? What do you do in year 3? I am not sure it solves the problem. There may be other ways of dividing up the curriculum to teach it in chunks where students are coming in with very low attainment.

The stepping stone is not really a stepping stone, because if they come in with a grade 1 or 2 GCSE, they already have the equivalent of a level 1 qualification. I am not sure it changes that much. The real issue is: how are we going to improve the English and maths skills of young people that are coming in with fairly poor attainment? My concern here is, really, the amount of time we give to them in the curriculum, the investment in English and maths tutors, and the huge gap in pay between school English and maths tutors and college English and maths tutors.

I know that not everything is about funding—I am probably the last person to constantly raise the question of funding—but I think if we are serious about this problem then we need to stop changing the qualifications and actually invest properly. If we are going to consider a post-16 pupil premium, I wouldn’t really support that, but what I would really support is a significant investment into excellent English and maths teaching, and the extension of the 16 to 18 phase to 16 to 19 for those who need it, now you can actually have three years’ funding. I think building that in for those with low English and maths right at the beginning and combining their vocational learning with their English and maths more effectively are better ways forward, if I am honest.
Daniel, would you like to add anything?
I have nothing further to add on that.

Q10 The Government have proposed changes to school accountability measures, such as Progress 8, that would cover English, maths, two sciences, two breadth subjects and two choices. Is that necessary and do you support that reform?

That is a brilliant question. It is one of the biggest questions that comes out of the technical education at 14 announcement, where the EBacc, Attainment 8 and Progress 8 all have to, to an extent, be relitigated with this new pathway that we don’t fully understand.

Our view at the Centre for Social Justice would be that the biggest issue with these measures was, as the Government said, their narrowness. If we can get technical education pathways at 14 right, that would be a very good way of addressing that while retaining what really works about them.

Take the EBacc; I know it is slightly separate, but it sits within the same design as it was implemented. If there were a TBacc as well—you retain your English, maths and science but instead of, say, history and French, you could do engineering, art and design—you could keep the rigour, ensure that there was no sense of a second rate option when it comes to breadth, and also have that wider breath.
There is an interesting opportunity here—I say that, but all those things are very difficult to do. But I do like that possibility as we reopen that question with this new announcement.

We would welcome a move towards recognising more breadth in school performance measures—particularly the inclusion of creative subjects and of technical awards. We think there is an opportunity to go a bit further: to think about how performance measures could recognise a wider set of qualifications more generally. We think it is really important to think about the qualifications suitable for children with a wide range of special educational needs, making sure that what are really good and appropriate qualifications for that wide range of children can be included in those performance measures. We do not think they currently are as much as they could be, and that brings all sorts of perverse incentives in terms of school admissions for children with additional needs.

There is a proposal to include an additional measure for children coming into secondary schools with low prior attainment. That is a helpful and overdue recognition for schools that have a particularly high proportion of children coming in with lower prior attainment.

We think this is heading in the right direction. There are clearly additional questions about the likely move towards an even greater focus on a broader range of technical subjects pre-16 and how those are recognised, but those can be approached in the same way as some of the thinking that has already started to be done around Progress 8.

I do not have a lot to add, apart from the fact that I agree with a lot of the earlier comments. We always have to be cautious when we change qualifications around dilution and lowering expectations. We have to keep our expectations high and encourage every individual to do absolutely the best that they can. When we make a lot of those kinds of changes, I am always slightly cautious about ending up inadvertently creating a high road and a low road. We have to be careful about that.

Q11 I would like to talk about enrichment. The previous Government published the enrichment framework in June this year and committed to additional funding, including the “Every Child Can” programme. What else do you think is needed to deliver the Government’s ambition of a strong enrichment offer, including access to sports, culture, civic engagement and—the one that I am really passionate about—outdoor learning and nature? I will start with you, Daniel.

We were very encouraged by the framework and announcement; it is something we have called for, but I think it is fair to say that it is not as substantive as it would need to be to make the kind of change that we would like to see. We at the Centre for Social Justice are publishing some research on this in the next fortnight or so, and we pick out three things within the scope of enrichment—actually, sport is within that as well.

First, we always focus on the provision offered, and mostly what focusing on inputs means is that those children who are already sporty or in lots of enrichment activities will do more. The number of children being enriched does not change substantially unless you focus specifically on participation, so it is a question of—I know it is a cliché to say this— moving from the input to the outcome.

Secondly, it is always sad to come to this conclusion, but there i s a reason why private schools do this phenomenally well and state schools do it much less wel l: it is really expensive . The funding pot that has been allocated and has been built just feels several times too small for the aspiration that has been outlined. On some things, we can see how much private schools spend to achieve what they manage to achieve; we can see how much money has been set aside .

That brings me to the third and final point, which is that a decision a bout priority has to be made in order for enrichment to be expanded so that every child can be physically active and doing other enriching activities like outdoor learning , theatre and debating. E nrichment has to move up the food chain for that to happen . It has to move up the food chain in terms of accountability measures —there are sharp edges , there are consequences , if th at does not happen — and it has to move up the food chain in terms of the resource associated with it . That will necessitate a question about what it move s up over — what it move s up in relation to . It is very hard to address th is issue —because it’s an expensive issue — without asking that question as well.
It doesn’t cost anything to take kids outside.
T hat is true.

A more enriched experience for children and young people is clearly a good thing , a nd I think it is really positive that this is receiving so much attention and policy focus. I agree with Daniel that there is an opportunity —that more could be done with this. I think it is important that e nrichment does not become synonymous with extracurricular . S ome of the things currently talked about in terms of enrichment really should be part of a core curricul ar offer , s o there is something to think about there.

This does need to be done in a way that is manageable by schools , particularly those serving more deprived communities , whose pupils probably need it most. T here is a danger that if schools that find this more challenging do not do as much of it as other schools, it could end up exacerbating gaps rather than closing them. That is something to be aware of. We need to be sure that it does not add to the already significant workloads of teachers and leaders. I suspect you will hear more about that from your next panel, but it could end up being counterproductive if it does that .

Daniel ’ s points about accountability are right. How do these increased expectations on schools sit alongside performance measures , Ofsted— is there an opportunity to rebalance what we hold schools to account for , what we see as important in what schools do , and make that more holistic? If it ends up going down that route, that w ill be hugely beneficial.

Q12 Alun, I have a huge rural constituency and one of the issues is that children cannot do after - school activities if they have to get the bus home, because there is only one bus —the school bus. Are you seeing any disparity between rural and urban areas in the provision of enrichment activities and extracurricular stuff? Have you noticed that in any of your work?

We do not have specific research on that, but I am aware of a whole range of things about access and participation relat ing to transport in rural areas, which comes up in lots of different guises , so I think that that does reinforce your point.
