I have been in the NHS almost four decades. As long as I have been in the NHS, we have always talked about capital slippage. It is a feature in NHS capital programming. We are not good at spending the money that we have. I think there are a couple of reasons for that. We have constant tension between governance and flexibility. We could delegate much more. Relatively small investments still require regional and national approval. That then means we have a very elongated approval process. That speaks to the point that I made earlier about developments not happening and the opportunity being lost. There needs to be much more agility and flexibility there, and much more trust as a consequence of some of these developments taking place. There will always be an issue in terms of governance from a public sector perspective and public expenditure. But I do think there could be more delegation than there currently is.
Q212 Where do you think the additional delegation should sit? At ICB level? Integrated care organisations? Community or foundation trusts?

I think most of the above. At a strategic level it is absolutely right for the ICB to determine what the priorities are for that area because they are the strategic commissioners, and the capital distribution should relate to what they wish to commission strategically. We have already got a greater level of delegation to NHS trusts with the change in the capital regime this year. There isn’t system capital in the way that there was before. The problem is that the oversight that used to exist, even at a level that is below the current size of ICBs, has gone. The temptation for NHS trusts in particular would be to deal with backlog and maintenance issues and not think bigger in terms of what they could do with that capital if they were to pull it together.
Q213 Is the logical conclusion of what you are saying, with the consequences of the NHS Bill, that health and wellbeing boards should be given their own specific budgets? What do you think?

That is an interesting question, as to whether health and wellbeing boards are at the right level to be able to do that and make those decisions. They should definitely be part of that decision making.

Q214 That is what the Government’s view is. We have been asking for clarity from the Department—we have found that challenging—on exactly how the place-based integration between local authorities and the NHS is going to work. We have challenged them on the boards issue because of the cultural point and, when they come back, they basically keep saying, “Health and wellbeing boards.” If that is it—if that is going to be the main mechanism by which place-based decisions happen—what do they need to have for it to be a success?

Given my experience of local government, if I were in the Department of Health and Social Care my concern about increased borrowing powers across the system would be that people may borrow too much money and not be able to pay it back. In the local authority context, there is a legal requirement to set a balanced budget every year, which you do not have in the NHS.
That is what I mean. Shouldn’t there be an NHS budget for the health and wellbeing board to spend?

A health and wellbeing board is a partnership, rather than a constituted organisation. It ensures a hard governance stop and accountability. As a local authority person, I am a huge supporter of devolved budgets, but we need an accountability mechanism that makes an organisation accountable overall for the spend. It should be the accountable body for that budget. The risk with boards is that accountability is diffused over a range of partners.

I agree with that. In principle, health and wellbeing boards having oversight makes a lot of sense because of the space that they occupy. The devil is in the detail, in terms of the governance arrangements, how you would delegate a budget to a non-statutory body, what would happen in the event that there is overspend and who is responsible for that. A regulatory framework needs to be understood and worked out if that is to be successfully done.

Q215 When we were in Cornwall—in my constituency—we saw a range of creative community methods of delivering neighbourhood health facilities, which achieved very substantial value for money. They worked to an extent outside the procurement rules, because they used, for example, community interest companies to deliver projects. To what extent are the rules within which you operate counterproductive in terms of value for money and of achieving the intended outcomes? [ Interruption. ] Sorry, it is so loud outside. I don’t know whether you even heard the question.

I did. I have worked in Cornwall in the past, so I am familiar with some of the things that you said, including community interest companies and LIFT C o schemes in Cornwall. When we are looking at alternative finance, whether it is LIFT, public-private partnerships or PFI, one of the issues is that the thing that works today also has to work in 10, 15, 20 or 25 years. The length of contracts and concessions in some of these arrangements is significant. The delivery of healthcare—the way that healthcare actually operates—is likely to change quite significantly over that period, so one of the issues that we have had is getting locked into very long-term arrangements.

It is seldom the case, even if there is significant risk transfer, that alternative finance will prove to be cheaper to the public purse than accessing Government borrowing, so we need to think carefully about what we do, the flexibility that will be delivered and whether that represents long-term value for money for the public sector, so I would urge a bit of caution there. With new types of public-private partnerships, the issues are still the same. The private sector will always price risk, and there will be a premium for that risk. The public sector is not as good at managing risk, and that means that over the period of the concession, it will be more expensive. Now, that might be the right thing to do. A PFI hospital will have lifecycle built in, which would not happen in a traditional construction. Therefore, at the end of the concession, the building should still be in the same state that it was in at the start. That is very different from the way that the NHS has built things.

When it comes to LIFT C o, one problem is that we have seen , in some cases, too many assets being constructed and people not always thinking about that , as I said, from a strategic perspective : “D o we actually need that development? Could we repurpose something that is already there? ” The public sector estate is significant, and I think we are quite guilty of not repurposing and using what we already have .

I agree with all that. For me, private finance and alternative financing models work best where you are dealing with portfolios of assets and you have the ability to swap assets in and out of the model . W here you hit a real challenge is that a lot of the LIFTC o facilities were let on 25 or 30 - year concessions that wrapped in the debt payment, the lease payment and facilities management costs , an d then if you have revenue cutbacks, you could have the situation where the services have all been cut back. When I was running One Public Estate in London from 2015 to 2017, it was littered with part ly or fully vacant LIFTCo assets, because there had been revenue funding reductions and services had closed down.

Where I could see a private finance model working is for, say, smaller GP surgeries , where you know there is a need for x number of years , bu t if the asset is no longer needed, it could be sol d by the JV partnership for a different use , or redeveloped. Waltham Forest have used that model for housing acquisition where we know we have an immediate need, but we have the ability to move assets out of the JV partnership s hould they no longer be needed. T raditional private finance and LIFTCo do not give you that flexibility.

Q216 Okay, but I am not talking just about LIFTCo; I am talking about the community interest companies —not-for- profit organisations —that are delivering those projects. On all the accounting and procurement rules within which you have to operate , I think you are saying, Bill, that it is preferable to work within those rules , constraints and straitjacket s even if that results in not achieving the value for money , in terms of the initial capital outlay on the building , that you could have achieved, in the first instance, significantly cheaper elsewhere, but by other models of delivery.

One significant change that ha s tak en place between a lot of the concessions commencing and now is IFRS 16. Op erating leases that were not on the balance sheet a re now on the balance sheet , so you have to account for those in both revenue and capital terms . Tha t counts against the capital delegated expenditure limit , and that then mi litates against the flexibility that we have seen in the past where operating leases did not. T hat is a very different environment from the one where—
Q217 Are you supporting IFRS 16 ? Sorry, I am not an accountant ; I find all these terms rather arcane. Are you supporting the use of that particular rule?

It is not a question of supporting it or not. It is part of generally accepted accounting practice, and the Government ha ve decided that they will adopt that , so we are required to be compliant with IFRS 16 . But it constrains flexibility.
Q218 You are required to use it, but can you see the sense in doing that?

I t ha s reduced flexibility. I n terms of having greater transparency in some of the financial instruments that we have utilised, it has reduced flexibility and reduced our ability to do these things over a longer period. I think it is the case that in accounting terms it is right , but in terms of flexibility and what makes sense for the things that we are trying to develop , it is very, very difficult.

Q219 Explain it in the simpleton terms in which I require it, because I am not an accountant . You are saying that the IFRS 16 rule protects the public interest in some manner, but creates an inflexibility that means that you can do less and it might end up being more expensive . As I understand it, it brings the value of the lease into capital budgets and can cause a trust or ICB to breach their capital limits where funding is otherwise available, which seems rather counterproductive to me .

I think that is an unintended consequence of having more transparent accounting. T he purpose of IFRS 16 was to ensure that leases were much more transparent. In the past, operating leases operated very differently from finance leases. It was possible for an organisation to lease an asset, whether it was a piece of equipment or a building, and that would not feature on the balance sheet. Internationally, accounting standards moved to ensure that those were on the balance sheet, to increase transparency. From a n accounting perspective, it is absolutely fantastic and really transparent; from a pragmatic perspective, it means that then counts against capital limits. That is very constraining, because it is almost like a double whammy—accounting for things in a revenue sense and in a capital sense. That really constrains the ability to look for alternative finance in the public sector and has been a massive constraint.

Q220 To take one example, we saw in the HSJ that your cluster pulled out of a £33 million neighbourhood fund. Presumably that was something that was desired. What was the basis of that decision? Had the estimates simply changed, or the valuations, or had the accounting rules caused it to trip up?

That is the other constraint working in the NHS at the moment. Across the cluster where I work, a significant number of organisations are in significant financial difficulty. Almost every one of the acute providers has a significant deficit. The choice we were faced with was continuing to preserve the transformation fund—this is always an issue, deciding between what will work in the long term and what has to happen for short-term requirements—and thereby facilitate the shifts we want to see from sickness to prevention and from acute to community, or support organisations and help them to deal with their deficits.

Non-recurrently, for this year only, we have used most of the transformation fund to support the deficit organisations, while being very clear that we still expect the proposals that we wanted them to bring forward to happen. We inevitably would not have been able to start everything on 1 April anyway, so we are still working through the proposals with the intention that from 1 April ’27 we will have this year’s transformation fund and next year’s transformation fund—and therefore £66 million—to facilitate and fund those changes. It is far from ideal, but we had to be pragmatic and recognise that it was not acceptable to have every organisation with a deficit.

Q221 What do you think about the financial reforms announced in the 10-year plan, in particular the setting of five-year capital budgets? You mentioned earlier the constraint of having to work within annual budgets while construction—the whole planning, pre-planning, predevelopment, development and aftermath—is clearly going to stretch beyond one single financial year. Do you think the new freedoms—presumably, they will be freedoms—will help? What else could help to create an environment of creativity and flexibility to achieve value for money and to deliver the projects?

First, yes, I agree that having five-year capital budgets will be advantageous. That will allow us to plan over a much more realistic and reasonable time horizon. Secondly, greater flexibility in terms of the ability to move capital and revenue, and vice versa, has traditionally not really happened, other than to support the revenue position, but we should be able to be much more flexible. If we have a development that has capital and revenue components, we should not be constrained by how much of that is capital and the capital limit we are working within.
Okay—so you want more flexibility in that area as well. I think that that that covers it.
Q222 Where is the financial risk for neighbourhood estate projects currently being held? Is it being held in the right place? Bill might be best placed to answer.

In terms of neighbourhood, to take the cluster where I work, there is a mixture. Some of that has been delegated, so it sits between the primary care provider board, particularly in Derbyshire, and one of the community providers. Going forward, we are working on developing governance arrangements for how we manage the risk: what would we delegate in terms of budgets, and what would be the governance arrangements around that?

We are still working through what the neighbourhood footprints will look like; we think there will be a range of them. Our experience is that if we do things at a very small scale, with a very small cohort, we can see some of the changes take place and actually observe them, but we have to do this at scale. We have to do this for 3.3 million people, not cohorts of 50,000 people. With the greatest respect to VCSE colleagues, they can help us to understand some of those things and be really nimble. One of the things that the NHS has struggled with is taking that nimbleness and some of those innovations and scaling them up. We have not been very good at that. We need to think about how we scale those things up and do them across the whole geography.

Q223 Joe, you probably sit in the middle of that, don’t you? You have a reasonable scale because you are place based, but you still have to be nimble. Do you recognise that in terms of trying to balance it?

Yes, that is a very common challenge with working with the VCS. A lot of organisations are hyper local. Exactly as Bill says, it is about how you take that learning, involvement and role in service provision and scale it up. The larger the geography, the harder that becomes.

In terms of the financial risk, from an immediate local authority perspective, one of the challenges is, as I mentioned, the track record of the NHS in following through on leasing spaces. At the moment, the financial risk for the health centre I referred to is sitting with us, in that it has sat vacant for three years. With a good wind, it will probably be at least another year before it is occupied. That is four years of lost rental income. We took the debt out to build the facility six or seven years ago. It is about £100,000 a year, so I reckon that we will have lost local taxpayers half a million pounds by the time it opens. That is money we could have spent on delivering other facilities for local people.
Q224 That is quite something, because you would expect the health service to understand the imperative. You have the asset there and you would think the NHS would fill it.

Obviously local authorities have had circa 40% budget cuts since 2010. That has presented huge challenges. But in local government there is also now a commerciality, and a real focus on needing to make the right investment and get the return. It is a different system in the NHS, where you have not had the same level of financial austerity as in local government.
I am a recovering local government cabinet member, so I understand that well.

It feels like an opportune time to talk about the VCSE sector from our perspective. I absolutely understand and agree about the financial pressures that NHS partners and local authorities face in terms of service delivery requirements. Bill made the point very well— Claire Fuller talked about this in her stocktake report—about the need to think much more expansively about the health estate, and not just about repurposing primary care, or building new GP NHS centres.

If we look directly back to the experience of the covid pandemic, the role of community spaces in the vaccination programme was fundamental to that working, because they knew where people were, and people who might otherwise not have come for their vaccination would come to those places to get it. Part of the very complex solution speaks to the point about the appetite and demand for community-led spaces. The community ownership fund, which closed at the beginning of last year—
Q225 You keep using the phrase “community-led spaces”; could you define that?

They are spaces that are run and led by community organisations. That could be a local charity or a type of social enterprise like a community benefit society or a CIO—that kind of thing— rather than spaces led by the local authority or the NHS, or a private space. A community centre, a community café—that sort of thing.
Q226 Is there a governance arrangement that people think would work better to allow the health service, local authorities and VCSE organisations to share space better?

In Waltham Forest, we have a VCS lettings policy, whereby we offer rental reductions of up to 80% of annual rent based on an organisation’s social impact. We look at the value that the organisation brings to local people, there is an assessment framework, and that is then reflected in a reduced rent.

Q227 When I look back at my days as a councillor, that feels like the kind of thing you would do for a few years and then, after a while, an officer would say, “We could also look at the rents again and see whether we could bring them into line.” How secure are they? I do not mean for you specifically, but that does not feel like a very secure model, unless there is a clearer national direction on stuff like that.
I agree that anything that is set locally can be changed with changing priorities. Equally, things that are set nationally can be changed with changing priorities.

On managing the financial risk, when we think about the delegation of budgets and of financial responsibility, it leads me to think of the lead provider arrangements. The organisation that manages the financial risk should be capable of dealing with that financial risk. The delegation of neighbourhood budgets is quite significant. If they are dealing with all the healthcare in that neighbourhood, it needs to be an organisation that has the ability to deal with that. That will militate against some of the smaller organisations leading that, but that does not mean they should not be involved in that arrangement.
Q228 We are moving towards the One Public Estate model, which helps to support integration. How does it work? Does it have potential?

One Public Estate is two main things. It is a method of partnership working—you bring together a board representing major public sector landholders in an area. If VCS organisations are major landholders in a particular community, it brings them into the board as well, so there is that partnership arrangement. You look at your assets in totality, and the opportunities, and then the programme has provided Cabinet Office funding to undertake feasibility studies. I have seen a huge amount of very positive projects move into delivery. They have been funded with a small feasibility grant from Cabinet Office—say, £200,000—and have gone on to be multimillion-pound programmes that have delivered very significant impacts for residents.
Sam, you look like you are itching to get in.

Yes. I want to make two points, one about demand and one about models of governance. One of the things that we found in the analysis of the community ownership fund, which is a £150 million fund that closed early last year, was that it was 12 times oversubscribed. The total value of the expressions of interest that communities made to that fund was about £1.8 billion. There was a huge amount of demand for assets of community value in those places to be brought into community ownership. There are examples of the health system, of the NHS, nationally and in local areas, taking that initiative and that focus.

What has been incredibly interesting, and seems to compare very starkly to the wider neighbourhood health centre agenda, is the neighbourhood mental health centre agenda. It started with very small pilots and is being grown out under the 10-year plan. There were six initial places nationally that took part in that pilot, four of which happened in spaces that were community-led, or rather that were not NHS or local authority-led.

There is an example of one in Whitehaven, in Cumbria. What happened there was that the community mental health trust had the funding from NHS England under the pilot. They bought a local shutdown Halifax bank on the high street, paid for the refurbishment and everything, and then they asset transferred that over to Whitehaven community trust locally, who now run that as a neighbourhood mental health centre. As the NHS lead on that programme talks about, it is an ordinary building on an ordinary street. They very much designed it not to have wipe-clean seats and clinical white hallways. There is an independent evaluation of the programme coming out later in the autumn, so I absolutely direct the Committee to look at that when it comes out. The anecdotal evidence across those places on the impact on just one metric—keeping people out of crisis—is huge.
We did an entire report on this, I am sure you are aware. We have looked at it in some detail.

I just wanted to compare that with what seems to be happening in the neighbourhood health centre agenda, which is very much not about that approach. It is very much about new build, PFI, or dealing with existing NHS estates. A lot needs to be learned from that when the evaluation comes out. There are a lot of reasons why that model can work equally as effectively for physical health and wider health, and not just for mental health conditions.

It is about marrying the level of demand for community-led spaces as part of the health infrastructure with the ability and success of those models, and trying to think very differently—in a cultural way, in a strategic way, locally, nationally or regionally, wherever it is—about how you use the community estate, if we want to call it that, as part of the wider health estate and as part of the wider One Public Estate. I don’t think that is happening at all to the level it needs to at the moment.

Q229 I have one final question, which I often ask. If there was just one thing that you would urge us to make sure that we press on when we are trying to knit some of this together and encourage the Department to do things differently—just one, I am afraid—what would it be?
A governance system that facilitates collaboration and accountability.

Greater flexibility and delegation in the ability to use capital funds, and also flexibility between capital and revenue. I think the points made earlier about multi-year allocations will help to support that.

To move away from what seems to be the recent direction in DHSC and NHS Property Services—this focus on NHS and public estate first—and think much more broadly about what a community health infrastructure estate looks like. [ Interruption. ]
Saved by the bell. Thank you very much.

sessions.iT: Multilateralism
sessions.w: Professor Stefan Dercon (University of Oxford); Professor Ian Goldin (University of Oxford)

segs.tx: International Relations and Defence Committee
C orrected oral evidence: Multilateralism
Wednesday 22 July 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Robertson of Port Ellen (The Chair); Lord Alderdice; Baroness Blackstone; Lord Bruce of Bennachie; Baroness Crawley; Lord Darroch of Kew; Lord De Mauley; Baroness Fraser of Craigmaddie; Lord Grocott; Lord Houghton of Richmond; Lord Lamont of Lerwick; Baroness Prashar.
Also present: Baroness Antrobus.
Evidence Session No. 8 Heard in Public Questions 83 – 9 5
Witnesses

Professor Stefan Dercon , Professor of Economic Policy, Blavatnik School of Government , Economics Department , University of Oxford ; Professor Ian Goldin , Professor of Globalisation and Development, Oxford Martin School , University of Oxford .
Examination of witnesses
Professor Stefan Dercon and Professor Ian Goldin.

Q83 Welcome to this, the eighth session of the committee looking at the issue of multilateralism. Welcome to our two expert witnesses here today; we look forward to this session. It is live on Parliament television, and I believe that there is an audience for it, apart from the large numbers we have in the Public Gallery today. You will get a transcript in due course which you can change for any minor defects that are there. I ask members of the committee to declare any interests that they have before they ask any questions.

I will ask the first question. I was the lead reviewer of the strategic defence rev iew last year, and I think it is probably the only relevant interest to this particular inquiry. Both of you have a lot of expertise in this area, and I just wonder whether, in introducing yourselves to the committee, you might also look at the main characteristics that you believe are in the existing multilateral system and whether or not you believe that it is, as a number of witnesses have said to us, actually in crisis, and if so, why. I will ask Professor Dercon to start off with.

Thank you very much for asking me to comment on this. My background is that I am an academic at the University of Oxford. I was also the chief economist of DfID for a considerable period of time in the 2010s. Then subsequently I advised various Ministers in the FCDO as well.

As far as I am concerned, the way I would look at it is that there is obviously a real challenge in the multilateral system, as you were implying. We should not forget it was built essentially on a bargain between, say, US and European countries and the rest of the world, where the design was done by the West, and in return access and also possibilities for stability in the rest of the world were essentially guaranteed . D efinitely after the end of the Cold War, for decades, that was its feature . Of course, the geopolitics has changed dramatically. I am not saying that the multilateral system is on the brink of disappearing, but its legitimacy and credibility for a lot of players internationally have definitely been being questioned, and indeed its powers of enforcement of the rules of the game internationally are weakened .

We are in a situation of huge fragmentation that is happening because, when legitimacy is questioned, other countries are looking for alternative ways of doing this. You get proliferation of the G20, the BRICs and new kinds of regional banks and so on in the whole system. In that sense, we are definitely facing huge challenges. In building a credible system, I do not think that you can rebuild the old system, but actually there need to be ways of rebuilding a system and starting again from the bottom, building partnerships and coalitions of the willing to actually make progress.

Maybe, finally, I will make a very quick point on what is probably my main expertise, international development. There we saw that the multilateral system of course, plays a huge role, but with massive proliferation and slippage of mandates and huge confusion in the system—who does what and how. A lot of multilateral organisations are not clear any more what their core business is. That creates unhelpful context in a lot of settings.
Thank you very much. Professor Goldin, will you introduce yourself and give your answer to the question?

Thank you very much. It is a huge honour and privilege to be here, and I appreciate the invitation. I am an economist who spent about half my career in policy and government and the other half since 2006 at the University of Oxford, where I am professor of globalisation and development and started something called the Oxford Martin School, which is the world’s leading centre for studying big global challenges and includes a lot of work in international relations but also on other topics.

I was born in South Africa. I came to the UK in 1978, involved in anti-apartheid, and lived here until 1994, when I was invited by President Mandela to go back and serve in his Government , be his economic adviser and run the Development Bank of Southern Africa. In that context, I was involved in many multilateral negotiations, including with the World Bank, which we barely borrowed from while I was in that role. When President Mandela stepped down, I went to the World Bank, where I became head of policy for the World Bank Group and the special representative to the UN for the World Bank, and also vice-president there under Jim Wolfensohn, was involved in many things with the UN—the millennium declaration, the beginning of the MDG process, and was also invited by Kofi Annan to be on the UN reform task force that he convened, along with Gordon Brown and many others at that time. Jim Wolfensohn retired and was replaced by Paul Wolfowitz. I resigned from the World Bank and, fortunately, the opportunity arose to come to Oxford in 2006, and I have been there ever since.

To respond to the question, I believe that the United Nations, the global multilateral system, is in crisis. You certainly would not want to look to the Security Council for help if you were in Ukraine or Palestine or Sudan. That and m any other parts of the system are totally unfit for 21st - century purpose. One should n o t beat up on the people who work in these institutions, although they certainly are in need of very major reforms. It i s the shareholders of these institutions , i n the end, the major Governments of the world , that are responsible for them. I t is to them that we need to look , which is why it is important that this c ommittee and the UK thinks about its role in them . These institutions should be servants of the Governments which own them.

The World Trade Organi z ation is completely stymied at the moment. The World Health Organi z ation — which , to me , must be the most important of the organisations that we need to save us for the future — is in a worse state than it was in 2019, before the Covid - 19 pandemic. The US, of course, is not funding it any longer . G lobal politics is making it a much more fractured operating environment .

We do not have a ‘ u nited n ations system ’ , but a ‘ divided nation s system ’ . Whether it is m ultilateralism , development or team sports , there i s a big tension between the need for Governments to work together and a growing need from taxpayers, from voters, to see their Governments do things that are in their narrow self-interests. T hat, I believe, is part of the reason that this is happening.

The most sophisticated of the systems , finance , in which I am involved, failed to stop the financial crisis. I was at the W orld Bank as head of policy in the run - up to that crisis. We never saw it coming. As you know, finance, the W orld Bank, the IMF, the Bank for International Settlements and other multilateral institutions, along with our central banks and treasuries in our national Governments, are by far the most data - intensive, well-paid and powerful institutions in our countries. T he fact that they failed to see the crisis coming led, for many people, to a collapse of trust in multilateralism and in metropolitan elites. Much of what we are seeing in the fractured world, in the democracies , follows from this failure of multilateralism. I t is not a new crisis of multilateralism ; it is one that ha s been building and brewing for many years . I t is important that we try to fix it, because it is of vital importance for the future of humanity.
Why did all these clever people, with all that data and information, not foresee the crisis that was coming?

I think one reason, which is very relevant today , was the failure to understand technological change by old men like me, who were in the multilateral institutions but were also in the audit c ommittees and were the CEOs of banks , but did not understand credit derivatives, which were the new gadgets. I did a BBC series called “ After the Crash ” , in which I interviewed some of these traders and said to them, “D id you foresee that your instruments would lead to this sort of thing? ” Th ey said, “O f course we saw that, but we felt like poker players on the decks of the Titanic, and we knew we would get out in time ” . So one reason w as this disconnect.

Of course, library shelves have been filled with books on the causes of the financial crisis. There were many reasons , and a nother was the political imperative of , “D o not prick the credit bubble while the party is going ” . Politicians did not want to reduce the feel - good feeling that the credit bubble was creating, particularly in the US but elsewhere too. T here i s a real tension between the advice . W hen you speak to economists and when you speak to politicians , m any of them now say, “W ell, we saw it coming ” . I think that is a rereading of history . S ome individuals did , b ut clearly the institutional consensus was that this was manageable at the time. I t was, I think, a failure of will. It could have taken an undergraduate to work out on the back of an envelope that credit derivatives were not sustainable , but this just was n o t something that was absorbed into the mainstream.

There was also clearly a failure of information . I think th at the UK and Gordon Brown w ere surprised at the time when Lehman Brothers took a very large sum of money out overnight back to the US. That institutional failure to keep track of what was happening also lay at the heart of it.

Q84 Can you tell us what you think the UK’s role should be in large multilateral organisations over the next decade ? I n particular, do you think that there is a trade - off between, on one hand, support for multilateral engagement and , at the same time, the pursuit of UK interests ?

It is important to always recognise who we are and what our role potentially can be, but also what our interest really is. We are a medium - sized economy these days , v ery open and very much exposed to global forces. It i s in our interest , as the UK , that there are rules of the game and a clear sense of order.

W e should be careful about national interest s becoming very transactional —u nfortunately, when I was working inside the system, I observed that too often —and about the q uick wins. Flag - waving seemed to be leading while you were , in fact, just a smaller player in the whole system . That was very much communicat ed towards the UK audience, but without constructively building , in the medium term , the stronger rules of the game that are in our interest.

I n a sense, a trade-off is not the right language, because it is in our interest that we have some form of functioning multilateral system. W e should be willing to be selective , b ut the main thing is that it is multilateral and multisided . We need to build coalitions. We usually hear , “W e ’ re going to lead the reforms ” . Why do we not say , “W e ’ re going to build the coalitions for reform ”? Otherwise , we just stand here flag - waving. I find it a bit unfortunate that , yesterday , the Foreign Secretary again said , “W e ’ re going to lead reform of the multilateral system ” . Why cannot we use the word s that we need, which is to build the coalitions so th at change can actually happen , rather than making it about p oint - scoring and flag - planting ?

The UK has to be selective. Professor Goldin has already alluded to that . The UK’s expertise lies i n financial architecture ; i t should lie there and look at the issues . That is wh at we are strong in ; we have been very good historically a t setting the rules of the game. Virtually all bonds held by any Government in the world are under UK law [1] . Those are things where we can keep on building, innovating, being stronger, probably do ing better scenario planning and being aware of where the weaknesses are.

T here are areas that are clearly in our immediate national interest as well, including for our own economy , but it has to be seen not transactionally but from the point of view of building a system that can serve us in the medium term, with coalitions of the willing . We can be a bit more imaginative. It is not just European countries or the US ; we can think more broad ly: w here can we find new partners to build the rules of the game that can help our societies and economies?

If one thinks about what the greatest threats to the UK are in the future , there i s not one that could be solved by the UK alone. It requires co - operation , w hether it is the next pandemic, climate change or the t hreat of Russia and conflict . W hatever it is — one can think of the growth of Britain and the free trade system —w e a re going to have to be part of a global coalition of countries meeting those threats . T he idea that we could build high walls , insulate ourselves from the risks and prosper is profoundly misguided, although some people seem to still believe it, not least in the US.

That does not imply that we need to rely on the existing system of global governance to solve the problems. P art of the challenge is that the word “ global ” in th at phrase makes us feel that everyone has to be part of every solution and agree to it. I ndeed, we find that that is the reason why there i s an impasse in many institutions, whether it is the UN Security Council , the World Trade Organization or the World Health O rgani z ation.

I believe that the UK should be at the centre of new thinking in creating creative coalitions that work to solve problems. E ven if we solve only half the problem , or 80% of it, we should be very proud of the coalition in making these advances and the demonstration effect of working with others.

“M ultilateralism ” also implies Governments working together. That is very much stuck in the post-Second World W ar frame that founded the system. O f course, the UK, with Churchill , Keynes and others, was absolutely at the heart of that construction — Bretton Woods, the UN and other systems —b ut now we have a very different constellation of actors. W hen we think of the future of the system, we should not automatically think that only Governments should be part of it, or necessarily even in the lead. In the case of pandemics, we have seen the important role of collaboration with pharmaceutical companies, for example, with the UK taking the lead on that. In the case of past successes , like the closure of the ozone l ayer, it was about working with a small number of companies. In the case of the fight against HIV / A IDS , it , too, was about working with pharmaceuticals. Increasingly, we will have to work with artificial intelligence companies , like DeepMind, based here in London.

Broader thinking about what that coalition would be and who the key actors in it would be to make headway in resolving the problem , is extremely important . It is not only p rivate sector actors but other actors, including professional associations, cities and, in the case of the US, states that have a vital role to play. S tarting with the problem and thinking about which minimum set of actors would get us to make progress on this is a better place to start than thinking , “Which other Governments can I automatically talk to in order to make headway on this ?”
Q85 ​​ Baroness Blackstone: ​ You both impl ied the need for selection . Can you tell us what your three main criteria for selection would be?

​​ ​ The first would be effectiveness and i mpact : w hich key actors will impact this outcome, be they Governments or others ? D epending on what one is targeting , it would be very different. A pandemic , incidentally, is the extreme case , because it is the only threat the UK faces that requires all countries in the world to be part of a solution. A pandemic could come from the poorest village in the poorest country, or the richest lab in the richest country . That does not mean that all countries need to be primary actors in finding the solution. One could create rapid response taskforces that come from elsewhere , but Governments would have to agree to sharing data and being part of that. That is the only one like that . In the case of c limate change , two dozen countries could resolve 80% of the problems of emission s—although not of adaptation —and in finance, it is an even smaller number of countries. So, the first selection criteria, depending on the problem, is identifying the key actor s to build a coalition around.

The second would be subsidiarity : w hat is the lowest level of action one can include? I believe it is extremely significant that we do not aim too high. In other words, you will never get 100% of the solution. What minimum set of actors will make you progress , a nd how can this be devolved to different groups? Again, depending on the questions, these would be very different sets of actors. As we saw in the fight against HIV /AIDS , for example, non- g overnment al organisations became very important . I n the case of pandemics , philanthropists would have to be part of a solutio n—the Gates Foundation is now the biggest funder of the World Health Organi z ation. So, the second criterion concerns which group —but the smallest number of groups .

The third criteri on needs to be a demonstration effect. Start modestly, build from that and show that you can make progress. There is a tension between being a team player and not waving the fla g within these coalitions, because that will certainly alienate all others , a nd proving to voters and the public that one is getting value for money and that the UK is engaged. T hat tension should be managed in favour of getting the quick wins first and then advertising them , rather than the other way around . P rove to the public that one is making progress after one has made progress, not before.

​​ ​ Let me try to give some other ones , rather than just agreeing. The way I would go about it alludes a bit to what Professor Goldin talked about earlier on the lack of ability to foresee the financial crisis and so on. I probably have a slightly different view on it . T he benefit of hindsight is very good but w e need much more thinking about possible worlds and scenarios and w hat is possible. We have to t hink about the big challenges in the world and be willing not to say , “T his is the scenario ” . Sometimes the reviews we have seem to settl e on, “ This is the challenge in the world ”. W e are not thinking enough , because there are quite a lot of different challenges in the world and some will dominate over others. It is about possible worlds and trying to identify the key and important challenges where we should focus .

T he second one is about asking what we, the UK, can do , which goes to the point about comparative advantage . T he comparative advantage we have —where it will filter, even in terms of what may be happening —is in issues to do with the global financial architecture, debt and norm - setting around illicit finance. They are definitely the area s where we should have a comparative advantage. A nother one is the area of science and applied science , and the norms and standards that come into issues.

The third one, although I sometimes fear that we are not as good at it as we like to claim , is our role in helping to stabilise the world . I do not mean that just from a defence point of view but from the complementarities in various ways of doing this. I know there used to be an extremely good collaboration between defence and the development side in the UK Government. Now it feels as though they are being played off against each other, which is not very sensible if the biggest challenge in a lot of setting s is stability and the externalities that could have on the UK.

Th ose are the possible areas of comparative advantage. The final thing to say is that you can only do things if you have entry points. Perhaps this is a version of what Professor Goldin was saying . It is about thinking about where there is a chance for change —not just arguing about what the most important things are but asking: where do we have a chance to make something happen? It comes back to the question of where we think we can find some like - minded people around particular issues . If we go back to re building an international rule s- based system , w e need to understand how we buil t it at the time . T he trade system used to not be there . I t took a long time , including GATT processes, endless negotiations and building from below before we got to the WTO and so on. We did not suddenly invent it at Bretton Woods. We need to think about where we can start . Get the entry points right , the right partners to begin to build on it and diversify your portfolio, because some things will fail and some will succeed.
​​ ​ That was very helpful ; thank you both.

Q86 ​​ Baroness Crawley: ​ Good morning, professors. My question follows on . You have given us areas where the UK can play to its strengths within the multilateral system. That is the key question for us with this committee inquiry: how should the UK approach multilateral engagement? You have given us some very useful examples. How do you prioritise that in a world where funding is tighter and tighter? We had a very welcome announcement today on UK bus fares, for instance. That was fantastic. Then you look at where the money is coming from and see that it is the international budget: where we were giving grants for climate change in developing countries, we are now thinking about loans. How do you prioritise? Should we engage where our strengths are? You talked about our financial strengths. Should we engage on future opportunities and problems , such as AI ? That is always within the context of tightening national budgets.

Sorry, I have a bit of déjà vu of when I was working in g overnment when the cuts came through , having to handle the spreadsheet and find £4 billion in five weeks and of being criticised that we did not do it well enough in five weeks.

There is a reality of tight budget s: they are too tight and choices are being made . But you as ked how to prioritise. I will link back to what I mentioned earlier. We sometimes have a tendency to want to do things because they are important. A very typical thing in g overnment that I have observed over all these years as a chief economist is that we identify a problem and think that we can solve it by putting money on it. In between, we do not think hard enough about how we can solve it and generally begin to think it through. T hat part of reasoning helps with prioritisation. It comes back to the question of whether we generally think through where the entry point is—where t here is a chance that you can make an impact, rather than doing everything problem - based .

In international development, there are endless problems and all kinds of things we can spend money on, but we cannot solve all the problems with our resources . The priority needs to be think ing: “Is there an entry point for us to make a difference here? ”, r ather than saying, “T his is an important problem ”. Going back to my time inside g overnment, it definitely helps a great deal if we do that a bit more systematically and do not just respond to problems . You mentioned AI . I am not an expert on it, but there is definitely a lot of expertise on it in the UK these days. In w hich bits and pieces w ould we have an entry point related to global norm - setting , for example? We can all cry about more global regulation tightening the hands of some of the biggest tech companies and so on , b ut where is the entry point? Where are the coalitions that can do it?

In my view, a s I always tell my students , the “ how ” is often far more important than the “ what ”. Having a way of doing something helps you to decide where you will have the biggest impact, rather than having an endless list of problems that we need to tackle.

To build on what Professor Dercon has said, I think it is important to reflect on the UK ’s soft and hard power , as the late Professor Nye distinguished them. It is often the case that soft power can be generated with small amounts of money and become more important. My personal opinion is that cuts to the BBC World Service, for example, are not in the UK ’s interests . O ne can also debate — Stefan was at the hard end of it—the cut s to the aspiration for 0.7 % for international aid and where they have ended up today. T he y are part of the UK’s global reputation and ability to influence other debates. They get us seats at the table and give us a power that goes way beyond the amount of money involved.

T here are other questions around what makes the UK special. I would argue that our commitment to human rights, democrac y, anti-corruption and activities associated with them are central to what we are about. T herefore, I believe that easing off on the monitoring of the Bribery A ct and of money laundering , for example, undermines in the process not only our hard power but, more importantly, our soft power and s tanding up for what we are . T here is a growing tension between us and the United States on this. It has removed some of these constraints on its activities . T here might also be growing tension with other democracies , in Europe and elsewhere. But I believe that at the heart of what the UK is able to offer other nations and people around the world is th is question of standards and norms , which Professor D ercon alluded to . C utting back on th em is not in the UK’s interests.

After that, prioritisation is necessarily very difficult. I was involved in it in many countries in my context as head of policy at the W orld Bank Group. In the future, the UK will be more, not less , dependent on the rest of the world , a nd forming these coalitions will become more important for safeguard ing our future than it is today. A key question is therefore: wh at budget cuts are we undertaking that will undermine that? Clearly, defence expenditure is one hard power issue , but it is only a small part of the future security of the UK . P andemics, climate change and other threats are at least as important to the future of the UK , a nd th ere is a growing case for AI, too.

C reative coalitions do not mean that we can work only with people who have the same principles as us. That would be impossible because we would have no one to work with on many of the key questions. What it does mean is being clear and grown up in our discussions about our differences , ensuring that they are not swept under the carpet .

Q87 Can you talk a bit abou t the impact of public attitudes towards multilateral politics and global governance? To what extent do you think the UK’s involvement in global governance and multilateral policies is constrained by public attitudes towards globalisation?

Th at is a really important question . There has definitely been a failure by many of us to first, properly make the case for global governance issues and issues to do with globalisation , and, secondly, to rethink it in the current circumstances —I will come to that in a moment. There is no doubt that globalisation, certainly around trade and so on, has been a huge driver in lifting the standard of living of huge amounts of people in poorer countries. For us, it has created a massive reduction in the cost of living and the prices of all kinds of goods. W e see that disruptions in trade flows are now a big driver in the cost of living crisis.

Of course , globalisation as it was practi sed and with the rules of the game it had , benefited everybody as consumers , but it hurt some people , as workers and producers in Western countries. F inding a way of balancing these two interests is something that we probably fail to do properly in Western countries. This is also well understood in a lot of emerging economies. It is not just a matter of communicating better the benefits ; there is a real task for us to build a case for a globalisation version 2.0 that can handle some of these issues better and t hat recognises that th ese liberalising forces in trade have lots of benefits but also come with at least temporary and sometimes longer - term costs , and then begin to build a system. It would serve the world very well and provide ways of building coalitions with all kinds of emerging economies which at the moment look at us more suspicious ly , not least with all the trade barriers that seem to be emerging , explicitly in some countries and implicitly in other s . There is a real case, and it is a matter of not just communication but design. It is about thinking carefully through what it should look like and not failing to communicate it this time.
Thank you. Would you like to add something, Professor Goldin?

Yes ; as professor of globalisation at Oxford , I probably should. It is a much - abused term. People have a very different sense of what the content of globalisation is. For me , it means flows across national borders of all types . The good flows are trade, investment and v accines, and the very bad flows are pandemics, financial crises, et cetera—what I call the butterfly d efect of globalisation. It is absolutely endogenous; it cannot be removed. We are entangled increasingly with others around the world. What we do has an impact on them and what they do has an impact on us. There is no reversing this. High walls will certainly not reverse it because, as China found after trying for over a year to keep out a pandemic, they will not stop pandemics, climate change or the big threats that we face.

The question is: how do we manage these flows? The problem arises from the ever-widening gap between the growing intensity of the flows and the governance of them, which is increasingly fractured and national. That is why we have more and more of them and why we face greater threats from pandemics, the climate and other threats.

The political response for domestic constituencies needs to be able to demonstrate both that these flows have been beneficial and that people are better off, as Professor Dercon mentioned, but in multiple ways. We are all certainly better off for these flows. Autarchy is a recipe for disaster for any economy; North Korea is, of course, the extreme case of what it does to you. We need to demonstrate that more forcefully, but we also need to demonstrate that our future depends on this in terms of the need not only for goods and services, ideas, digital traffic and everything else but for co-ordination with others.

It is not going to be politically popular but it is the case that we need more globalisation, not less—but not of everything. We do not need more of the bads, such as illicit traffic or the many other bad things of globalisation—including, increasingly, illicit movements in cyber space—and we certainly do not need any of the bad flows, such as climate change and pandemics. Those require more management. We need to be able to differentiate between them. We need to identify them and work with others both to reduce the harms of globalisation and to enhance the goods.

This is true domestically as well. Communities in our country and in other countries have been hollowed out by these flows. We need to empathise with those people and think about trade reform and multiple other ways in which we can demonstrate to them, too, that they will have a better future not by being less integrated but by being more integrated with the world.

The race to the bottom on taxation is one of the very negative features of globalisation, with the creation of offshore tax havens and islands, and the incorporation of companies in other jurisdictions over which we have no power. The revenue-raising ability of Governments has been greatly undermined by this lack of governance. The OECD is trying to come up with principles as a basic low base for it, but it is being undermined. The UK being at the forefront of that discussion will be an important contribution to restoring faith that we can be integrated and still shape our own destiny.

A recent survey that I read showed that young people in particular are becoming less globally minded , are less trusting of traditional allies and so on. T his is against the background of digital, where they get information —in particula r, TikTok . H ow does one deal with that ? W here do Governments have to put their effort s ? I hear what you are saying in terms of “ what ”, but it is about the “ ho w” as well .

Pr ofessor Ian Goldin: Yes. There is an irony in people using global digital tools to be anti-global , but that is absolutely the case . It is true that many of the anti-globali s ation movements are among the most globalised institutions. We—academics, Members of Parliament and businesses —need to be on the front foot much more here.

There is one thing about which I am always surprised . I was involved in the Uruguay round of trade negotiations, which shows how old I am. Business es did not speak up on the benefits of lower tariffs and removing trade barriers. They were silent. If you read the FT , the Wall Street Journal and so on, there was virtually nothing from business leaders at that time talking in favour of trade reform and lowering tariffs. T hose who believe in the importance of these things need to be more vocal in defending them.

Part of the challenge is that we do not use TikTok —I do not use it, anyway; it is a generational thing. Thinking about how we can use influencers is important. The UK was phenomenally successful with campaigns such as Make Poverty History, Band Aid, Live Aid and so on . It used icons of the time , such as Geldof and Bono , to get these messages out to young people , and it had extraordinary success, but we have done nothing like that since . In recent years, we have lost the ability to talk to multiple generations , as has Parliament.

I do not have much to add beyond that . This is an issue not just of globalisation but of the whole way in which we reach people . It is about how we can educate new generations on critical thinking and being willing to be critical . I am generally an optimist about many things but I think that, in a decade or so, we may look back at this period and say , “ This was something that was possible ”.

I come back to the point that with strong coalition - building , given the expertise that we have in the UK, one should begin to think about what a governance system could look like . However, we should recognise that, if we do not have India or Colombia [2] in this tent, we will undermine ourselves . We need to be willing to build a broad church around these things —not simply an on/off switch but something with a sensible regulatory role .

There are so many parallels here with the role in the economy and in society that robber barons played a long time ago. It took several decades , historically, before we found a way to manage that sensibly. I am optimistic that we can do it, but we all have to work on it.
We have a former Chancellor of the Exchequer on our committee; he has a quick follow-up question.

The problem is becoming worse , in a sense, with so much emphasis on security of supply — in some cases , it is just hidden protectionism —but do you not think that, to some extent, the fault lies with advanced countries , rather than the “Global South” ? Protectionism is growing in the advanced world and being used very much against , in particular, agricultur al producing countries in the developing world. I absolutely agree . We have killed it off against our own interest. The advanced economies have been trying to do this for a while . Quite a lot happened — definitely in the 2010s—and we did not react to it. So , I agree 100% with you. It is on our side and it is where we need to come from.

In fact, if you look at a lot of the “Global South” economies , there are issues to do with China and its role in all this, but the problem goes well beyond that . Other economies have been gradually opening up and doing more, but we are the ones who are going backwards. [3] I agree with you. Perhaps I could ask you to give briefer answers to some of our questions; I ask members of the committee to keep their questions relatively brief as well.

Q89 Thank you very much for your answers so far. A lot of countries outside the establishment of the current multilateral system are now agitating for more attention and more focus . They are very different : you have, say, Indonesia, Brazil, India and Nigeria . How do we involve them in a reassessment of multilateralism ? We have a number of existing instruments that are powerful. The Commonwealth is very much one of them. It is a wonderful convening platform. There is a lot of good will in our relationships with many countries that could be nurtured.

It comes back to this question: where is our leverage? On the point you are making, are there one or two pressing global issues where we could make a significant difference? Let us start with those, despite the cuts in budgets and everything else . I would be driven by those. We are very powerful on the climate in many respects , and we are doing the right thing on climate change. It gives us a moral advantage. We are very powerful when it comes to pandemics. We have great pharmaceutical industries. There are certain areas where we are very powerful on AI. Could we leverage one of these things to make real progress that goes beyond statements and into some institutional continuity?

Your question was also a bit about the “how” , given that budgets are low and diplomatic posts are being cut. From my experience of working in the FCDO, I was very surprised by how centralised everything is . As a result, initiatives from extremely skilled diplomats on the ground that begin to build partnerships ha ve very little resonance in London. There is a sense that the system is still designed for a very clear set of global rules and that our role is simply to make sure that everybody follows them , but given that these rules have disappeared , where new partnerships need to be built , as you alluded to, you need a very different type of diplomacy , whether in development or in other areas of multilateral co - operation. You need to have people who have the liberty to try , within a broad and general framework , to build up these relationships and so on.

Whenever I travel—I still do , an awful lot —and I go to high commissions or embassies , I am amazingly impressed by the quality of the people on the ground and their local knowledge. However, it has to go through a desk here , then it goes into a semi - quagmire in the system where those kinds of things do not get translated. For me, a lot of what you are asking around, “How can we begin to do this ?”, is about empowering on-the-ground missions much more to do what you just described.

Money does not buy you influence in these countries. It is not about the fact that they have less money. Again, it is about how you use resources to build up partnerships and links with well-meaning Governments. There are plenty of Governments who do not mean well, so you want to be careful and selective in build ing partnerships up in particular areas where you can say, “Look, we can begin to build here”. You must make sure that you communicate across different missions and embassies in new ways to build, from the bottom up , a rule s- based system.

Lord Bruce of Bennachie : I have some quick supplementary questions. We seem to be reticent to use the Commonwealth because it is not the British Commonwealth, but it does share our values. How much more can we do?

Y ou have said two things . One is that London is not only not listening to our posts —what is the point of them in the first place if they are not being listen ed to ?— but dismantling them . Q90 My question follow s on from Lord Bruce’s question. One thing on which I am sure absolutely everyone can agree is that the structures of the UN , when it was formed , spoke to a world that would be unrecognisable to what we have in front of us today. Yet the structures now are, in essence, the same. Am I right in thinking that a lot of the growth and interest in the “Global South” is a reflection of lots of countries that are relatively disfranchised within the structures of the UN trying to effect changes that reflect the modern world , not some world from the 1940s ?

If you agree with that , my question to you is: should Britain’s role be to put reform of the UN and its structures in the “too difficult” box—I do not necessarily dismiss that, as an awful lot of issues go into the “too difficult” box—or should we be more engaged with the “Global South” on this, recognising the injustice? I do not know whether “injustice” is too heavy a word, but should we recognise the present structure in relation to the “Global South ’ s ” needs and ambitions ? Should we take a lead on this, even though doing so would be to our apparent short-term disadvantage , because , relatively speaking, if they grow, we diminish?

It is in the “too difficult” box . I say that having been on the UN reform taskforce, which is just gathering dust , like many other taskforce s before and after it. That is not to say that one should not say that it is necessary and align oneself with the countries that say , “This is unjust; t he shareholding of all the institutions is unjust ”. Also, “one country, one vote” is unworkable . We need constituencies. We need different ways of doing things . The whole system needs reform. I do not think that that is going to happen in my lifetime, but that does not mean that one should not be arguing for it and aligning oneself. Again, that is part of soft power positioning.

W hether one can take a piece of the spaghetti bowl of overlapping UN mandates and try to fix it on a particular topic is a different question . O ne coul d do so, I think. I would certainly prioritise health and the climate , for example, as areas of need . We need to build institutions that work on these key global challenges. One would get tremendous support, and not only from the “Global South” . Incidentally, I do not like that term because most of the countries in the “Global South” are not in the southern hemisphere and some countries in the southern hemisphere, such as Australia, are very rich, but including countries such as India and China on those two questions would certainly be absolutely central to a coalition of the working.

I would not give up. It is difficult . T he current crisis in the UN system — especially in New York, which has a lot to do with finance being massively curtailed —is an opportunity. It focus es people’s minds a bit .

T his is probably the right moment to ask ourselves more generally about the relatively overstated position that we have in the system , whether in the shareholding or in the Security Council . We need to be willing to discuss this and, in return , to be part of the designers of the new system and to play a role in it. I am not suggesting a negotiation strategy here, but, again, we need buy - in from some of the other players across developing and emerging economies , as has been mentioned. A s Professor Goldin implied , this is a huge ly diverse set of countries , but, unless we build coalitions with them on this and give them a bit more voice— as it is often referred to in these organisations — we can not make them relevant again . The alternative is that we will keep on creating the incentives that continue to emerge, and the system will have even fewer game rules than we would like .

The important thing is that shareholding or voting power is one way of having influence —i t goes through power —but, if the power diminishes all the time , that is not very useful. There are other ways of having influence . Again, I come b ack to the UK. Historically, w e are designers ; John Maynard Keynes was mentioned . W e were designers of the system . W e are a place of ideas and convenors. We play that role. O ur influence can come from that form of power in the system because people come to us . I remember the way in which they did so when I was in development; t he German side said that it would not decide anything until it had checked what DfID was doing first . These are the kind s of thing we can do across the whole system . It is about giving up a bit of hard power for a space in this current crisis to build up our own soft power , with good ideas being the convenors of new ideas.
Q91 Professor Dercon , to the extent that it is still current and relevant, can you comment on the effectiveness of the multilateral development review processes undertaken in DfID?

That takes us back. It started with a multilateral aid review in 2011. The follow - up multilateral development review must have been in 20 16 or 20 17 , but that was another age. Money was going up , and it was right to question whether we would simply put an extra zero on someone’s cheque. We were inspired to ask, “What does that get us?”

T he instrument that we were using at the time , so to speak, was the belief that more money on the table gave us more influence ; t hat is a fair assessment. Back then , it was definitely important to review performance and alignment with broader UK objectives. I noticed that the House of Commons International Development Committee was arguing that they should have one. To be honest, at the current time , in this age, I do not see what its role would be, because this is not about huge amounts of resources being shifted. It is now much less than at the time. Also, the risk is that , given that the entire environment is a bit more transactional, we start looking at much more short - term benefits . One example is whether people vote in favour of us or support us in a vote . I do not think that that is going to help the system ; I worry that the criteria that you would use for assessment would be far more short - term , rushed and transactional in the current age . It will not earn us that much.

There are other processes that are being monitored. It would be much better to focus on rethinking what a reasonable future structure could look like and hav ing some scenarios for that. Using our influence, can we nudge some of these institutions in a certain direction, working with others , rather than trying to think that this process will now decide our ever - smaller cheques? I am not sure that that is the best way of using resources.

Q92 We have touched on this a little already, with regard to the Carney speech about middle order powers and forming alliances. Is that realistic when one considers the diversity of middle powers? O ne thinks of countries such as Indonesia or Japan , as well as European countries. One of our witnesses said that we should not necessarily look for people who have the same values or principles , but surely the middle order powers can be used only on a one - off basis for particular crises . S urely Britain has no permanent allies, only permanent interests .

You have put it very succinctly. Mark Carney’s speech was welcome. He articulat ed what has been part of international relations literature for a long time regarding middle, super and lesser powers. Underlining the point of a more variable geometry — that is, we should not be just bystanders because we have a role to play in addressing key questions —is welcome.

I am not a great fan of the idea of m iddle p owers for two main reasons. First, it is exclusionary : it impl ies, “That’s the group you ’ re going to work with ”, when , sometimes , you may want to work with both superpowers and with lesser powers —although that is a rather derogatory term; it puts a lot of developing countries ’ backs out of joint . They think, “What about us?”, which is legitimate. A bridge power is a more attractive concept to me than a middle power —that is, someone who is able to build coalitions with who m ever one needs to do so .

Secondly, it goes back to this idea that it is about just Governments’ powers. As I mentioned earlier, we need to be thinking more creatively about other actors in this , such as the private sector. The challenges that we face will not only be resolved by Governments speaking to one another , whether they are middle powers or otherwise . That is my second concern around how we are going to resolve the se issues.
I would briefly add that, as Professor Goldin implied , this was first raised as a concept in the 16th century. I t is a pretty old concept going back to Renaissance Italy and the princely states.

I am less negative about it as a discourse for the simple reason that, as seen from the UK, it is a useful disciplining device for us to recognise that we are not simply there as a superpower . W e need to build coalition s , and we cannot simply be the top dog in everything. I would not go out and encourage politicians to make speeches like Mark Carney did, but, within the system, it would be useful to recognise that we can achieve things only if we begin to build coalitions of the willing. That could be with Indonesia, Brazil and Mexico—that is, different types of player .

I am probably less negative about it because, if we want to rebuild a global system, we will need to bring some of these countries along. We will need to begin to have that conversation, whether it is about trade, financial architecture or human rights. We need to find coalitions of the willing to begin to reset these things. I am less negative, but I would use it as an internal disciplining device, rather than something that we keep making speeches about.
We will now bring together two questions to save time , s ince we are covering the same ground. Lord Houghton will start.

Q93 To p ut this in context , o ur study is being done in two parts ; we are attempting to go into the second part before the first part. The first part is to assess the state of globalisation in the context of the human journey. We will then make recommendations on what to do about all that . It is important to get the first part right because the second part depends on it: you embark either on a set of recommendations that are all about pragmatism and survival or a set of recommendations encompassing idealism and values. During the second half of this morning , we will attempt to clarify our thoughts on the first part . You a re our last chance saloon to get this right.

On the start point of our inquiry — the great , macro challenges to globalisation and its place in history — are we still believers in a teleological certainty of human destiny towards ultimate harmony, which is what we grew up with , o r do we lean more towards the philosophical pessimism of John Gr a y ? A re there inherent behaviours in human nature that make the establishment of a coherent world order inevitably elusive? A re you two really no more than professors of delusion? Your answer will help us b ecause , at the moment, we are veering all over the place on this ; we must anchor it today before going on holiday .
It takes a field marshal to ask that question. H old that in mind while Baroness Fraser ask s another , related question.

I am not a field marshal, so I will be a bit kinder. O ur role is to make a recommendation to the Government, and I am really interested in the question of what the Government need to do. It is about the “how”: how can they do it? Do the UK Government need some sort of strategy ? How d oes that involve the creative thinking and other players about which you have talked today? Ho w does that strategy come together given the fragmented responsibilities across different departments ? W e are on something like our sixth F oreign S ecretary in five years. How long - term can such a strategy, if the UK needs one, realistically be ? It would help us if you could say a bit more on the “how”, so that we are not delusional .
You ha ve the two sides of the question. Who will go first?

O n the question of the direction of travel, there i s no foregone conclusion. I am with Martin Rees — Lord Rees —with regard to the idea that this could be our final century. T he decisions that we make , and the decisions that this Parliament and others make , are consequential to this end. He is perhaps more pessimistic than I am, because he puts a 50% probability on the idea, whereas I would suggest that it is much lower. E ven if it were 1%, though, that would be too much. It matters , therefore, and there i s no inevitable outcome.

In my short career, w e have clearly gone from a world of the m illennium d eclaration and harmonisation agendas —with the seeming utopia of the collapse of the Berlin Wall , the opening up of China and everything else in the 19 90s — to a very different world today . This difference is in not only the fractious power structure but the emergence of serious existential risks, such as pandemic s and other emergencies , as well as new ones such as AI. There is no inevitability; it all depends on what Governments and people around the world do, which is why this is an important conversation.

The question of “ how ?” flows from that. For the reasons you have outlined , g overnment grant strategies are tasks that probably absorb too much attention. It i s important to have civil servants and g overnment departments that provide continuity and have a road map to what is important. Values are at the heart of this, as I mentioned earlier . What does Britain stand for in all this? H opefully , that is not something to be negotiated by each incoming P rime Minister .
