When somebody is searching for something about the news, you can show a set of providers that are deemed to be appropriate. All of that is part of the Green Paper discussion.
The Chair: Thank you, we need to move on now .

Q86 Lord Knight of Weymouth: There is a clear logic around going where the audience is. The Government announced that they want to ban social media for under -16s . I f you , as a public service broadcaster, are going to go with the spirit of that ban , h ow will that affect your distribution and gaining an audience share among under-16s i f you then cannot use YouTube as the platform for that?

Matt Brittin: We are starting from a position of greater strength than I anticipated before I started at the BBC. “ Newsround ” is viewed by 3.5 million children a week in term time in schools. It i s a phenomenal product , a nd it means that under -16s trust their parents and the BBC more than other information sources . I would love us to partner more with the Department for E ducation and others to look at how we can go further with that.

In secondary schools, Bitesize is used by 80% of pupils, and I think we could go further with that. I ha ve talked to colleagues about the big structural problem we have in the UK about the 1 million young people not in education, employment or training. We ought to be working with g overnment and others to try to equip those people with the skills they need to get the jobs of the future, just as the BBC did back in the day , around the time of the M icrocomputer ’s introduction. There is an array of things we can do .

O n the social media band specifically , the answer is that we do not know yet h ow that is going to pan out. It i s in discussion. We can look at Australia and learn some things, but in general, the principle of velocity that I tr ied to lay out on day one was about being closer to the audience, simpler to navigate and faster to the future. We therefore need to be more about experimenting and learning as these social things change.

T he final point is that this whole conversation is driven by the pace of change in behaviour. That is what has driven ITV and Sky to merge. That i s what has driven consolidation in the TV production sector. That is what ha s driven big reductions in local journalism over time. It is all about how consumers, citizens and audiences are changing their behaviour , and that is only going to accelerate.

Q87 Lord Knight of Weymouth: In Australia, they did not list YouTube, but there is now discussion that they should. The indications are that it would be listed here. I am interested in whether or not there i s any conversation going on , particularly with 16 year - olds being enfranchised , a s the current legislation that is in the House of Commons suggests, around whether there i s a role for the BBC in creating a platform specifically for teens to keep them informed about what is going on in the world in a way that is compliant with where public policy has now landed.

Matt Brittin: I have spoken to our team who deal with children’s and education, and that is an important part of our mission , and a dapting to these changes is important. To do that, we will need to look at the funding, and that is part of the discussion on the charter. W e will also need to look at partnerships : how do we partner more deeply with educators , NGOs and potentially even with tech companies on how you train people on digital skills ? I n my previous life , I began a programme on training people in digital skills. We ended up training 100 million people across the world and over 1 million in the UK. There was a big focus outside London. We found that the main issue people have is a degree of confidence about how to use this and how it could be useful. We are going to need to do that as a country for the jobs of the future as well. I absolutely agree with you , and subject to the opportunity for funding and partnership, I would love for us to be accelerating work there.

Q88 Baroness Owen of Alderley Edge: We have heard about the increas ed collaboration between public service broadcasters and the need to enable them to respond to the challenges posed by global platforms. The Government have proposed giving the BBC a specific duty to partner with public service providers, which you obviously support. What practical difference would this make?

Matt Brittin: There is plenty we can discuss around public service media more broadly in the UK. We touched last week on discussions about iPlayer becoming a sovereign media platform. You could imagine, whether it is iPlayer or structured in a different way, a destination where homegrown storytelling and the quality of journalism that the BBC and other public service broadcasters aspire to can be found and where we are not subject to third-party algorithmic decisions.

One thing that I have talked to our technology team about at the BBC is that iPlayer could be better at recommendations. It is not as good as YouTube or Netflix, candidly. We have great shows that people do not necessarily discover. But we should have a public service values recommendation engine at the heart of what we do.

I read the 100-year history of the BBC. In the early days of broadcast radio, the schedule would include incredibly challenging classical music next to a popular drama. TV schedules would often introduce something that you needed to be seduced into watching, or when you read a paper newspaper, you will see an article that you might not otherwise have chosen to read. That is what an algorithm can do for us, if we tune it in the right way, so that we are encouraged to explore things.

We just launched a brilliant new show called “Evolution” with Chris Packham hosting. It explains how a cell became an elephant. That type of content might not be something that somebody seeks out, but if they come to watch a comedy and they see that suggested afterwards, that is the kind of thing we should be looking at.
Q89 Baroness Owen of Alderley Edge: Can we pin down specifically whether the BBC would do anything differently under a strengthened duty that it is not already free to do?

Matt Brittin: There are lots of things. W e have the charter, the agreement, the Ofcom code and the terms of trade we have with the industry. Many things have changed since those things were put in place. O ne example we have talked about is I think that licence fee payers believe that the BBC owns its whole archive. People expect that everything we have produced is owned by the BBC. I get so many people asking , as does Samir, “Why we do not have i Player globally? Surely we could make that available to the world. Would it not be an amazing thing to do ? P eople would pay ” . W e have BritBox in the US , which is doing very well, but has a smaller selection because of the rights ownership , and that is a challenge.

It i s also an opportunity , because of the way we do rights . First, s ince 2003, the Communications Act has open ed up all of our commissioning outside of news to third - party independent producers, and it has created a huge industry of independent production, but they have now largely consolidated into scale players. So we should think again about how those things work. T hat is another example. Secondly, there is broadcasters and platforms piece. There i s the creative side of it. W e have got a creative powerhouse, but the dynamics are changing. How do we do that?

T hirdly, we have invested across the UK. I was in Cardiff , and 25 years ago in Cardiff, aside from producing the daily soap, “Pobol y Cwm”, for S4 C, t here was no drama production. The BBC chose to put “ Doctor Who ” there ; 26 years later, I visit Cardiff , and I can see shows being made at BBC S tudios and an independent studio , with productions from six streamers and networks , including the BBC , being made. I go to the Bad Wolf s tudios, where we made “The O ther Bennet S ister ” and Doctor Who’s TARDIS sits waiting for the next D octor, and a big Netflix show is being made there. Al l that is because of the investment that the BBC made in creating those skills in the industry. You have to zoom out and look again at the structure of competition, where we are today and how to do something bigger in the future.

The final point I will make is S teven Knight, the creator of “ Peaky Blinders ” , among other things, spoke to the Commons S elect Committee recently in the charter meeting . H e talked about how when he makes a show for Netflix or for Amazon, they might come and hire talent, which is helpful —j obs are created or careers continue — but they do not leave behind any of the profit. That is something we should be thinking about in how we structure our industry for the future. People want to come and work here because we have great talent and incredible storytelling capabilities like Steven’s, but we should think again about the intellectual property and the value.

May I add to and reflect on the question you raised, particularly about iPlayer and the desire for people to watch it around the world ? Matt mentioned the point about rights . W e know that the Communication s Act 2003 gave the rights to independent producers ; I benefited from tha t, having been an independent producer . I t was a very successful strategy , and w e now have an incredibly strong and talented independent sector. But the rights question — the terms of trade — falls into the same bucket as many of the other things we will discuss, such as the funding model, the governance structure and the regulatory structure . They are a ll terrific, but they were made for a period in the past , which is disappearing in the rearview mirror . We need to rethink all those areas as we create a new charter for the future. T hat means that everything should be rethought. What will enable the BBC to thrive and survive in the future and to compete with the forces we have talked about in all these areas ? Should we revisit the terms of trade? We must revisit the licence fee and the way we are regulated : t h ose have done their job and have been very successful, but we need a new vision for them .

I make one other point about that new vision , which has come through in some of these conversations, and I cannot emphasise it enough: t he BBC is much more than a broadcaster. It is a public good. It has a role to play in the civic and cultural life of the nation. That is why we talked about what we do with under - 16 s. It is a role we have to play . I n all the roles , we have to ensure that everything that we do in our new charter supports that central idea that the BBC is much more than just a broadcast er. The £18 0 from e very household pays for the great content , but it also pays for reaching schools and for skills and training. It pays for a whole lot of things, quite rightly, because that is what the licence fee payer wants . That is why our relationship to licence fee payers is much more than just transactional , a s it is with subscriptions. It is important ; it is to do with our role in civic life.
Thank you. Lord Storey?

Q90 Good afternoon, and thank you for joining us. B y the way, your licence fee does not pay just for your iPlayer or television but for local and national radio, which is hugely i mportant. My question is to you, Matt. When you gave evidence to the Culture, Media and Sport Committee last week , you pointed out the recent market consolidation . W e know that, of the public service broadcasters , Channel 5 is owned by Paramount ; S ky is owned by Comcast ; and , some might say bizarrely , Sky is now bidding or is in the frame for ITV. W e are left, in a sense, with only two national public service broadcasters. Comcast has ambitions to take on Netflix as a streamer. How do you see that situation evolving, or is it a crystal ball you do not really want to look in to at the moment ?

A key point I would like to get across—and if I have not done that c learly , then I give my apologies — is that, globally , changes in audience behaviour are driving all this change in the industry . T he challenges the BBC faces are not different from the challenges that Sky , ITV , Comcast and so on face. Changing behaviours mean that people need to have more scale in order to invest in reaching those audiences and , in the case of the commercial players, monetising them. C hanging behaviours is one of the reasons that we have a shortfall in the licence fee funding versus where it was previously.

B y the way, you are right to mention some of the things we have no t , such as local radio and radio more broadly, which is not covered — you listen to radio and it is free ; t here is not a licence fee connection there, which is a slight anomaly as well , b ut we reach 30 million people a week through our local radio services and the Scottish, Irish and Welsh services.

T he consolidation is all driven by the same forces. What does that mean for the UK? As you rightly point out, Sky - ITV will be owned by an American company. I am impressed with the commitments they have laid out on supporting local news and PSB content and two separate news services , b ut they are already some way behind the BBC . W e are the biggest funder of domestic content : w e fund something like 86% of public service broadcast children’s content. W e are in a world of jeopardy in the British media ecosystem as well , and I believe those forces will get only more powerful. W e will need public service media and regulation , and our brilliant creative skills , to be able to succeed in that world.

T hat is w hat I am trying to get across : this is not just about the BBC , and not just about it as a broadcaster, but about national values, sovereignty and trust . W hat the BBC has always done well is show us , and the world , who we are. T he evidence from the World Service and our international reach and growth is that people around the world want that : they want that storytelling and that journalism.

Q91 That is important. I slightly worry that we could follow what people want , or we could lead people to what we think they should have in what we offer them. I t is not just a question of sitting back and saying, “O h, people want to spend all their time streaming now” . T here are other things that , through innovation and change , we should ensure that people perhaps do want. I am a great advocate of local news ; I worry about the fact that , in 20 years, local news in my city has virtually gone , and w e have sat back and allowed that to happen , as a nation .

I share your concern, and I think you are absolutely right . We need to continue to be bold and brave in our journalism. That is why I said that one of my three priorities was editorial excellence — making sure that we continue to innovate and be brave in what we are investigating but also in the storytelling.

I actually worked in local press 20 - plus years ago . Ahead of the Select Committee last week, I looked this up : when I was working in local press , t here were around 9 , 000 journalists employed by the biggest three local press companies , and t here are now only 3 , 000. Why is that? Well, the economic model has changed . A dvertising, particularly recruitment advertising, which is high - margin , shifted online — thanks to Craigslist in particular — at zero cost. The margin just collapsed. It was t he same with motors advertising and property advertising. T hat led to an inability to fund local journalism. T he funding of the BBC and its journalism is really important .

I have been impressed by seeing what colleagues at the BBC have done over recent years a cross the UK . Some 60% of the BBC’s network spend and 55% of staff are outside London. A lthough we are wedded to the historic transmitters in terms of our local radio network —there are 39 local radio stations in England alone — they have broadened the offer to ensure that there i s digital content online in terms of local news and local services as audience habits shift. O ne of the challenges is to continue to support all those linear services as well as supporting audiences where they are. I t is not just young people : I suspect these are habits around the room, with many of us going online for BBC News or enjoying local video and other reporting services.

Q92 Could I ask a follow-up question? I n that session with the Commons Select Committee, you talked about how the BBC could use its scale and platform to ensure that Channel 4 ’s content could cut through —y ou specifically talked about Channel 4—but Lord Storey is quite rightly raising the issue about local news , and that is of concern. W ould there be scope for the BBC to use the BBC News app and website — your own platforms — to ensure that news content from a range of different news publishers could reach audiences? Is that something you would consider?

We already have the Local Democracy Reporting Service , which I visited in Birmingham and spent some time with . It is an intervention that has produced over half a million stories , which have been carried by 1 , 000 local media organisations and about 165 journalists as part of that collaboration with the industry. T hat lead s to stories surfacing on their apps and on BBC platforms. M ore could be done there. Obviously, the BBC’s charter , its editorial guidelines and the standards to which it is rightly held by g overnment differ from the standards to which other media organisations are held , s o one would have to be thoughtful about further developm ents in standards and editorial.

Aside from those traditional media publishers, there are many local creators who are working with the platforms we mentioned earlier and want to work with the BBC. My colleagues have had meetings across the country with many of those creators, and there are things that the BBC could learn from them, and there are things that they can learn from the BBC. I would be excited to extend that further. With the right scope of charter and funding, I think we could go more local. You no longer need a capital-intensive model to do the kinds of things that we used to do with studios and offices, as we saw during the pandemic. We had people broadcasting from home, and the technology keeps advancing, so we can make very high-quality video and audio content with much less investment. A capital-light model that allows us to get closer to the audiences where they are geographically is one that I would see having real promise.

My last point: every pound that we spend in the UK returns three and a half times that to the UK economy, because it creates that market. We have over 7,000 suppliers that we support outside the independent production sector. There is real value for money for the Exchequer in continuing that investment. Equally, there is jeopardy, because for us to keep that investment out across the country has costs. There is duplication and so on; we try to minimise that, but it has some cost.

Q93 As you know, the Government have proposed the need to make economic growth a distinct public purpose in the next charter. Your recent economic impact report demonstrates that the BBC already supports growth across the creative industries through its existing remit. What difference do you think making that a distinct purpose would make and, if they did it, what could you do that you cannot do now?

I will ask Matt to pursue that. First, though, as we have mentioned, the BBC has been committed to growing the economy, especially the cultural industries, for a long time now. We have done a great deal of work there. In some ways, I can say that it almost does not need the public purpose because we are already doing it. We have a lot of data on this. Our spend out of London is huge. My personal interest when I first started as chair was that I was keen that we turbocharged the Across the UK strategy, which we had had in place for some time. We have been very successful in moving programmes and production, and I am keen now that we also move power because it is important that power does not just stay in London but gets closer to the communities that we reach. That drives growth. It is important to look at the data about how much growth we drive by pushing out from London to all around the country. So we are doing a great deal here. If it is to be a public purpose then I personally am open to that, but I would say we are already doing that.

There are other elements of the public service we could talk about. Media literacy, for example, could be part of it in terms of our public purpose of supporting learning. That is a really important role for the BBC to play. It is new because of the rise of disinformation and misinformation. So my own view is that we do this a great deal. We do not necessarily need a further public purpose for us to do it because it is good for the BBC, it matters and it is part of our role.
Q94 Is there anything, if it becomes a public purpose, that you will be able to do that you cannot do now?
That depends on the detail. Before my time, the BBC declared in the response to the Green Paper, as Samir said, that it was very open to this.

Personally, I would be a bit more cautious. Growth is an outcome but the purposes of the BBC are about its purpose. Impartial news and information, supporting learning, creative industry, community representation and reflecting the UK feel to me like a different order of magnitude. Having worked in business, I was always concerned when I found a business that said its purpose was shareholder value. Actually, your purpose should be delighting your customers, serving your audiences, serving your readers and so on, and shareholder value is an outcome from doing that well. So I am a bit more concerned about that. As Samir says, we are seeing an outcome in terms of growth that is really positive, and reporting on that is good, but my concern would be that we were diluting the focus that we need to have at the moment—and possibly adding bureaucracy and reporting, but we could agree how best to do that. So we are open to it, but we should bear in mind that it is of a different order from the central purposes that are so critical to public service today.

Q95 I think a number of us agree with you that a blanket commitment to growth could just end up as a stick to beat the BBC with, that achieving growth is an objective for the Government and for the nation that the BBC will report and reflect on and that your scepticism is justified. We are all in favour of growth, so why make it one of the things that the BBC is failing on or not?

I am much more in favour of the whole concept of supporting growth. I agree with what the Chairman just said: the licence fee is not just a subscription to the broadcaster; it is the broad contribution to our activities as a liberal democracy, with the access to debate underpinned by a trust in the news services that you provide.

In another part of the forest, this committee is looking at the impact of artificial intelligence. This seems to be an area where the BBC, using its old Reithian mantra to educate, could be very useful. The implications of artificial intelligence—
I think we are coming on to that in a moment with further questions, if you could leave that.

I am not sure what else I need to ask, though there is a specific question. Matt rightly mentioned the importance of journalism, and a number of our colleagues are very interested in that. Something that we often hear from critics of the BBC is, “I know all about the BBC. I was trained by it”. That pipeline of trained journalists has been a victim of some of the cutbacks. I wonder, in your vision of the BBC, how far it is willing to look at the skills and the development of the broader, sustainable pipeline of journalism talent across the UK.
I think you are straying into the questions that other people are going to ask. I think that we are going to come on to that in a moment.

I want to ask a different question about purpose. We were trying to get to the point, with regard to what Lord McNally just said, where the growth purpose pushes you to prioritise commercially exportable content or measurable economic impact, but I think you have given us your answer.

That would be the concern. If you are focused on growth then “Newsround”, local journalism and investment in things such as training might be deprioritised in favour of bigger shows that you could sell internationally, the larger-scale productions. I do not have all the economics for every type of show that we do, but you would be at risk of losing some of the key public purpose things that Samir talked about.

Q96 You mentioned music and musicians, which I was glad to hear. The BBC has an important role as the largest employer of musicians and the biggest commissioner of new music in the UK, and it has always played a role in championing new talent with Young Musician of the Year, BBC Introducing and the music education initiative. However, when I read your economic impact report, that important role just did not seem to be covered.
I noticed that as well.

There is a mention of it in what you have just published. I was an MP in Salford and when the BBC moved there, having the BBC Philharmonic there, working with our communities, working with our schools, opening itself up with its concerts was a remarkable thing. It has a lot of impact on a community to have those musicians there. It makes a difference to what can be achieved locally. So why do you not mention it? You need to play it up.

The report was written before I joined but I can tell you that I went to Salford in the first week that I started to tour the country before taking the role. One of my greatest joys was when I had the opportunity to sit in a rehearsal of the orchestra and see the talent. The commitment there was phenomenal. I, like many licence fee payers, had not realised the BBC was perhaps the second-biggest employer of musicians.
No, the largest.

After the military, I think. It is pretty big and most licence fee payers would have had, as I had, little idea of that. This is an important part of what the BBC has done incredibly well. I also went to join the Radio 3 breakfast programme hosted by Tom McKinney in Salford, and it was a joy. I discovered, “Not the Nine O’clock News”. If anyone is stressed and at 9 o’clock they want an antidote to the news, then that is a wonderful, relaxing piece of classical music. So, I absolutely agree with you. By the way, this week we kick off the world’s largest and longest-running classical music festival in the Proms. The impact of our music operations shapes the UK and it is a big and important intervention. Again, we need to ensure that it can be funded and protected under the licence fee.

Of course, it is not just classical music. I think about Radio 1’s Big Weekend that was in Sunderland recently, and Radio 2 In the Park, which is going ahead in Stirling in September. These things bring people together. An important public purpose in these divided times is the role that we and other public service broadcasters play in bringing people together. Music is a key part of that. It creates economic value. Those “In the Park” and “Big Weekend” events typically generate £3 million to £6 million for the local economy, as well as obviously a huge moment of togetherness. As does sport—we are facing some sport later today. I was staggered. Samir and I had a bet on what the overnight audience for the Mexico-England game would be.
I won , by the way

He won. It was 9.1 million. Another 5 million watched it on catch-up. Another one point something million watched it replayed on BBC2—with fingers in ears, do not hear the score beforehand. These moments are really important in a fragmenting world. That is one of the things that could be in jeopardy if we are at the mercy of other platforms and are not able to continue that sort of investment.
We hope it does get some attention and priority.
It definitely gets the priority from the BBC to continue the impact. That is part of the concern within charter, because we will need to make difficult choices in every area.

Gathering the nation, bringing the country together is an important role the BBC plays in our civic life. We can all guess how many are going to turn up tonight and it will be quite something. It is true. We cannot lose it. It is a really important part of it.
I think most of us are sold on that.

Q97 I will be getting away from debating the Sporting Events Bill to watch the match later. I want to reflect on R&D and the role of the BBC. I want to start with you, Dr Shah, because I am going back into the past briefly, before handing over to Lionel to take us into the future. The Green Paper tells us that under the current charter the BBC’s R&D spend has fallen. The previous one had a public purpose on emerging technologies. Has that removal played a part in the decline in the role of the BBC in emerging technologies?

I do not think they are connected. When you refer to decline in the BBC, we have already discussed why licence fee payers are leaving—because of changing audience behaviour. The latest statistics say that 94% of the British population consume the BBC every month. I challenge “decline”. The key thing is that only 80% of households pay for it. So there is a gap we need to bridge. Matt can talk more authoritatively about the technology. In our history, we were leaders in technology and innovation. Right from the start, we led it, from radio to television. I lived through quite a bit of it myself—when we went to colour. We all remember Wimbledon in colour. The world has changed.
BBC computers played a huge part in the computer science capability.

We talk about this a lot but the world really has changed. If you look at the money that is being put into artificial intelligence, we cannot match it. Seriously, we are talking trillions of dollars being poured in by the big tech players. We do not have anything like that. The technology is going to be very important, and I am an optimist about AI. We can harness it to human creativity. I do not think it is an evil thing that we need to contain but we need to be realistic. We do not have the money to develop AI to compete. Matt can talk about the role we can play in modern technology and how we can harness it. But the days when we could develop our own large language model—I do not think so.

We will perhaps come on to AI. Perhaps I might address the first part of your question. Samir is right to say the BBC harnessed technology and creativity together, with radio, television and then with streaming. In recent years, as the challenges of funding have appeared—we have lost £1.3 billion of public service funding in the last 10 years—the management team has focused on content, channels and services, and keeping the content as high-quality as possible, which you can see in the BAFTA wins, audience responses and so on, and keeping as many channels and services active as possible. That is been at the expense of technology investment. There are some great people in the BBC who are brilliant technicians and engineers but, as I mentioned, things such as recommendations, the news app and so on could be better. A choice has been made in that respect.
Q98 Does that imply that that decline in R&D meant that perhaps the BBC might have dropped the ball on AI?

Well, let us move on to AI. There has been less investment in some of the technology areas than there could have been to maintain the user experience part of it. If you move on to AI, it is a very broad field. I am wary of experts in the room but I have worked with Google DeepMind and many colleagues over many years in this field. It is the application of AI to specific areas that will be both risky and beneficial to society. As Samir rightly says, we in the UK are not going to suddenly magic up a multi-trillion-dollar foundation model or anything of that scale. What we have the opportunity to do, and what I am keen for us to try to do at the BBC, is to pioneer in the application of AI to improve what we can offer in public service. Your Lordships will be looking at this in the public sector completely. We also want to understand the risks of AI. There are really serious risks around information integrity, data security, media literacy, the corruption of content and the generation of fakes. We have to use these technologies, and our teams do, but we are going to need to do more in order to benefit our audiences and to maintain the integrity of our journalism.

Q99 Lord Tarassenko : What a long lead-in to AI. I will come on to AI but I have a couple of general questions first. But before that, even, what I wanted to say is I worked in AI research for the past three decades as a professor of electro engineering in Oxford. The reason why I mentioned that is, as the Department of Engineering Science at Oxford, we are proud that one of our alumni is a former director-general, John Birt. He trained as an Oxford engineer. He was in the House yesterday and spoke in the Cyber Security and Resilience ( Network and Information Systems ) Bill Second Reading debate. So it is nice to have two directors-general in the House of Lords on consecutive days. Indeed, in the three decades I have been a professor, we have trained many engineers who have gone on to work in the R&D department of the BBC—perhaps fewer in the past few years, as we have just discussed. But, looking forward, obviously I am biased in terms of R&D , but in terms of your commitment to R&D innovation should it be included in the BBC’s public purposes? If so, how should it be framed so that BBC innovation serves public interests and how will you make sure that it does that?

The application of technology in the fields in which we work should be critical to the BBC’s future. On the purpose, I may be in a different place from the Green Paper response. It feels to me that this is a means, not an end. The purpose is having clarity. In a time of uncertainty, the greater clarity you have, the easier it is for an organisation to galvanise behind it.

Just as growth is an output, harnessing technology well is a question of how we fulfil our purposes—it is not a purpose in and of itself. I am open to debating that, because I think we are a part of critical national infrastructure. The BBC, subject to sufficient funding, should be working with the security services and the Government on information integrity. There are questions about identity and logins and all the kinds of things we encounter in our everyday lives. There is a question about who we should trust to do these things. So there is a big opportunity to think strategically as a nation at this moment.
Q100 Lord Tarassenko : The Government have proposed to house this with a new purpose on driving growth, but maybe you have already discussed that. Do you think it makes sense or not?

Matt Brittin: As I say, we should be open to discussing the modernised remit for the BBC, and we absolutely are. We have lots of pretty intensive detailed sessions with the department coming up in the summer.

I personally believe that an enduring purpose, one of the five that we have, of serving audiences is a helpful and clear purpose for the BBC. Harnessing technology, delivering growth, delighting audiences and enhancing our reputation internationally are all outcomes we achieve by doing that well. If we fulfil our purposes well, we will automatically be embracing these things. The cost implications and the capability would need to support that. I would want to understand how that would impact Bitesize, classical music and all the other services we need to provide.

Q101 Lord Tarassenko : Bitesize will feature in my next question, because we finally come to AI. I disagree with you on the claim about trillions of dollars for models, because it is becoming increasingly clear that there are , in fact, three types of AI models : there are the ones you mentioned, the frontier AI models ; the ones that Mr Bri ttin will be familiar with, such as Gemini from Google . It takes trillions of dollars to train them and keep them in the frontier. There are the open - source or , more likely , open - weight models , such as Gemma and so on. There is third category, which has very much been discussed in the House of Lords recently, which is sovereign AI models. They are n ot at the frontier ; they are maybe six to eight months be hind the frontier. It would take in the order of millions of dollars or pounds to train. I ndeed, as a senior adviser to our national AI institute, the Alan Turing Institute, I have been discussing that, and I ha ve been to see the BBC, Peter Archer specifically , to discuss that with you. W here do es the BBC play in that spectrum? Would you want the capability to own it , or would you want to partner , procure or adapt ?

Matt Brittin: That is why I intervened when Dr Shah was talking about this. Y ou are right ; it is not common public parlance to talk about these things in these ways. W hen I am talking about the application of AI, I am talking about the area that you mentioned there. There are already things that the BBC is doing. I talk to colleagues in other newsrooms around the world , using tools , such as N otebookLM , that allow you to upload and research documents using large language capabilities but without the hallucination concerns. T here are tools off the shelf that we can and should use, and we should do more. I have begun conversations on p artnering with other members of the European Broadcasting Union and other big newsrooms around the world .

I think your implication is “Buy or build?” in some of these things. There is an opportunity for us. It would need to be in partnership to participate in building a sovereign model. That would have impact for the UK only if it was to partner with a programme around skill development. What would a 21st century version of the BBC microcomputer project look like? Is there a sovereign model and a programme of education , training and exploration? Who would you need to work with in order to do this? What sovereign infrastructure would one need in order to promote it? The other day, I spoke to the CEO of BT. We were talking about digital switchover and IP TV — all these things come together. This is a moment of jeopardy but also opportunity for us in the UK to be brilliant at bringing our engineering, scientific and creative industries together around sovereign AI and the application of other AI models, as you suggest , Lord Tarassenko .

Q102 Lord Tarassenko : I think that we are all on the same page . You mentioned sovereign ty and trustworthiness. The key thing, which is important to remember about these and would be different from Gemini or Gemma, is that you would have full control of the training data set and you would train the model according to UK law. T rustworthiness is very much part of what the BBC does , s o it needs to be in the conversation , without necessarily designing the model itself.

Matt Brittin: I agree . O ne of the things that we are concerned about with the BBC is that the public tell us they want us to be independent of Government , so part of charter is about that. One would need to think , in a project such as that , about the role of g overnment and other bodies in building and earning that public trust. It is a big opportunity.

Dr Samir Shah: I would hesitate to interrupt a conversation between two people who know a great deal more about AI than I do, but on acting in the public interest , your point about trustworthiness is central to it. The public rely up on the BBC to help them through this new world of technology, and we need to maintain that. W hatever our relationship and whatever partnerships we make, that central value that t he BBC has in being trusted by the public needs to remain there. That is important.
The Chair: W e need to move on to the next questions . Baroness Caine has some questions on skills.

Q103 Baroness Caine of Kentish Town: Yes, and on nations and regions . Hello. Obviously, the BBC — you say it , and others say it too —is recognise d as the venture capital for the creative industries and as the cornerstone of the creative industries. T he current charter requires you to serve the UK’s nations and regions and to support the creative economy across the UK. It also requires you to work collaboratively with a wide range of organisations , where that is in the public interest. I n many ways, arguably , that is your growth agenda within the charter . I s that one that you would still see as being relevant to your future? I know you said to the C ommons that you were terribly excited about it , and you both articulated the progress and the work with the nations and regions.

Matt Brittin: Yes, absolutely . I mentioned a couple of things that had surprised and delighted me about travelling around the country , a nd one was the real progress that had been made . We are i n a world where , rightly, we are looking at devolution in order to respond to uncertainty and to serve people by understanding their needs better , wherever they may b e.

T he BBC is actually doing incredibly well , with, as I said, 60% of network spend and 55% of staff outside London. Since I joined, we have another two commissioners who will be based outside London. I ha ve appointed a deputy director - general who is based outside London. The leadership team and the people making decisions about commissioning content being more decentralised is important . That is what gives you the Cardiff story, the Salford story and similar stories in Glasgow and elsewhere.

To sustain that, we need the funding . T he other part of our growth strategy needs to be BBC S tudios and our commercial growth. W e need to complement the public funding with as much commercial revenue as we can , within the scope of the charter and remit.

Q104 Baroness Caine of Kentish Town: I n relation to that success in the nations and regions, to what degree do you feel that has been powered by your partnership with independent producers and their ability to have scaled and grow n as a result of your investment?

Matt Brittin: Hugely, because since 2003, producer choice and its successive changes to terms of trade mean that we are commissioning out to tender all the time. Samir mentioned that h e and others have benefited from that, and it has created an incredibly vibrant production sector. That sector has consolidated. We see Ban ijay and All3Media coming together to create a £ 5 million revenue business, and that is partly because the funding for original content had a boom a s the streamers invested heavily in the acquisition of new subscribers ; that has fallen away a bit. W e face the same situation in BBC S tudios, which is our commercial competitor.

I am excited about the next generation of independent producers as well as the fantastic skills within the existing producers: smaller content creators in audio , video , drama and music that we c an work with. W e have seen that when we have run sessions across the country. That could allow us to operate in a capital-lighter way, as I mentioned earlier. I hope that we can do that.

Baroness Caine of Kentish Town: Obviously, o wning rights allows those companies to scale up and , therefore , to succeed , move on and move forward. I think you also mentioned in the Commons session that you were potentially looking at size as a variant in relation to the rights issues going forward. It seems to me that there might be a tension between growing the economies in the nations and regions and removing rights from independent producers. I am just giving you the opportunity to clarify because I think there is potentially concern and confusion about some of what has been said.
Absolutely, it is not from an intention to sow any concern and confusion, but probably from answering a lot of questions briefly, so thank you for the chance to do that.

First, we should recognise the huge success of that sector. We partner with it, we work with it every day and we really support it. We do not want to disrupt that in any way. The point I was trying to make was that, if you zoom out and look at the UK, as we have tried to do on a number of the questions that your Lordships have asked, we need to think strategically about our industry and how we can together make changes to how the economics, rights and opportunities work so that we can continue to punch above our weight as a creative industry as a whole.

I am conscious that the BBC has a role as one of the key cornerstones of that industry, but it is only a part of the industry; commercial competition and innovation is part of it. Also, coming from where I come from, I think we should see it as not just those players but all the new types of content creators. There is lots of innovation in local journalism as well, as you will know. We should be rather expansive in our thinking, but we need to think about scale and how we introduce the next generation of production success as well.

Q105 Okay, great. I will move on in terms of next generations to the skills and training issues, because, again, we have heard from witnesses and it is known that the BBC is an incredibly important part of that training and skills infrastructure. Everybody recognises that but, interestingly, nobody seemed to pick up on the difference and the mistake made in the DCMS Green Paper, which said that the BBC spent £10 million on training and your response to that paper, which said it was £45 million. In effect, the DCMS Green Paper is wrong. My point is that nobody picked up on it. In a way, that relates to the focus that potentially is given to the skills and training agenda, in terms not of investment but of purpose and strategy.

We have talked to other public service broadcasters. They identify it as an area where they collaborate across the industry with you, but nevertheless, there are still huge skills gaps and shortages within the workforce, even though there is underemployment at the moment . In your response to the charter review, you talk about 1,000 apprentices, which is marvellous, but what is the missing link? Where is the strategy? Is the strategy being developed in partnership with others in the industry? Is it actually addressing the skills gaps and shortages that are there?

L et me just begin on that and I will let Matt follow up. The first thing to say is that I am very pleased that you have raised this, because we have discussed before, and I have said quite often, that the BBC is much more than a broadcaster, and one of its key roles is this: skills and training. I, the board and the BBC see it as absolutely central to our purpose to develop the workforce that underpins the creative industry. That is central to what we do, in addition to being a broadcaster.

At a general level, I am aware that our skills and training go across the board. We go to schools in what are called taster days, where we try, especially in disadvantaged schools, to get them to enter the pipeline. We have the apprentice scheme for older people, and it is worth saying, although we have 1,000 places, last year, 47,000 people applied for it. You can see that the demand is much greater. Later on , when you enter the industry, we have a whole load of training, master classes, all sorts of writers’ workshops to try to develop skills. So we have a great commitment to skills and training, because we want to create the next generational pipeline. It is a really important part of what we do.

The number I have here is £47 million, but I think we could do more. Let me just address those 1,000 apprentices and 47,000 applying. Training costs, and we have to have a funding model. I am sorry it goes back to money, but we need to continue. We cannot take the talent pipeline for granted. We need to develop it, to build it and to build it around the country. But that will cost. It is part of our civic duty to do that. I have a little thing about other streamers that fly in and fly out, live off our talent and do not contribute. But we have to do this.
First, I apologise for the error in the report. It is unforgivable, because the work that goes on is big and—
It is not your report that made the mistake , it was DCMS’s.

Maybe we should have spotted it in the draft anyway. The good news is it is bigger than the report says; the bad news is that there is still a big skills gap. I know you have a lifetime of working in skills, and I share your passion personally, as I have mentioned.

As Samir says, I would love us to do more. It requires funding, but it also requires collaboration and partnership. I am struck by the fact that we have 45 different industry schemes ongoing. On arrival, when I started to look at this, I worried that we were subscale in a number of areas and actually we need to think again about the scale of our intervention. I would love to talk to you and other experts about this. I am only just short of two months in, so it will be a priority.

Another thing we will have to do, I think, as we reinvent the BBC for the future, is the fact that we have to make savings and that means job losses means it is harder for us to employ people. But the size and shape of the BBC for the future needs to be one which will attract young and rising talent and offer them the chance to build and grow their careers. So we have to sort of deal with that conundrum as well. That is why I am encouraging us to think at an industry level collectively with government so that we can think about how we create those jobs of the future together.
We have to move on .

Q106 I just want to pick up something that witnesses have talked about, which is very good to hear. You talk about partnerships and collaboration. It used to be said for many years that the BBC did partnership to people rather than partner with people. That is a critical difference. As you rightly say, a number of these things require the BBC to do that without necessarily reinventing wheels or not working with existing organisations such as ScreenSkills , which you may or may not have heard of, Matt. I am very happy to come and talk about all of this, but it is key to the regional clusters as well, and witnesses have talked really positively about those clusters.
I have had conversations with a couple of the mayors already about exactly that.

We have a couple more areas . I will touch on funding. You have mentioned it as we were going through, but I will come back to that just before we finish the session. Veronica, you have a question around editorial standards and impartiality.

Q107 Thank you so much for the time and detail that you have given us today. It really is very helpful to us. I will start with Dr Shah, the chairman, because I know it is something we have as a shared interest and lifelong activity in journalism. You have talked about trust, and I think we all believe that trust is an absolute bedrock of the BBC. Whether you are talking about anything that is new, that is old, the future, or AI, you are also talking about journalism.

You have recently—I think, in fact, yesterday—acknowledged again that there have been some recent and very serious failings of BBC journalism. Obviously, we are also aware of the very important report that was produced by Michael Prescott last year. We do not need to go into that now, but I would like to know how your thinking has been refreshed with the arrival of the new DG. You did, after all, lose your last DG and head of news as a result of a failure in journalism. What steps will you, as a new team, take to bolster journalistic standards and impartiality? What is your current thinking?

Thank you for that. As I said before, it was a difficult year last year, and we had a number of failings, which I acknowledged publicly. Since then, we have taken a number of steps. We have changed both personnel and policies. I will not go into great detail , but I can let you know the detail if you wish. We have changed the leadership of the Arabic service, which has always been an issue. We have changed the leadership of long-form journalism. We have a new deputy director-general in charge who can focus on it, and soon Matt is going to be appointing a new director of news. So there has been quite a big change just in personnel to address the question . We have also had a great deal of change in policies and practices in that to try to address it. For example, we have a new system of oversight of high-risk long-form journalism, which has always been an issue at the BBC, pre-dating last year . You mentioned Michael Prescott , and I note that the s tandards c ommittee has been reshaped. It has a new remit, a new purpose, new membership and a new c hair. With the changes we have made , I feel confident now that , should such instances arise again, we will be able to deal with them with greater speed.

S peed was one of the big questions that arose, because most of the issues that came up were as a result of the BBC’s own investigation into our journalism . We were slow to act, and we need to be faster . But I feel confident that , under our new leadership , along with Matt, we will address issues that come up, as they will , with speed and decisiveness.

Q108 T hat is encouraging, and we all hope that that is the case. You will be aware that , only today , the former director of BBC T elevision, Danny Cohen, has written a n important piece , and I am sure you are up to speed on that. I will quote it because it is important. He say s: “ The prevailing culture at the BBC — long denied — is more sympathetic to L eft-of-centre perspectives .. . We have seen this in coverage of a range of issues from trans rights to the Gaza War, Reform, immigration and US politics ”. F or him to say that now, when we have a new team in place, is quite significant. W hat is your reaction to that ? How confident are you ? Y ou still have the same board and many of the same systems. You may have one or two new people, and you have to appoint a new head of news. But have you really got to the root of the problem? It is not just about structures ; it is about judgment, is it not?

I understand the question and I understand Danny, who m I ha ve known for a long time. He is a close watcher of our journalism , a nd he make s these points. My reflection on this is that we have done a pretty good job in trying to tackle this and make sure that our journalists understand what it is to be impartial , fair and accurate.

We are talking about the newsroom , journalists as a whole and indeed the BBC and our recruitment. It is not a surprise to learn that we tend to recruit liberal arts graduates , who tend to have a metropolitan outlook , which they bring to the culture of the organisation. E verybody has a political position ; that does not bother me. What matters is that we do not see that in the journalism we do . We need to be constantly vigilant on that , and we will be.

You dismiss ed the changes in leadership , but I would not dismiss them that much. I think both leadership and policies need ed to change , and they have changed pretty significantly . I ask Danny and you to have a look at our journalism and see how we go forward. We have a new team in place , and the d eputy d irector -general will be a n important factor in that. So we shall see . I am confident that we will address the questions that Danny raises with me and generally.
We need to move on.
Q109 Very briefly, can I ask Matt Brittin what exactly he means by a “satnav for bias”? Do you think that judgment is a technical issue?

It is hard to answer that question briefly , because you quoted a small fragment of what I said, but I woul d be happy to talk more broadly about it. One of the issues we face with the criticism of journalism is understand ing the volume and character of the output. I have suggested that we can use technology to help us to understand and guide where we might be covering more or less, because there i s a huge volume of output and it is right that we hold ourselves to the highest possible standards. But that is only one element of the ingredients we need.

O bviously , you have huge experience in journalism, so you will understand that standards, structures, culture, training, behaviours and management are all parts of what we need. In answer to a question , I suggested that we could also use technology s o that, when there are criticisms, we have the data to help us to investigate them better. T he team has begun to do that.
We need to move on because we are nearly out of time. We have a couple of questions about funding.

Q110 Obviously, t he BBC positions itself as a trusted source of information , and I am concerned that some of these big cuts that are being made will affect that . Getting rid of “The World Tonight ” , for instance, and reduc ing the funding for the “T oday ” program me— the absolute flagships of information for R adio 4— seem s to me to be a retrograde step in trying to push the BBC forward for the future as the place for the most trusted news information.
And the question is?
The question is: why are you doing that?

The answer is that we have to make £500 million of savings. That is a huge number. It i s in excess of the budget for drama and sport , and for news. S o we have to make some tough choices. Y ou are absolutely right : t rust is earned. As we just discussed, it is earned through the story selection, the way those stories are told, where they appear , and the expertise and eyewitness nature of the journalism . I n journalism , i t has to be earned, because we are accountable for due impartiality across all our outputs.

W hen you look at what we have to do and the scale of those changes, which are driven by the challenges in funding that we talked about , we have to make some tough choices. S o we try to focus on audience value , reducing duplication and making sure that we are going closer to the audiences. I do not want to get drawn into individual programme choices, but the example you gave is about two similar, but not identical , programmes. By the way , a ll our programmes are there only because they have audiences , many of which love them —s ometimes , they angrily shout at the radio — and brilliant people working on them, so it is always a tough call. Th ose are two somewhat similar programmes and , if we zoom out to the scale of what we have to do, some choices have to be made. We cannot just salami slice .

There is more to come , because the savings that we have announced so far and that t he teams have worked on over recent months amount only to the beginning of the total that we need to save. So we will need to look further at program me s and services, and at how we get the balance of trying to preserve audience. Tha t may mean that, in some cases , we focus on doing less but raising the quality. We have to understand how to do that in the context of the charter. Th e BBC at its best is bold , brave and innovative, as we have discussed, whether creatively, journalistically or through technology . W hatever the size of the funding, we need to reinvent the BBC for that world.

Q111 W e can end by talking about funding , g iven that we have touched on the cuts . I n your session with the C ulture, Media and Sport Committee, you discuss ed the possibility of a household levy as an alternative funding model for the BBC. I wanted to give you a final chance to comment on that . In that session, there was discussion about a household levy being taken off the table, but since then Lisa Nandy has said that no options have been taken off the table. So how would a household levy work in practice? H ave you done any economic modelling to understand how it would affect the BBC’s finances?

As we we re saying to the S elect Committee last week : how do we come to be in this situation? We have touched on that in terms of the drop in public funding. The majority of the drop came from licence fee freezes and the increases in scope to cover the over - 75 s and so on. So the majority of the drop came from interventions. Some came from behaviour change. T hat is why we are where we are .

W ith Dr Shah and colleagues , I have asked: what do you need to maintain that universal remit under charter with a level of funding that is sustainable ? It is very hard to run an organisation that can attract and develop the best creative, journalistic and technical people i f you have to cut costs every year in an unpredictable but downward spiral. So we need universality, sufficiency and the scale to be able to do whatever set of purposes the charter sets us in the best possible way —w e have talked about that —w hether it is at a programme level, a genre level such as music , or a technology level. Y ou have rightly illustrated some of those choices. T hat is what we need centrally .

There are many mechanisms and variants that could achieve that. We talk ed particularly about the household lev y because the c ommittee had heard from various witnesses who had pointed at that as something that might be a solution, and I think we should be open to all options that could deliver that set of outcomes.

I have spoken to the European Broadcasting Union, and I know that this is in place in a number of European countries in different ways . T here are advantages in some areas. In some cases, it is collected through a utility bill payment and , generally , evasion reduces significantly. There are obviously some people who absolutely do not want to pay for those services , so there i s a question about enforcement there. But , generally , collection costs are lower and universality increases. T hose who favour that solution would say that, if the BBC licence fee is £15 a month today, could it be £12 a month if it was more universal? W ould that allow the Government to consider social interventions around people with lower incomes , older groups and so on? So there is some merit in that, particularly in the cost of collection, evasion and universality.

There are also questions, obviously, about the willingness politically from a leadership standpoint . P eople are facing a real income challenge in their homes , a nd we are very conscious of that — that is our audience as well. So that is one of the options and, through the summer, we will engag e intensively to look at those different alternatives with the department.
Q112 Do you expect, by the time you have finished this exercise, to be able to say, “This is what the BBC thinks it needs to fulfil the commitment asked for in the charter”?

Obviously, w e have built models of the cost of the BBC and its services. It i s hard to answer that question specifically because we have to deliver against the charter. So there i s a question of what the charter asks us to do and what the funding model for that is. W ithin that scope, we would like to do more across the UK , to do more in education and in technology , and to be more confident in our contribution to growth and skills. There are an awful lot of things we would like to be able to do more of , but i t depends on where we get to on scope.

There is also a load of the industry factors that we talked about. If we are able to collaborate more with other parties, can we do more to protect the UK’s incredible creative industries as part of this? T here i s an awful lot of detail to work through. It is welcome that , here and in the Commons Select Committee, the sense of the moment we are in and its importance are well understood by the d epartment and the industry. I ha ve been struck , on my way into this job , by h ow many people from the industry — whether from news publications that are critical of the BBC but understand its role, from technology companies , from broadcasters , or from production companies —have a will for us to continue to play a key part in the UK . That is very much there. So I hope we can find a solution that allows us to do exactly that.

I would just add to that. I welcome the Secretary of State’s thinking about the funding model, opening up issues such as the hous ehold levy and extending scope. We will be in negotiation or discussions with them , because it is for the Government to decide. One point that is really important to note is that , apart from universality and scale, we need stable funding because , right now , funding income is going down. It is very difficult to run a major and complex organisation if you do not know what your incomes are. Obviously, a household levy would achieve that . S tability — being guaranteed a level of income —is critical to this to be able to deliver our purposes.

Q113 We are just about out of time. We had a couple of points and questions that we did not fully put to you, and I will just state what they are. C ould you let us know afterwards, rather than have us try to extend the sessio n? O ne is about opening iPlayer and BBC S ounds to other public sector broadcasters . W e wanted to know how that would work in practice, given that other PSBs have their different funding models . W e were talking about C hannel 4.
In short, the answer is: yes, in principle, but ad serving and the ad technology is something we do not have.

If there i s anything extra to add to that, could you write to us ? On skills development work, it is important that the BBC continues to support and sustain that pipeline of journalism talent across the UK. There are real concerns about that. I know it all hinges on the funding .
It is absolutely on the priority list.
I am glad it is. It is useful to end on that point about funding. You have answered a very wide range of questions for us. Thank you for your time.

sessions.iT: The Humanitarian Situation in Yemen
sessions.w: London School of Economics (LSE); SOAS Middle East Institute

segs.tx: International Development Committee
Oral evidence: The Humanitarian Situation in Yemen , HC 553
Tuesday 14 July 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 14 July 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Sarah Champion (Chair); Janet Daby; Tracy Gilbert; Monica Harding; Alicia Kearns; Noah Law; Brian M a thew; David Mundell; James Naish; Sam Rushworth; David Taylor.
Questions 1 - 6 3
Witnesses

I : El-Khidir Daloum , Country Director, Yemen, World Food Programme; Konstantinos Psykakos, Deputy Programme Manager Cell 5, Médecins Sans Frontières; Noha Yehya, Gender and gender-based violence specialist.
II : Dr Richard Barltrop, Visiting Senior Fellow, Middle East Centre, London School of Economics (LSE); Helen Lackner, Associate, SOAS Middle East Institute.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: El-Khidir Daloum, Konstantinos Psykakos and Noha Yehya .

Q1 Chair : This is the International Development Committee’s one-off session on the humanitarian situation in Yemen. As a C ommittee, we repeatedly come back to this topic because the humanitarian situation out there is truly horrendous. It has been going on for over a decade, and unfortunately it gets very little attention . T hat is partly the short attention span of the media . They like a crisis and this is an ongoing protracted disaster. I t is l argely hidden, as this session will show , because it is very difficult to get current information into the public domain. All that said, we are very fortunate to be joined by a number of witnesses today who we will separate into two panels. Mr El-Khidir is here in the room but o ur other witnesses are virtual. Mr El-Khidir, could I ask you to introduce yourself and your organisation, please ?

El-Khidir Daloum : T hank you very much, honourable m embers of the International Development Committee. It is a great honour and privilege to stand in front of you today . I am the representative of World Food P rogramme in Yemen. We have been working in Yemen for over three decades and are honoured to have a long-lasting partnership with the UK Government and p eople. I am really grateful to be here with you.
Q2 Chair : For those people who do not know, could you explain what the World Food P rogramme is and what it does around the world?

El-Khidir Daloum : The World Food P rogramme was established in 1963 and stands to achiev e zero hunger. The sustainable development goals ha ve identified the second goal of achieving zero hunger and WFP stands for that. WFP operates in 84 countries. It saves lives . S aving lives is basically a humanitarian response and we work on survival, feeding people and addressing hunger to prevent the worst outcomes . At the same time, we work on the development side ; w e call it changing life. It is about addressing the root causes of hunger. We translate those root causes into positive programmes such as resilience, food systems, and school meals , and so on .

In addition, WFP work s in enabling the humanitarian space, especially agencies , to deliver humanitarian response in hard-to-reach areas where access is limited . WFP provid es logistic support , such as the logistic cluster , when there is an on-surface demand for agencies that are not able to deliver . T hat is across the world. WFP is the leading agency trying to address most of the famines that happen in the world , which happen as a result of climate , conflict , or the outbreak of diseases. Those are the main reasons for famines and crisis.

I have to mention that, because of the volume of the humanitarian response, WFP is often perceived as only a humanitarian agency. Yes, we are the largest humanitarian agency in the world , but we also have a developmental side.
Q3 Chair : Are you part of the United Nations?

El-Khidir Daloum : Yes , w e are part of the United Nations . I n any country you will find agencies called resident and non-resident agencies. WFP continues to be a resident agency because it is operational and work s deep in the field. You will find us in the capitals , but you will also find us closer to the people we serve.

Chair : WFP is one of the best values for money on public record ; y ou are one of the leanest organisations. I have seen you on the ground and w hat you are able to do is remarkable. Thank you for everything that you and your colleagues do. We can now turn specifically to Yemen.
Q4 Janet Daby : What is the impact of food insecurity in the current conflict in Yemen?
El-Khidir Daloum : I want to start with the trajectory. In the last decade, Yemen has gone through a very challenging moment.

Until 2015, the World Food Programme ’s developmental programme was the major component and humanitarian programme was the smaller one. As a result of conflict, we have reached a situation where 50% of the total population of Yemen is food insecure. That constitutes about 18.3 million people. Further, 3.5 million are acutely malnourished, 55% of children are chronically malnourished, and 5.2 million are internally displaced as a result or war or the climate crisis. It has affected boys and girls. About 3.2 million children of school age are currently out of school.

I started this role on 5 March this year. I have travelled in the southern part, under the control of the in ternationally recognised go vernment, where I met the IDPs —internally displaced persons—and refugees, and people who are affected by climate and conflict. I have to say that it hit hard. Any conflict is hard for women, children, and the elderly. Those are the three categories that have been hit hard.

We have also marginalised communities in Yemen, called Muhamasheen in Arabic. Those Muhamasheen, or marginalised communities, have paid the largest price. I want to give you an example of what will happen to the household when hit by crisis. Whether this crisis is as a result of climate change, conflict, or outbreak, the first thing the household will do is cut meals. Three will go to two , and two will go to one . If one, it will go to the quality of the food they take. The quality is going to be compromised. As a result, malnutrition will happen. They will then try to borrow from their local community. Everyone will know what you have in terms of assets, so they will not give you more than the value of your assets. When you then go for the third strategy, which is to sell your assets, you will find that the terms of trade are not in your favour. You sell all your assets and are not able to pay your debts, so you will be indebted. When you reach this stage you have only two options ; to stay in the land or to leave. If you stay, you will be malnourished and the whole issue of a declaration of famine could happen. Otherwise, you become an IDP. That is why , as a result of that push factor, there are 5.2 million IDPs. Th at is the situation in Yemen right now .

Q5 Janet Daby : That is quite shocking to hear and very concerning. In terms of the long-term impact of malnutrition and Yemen’s stability, how do you perceive its ability to recover and improve? What are your thoughts around that?

El-Khidir Daloum : One thing I have learned from my humanitarian work over the last 35 years — 10 of them in the United Nations and 25 in international NGOs —is that you have to be optimistic in this sector. There is always hope. Yemen was not dependent on aid, especially humanitarian aid , until 2015 . That will tell you the story that you focus on resilience , food systems , and the value chain . Yemen is rich in three food economy zones : agriculture, livestock, and fishery. I f we work hard with support from the UK Government and others, and we have examples of WFP working in resilience , then all those food economy zones can turn around the lives of the people. We have operational research to show that whenever you invest $1 in resilience, it can save between $3 to $7 during times of emergency or shocks. These are examples of how Yemen can easily go through recovery programmes. We have a number of recovery programmes that have been successful and paid back in terms of turning the lives of the people around and created hope for marginalised groups.
Q6 Monica Harding : The rates of disability in Yemen seem to be very high as a population. Why is that?

El-Khidir Daloum : Disability in Yemen is sometimes the result of war. Some is the result of immunisation coverage being very low . We also have an issue of stunting . R ecently I went from Yemen to the western coast and about 40% to 60% of kids were stunted. Stunting has a lasting effect, especially after the age of five but s ome nutritionists say after the age of two. It is e ither the conflict , the polio coverage not being as good as it should be —but that has now been improved —or i t is the result of a chronic malnutrition situation, especially the stunting form of malnutrition.

Q7 David Mundell : A re there any resources or attempts to pursue food security initiatives to ensure th at the Yemeni population can shift from this dependency model to a more self-sufficien t model?

El-Khidir Daloum : Yes; this is not only WFP ; there are other agencies. I can give an example from the World Food P rogramme. We worked with farmers in Mukalla in resilience —w e call it resilience programmes —and w e provide them w ith agricultural inputs and approaches to agriculture. We also engaged them in the value chain ; how they can be in aggregation. A number of them come as associations . T hey then link them to the market , and they sell their commodities to the market. We have help ed them to bring back a lmost 3,000 hectares of land. It is now active. M y deputy was there recently . I was not in M u kalla, but my deputy was retained by M u kalla ’s govern ors . T hey have reached this situation and w e now would like to work in the Bab -el -Mand e b Strait . W e are trying to work with a fishery association to bring them together and try to link them to the market. They are mainly producers but they are not linked to the market , which is the biggest issue. It is th e transport, connection, and cold chain systems ; a l l these things together.
Q8 David Mundell : W hat are the main barriers to tackling food insecurity? Have you just set out what you see as the main barriers to tackling it , o ut with the conflict itself ?

El-Khidir Daloum : T he agriculture , livestock , and fishery food economy zone s are the most vibrant food economy zones. In these zones, people should be well off. W e need to ask ourselves why they are not well off. The main reason is that between the production , value chain , and the market there are many aggregators. They are not able to sell their products at the right time. For example, if they have fisheries they have no cold chain for it. If they have fruit and vegetables, they have no cold chain for it. If they produc e milk, they cannot link to the market . Th at is one thing. The other is to group themselves into proper associations. They study the market and become one group. Instead of having many mediators between them and the consumers, you minimise the mediators and they c an engage directly with consumers. The more they engage directly with consumers, they more they will be winners. The consumers will be winners. The economy in total will be a winner.
Q9 David Mundell : Do you think that is achievable?

El-Khidir Daloum : It is achievable because our experience in Mukalla has demonstrated it. To give you another example, we are working on something called home-grown school feeding. In the past, we have brought food from the UK, the United States, Australia, Canada, and different places and distributed it in the schools to attract more children. We have now introduced something called home-grown school feeding. If you are in agriculture, we link you with the agriculture food economy. Schools buy from local farmers instead of from outside. It is the same for livestock and the fisheries. We found that, once linked, it stimulates the local market. The UK Government gave us funding for cash transfers during the humanitarian assistance. We have a study that shows that w hen you are providing assistance in kind, it will stimulate in the local economy by only $1. For ever y $1 in cash , the local economy will be stimulated by b etween $1.7 and $2.5. It is a humanitarian response but it will have a lasting impact on the local economy.

Q10 David Mundell : Y ou have essentially been talking about the southern part of Yemen and what is happening there. How or to what extent are you or others able to operate in the northern Houthi-controlled territories?

El-Khidir Daloum : As I stand in front of you, 38 out of 73 of my beloved colleagues are detained by the Houthis for doing the noble job of delivering humanitarian assistance to the Yemeni people, irrespective of where they are and under which authority they are controlled. That is the situation we are in.

I would like to say that we are not operational there . T he Secretary-General took the decision about the UN post in the north for two reasons. First, it is because of the 73 detainees. Secondly, it is because of limited humanitarian space that respects international humanitarian laws and the humanitarian imperative. Having said that, World Food Programme and other humanitarians work with all people i r respective of where they are and who they are. It is not going to dictate our work for us. For the time being, we are in post.

The situation in the north is not good. I do not have a high level of confidence to speak about it because we do not have ground colleagues who can provide us with the data.
