Generally, when I talk about the 18.3 million we have information on, they are not only in the southern part of the country but are also in the northern part under the Houthi authorities.
Q11 David Mundell : D o you feel you have an accurate picture of the food insecurity position in the north?

El-Khidir Daloum : We have an estimate. The estimate talks about 18.3 million. Out of them, about 12 million are in the north. These remain estimates. As long as we are not operational, WFP cannot speak with authority on how bad the situation is in terms of malnutrition and food insecurity.

Q12 Chair : Mr El-Khidir , can I send my solidarity to your colleagues ? Detaining international humanitarian workers is a clear violation of international law. I am disgusted that it is going on and deeply sorry for the individuals , their famil ies, and the wider humanitarian family. I wonder if I could just pause and bring in Noha and Konstantinos. I know we have some problems with the connection. Konstantinos, can I ask you to introduce yourself and your organisation to us, please ?
Konstantinos Psykakos : I work for Doctors Without Borders, Switzerland. One countr y we are operating in is Yemen, along with other colleagues of MSF in the country.
Q13 Chair : Noha, can you introduce yourself and your organisation to us, please?
Noha Yehya : I work as a gender and GBV specialist for a national NGO.
Q14 Tracy Gilbert : Can you tell me what unique challenges women and girls are facing today?
Noha Yehya : T he problem in Yemen is that, in the south and the north, women are exposed to violence and used as a weapon.

One big problem women and girls in Yemen are facing is our laws and institutions. They give us no way to protect ourselves or to find safety. No law in the country bans discrimination against women. Marital rape is normalised and never considered a crime. Even getting a basic legal right such as inheritance is a battle for a woman in Yemen. To make it worse, there is adultery law in Yemen , or Zima law as we call it. If a woman who is exposed to rape tries to report or file a case against the rap ist then she might be prosecuted for adultery unless she can prove that she was raped. This cannot happen in Yemen. If she is not imprisoned for adultery, she might be exposed to an honour killing. Under the laws in Yemen, if a male in the family kill s his mother, sister, or daughter for adultery then it is only one year in prison or a fine. This exposes women to a lot of risks.

There is also a total lack of accountability everywhere in Yemen, north and south. It is kept alive by the m ahram rule. It is more in the north than the south, but every woman who needs to travel needs m ahram . It means that she needs to be accompanied by a male or get permission f rom a male to move from one place to another. This is a kind of violence because women who are exposed to domestic or gender- based violence cannot go and seek services. It is the same f or service providers. Most service providers of specialised services for gender - based violence are women. If they cannot travel or move freely to service provide rs then services will be stopped and women will be exposed to more violence. T here is also a stigma issue. W omen cannot always speak out about v iolence or their expos ure to violence by a male abuser because it is known and normalised . E ven if a male is an abuser, he is also the protector. She cannot speak about this , o therwise she will be considered disobedient.

The n orth and s outh have different dynamics. When we look into the violence against women, it is hidden everywhere and is equally in the n orth and the s outh. In the n orth, we have a serious issue relat ing to the security of women. It is Zainabiyat , which is a female force. In the n orth, t he Yemeni Network for Rights and Freedoms documented between 1,400 and 1,654 cases of violence against women. T here are also testimonies f rom prisoners who were recently freed from prison that say Zainabiyat facilitated all kinds of violence against the women in detention. Zainabiyat i s the one monitoring women working in the field s of GBV , protection , and humanitarian field s in general.

No ne of our colleagues or researchers can even speak about gender-based violence. That is why some colleagues , who were supposed to be here today , could not join ; t hey are based there where are different dynamics. In the s outh, there are armed groups that can do whatever they want to do to expose women to risk or violence. There is no clear mechanism or way to appeal for any support for women . I t is also difficult because of the divided ministries and armed groups that are connected to the Government and different political parties. It is a bit chaotic in the s outh.
Q15 Chair : C ould I bring you back to a point you made earlier? You spoke about Zainabiyat . Could you tell us what and who that is?
Noha Yehya : It is a female force.
Chair : A female force?

Noha Yehya : Yes, it is a female police force formulated by the Houthis in order to monitor and detain women because of the culture. Men cannot touch or monitor women so t hey created this group in order to control women and make sure they keep their mouths shut. They cannot speak because they are reachable and can be detained.
Q16 Chair : You said in prison s , the Zainabiyat were carr ying out violence against women?
Noha Yehya : Yes . T hey facilitate the process by a ll kinds of v iolence you can imagine , which I prefer not to talk about.
Chair : Could we bring Konstantinos in to talk about it from a medical perspective?

Q17 Tracy Gilbert : If there is anything to add, that would be great. Are you aware of any protective funding or dedicated programmes designed to aid the needs of women and girls facing these circumstances?

Konstantinos Psykakos : B efore starting on dedicated prog rammes to address those needs, I have to complement what my colleague Noha ha s said. In the no rth, especially where women are already deprived of access to health care and with the pause over the past month that the administration had to face in the n orth of Yemen, those limited services are already extremely scarce. They are already hindered and access to them put s them more at risk as we speak. Where you had a network of PHCCs that would be able to screen and identify women at risk and refer them to appropriate secondary health facilities for support and to provide services, they are now even scarce r . Women already have barriers and issues to access at a local level , let alone when they have to cover further distances to reach that access to care. Keep in mind the context ; t he restrictions are many. A year or so ago , we were relying on other partners in the vicinity to provide those needed services. Today, we are very worried and raise d the alarm that we might not se e the majority of those cases access our facilities or the care they need for the matter at hand.
Q18 Tracy Gilbert : Are you aware of any reserve funding or any projects that are trying to exist in either the north or the south?

Konstantinos Psykakos : A s my colleague has already said, the north and the south have a different reality. In the south, while you have the availability of funds, it is more about feasibility and implementation on the ground . T o what extent the efficiency of it happens and is applie d . In the north, we are facing a more c hallenging environment where restrictions and barriers exist for different re gions . F unding has been scarce but, even if it is available , it needs help and support to be implemented on the ground. We can elaborate further on this specific point.

Q19 Chair : While I was researching for this session, I was shocked to discover that three women are dying in pregnancy or delivery daily, which in June of this year was the highest maternal mortality rate in the Arab region. A re there any specific programmes to encourage training and the support of midwives and doctors specifically around sexual and reproductive health rights?

Konstantinos Psykakos : On that matter, I can tell you that there were a lot of activities at a primary healthcare level that would engage with the communities, through the modalities of the Ministry of Public Health and Population , to train TBAs in the traditional delivery system of the community in Yemen. We were trying to train the communities to refer to the PHCC for stabilisation and treatment if possible , or at least timely referral to a secondary healthcare facility where antenatal care could be followed , when they identify early complications.

Y ou have already mentioned the 2025 numbers . Alarmingly, i n 2026, we have a different problem that insinuates the situation has been exacerbated on its own . W e do not see as many cases anymore . Th is has led to the conclusion that, if the trend continues, women have lost access because the support to the primary healthcare level has been reduced drastically due to the UN pause and other reasons.

Those women do not have the means to access secondary health facilities. Of t he ones we received in 2025, 40% of cases were late arrivals to the hospital hence complicated cases. If there was a system in place, we would be able to treat them earlier and with fewer complications .

I can share this experience myself because I was in Ad -D ahi, Hudaydah two weeks ago. I was visiting one of the primary healthcare centres we are supporting to refer to another hospital in Hudaydah , Al-Qanawis . It offers maternal care and sexual and reproductive health facilities . The team mention ed that in 2025 they saw cases referred to Al-Qanawis , but until June 2026 they have seen far less cases. I do not think we are in a situation where we have trained the communities enough to deal with complications at local level with the means that they have. T hose women have lost access , or it has been severely hindered and p robably will be hindered further in the future the more we progress in this timeline.
Chair : That is chilling.
Q20 Janet Daby : Noha, I was thinking about female children, teenagers , and young women in terms of their mental health. What protections, if any, are in place for them?
Noha Yehya : Do y ou mean services for them?
Janet Daby : Yes .

Noha Yehya : Since the war started, the percentage of early marriage s has increased sharply. G irls less than 18 years old are getting married or getting pregnan t before they are ready. This has increased mortality among the children and exposed the ir health to a lot of risks.

UNFPA , through national NGOs , is running some health facilities. Due to the pause in the north and a lack of funds, almost 70% of these protection or health services ha ve been shut down, which means women are now left behind . They cannot seek services . T hey cannot access case management, psycho - social support through the protection centres or safe spaces , and they cannot get the health services needed. They are exposed to unsafe abortions and childbirth , which can cause a lot of issues for them. This is one of the biggest challenges that we are facing; many services have been shut down or are on the edge of being shut down.

UNFPA is trying . It asked for $ 71 million this year to ensure that services c ould be sustained and continued. Unfortunately, up to now, only $ 9 million has been received and used by the partners for the implementation of sustaining some health facilities and safe spaces . Out of 103 safe spaces in the north, now only eight are operating. You can see the variance and t he massive need .

Q21 Brian Mathew : Konstantinos, I want to take it to a higher level now b ut want you to dig down. I will ask you three questions in one . W hat is the current state of healthcare in Yemen? How does MSF meet those needs? W hat are the long-term implications of those needs not being addressed?

Konstantinos Psykakos : What is the status of the current health state of Yemen? In north and south, we have different situations and the same in parallel. What do I mean ? In Yemen, people are in need in the north and south . The Ministry of Public Health and Population and PHCC level s are in need of support, technical supervision , and more knowledge on the ground to support them in mov ing forward and address ing those needs. The difference is that you have more resources available in the south compared to the north , as in the past year more funds have been concentrated in the south rather than the north. That is the big difference. It is the same needs but different . The south has the funds, tools, and NGOs to operate and move ahead with whatever needs to be addressed at a health level. The north has been defunded and isolated. Its needs are still the same though and will accelerate in the months or years to come. That is what we anticipate as of today.

T o connect the first point with the third point : what do we foresee in the long term if those needs remain unattained? In any given country where the health needs of the population remain unattained, we do not expect this part of the population of the country to be able to recover themselves or enter any trajectory other than one of prolonged humanitarian disaster need or the prolonged management of outbreaks . T here are no more outbreaks ; i t is a regularised situation that we are manag ing week after week to address those needs but without being able to outpace th e curve. W hen it comes to the north, w hat we at MSF are trying to do is keep a modus operandi that can reflect the needs of the population in a versatile way and address outbreaks and emergency response s because the humanitarian landscape has changed.

M any NGOs were able to collaborate and co-ordinate their responses before. W e now need to keep a focus on how we can better address the needs of areas , k eeping in mind that we have already reached our maximum capacity in terms of operations over the past years . O ur further growth is not a matter of financial support but it is a matter of the feasibility of having a wider operation.

W e are collaborating with ICRC — International Committee of the Red Cross, the other actor in the north of the country — to be able to have maximum efficiency and not overlap in geographical areas. For the south, we are attending to different health needs in some areas because we have activities and programmes . B esides focusing on malnutrition or paediatrics, we are also focusing on activities for the migration population that cross es from the Horn of Africa to the south of Yemen to reach the rest of the Arabic Peninsula. Tha t is another population in need ; i t is not a Yemeni population but they have needs.
In the meantime, in the same modality, we are try ing to engag e with other actors to avoid the duplication of activities and to maximise the geographical coverage.
Q22 Noah Law : The needs you have described persist at a time of global aid cuts. To what extent are you confident in your own organisation’s funding in the years ahead?

Konstantinos Psykakos : That is the question. If I had the answer today, I would be able to organise my operations for the next five years. Every year dictates the next one. Today, in the north, you have a different situation. It is not only the funding cuts that are global. We experience it in every country ; i t is not only a reality in Yemen itself.

What we see in the north of Yemen is that it is not only the global funding cuts ; i t is also that decisions have been taken to restrict any little funds that might have remained . If there is a ny willingness for those funds to be injected in the north, there is no facilitation for those funds to find their way north . For MSF or ICRC, we can navigate t hings such as a l ack of access for UN H AS f lights and i mportation, and flagging a terrorist organisation of Ansar Allah, the de facto authorities , to deliver activities and services to the people of the north , but o ther NGOs might not have the same capacity. It might create an activity of fear about operating in the north . It is not only a matter of global funding cuts that we see less services on its own , we see other effects and additional pressure s coming to the northern part. In the south, it is as we said but the north and the south share different realities in some ways.
Q23 Noah Law : Noha, h as your organisation specifically been hit by UK aid cuts?

Noha Yehya : Of course. My organisation is one of the biggest organisations providing gender-based violence and health services for women and girls in Yemen. W e are one of the biggest recipients from UNFPA and a few other donors. With the UK cutting the fund , 70% of our services have been shut down including health services or safe spaces for women and girls. It means that women cannot reach these services and the consequences will last for a generation. Women are exposed to psychosocial stress and violence , which will be passed to their children. It will increase poverty and the consequences will be difficult. Cutting the fund now will not stop violence ; i t will only stop the help for women in Yemen. That is what is going on now.

We are trying with our resources to downsize the interventions or services , but that means we have more than 6,500 women on the waiting list. In the n orth, 2,300 are on the waiting list for safe spaces and t o get some psychosocial support . T his is the only door open for women seek ing services ; i f we shut it down, w e will face a lot of consequences. One is structured violence , which will not be easy to address later. We are destroying the structure of the community by leaving women exposed to this violence and not provid ing any support for them. Girls will be deprived of schools. Poverty will add stress to women and their families, which will increase domestic violence. It is a cycle. If we d o not find a way to restore the services, we are destroying a community and we will not be able to fix it easily.
Noah Law : That is incredibly disturbing to hear.

Chair : Noha, it sounds like you are describing hell and it is getting worse. I hope that the international community hears what you are saying and a solution is negotiated fast because it take s away future potential —

Noha Yehya : C an I add something ? T h e international community, by cutting fund ing , is adding another kind of violence against women in Yemen , especially in the north. W e are punishing them for being in places where the Houthis are. We do not give them money or services because they are there. It is heartbreaking and, I am sorry to say, unhumanitarian .
Chair : I agree.
Q24 Noah Law : Can I make a quick clarification, please ? How much of what you have described is about cuts versus the restrictions that Konstantinos referred to earlier?

Noha Yehya : There is a restriction of access but, for the national NGOs, we have our own way to provide services for women. We are an experienced organisation and we have been there for decades. We are using informal trust an d personal relationships to ensure that we have access to women and provide services in any way. We are always sensitive to the situation and know how to reach women. Restrictions are difficult ; they take time and expose our team to risk. Our team and national teams working in humanitarian areas , especially in GBV, are exposing themselves to risk at a level no humanitarian in any other country would accept. W e do not have any protection from the state or humanitarian actors. We do not even have policies to protect our staff. We are implementing partners. Not all donors or organisations can provide us with this kind of protection. We know our ways. For years, we have been working with restrictions , but the restrictions do not mean that we will not find a way to do our job.

Q25 Sam Rushworth : Can I ask one question that is off script? Noha, th ank you for talking with such candour about some really challenging situations people are facing. You have talked about some services that are being provided to women to relieve suffering. Are there also any civil society level forms of resistance ? T o what extent is it possible for women to organise and challenge Government around their rights in this space?

Noha Yehya : I t is not easy. It has exposed them to a different kind of risk. Y ou can consider me an example. Because I was talking about so many issues in an online meeting , I am out of my country, under stress, away from my family , and cannot go back . Q26 Sam Rushworth : I want to change topic now and talk about humanitarian aid access. Would you mind setting out what you see as the main barriers to humanitarian aid in the area?
Noha Yehya : Humanitarian aid access?
Sam Rushworth : Yes.
Noha Yehya : In general or for women and girls?
Sam Rushworth : You can speak to both.

Noha Yehya : I n general, there are different dynamics in the n orth and the s outh. In the n orth, we have the Houthis and we need a lot of approvals. They ask for details ; s ometimes they try to force us to provide the name s of staff with their addresses and mobile number s — private information — in order to give us permission to implement. We do not do it. It is a problem that might delay implementation of some activities in the field. As for physical movement, as I mentioned earlier, for access to women and girls we now need m ahram. This is one of the biggest challenge s . Women cannot move around to either get a service or provide a service unless she is accompanied by a man or get s written permission by a man so that she can move freely or provide services. At the country level for other humanitarian actors, they are usually requested to provide a list of the beneficiaries, which is against humanitarian principles. No one can provide this i nformation. T here are also sensitive areas in Yemen, both in the n orth and the s outh . T hey can give you permission to work there, but you will be monitored. Sam Rushworth : If I understand it correctly, it is more difficult in the n orth than in the s outh but not impossible thinking about —
Noha Yehya : It is more difficult in the n orth definitely than the s outh. In the s outh, we have this armed group that is also doing these things , not in Aden but in some other governorates.

Q27 Sam Rushworth : It is not impossible to get humanitarian assistance in, but the effect of monitoring is severe. I n terms of your organisation, how does that sense of being constantly monitored impact on you ?

Noha Yehya : As I told you, we are all monitored. All the women who are working in protection and in GBV are monitored. It is a matter of how clear you are with the authorities. If you provid e full details about what you are planning to do and necessary information then it may take long er . It might take a lot of mutual trust. It might need a lot of personal relations between some authorities in order to manage and get permissions to implement. It is not an easy way. It is the only way many national NGOs ha ve to implement , but i t does not mean that we compromise o ur humanitarian principle s . It does not mean we are trying to work against these principles. As nationals, we always find a way to negotiate it. We are Yemenis at the end of the day, either north or south.

Q28 Noah Law : T o come back briefly to the question of the UK’s impact , y ou mentioned that your programme is one of the main implementations of the FPA. T o what extent do you believe the UK is responsible versus the broader global cuts to that programme ? Does the UK have a very specific role and contribution that it is failing to meet?

Noha Yehya : T he UK can advocate and provide funds to Yemen. It can support a diplomatic process for peacebuilding. It can do a lot. By providing funds to us, and I will talk about women and girls , you are helping the community in other ways. You are helping the peacebuilding process. Without wom e n empowerment and the inclusion of women, we cannot talk . W e cannot speak about genuine peacebuilding. There is no real peacebuilding. I f we want real peacebuilding, we need women to be part of the transitional justice. If women are excluded because of this violence , cannot get services , be empowered or be included , then this will not help the stability of Yemen. The UK and FCDO can do a lot of things to support Yemen.

When we talk about locali sa tion, the majority of organisations that work in the north are national NGOs. The UN was in both north and south, but it was forced to move its operation to the south. Only national NGOs have been left behind in the north , trying to fight and not collapse due to the lack of funding. N egotiating and returning operations of the UN to the north will help national NGOs respond. It will improve the f unding situation in the north as well .
Q29 Noah Law : A re you mainly feeling that hit through the fact that UNFPA has been cut? I s there anything the UK can do to fill the void?

Noha Yehya : Help us to respond diplomatically and financially. This is what we need . I f I say only financially, it does not mean there will be stability. W e can work on stability diplomatically and financially .

Q30 Sam Rushworth : Noha, t hank you very much for those responses. I am conscious of the time and what we still need to get through. This is a question that I am going to pose to our other participants. It is about the protections in place for aid workers. El-Khidir, could you share your experience of what protection is in place. Konstantinos, is there anything you would like to add on this topic before I com e back to the C hair and move on?

El-Khidir Daloum : T hank you very much. Aid workers are at the front line and are always there. We are tr ying to do everything under our duty of care for the people who work and serve and the people we serve. We are very conscious of the transfer of risk, including to co-operating partners. Even when we are working with international or national NGOs or civil societies, we are try ing to do our level best. However, whether they are non-state actors or a Government, we expect them to observe the humanitarian imperative and respect humanitarian law. That is a big issue. WFP and other agencies have lost lives on the front line.

Y ou ask ed a question about the humanitarian space and monitoring : w as it because of the cut s or because of access ? I want to say that when access is not there, access is not there. Therefore , it will compromise the integrity of the response. WFP has four ways of monitoring. First , we do it oursel ves in person. Secondly, we do it through mobile s . Th irdly, we do it through co - operating partners. Fourthly , we do it through third party monitors such as private compan ies. O n the funding side, Yemen i s placed at number four o n the hot spot map in terms of those affected. T he funding has been affected severely. In 2025, WFP reach ed $ 8 million. This year we have done what I call a brutal prioritisation to go for $ 3.4 million .
Q31 Sam Rushworth : You have gone from $ 8 million to $ 3.4 million ?
El-Khidir Daloum : We have gone from $ 8 million to $ 3.4 million.
Q32 Sam Rushworth : Where was that funding coming from?

El-Khidir Daloum : Of the $ 3.4 million we are speak ing about right now, we have only reached $ 2 million. The US has done a bigger cut . L ast year , we had $ 54 million from the UK , this year we had only $ 17 million from the UK. I have to commend your team. Y ou r ambassador and t he FCDO team tr ied to leverage their funding with the Kuwaiti s and the Saudis. They tr ied to ask, if the UK put this amount of money in then how much would they put ahead of it ? I will appeal to the Committee . I f we do not secur e £ 118 million for food security and monetary relief by the end of this year, we will not be able to provide service s in the south. I am talking about the south where we have access. A ccess is not an issue for us.
Q33 Sam Rushworth : You do not have access in the north, is that right ?
El-Khidir Daloum : No . W e have access for every place in the south except for three places , which are hot spots between the Houthis and the IRG, the i nternational ly r ecognised g overnment.

In the north, as I mentioned earlier, there are two reasons. One is the detainees and the other is the humanitarian imperative. O ur offices and assets have been taken ; those humanitarian imperative s are not there. If those issues a re addressed, we are more than happy to go back to the north and respond to the ir needs . As I mentioned, needs are needs for us . N o matter who they are, we will respond to them. The situation in the north is not conducive enough for us to go there and respond.

Q34 Sam Rushworth : Can I quickly bring Konstantinos in before we finish this section? B riefly, i s Médecins S ans F rontières everywhere in Yemen? W hat barriers and protections do you have in place?

Konstantinos Psykakos : I will not stretch my answer too much because it is what my colleague Noha has already said. It is e ngagement with the authorities, local actors, and communities , and b eing clear on what we do, what we deliver, and what the purpose of that delivery is in terms of services towards the people. That brings mitigation to the risk, if there is a risk of exposure. If we want to talk about barriers of protection, it brings a barrier of protection.

A ccess is easier in the south as it has different ways and environments in terms of engagement strategy with authorities , non-sta te groups , and so on . It always brings the safety you need and the guarantees on the ground.

When it comes to the north, it is a complex operating environment. It is not being treated as an excuse to withdraw or not to deliver services on the ground. We need to remember that th ese discussion s over barriers and issues of access affect people on the ground and patients who are not always related to those discussions. They are being affected, and they will keep being affected.

MSF is operating in only 10 different governorates in the north. I am not saying operating in the north is easy and I do not want to tone down any of the issues we have discussed so far, but with international teams and national colleagues it is not impossible. It is still feasible. I f we ask other operating partners in the north, they will tell you the same. I t is not easy . I s it feasible? Yes. Can we keep doing it? I want to believe that we can keep doing it , and others would be able to do it as well if they had the support to regain that access. T he complexity of the north should not be used as an excuse not to have services. That would be my main point here.

Chair : You have made that point very powerfully, as have all the witnesses. We are really grateful to you for joining us today and tell ing us the reality on the ground. As I said at the beginning, it is incredibly diffi cult for us to get that reality so t hank you for sharing your experiences. Please pass on our gratitude to all your colleagues and volunteers for what they are doing day in and day out. We admire them enormously . W e have heard your call and will keep pushing the international community to step up and do more. Noha, as you said, it is absolutely morally the right thing to do, particularly with the landscape of horror that you have painted for us . Thank you all very much for your time today.
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Dr Richard Barltrop and Helen Lackner .

Q35 We are fortunate to have a second panel. My apologies that we are running a little later than planned; it is always a challenge when we try to get first-hand testimony, not least because the internet does not always want to assist us in getting that evidence. Thank you both for being here in the room. Helen, I will start by asking you to introduce yourself and your vast experience in this field.

I have been involved with Yemen for 53 years this year, working mainly in rural development activities; I have held a number of other jobs in Yemen, and have lived in the three Yemeni states that have existed during that period. I might possibly get to see another one, or not, as the case may be. In recent years I have largely recycled myself as an analyst and author, writing about politics, economy, and society; I am leaving the peace stuff to Richard.
Q36 That hands us beautifully over to Richard: what is your role?

I am a visiting senior fellow at the London School of Economics Middle East Centre. I research international and local approaches to peacemaking. I have a background in academic research on peace processes and carry out professional work for the United Nations and peacebuilding NGOs in the Middle East and the Horn of Africa. I have worked for the UN in Yemen, in particular in the capital Sana’a, where I was based in 2020; from 2022-23, I worked for UN mediation efforts. I am speaking here in an independent capacity and as a researcher on what determines failure and success in peace processes.
Q37 Helen, can I ask you to give a brief overview of developments in the war over the past year?

Since 2022, there has been an unofficial truce between the Houthis and the internationally recognised g overnment. Let me take this opportunity to say that it is a problem when people talk about north and south. It is geographically not technically correct and it is politically weighted. There are people—we might talk about them later—who want to recreate the pre-1990 borders, so when one talks about north and south it presents a problem. I personally use the term internationally recognised government , IRG. Otherwise, officially, people use DFA—de facto authority—when referring to the Houthis in Sana’a if they do not want to use the word Houthis or Ansar Allah, as they choose to call themselves.

Until 2022 the main actors in the war were the Saudis and the then internationally recognised government . In April 2022 two major things happened. First, a truce was declared, thanks to the United Nations — the special envoy played a role, but the main reason the truce happened is that both sides wanted it. Primarily the Saudis wanted to get out. The Saudi regime changed when the new King and his son took over in 2015; the son was enthusiastic about the war in Yemen and thought he could win it in a few weeks. By 2022 it had become apparent that this was not the case. The other thing that happened was that the ex-President Hadi, who died a couple of months ago, was replaced by a Presidential Leadership Council , or PLC.

That is the political situation. Militarily , since 2022—in fact since early 2021—there are a number of fronts that have largely remained unchanged; the situation is static in terms of military control and is not that much different from 2016.

The main political developments of the past three or four years have been a basic absence of change and absence of improvement , since the Presidential Leadership Council took over . The PLC has eight members—all men of course—but they are not united, they are extremely divided. They spend more time in disagreements, rivalry and internal fighting—not military fighting except on one occasion—than they spend thinking or worrying about how to solve the problem with the Houthis .

The PLC was formed in April 2022 by agreement between the Saudis and the Emiratis who each had four supporters on it . The big change that has happened is related to the much wider change of the growing Emirati-Saudi rivalry —this is not the topic here , but I can go on to speak about it.

In December, possibly as a result of something that the Saudis said to Trump about Sudan, the Southern Transitional Council, which is one of many southern separatist factions —which is why I am not into talking about southerners— took over the two northeastern governorates of Yemen: Hadhramaut and Mahra on the border of Oman and Saudi Arabia. It did that extremely quickly and without any major fighting; it was told to withdraw and it refused. As a result, for the first time the Saudis bombed two Emirati ships carrying military equipment in the port of Mukalla.

I am going to interrupt you: we are straying into the remit of both the Foreign Affairs Committee and the Defence Committee with your comprehensive answer. Please can we focus on the humanitarian and development situation? I am going to pass to Monica for the next question.
It is complicated—
Could I just finish with one sentence?
Just one sentence, please.

In January, the internationally recognised government and the PLC ousted the Emiratis and the Southern Transitional Council, so the PLC has now been reformed with a different membership, or at least two different members. They are still divided but that issue is solved; or rather it is not solved but that would take another sentence.
Q38 What will the next role of Saudi Arabia be in Yemen, and how will it evolve in the coming months, Helen?

The Saudis have two options. One is that they do what they were planning in 2023, which is to make a deal with the Houthis and then force the internationally recognised government to accept it. The other option is to go with the internationally recognised government , which is now 99% under their authority , and fight the Houthis to recreate a united Yemen. My past understanding was that they were in favour of option number one but, for international reasons, they have not taken it. You can imagine the international outcry in relation to the Iran war if they signed a deal with the Houthis at the moment; it would be impossible.

On the other hand, although the internationally recognised government have been very active in military restructuring, military reorganisation and so on in the last six months, they have not yet reached the stage where most people who know more about military things than I do would say that they are capable of fighting back. At the moment, the Saudis are just sitting there trying to control the IRG. They are not putting in enough money to finance salaries, fuel, and other needs. There are major electricity problems and so on because they are not putting in enough funds, whic h would be important in strengthening the internationally recognised government ; at the same time they are not letting go. As far as I can tell, they are hedging the situation.
Q39 Richard, would you like to come in there? What is your opinion on the removal of the STC; has it improved governance or stability across Yemen?

At the moment, it has an impact within the south; as Helen explained, it has a political impact on the Presidential Leadership Council or the PLC. That does not mean a transformation in the governance situation in southern and eastern Yemen. T he aspirations of the Southern Transitional Council remain intact , even though the party has taken a hit ; the aspirations—greater and smaller—of other sections of the population also remain. The events early this year will have caused ripples in local governance but are not going to lastingly alter the situation.
The Southern Transitional Council is now completely split. Half of the members have gone with the Government, and the other half are trying to continue being separatists.
Q40 Helen, turning to the issue of displacement and playing into the situation you have described, how has that affected national stability?

About four and a half million people are displaced; many are in communities with relatives or friends or have moved from one village to another. There are a lot of small displacement camps, mainly in the Marib Governorate, where the population has risen from around 300,000 to 3 million in the course of the last 10 years; there are large numbers of displaced people in Marib, mostly in a large number of very small camps.

Politically, I do not think the displacement issue is making much difference to the Yemeni situation. The main aspect is humanitarian. In the case of Marib—where you have a very large number of displaced people—the impact on the water supply is another important factor. Water is a fundamental issue, so that again is something one could talk about; the water supply and potential for economic activities and so on in Marib is very much affected. The availability of water has an indirect impact on stability. At that level, you have a connection.

Relative to conflicts elsewhere in the world, there have not been large population displacements in the past year or two—or three or four . As Helen mentioned, there has been an informal truce since the official renewable two-month truce expired in October 2022. That has meant there has only been low-level limited skirmishing or fighting within the country and there have been no major cross-border hostilities with Saudi Arabia from the Houthi side. There have been no significant population displacements as there have been in dynamic conflicts such as in Sudan. The conflict in Yemen is not dynamic; it is much more static.

Most of the political and military displacement was in the early years. Most of the displacement that has happened in the last two or three years has been due to environmental causes—including droughts and floods—but the figures are much lower.

Q41 That is interesting. A few years ago a witness said to us, “Always follow the movement of people to see what is going on in a country.” While the conflict is not happening, you are seeing environmental movement; I also wonder if people have given up hope, so there is not anywhere for them to move to?

I do not think so. People move when they are desperate—that is quite straightforward—and they move when they are pushed. Either they are pushed by fighting, or on a lower basis by a flood. At another level you have a general level of displacement that started before the fighting and is going to go on. For example, in areas where the water has completely run out, people have had to move. Their villages have been abandoned and they have moved to the cities, which creates another set of tensions. It creates in stability when you suddenly have thousands of people from villages moving into a town or city where there is also a shortage of water, schools, medical services, and everything. That creates social tension, which can become political tension. Those who are militarily displaced, or who are going to camps, more or less end up in empty areas. Referring to your earlier question on agriculture and development, less than 3% of Yemen land is suitable for agriculture , so there are plenty of desert spaces in which to create a refugee camp —and when you get into the situation with water, it is much worse .
I would add that the environmental stresses are probably stronger or more acute in the more arid lowland regions. The highlands are the agricultural heartlands to some extent.
I am not sure I would agree with that.
There are also environmental pressures.
It is a matter of water tables. Yemen has no permanent rivers; it only has one tiny one.
We have a water expert on our panel; Brian, is there anything you want to come in on?
I nearly had a job doing the water supply in Sana’a, but I decided against it.

Q42 Helen, do you think the static situation that you have described over the last short number of years has led to international actors being more concerned with managing the situation than trying to resolve it?
I agree with what people said in the previous panel: international actors are just not interested in Yemen.
Q43 Why?

It is a long way away; it is isolated. It controls the Bab -e l-Mandeb Strait , which is the one point that could get the international community interested. It has a large population and it is poor. It has no significant oil or other goodies unless some rare earths are discovered, in which case maybe they will get excited and start trying to get things out. I do not know, to be honest. I have been involved there for 50 years and I love the place— I know lots of people who do—so I am not the best person to say why nobody cares.
Q44 You have touched on the fact that, given the Houthi’s previous and probably ongoing relationship with Iran, the current Iran conflict means that a dialogue with the Houthis is more difficult.
It is more difficult for the Saudis; nobody else wanted to talk to the Houthis in the first place. Did the UN want to talk to the Houthis?

Yes, it did; it is the mandate for the UN special envoy to use their good offices to mediate. You asked why the situation is static; it is the peace process or peace efforts that are static or stagnant. One illustration is that a two-month truce was renewed only twice in 2022 and there has been no subsequent agreement, although there was a prisoner exchange agreement this year.
That was supposed to happen last week but it has been cancelled indefinitely.

It built on previous prisoner exchange agreements, but it is not a core peace process. The core peace process is static, like the conflict. Why is it static? Helen mentioned that in effect Yemen does not matter enough to some international actors. Another part of the answer would be that the international vision and framework for the peace process is rigid. It is fixed by a UN Security Council resolution 2216 dating from April 2015— 11 years ago—and the interpretation of that resolution. That resolution is being adhered to by those international actors that talk about and try to involve themselves or give diplomatic support to a p eace process for Yemen, but it does not fit with the realities; in many respects it is obsolete.

Q45 We have considered and taken evidence on other conflicts, for example in Sudan, which is a hugely complex conflict. Even if there was a will to resolve that, it would be incredibly difficult. Do you think that if there was a will to resolve this conflict it could be done?

Yes. At the moment, the configuration of the peace process for Yemen is an international vision and framework. The terms and the framework included in Security Council resolution 2216 envisage an eventual Yemeni-led political process. That process or that element has never been reached in the past 11 years. As peace processes elsewhere in the world show, it is ultimately for the people whose country it is to shape and lead a peace process; they can do it best.

Among the Yemeni leaders of the conflict—on both sides—there is no will to bring an end to this. Some of them, o n both sides, are profiting massively from the war situation. On the IRG side they are still divided—slightly differently this year from last year—and competing with each other. The leaders are profiting from this war and they do not particularly want to solve it. My view is that mediators can do and say what they want but if the parties concerned do not want to solve it, they will not.

Most of the 35 million or so Yemenis, however, do want to solve it. They do not want to live in this war. They do not want to suffer all the things we have talked about and not talked about; but they have no control over the military. In the Houthi area, there is a very efficient, effective and unpleasant, repressive regime. You heard some examples of that earlier. On the IRG area, there are different factions running their own unpleasant regimes and fighting each other. The Saudis are now in a position to try to dictate something, but they are not —they are not trying to solve this rivalry.
Q46 Could I ask a slightly off the wall question; it might be interesting to hear the answer. Was there ever a golden age when Yemen regarded itself as being a happy place?

Yes; it lasted from 1990 to 1992 or just about 1993. That was the best time. It was just after unification, and everybody was very enthusiastic about it. There was freedom of expression and a multiplication of newspapers and media all over the place. Everybody was really enthusiastic about elections, about progress, and about how they were going to get democracy and development. Those were good days, and everybody was hopeful. Yes, Ali Abdullah Saleh was murdering a whole load of socialists on the quiet, but they thought, “That won’t last, we’ll sort it.” People were hopeful until the 1993 elections: everywhere you went, people were enthusiastic. I remember at one point sitting with some guys trying to count the number of new political parties and we gave up when we got to about 40. People were really hopeful that there would be development, that education, health, development and activities were going to be the thing and that there would be democracy —all the things that they hoped for . But as I said, it did not last.

Q47 We want to get back to that effective, great, good governance. You have answered my question already—do not feel you need to repeat things you have said—but I want to get a sense of what the biggest barriers are to restoring effective governance in Yemen.

Obviously, the war and the divisions. In the long run, the way to solve these problems is through federalism; that is the only thing that would work in Yemen. There are long-lasting and long-standing divisions, both politically between the states and socially and politically between tribal and other groups and different regions, so a well-designed federal state would make a lot of sense. There was discussion of a federal state and it was decided to have one after the National Dialogue Conference, but in a completely bure aucratic manner: for instance, “X, Y, Z is governor of here, X, Y, Z is governor of there , let’s mix it together .” That is not the basis on which to create a federal state. You have to look at the social structure balance, at social groups, and at naturally available resources so that you do not end up with one place that has loads of stuff while the next one has nothing. In Yemen, water is absolutely fundamental. That is the basis on which one could hope to plan. People are still talking about it but not with interest because they do not want to solve the problem.
Q48 Are you aware of anyone working towards that?

There are still people talking about it but most of the people I know who are hopeful or interested in politics are pretty depressed. They are a bit lacking. I was talking to someone yesterday, asking him, “What’s the future?” He said, “I have my vision but nobody wants to listen.” I said, “Well, I’ll listen.” He said, “Yes, but nobody listens to you, either.”
Q49 We are listening. Richard, what role do you think local actors and civil society in Yemen can play to help stabilise the country?

Freedoms are lacking, but that is a reality in many countries in the Middle East and more widely. Among civil society, civil organised groups and NGOs, the desire to be more influential is there, as indicated in the previous witnesses’ responses. The enabling environment will come as and when there is a facilitation and creation of space for inter-Yemeni dialogue. As I said earlier, a fundamental problem is that the prevailing framework for the peace process in Yemen is inappropriate: it does not foster gro wth in the space for civil society activity. At the moment it is difficult for those civil society groups to act, to do local peacebuilding, to engage in Track III or Track II initiatives in support of higher-level peace mediation, or to engage in areas of developmental work involving terms that some governing authorities dislike. As Noha said, they have to struggle and find ways to work around and relabel the things they want to do. The desire and capability is there, without doubt. The skills and capabili ty of Yemeni civil society groups and NGOs should not be doubted.

Q50 Richard, the UK is the penholder for Yemen, as we are for many difficult conflicts at the moment. What leverage do you feel the UK has? As a follow-up to that question, how can we be more effective in our role as penholders?

As a penholder, you have the leverage of drafting resolutions or opening the way for discussions on potential resolutions around the Security Council. That leverage has not been used well, and I am not the only person who would say that: researchers and people who have worked on peace processes have written on this from as long as eight years ago, remarking that the rigidity and inflexibility and the refusal to reconsider resolution 2216 was unhelpful. It was limiting mediation and the potential for the pea ce process to make gains. The question for the UK is that, as penholder, has it used that penholding well?
Q51 Do you feel that the UN has leverage? If the UK were to use its role as penholder better, do you feel there would be leverage over the actual situation on the ground?

It would be welcome. It is not just the Ansar Allah in Sana’a that would welcome easing in the international framework for the peace process and the picking up of a pen for drafting a new resolution addressing the peace process. There are other Yemeni parties that would welcome that also. What was the other part of your question?

Q52 I am wondering whether anyone has leverage. In your first answer, you suggested that the UK has not effectively used its role as penholder at the UN; even if it did, what leverage do you feel it could have?

The UK is very limited in its leverage. It can facilitate in the capacity of penholder but subsequent leverage is limited, partly due to the very limited diplomatic engagement with some parties in Yemen. The absence of foreign diplomatic missions—largely speaking—from Sana’a and northern Yemen has consequences for limiting its diplomatic leverage.
Q53 Helen, what about the UK’s regional relationships? Are we sufficiently leveraging those relationships to have any impact?
The UK could suggest to the Emirates that they completely stop being involved in Yemen.
We could suggest it, but what is the likelihood that it would work?
You have seen how much impact other suggestions to the UAE have had, particularly on Sudan. I do not know what else could be done.

Q54 You talked about the rigidity and inflexibility of the UK approach, or maybe the framework that the UK is proposing. Why has the UK come to that inflexibility? What is the reason they propose that?

I think because of group-think, a diplomatic bubble and lack of contact with the country; lack of contact with realities in the country, lack of on-the-ground experience, observation and interaction with Yemenis of all political and non-political backgrounds.
Q55 Do you know the size of the UK’s diplomatic mission in Yemen or what it has been historically?

I do not know the numbers, but obviously they do not have an office inside Yemen. That is a question you can put to the FCDO and the ambassador. How many days a year does the ambassador spend in Yemen? It is vanishingly few.

Q56 More diplomatic engagement with Yemen would perhaps unlock this inflexibility and the rigidity of the framework. From the British taxpayer’s point of view, Yemen is surrounded by very wealthy countries that are absolutely involved in Yemen. Why should the UK get involved in this?

I do not think that the UK necessarily has a lot to offer. The neighbouring countries are much more important, and the reputation of the UK in Yemen—at least for some Yemenis—is tarnished by its history and its role in the Saudi-led military intervention since 2015.

A lot of people look back to the days of British rule in the south and in Aden, and many Yemenis think Britain should be involved because of that involvement. Many of them would welcome it, at least among the southerners.
Q57 Do you think there is any point whatsoever in the UK playing this role as penholder in Yemen? If not, who would better play that role?
That question might apply to most penholders. It is about the power of the UN; that brings up the issue that the UN’s influence has gradually become weaker and weaker as the decades have gone by.

Countries can feel flattered by the penholding role, as though it is a testimony to their diplomatic finesse and skill at drafting. But there are 15 countries in the Security Council; even in the Security Council discussions yesterday about Yemen, the issue of resolution 2216 was raised, and the question of its age or obsolescence.

Q58 It is no criticism of you, but I feel as if we are struggling to answer this question. I am not asking it as a challenge so much as I am trying to think through what would be the most meaningful diplomatic action that the UK could take. Do you have any thoughts on that? Can you just take 30 seconds to reply?

Diplomatically, I would say try to push the neighbouring countries to be more involved and possibly talk to the different Yemeni politicians—if they are interested in listening—and try to persuade them, not to change their views but to start thinking about the millions of people who are suffering.

I would agree with that , and would add that the UK could do more to acknowledge the realities of governance within Yemen and engage with those realities. There is an administration, a go vernment in Sana’a led by Ansar Allah and minority partners. It should not be a complete taboo to acknowledge that.
Q59 Just to come back to what you said was group-think, where does that come from? Is it UK group-think, or diplomatic group-think?

It is my observation—I have not been part of it—that there is group-think among the diplomatic community that is engaging with Yemen but based outside the country in Riyadh, and to a lesser extent in Amman in Jordan. They are interacting with other out-of-country embassies to Yemen and with a limited section of the internationally recognised government of Yemen and their embassies abroad; they are staying within the comfortable space of a discourse about a political path for Yemen, without questioning it.

You could say it goes back to the Friends of Yemen, which if I remember rightly was set up in 2009. That developed into a group of 10 ambassadors, which then created the GCC initiative and agreement. So there is a corpus; obviously, the individuals have changed, but we are now well into the second decade of its operation. That may be an element.
To add to that, of course, there is the standard diplomatic turnover of staff moving every two or three years.
Q60 Helen, does the UK have a strategy for Yemen other than humanitarian assistance?
I do not know, but I could suggest one. I could suggest things to do with development, which is what I am keen on.
To the extent that it has a strategy, that strategy is unrealistic and unhelpful for the prospects for peace in Yemen. That is the final reckoning.

Q61 Let’s go there, Helen. T he last two hours have been pretty bleak about the humanitarian situation and life for civilians; the development situation has not even been touched upon because there does not seem to be the ability to operate in that space. Let us try to end with something hopeful to aim for. Let us say that there is a foreseeably lasting peace, and an opportunity to stabilise and rebuild Yemen. Helen, you said that you could offer a development solution . What would be the priorities and how would it come into reality, with international money or private money? What would you foresee?

Yemen’s crisis is very deep and goes back way before the war started. There are incredible, basic, fundamental things that need to be done. Some can start now. You do not have to wait; you must not wait. In my view the two major sectors that need to be addressed are first, water and environmental issues, and secondly, education. The Yemeni education system is not appropriate to the 21st century. The population of Yemen is still growing at almost 3% a year. There is an absolutely desperate need if the new ge neration is to fit into a modern economy. Even when the education system works it is crudely more 19th century than 21st. It is something that cannot wait and does not have to wait; you do not need to wait until you have peace to do things such as developing appropriate syllabi, training potential teachers, and preparing and designing an education system that will create a labour force that is able to survive and be operative. It takes about 15 years to get that going; the later you start, the worse it will be.

Working on the education thing is one element, and something that the UK could fund and participate in. That could start now and it does not have to address—at least not directly—the split between Houthi-controlled areas and IRG-controlled areas. Let us remember that two-thirds of the population are in the Houthi-controlled areas: they are the vast majority. To me, working on education is one of the two basics that need to be addressed.
Q62 Richard, what are your thoughts? What development needs should the international community focus on?

It should be led by the Yemenis now and in that hypothetical or hopeful future of greater and widening peace. The capabilities of Yemenis regarding development and the economy should not be underestimated; they must not be. The narrative of precariousness around Yemen regarding its economy and humanitarian conditions has long prevailed internationally, but within the country there are a lot of capabilities. There are economic strengths and sectors that have resilience and capability. There are large numbers of Yemenis working in neighbouring countries and further afield remitting back to the country.
Q63 Is the banking system still operational, so that remittances will get through to the right people?
As far as I know, yes.

That has given us a little window of opportunity. Going back to what you were saying at the start: in the last two years, the movement of people is more environmentally than conflict-driven; that is a topic that this Committee has sadly come back to over many years. I hope the next time we meet to discuss the situation in Yemen—both from a humanitarian and developmental point of view—we will be looking at the successes that have been made. Thank you both for all that you have done over many years. We have l istened, Helen; tell your colleague we have listened and we have broadcast, and that we will continue pushing the UK Government to do everything that is within its power to try to get the stability that everybody so dearly wants. Thank you very much for your time. Thank you, Committee.

sessions.iT: New Towns: Bricks and Mortar
sessions.w: Saïd Business School, University of Oxford; University College London (UCL)

segs.tx: Built Environment Committee
C orrected oral evidence: New towns: bricks and mortar
Tuesday 14 July 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Gascoigne (The Chair) ; Baroness Andrews; Lord Bailey of Paddington; Baroness Barran; Lord Bassam of Brighton; Lord Cameron of Dillington; Baroness Griffin of Princethorpe; Baroness Janke; Baroness Lawrence of Clarendon; Baroness Miller of Chilthorne Domer; Lord Porter of Spalding; Lord Ravensdale.
Evidence Session No. 5 Heard in Public Questions 44 – 5 7
Witnesses
Professor Juliano Denicol, Professor of Megaproject Management, University College London; Dr Alexander Budzier, Saïd Business School, University of Oxford.
USE OF THE TRANSCRIPT
Examination of witnesses
Professor Juliano Denicol and Dr Alexander Budzier.

Q44 Good morning and welcome to the House of Lords Built Environment Committee. As everybody knows, over the p ast 18 months or so , we have been looking into the subject of new towns. Our third module has been specifically on what we have called bricks and mortar , which includes some of the stumbling blocks to making these new towns happen. This is our final public session before the Summer Recess . P eople will be pleased to know that we will return after the summer to conclude this inquiry. Today is not just the end of this module but , in effect , the end of our discussions on new towns, so we are seeking to bring the whole debate on this programme to a conclusion and to raise some of the issues around delivering what we would term megaprojects, or big projects, as new towns , as well as whether it can and should be done.

We are delighted to welcome two guests to talk to us about that: Dr Budzier from the Saïd Business School at the University of Oxford, and Professor Denicol, who is a professor of megaproject management at UCL . I w elcome you both. We have a series of questions from around our horseshoe. My request to our witnesses and members alike is to keep the questions and answers as short as possible. If there are any bits where you do not have anything to add or on which you want to write to us, please say so.
This question is for both of you. What would the successful delivery of the new towns programme look like to you?

It is all about the outcomes; it is not about the announcements. It is about towns that have an established population with lived-in housing units that function. That is a successful outcome. It can probably be judged only in the decades to come. Milton Keynes was 50 years ago , and now we see a flourishing town. Ebbsfleet has not flourished so much. Success should look more like Milton Keynes than Ebbsfleet.

It should be about infrastructure first —that is, be infrastructure-led and systems-led. We have a collection of interdependent major projects to be delivered together. It cannot be about only housing. There is confusion in previous reports around the narrative. Is this housing or is it economic growth as well? How do we square that vision and proposition? People need to have a place. The place - making perspective needs to be beyond housing and assets. It needs to have an identity. It needs to have access to jobs. There is a collection of assets , from transportation to hospitals and schools , that need to be in place before you start a discussion with the private sector on unblocking the delivery aspects. For the people living there, it needs to have an identity.

Can I go a bit further? Some of our witnesses have raised the spectre of decades-long building sites. How do you think we can move forward without ending up with these sorts of projects that seem to go on for ever and do not end up delivering what we are looking for?

If we unpack some of the findings from your previous reports, it seems that there is a consensus that development corporations are the way to go and the delivery model for these things. Equally, it is missing a central body, such as central government oversight of the delivery of towns across the country. If we are to unpack the concepts of central oversight and government leadership, along with several terms and expressions from previous reports, what does that look like? It is missing an entity or agency that would be there for 50 or 60 years and have C abinet-level oversight , would report and would have influence , because you need to unpack and herd several sectors and money from different departments. That is a systemic effort that I doubt local development corporations will have the power to do. In terms of a governance structure , we need an entity that will be there for much longer and ensure consistency and standardisation.

T hat should also deal with the argument of speed. If you think about it, what are the current choke points? A lot of that is about local co-ordination and consenting processes. In the current powers, a local master plan does not automatically imply consent. If we look at successful development corporations, such as the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, the power was delegated or taken away from local authorities and given to the development corporation for a limited time. Therefore, the choke point was taken away. E qually , we see where that is not taken away. Take, f or instance, the Social Housing Innovation Fund and how quickly it rolls out projects, or the school rebuilding programme , where announcements and local support for a scheme do not necessarily mean that it gets built or built quickly. It is then held up in all sorts of co-ordination and consenting things.

As I was coming here , I thought I would look at some numbers. If you have a development consent order, the statutory limit is 15 to 18 months until it should be granted. I looked through the last 75 DCOs. Only 40% of those achieved 18 months or fewer . Some 60% of all DCO processes take longer than that, which is already an expedited process. That is a real choke point right at the beginning. As Juliano said, without a system in place to deliver this or have some sort of capability, announcements and small enablement projects will lead to small developments but not reach the required scale.
Do you see financial barriers as a significant issue?

It is a question of sequencing as well. Do we have the money to afford it? Where is the evidence for that? We have a big vision and a big ambition. We had 40 new hospitals. We had many different PowerPoint presentations. Where is the infrastructure delivery road map sequencing for each town? Can we afford them all? Should we prioritise? What is the plan to bring money in and attract private sector investment?

If you think about it in terms of building a new town with 10,000 units, the infrastructure and public buildings alone , such as hospitals and schools —Juliano mentioned these— will cost about £ 4 billion. We have the announcements and the bank under Homes England now, but these are all numbers that have been announced but not actually committed to . There is a real difference there in terms of the commitment.

Q45 On that ever-decreasing list of what is up and running, do any of them look like they could be a perfect new town? This is not just an academic exercise now, is it? We know where they are going to be — at least , we know the list they might be on , even though it gets shorter on a monthly basis.

If you look back, the sequencing was done in the wrong way. The longlist was announced first, then that was whittled down by the Government to the seven sites. Now , finally , the environmental and delivery studies have been done, so are we allowed to construct on the site ? That kind of sequencing was completely out of sync. In an ideal world, you would have done an investigation survey for all the sites and then land on one. Why? B ecause of the whole thing around land uplift values , which has happened: as soon as you announce the 12 sites, everybody increases the options on the site s and the money is gone. The sites are less viable so there is less public infrastructure, Section 106 and so on.

We know about the sequencing. We complained about that a year or two ago — probably before they even started. Do any of the ones left on the list, even though they might not be on it tomorrow, look like they could be a perfect new town? Is it one or all of them ?

The problem is fixable now. You can make them all successful. If it were me, I would first publish the funding model concurrently with the arising environmental impact assessments so that things do not come one after the other but are done in one package. There are safeguarding powers in statute that could be used to safeguard the land value now and take away the hope value, which just increases the cost of these projects rather than delivering something. Exercise these powers now , be very clear that this is the funding for the projects , and give the constructability study and the environmental impact assessment. As Juliano said, create something that is a single accountable owner for the seven together, not just a random collection of seven projects.
So w e can still hope that the Government can retrieve this and do at least some of it if so meone says, “I ’ m owning it”.

To that point, you need more than individuals who are behind that. What is the structural mechanism, entity or agency that will match the policy announcement and the ambition? Nobody disagrees with the ambition — we need 1.5 million houses and so on — but how do you make that happen in a co-ordinated manner? We can go back to multiple examples from different megaprojects around the world on the accountability of the client. At the Megaproject Delivery Centre at UCL, we look at the client as one of the most important actors in the system — that is, the guiding mind or co-ordinating view. Mark Wild made that point on Crossrail, and again on High Speed 2, and Sir Andy Mitchell did so on Tideway. We have many examples in the UK , such as CLM and the Olympics model , or ODA ; I am sure you heard from Nick Smallwood and Sir John Armitt. It will not be successful without that agency, whatever that is and whatever its capabilities .
Q46 We look back historically at the immediate ly post-war new towns and we probably assume that that was a successful programme. Do you think that there are lessons to be learned from it?
I like Milton Keynes and the single development corporation. You might think that it is funny with its little road layout, and its house numbering system is a bit odd —
With all its roundabouts.

U ltimately, for most people who come from Milton Keynes and live there, it is a thriving town; it is a definite success. How did that happen? You had the development corporation and the powers and funding associated with it. Most importantly, so that it did not just create its own inflation bubble—Juliano mentioned things such as HS2 , which makes itself more and more expensive —in Milton Keynes, t he land was assembled by the public purse, not private developers . I t was assembled by use value. They bought it at the price for agricultural land and took the value uplift that came from making it developable , so that it could be borrowed against , and put that into the infrastructure that needed to be built. The financing mechanism used was to finance it from the agricultural-use land to the future-use land, to borrow against that gap and to put it into the financing of the infrastructure. It was a very successful model.
Are there ways in which we can replicate that with the current new towns programme? Wh ich similarities we could focus on to deliver the thing I think we all want : new homes for people?

There is nothing that we could not sort out. Give the development corporations similar powers and find a similar financing arrangement, which means stopping any land value speculation because those powers exist. The Government could do that and address the hope value debate by recycling it into paying for the infrastructure needed to enable the sites and lay the foundation al fabric for future successful towns.

I would add to that the need for the consideration of speed. The post-war landscape was significantly different , in terms of planning and consent , to what we have now. Hinkley Point C ’s develop ment took around 10,000 pages to get permission to build. Sizewell C was seven to eight times more, with supplementary documentation—80,000 pages in a space of how many years? There is a new network and infrastructure working group at the OECD, which is the first new network created by the OECD in 17 years for infrastructure delivery, recognising the challenge that multiple countries are facing.

It raises th is question: how do you have accountability for these things ? W ho owns the model ? H ow do we learn from planning and the expansion of requirements? That takes time. Once you address all the pillars you have, you start again because the regulations changed. How fast do we want the cities to be there? We have a housing crisis . There will be trade- offs; we need to be honest about those . What are we willing to do to have economic growth and housing ready for people without damaging the environment? There must be another way, and trade-offs are needed; otherwise , it will take as long as it is taking to build major projects . I have plenty of examples.

Q47 Good morning , gentlemen . I am sorry not to be with you in person. This is a pretty blunt question in relation to everything you have said so far: do you think this is worth it? W e have failed to project the same imperative as in 1945 on central funding or a plan for sequencing, as you call it, and we have done things in the wrong order, yet we are lumbered with a big political image of new towns . W ould it not be better at this point to say, “ W e’re just going to build a few additional settlements in key growth areas”, or is that now too late and too politically expensive?

Honestly, you would not make up the numbers. Private sector developers would easily build infill projects, and perhaps densification projects in urban areas , because there are clear profits to be had. That is something the market can sort out if there is a shortage of appropriate rents and prices for housing or other real estate.

The key role of g overnment is not in those kinds of projects . It is about whether we should and can build new towns . Given the need, we are not going to make up the numbers. We know that parts of this building other than this committee talk about social cohesion and such things. L ook at places such as Hong Kong, where a lack of housing led to unrest . Once you get two generations who never have the opportunity or even the faint hope of owning, or even renting, a property on their own, that has more negative consequences than high rent and a high cost of living in the long run.
You are saying that this must remain a national and coherent government project, badged as a new towns programme .

Yes. It needs to be a national endeavour , but you need the capabilities and resources to match the ambition. That requires building capability and long-term investment in institutional structures because it needs to be led by the Government. Going back to your question, if we need as many cities as was announced, we do not know the sequencing, the cost or how long it will take. Before an answer to that question could be provided, I would like to see the analysis and data to back , say, seven cities instead of three. Should we prioritise where we have ongoing infrastructure , a long the lines of East West Rail, which is already progressing and taking years ? If you have to build infrastructure, how many years are you taking to build it first so that you can attract the private sector for housing? There could be an investigation into which ones will have more infrastructure . Y ou could deliver housing but the infrastructure needs to be there first; there is no way round it.

In addition to those arcs and corridors that have been designated, such as Leeds South Bank or Victoria North in Manchester, which already have that existing infrastructure and those kinds of things in place, a new town could tap into things at speed without the long development timeline that is usually required if you have to put in all that infrastructure, create jobs and build the transportation , schools and hospitals that are needed.
That is an interesting alternative model; thank you.

Q48 Y ou seem to be saying that there needs to be a government body or central mechanism to ensure that this happens. Are you talking about a Minister or a ministry? Is it something that the Deputy Prime Minister could do? Who needs to drive this?

It cannot be your job on a Tuesday morning. You need dedicated capability in an organisation , not just a team of people . Y ou need to establish an entity to manage the portfolio , find synergies across all the towns and deal with the supply chains and markets to create savings , in terms of managing this as a portfolio and having a strategy across the country. For that, you need an agency with the right seniority and people who can go around multiple government departments to bring in the right people to talk about schools, hospitals, transport, water, utilities, the grid, EV, climate change and resilience, which are the multiple sectors you need to address. Without th at seniority , this will not happen.
