One key thing, p arallel to whatever the Government decide on policy for setting limits and guidance to achieve a widespread increase in reductions in speed, is a n awareness campaign, so that the public and policymakers understand how very small changes in average speed have a massive impact on the severity of injuries, the risk of death and the costs. At the moment , we are out of balance with the real harms and costs and the priority and urgency that is focused on saving lives.
Q156 Adrian, t he written evidence from 20’s Plenty for Us said that you “doubt that the proposed measures will deliver the casualty reduction targets”. Why is that?

Because there is no commitment to a 20 mph speed limit on residential streets . S ince around 50% of KSIs occur on 30 mph roads, without reducing that speed limit to 20 mph you simply cannot achieve the target of 65% . It is interesting . W e have modelled it , and I think you heard it from an earlier witness that the contribution of 20 mph to the Government’s target is far and away the biggest single measure that could help. I think Dan Campsall said it is something like 10% to 15%, and we would concur with that .

B ut it goes further, because 20 mph not only bring s down casualties but enables other measures to come in much more cheaply. I have seen that in projects that I have been involved in. Once you have the lower speed limit it enables you, for example, to do an informa l crossing , rather than a formal one. It makes all the other measures much easier to implement.

It also changes the relationship between road users—between the driver and the cyclist, or the cyclist and the pedestrian—so that they look out for each other more. Your field of vision widens when you are doing a lower speed. Rather than being surprised that somebody suddenly jumped out in front of you, you have anticipated it. It has a sort of cumulative effect. It is not instead of all the other measures; it is complementary to th em .
. We will drill down a bit more into the mechanics of 20 mph .

Can I add in the moral dut y part of a chieving the 20 mph limit ? U rban areas and villages , and roads w ith vulnerable, innocent, unprotected pedestrians — children, the frail, cyclists and non-motorised vehicles, horses and horse-drawn vehicles —are disproportionate ly within the areas where we would consider 20 mph limits. The re is a moral obligation and duty to protect the unprotected, to rebalance things away from a focus on motorised vehicles and to save our children and the unprotected . There is a host of other health benefits in terms of active lifestyles, mobility and the climate , the sense of security and lack of isolation of people that then allows community involvement, access to health and so on—t here is such a raft of other benefits. I would just like to emphasise that.
Thank you.

Q157 The Department told us that the strategy is evidence - based , and there was recognition of that in a lot of the submissions. While organisations like Brake recognised the evidence base of a lot of the strategy, they thought it did not go far enough in looking at best practice in terms of speed. What is the assessment of the evidence-based nature of the strategy when it comes to speed? Is there more evidence out there that the Department could draw on, perhaps to have a slightly more nuanced strategy?

Let m e look at some of the evidence we provided to the Government on speed, to make sure that everyone is aware of i t. A t Transport for London we analysed the impact of 20 mph spe ed limits across London boroughs over a very long period of time —about 10 year s . The results were un equivocal and showed that over that time the introduction of 20 mph speed limits achieved a reduction of around 3 4 % in people being killed or seriously injured. That was set against comparator roads, so it was controlled for. For children, t here was a much greater 70% reduction.

When you look at the detailed nature of th at evidence—it is the most comprehensive piece of evidence about 20 mph limits , across areas—I do not feel that it was pulled through clearly enough to demonstrate the area- wide benefits of 20 mph limits and the real need to put that at the heart of a strategy that reduces danger on our roads.

I will add to that. I t is s urprising that there is no reference to the outcomes of the full 20 mph speed limit in Wales, which is effectively the largest application of 20 mph that we have seen in the UK.

Q158 W e have a broadly one - third reduction i n Edinburgh as well because of 20 mph , and that has been subject to peer-reviewed research. I guess the challenge with Wales is that it may be too soon to work its way through the peer - review process.
No , I think the evidence is quite clear.
But in terms of peer review and independent analysis. Lilli , i s the evidence you were talking about TfL’s analysis, or was it done independently?
It was done by one of our analytical teams and peer reviewed by academic institutions.
And you feel that that has not been taken on board, despite the real results there , particularly for children.

Clearly , the strategy mention s that they are looking at this . I really know, through our Vision Zero action plan, that to move forward you need c lear and unequivocal determination that you are going to do something. We are very clear at the London level that we will move residential roads to 20 mph and work with London boroughs to do that. Now , 21 out of 33 London boroughs have this, and that is what is continuing to build and deliver further changes.

I feel the strategy is currently a bit h esitant at the national level, and that there is an opportunity with the policy to really go further and be much clearer. If you do not do that , too many people will find reasons not to do it, and we are back to the moral choices we have been hearing about.

You ask ed about the strength of evidence. The evidence has been there internationally. The World Health Organi s ation signed off many papers on the importance of speed , and even the real impact of 1% or 2% reductions in speed , which significantly reduce the number of killed and seriously injured. My favourite paper is a comprehensive unified framework for analysis by Rune Elvik. It really goes into the detail of not just the average speeds but the distribution of speeds. You have theory , and w e have —
Q159 We are guilty of talking a lot about 20 mph; does that paper go beyond 20?

It specifically looks at the incremental changes. I think 20 mph is a mechanism to make people more aware of how important speed is , and it also achieves a reduction in speeds. Where it has been implemented in other areas , it has not always been preceded by capture of the public’s understanding and awareness of it, initially , with f ocused interventions to make them more aware and understand the central role of their choice of speed , and then their support for and engagement with the measures. If we did that, and got it right, they would be d emanding that we introduce 20 mph limits in their areas and would be much less resistant and form much less opposition , because i t is absolutely clear . You have theory and ob served effects of the actual power of small reductions in speed wherever it has happened internationally. There is not a lack of evidence. There is a lack of willpower , following through, and putting it into action and intervention.
I cut you off earlier , Philip—sorry.

I was going to say, in terms of academic peer rev i ew, no, but in the sheer scale of the change that has been made—let us call it the experiment —there is no doubt that it has had the effect. It was entirely predictable, as Rob said. The evidence is clear. The report of the taskforce that I chaired was very clear. The evidence was collected and it said t his will happen and this will benefit. The relative changes in speed and the reduction in casualties were in line with what was predicted . W e know there is absolutely no doubt that this can and will be successful. The road safety strategy, in my view, does not pay enough heed to that evidence.

T o your point, urban areas are hugely important . I just looked at the numbers, and 45% of KSIs are in built - up areas, so we have to focus on built - up areas. We have to think about 20 mph as central , but we must not ignore the contribution that we need to make on rural roads , particularly single carriageways.
Q160 We have some specific questions about the Welsh experience. Rob, you referred to an international study. Could you name it? If we do not already have it, could you send it to us?

It was in the submission. It ’ s by Rune Elvik . I t is not an international study ; i t is the expertise that the World Health Organi s ation base d its speed impact tool on. Its formal title is “A comprehensive and unified framework for analysing the effects on injuries of measures influencing speed”, by Rune Elvik, in Accident Analysis & Prevention, 2019.
A nd it is referenced in the writ ten evidence you submitted so it is discoverable on our website.

Can I add something briefly ? I t talks about the effect of small reductions in speed —I think 1 kph is an 8% reduction in casualties . The focus of so much speeding policy is on compliance. It is interesting that one of the indicators in the road strategy is about compliance. Compliance is not the end. You can be complying with the wrong speed limit. We should be measuring actual speed and reductions in speed — the small changes in speed that have a disproportionate effect on reducin g casualties. That is the key message from that Elvik paper.

Can I add to what Phil was saying about Wales, and whether the evidence was peer reviewed ? It is interesting that if you compare the 20 mph and 30 mph roads in Wales with other roads, those other roads did not see any change in casualties. By the same token , you can compare it with England. Again, there was no change in that period. I think the benchmarking is pretty clear .

It is interesting that when the Wales default was declared, we were slightly nervous at 20’s Plenty for Us. We had seen the evidence from Bristol, London, Edinburgh and all sorts of places , and we thought, “I s this also going to happen in Wales? ” Of course it did, so we were absolutely delighted. After a year we thought, “Maybe next year’s results are not going to be quite as good,” and they were. If you look at the change quarter by quarter, it is very consistent. I am almost certain that a peer review would come up with that.
Q161 I always think it is a shame that we do not know which lives have been saved. If you were able to present that , it would change everything.
You can’t identify them.
We ’ re not going to rerun the model —sorry . [ Laughter. ]

Can I put it very briefly in numbers ? The paper I referred to is behind the speed impact tool , which is a way of predicting what a change in speed would achieve. I will give t wo figures . D rivers choosing to travel at 27 mph rather than 30 mph reduce the risk of fatalities by 33% and of seriously injuring people by 26%. If we look at an average speed going from 30 mph to 20 mph, which obviously is not the same as applying a 20 mph limit , but if we achieve compliance , it reduces fatal collisions to 72% of what they were and reduces serious injuries by 62%. That is the magnitude that the models predict, and it is the best model that we have at the moment . Wherever it is actually seen —those reductions in actual speeds are average speeds—it replicates the model.
T hank you very much.

Q162 You talked about your views on the strategy’s level of ambition for reducing killed or severely injured rates. One thing that is not talked about much in the strategy is Vision Zero. Do you feel that adopting Vision Zero at national level is realistic, and should have been considered in the strategy?

I am the author of the original Vision Zero strategy for London and worked on this for many years with other international cities and countries. I can understand the hesitation, perhaps, of officials and Ministers at that point, because when we launched the Vision Zero action plan in London and set the goal of eliminating death and serious injury from the roads by 2041, it was considered quite audacious. Yet driving that through and changing the tone of the debate to say, “This is not an everyday occurrence, or an acceptable outcome of how we use the road network , ” has fundamentally changed the way we make decisions as a city, both in London boroughs and in Transport for London. As the chief safety officer I know that , because it allows intolerance of an acceptability that death and injury will happen . Clearly, things are not perfect in London and road danger still exists, but there is that intolerance of it, so when something happens you go further and question every investment decision you make.

I feel, emotionally—which is at the heart of what politics is ultimately about—that it is hugely important to have that kind of commitment and strength . Actually, do we really want to change things? Yes. What number is acceptable: 13 or 25? Last year 96 people were killed on London’s roads. To me that is unacceptable. It will not be acceptable until it is zero.
Any other though t s?

As Lilli said, what other number would you choose? Yes, it is audacious—a really good word. It is ambitious, but it has to be, in the end, doesn’t it ? In any other industry or mode of transport , what would be an acceptable target for killing people—for the railways or airlines? We could not put a number on it, so why would we say anything else as the long-term objective?

I have a slightly different take on that . Y es, absolutely , it has to be the principle, because there should not be a level of harm that we accept, but I think messaging, public engagement and the understanding of drivers are important. In some areas, if you say “Vision Zero”, people react against it, because they see zero as absolute; it is never going to be achieved and is unrealistic. It is so far away from where we are that it seems impossible, so they give up. It should absolutely be the principle driving things —i t is zero avoidable deaths . E ven if you just put that little “avoidable” in, it makes it more understandable to people, because it is not so absolute or like saying infinity or zero. Yes, it should be the principle, but it is brilliant if we achieve a 65% reduction in the next 10 years and a 70% reduction in children. That would go further than we have in the last couple of decades. So the principle is absolutely right ; h ow best to engage policymakers and the public is a different question.
Q163 We are going to be exploring some of that a bit later. Adrian, do you have any thoughts on Vision Zero?

I would just echo what other people said. You need that as a long-term goal , but 65% by 2035 is pretty ambitious and gets you a long way. We probably need some interim targets as well . H ow are we doing by 2028 and 2030? It is a journey that we are going towards. Y es, absolutely, Vision Zero must be the end goal.
Thank you very much. We are now going on to speed and road danger.

Q164 I will ask a slightly leading question. We have established that speed is a factor. Is that because when we reduce speeds the severity is less significant, or is it because accidents themselves are less likely?
Both.
Does a nyone want to expand on that one-word answer?

K inetic energy is ½ mv 2 . T hat ’ s how it works —y ou cannot argue with physics. A small increase in speed , as the square of the velocity , is the energy that is dissipated on impact. It is simple. In terms of reaction time , it changes the driver’s perception of the road ahead. It g i ves them more time to look , to avoid a casualty and to brake. If you are doing a certain speed and you stop a metre from a child, no injury takes place, while at 1 mph faster you might not be able to do that.

T o expand on that, we talked a lot about 20 mph but it is also manifest on strategic roads as well, and we have reduced top-level speed limits on some strategic roads in London. It allows more time to react and reduces the severity, because of the physical impact. On both those factors , it is absolutely critical .

Q165 Rob, you said in your written evidence : “ Speed is the predominant risk factor and controllable variable within our road safety system. ” The predominant risk factor is different from the cause, isn’t it ?
I would probably equate them.
Lots of people tell me they are great drivers and should be able to drive in line with the road conditions, but you are saying that speed is an issue.

Speed is the predominant issue, because increased speed increases the risk of collisions. Unexpected things happen on our roads every day. Sometimes when we are thinking or talking about speeds there is an assumption that everyone else is obeying the rules and driving sensibly, and that there will not be children or vulnerable adults doing odd things, or vehicles or animals, or trees down, or anything of that nature.

If we can reduce the speed at impact, that relates to the forces on the human body. Our frail mammalian bodies of blood and bone have a biomechanical tolerance, which is pretty much 20 mph for pedestrians. If you exceed that, the risk of death and injury is much greater than if you can achieve enough safety reserve in our systems when there are collisions—and there will be, as errors happen . B ut errors are different from people choosing to ignore the rules and drive too fast for the conditions. That is the absolute key.

W e know from the analysis of collisions in London that excess speed—which does not mean exceeding the speed limit ; it is speeding too fast for the conditions—is involved in at least 50% of serious and fatal injuries. It is the main causal contributory factor, to go directly to your question.

Coming back to the control, we have a system. Roads and mobility are a system—a man-made construct. Every bit of it is in our control. We create the cars, regulate the human drivers and decide how often they are licensed and checked, and the regulation, enforcement and penalties are the outcomes when people transgress the rules. It is a balance between mobility and speed, and a choice of restrictions and regulation , versus safety for drivers and other road users. At the moment , the pivot point—where we are on the seesaw—is far too much away from safety.

If we introduced a ban on speed—zero speed—there would be no injuries. Clearly , that is not viable or practical, because then we would lose mobility and all the other benefits, but we need to come much more back towards the realities of safety. That is where Vision Zero really has power, because you really start to think, every time there is an incident or even a near miss , t h at t h ere are things you can learn. Why did those drivers choose, and think it acceptable, to drive at those speeds or undertake that risk, or cause that risk to others and themselves?

Causation is always very subjective. Accidents, collisions and casualties always have multiple causations : i f this happens, this happens . Yet speed—the energy embodied in the moving vehicle—is common to every collision. Some factors, whether they are drug driving or drink driving, are only a subset of the population and of incidents, but speed is common to everything. It is the most important factor, in our view.

I have seen a report that was sent to me just this week by a local council, about a particular road where there have been six incidents. In the detail it says that in three of them speed was a cause. When I looked at the detail I thought, “Speed has been a cause or a factor in all six.” If one of the people had been driving a bit slower maybe it would not have happened. I think it is under-reported, which is part of the problem. We feel different when we are walking from when we are cycling and when we are in a car. Yes, when I am in a car , I feel a bit invulnerable, and I probably do not always drive as well for the conditions as I think. It is that perception of how you are doing. The average driver thinks they are better than the average driver. That is what all the data tells us. I am not going to say whether I am or not.
Q166 Yes — the rules are for other people. If w e have established that speed is a big factor, what other things can we manage to improve road safety?

I am glad you asked, because it is really important to see speed as part of the system. Our Vision Zero action plan clearly sets out a range of actions across all elements of what we call a safe system . In terms of vehicles in particular, one thing that we think the strategy could go further on is the safety of heavy goods vehicles. In London, for example, we have required additional safety features to enhance the visibility of the surroundings for the driver, through what we call our direct vision standard. That halved the number of casualties resulting, so on average six fewer people are now killed by heavy goods vehicles and around 15 or 17 fewer people are seriously injured. The European Commission has adopted that as part of vehicle standards. That ethos needs to drive through into the strategy.

Similarly, we have a bus safety standard that goes much further than a normal safety standard, so you can do things with vehicles. One great thing in the strategy was the recognition of technology. All those measures should be required and adopted because, with very little impediment or hindrance to drivers, it would make the drives easier, more relaxing and definitely safer , so all those measures are hugely important.

You need to change the roads. You will see outside Parliament that there are cycle lanes. There are ways of creating and segregating vulnerable road users from main roads. That is essential, as is education.

Finally, there is enforcement. The role of the police is critical. Our plan is a joint plan between the London boroughs , which manage 95% of the road network, London police, Transport for London and other agencies. Collaboration is a key part of it, and I think that could come through even more strongly in the strategy.
It is a shame that the Road Haulage Association is not here today to answer some of those points.
Yes.
Is there anything else on that?

Essentially, what we were talking about was speed. Of course, there are other factors. The safe system , which is referenced in the strategy, divides it into the five pillars or components. I believe that insufficient focus is placed on the writing around the circle. You have your five components —safe roads and roadsides, safe road users, safe speeds, safe vehicles, post-crash response—but the leadership, co-ordination, messaging, public awareness and attitudes and cultures around road safety are missing elements. Not enough is put into that. There are behavioural scientists and research academics who have tools to measure where a population is, introduce interventions in real time , not causing waiting and delay, and observe the impact. We need to harness those to a much greater degree.

As I said earlier, if we got it right and people understood the harsh realities out there, they would demand this and they would not choose to drive in the manner they are because they would understand that the driver has ultimate responsibility. At the end of the day, we have a system with all sorts of components, but , ultimately, the final decision is that a driver decides consciously to get into a car, whatever condition it is in and whatever condition they are in, and chooses at what speed to drive around other human beings. This is not about blaming a driver. We see it in the context of the system and try to understand why they are making unwise decisions where they are, and we have put in awareness enforcement regulation that will reduce the tragedy that is happening out there.
It is also the choice of car people buy. In particular, people do not understand the relationship with bonnet height and the impact it has on pedestrians, particularly children.
That is important, but we will come to it later .

Q167 On people’s attitudes to speed, it is interesting that sometimes when someone is caught speeding and fined it is treated as being unlucky . It is not unusual to see o n a local community Facebook page a warning that the speed cops are out trying to catch criminals. We don’t warn burglars or shoplifters that they might get caught, but for some reason it is acceptable to speed , is n’t it?

There are a couple of points on that. The reality is that we are in a blind spot. We have evolved, lived and grown up with vehicle mobility as part of the background of our everyday lives. Somehow, things have got out of kilter , and we have got out of touch.

I would like to introduce some concepts from Professor Ian Walker, a British environmental psychologist , who uses the term “motonormativity”. One of the Committee’s previous inquiries made reference to it. He describes it as society’s unconscious bias towards cars. It refers to a cultural blind spot where people automatically accept driving as the default and normal transport mode, often suspending their usual ethical and moral standards when judging driving behaviours. It explains how people are able to apply double standards to road use that would be completely unacceptable anywhere else, like flying and drink or drugs. They ignore alternative options to driving that are often healthier and possible , and they defend the status quo . They are resistant to our introduction of measures that will make it safer for everyone. I think there are some really interesting things in there.

One other thing mentioned was the concept of pluralistic ignorance. That is really interesting . I think it arose in the previous session. It is not a term I had been familiar with, but I think it is real. It is described as a number of vociferous opponents who are much louder in their expression of opposition and resistance to interventions like 20 mph limits and anything else that makes t hings safer. People who hold the majority view and are in favour and support of more safety and 20 mph limits remain muted and quiete r because they believe they are part of a minority and might be ostracised. For policymakers and the general perception , it seems that the minority louder group are the majority , but they are not . I t ’ s actually the reverse. We have lots of question naires and surveys showing how important road safety is to people and how they want their communities to feel safer and reduce the costs, deaths and injuries.

Q168 Within that context, the Government are devolving powers to local authorities across the UK , in Scotland and Wales, to look at speed. Is that the right thing to do? Do you think they should just do what happened in Wales and take that central decision?
They did not do that in Wales.
Apologies. Do you think devolv ing it is the right thing to do?

Personally, I do not . I think i t should be nationally set. How the G overnment and things like that work something out, I do not know — I am a frontline clinician and I do not know how the Government s work — but I think it has to be nationally set, delivered and prioritised. I do not understand the dynamics of h ow that gets localised to an appropriat e degree , so I defer to your expertise on that.
I think national leadership and policy setting is absolutely critical , but it is clear that regions and cities can make progress in the absence of it.
It is happening, is n’ t i t?

Yes. Fatalities have fallen faster and further in London than in any other national city. That is a clear trend year on year because of policies, but you need that leadership , and that commitment in the strategy to set policy, review it and be bold.

There is something very important about what Dr Török said about challenging the tenor of the whole discussion. If reducing road deaths is never talked about at national level as a priority— it is now that we have a strategy, but there was a period when we did not—it is very difficult for regions to make the progress they need. Local highways already set the standards. That is what happens now. I believe there is some merit in that, but it definitely needs national leadership.
Q169 The UK Government c ould set a national limit of 20 mph in urban areas and individual local authorities c ould opt out of that. That is happening, is n’t it?
What is the most effective and urgent way we can do this? Every day we do not , more people are dying and their deaths could have been prevented.

There are some things that require national action. For example, if they were to mandate the 18 safety technical features in all vehicles , at a stroke you would have vehicles being intelligently adapted to the speed limit in their area.
But only in new cars.
Well, w e have retrofitted our vehicle fleet at Transport for London.
It will take time for most cars to have this.

It would, but that reduced speeding incidents by 63% in our fleet. Very quickly, i f you take the leadership and mandate those kinds of technological changes, you will already reap the benefits from the limits we have , and then you reduce those to lower limits . That kind of speed of action needs to be aligned with the targets we have set at national level.

On the question of public attitudes, we must not think that public attitudes are immutable . T hey change. What we are seeing in London and Wales increasingly is that , once we have wide areas of 20 mph and that becomes the norm , there is increased normalisation. The view at the taskforce stage was that we would see compliance increase over time. At the moment , it is pretty flat . There was a concern that we would see a dip and it would creep back to normal again . Tha t is not happening . I t is certainly flat and we will get increasing vehicle technology.

On the pace car point, we recommended to the Welsh Government that if all the public fleet—there are millions of vehicles run by the public sector—were retrofitted with ISA and acted as pace cars , we could also get the public themselves to opt in and become pace car drivers. We do not need every vehicle to obey the speed limit to influence the majority of the traffic flow. We can do a lot.

Interestingly , o n the point about pluralistic ignorance, there was that concern. The re was a view that this was tremendously unpopular. Actually, a silent majority in Wales support ed this, but we had this very loud minority. There was reluctance on the part of public authorities to take those steps , because of the fear of backlash. The point about having leadership to show the need for this is hugely important. Whether it is an immediate law change, as wa s done in Wales, or a policy change that sets a very clear sense of direction, that is what is needed , and local authorities will be given support to make the changes.

Q170 On the attitude point, the big criticism of the 20 mph scheme in Edinburgh is that it has reduced average speeds by less than 2 mph, but it has also reduced the speeds of the fastest vehicles. I guess that on the attitude point maybe the counter-argument is: why bother reducing speed limits? Should we not just be educating drivers to stick to the existing speed limit?
Because you cannot achieve that through education.
You have to reduce limits —

Would you rather be hit by a car doing 29 mph in a 30 mph area or a car doing 25 mph in a 20 mph area? It is about speed, not compliance. Compliance with the wrong speed limit is no success, which is the point I made. The indicator in the road safety strategy that it is going to measure speed compliance is in my view the wrong measure , unless we have the right speed limits to begin with.
Q171 There is no hope of changing attitudes , then .
No, I am saying the exact opposite. I think there is huge hope for change.
But you would do it via changing speed limits . That is how we change attitudes .

It is one way. The two go hand in hand. We need to change public attitudes. If we demonstrate to politicians that there is a silent majority in favour of this, they will make the right choices , because of the pluralistic ignorance point that Rob made.

Recruit the expertise of the behavioural scientists to get them to understand and map out what the current attitude is, because we do not know. I do not think that work has been done. You get windows into it. Once you know where the starting point is , you can launch campaigns and educational awareness , try to change it and understand which identities people are relating to that are keeping them in unsafe decision-making modes . I t is about doing both.

C ompliance is really important . We have a technological, behavioural and social system of road use, do n’t we? It is roads, vehicles and people. If the message we are giving is that we are setting speed limits, but we are not really going to take them seriously and it does not really matter whether you comply, we totally lose control of the whole system. It is the predominant factor that can change this.

You mentioned V ision Z ero. We could have zero tolerance for excess speeding . Zero tolerance for breaking the speed limit would be a start , and for speeding in inappropriate conditions would be more complicated but desirable . But zero tolerance for wilful choice in exceeding the speed limit would be a brilliant start, and it is doable. There is technology out there and data in vehicles that measure how fast they are going and know what the speed limits on the roads are. It may be seen as unpopular and there may be hesitancy from a popularity and support point of view, but if you have road safety literacy and consistent messaging, understanding and awareness and people saw, underst oo d or realise d how the impact of their choice s to go a bit faster or closer massively increases the risk of serious injury and death, they would choose otherwise. It is both — it is all these components acting together. The big missing component at the moment is public awareness and attitudes , and focusing on that to gain support for everything else we are talking about.
Q172 In your evidence you said that drivers do not always understand the impact of relatively small increases in speed.

I do not think they do and I do not think policymakers do. That is partly what that paper and others referred to as well. It is intuitive to all of us that if someone speeds massively there is massively increased risk. You need a broader understanding of systems and whole-system s behaviour and risk levels to appreciate it.

It has been understood only fairly recently , in the past few years , that a greater number of people going a little bit too fast across our network massively increases the risks to everyone in a way that is probably more significant than the few who are exceptionally speeding. Part of it is the number of interactions , because there are so many more vehicles on the road , they are driving much closer together and people are behaving in slightly different ways. The net effect across the system of small changes in averages is really impactful in reducing injuries and deaths. You have to focus on the excessive speeds as well — d on ’ t get me wrong : t hey are disproportionately high — but it is a much smaller number of interactions than people who habitually choose to go a bit faster.

I am not saying that compliance is not important. I am saying do not start by measuring compliance , because if you are m easuring it with the wrong speed limits , you may get the wrong measure of success. I am not saying that 25 mph in a 20 mph area is acceptable, but let us set the speed limit s first and then achieve compliance later in the long term, whether it is through technology, greater enforcement or whatever.

I want to pick up what Rob said about public attitudes. What we recommended in the Welsh taskforce was that before the Welsh Government brought in the legislation to change the default speed limit, they would carry out what was called a national conversation with the Welsh population about what residential roads and streets were for. The expectation was—
We will come to Wales later, won’t we?
We are going to come on to Wales. I also have a question o n behaviour .

My point is that they did not do that. That understanding of the motivation of people speeding and their attitudes to speed was exactly what was recommended, as Rob said, by university behavioural scientists, but it was not done.

Q173 We talked about the more carrot side and the behaviour side. Obviously, in outer London , where I am , there are lots of 20 mph residential roads. What I do not see is much enforcement. Am I right that there is not much enforcement? If so, why is that? I have been caught doing 24 mph in a 20 mph area. You see an awful lot of people clearly proceeding on the basis of , “I know there ’ s no speed camera and I ’ ve always driven at 30 + mph, so I w on’t slow down here now.” I know why the roads have been designated as 20 mph, but that is because I live and breathe this stuff, but where does enforcement fit into the 20 mph element?

I will pick up the position in London, but it would be the same everywhere. It is really important from an educational point of view. We do have a lot of marketing and communications that make that critical point—“I didn’t know I was going a bit too fast , ” and that that can have devastating outcomes.

We work with the M etropolitan police who enforce in 20 mph areas. London is a very big place with around 27 million journeys taking place every day. One objective they took on in the last Vision Zero action plan was greatly to increase the number of enforcement notices issued each year. That increased from around 150,000 or 200,000 to over 800,000 notices of prosecution. Those are not just on high-speed roads; they include 20 mph roads. We have also now remodelled and changed the deployment of the roads policing force in London with the road danger team , which will be much more mobile and will be moving around . That will create more of a presence that hopefully you will see and feel.
Nevertheless, to go back to the point Phil was making, there is too much speeding in those 20 mph zones.
You can see it .

You can see it , and it really annoys me and local citizens. Th ose are still delivering safety benefits. We know that from the 10-year research we have done , because those results were delivered with the current deployment and less enforcement happening , j ust because you bring down average speeds. I want people to drive at the speed limit or less, so that would really get me towards my V ision Z ero goal. That is why we will continue to work really hard with the Met police on this, but it is also about technologies such as speed limiters. We will come later, hopefully, to much greater access to new camera technology , which is being blocked through the Home Office - type approval system. We need to be able to use that much more intelligently and unlock the power of enforcement.
It would be good if you could give a breakdown of those tickets for speeding to see what proportion arise in 20 mph zones.
We absolutely can do that.

Q174 That would be really good . Just for a bit more detail, i f I live in London on a street with a 20 mph limit and the average speed is way above that, how do you react to that? Do you just phone up the police and hope they will enforce, or do you come along and think about installing physical measures on the street?
It depends on which highway authority it is. Ninety-five per cent of the roads in London are owned and managed by the local borough.
Apologies, okay.

No, don’t worry. The main roads are Transport for London. This is what local communities do every day. Probably the biggest postbag of a ward councillor is about speeding and road danger concerns . They will work with the local polic ing forces . The new road danger reduction team , in terms of their deployment, can go in and do mobile camera enforcement, for example, on your road, if that were the case. If there is a need for physical changes, the local borough can introduce them or maybe do mobile deployment. There is a range of measures , but obviously it is very seldom that you will have an impact road by road; you need to think about it across the whole borough . B ut sanctions do apply and people do get speeding notices.
It would be good to see that data.
We will send that.

T o add o n the data for enforcement, 20’s Plenty for Us has made a freedom of information request to all police forces in Great Britain over the past three or four years. The level of enforcement of different speed limits does not relate to the risk in those speed limits. It is highly variable.
Q175 Lilli was saying that in London they are being more nuanced about where they plac e enforcement based on risk .
London is showing us the way. There are other forces. If you go to Avon and Somerset, they are good about this stuff . Ot her forces are not relating the enforcement to the risk.
There is a clear message there.

Can I pick up on the enforcement and policing side of things? Particularly for 20 mph, I do not think we should lean too much on the police and enforcement to expect them to achieve that for us. If we get the messaging and public awareness right, it will drive itself. Police monitoring and enforcement is for occasional transgressors, not the mainstay. We know it is effective . We know that p eople currently have very low perceived risk of being caught and the penalties do not reflect the risks.

At the moment , the ACPO recommendation for speeding in 30 mph areas—I will relate to 30 mph—is that enforcement does not kick in until 35 mph. The risk of 35 mph rather than 30 mph is an increase in fatalities of 90% and an increase in severe injuries of 62%. The penalties we see that kick in only at 35 mph do not relate to those. People actually laugh about it and say, “I got sent on an enforcement campaign , ” which is now online, is n’t it? It should be severe points and severe penalties so the negative consequences that people perceive and experience are true inhibitors.
Q176 Are the Government spending enough on the public information messaging that I remember in my youth?
We are not tapping into what is now known by behavioural scientists about behavioural change units.

For me, this is where the strategy is really lacking. There is very little in there about what will be the strategy to increase compliance and reduc e speed s. It could be about greater resources for police enforcement . I t could be about local authorities being given powers to enforce speed limits , which ha s been proposed in London. It could be about community policing systems . I t could be about pace cars and a stronger commitment to ISA. B ut it is really silent . What are we going to do to increase compliance? That should be an absolute focus of the strategy, but it is silent on that at the moment . I t does not really talk about that at all.

I have an anecdote. I us ed a L ime bike to get here today. I was zipping along at 15 mph on a main road and then I went off on to the E mbankment where there are lots of residential properties , and I could not do more than 6 mph or 7 mph. Then I g o t back on the main road and could do 15 mph. That is great using bikes . We can do that with cars. The technology is not the problem. We could do that now. It is about education.
Along would come someone saying you are restricting their freedoms, but never mind — that is the world we live in these days.
But it is freedom to harm other people.
Exactly.
Going back decades, I have an image in my mind of a TV advert put out by the Government around a child in a car. It is really our fault.

They are completely absent. The public information film has disappeared. We just do not see them any more . There is a huge role for G overnment here to increase people’s understanding of the reality.

Q177 T o ask another slightly leading question, should we be do ing 20 mph at scale ? O r should we just do it where we know there have been accidents, or perhaps outside schools and things like that? Why not focus on outside schools and where there are accidents?

It is as if children exist only at school. Rod King put this really well : w e do not see children in the public domain any more . We just don’t see them. The only time adults see children is at the start and end of school time s . We think that is the only place where they exist so that is wh ere you need 20 mph. That view is really unfortunate and it speaks to the loss of children’s independence. I will leave Adrian to comment, but f or me there is absolute evidence that a wide area of 20 mph is cheaper, more effective and more understandable.
Does the evidence show that?
Yes, absolutely.

I agree with Phil , as you would expect, but our analysis is that at least 80% of child casualties do not occur outside school gates. Everybody agrees that you should have 25 mph around schools — I do not think there is anyone in this room who does not say that — but that is not where the casualties are. They are in every other walk of life for children. Interestingly, the target for children reduced KSIs is 70%, not 65%, and something like 80% of those occur in urban areas. So if you are going to reach 70% , 20 mph is even more important for that particular target .

To add something as a highway authority, it is much cheaper and more efficient to introduce it on an area basis, in that you r obliga tion is to indicate very clearly to the driver that they are entering that zone, but if you are doing it street by street you literally have to change the signs at the end of every single street and the cost is prohibitive and not effective.

It is also confusing for drivers : I am driving down one street a nd i t is 30 mph ; I driv e down the next street and it is 20 mph ; I driv e down the next street and it goes from a 20 mph limit to a 20 mph zone, so there is a big sign saying , “End of 20 mph . ” But i t is still 20 mph. It ’ s a complete mess . Y ou have to do it by area . If you look at any town in England, Wales or Scotland , draw a kilometre radius around every school and say, “We’re going to have 20 mph for a kilometre around every school , ” that would be the whole town. You then say, “We will do the whole town and set the gateways, but that road has protected cycleways and there are not many pedestrians or cyclists, so we can raise it to 30 mph.”

Q178 I was going to come to signage later, but let me ask about it now. Living in and representing an outer London borough area, one of the most confusing things to drivers — asking for a friend, constituents and fellow London MPs — is the clutter. Seeing the signage, apparently 20 mph painted on the road is not a statutory requirement. The repeater signs are, yet as a driver the painting on the road is much clearer because it does not get messed up with the clutter. You can miss a repeater sign because there is a van in the way or a bush is overgrown. To me, how clear the signage is should be a factor, but there is also the disjoint. In Windmill Lane go ing up from Syon Lane towards Three Bridges it is 30 mph, 40 mph, 30 mph, 40 mph, or the other way round. The A4 going through the borough of Hounslow is 40 mph, 30 mph, 40 mph. That is a TfL road ; Windmill Lane is an Ealing and Hounslow road . What can be done to make life consistent for drivers, even within a single local authority area? We will come on to different local authority areas later.

You articulated the problem brilliantly. Some of this is because highway authorities are required under the manual for street design to use signage in that way. The Government have committed to revising that guidance and it is a brilliant opportunity to streamline it and make it much simpler. We would welcome that and could bring your experience and that of others to do so .

Our experience is that a more consistent driving experience will improve that goal of compliance, which is what we are seeking to do. Our road network is not perfect and we have committed to reviewing speed limits and to bring them down on strategic roads where appropriate , so you get that more consistent experience. It also goes back to the original point about having default policies because of people’s expectations. If we knew that residential roads were 20 mph by default, unless they were signed differently, you would not have to have all the clutter to tell you that . I t is something you know because you are taught it. That is my point of view. I think there is an opportunity with the revision of national guidance to streamline this .
Meanwhile, will TfL look at the required speed limits on the A roads in London?

Yes, we are. The Vision Zero action plan definitely commits to doing that: both extending 20 mph by around a further 65 k m and reviewing the speed limits on the other strategic roads to make sure they are consistent .
Because they are coming from 40 mph down to 30 mph.
They will not all do that, but there is an intention—
There are inconsistencies on the same stretch of road, which people see as just a money spinner for TfL or the council.
To be really clear , none of the speed enforcement money in London or elsewhere goes to the local authority.
We know that. It is the political pushback that we get.

On the consistency point, there was a big backlash in Wales. We know that and we can explore the reasons. Much of that came from the inconsistencies. A big area of concern for drivers was that change from 20 mph to 30 mph to 20 mph to 30 mph. There is a real benefit to consistency as well as, as Lilli said, cost-effectiveness. On the roundels point, certainly our understanding is that a roundel — a painting on the road — is perfectly legal as an alternative.
It is not illegal, but it is not a statutory requirement.
As an alternative to the upright sign —t hat is our understanding. The two are equated. I agree with you. A painted roundel is very hard for a driver to miss. It is much more effective.

To go back to the questions from Scott, I thought I would leave you with this lovely quote. I was at a road safety conference recently in Birmingham. Modeshift STARS work with schools to encourage more children to walk and cycle , and t hey have set up active travel ambassadors for schools and young people. There was a young girl on the stage and she said , “ We can’t have a childhood that you can’t walk through,” which I thought was quite profound. We have to have a childhood that we can walk through. In other words, “W e have to have an environment that we can experience. We can ’ t be in our bedrooms on screens .” This is about much more than areas a round schools . This is about an urban environment that children feel able to be in and in which to have an element of independence. We have seen the loss of children’s independence. We must not ignore the benefits of lower speed limits, not just in terms of road safety but in the way in which people, young people particularly, can live their lives.

To your point about street clutter, in terms of speed limit signing, this comes because we are setting national speed limits that are too high, and then you have to tell drivers you can only do a lower speed than that. If the national speed limits were lower but you could go faster on certain roads, you would not need a sign, would you?
We are coming on to who sets speed limits.

Q179 You have all been very clear on the advantages you see in 20 mph speed limits and the benefits that they bring. Given that very clear evidence , and that most of the road safety and road design experts are of a similar view , why is there such a culture war? Why is there this resistance?

It is change management. We have got used to 30 mph as the limit, and that has been with us for 100 years or so. Whenever you change, people are going to get uncomfortable. “Oh, why do we need to change? I haven’t been involved in a crash, and I’ve been quite happily driving at 30 mph.” It is just about getting used to it. We saw the petition in Wales. At the point of the change, over 400,000 people signed this. By the way, that was before many of the signs were in place, but leave that aside. There was an identical petition two years later, and it attracted 2,378 signatures. It was less than—sorry, I can’t even do the maths. It was a tiny number of signatures. Of course o n social media it is still there, but people just get used to it.

There is some truth in that. I come back to question the level of resistance. The fact that there are groups that are loudly opposing or resistant to this change does not mean that the majority are not in support. The surveys that the RAC and similar bodies do tell us that people want reductions in speed limits and safer roads. There are 1,600 people killed on our roads, 29,000 seriously injured every year, 134,000 involved in other injuries, and a potential saving to the economy of £54 billion. Is that not reason enough to make people more aware of the real costs of this and the benefits of increased safety, and whether it is popular or not to do the right thing to prevent that harm and those deaths? Allowing it to continue is within our decision making: what are the policies and legislation and how we align things to that reality.

Q180 I completely agree with that. Of course, we should have policy that should be trying to do the right thing, but there is this tension. I am speaking in general, not just on this. There is that tension of people in democratic politics about how you strike the right balance between doing the right thing and then also not doing the thing that is going to get you booted out of office, or the thing that you think might get you booted out of office. That is why this whole public engagement and bringing people with us thing is important.

And it is important to depoliticise it. Give this decision making to a body like the RSIB. Make it cross-party , independent of politics or whichever Government happen to be in at the time. Give it the authority to review the evidence, what is already known and recommend actions and interventions that are going to save lives. There are barriers to this within the driving public and their decision making and within legislation and policymakers, and we need to understand that. What are the barriers? What are the opportunities? What are the enablers? Let us get everything lined up and achieve a reduction in death s and serious injur ies .

If you look at London boroughs that very recently will have introduced this, there are local politicians who are taking it on the chin and being very brave in introducing it. There is always a lot of local discussion. It has been most successfully framed when the limit is not what is so important but it is actually about what you want to do with your streets, and when it is married with creating safe routes to school, reformatting the high street, making the environment look nicer for people walking and cycling, or for older people to access shops. These are real, tangible benefits that people do not want to lose once they have them. There are lots of bits of communities that have been remodelled along this. We have seen in local elections that people have secured greater public support in the wake of doing this, and there is quite a lot of evidence of that. Being really clear on the benefits and what you are trying to achieve with it is absolutely critical , and you can see that rolling out. The point of the national strategy is that it creates that really helpful strategic steer at national level to say this is important and something that we are behind local authorities doing.

A clearer strategy and technical guidance also enables officers. I know in some authorities you have pro-20 mph members, but officers may say to those members, “Yes, but of course if we follow the Government’s current guidance you can’t have 20 mph.” We will perhaps come on to this, but there is the “Catch-24”, which I will steal from Adrian. If speeds are above 24 mph, you cannot have 20 mph, which is a completely perverse position that we have in current national guidance. That certainly needs to be swept away urgently. That is holding back a lot of authorities where officers are strictly following the current Government guidance even in the face of elected members who want to bring in 20 mph. That is a real problem. We have to do something about that.

Q181 I have one more question on this , and I would ideally like a couple of short sentence answers from each of you so that we can move on. A lot of the anti-20 mph rhetoric that one sees is that 20 mph limits increase journey times, increase congestion and have a wider economic cost. Is that supported by evidence?
No.
No, because most delay in London is incurred at the junctions, not on the road network .

You get more consistent, reliable, predictable travel times, which is of more benefit than the small reductions in some journeys, and you avoid the disruption when there is an incident and the delays and all that side of things. Commercially and individually it is positive.

In preparation, I looked at the latest monitoring data of Transport for Wales up to March 2025, and it is showing for a whole range of journeys increasing journey time of no more than about two minutes on average, really small increases in journey times, and, as you said, Rob, an increase in journey time consistency so that you know your journey ; all you have to do is leave another two minutes earlier and you will be there. In terms of the economic effect, there is lots of research. If you multiply millions of journeys by two minutes by the value of time that transport economics uses, you get a very big number. The reality is that makes no difference at all.
You have to take off the saving of the consistency and the lack of disruption from getting in a big tailback because there has been a big incident.
Reducing the speed limit on the M25 actually increased the capacity of the M25.

Indeed. The net economic benefits of this are massive. We have a calculator that shows to each local authority how much it would cost to implement this and what the economic benefits would be . T he payback is never more than six months, and it is often one or two months.

Q182 While we are on the subject of economic payback, we are going to come on to the concerns raised by a Conservative Member of the Senedd , who sa id that the Welsh Government’s own figures stated it will cost the Welsh economy about £8 billion. Where did she get that from?

That is exactly what I was saying. If you take small slivers of time like two minutes over 60 years and over millions of journeys , times the value of time that transport economists use, you get a very big number. That is not a real—
It has not taken into account the other costs.
No. Regardless of that, it is not a real figure.
I see.
It is not real money. In theory, what would you pay to get to your destination two minutes earlier? You put a number to that—50p.
I see.
There is lots of academic research. People cannot use that two minutes. They get there and they sit down and watch “N eighbours ” for two more minutes.
It is the same as the old-fashioned WebTAG .
Exactly right. It is just WebTAG . It is nothing to do with the economy.
Q183 That is , I guess, the consequence of the change. In terms of the benefits, does the same analysis put a monetary value on a life saved?

Of course, yes. In my view, those are much more tied to the real costs of the economy like the health service. It really costs money to patch people up. It really costs money to send out investigators and to clean up the road . These are real costs , regardless of the human suffering that is caused. The value of time savings, in my view, is entirely illusory. The Welsh Government’s impact assessment that came up with that figure quoted academic research to say it does not really matter, but of course people ignore that and they just focus on the £8 billion.

Even if you believed it, a full business case would absolutely take on board the quantified value of lives saved plus the additional potential public health benefits and lives saved through enabling more journeys to be made actively. When we do a full business case, we will look at all these costs in the round. As Adrian said, there is a very strong business case and very strong cost - benefit assessment for 20 mph.

It is not just to the authorities; it is to the individual driver, because they use less fuel and their insurance costs come down. I do not think that has come across to people. “ Oh, i f I had 20 mph in my area and everybody was driving a bit slower, my insurance would be £50 a year less. ” I think I might buy that.
The insurance thing is the real sell, actually . It has not been made enough of.
Yes , I have only just learned about that. I didn ’ t know. I will have to tell him indoors as he is in charge of insurance .
Q184 Should England follow Wales and move towards a 20 mph zone as a national default speed limit on roads?

First, let us get away from the word “zone”. The 20 mph zones are hopelessly confusing. We need to get rid of 20 mph zones. They are a nonsense. In Wales now , there are no 20 mph zones. They are not lawful in Wales. The idea of a special little zone and everything else is 30 mph is —
Getting over the border is problematic.

It is n ot even that. Even in England, the days of the 20 mph zone have gone. Let us just treat 20 mph as a speed limit. Should England do what Wales did? Ideally, I would say yes. It was extremely effective. Will it do it politically? I do not know. It was interesting that Scotland was minded to make the same legislative change that Wales did , took fright politically and decided not to do it. What Scotland now has is a much firmer policy default: 20 mph is the norm and town by town we will implement this. That is where England certainly should go to. I would like it if England did what Wales did but , realistically, it may just be too much of a political ask at the moment , it’s sad to say.
Can’t we do it, but do it better? Do it with that awareness and public campaign beforehand so that you have support and achieve all the benefits.

Indeed. I alluded earlier that the intention was that the Welsh Government would roll the pitch, carry out that engagement with the public and almost gain consent of the public to bring in the legislative change, but they did not do that partly because of covid and partly because of budgets or whatever. They only began to engage with the public once they had taken the decision and then were informing the public about the change rather than gaining their consent. England could perhaps do that. We do not talk enough about Northern Ireland , which recently consulted on changes to its speed limit guidance, and I am hopeful that that will also move. The Republic of Ireland also has a default policy of 30 mph.
The Republic of Ireland has default 30 mph—
In urban areas. It has defined urban areas in legislat i on.
That is what we have in England.
Is that not in kilometres per hour?
Sorry — kilometres. I t i s 30 kph , which is 19 mph. Very soon, England will be the only nation in the British Isles that does not have a policy default of 20 mph, or 30 kph, in urban areas.

20’s Plenty for Us was set up to advocate for a 20 mph national speed limit actually across the UK. We were clearly delighted with what Wales has done. One of the reasons why Wales had to go down that legislative route was that there were very few 20 mph places in Wales already. In Scotland and England, you have many more areas of 20 mph. Sixty-eight out of 154 local authorities in England are already committed to 20 mph. We have already made huge progress. You could argue that a national legislative default would therefore be easier because a lot of people are already doing it. You could also say we are setting a national value of 20 mph, an expectation that it is going to be 20 mph, and assume that everywhere , and let local authorities exempt out without changing the legislation. You could get almost the same effect. It might be a bit more expensive, but it might be a bit easier.
And it might take longer.
It might take a bit longer.
That is what will happen. That is the price to be paid.

We have extrapolated the Welsh results to England, and our calculation is nine fewer KSIs. There are nine more KSIs per day in England because we have 30 mph rather than 20 mph. There are nine people being seriously injured or dying today, tomorrow and every day until we make the change. Speed is of the essence in this context.

Q185 W e have talked about Wales a bit. I am an even more out-of-London MP than you, Chair. M y borough, Bexley, does not have many 20 mph zones, and if you go on Facebook groups, you will see they say, “Don’t go to Lewisham. It’s terrible. It’s all 20 mph.” How do we learn from Wales—you touched on this a little bit—in terms of communication and engagement if we were going to spread that across England?
We learn how not to do it.
What lessons would we learn in terms of communication and engagement?

We learn how not to do it. It had a very strong politician who carried it through and is no longer a Member of the Senedd. He took the political hit and was willing to do so. Not all politicians are like that. There needs to be much more engagement to gain the demonstrable consent of the silent majority so that politicians can say in the face of the vociferous opposition that will come, “We ’ re doing this for these people. W e’ re holding up a mirror to society, and this is what people want.” We are very confident that if you do representative surveys and proper market research that is balanced across the community of every age, every gender, disability and ethnicity , you will get probably about a two-thirds majority in favour of 20 mph. You do that before you then make the change. You do that change, and w hen the loud voices come, you can say, “Yes, but you are the minority. Look, w e know that you are the minority. We are doing this on behalf of the silent majority.”

What you will find will strengthen every politician who then has to implement this. There are two things. One, if it is a policy default, you have to argue why you are not doing it as opposed to why you should. In many of our outer London conversations, that would change the balance quite significantly, because the evidence is so clear now. You are literally having to argue why it is acceptable that your children and citizens on your streets are more at risk than they should be.

It is not just that. You mentioned earlier selling and promoting all the other benefits to communities and linking it to other agendas, particularly the physical health and mental health of the whole community and nation. There is really something in that. That is a really positive approach to it.

Can I give you some examples of what 20’s Plenty for Us has experienced in Kent? First, it is worth saying that KCC did a study a few years ago in which it did representative market research and found that across all the districts in Kent between 60% and 80% of people were supportive of 20 mph, and that helped to change the policy. The KCC policy is not perfect, but it has gone as far as it can within the existing guidance.

At the time of covid i t introduced two 20 mph places, one in Tonbridge and one in Faversham. The level of opposition in both places was about the same. The difference was that in Faversham there was a huge amount of support, which there was not in Tonbridge, and that was simply because of much better engagement at a local level. In fact, 20 mph has gone into both places, and it has been just as successful in both and it is accepted and so on. That level of pre-engagement is really important . I think I am right in saying that , when 20’s Plenty for Us was part of the initial thought process in Wales , there was a recommendation that 10% of the budget should be on marketing , advertising and PR. If you look at places like Cornwall, the marketing and PR around lower speeds , particularly 20 mph , is really good . There are lots of examples around the country as to how we can do this better.

Q186 On m arketing and PR , y ou mentioned the covid regulations and funding that are no more. There is a local example to me where there had been prior concerns about rat running and speeding in a residential area. The covid regulations and funding were used to do what had not been possible before. An election switch ed on that basis and i t turned out that people quite liked it once it was in. Is there some justification for looking at the way regulations can be done on a temporary basis in areas where there is already a certain amount of popular ask? Have we gone back to experimenting with overly restrictive regulations?
This is a little technical point.
I am thinking of low-traffic neighbourhoods.

Yes, but it applies to speed limits, too. We were involved in the Faversham scheme that Adrian mentioned. Kent County Council during covid introduced a whole town 20 mph limit using an experimental traffic regulation order. It monitored that and it was popular, and then it made tha t permanent. Some traffic engineers and highway engineers point to very arcane bits of law and say you cannot use experimental orders for speed limits. Some people think you can. Some people think you cannot. There is a difference of view among traffic engineers.
We are Parliament , so w e make the laws.

I see no reason why you could not have experimental speed limits. That w ould be very valuable. You could see how it works and monitor the journey times. That was certainly very powerful in Faversham and then it made it easier. It is done in London. It is done in lots of places. I have heard it said in many cases that you cannot do that. Clarification would be really helpful on that.

Q187 Are experimental schemes part of the solution, then? The general thing people believe is that you make a change that might not be universally popular but after six months they get used to it. The problem with the experimental schemes is that the campaign against schemes can grow because there is a feeling that there is still a hope that it can be changed or reversed. Is it not better to take that traditional approach where w e consult, we have a well-designed scheme, we implement it, we know there are going to be some initial issues, but we get through it ? I am speaking through experience. I have scars on my back.

There is a value in it, but you do not make it a referendum. You say these are our expected outcomes, this is what we think is going to happen, and we monitor against those. We monitor against the evidence, not against people’s opinions. We can do them as long as it is done in a very careful and controlled way.
Don ’ t forget we are trying to get to an outcome. Sometimes what we as highways authorities introduce do es not work. The benefit of having an experimental scheme is that you can make changes.
If t here is a genuine question that you are asking.

Yes. You could get perverse travel outcomes that you did not understand. Experimentation can be extremely powerful, and it also allows an ongoing and more mature dialogue with local communities, so I am very supportive of it. In the low traffic neighbourhood experiment it proved to be very helpful in getting better outcomes. You do not need it universally, but it has its role.
In the Tonbridge example, which was done under the same legislation, we removed small bits of one or two roads from 20 mph and put them back to 30 mph. That was helpful.

Can I step sideways on this a little? I completely agree that local experimentation can inform some things. I would certainly welcome experimental and exceptional legislation and policy because it is a proportionate response to the urgent level of problem that we have. I f the Road Safety Investigation Branch was a national oversight body , not investigating individual collisions but looking at the global background factors, looking at different schemes and seeing what can be brought back and then nationalised and spread out, s urely that w ould be a structural, systematic way of approaching this problem. The RSIB is absolutely key .
That has come up in other sessions.
Q188 The only other thing on Wales I want to ask is about the effectiveness of the policy where some roads moved from 20 mph back to 30 mph. I know we have touched on that.

It is very few. Some of the press would have you believe that there was a wholesale reversion. It was really very small. We use the term “exceptions”. There is the default 20 mph, but you could set exceptions where you saved a 30 mph , as it were . The authority with the greatest number of exceptions in south Wales was Blaenau Gwent: 10% of its network was saved at 30 mph. Wrexham had the fewest, about 2% of the network. Interestingly, Wrexham is the authority that has probably put the most roads back to 30 mph. It is still levelling up—about 50 roads. Across the 22 local authorities in Wales, the majority have done five or 10 roads. Some have done none at all . It has really been a quiet tinkering. There has been a little bit of reversion, but really very small and much less than what you hear in some of the press.

That should not be interpreted as failure, should it? All those areas where it has been introduced will have been safer for that period where those lower speeds were achieved. If we then find that there are other reasons we want to de-restrict them a bit, that is fine. At the moment , we need to accept that we need to move things to saving people and injuries, and then where we can in a structured, systematic way release restrictions where that is possible without increasing risk disproportionately.
Some people say Wales is a failure because of all the controversy and so on, but it is a massive success. It is absolutely a massive success.
In s aving people and injuries.
Right, okay.

On the Wrexham point, they moved 55 roads back to 30 mph. Quite a lot of those should have already been accepted in the first round. That is the point of getting the design right , so you know which road you are going to except when you change the majority of roads to 20 mph. That is where the local information comes.
With exceptions and being clear about why the exceptions are there.

Q189 I need to go shortly, but I will talk about the greatest part of the world first — of course , that ’ s London. Lilli, can you talk to us about the roll-out of 20 mph zones in London and the greatest challenges you have faced?

Again, they are not zones, they are limits. The local boroughs in London pioneered this, and then TfL came along. There were already 20 mph limits in large parts of London , right back in the late 1980s. This has been an early adopted policy. When we looked at our evidence, we were looking right back to that period up into current times.

With the introduction of 20 mph on all the strategic roads in central London from 2020 on and then Westminster going to a 20 mph speed limit, we now have all of central London and all of inner London being 20 mph as well. There are 11 boroughs in London out of the 33 that do not have at least 75% of their roads being 20 mph. That is generally aligned with political alliance. It tends to be more of the Conservative boroughs that do not have 20 mph, and that goes back to the conversations we have about the perceptions and attitudes in local areas to these kinds of measures. Many of them are working with us, and we are providing evidence as to how they might take forward those measures. There will be change in coming years to make sure that we continue to see the benefits. That is why we have talked about having a stronger national policy on this that really makes it clear that local politicians are making decisions within a context and against an evidence base now that is unequivocal: reducing speed limits on residential roads will save lives.

As highway authorities, you also have a duty to improve road safety. As a public servant, you have that duty. That needs to be brought out and made much clearer. If you can reduce risk, you should be reducing risk on your roads, and we now have the measures that we know can make it happen. As Transport for London, the other thing we do is to fund the local boroughs through their transport. We fund the local boroughs’ transport plans so that money can be made available for 20 mph limits to be introduced.

On th e duty Lilli referred to, t here are very few duties that high way authorities have. They have a lot of powers, but they do not have so many duties. Reducing casualties is one of them, and perhaps it is time that that was given greater emphasis by G overnment.

Q190 You said earlier there are 11 boroughs in London that do not have 20 mph limits, and in the main they are going to be the outer boroughs — boroughs like mine, of course. The last 20 mph area in my borough was introduced about 22 years ago. I was the c abinet member. It was a long time ago. Since then, the world has changed. We have social media. We have disinformation. I am sure like me, Chair, you went through the experience of ULEZ and what that did in outer London boroughs. What would we learn from that experience ? It was full of different levels of information — let ’ s put it that way — in a social media context , to the extent that i n my borough there was a terrorist incident over it , as you may well know . What would we learn from that if we were then looking at trying to persuade a further roll - out in some of those areas?

We have already gone over some of the key lessons for success. With ULEZ, we got there. If we reflect, maybe we could have done more on the pre-communication as to why those measures were needed to bring communities with us. There are very high levels of compliance now and it is delivering enormous benefits to air quality in London. Looking in the rearview mirror, it is much easier to justify it.

With speed, we are now in a really good position that we have such good evidence from London. We need to help and support, and we are doing this now post the local elections in London to provide that evidence to all local councillors and say, “This is what works. This is how you can discuss it with your local communities.” The demand is there. With ULEZ too , even though there was a very vocal campaign, that was not the majority. That was a minority that made their voices very loud. We know that most people comply, because we have about 90% compliance levels with ULEZ. We can have similar impacts with speed as well. It is really making sure of that voice and campaign , and knowing that that evidence is there to support local politicians in taking those measures forward.

This goes way beyond 20 mph. It is about e quipping local politicians to understand the backlash that will come, and perhaps making those politicians who have been through difficult experiences understand that it is not representative. Perhaps what they need to do is log off Facebook and stop looking at it, because it is not the truth. It is a distortion of reality. It is disinformation.
You have to ask the same people if they want to reopen a closed - off cul-de-sac that was done 40 years ago . T hey go, “Oh, no, we wouldn’t want that.”
