Speed limits do not go back up. That is the lesson that we can all take away. A part from one or two trimmings on experimental ones , as a rule of thumb, they do not go back up once they have come down and people have got used to it.

If you set the national assumption at 20 mph, whether you do it legislatively or by values and encouragement, and then have the local authority justify where and how they can move it to 30 mph, you get a completely different question. It is a completely different discussion.

Q191 I have one last question. We politicians spend too much time looking on social media. The challenge always is how you convince Mrs Jones, because it is Mrs Jones when she sees you at the bus stop who gets convinced by what she is reading. The experience, as I am sure you know, Chair, was that the level of information out there was wild, quite frankly. There has been a lot of discussion about 20 mph limits. Are there other speed limit interventions that could produce equally beneficial effects?

Monitoring and the use of technology. Many modern vehicles integrate computers that monitor and can record speeds and all sorts of other parameters, and we are not systematically having access to those as part of our monitoring and enforcement structure.
Alex has some questions on new technology. Anyone else?

The biggest one for me is 60 mph on inter - urban single-carriageway roads. It is far too high. We know that head-on collisions, which is what you get a lot, and run-off incidents on single-carriageway roads are not survivable with a combined head-on speed of 120 mph. So I think w e have to do that. Scotland was considering reducing its rural speed limit again. It has kind of gone by the wayside. For me, t hat is the other one that we really should focus on.

Surrey county council is doing some very interesting work on reducing its rural speed limit, but again it is constrained by the guidance. If the guidance were a bit more liberal, it would have been able to go even further.

Q192 Before I go, on London and the boundary issues, like your example, Chair, I can think of one on the Bexley and Dartford boundary where you go from 70 mph to 50 mph to 40 mph to 30 mph to 20 mph back to 30 mph within two miles. How do you see that working from a London perspective? How do we work some of that out under the current rules on the cross-boundary issues?
I am not quite sure how to answer that question.
All that is because the initial speed limit is too high, so you are having to justify the lower speed. I can justify it there, but I cannot do it there. Oh I can do it there. Start lower and go up.
It is also to do with regs and boundaries, which we are going to come on to in terms of who is responsible.

Q193 Adrian, the written evidence from 20’s Plenty for Us argued that the strategy is “ informed ” by safe system principles but not truly aligned with those principles. Can you tell us what you mean by that?

Yes . T he human body could probably not survive an impact at 30 mph , y et i n theme 3 there is a picture of a “ T hank you” sign for somebody going 27 mph on what is clearly a residential street. It needs to say it is 20 mph unless you can justify a higher speed limit. That is the nub of it.

I do not know whether anyone has introduced i t in evidence so far, but has the Committee heard of the Stockholm d eclaration of 2020 , from the t hird Global Ministerial Conference on Road Safety ? Article 11 of that underpinned the Welsh guidance on setting exceptions . It says to set in Europe a 30 kph speed limit wherever “ vulnerable road users and vehicles mix in a frequent … manner ” . That is absolutely core to the safe system s principle when it comes to applying to speed. That is missing from the strategy and i t would be very helpful if that was in the re , and then that could carry through into the guidance. It is a fundamental principle that underpins all the evidence. It goes back to Rob’s point about the survivability of the human body, basically.

I agree with those points. I would like to make a point about the safe system as a whole and s omething that we do not capture between our organisations and the population. For a system to work, we need to have a really mature understanding and embedding of all its components in a balanced fashion according to a weighting of how they influence the injuries and deaths that occur, and that is rarely done.

Often, we will relate that we have a safe system because we are thinking about the independent components, but until you marry them up and they are singing in harmony the whole system is not as effective. If you put too much emphasis on some components at the expense of some other critical ones—I would put driver responsibility, speed and leadership at the top of those—you can put an awful lot of work into those other pillars , and y ou can say, “Yes, we have a safe system ,” but it does not achieve the outcomes you expect because it is not a mature, embedded, deep system.

That parallels something that we have seen across other industries. In medicine, we had it with risk and risk management maturity models. There are matrices that describe this concept that people are aware of safety, they talk about it a little bit, there are a few segments of it that are done, and then it is completely systematically embedded in our systems. Sometimes , this really has power across the outcomes that we are seeing. People are not marrying the whole system up, and therefore the system falls to pieces as far as the effectiveness that we predict.

The re is a danger of not treating it as a system. We really try to take a systemic approach. We will prioritise all our investment decisions by their ability to deliver on reducing the greatest risk, which is how you get that focus. If you do not do that and you just say we have elements of a safe system , you can focus on the really nice to haves and the easy to dos that do not have much impact. You really need to have a systemic approach , which is driving the greatest focus on the greatest change, which is why we have been talking so much and so passionately about speed limits.

Q194 We have covered this to some extent, so you can keep some answers short. Is there a contradiction in the Government’s approach to reducing the number of those killed and seriously injured on our roads , given that speed management is a key lever for achieving this objective but is left to local discretion?

Yes, there is a tension, is n’t there? Is it possible for a national body or national Government to understand the right speed limit on every road and street across the country? There has to be a role for local decision making and local knowledge. We liv e in a world where the Government are probably pushing even further down the devolution role. The idea that we are going to take it completely out of the hands of local authorities to set speed limits on their roads I am not sure is practicable. However, we can set a framework in which those decisions are taken that is much more controlled and accountable.

I mentioned the road safety conference . There was a very impassioned ex-councillor who had just lost his seat in Felixstowe , I think . He had achieved a 20 mph speed limit in the town. It was all ready and set to go. Elections happened, a new individual came in — a new portfolio hold er — and just scrapped the law. There is no consequence on that individual for taking that decision. We are talking about systemic action .

We need to set up a system of checks and balances and accountability. What would the impact be? What would that politician have to do to justify that decision? Let us make it more explicit : “Yes, I will sign this piece of paper and this committee report that says I ’ m going to set the speed limit 10 mph higher than the national guidance sets, and I am signing off that it will cause five more casualties a year. I am putting my name to tha t. ”
There is the ballot box, I suppose.

There is the ballot box, but that is a very weak check and balance. It needs to be much more explicit and much more in black and white accountability. Then the public attitude and those people who care passionately will see the evidence. “What do you mean, y ou signed off this piece of paper in the full knowledge that this is leading to a greater degree of road casualties ?” We can change this. We can keep local decision making, but we need to think about the system and perhaps use things like the local outcomes framework. The Government are setting a local outcomes framework for every local authority to have targets and meet them in terms of KSIs per billion vehicular kilometres. Let us make those metrics front and centre in the decisions that politicians take at local level.

I have two brief points. We have covered a lot of this already, so I will not repeat that. As far as the ballot box is concerned , remove these decisions from popularity contests and concerns about ongoing votes and things. It is about the leadership , co-ordination , the accountability and governance structures we put around it. It can be local or central. As long as we have the correct governance mechanisms and accountability for the outcomes, the deaths and injuries, it does not matter how we do it. There are a number of ways of skinning the same cat.

Q195 Wales as a country is a reasonably large geographical area. The equivalent in terms of square miles in my part of the world would be the whole of the east of England. Y et these decisions are taken by individual local highway authorities. Is there a sense of how big a geography such a decision needs to be taken over for it to be unconfusing to the driver?

Again, t his is a misunderstanding. The Welsh Government did not set the speed limits across Wales. It didn’t do that. It just changed the national default , at this moment in time, from street lights mean ing 30 mph to them now mean ing 20 mph. Local highway authorities across Wales are still completely empowered to change the speed limit on any road in their area. There was no central decision making. That is a fundamental misunderstanding of what happened in Wales. It was simply changing the national default. If they sat on their hands and did nothing, the speed limit would come down to 20 mph. So i t is not quite the same thing.

You mentioned the east of England. A few years ago, Birmingham lobbied the Government for similar powers to Wales to change the default speed limit of street lighting in Birmingham. Street lights in Birmingham would mean 20 mph and in Sandwell they would mean 30 mph. I do not think that is feasible or possible. It could be changed across the whole of England, and we could do that. It was difficult enough for one nation within the United Kingdom to do it. There was talk at the time of European-style signs on the boundaries of “You are now entering this nation” and “In towns and villages we drive like this”. That was not done. It is acceptable at that scale , but I do not think it is feasible to have a region or city where the default speed limit is set without any signs to tell drivers.

Q196 I am keen to understand to what extent road design has an impact on the speed at which drivers use the road. It is worth thinking about existing roads and how good we are at getting new developments and a place where speed is in a good place as well.

Road design is critical to how drivers interpret and use the road , and to the choices that are available to other road users to decide whether they feel safe using it. It was traditionally a bit of a block on the introduction of 20 mph because the police would be hesitant. They would say, “If the road doesn ’ t look and feel like 20 mph” — undefined — “we won’t enforce on it.” Certainly in London , we have moved beyond that conversation. Equally, to elicit the right psychological response from drivers, if you can use the reduced limits to build out sidewalks and to provide more facilities for walking and cycling or even to do more tree planting, you will get a better response in terms of compliance. I do not think of 20 mph as an end in itself . It is really not . It is about creating a healthy street environment that unlocks the kind of activity that we want to see in town centres, and that is economic activity as well as people travelling actively.

The ideal design structure would segregate pedestrians and other road users from vehicles, would it not, and separate vehicles in different directions? Britain does not really lend itself to that geographically.
I don ’ t really like that road design.

There are different opinions, obviously. Road s engineering can be quite critical in hotspots. Where we find that there are recurrent problems, it is understanding what we can do to change the road design to prevent future incidents. In a previous session, it was mentioned that there are 192,000 miles of roads, and the cost and delays in managing all that makes it an impossible task, does it not?

We know how we can design roads that reduce this . There is traditional traffic calming. We are learning that with more subtle, cheaper changes we can make a difference. Traffic engineers historically have assumed a design speed , and thinking through the needs of the motor vehicle have said, “We must engineer the road for drivers to be able to travel at that speed.” If you look at the D esign M anual for R oads and B ridges , it says we should design our urban roads for 60 kph, which is 37 mph, just in case drivers want to go a little bit quicker. We have a problem : t he central tenet of many highway engineers, the DMRB , is sending completely the wrong signal. We need to be much clearer and say , “T he design speed is now 30 kph and we engineer our roads to achieve that. ” That is going to take a long time. There are many low-cost changes you can make in the short term.
Such as?

Narrower traffic lanes. We have a standard traffic lane in this country that is oddly 3.65 metres, which is just a metrication of 12 feet. Many highway engineers believe there is something magic about the 12-f ee t lane. We know from lots of evidence that narrower lanes carry just as much traffic , are much safer and will lead to slower speed. Narrower traffic lanes would be one good thing, and then you could make more space for walking , cycling and all the rest of it. There are e ven things like removing the centre line. They are v ery simple things. If you resurface the road and do not put the centre line back, that will reduce speeds by 1 mph or 2 mph , and it is cheaper. People think it is less safe , but a ctually, no : d rivers react to the environment. If there is no centre line , that does not give them quite that much certainty, and they react by slowing down a little bit. There are lots of little psychological cues.

Making the turns tighter is absolutely critical . You have to turn hard. Sweeping turns are incredibly dangerous. A very high number—I think it is about 50%—of serious injuries in London are people turning into side roads. We are tightening those turns up because it requires you to slow down to make the turn, and you are also more visible. These are not massively expensive design changes.
Q197 Is that in consultation with the fleet managers of large vehicles? Will they still be able to get round the corner?
Yes, you still need to make sure that the road width or the turn is sufficient for that. In terms of heavy goods vehicles or service vehicles, yes.
And b uses, of course.
Yes.

There probably are opportunities wherever a new road scheme or a new road is being built or something is being maintained to ask, “A re we applying what road engineers know will achieve the outcomes we need? ” I do not know the answer to that question, but that is a very valid point .
Q198 Are we getting new roads right?
No. There is a document called Manual for Streets , which some of you will know.
It has been raised by witnesses in previous sessions .

I was involved with the first edition. The new Manual for Streets , which some people call Manual for Streets 3 , has been promised since 2019. It is good to see all these documents like the road safety strategy , Better Connected and a ll these things , and promising the new Manual for Streets . We so desperately need it. We know that. There has been so much learning since the first edition came out.
Some previous witnesses said that it is in contradiction to the current road safety strategy.
Q199 Is there a chance that the new Manual for Streets could lead to better design — to design for lower speed ?

Absolutely. It should be front and centre. I would say this, wouldn’t I? The first Manual for Streets is pretty good when it comes to designing for speed, but we have learnt much more, and we could go further.
Q200 To what extent is fear of traffic among pedestrians, cyclists and other more vulnerable road users influenced by high speeds in cars? What does the evidence say on that?

We do an awful lot of interviews and understanding of behaviour in London of people who potentially would cycle or are walking. Fear of traffic is the main thing. Volume and speed are the main barriers to people walking and cycling. It is particularly the main barrier to allowing children to walk or cycle to school. We know that , when local authorities introduced measures such as low traffic neighbourhoods that either temporarily or permanently remove traffic , you get very large uplifts in people walking and cycling , and in safety outcomes.

It particularly impacts on women, does n’t it? There is evidence of that. Disproportionately, women are more fearful particularly when it comes to cycling. In London , there is probably about a 2:1 ratio of male to female people cycling. If we are going to get the uptake in cycling that is G overnment policy, we have to get more women cycling. We have to do something about the fear of traffic.
That all links into mental health and that agenda as well.

Q201 To come back to the discussion around the previous question, tell me whether I have misunderstood. G iven that that is one of the main barriers, the l ogic would therefore be that you either have to significantly reduce speeds on roads consistently or you have to provide dedicated infrastructure.

Yes and yes. If you are the strategic transport authority of London, it is clear that the roads also have to function for volumes of traffic. Fifty per cent of journeys are made by car in London, and there is an enormous amount of vehicle traffic as well to service the city. In designing streets to make them safer, there is a clear set of guidance and advice that we have developed for our own network and for the boroughs. It helps them identify that , on strategic roads or roads where the volumes of traffic are higher , you physically need to segregate cyclists or pedestrians from moving traffic. On residential roads where speeds can be kept to 20 mph and there are lower traffic volumes, you can mix traffic safely. There is a very clear hierarchy of how you need to manage and physically change the road network depending on speed and volume, and it does not mean that in every case everything needs to be segregated.

Q202 I am going to test the Chair’s patience. For all that Transport for London is quite eager to boast about what it has achieved on this , I gently suggest that compared with comparable Dutch cities there is a long way to go.
There is a long way to go, yes.

As someone who goes across it every day, the traffic light programming at Hyde Park Corner definitely does not seem to support the vast numbers of pedestrians and cyclists who go across. The wait times are unbelievable.

I want to make sure I understood what you said in the previous discussion, Rob, about how hard it would be to change these things in terms of road design or whatever . The Netherlands is more densely populated. Only one of its cities was destroyed in world war two, yet it has been able to do this. It has also provided for road traffic. It has the densest motorway network in Europe. It is not either/or ; it is about the right tool for the job. What policy levers need to be pulled nationally or for devolved Administrations so that we can move further to address the fear of traffic that is the main barrier to walking and cycling uptake?

If we go back to the Government’s road safety strategy, it had lots of good components, but it lack s the commitment to making change , the pace at which those measures need to be introduced and the clarity that they are committed to certain goals such as eliminating death and injury. The Netherlands has been pursuing very positive policies in terms of promoting cycling for a lot longer than we have. You need consistency of policy, you need consistency of investment, and you need very strong policy direction from a national level to support that local direction . T hat will drive through some of the inconsistencies and the sluggishness that you see both in London and elsewhere.
Q203 Do you feel we are getting that clear policy determination from the national level?
The strategy is definitely a step forward, but I would really hope that we see less consultation and more action. We need to move through to delivery.
That is a wonderful note on which to move on to the next question, Chair.
And now to new technologies .
Q204 What role should intelligent speed assistance play in helping drivers to comply with speed limits?

We should embrace the new technologies and particularly things like the absolute limit. It should be physically and technologically impossible for a vehicle to exceed a legal speed limit on the roads. We have the technical capability, we have the infrastructure, and where there are glitches they can be ironed out. That will be a starting point.
Q205 Would it be down to the private sector to do that?

It is required on all new buses in London, and we are retrofitting all our buses ; 3,000 of the 9,000 buses in London have what we call ISA. That is mandatory ISA. You cannot override it. We are a public body, and we are doing it. We also require that in our own vehicle fleet. It could be a national requirement .

Absolutely. The Government are consulting on that, which is great , but we need them to take a step further . Vehicle manufacturers are required to do it for the EU. B ecause Northern Ireland is in the single market, if you hire a car in Northern Ireland it will come with ISA. It is already happening in parts of the UK, but we need to bring it in. It will probably come in with manufacturers, but the Government need to be much more positive about it.

It is not perfect at the moment . My car has it, but I have to choose to turn it on, which I do most of the time. It is not always reliable in detecting the speed limit. There is a credibility problem. It has to go hand in hand with making digital speed limits available so that the in-car systems can read them so that you get that consistency. If it comes in every new vehicle but does not work very well, there will be pushback against it. For me, it has great potential. One of the arguments against lower speed limits is always the enforcement argument. Over time, ISA removes that as a reason not to do it.

That is o nly proper ISA that is absolutely compulsory , mandatory and you cannot override it. At the moment , the ISA that is legislated for, I understand, is not absolutely compulsory , and you can turn it off when it does not absolutely adhere to the speed limits on the road. We ought to be careful about what we are talking about.

Q206 When you have a speedometer in front of you, the middle — the bit you look at as a driver — is around 60 mph, and there are a whole load of speeds that you are obviously not allowed to do on that side. Should that middle point be moved?
That is a really interesting idea.
Sorry, this is not my specialist subject, but it is completely bizarre that any car is allowed to be sold that can do more than 70 mph. Tha t is really weird .
Q207 Do you think the strategy in any way overstates the potential impact of new technologies?
No, I don ’ t think so. It is there. To some extent, I feel it is too lukewarm on them. It points to their advantages, but it does not really—

I do not think it embraces enough the monitoring and behavioural change that could come from continuous data monitoring and dashcam footage. One of the things that we know from serious collision investigators is that , even after a fatality or a serious injury , they do not have access reliably and early to the data that onboard computers and mobile devices that people are carrying have, because there are all sorts of blockages from companies saying, “Oh, no, that ’s the car owner’s data, and we have to have their permission to release it.” It is not uncommon for serious collision investigators to have the option of having to pay £4,000 to have access to that data. It comes six months later, and there are reams of data that are uninterpretable without the expert knowledge of the motor manufacturer. That is a very simple example.

Why do we not align legislation so that it has to be immediately released in a meaningful manner for those instances where there has been a death or serious injury? Why do we not extend it to a requirement for the benefits of accessing vehicle use to have continuous telematics and dashcam footage that is recording all the time and is then reviewed , and the hour before reviewed , by investigating authorities so that they understand what part behaviour and the way that car wa s being driven played in the lead-up to the incident? At the moment , the event recorders only capture five seconds of data, and that is prior to an impact or incident. That only captures the engineering components. It totally misses the driver behaviour choices and all the other things.

I know there are issues around accuracy and precision , particularly if you are thinking about prosecution, but we are not necessarily thinking about that. We are thinking that , if you had a visual dashcam record of what actually happened , you can immediately understand what happened and then build your evidence around the appropriate bits of information from that. Chatting to police serious collision investigators, th ere is a real frustration at that blockage and that lack of access to information.

I would extend it. Can I just highlight new and novice drivers? Six per cent of licence holders are new and novice drivers—younger drivers. We know that in the first year 18% will have a collision. They represent 24% of the killed and seriously injured. They are killing themselves. They are killing other people. If we are a bit nervous about introducing widespread telematics and dashcams to everyone, which is what my preference would be but I know that is seen as extreme, why do we not at least start with saying that every new driver has to have it for the first five years of their journey? That would change their behaviour because they know they are being monitored. It would give us the evidence from this excess disproportionate number of collisions that we can then focus the RSIB or investigators on understanding what is actually happening and capture all these human elements.

Q208 On the disjoint between speed limits changing on the road, which presumably is the one the driver has to comply with, and the data coming in in real time in their car, I have driven a number of times on a road that I can see from the repeaters on it is 20 mph, but in my case Google Maps, or whatever technology one is using , says that it is still 30 mph. Why is there a disjoint? Surely, that is pretty important if we are to make use of telematics much more actively.
T hat was the point I was referring to. There is a credibility problem at the moment . They are not accurate enough.
Why is that, and what needs to happen?
Nobody has prioritised it and said, “This is how we are going to run the system.”

Q209 Who is responsible for making sure what comes through on the sat nav, or whatever the generic name is for that now, and the actual speed limit? You have a legal process to change the speed limit. Should that not immediately switch the data over?
There should be a national digital speed map, which there is not, as far as I understand. We have created one in London that is available on the website.
Really?
Yes. Because speed limits change street by street due to traffic regulation orders, we then have to monitor every single TRO and make sure that we then update the map. That is how it is done.
That disjoint also happens in terms of road closures , lane closures and so on.
Absolutely. It is perfectly fit for a national view on this and a streamlining of processes.
It ’ s not rocket science.
It is not. This could be digitised and made so much more straightforward.

The Government many years ago considered how to streamline, improve and bring up to date the TRO process. It is an analogue process. It is very paper - based. It is very clunky, advertising in the London Gazette . We have to bring that into the 21st century.

On the digital point, i t is astonishing that I cannot go on to the web and see the speed limit in this part of the UK. The Ordnance Survey has a map of speeds and speed limits, but you have to pay for it. It is astonishing. There is a gap there, and it has to be the G overnment that plug that gap.
Q210 You touched on EU vehicle safety standards. Should the UK adopt the current EU vehicle safety standards?

Yes. That is the indication of the direction of travel . M anufacturers would find it difficult to make a special UK car. It is in their interest to bring it in, but it would make it again much simpler and more acceptable to the public if it said, “This is in conformity with regulation.”
Q211 Does the Department for Transport collect the right data to best understand driver compliance with speed limits?
No.
What should it do?

It should use in-car data, the connected vehicle data, which is available. It does not need these speed tubes down in various random places. Every time these free-flow speeds come out, we have to then explain to the people we talk to that they are not very relevant because they are in specific places. The connected vehicle data now is so good that we just do not need to do this free-flow speed analysis. We can get it from the connected vehicle data.

My understanding is that it is based on 77 automatic vehicle camera -type set-ups across the country. That is a fairly temporary small picture of the whole. I completely agree. The data is there within vehicles at the moment .

For 20 mph places, it is only seven. Most of those are atypical of 20 mph places. They just happen to be where they have those speed tubes, and at some point in time the speed limits change d from 30 mph to 20 mph and so it is, “ Oh, w e can monitor them at 20 mph now.”
We need a deeper understanding of the actual speeds and the range of speeds. It is not just speed limits and proportions, is it? It is the shape of the curve.

It is interesting. In preparation, I went on the website to have a look at the latest data on compliance, and the Government have acknowledged that for 2025 they are no longer collecting data on the old basis. There is an acceptance by the Department that the system that it was using has 78 sites for the whole of Great Britain to monitor speed. It is really insufficient . Interestingly, T ransport for Wales in its monitoring of the 20 mph speed limit in Wales is using in-car GPS data as part of its assessment. Wales is moving on a little bit there.

Q212 If there are no further questions, I am going to come to the final one . Naturally, we have heard from many families and people who have suffered a loss because of avoidable collisions. Looking specifically at speed, what is the single most important recommendation that this Committee could make to strengthen the Government’s road safety strategy?

Get t he RSIB launched and appropriately focused action interventions to specifically look at driver responsibilities and awareness about the influence that their choices around speeds have on the risk to others , and the public engagement and awareness piece.
I think that was two or three.
The RSIB—one.
M aking the policy on 20 mph clear and default in urban areas would be probably the most important thing that they need to lead on. I will leave it at that.

Make speed limits fit the function, the use r s and the characteristics of the road, not the existing speed. Too many of our speed limits are set based on what drivers want to travel at, the old 85th percentile, and it leads to this nonsense of 24 mph being the barrier. Once you make the decision that the speed limit should follow the function of the road and who is using it, immediately 20 mph becomes the speed limit where there are people—back to my Stockholm d eclaration—and then everything flows from that.
Can you guess what I am going to say? It is 20 mph at a national level, either legislatively defined or with very strict guidance about how you implement it at local authority level.
Q213 What would be the disadvantage of not doing it nationally but by local authority area? Would it be about clutter and confusion for drivers?
No. If you went with the Wales approach, which is we change what street lights mean— street lights mean 20 mph; they do not mean 30 mph—
As you are moving from one local authority area to another.
By its nature, that will iron out the differences because street lighting is there. Most 30 mph roads do not have a speed limit put on them by the local authority.
They have a default 30 mph.
They have a default 30 mph because of the street lighting.
Q214 If that road passed from one local authority that had one policy into another authority that had another default policy, how would that be managed?

If neither authority A nor authority B have a speed limit that they have set , and they have street lighting, the speed limit is 30 mph by default on the street lighting . If you change the national law, they immediately become 20 mph. That local authority would then have to take a conscious decision to raise the speed limit back up. That is more difficult.

Q215 I am obviously not being very clear. My understanding is that the road safety strategy is delegating to local authorities if they want to change the default speed limit in their areas — or it is just on specific roads as it is in London ?
It depends what you mean by default . Is it a legal default or a policy default? At the moment , there is no intention in the road safety strategy to change the legal default.
No, that ’ s correct.

Ideally, that would be what we would do. If you did that, you would iron out most of the differences. If you leave it as it is and the Government set a clear policy default of 20 mph, which is what we have in Scotland, it will not eliminate the possibility of differences at the boundary, but if you bring in much greater checks and balances, things like a requirement to sign off, as I suggested, you place a greater burden and a greater degree of difficulty to not comply with the clear guidance that is written.

Q216 So y ou think the way the road safety strategy is worded at the moment gives the right sense of direction , but w hat I am trying to get at is that t he Government are not going for a default. They are going for local area by local area. What do you see as the specific problems with that? Given , as we know from Daniel’s examples from south-east London , that different local authorities have very different attitudes, they are therefore going to implement the policy differently.

They are committed to new guidance , which is fine , so there is a ti ck in the box for new guidance. What it does not say is that guidance is going to be really strong , and strong enough to eliminate, as far as we possibly can, those boundary difficulties.

Nationally, it should set out that the evidence would suggest that the expectation is that it is 20 mph, and therefore if you are not implementing that you have to justify why that is acceptable in safety terms. If I was using the analogy of the railway, which I also look after, you have to reduce risk as low as reasonably practical. If you are not doing that through one measure, you have to have other mitigations. They need to demonstrate why that road is safe even though the speed limit was not the safest one we know it is. It creates a dialogue that does not exist at the moment because people can abdicate from making decisions on it because the default currently is 30 mph.
The risk is distraction and inefficiency, is it not, and, as a driver, inconsistencies and then confusion?

Q217 That is what I am trying to get at. This is not being consulted on. This is the strategy. It is quite clear that at the moment the Government are not likely to move away from that and are not going to move towards what you are all asking for, which is default 20 mph in urban areas. That is what I am trying to ask. Given that this is the Government policy, the re are the practical difficulties of the way they have worded it rather than what you are saying.
Get the RSIB launched, and it can focus on this and manage that so that it is consistently applied in the best way possible.
If the guidance is sufficiently clear that this is what we are expecting you to do—20 mph—
The guidance is not there.
They are committed to it.
They said they are going to do guidance.
The second commitment is to a safe system , and you cannot have a safe system without 20 mph as a default in policy terms , even if not legislatively.

It is a contradiction. Okay. Thank you very much for your evidence and the time you spent preparing to come to us today. If there is anything you think you did not get a chance to cover or cover in sufficient detail, please feel free to write to us. We are going to resume our oral evidence sessions for this inquiry in the autumn, but for now that concludes today’s meeting. Thank you very much.

sessions.iT: Article 2 of the Protocol/Windsor Framework
sessions.w: Dermot Nesbitt

segs.tx: N orthern Ireland Scrutiny Committee
C orrected oral evidence: Article 2 of the protocol/Windsor Framework
Wednesday 15 July 2026
Watch the meeting

Members present: Lord Carlile of Berriew ( The Chair); Lord Dodds of Duncairn ; Lord Elliott of Ballinamallard; Baroness Foster of Aghadrumsee ; Baroness Goudie; Baroness Ludford; Baroness O’Loan; Baroness Ritchie of Downpatrick; Baroness Sanderson of Welton; Lord Thomas of Gresford .
Evidence Session No. 6 Heard in Public Questions 76 - 81
Witness
Dermot Nesbitt, lead negotiator , Ulster Unionist Party , to the multiparty negotiations 1998, regarding human rights and equality.
Examination of witness
Dermot Nesbitt.

Q76 Good morning and welcome to the public meeting of the Northern Ireland Scrutiny Committee. We are today holding our sixth public evidence session of our inquiry on Article 2 of the protocol and Windsor Framework, which is the so-called non-diminution of rights provision. We are joined this morning by Dermot Nesbitt, who was the lead negotiator for the Ulster Unionist Party to the multiparty negotiations regarding human rights and equality that led to the 1998 Belfast/Good Friday agreement. We are concerned in particular today with the rights, safeguards and equality of opportunity chapter—the RSEO chapter of the agreement—which is referenced explicitly in Article 2(1) of the protocol/Windsor Framework.

You are very welcome, Mr Nesbitt, and we very much look forward to your evidence. The first time you speak, perhaps you would briefly introduce yourself. Today’s meeting is being broadcast and a verbatim transcript will be taken for subsequent publication. It will be sent to you to check for accuracy. I refer to the register of m embers’ interests as published on the committee’s website. I am going to start the session now by asking the first question. What was the starting point for the negotiations on equality and human rights provisions during the multiparty talks, and how did this relate to the six rights listed in the Downing Street declaration of 1993?

Good morning again. What was the starting point? I had been involved in rights and equality before the talks and I was very conscious of the developments that were occurring in Europe in the late 1980s and early 1990s. I was conscious of the Dublin forum that the Irish Government proposed on their documentation, and that led me to the starting point.

The starting point is from a European point of view, and this is where I believe it is very important, because we are part of Europe. You go back to the Treaty of Versailles, where there were many countries newly formed after the First World War. Those new countries comprised some with minorities. I will give a quotation from the emeritus professor of Irish studies, Brian Walker at Queen’s. He said that some of those countries had majorities where they agreed with the changes and others had minorities where they did not agree. He said that this was common to the Northern Ireland problem. I say at the very outset that Northern Ireland was not, and is not, unique, although it is often treated as unique, as we will see in our discussion.

That was the First World War. Roll forward to the end of the Second World War and you come to 1989, with the demise of the USSR. You now have the Russian Federation. That created a lot more countries: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Czech Republic, Slovakia, Poland, Hungary. These were all now separate countries. The Council of Europe, a very important international body and home of the European Convention on Human Rights and of the European Court of Human Rights, decided that it had to act, because it was mindful of what happened at the end of the First World War with minorities and did not want the same to happen. I quoted what it said in paragraph 6 [See written submission, 8 July 2026] , where it brought together the members of the Council of Europe and “ agreed that the national minorities which the upheavals of history have established in Europe had to be protected and respected as a contribution to peace and stability ”. That led to the Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities. That was a very important framework.

As I say that, I am mindful of having read the transcript [ 8 July meeting] , where you asked at the end for the m embers to read my submission, and Mark Durkan said, “ I imagine that the framework convention features in it ”. Yes, it does. Therefore, he and others were conscious that that was something I mentioned a lot, because it was and is important.

From my background point of view, I was the lead person on rights and equality. As I indicate, I have been involved in politics for over 50 years. I have held a very moderate view from way back in the 1970s, when I believed nationalists and unionists had to work together in a Government so as the community could support the Government.

Moving forward, I am trying, and I will try in this submission, orally as well as in what is written, to be objective and evidence-based, as you will see from my first quotation, which goes way back to September 1996, when the forum was established with the talks. I said that, were all participants in the talks to abide by international consensus on how to solve our problems, we would make progress. Indeed, I said that these principles have been derived from international human rights law. What does it do? It balances majority rights and secure borders with minority rights. Everyone should feel communally together within the community. That was my aim at the beginning of the talks.

From a European point of view and from a Dublin forum point of view in their documentation, it led me to be very clear. There is a saying that, if you are sailing in a boat, unless you know which port you are going to, no wind is favourable. I was very conscious of what I wished to achieve: rights and equality of opportunity, based on international standards, as established by the Council of Europe.

Can I ask you a supplementary question, Mr Nesbitt? When these negotiations took place, the background to the negotiations was the Troubles. The talks were a resolution of the Troubles. How far was the conversation about rights that took place brought about by the Troubles? How far was it rather an attempt to ensure that what were regarded as internationally secured rights continued in Northern Ireland?

A way had to be found to eliminate the Troubles. It was a sectarian conflict, basically. When I say sectarian, I do not mean all Catholics are nationalists, or all Protestants are unionists, but it was primarily a sectarian conflict. We had to find a way to have a community that was at ease with itself and there had to be standards. The only way you could probably get acceptable standards to all is to go to what was, as I keep saying, international consensus as to a way forward. Rights were important in a way forward. I viewed it, in terms of the contribution I had to make, that I had to secure certain positions on rights, which, as we see, took a little while to get.

Q77 Baroness Ritchie of Downpatrick : Dermot, you are very welcome. At this stage, I would say that I served with Dermot on Down District Council and then as Assembly Member s for South Down in the Northern Ireland Assembly. That is a few years ago.

Moving on to my question, what viewpoints concerning equality and human rights did you present to the negotiations on behalf of your party? How did these relate to the conflict; to other types of rights, such as those for the disabled and gender rights; to other things that are specified in the Downing Street declaration and RSEO; and to the future of Northern Ireland and north-south or east-west relations?

Good morning. That is a four-point question. There is nothing like making it complicated at the start. I smile though. We know each other very well. I will take the first part of your question and then the other supplementary parts. I led, as you see in paragraph 9—and it is important that it is the Dublin forum. This is not a unionist forum. This is a forum that was created at the time of the 1996 elections in Northern Ireland.
Of which I was a member.

Yes. As I comment in paragraph 9, Professors Boyle, Campbell and Hadden made it very clear that the fundamental rights are determined by international agreement. There is an obligation there for all states. It is not a matter of bargaining, so we do not bargain. They are there, they are clear and they should be dealt with. Asbjorn Eide —and this is why I view the framework convention as very important—said then that it was the first significant hard law dealing with human rights of minorities.

I look at what P rofessor Monica McWilliams said, as I read the transcript [8 July] . She said, “ p r obably the biggest mistake that we made in the Good Friday agreement was that we did not establish a validation committee ”. She gave an example where Colombia was overseen by the United Nations, whereas here this framework convention was overseen by the Council of Europe. As you see in the footnote, each member state that ratified that framework convention—and that is why I viewed it as very important—was subject to monitoring by the monitoring committee of the Council of Europe every few years, so it was being validated by a respected international body.

I made it clear as well in the talks that, as stated by Professors Boyle, Campbell and Hadden in paragraph 10, we should incorporate a major provision of the framework convention for national minorities into a Bill of Rights. Also in the talks, I was very conscious of something —I am sorry I was not doing it last week with Mark Durkan , because Mark would have remembered. During the talks, I vividly remember him saying to me, “Dermot, I never want to hear you mentioning ‘ minority ’ again”. He did not like the word “minority” because it made him feel that they were somewhat less important. That is why I say, in paragraph 11 onwards, that minorities display a distinctive cultural, linguistic, educational and religious dimension. They have an identity that they wish to preserve. That is something that is common not just in Northern Ireland, but throughout Europe.

I gave one example there of the Celtic Romansh in Switzerland. This is a point I tried to get across. They did not view themselves as somehow inferior because they were a minority. They just viewed themselves as a smaller one of four. The others were French, German and Italian. Michael Breisky , who was the Austrian ambassador to Dublin, made very pertinent comments that protection of minorities must be based on international consensus. We have to break down the barriers and the sense of being superior or being inferior. That was intrinsically important within the human rights concept that I viewed right back since the 1970s, where unionism and nationalism must be viewed each with respect of each other and each of equal importance. That was one of the key things I tried to convey in the rights process.

If I can continue, as you see, the United Kingdom and Irish Government viewed treatment and equality of opportunity as very important, but they were reticent initially to recognise international law fundamentally, because they talked about having regard for international law. My position was summarised in a statement I made that they have to accept the framework convention, we should ratify it—because I viewed it as important—and it is the European model for solving problems. What better body than the Council of Europe . We have minorities and of course they have their own particular characteristics , but the principles that apply to them all are not unique . Eventually, the UK ratified the framework convention in January 1998.
Forgive me for interrupting you, Mr Nesbitt. Can I bring in Lord Thomas of Gresford ?

Lord Thomas of Gresford : Did you ever think at any time that you were promulgating rights enforceable by individuals in those bulleted points, or did you think you were setting out principles from which enforceable rights could be drawn?

I was doing the latter, setting out principles, but I also had to give examples of rights. The framework convention is, as Asbjorn Eide said, the most important volume of rights dealing with minorities ever to have been derived. I give an example at the end of the annexe on the 30 rights that are possible, but they were the principles of rights.

It is called a framework convention. The reason it is called a framework convention is that it lays out the framework of how you deal with it, but it allows each individual state to decide how it applies. It allows each individual member to decide whether they wish to be part of a minority. You do not have to be a nationalist minority. In fact, now Ulster Scots are recognised as a national minority as well in the framework convention. You do not have to be an Ulster Scot unless you want to be. You do not have to be a nationalist unless you want to be. You choose. I am laying down principles that are to be applied through law and application in Northern Ireland.

Baroness Foster of Aghadrumsee : I think the Chair stopped you. You were about to say that the framework convention was adopted by the UK Government. Remind me, did the Republic of Ireland ever adopt the framework convention on national minorities?

Yes, it did. It gave a commitment where it said that it will proceed with arrangements as quickly as possible to ratify the Council of Europe. That is in the section that you are dealing with. It gives a commitment to do that. When it actually gave that commitment, as part of the monitoring process, it said that, in dealing with states, it will abide by the principles of international law. Northern Ireland is another state. It is recognised in international law as part of the United Kingdom. Eventually, therefore, the United Kingdom said it would implement international regulations or international law as necessary to ensure its obligations are met.

I notice the words that the Belfast agreement is a political text, not a legal text, but there is the Northern Ireland Act 1998, which is the legal text. For example, it says in Schedule 2 to the Northern Ireland Act 1998 “ observing and implementing international obligations ”. That is an accepted matter. They will observe and implement international obligations. The Irish Government gave the same commitment to do so. That is why—as we may deal with one of my greatest disappointments—as a moderate unionist throughout my life and one who wrote about recognising territorial integrity, I find it extremely difficult to accept the protocol with respect to the contribution that Leo Varadkar made. He was breaching international law.
You will have to forgive me for interrupting you, but I want to be sure that we have the questions from members of the committee, which is the purpose of the meeting.

Q78 Lord Dodds of Duncairn : It is good to see you, Dermot. In terms of the emphasis you placed on the framework convention on minorities then, and even today, and the final outcome of the RSEO chapter of the Belfast agreement, how satisfied were you and are you that that adequately took cognisance and recognised your emphasis on the convention? At the end of the day, the chapter was written and agreed. How satisfied were you at the time that all the issues that you raised about the framework were reflected in that chapter?

I was somewhat satisfied. Those rights were mentioned, the six or eight in that section, but it also said in that section that the Northern Ireland Human Rights Commission that would be established would deal with international law and look at rights supplementary to the European convention to form a Bill of Rights. That is where I was agreeing with the Dublin forum that the framework convention should form the basis for consideration of a Bill of Rights. I was somewhat satisfied as to the rights that were actually mentioned in the agreement, but also the implementation required the Northern Ireland Human Rights Commission to carry it through to its conclusion, which regrettably did not happen.
We have a related question from Baroness Goudie.

Good morning. How are you? Did you foresee that the rights would ultimately include the rights, safeguards and equality of opportunity and that the chapter would be enforced into the Belfast/Good Friday agreement as a political text and not as a legal text? How do you feel about that?

As I said a moment ago, yes, it was a political text, but that was translated into a legal text by the Northern Ireland Act 1998. You have Article 69, which talks about the Northern Ireland human rights. You have Article 75, which talks about the Equality Commission. You have listed the various bodies, including the North South Ministerial Council and the Assembly of Northern Ireland, and how it is formed and constituted. All of that is in law to reflect and to mirror the Good Friday/Belfast agreement. While I accept it is not a legal document, I emphasise that there is a complementary legal document that reflects the key ingredients of the Belfast/Good Friday agreement.

Lord Dodds of Duncairn : How would you assess the success or otherwise of the implementation of the RSEO chapter of the Belfast agreement? Has it worked out differently in practice from what you envisaged in 1998?

To some extent, yes. To another extent, no. Yes, we have had the Human Rights Commission and the Equality Commission. The Equality Commission is doing its job. People can go to it. If the Equality Commission thinks it valid, it will take its case for lack of equality of opportunity. That equality of opportunity is right across the spectrum.

What is important is that the persons and institutions that are involved need to implement what was agreed. As I said earlier, my biggest concern, and annoyance I would even say, was that a fundamental principle of international law, which I referred to at the very beginning, in 1996, of respect for territorial integrity, was not respected by the then Taoiseach Leo Varadkar. It takes a balance. We have to have compromises: minority rights, majority rights, respect for territorial integrity.

That balance did not materialise. I never thought for one minute, when I referred to territorial integrity in 1998, that somehow it would be fundamentally breached, because integrity means whole and undivided, which is not the position at the moment . I never thought that that would have happened, but it has happened and I am extremely disappointed.
Presumably, what you were thinking then was predicated on the assumption that the United Kingdom would remain a member of the European Union.

I am conscious that there were beneficial aspects of the European Union. On my point of view on rights and the element that I was dealing with, I was dealing with rights that are enshrined in international law. Those are implemented whether or not you are in the European Union. You are in the Council of Europe. The United Kingdom Government ratified the framework convention that would ensure their international obligations were met. The Irish Government did the same. There is not a prerequisite that you need to be a member of the European Union to implement those rights. Therefore I do not believe that the part that you are talking about—Article 2 of the protocol—is relevant.
You did not think that membership of the European Union in some way would underpin the rights of which you were speaking.

No, I was not conscious that the European Union would underpin the rights. What underpinned the rights was the monitoring procedure of the Council of Europe. In fact, the sixth monitoring procedure of the United Kingdom is under way now. It has to give an account of how it is implementing that. The account is to the Council of Europe, not to the European Union. That happens whether or not we are in the European Union.

Bearing in mind your focus upon the Council of Europe and the European Convention on Human Rights, what account did you give to subsidiarity under the European Convention on Human Rights, which is quite a significant feature, and jurisprudence of the European Court of Human Rights?

Y ou are asking me a legal question and I am not a lawyer. I am not sure what the answer would be for that. All I know is that, in law, it actually says , in the 1998 agreement or the 1998 Act, that the Secretary of State would request the Human Rights Commission to draw up a Bill of Rights to supplement the European Convention on Human Rights based on international agreements. That was what I was focused on and what was in the Belfast agreement. On your legal part—and I know you are a lawyer and I am not—I probably cannot answer that question specifically.

As a supplementary to your question, in discussing and negotiating that section on behalf of the Ulster Unionist Party, what was your lodestar, guiding principle or driving force in terms of rights? Was it the ECHR or something else?

I am sorry to come back to it. The Framework Convention for the Protection of National Minorities was my guiding principle. Asbjorn Eide said, “ i t contains much more detailed provisions on such protection than any other international instrument ”. That is some standard; that is some standard to follow. Therefore that was my guiding principle. Having got the framework convention, I wanted the UK and Irish Government to ratify it and I wanted them, in turn, to implement it.

Q79 Thank you, Dermot, for that. You partly touched on my question in answer to your last one. I am wondering what role you have seen the Equality Commission for Northern Ireland and the Human Rights Commission play in protecting and promoting the rights and equalities in Northern Ireland. Has that been positive?

Also, you had started to answer a question earlier around your points 39 and 40 of the submission. You have mentioned the Leo Varadkar quote a few times. You said that both the UK and Irish Governments are breaching international law due to the protocol/Windsor Framework and particular commitments provided in the Belfast agreement. Could you expand on that a little please?
Could I expand a little on precisely what?

Could you expand on your comments that were added in your submission around the Leo Varadkar comment, which indicated that the UK and Irish Governments were both in breach of the Belfast agreement around the protocol/Windsor Framework.

That is an interesting one. As I say in paragraph 35, Leo Varadkar said, “ To the nationalist people in Northern Ireland ”. That is a national minority. He is addressing them. He says, “ I want to assure you that we have protected your interests throughout these negotiations … There will be no hard border ”. It is a very interesting small point, but he said, “There will be no hard border on our island”. That was agreed and ratified.

As you see from Lord Jonathan Caine , they had a debate in the House of Lords in 2021. He said of the document that was agreed, “ At a meeting the following day in the Cabinet Ro om, I stated that the document had every hallmark of having been drafted in Dublin, at which point one very, very senior official replied, ‘ That’s because it largely was ’”. It is very sad that they wrote something that breaches international law and that the UK Government supported that.

What is also important—dare I use the word “hypocritical”? That is a strong word. The European Union was a very strong advocate for the protocol and for breaching territorial integrity. Yet, as I deal with in paragraphs 40 onwards, when it came to countries wishing to join the European Union with the demise of the USSR ; Estonia , Latvia, Lithuania, the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Poland and Hungary, the European Union stepped up and called for a stability pact to be implemented.

As you see, paragraph 41 lists all the international treaties that deal with it. Then it said what these principles were: refraining from the threat or use of force, inviolability of frontiers, territorial integrity of states and respect for internationally recognised frontiers. It was conscious that there were minority conflicts and it wanted the territorial integrity of states to be recognised by countries that were hoping to join the European Union. The Secretary of State was asked, as I say in paragraph 43—
On that, there is a correction, is there not? It should be Douglas Hurd, not Douglas Hogg.

Sorry, yes. You are quite correct [1] ; it is one of these typographical things. He said that part of this was to resolve problems especially concerning frontiers and minorities. There were Russians in Estonia and what have you. Here was the European Union wanting to respect the territorial integrity when it comes to countries joining the European Union and being in the European Union. If you are not in the European Union, so Northern Ireland and the United Kingdom, we can breach the territorial integrity of the state. As we know today, hardly a week passes in the news that international law is not mentioned with the USA, Venezuela, Greenland, Gaza Strip and Ukraine. There was a quote from Yvette Cooper. I think I got her name right, Chair.
I think we have got the point, Mr Nesbitt. Can I bring in Lord Thomas? Then I am going to ask Lord Elliott to go back to the original question.

Lord Thomas of Gresford : Was Mr Varadkar doing no more than giving assurance to the nationalist community in Northern Ireland that the border would remain open? I do not see that there is a great breach of international law in what he said. He was simply giving an assurance, was he not?

You say he was giving an assurance and there is no breach of international law. As a very important committee of the House of Lords said, there are many acts from the European Union that are applied to Northern Ireland that Westminster and Stormont have no say in. It breaches territorial integrity of the United Kingdom.

As regards the hard border, as I mentioned quite clearly, there is no problem. The border is quite open. We have a common travel area. Of course, there are slight problems at the moment , but the Secretary of State for Northern Ireland has said that he will address that. That is an open border.

As you notice, I have said that Niall Cody gave evidence in May 2017 to the Oireachtas where he said that less than 2% of goods would be physically checked, the vast majority would be checked in warehouses and it was being managed entirely electronically. I quote : “ w e are not looking for sites for customs posts ”. The border would have remained technically open as it was, whether or not we were within the European Union, but, no, that did not buy into Leo Varadkar—
I want to move on because we have very little time left. Can we go back to your original planned question?
Dermot, my original question was around the Equality Commission and the Human Rights Commission, and what role they have played since their establishment. In your view, has it been positive?

Yes, it generally has been positive. I was a member of the Equality Commission, so I do not make too much of a comment because there were various discussions we had. It is positive in one sense of the Human Rights Commission monitoring the law, but it has not been positive in not devising a Bill of Rights. As I tried to indicate, it refused to take a narrow view. As Tom Hadden rightly said, initially, under Bryce Di cks on , it had a whole lot of sub-committees on various interests. Of course, it wanted maximum rights. As Tom Hadden rightly said as well, the United Kingdom Government said that it did not stick to the remit of a Bill of Rights.

He went on to say that Professor Monica McWilliams did not learn from that, which I find quite disturbing. She said, “We’re not going to do a mere tick box”. That is disrespectful to the two referenda held in Ireland and Northern Ireland on 22 May that endorsed the Belfast/Good Friday agreement, which had in it a Bill of Rights to reflect the particular circumstances of Northern Ireland, building on the European Convention on Human Rights. It has been successful, yes, but on other occasions, particularly in the non-formation of a Bill of Rights, it was not successful.
We will come back to a Bill of Rights at the end.

Q80 I wanted to be clear in my own mind about what you think the significance was of the UK vote to leave the EU for the RSEO chapter of the Belfast/Good Friday agreement. You said in your written submission in paragraph 40—and you have been discussing some of this—that both the UK and Irish Governments breached international law, and particularly commitments provided in the Belfast agreement, when they agreed the protocol and the Windsor Framework.

Then, during your answer today, you referred to Article 2 of the protocol not being relevant because—this is in paragraph 70 of your submission—the Belfast agreement “is a stand - alone international agreement, and its central reconciliation elements will be sustained into the future, notwithstanding the UK’s withdrawal from the EU”. On the one hand you say that Article 2 of the protocol is irrelevant, but on the other hand you have said that it is a breach of international law. It is probably just me, but I was struggling to put all that together.

I put Article 2. I see Article 2, but I say it is not relevant because what really is relevant is implementation of the Good Friday agreement through the Northern Ireland Act—it is statute there and what has to be done—and implementation of the framework convention and monitoring through the Council of Europe. Those are the key things.

As I mentioned, I accept that the European Union says that the European market is important and needs to be protected. I also say at the very end, I think in the last paragraph, that you could have a European harmonisation Act UK. In other words, companies that want to trade with Europe would have to subscribe to that particular law . Therefore, you would have a law for those that want to trade.

What we have now is a law that applies to all of Northern Ireland, whether or not you are trading, and all the other companies that might not be trading with Europe. We have lots of documentation complications because of the border between GB and Northern Ireland. Therefore they are subject to problems that they need not be. The only ones that need to be subject to European law are those that are trading, and that could be done. There are also other suggestions, where they both give guarantees of those coming north and those going south.

The protocol is not needed, as it says in Article 2, to protect rights. Rights are protected by those who implement them, namely the Human Rights Commission, the Equality Commission, the Assembly, government, potentially the Bill of Rights et cetera.

Q81 Let us go back to a Bill of Rights as our final subject. I am looking at the annexe to your written document, which sets out a recipe of 30 rights that might be included in a Bill of Rights. I am sure you recognise that having a Bill of Rights like that would be unusual in the context of the whole of the United Kingdom, because there is no such Bill of Rights for the United Kingdom comparable to the document you have set out.

I wanted to ask you a practical question. Which of the important rights set out in your list of 30 are not enforceable by current legal mechanisms available in Northern Ireland, even though those legal mechanisms are not in one document?

I cannot answer what is not legally enforceable, again back to the legal position. This is where I say you, as a committee, should be taking a position where you say, “Here are 30 rights of the framework convention. As a Human Rights Commission, could you look at them, see which ones are particularly relevant to Northern Ireland and what you can add and make into a Bill of Rights?” It would have the expertise, knowledge, time and commitment to dissect those 30 rights, as to which would be relevant or not relevant, given Northern Ireland or the UK.

I am very conscious that they are very expansive rights. If you look at these, the last three mentioned talk about endeavouring to conclude, where necessary, bilateral or multilateral agreements with other states. That is what we have done here. Taking measures to encourage trans-frontier co-operation: we have done that. That is a right that does not need to be implemented as such.

Exactly, that is why I am asking for your expertise. You have spent half a lifetime looking at these issues and we take what you have written very seriously indeed. I am wondering whether there are any rights in your list that stand out to you as not being enforceable under the existing, if somewhat diverse, provisions available for the enforcement of rights in Northern Ireland.

There is none that stand s out as not enforceable, I do not think. Having put in my mind the 30 rights, I do not think that there are any that are not enforceable, although some are not enforceable maybe because they are not needed. I gave that example of trans-frontier co-operation. That need not be a right because we have that.

P art of my problem is the North South Ministerial Council. Part of its remit was to deal with complications and difficulties, including the EU. We never dealt with that. The protocol was imposed upon us. The Northern Ireland Assembly was not consulted or asked for a view as such.

Do you want to make any comments about the Dillon judgment? It may be that you will say, understandably, that that is an issue for the lawyers. If you had any comments about whether the Dillon judgment creates certainty or uncertainty, or maybe certain uncertainty or uncertain certainty, we would be interested in them.

I view the Dillon judgment as the Supreme Court exercising its authority. The Supreme Court means the highest court in the land. It is exercising its authority. Therefore I do not see the Dillon judgment as of any great significance. I come back to the same thing I repeated: it is implementation of the Northern Ireland Act and the framework convention. I repeat that the reason I highlight the framework convention is that I go back to the Council of Europe when it was derived historically because of conflicts. It did not want conflicts among minorities to continue as they did, especially after the First World War with Germans in Poland. We know what conflict that caused.

Those are all the key things that are needed. This is a one-off judgment on Dillon. I noticed the use of words. One of the questions written to me is about sectarian conflict, and the Good Friday agreement talks about communal conflict. Sectarian conflict is a better description of the conflict we had in Northern Ireland.

As I understand from your submission and what you have been saying, your interpretation of the Dillon judgment in relation to rights is that it dealt specifically with sectarian conflict as opposed to forward-facing rights.

I could not disagree with Dillon where it said that the rights listed in the bullet points were all concerned with ending sectarian conflict in Northern Ireland. I could not disagree with that. All I would say is that those rights listed were not encapsulating all that was needed. You had to look at the whole section of that Belfast agreement to see what was needed and whether it has been properly implemented.

This goes back to the question about the Human Rights Commission, the Equality Commission and whether they are doing their job. Yes, to an extent they are. To an extent, the Human Rights Commission did not fulfil its job of getting a Bill of Rights.

Thank you very much, Mr Nesbitt. You have been a very valuable witness to the committee. I am now going to bring the public part of the meeting to a close. Can I remind you that a verbatim transcript will be sent to you for correction? Thank you on behalf of us all for your evidence.

[1] Mr Nesbitt subsequently c larified that his written submission was correct to refer to Douglas Hogg, but that he was mistitled as Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs. Mr Hogg was Minister of State, Foreign and Commonwealth Office.

sessions.iT: Equality at work: flexible working and disability
sessions.w: Action for ME; Arthritis UK; Disability Rights UK; Alison Thwaite (The Down's Syndrome Association); Scope

segs.tx: Women and Equalities Committee
Oral evidence: Equality at work: flexible working and disability , HC 177
Wednesday 15 July 2026
Ordered by the House of Commons to be published on 15 July 2026 .
Watch the meeting
Members present: Sarah Owen (Chair); Alex Brewer; Rosie Duffield; Kim Leadbeater; Rebecca Paul; Richard Quigley; Rachel Taylor.
Questions 1 - 4 1
Witnesses

I : Clare Ogden, Head of Support Services, Action for ME; Patricia Stapleton, Senior Policy Manager, Arthritis UK; Fazilet Hadi MBE, Head of Policy, Advice and Information, Disability Rights UK; Alison Thwaite, Head of Employment Services, The Down's Syndrome Association; James Taylor, Executive Director of Strategy, Impact and Social Change, Scope.
Written evidence from witnesses:
SCOPE [ FWD0020 ]
The Down’s S yndrome Association [ FWD0021 ]
Action for ME [ FWD00 24 ]
Disability Rights UK [ FWD0033 ]
Arthritis UK [ FWD0038 ]
Examination of witnesses
Witnesses: Clare Ogden, Patricia Stapleton, Fazilet Hadi MBE, Alison Thwaite and James Taylor.

Good afternoon and welcome to the Women and Equalities Committee. Today we are holding the first oral evidence session as part of our inquiry into flexible working and disability. This inquiry forms part of the Committee ’s series of inquiries into equality at work and follows on from some of our other work on equalities in the workplace. I am really glad that we have a brilliant and large panel with us. We have Clare Ogden, h ead of s upport s ervices at Action for ME ; Faz i l e t Hadi MBE, h ead of p olicy a dvice i nformation at Disability Rights UK ; Patricia Stapleton, s enior p olicy m anager at Arthritis UK ; Alison Thwaite, h ead of e mployment s ervices at the Down ’ s Syndrome Association ; and James Taylor, e xecutive d irector of s trategy , i mpact and s ocial c hange at Scope. Welcome to you all. The Committee will ask questions and there will be some follow-ups. If you want to go into greater detail about anything than we have time for today, you can submit written evidence afterward s . If you leave here thinking, “O h, I should have said that, ” the same rules apply ; y ou can send it in writing afterward s . I am going to hand straight over to Rachel.

Q1 Thank you all for joini ng us today . It is a very hot day and London has been difficult to navigate so w e really appreciate you being here , and Clare for joining us online. It is always difficult w hen we have big panels as p eople feel they need to get in on the first question. You do not ; you will all have your opportunity. Fazilet , you and James both have a disability and have built successful careers. To what extent have you required flexible working arrangements to overcome barriers? W hat are your experiences of accessing the flexibilities that you need?

When I reflect on my world of work, and I have worked for many decades, the single thing that ha s helped me most has been the A ccess to W ork scheme. When I started work, digital a nd computers were not a thing. Obviously things became a bit easier for blind people with the advent of digital technologies. That enabled me to present myself to an employer as someone who could work on a level playing field to others. That was really important and is the standout factor for me. In terms of flexibilities, it was not so much that I needed flexibility in terms of the hours or which days of the week I worked and so on . I needed people to change the way they did things ; for people who were presenting things to speak to their slides ; people who were sending me documents to use a narrative word format and not complicated tables ; people in team meetings to go round the table and say who they were. As I say, f or me the flexibilities were not about hours ; t hey were more about adapting to what I needed to be part of the team and creat e a more inclusive environment for me.
James, is there anything you want to add?

I have a physical disability and a different experience to Fazilet. For a long time I thought it was about me trying to get a job despite my disability. My world view has now completely changed ; it is about getting a job because I have a disability and being proud of it , and m aybe we will talk about that a bit more later.

I am really privileged to work for a disability charity and effectively get paid for being disabled and t alking about my disability . N ot every disabled person can say that. When I was younger, certainly in retail and temporary jobs that were often physically demanding, I would often mask or hide things that I needed because I did not want to ask for them. I felt that I was perhaps putting the employer out of its way to do something different for me. That is an experience that lots of young disabled people still have despite the progress we have made. Personally, just on flexible working, I have certainly noticed a difference. It takes me a long time to get to places, to walk places, and to get around. Having the flexibility to work from home has enabled me to be far more effective in my career.
